en: [======= JNys_1.1.I: The Section on Birth (Janmādhikaraṇam) =======] // Now begins the Section on the Desire to Know (Jijñāsādhikaraṇam) in the Illustrious Nyāyasudhā.

**Invocation** Salutation to Hari, the Lord of Śrī; whose mass of pure radiance from the jewels of his eternally innumerable virtues dispels all the darkness of evil; whose body is characterized by the fashioning of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the world; and who shines as the heart of all the Vedas and Smṛtis. (1)

May that Sun-like Vyāsa never forsake my mind—he who appeared upon the circle of the earth and spread forth the lineage of the Vedas; who, out of compassion, awakened the lotus of the Śruti and revealed the supreme reality; who destroyed the darkness [of ignorance] and established the hand of the virtuous on the path of truth.

He whose pervasion (*vyāpti*) resides in his own side by virtue of his own light, whose presence is in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and whose exclusion is from the contrary class (*vipakṣa*); and who has no attachment to an object that is sublated (*bādhita*).

There exists no peerless, pure means of valid cognition endowed with a counter-argument; may that Blessed One, the sage Ānandatīrtha, be my authority for the definitive determination of reality. (3) May that Goddess Bhāratī, the deity of all speech and mind, who makes even a mute eloquent through her experience and turns even a dull-witted creature into the crest-jewel of the wise—may she establish her presence within my words and my mind. (4)
May Padmanābhatīrtha—the dwelling place of Ramā, the birthplace of the *Sannyāyaratnāvalī*, and an ocean of the nectar of dispassion—be for my prosperity. (5)

I pay homage to my gurus, known as the venerable Akṣobhyatīrtha, who are knowers of words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition, and who crush the pride of their opponents. [6] Upon the ground of the lotus-lake of the mind of the noble and venerable Ānandatīrtha...
My mind acts like a bee hovering over the lotus of the *Anuvyākhyāna*.
(7) We are neither deeply rooted in the ocean of grammar, nor clever in the discussions of the Vedas, nor proficient in logic, nor even those who have known all that is to be known;
yet, having taken refuge in the path of the compassion of our venerable teacher Pūrṇaprajña, we are somehow worthy of honor even as we speak of the Great Ones. (8)

Although the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā-śāstra* was composed by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa for the ultimate liberation of living beings, the venerable sage Ānanda-tīrtha, considering it as if uncomposed because it was obscured by the blinding darkness of faulty commentaries, composed a commentary on it in accordance with the Teacher’s intention. Furthermore, intending to compose an *Anubhāṣya* as well, he—

though naturally free from obstacles due to his dissolved material nature (*vilīna-prakṛti*) and though his bodily, sensory, and mental activities were incessantly directed toward the Lord— [proceeded].

Having understood through the unbroken tradition of the conduct of disciples that acts such as salutation to Nārāyaṇa must necessarily be performed— as they are the cause for the unimpeded completion and the proliferation of the work he intends to begin—
he composes at the beginning of the book [the verse] "Nārāyaṇam" in order to instill this practice in his students:
"Nārāyaṇa, whose singular body consists of all perfect qualities, who is free from defects, and who is attainable by all through excellent words..."
Because it is the source of this entire universe in all its particularity, I always bow down to that which is most dear to me. 1.1.1.
In this context, the grammatical construction is "I bow down to Nārāyaṇa.
From the very use of the first person pronoun (*uttamapuruṣa*), the word "I" is understood.
By the prefix *sam*, he expresses the correctness of the means of knowledge, characterized by its association with excellence such as devotion and so forth.
For only such a prostration to Nārāyaṇa becomes an auxiliary factor for the attainment of one's desired goal.

However, the connection of the words beginning with "nikhila" (all) is with Nārāyaṇa as a qualifying attribute through the function of providing valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And the purpose of these words of praise is precisely the glorification of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) itself.
In this regard, the resolution for the objection regarding redundancy is precisely that it constitutes praise (*stuti*).
Alternatively, it may be explained as being intended to convey the qualities that serve as the basis for bowing down (*namyatva*).

Whence comes the state of being worthy of salutation for Nārāyaṇa? Even if that were so, why is there salutation to him alone while other deities exist? To this it is said: "He is to be worshipped even by way of all his specific attributes. "Specific attributes" (*viśeṣāḥ*) are those qualities (*asādhāraṇa-dharmāḥ*) by which a thing is distinguished; and these are both "all" (*aśeṣāḥ*) and "specific attributes" (*viśeṣāḥ*).
The particle *api* signifies pervasion (*abhivyāpti*).

He is worthy of worship not only because of those specific qualities that serve as the causes for being worshipped, but also because of his excellence—that is, his superiority—over the entire world, including Brahmā and others, who might otherwise be suspected of being worthy of worship; this "entirety" refers to his state of being the supreme among all.

Therefore, since he is to be worshipped even when other deities exist, and as to how both of these qualities belong to Nārāyaṇa, it is said: "entirely," and so forth. For there are three kinds of deities who are worthy of worship.
And it is intended for those who are qualified [for this practice].
For the salutation to the deity is not performed out of mere habit;
rather, it is done with a view toward purposes such as the removal of obstacles.
I seek a particularly distinguished deity for this purpose;
such a deity, being authorized, brings about the awakening to the texts concerning its own domain and so forth.
Indeed, salutation becomes fruitful only when it is accompanied by devotion and other such qualities.
It is held that he is reborn in that very same deity.

To establish his superiority therein, there are three qualifiers for this [deity]—his birth and so forth—namely: "the sole embodiment of all perfect qualities" and "faultless. "All" means without exception; "perfect" means that each quality, such as bliss and the rest, is individually limitless.
The word *eka* has the sense of "exclusive" (*kevala*).
He is so described because his body consists of those [elements] alone and not of the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
He is "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*) because he has emerged from defects such as dependence on others.

Since this world, which is present to the intellect by being established through means of valid cognition such as perception, has its "origin" (udbhava)—meaning birth—as its beginning, it is called "udbhavādi. The group of eight [states] beginning with birth is thus referred to as "udbhavādi.
That which "gives" (dadāti) these states as they occur is "udbhavādid.
The genitive case in the word "asya" (of this) expresses mere relationship.
The phrase "even in its entirety with all its specific distinctions" is also connected with the words "this arises from that.

This refers to the arising [of the universe] along with all its intermediate subdivisions to be established in the section on ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*) and so forth, as expressed by "this arises from that.
Furthermore, the phrase "by all excellent statements" is used to demonstrate that this subject is the most authoritative.
The word *api* serves either to collect the reasons for being worthy of worship or to indicate pervasion (*abhivyāpti*).

Because they are not suspected of having defects—either by virtue of being non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*) or by virtue of being rooted in that [non-human source]—the Vedas and so forth, as well as the *Brahma-sūtras* and so forth, are "excellent utterances" (*suvākya*); by all of these, [He] is most fully attained.
It must be established as preeminent.

If Nārāyaṇa is to be saluted because he is to be propounded by the Brahma-mīmāṃsā Śāstra— which one intends to explain— and by the Veda and other texts whose subject matter is to be determined by that Śāstra,
then, alas, for that very same reason, Dharma and so forth, or even the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth, would have to be objects of salutation.
It would not be so;
for that [knowledge] is taught in certain portions of the Vedas and other texts as being a subsidiary means (*aṅga*) for the realization of Nārāyaṇa,
whereas this [knowledge], however, is to be known through the entirety of the Vedas and other scriptures because it has no other purpose.
With the intention that only such [a person] as described is the qualified subject, it was stated by him [the author] that [the Lord] is "dearest" (*atamam*) and "by all" (*akhilaiḥ*).
To demonstrate this state of being desired, he said, "He is always my dearest" (*sadā priyatamaṃ mama*).
Here too, as before, the purpose of the word *sadā* (always) and the suffix *-tama* (superlative) should be understood.
Alternatively, there is an explanation based on the focus on the definition (*lakṣaṇaparatayā vyākhyānam*):
nor is it appropriate to offer salutation to one whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) has not been determined.
Since the determination of a reality is not possible without a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), many characteristics of Nārāyaṇa are stated here by way of their various manifestations.

Among them, by the word "entire" (*nikhila*), three characteristics are declared through their distinction from the opposite [of the defects]: the state of possessing all qualities, the state of having complete qualities, and the state of being whose very body consists solely of qualities.
By the phrase "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*), one characteristic is expressed.
By the word *āpyatamam* ("most attainable"), two things are indicated: its status as the primary object of the Vedas and so forth, and its status as the object of all the Vedas and so forth.
By the word *asya* ("of this [one]"), the two feet are indicated.
By the word *aśeṣa* ("without remainder"), its status as the foremost object of worship is expressed; that is, it is to be worshipped preeminently by everyone without exception.
By the word "always" (*sadā*), its fitness for supreme love is indicated. Anticipating the objection that this might be impossible because it is not experienced [by others], it is said, "always mine.
While this is experienced by others only after the attainment of knowledge, for me, it is so always.
The word "api" (also/even) serves to aggregate the defining characteristics.

Alternatively, since Nārāyaṇa is endowed with the characteristics previously described by the words "entire" (*nikhila*) and so forth, one might ask: by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is he to be understood? To this [the author replies]:
It has been stated that [the goal] is attainable through well-spoken words.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that in certain parts of the Vedas and other scriptures, it is described otherwise? No;
with the intention that such perceptions are preceded by a lack of thorough reflection, it was said "[by] all."
In that case, there would be no establishment of dharma and so forth,
because it is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition.
Not so.

The word "also" (*api*) is intended to include the fact that even dharma and other such things are known through the Vedas and so forth, though only in a secondary sense (*amukhyayā vṛttyā*). The particle "also" (*api*) serves to aggregate the proofs that will be stated hereafter.

With the intention that Nārāyaṇa, characterized as previously described, is to be understood by means of reasons such as being the instrumental cause of the entire universe, it was said: "of him" (*asya*).
*1.68* An explanation directed toward the refutation of objections:
Alternatively, if Nārāyaṇa possesses a body, there would be the consequence of defects such as suffering;
if he lacks one, there would be an absence of qualities such as knowledge.
Anticipating the objection that the causality of the world's birth and so forth is impossible in either case, it is stated:
"The embodiment of all perfect qualities and devoid of defects.
Because He possesses a body, He is full of qualities such as knowledge.
Furthermore, because He consists solely of all perfect qualities, He is free from defects such as suffering.
Alternatively, this word "Nārāyaṇa" does not refer to the Blessed One through a conventional etymology like the word "Ḍittha," nor is it applied through mere conventional usage like the word "jar";
rather, it also expresses His specific, distinguished qualities.
*1.70* Alternatively, for the sake of explaining the subject matter of all the treatises (*sakalaśāstrārtha*),
he expresses it in brief by means of this [verse], in order to conform to the intellects of the listeners;
for those who have understood the summary are eager to learn the detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
In this context, "always to be revered" is the statement of the meaning of the first aphorism.
For reverence consists in the inclination of the mental faculty toward that [object];
even the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is merely a particular form of that same [inclination].
To exclude [the meaning of] "Brahman" from living beings (jīva) and so forth, it was stated that it is "that which is Brahman"; the meaning of that is expressed by the word "entirety" (nikhila).
To establish that, the definition was set forth in the second sūtra.
He states this with the words: "of this" (asya).

Having stated in the third sūtra that the treatise (śāstra) is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding that [subject], its status as the object of that [knowledge] was established by the remainder of that chapter. Thus, it has been explained that [the treatise] is the most excellent means of attainment. Now, he states the removal of the suspected defects concerning the subject matter of the first chapter, which was set forth in the second [chapter]: "It is faultless" (nirdoṣam).

Thus, the nature of Brahman having been established, for the sake of generating the direct realization of Him—which serves as the means for the qualified seeker to attain His grace—the author offers salutation to Vyāsa as the third Guru, [preceded by] the hearing of the meaning of the entire Veda through detachment and devotion.
Having bowed to that very source of the scripture, the Guru of the Gurus of the world, with ease: *1.75* [The salutation to Vyāsa as the Guru].
Furthermore, I myself shall provide a detailed exposition of my supreme Vidyā.

Since the salutation to the Guru, like the salutation to Nārāyaṇa, must necessarily be performed at the commencement of any undertaking as a constituent part for the attainment of one's desired goal, the author—establishing his commentary on the Brahma-Mīmāṃsā Śāstra by first performing that practice—makes his formal declaration with the words: "To Him alone... (tameva).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having bowed again with devotion—that is, having saluted with excellence characterized by the possession of such qualities—to that very Nārāyaṇa who was previously saluted, I shall provide an exposition (*vyākhyā*) of the supreme science (*paramākhyavidyā*), which consists of the treatise on the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsāśāstra*). The use of the present tense is intended to indicate immediate proximity to the present action.
Alternatively, it is because the explanation has been undertaken in brief.
[Objection: But for one who has already prostrated, what is the purpose of prostrating again?
For there is no determining factor here that the repetition of prostration is a cause for the destruction of obstacles and so forth.
Or, if you argue that one should have said "I bow repeatedly" in the previous verse itself,
it is not so;
for here, a prostration is performed out of respect [for the Teacher].
To the question of how Nārāyaṇa possesses the status of a teacher, he says: "Originating from the scripture."

By the word "śāstra," both the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* treatise and the Veda and so forth are denoted because they are the subject under discussion. That from which something originates, arises, or is first perceived is its "source" (*prabhava*).
The compound *śāstraprabhava* means the source of the *śāstra*, according to what is appropriate in each case; [the term refers to Him] who is such a source.
For it is well known that whoever initiates a particular scripture is its authoritative teacher (*guru*);
and because he is the initiator of the tradition of this present scripture, Nārāyaṇa possesses the status of a teacher—thus [the author] says: "of the teachers of the world."
[He is] the Guru of this world and of those who proclaim this scripture, such as Brahmā and others, directly and primarily—not merely by virtue of being older in age or the like;
that is to say, the proclaimer of this scripture. He supports Nārāyaṇa’s status as Guru through another way: "especially" (viśeṣataḥ).
The word "guru" (teacher) is understood [from the previous context].
"Especially" means as one who gives direct instruction, and not through a lineage like that of the world.

In this regard, if only the phrase beginning with "originating from the scripture" were stated, then there might arise a suspicion of a distinction between the deity and the teacher due to their being presented separately.
For that reason, it was stated, "to him alone. Nor does this render a separate salutation untenable,
because there is no rule that the occurrence of two causes necessitates the disappearance of the respective effects.
This inclusion in the text is for the sake of training the disciples;
furthermore, among disciples there exists a distinction between the guru and the deity,
and it is with reference to that very distinction that the term "of the gurus of the world" was used.
Otherwise, what was stated specifically as "not mine" would be improper.
[This concludes] the justification for the fact that [the self] must be explained.
It might be argued as follows:

Now, this salutation to the deity and others is intended for the purpose of explaining the text beginning with "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (athāto brahmajijñāsā). However, it need not be explained;
for only those human-authored statements that are preceded by a desire to convey a specific meaning are fit to be explained.
For a discerning person does not engage in the mere explanation of the *mātṛkā* alone;
nor is there any evidence that this [text] was preceded by a desire to convey a specific meaning,
since the mere act of composition is subject to deviation.
Furthermore, there is no certainty regarding the composition [of scripture] by a discerning person;
or, if there were certainty, it would follow that a creation [of scripture] is possible for the sake of achieving prosperity through recitation and so forth, just like a poison-removing mantra.
For the appearance of an object based on grasped linguistic conventions is the same even in the case of a poison-removing mantra.
It is not appropriate to accept an explanation merely on the grounds that it is preceded by a desire to convey a meaning;
for that would lead to the absurd consequence of explaining the speech of deceivers and the like.
Rather, it must also be in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its being true to reality.

Even if that were the case, one would have to state the reason for explaining this particular [text] while abandoning other similar statements; it is to dispel such a doubt that the term "supreme knowledge" (*paramākhyavidyā*) is employed.
This is the underlying intention.
In this treatise, there is indeed the designation "higher knowledge" (*paravidyā*) in such passages as, "Two knowledges are to be known: the higher and the lower.
Here, by the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*), the intended meaning is understood, as well as its correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*).
This is because the word *vidyā* functions through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) with respect to knowledge of reality and its means;
for in the rule *“saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣada...”* (Pāṇini 3.3.99), the term *“in the sense of a name”* (*saṃjñāyām*) is understood as a governing requirement (*anuvṛtti*).

Furthermore, by the word "para" (supreme), there is a distinction from other statements due to its accordance with reality (*yāthārthya*). Thus, since it is understood through scripture (*āgama*) that this [work] is worthy of the highest salutation and because of its profound meaning (*gahanārthatva*), it is appropriate to provide a commentary on this very work alone, setting aside others.
Nevertheless, one might object that since it has already been commented upon by others, it need not be commented upon again; therefore, the author says, "I shall provide a commentary."
The term *viśiṣṭā* means "excellent" (*vyākhyā*). By this, he intends to indicate that the explanations composed by others are erroneous;
and he will demonstrate this point by point as he proceeds.

Nevertheless, since this treatise has already been explained by the commentary composed by [the author] himself, one might ask: "What is the purpose of this further explanation? To address this, he says, "And also" (*anvapi ca*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), he combines the existence of a specific purpose for the *Anuvyākhyāna* (Sub-commentary);
that purpose will be stated later.
Since the disciples themselves would have provided the further explanation once the purpose was established according to the method of the Bhāṣya, he said "I myself";
by the word "myself," he indicates the incapacity of others.
[The authority of the treatise is established] through scripture. 1.96.

Having appeared as Vyāsa, Hari was requested by Viriñca, Bhava, and others, and he composed this unsurpassed scripture known as the Paravidyā. [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.3] As for the statement that Nārāyaṇa is the source of this scripture, that is incorrect.
Because it contradicts the well-known fact that [the Mahābhārata] originated with Vyāsa;
nor is Nārāyaṇa himself Vyāsa, because that would contradict the account of his birth.

Furthermore, because one who has accomplished all that was to be done lacks any further purpose, the composition of a treatise would be impossible. As for the claim that its status as the supreme authority is established by its being called "higher knowledge" (*paravidyā*) in the Śruti, that too is incorrect;

for the word *para* has multiple meanings, and the word *vidyā* is seen to be used even for mantras that lack the intended meaning [of "knowledge"], such that the designation "higher knowledge" does not definitively establish supreme authority.
Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule here that this [knowledge] is called "higher knowledge" (paravidyā) and has this as its object; therefore, he says: "having appeared."

In this context, by the statement that Vyāsa— though he had already accomplished his purpose— manifested at the request of the immortals headed by Viriñca and Bhava, who were the objects of Hari’s grace,
and did not merely "take birth," any inconsistency regarding Nārāyaṇa being the source of the scripture is resolved.
For it is observed that those who act solely out of the compulsion of compassion for the sake of benefiting others are all the more so when requested by them.

For this very reason, the use of the middle voice (ātmanepada) is employed to indicate that the Blessed One’s composition of this treatise was performed while regarding even the purpose of others as if it were his own.
And in this regard, the scriptural authority beginning with "produced from Nārāyaṇa" serves as the proof.

In order to establish that this [work] possesses the status of the supreme authority by means of its designation as "higher knowledge" (*paravidyā*), the term "designated as higher knowledge" is restated and explained as "the unsurpassed scripture.

It is "unsurpassed" (*anuttama*) because there is no scripture superior to it. It is a "scripture" (*śāstra*) because, through it, reality (*tattva*) is taught—that is, it is established and presented exactly as it exists. (1.100)

This is what is meant: having pointed out two types of knowledge with the words, "Two kinds of knowledge are to be known— the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā)," [the text] refers to the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs as the lower knowledge by saying "therein, the lower," and so forth, and then states, "Now, the higher is that by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained."
Thus, the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) has been demonstrated.

That [knowledge], being derived from the treatises of the Vedas and other scriptures, and because it possesses the characteristic of being the means for attaining the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), must indeed be a scripture; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of assuming multiple meanings for the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) when it is mentioned only once.
Furthermore, it is a contradiction to claim that a scripture is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
And since no other form of supremacy is possible for it, its very nature is that of being unsurpassed;
moreover, this is due to its proximity [to the goal], precisely as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because, by virtue of the co-occurrence with another word, a general term must be understood as having a specific meaning;
for example, when "supremely righteous" (*paramadhārmika*) is stated, it is understood that the supremacy pertains to righteousness.
And it is this very [work] that is intended to be the unsurpassed scripture.
This is because all scriptures, indicated by the words "Ṛg" and so forth, whose meanings are to be determined, have been described as *aparavidyā* (lower knowledge);
for nothing else is applicable, and because [the latter] cannot be considered supreme.
However, supremacy is possible for this [knowledge], since it is supportive.
By this, the explanation that the Upaniṣads constitute "higher knowledge" (paravidyā) is refuted;

for they too are included by the mention of the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas. Furthermore, the "maxim of the Brahmin mendicants" (brāhmaṇaparivrājaka-nyāya) is a resort only when no other way is possible.
Nor is it tenable to claim that the knowledge produced by that [scripture] is "higher knowledge" (paravidyā),
because it would be impossible for it to function as an instrument of realization,
and because it would entail the fallacy of attributing multiple meanings [to a single term].
Therefore, it is logical that by means of this [work] called "higher knowledge" (paravidyā), the establishment of this scripture's status as the supreme authority is proven.
Regarding the identity of meaning between the words "knowledge" (vidyā) and "scripture" (śāstra):

although the terms "knowledge" and "scripture" are associated with the respective activities of the disciple and the teacher, it should be understood that their identity of meaning is stated here by taking into account only their commonality as instruments for producing the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).

The commentary of the venerable Bhagavatpāda also indicates this very meaning: "When the Ṛgveda and other [Vedas] are not expressive of Viṣṇu, they are inferior knowledge (aparā vidyā); when they are indeed expressive of Viṣṇu, they are supreme knowledge (parā vidyā)."
For the Vedas and other scriptures, when not assisted by the principles expounded in the treatise of Brahma-mīmāṃsā, do not denote Viṣṇu; however, when assisted by them, they become denoters of him.
If it is argued that even so, the status of being a "higher knowledge" (paravidyā) is not obtained for the [Veda] alone, let it not be obtained.
Since this [Smṛti], which consists of the procedural forms (*itikartavyatā*) beginning with the Vedas, is not admitted to have independent authority,
its authority is established solely through inference (*anumāna*).
Bādarāyaṇa is the teacher of teachers and the source of the scriptures.
For that reason, the authority [of this work] has been declared by Manu and others for the sake of that [dharma].

Having thus established the unsurpassed authority of this treatise through scripture (*āgama*), he now wishes to establish it through inference (*anumāna*) as well; first, therefore, in order to state an inference regarding its mere authority, he says: "The Guru" (*guruḥ*). For this reason—that is, because Bādarāyaṇa is the teacher (*guruḥ*), the instructor, of the Gurus, namely Brahmā and the others who teach the reality of the world—and because he is the source (*prabhavaḥ*) of the scriptures, such as the Vedas and the *Mahābhārata*, as appropriate, which are the teachers that convey all matters without exception.
Or, it means that he is the primary source (*mukhyaprabhava*) of the extensive scriptures such as the Vedas, rather than merely the founder of a tradition (*sampradāya*).
And because their purpose—namely liberation—is for listeners beginning with Brahmā, it is "for that purpose" (*tadarthataḥ*).
Since this scripture was taught by him, Bādarāyaṇa, it ought to be authoritative (*māna*). (1.1.14)
Regarding the phrase "the direct statement of the probandum for the reasons":

here, the favorable conditions for the speaker, the listener, and the context—such as "the teacher of teachers" and so forth—are themselves the direct probanda; however, it should be understood that the phrase "mental [perception]" is the statement of the ultimate probandum.
For instance:

The triad consisting of knowledge of the reality of the intended meaning, proficiency of the instruments [of speech], and the desire to speak constitutes what is called the "favorableness of the speaker.
The dyad consisting of fitness for the knowledge of reality and being an object of the speaker's affection belongs to the listener.
The aim of the listener's purpose is the occasion [for the discourse].
In this context, the statement "the teacher of teachers" serves as the reason for the author Bādarāyaṇa’s intended meaning regarding the means of attaining knowledge of reality.
For it is observed that whoever is the instructor of reality to someone else possesses a superior knowledge of reality than that person.

And it is understood from such scriptures (*āgama*) as "among the gods beginning with Brahmā and Rudra," that he is the instructor of reality even to those such as Brahmā and Rudra, who are nearly omniscient.
Therefore, he ought to be omniscient.
By the statement that he is the "teacher and source of the teachers' scriptures," both his knowledge of reality and his proficiency in the instruments [of cognition] are established.
For whoever is the source of a scripture that sets forth a certain extent of meaning is understood to know that much of that meaning in accordance with reality.

Furthermore, the source of this scripture (*āgama*), which establishes all meanings without exception, is understood from such statements as "the Blessed One [recovered] the Vedas that had been lost" and "he taught what was not spoken by the five Vedas.
Therefore, there must exist this omniscient one.
Moreover, it is observed that whoever is the source of an extensive scripture possesses keen faculties, provided no other cause is present.
And how could this [Veda] be the source of another [scripture], such as the Vedas, if its instruments were not proficient?
By the statement "it was uttered by them," the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), which is the cause, is established through its effect.
The phrase "by the teachers" is the reason for establishing the capacity of the listeners to understand the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
For one who is himself unfit for the knowledge of reality is not seen to be a teacher of reality to others.
The phrase "from Brahmā and the rest" serves to establish that they are objects of the speaker’s affection;
indeed, it is well known that Brahmā and the others are the objects of the Supreme Lord’s love.
The phrase "for that purpose" (*tadarthatā*) serves to establish the suitability of the context.

Here, in every case, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*)—such as the arising of an effect without a cause—is to be inferred as the subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) against the opposing position.
Why then should one imagine the interpolation of another probandum (*sādhyāntara*) in the middle?

Now, one might argue: "Let the relationship between the probandum and the probans in these passages, such as 'the guru of gurus,' be explained exactly as they are heard according to the authority of the scripture;
why should there be the conceptualization of interpolating another probandum in the middle?
Even though these [passages] taken literally possess a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (vyadhikaraṇatā)..."
Nevertheless, because of the statement "that has been stated," there will be a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatā*) through the transformation of case endings.
Regarding the "non-deviation of reasons" (*hetūnām avyabhicaritatvam*):
although these [reasons] individually deviate from being authoritative in the Buddhist scriptures and so forth;
Nevertheless, let there be causality for the [combined] factors taken together.

If it is argued that the factor of "being composed by one who is the source of all the excellent scriptures such as the Mahābhārata" would be an *asādhāraṇa* (uniquely inconclusive) reason because it does not enter into the set of similar instances (*sapakṣa*), we say no;
for the presence of the reason is possible within those very [scriptures] themselves.
Because its authority is established through the acceptance by the great multitude of people and other such factors.

If it is argued that, in that case, since they were not actually composed by Bādarāyaṇa—who was distinguished by the authorship of the *Bhārata* and other works—the reason would merely be that they were taught by him to Brahmā and others for the sake of their liberation, we reply: certainly so.
Because there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to that much alone.

If this were so, one might object that the statement "the Guru is the source of Gurus and of scriptures" would become redundant; but this is not the case, because even though he does not enter into the formal body of the logical reason (hetu), his utility is established through such means as the presentation of examples (dṛṣṭānta). *1,125*
[Response: True, [the opponent] supports the necessity of supplying a different probandum;
nevertheless, it is not possible to understand it in this way.
If that were the case, it would be inconsistent to establish the relationship between the probandum and the speaker’s conformity [to the truth] within the subsequent statement.
If it is argued that this will constitute a separate inference, we say no; for if that were so, validity would be of three kinds. (*1.129*)
The arising [of this treatise] from a source is not inconsistent, because there is a correspondence between the speaker, the listener, and the resulting comprehension;
for it is the word of a reliable authority (*āpta*) and likewise rooted in the Vedas (*śruti*). (Manu Smṛti 1.5)
And because it is rooted in reasoning, the great threefold authority of the Brahmasūtras is seen everywhere in one way and not otherwise.
In that case, does this not imply the following:
"This treatise is authoritative because it possesses a favorable speaker and so forth, like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works;
and the favorability of the speaker and other factors is established by the reason already stated"?
This is untenable,
because being the word of a reliable authority (*āptavākyatva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in that case.

Nor should it be argued that this is not a valid limiting adjunct because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhyāvyāpaka*), on the grounds that while perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) and the like possess validity, they lack the status of being the word of a reliable authority.
This is because it is established as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) by virtue of its pervading the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the property of being a sentence.
If it is argued that even so, it is not a limiting adjunct because of its absence in the non-human Veda, we say no;
for the non-human authorship of the Veda is impossible.

Or [if it is argued that] this is established as a limiting condition (upādhi) because it is possible for it to be such when the probandum is delimited by being "consensual" or delimited by being "a human statement"—
it is not so, because your intention has not been understood.

We are not endeavoring to establish the authority of the treatise directly through the suitability of the speaker and other factors, such that the introduction of a "limiting condition" (upādhi) here would be relevant. Rather, since the possession of a suitable speaker and so forth is pervaded by being the word of a trustworthy person (āptavākyatva), one establishes that [trustworthiness] by means of it, and thereby establishes the authority of the treatise. Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "Of the speakers, listeners, and connections..."

In this context, "authoritativeness" (*āpti*) refers to the suitability of the speaker, the listener, and the [subject] matter within a statement; that is to say, a statement endowed with such suitability on the part of the speaker and others is an authoritative statement (*āptavākya*). Since this pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists, and since this treatise possesses a suitable speaker and so forth, [it is authoritative].

The connection with the preceding [verse] is that this treatise is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it consists of the words of a perfected person (*siddha*). Who is this "perfected person" (*āpta*)? This is what is meant: *Note: The asterisk (*) and dollar signs ($) indicate verse numbering and commentary markers in the source text.*

The subject of dispute (the word of an authoritative person) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is taught by a speaker who is favorable toward listeners who are likewise favorable, for the purpose of making them understand the means to achieve their own welfare, just like [other] accepted [authoritative statements]. The subject of dispute is a means of valid cognition because it is the word of an authoritative person, as in the case of what is already accepted.
The words of non-authoritative persons such as the Jainas lack the favorability of the speaker.
[The speech of] Buddhists and others lacks conformity to the ear;
[the speech of] jesters and others lacks conformity to the context.
Now, who indeed is this so-called "reliable person" (āpta), whose status as such is being established by the property of being the speaker of the words?
If it is argued that [the Buddha] is one who speaks of things exactly as they have been perceived, this is not so;
for the same consequence would apply even to one who speaks of things perceived through delusion.

Even if the qualification "perceived by a valid means of cognition" (*pramāṇadṛṣṭa*) were added, the same consequence would still apply to one who, despite having perceived something through a valid means of cognition, speaks of it otherwise due to negligence or other causes.
If it is argued that a speaker speaks exactly as something has been perceived by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no;
for even if one speaks truthfully regarding a certain part, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they might speak untruthfully regarding other parts.
If it is argued that one speaks only as much as has been perceived by a means of valid cognition, we say no.
This is because, for the most part, the definitions do not pervade the objects to be defined precisely because those objects are not of that nature;
for no one expresses everything exactly as it has been measured by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that one speaks only of what has been seen according to the extent of its measurement, we say no.

Because it would follow that one who employs a statement that is unknown, doubtful, or a mere restatement (anuvāda) would be an unreliable authority (anāpta); and because even the elder brother of Bhīma could occasionally speak with flattery, he too would incur the status of being an unreliable authority.
If it is argued that an "authoritative person" (āpta) is one who is free from defects, [we reply: no.

If it is argued that even among authoritative persons (*āpta*), since defects such as passion may occasionally arise, one is considered authoritative only with respect to a specific subject where they are free from defects—this is not so. Because the words "that" (*yat*) and "which" (*tat*) refer to specific instances, the definition would lack generality and thus fail to apply universally (*avyāpti*). (1.140)
[The Definition of Reliability] This is not so.
Reliability (*āpti*) consists of this: knowledge of the true nature of the intended object, the absence of a desire to deceive, the intention to speak, and proficiency of the instruments [of speech].
For it is accepted that one who possesses such [knowledge] is an authoritative person (*āpta*).
If it is argued that even in one who is considered authoritative, this [knowledge] might sometimes not exist, let it be so; for at such a time, he is accepted as being non-authoritative (*anāpta*).
Because there is no contradiction due to differences in time and other factors.
If this is so, one might object: "In that case, it would be said that whoever is of such a nature in a particular instance is an authority (*āpta*) therein. Let it be so; what is the fault?
If you say, "The referents of the words 'whoever' (*yaḥ*) and 'therein' (*tatra*) lack universal application (*ananugama*)," [we reply:]...
What is this so-called "non-concomitance"? Is it the unsuitability for universal linguistic usage, or the absence of one thing's subsistence in many?
It is not the first, because we observe its status as a cause for universal linguistic usage in such cases as: "He who is someone's son is entitled to that person's wealth."
The second [alternative] is not [tenable], because it is free from fault.

We shall explain in the "Examination of the Universal" (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*) how there is no lack of pervasion even for that which is not a universal, and how it serves as the cause for universal linguistic usage. *1,145*

By this, another definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*)— namely, "one who is faultless" and "one who speaks only of what has been cognized"— should be understood as being established. This is because reiteration (*anuvāda*), being within the scope of formal discourse (*vāda*), does not contradict the authoritativeness of its speaker.

And thus, the status of being an *āpta* (reliable authority) pertains only to a portion [of the speaker's qualities], namely, his favorability toward the speaker. Furthermore, the desire to deceive (*vipralipsā*) is based solely on the speaker’s inclination toward the interests of the listener; it ceases when that inclination is absent. Therefore, the logical concomitance (*pratibandha*) is well-established through the fact that the words of an *āpta* possess this favorability toward the speaker and others. [Objection: But does not the status of being the word of an *āpta* fail to be invariably concomitant with validity (*prāmāṇya*), as seen in works like the *Mālatīmādhava*, which were composed from the mere imagination of one's own mind?
If it is argued that Bhavabhūti, even while composing works such as dramas, was not at times endowed with the aforementioned characteristics [of an authoritative person], we say no;

for this objection has already been answered by the very statement, "one who is such in that regard," and because a sentence rooted in trustworthiness is intended here as the speech of a trustworthy person (*āpta*).

A statement that is non-informative or informative of a contrary [meaning] is said to be invalid (*apramāṇa*). Among these, a non-informative statement arises from the speaker’s lack of proficiency, while a statement informative of a contrary [meaning] arises from such things as erroneous knowledge. Thus, the pervasion (*pratibandha*) is established: the state of being a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is necessarily concomitant with the quality of being a statement preceded by [the speaker’s] reliability (*āpti*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an effect arising without a cause. [Objection:
What is the proof for the status of being the word of a reliable person (*āptavākyatā*) in this intermediate context?
Surely, one should instead explain here the proof for its validity (*prāmāṇya*) by way of its possessing a favorable speaker and so forth.
Why is the proof for the status of being the word of a reliable person (*āptavākyatā*) explained in the middle?
Because there is no parity between pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
For it is not possible that whatever is the pervader of a pervader would be a non-pervader of that [pervader].

If one were to establish that a statement is "the word of a reliable person" (*āptavākyatā*) on the grounds that it possesses a speaker who is favorable and so forth, then the favorability of the speaker would be indistinguishable from the probandum itself, since it is merely a part of what constitutes reliability.

Furthermore, the phrase "of the speaker, the hearer, and the connection [between them]" will serve to demonstrate that the suspected *upādhi* (limiting condition) is not co-extensive with the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*).
This is not so.
Because it would follow that the subsequent statement [beginning with] "by him as an authoritative word" (*āptavākyatayā*) would be redundant;
for the fact that the adjunct (*upādhi*) pervades the probans (*sādhana*) has already been established by the very phrase "of the speaker, the hearer, and the consequences.

Indeed, it is not the rule of the tradition that one who refutes an adjunct, having first demonstrated its pervasion of the probans, should then establish the presence of the adjunct in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of the probans, and thereby prove the probandum (*sādhya*) through that. (1.152)
If it is argued that, having shown the non-difference of the probans from the adjunct (*upādhi*), the probandum is thereby established, we say no;
for since trustworthiness (*āpti*) is a property belonging solely to the speaker, its non-difference from the probans is untenable.
Furthermore, there is certainly no lack of distinction [of the adjunct] from the probandum.
If it is argued that when the speaker's reliability is established through the favorability of the speaker’s mouth and other such factors, that reliability would indeed be established only partially;
and furthermore, it has been stated that the status of being a reliable person's statement is proven by the possession of a favorable mouth and so forth—
nevertheless, there is still an overlap between the probandum and the probans insofar as both involve a single part of reliability.
True;
nevertheless, there is no fault because of the distinction of specific differences (*viśiṣṭabheda*).
Otherwise, even the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*)—such as "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire"—would not exist.
This is because the qualified element (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) enters into both [the definition of the probans and the definition of the trustworthy person].

Furthermore, even though "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) enter into "existence" (*sattā*), others accept the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between them.

However, when it is maintained that a "trustworthy person" (*āpta*) is one who is faultless and speaks only of what has been correctly cognized, then there is not even a suspicion of the [probans] being qualified by the probandum. (1.156)
If it is asked why the author of the treatise also relied upon this tradition when the reason for the commentator’s reliance on the tradition has already been stated:
[the answer is] that even while establishing validity through the favorability of the speaker and other factors, one must ultimately rely on this very point.

Otherwise, who could prevent the following doubt: "Let there be conformity with the speaker's intention and so forth, yet let there be invalidity because it is rooted in the speaker's desire to deceive"?
Even though the view of Bādarāyaṇa is that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), as he will state: "Not so, because of the difference in nature."
Jaimini also states: "The authority of that [Veda] belongs to Bādarāyaṇa because of its independence.
Nevertheless, there is no contradiction, as this effort is for the purpose of dispelling doubts regarding its lack of authority.
That which accords with scripture and that which accords with reasoning is authoritative.

Having thus established the authority of this scripture through corroboration by a dissimilar source, he states the corroboration by two similar sources as well, in order to prove its unsurpassed nature, beginning with the word "śruti."
The two words *tathā* and *ca* have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Alternatively, they serve to draw back the word *mānam* (as a means of knowledge).
Or, the word *tathā* has the sense of a comparison, meaning "just as [it is so] by virtue of being the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*), so too is it by virtue of being rooted in the Śruti."
Although the two words "based on scripture" (*śruti*) and "based on reasoning" (*yukti*) denote that which is composed after having apprehended the dharma through scripture and reasoning,

nevertheless, here they should be explained as having meanings that accord with scripture and reasoning by means of a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*), due to the similarity of their common purpose.
This is because, for the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, who is inherently omniscient, a literal sense is impossible.
And if he had stated "because of the agreement with scripture and reasoning," then even a coincidental agreement would have been understood;
so that this might not be understood, he uses the term "secondary" (gauṇa).
For by using it in this way, the relationship of principal and subordinate (aṅgāṅgibhāva) is further understood.
And that will establish the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Consequently, this is the meaning:
that which is in agreement with scripture is authoritative (*pramāṇa*).
Just like the statements of Manu and others,
this treatise is in harmony with the Vedas,
because it is devoted to the investigation of their meaning.
Because that [cognition] would be impossible in the case of non-correspondence;
and that [is stated in the verse]:
"Furthermore, for the sake of knowing its object."
This is established by such scriptural authority (*āgama*).
Furthermore, that which is consistent with reasoning (*yukti*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
such as the statement "this mountain possesses fire" made with reference to a smoky mountain.
And this is consistent with reason,
because it has the nature of inquiry (mīmāṃsā),
and because inquiry consists in the investigation of reasoning.

Therefore, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, there would follow the consequence that both scripture (*śruti*) and reasoning (*yukti*) lack authority, because a partial contradiction (*ardhavaiśasa*) is impossible. *1,163*
The embodied self is indeed the supreme Self.
To the question "What follows from this, that it is God?", he says: "Thus, its authority [is established]."
The word *eva* (only/itself) is connected with the phrase "of the Brahma-sūtras. *Trividham* (threefold) is an adverbial modifier.
*Brahman* refers to the Veda, its meaning, or the Supreme Brahman; the *sūtras* of that [Brahman] are the *brahmasūtras*.
That is to say, these are the aphorisms (sūtras) for the purpose of determining the essential nature of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman, who is the meaning of the entire Veda.
The meaning of the word "sūtra" is to be understood from such traditional authorities (āgama) as: "that which consists of few syllables," and so forth.

By this, the meaning of the term *Śārīraka*, which denotes this very treatise, is as follows: the body itself is the "little body" (*śarīraka*); that which exists therein is the "embodied one" (*śārīraka*), namely, the individual soul (*jīva*).
The interpretation that this work is called *Śārīraka* because it was composed concerning that [embodied soul] (*śārīra*) is refuted,
as it contradicts the meaning of the term *Brahmasūtra*.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the work is an investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) into the nature of the Brahman denoted by the word *tat* as being identical with that which is denoted by the word *tvam*, we say no.
Because it is impossible;
for the sūtras beginning with "janmādy asya" (the origin, etc., of this) do not aim at non-difference,
but rather, as will be stated, they aim at the refutation thereof.
Therefore, the one denoted by the term *śārīraka* is indeed the supreme self (*paramātman*).
As it has been said:
"Both of those are embodied (*śarīrin*)."
"The individual soul (jīva) and the one designated as the Lord (īśvara) are to be known.
The investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) into His being the teacher of all and His perfection, etc., is indeed the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā.
Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa: "The state of being free from all defects," and so forth. *1,167*
The authority of the *Brahmasūtras* is indeed threefold;
for in this way, the threefold authority of the *Brahmasūtras* is observed—
meaning, it is observed by means of the three types of evidence, such as being the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*).
Therefore, that [authority] should be considered great and unsurpassed.

If the authority established by the three marks—such as the threefold testimony of a reliable person (āptavākya)—were to exist elsewhere as well, then how could this [authority] of theirs be unsurpassed? For this reason, it is said: "of the Brahma-sūtras alone.
To the question "How so?", he says: "In one way... (ekadhā).
Because of the expression "in every way" (*sarvaśas*), the term "in one way" (*ekadhā*) is an elliptical indication;
for instance, in some cases it is "in one way."

Just as, in the case of worldly objects, there is reliance on the words of a father because they are rooted in trustworthiness; in the case of matters such as dharma, there is reliance on the speech uttered by an opponent due to its agreement with the Veda;
and in the case of a statement such as "the mountain possesses fire" when it is precisely as stated, there is reliance due to its agreement with reasoning.
In some cases, it is twofold:
for example, by means of authoritative testimony (*āpti*) and scripture (*śruti*), as in the statements of Manu and others;
or by means of authoritative testimony and reasoning (*yukti*), as in the paternal statement "the mountain possesses fire," and so forth.
If it is argued that the statement uttered by the opponent— that "the Lord is omniscient" is established through both scripture and reasoning—
and that this exists in three ways even in the words of Jaimini and others,
that is true.

It is not as it is in the *Brahmasūtras*, for in those [texts], attainment and so forth are indeed limitless. For this reason as well, the term "great" (*mahat*) should be construed with the phrase "this is threefold."
[Objection: But surely, since the object of cognition remains exactly as it was regardless of whether the means of cognition is one or many, how can this be so?
[Reply: It is thus:
for it is not the mere means of cognition that is useful for action free from doubt.
What indeed is that which is cognized as being valid?
And it is an established fact of experience that to whatever extent something is cognized with greater validity, it produces a corresponding, unhesitating, and rapid engagement.
Therefore, validity itself is said to possess excellence by virtue of the excellence of its own effect.

In this way, excellence should also be understood by virtue of the excellence of its subject matter and purpose. Thus, nothing such as this is accepted as being the most authoritative means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatama*).
Although this commentary was composed by himself, it is being set forth for the sake of clarity.

Thus, concluding that by means of both scripture and inference this very scripture alone is the most authoritative means of knowledge and that there exists no other such as this, he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
The phrase "is accepted by those who follow authoritative means of knowledge" (*prāmāṇikaiḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Thus, the underlying intention is that it is proper to provide an explanation of this very [text] while setting aside others.
Now, one might object: "The *Bhārata* is said to be the best among all scriptures."
True;
there is no contradiction, for that [is the case] regarding those treatises which are subject to investigation.
But surely the author of the Sūtras himself establishes the necessity of undertaking this treatise in the very first Sūtra?
Everything is accomplished by the explanation of that alone;
what is the use of this?
If it is asked, "How does the engagement [of the treatise] occur in the very first sūtra? [the answer follows].
If it is asked how this applies even to the first commentary—
namely, that for one who has proceeded from doubt, there is a final determination by means of further proofs— that is the same in the case of the first sūtra as well.
Not so;
that [desire] arises precisely through the accomplishment of the object and other factors,
and it does not follow from that alone that [the treatise] must be undertaken.

For it is only when validity is established that the exposition of the object and other factors becomes useful for the purpose of distinguishing this work from treatises such as the *Kākadantaparīkṣā*.
Therefore, although this was already implied by the Sūtra, it has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya for the sake of purifying the intellects of the students. (*1,176*) [The meaning is clear.]

Nevertheless, although it has already been explained that this [sūtra] need not be further explained because it has already been explained, he says "svayam" (himself) in order to elaborate on that other purpose which was indicated by the phrase "anvapi ca" (and even though...).
Although the commentary on those Brahma-sutras was composed by me myself in the Bhāṣya, nevertheless, the purpose here is clarity alone— that is,
for the sake of clarity.
It is undertaken in order to clarify the meaning that was not made clear in the Bhāṣya.
Clarification is of many kinds:
in some cases, it is the statement of what has not been mentioned; in others, it is the expansion of what was stated too concisely.
In some places there is a condensation of that which, due to being excessively extensive, has not entered the intellect;
in other places, there is a unification of that which is scattered; and in yet other places, there is a substantiation of what has already been stated.
In various places, one should observe such matters as the strengthening [of the doctrine] by refuting erroneous explanations.
Now, one might object: "Should everything not be stated in a single place? What is the use of these different systems?
Do not say so.
For what is taught through both summary and detail becomes easy for listeners to grasp and purposeful.
As it has been said:
"The wise explain by means of both summary and detail."
"Because of his memory of many [past] births, it is the cause of a great abundance of fruits.
Thus, the meaning of the first verse of the Bhāṣya has been explained here by these three verses. To explain:

The doubt regarding a distinction between qualities and the possessor of qualities (*guṇa-guṇin*), which arose from the statement that [the Lord] is "surpassing in all qualities," has been dispelled by the words "entirely," and so forth.

The objection as to how "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) and "perceptibility" (*gamyatva*) can function as qualifiers—given that they are common to others—is resolved by the phrase "most accessible" (*āpyatama*).
The word "also" (*api*) serves to include other qualifiers.
The phrase "its exposition is this," and so forth,

explains the word "the gurus" (gurūn) in the plural by means of the extensive demonstration of their greatness through various modes such as "originating from the treatise" (*śāstraprabhavam*) and others. Furthermore,
although there is a distinction between the guru and the deity, the author's lack of preference for such a distinction is indicated by the use of the word "api."

The phrase "its exposition is that very [text]" is qualified by the words "sam" and "pra," meaning "not however. By the inclusion of the *sūtra* without any prefix, the supreme authority of the *Brahma-sūtras* is indicated; the demonstration of that is [the section] called "Parama."
The commentary beginning with "yaddvāpara" is inconsistent;
for, having promised to state the meaning of the Sūtra, no utility is seen in explaining the order of its origination.
Not so.

He shows that this is so by means of the passage beginning with "The Guru of Gurus," etc., in order to establish the supreme authority of the Brahma-sūtras even through such reasoning as their being rooted in authoritative tradition (*āpta*). [This concludes] the discussion on auspiciousness (*maṅgalavāda*).
Nevertheless, it might be argued that this treatise should not be expounded because it is devoid of an introductory rite of auspiciousness (*maṅgalācaraṇa*).
Indeed, actions preceded by auspicious rites (maṅgalācaraṇa) are completed without obstacles and reach fulfillment.

It is not correct to argue that these rites are not the cause [of success] because we observe the completion of tasks even for those who have not performed auspicious rites, and the failure to complete them even for those who have performed such rites.
For if that were the case, it would follow that rituals such as the Kārīrī sacrifice would likewise lack causality with respect to rain and other results.
This might be so, provided that the causality of the *kārīrī* sacrifice and the like with respect to rain and such were without proof; but this is not the case.

For when the relationship between the means and the end is established by the *śruti*, the fact that [the result] occurs even in its absence serves as the basis for postulating that it has multiple causes.
For even through the service of the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) and so forth, heaven is attained just as it is through the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices;
however, even when [the cause] exists, its non-existence [in the effect] occurs due to defects in the agent, the instruments, and so forth.
Indeed, a cause that deviates from its effect due to a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) would not truly be a cause.
Alternatively, when there is excellence in the agent and other factors, the existence of a powerful obstructing factor is postulated;
for a cause that does not produce its obstructed effect does not thereby cease to be a cause,
as that would lead to the undesirable consequence that even fire would not be a cause with respect to the bursting of a seed-corn.

And it cannot be argued that, because such a suspicion of a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrīvaiguṇya*) is easily available everywhere, this would lead to the collapse of all purposeful activity;
for this [objection] applies equally to the present case as well.

This is because the fact that the performance of an auspicious rite (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) is a cause for the unimpeded completion [of a work] and so forth is established by a Vedic text inferred from the undisputed practice of students.
The activity of a discerning person cannot possibly be fruitless,
nor can it be for the sake of some other purpose,
because that would entail abandoning what is perceived and imagining what is unperceived.
It is established by experience that one who intends to begin an action indeed desires its completion and so forth;
furthermore, there is no evidence for the pursuit of any other fruit. Nor is this perception of the relationship between means and end a delusion on their part.
Since no contradiction [with other means of knowledge] would thus arise,
and since perception and the other means of knowledge have no scope here, it is the Śruti itself that is postulated as the basis for the conduct of the disciple.
Nor should this [rite] not be performed on the grounds of uncertainty regarding the existence of obstacles.
Even when there is doubt regarding that [performance], it is established by logical principle that "even a partial defect must be avoided";
nor is it correct to argue that since the venerable author of the Sūtras has no obstacles at all, his failure to perform the rites for their removal does not constitute a fault.
This is because it must also be performed for the sake of the disciples;
for treatises preceded by auspicious rites become powerful and are undertaken by long-lived persons.
Otherwise, one would not have done so even in the case of the *Mahābhārata* and other such works.
By this, it is refuted [by the author] that the author of the Sūtra has indeed performed the auspicious invocation;
for even the objection— "Why was it not placed at the beginning of the book?"— is rejected,
since placing it in the book is also required by the traditional conduct of disciples.
And because it is for the sake of the disciples;
for this very reason, the claim that the author of the Sūtras performed some other act for the purpose of destroying obstacles and so forth is refuted.
To this, it is replied:
An auspicious invocation must indeed be performed at the commencement of any undertaking,
and it has been performed by the Blessed Author of the Sūtra and placed at the beginning of the work.
Because he placed the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha* at the beginning,
since those two are auspicious;
as it has been said:
“The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the throat of Brahmā in ancient times; therefore, both are auspicious.
Thus, the word *atha* has the sense of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
In this regard, Tārā is intended to be the root of all weapons;
because she is present everywhere, she is honored separately by everyone.
But surely this is untenable;

for if that were the case, since these two would serve as causes for the removal of obstacles and so forth, they would lack the status of being constituent parts of the first aphorism as members of the entire treatise.
And if that were so, the first aphorism would become deficient.
Because there is no other [text] that establishes the qualified student (adhikārin) and so forth,
and because such an establishment is necessary—

otherwise, the doubt that the treatise should not be commenced due to the absence of a qualified student and a subject matter would remain unrefuted, and the Sūtra would consequently be rendered useless— he says: "In that regard" (tatra).
The *oṃkāra* is called *tāra* because by means of it one crosses over the mass of suffering (*aniṣyanicaya*).
*Tāra* and *atha*: their status as the "root" refers respectively to their being the first [syllables].
Because they are employed at the beginning, the *oṃkāra* is *tāra*.
*Tāra* (Oṃ) and *atha* (then); their status as the "root" means they are uttered in sequence—that is to say, the syllable Oṃ and the word *atha* are employed at the beginning.
In that regard, it is intended and accepted by the author of the Sūtras, as a part of the first Sūtra and as a limb of the entire treatise; this is the implied meaning.
This is what is meant:

the syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*, employed in the first sūtra for the purpose of establishing the subject matter (*adhikārin*) and so forth, produce the unimpeded completion and other such results for the entire treatise because they are auspicious by their very sound, like the sounds of a conch, a lute, or a flute.

It is like seeing a full water-jar being brought for another purpose. By the mere statement "tārāthau," the fact that these two constitute the root [of the science] is established; this indicates the sign of the author of the Sūtras' own acceptance of this.

Because, having set aside other synonyms and having abandoned a different order, these two are placed at the very beginning, we understand—by virtue of their being indicators (*jñāpaka*) for the first Sūtra and by virtue of their being the causal factors (*kāraka*) for the entire treatise—that these two are of utility.
These two are intended by the author of the Sūtra;
nor is this arbitrary,
because all authors of Sūtras employ them in this very manner.
Nor is it observed that the activity of many discerning persons occurs in a uniform manner by mere chance;
by this, the commentary stating that the word "atha" (then/therefore) has the sense of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and so forth is explained.
*A Consideration of the Views of the Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa Commentaries*
In this regard, as for the criticism of others that "there is no syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) of the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) with the meaning of the sentence," it is as follows:
"For it is only the meaning of the individual words (*padārtha*) that is connected to the meaning of the sentence."
And that [meaning] must be either the expressed (vācya) or the indicated (lakṣya) meaning; however,
in this case, auspiciousness is neither the expressed nor the indicated meaning of the word *atha*,
but rather it is the effect (*kārya*) of the word *atha*, like the sound of a drum.
"Furthermore, the syntactic integration (*samanvaya*) of both the effect and the signified into the sentence-meaning is not observed in verbal usage.
"Or, let it be granted that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) has the status of a word-meaning; nevertheless, there is no syntactic integration into the sentence-meaning."
For instance: first of all, auspiciousness does not connect with the meaning of the sentence as the *brahmajijñāsā* through the relation of agent, object, or instrument,
because there is no evidence for its being any one of these [roles], such as the agent.
Furthermore, because other grammatical factors (*kāraka*) are present,
there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);

for that would result in the undesirable consequence of the passage being a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), as it would be intended merely to glorify the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) by calling it "auspicious."

Thus, this [objection] is refuted by us as well, because we accept that the word *atha*, which denotes "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), serves the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) according to its direct meaning (*śruti*).
Now, one might object: "But is it not the case that the syllable *oṃ* itself does not even exist at the beginning of this Sūtra?"
How, then, can it be said that [the work] has Tārā as its root?
Although it is established by direct perception as being recited by disciples and students, nevertheless, this is not a constituent part of the Sūtra.
Because it is recited by everyone in its uncombined form when there is an absence of other [phonetic] characteristics,
just like the syllable *oṃ* uttered by students at the commencement of Vedic study;
otherwise, like the word *atha*, it would have been indicated in its combined form.
Nor is the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) deficient in the property to be proven (sādhyavikala).

For it is well-established that when Vedic sentences are recited by all [reciters] at various different locations—due to the diversity in the commencement and cessation of study and through the abandonment of this or that particular place—they lack the status of being constituent parts (avayava) of a single sentence.
Otherwise, even if there were such diversity in the commencement and cessation of study, they would necessarily be recited in fixed positions, as in the case of "Oṃ" and "Brahman."
Let it be granted that the initial utterance of the *pakṣa* and *sapakṣa* [terms] is practiced by students as part of the rules of recitation, just like facing east and so forth.
However, the claim that this *oṃkāra* was placed at the beginning of the Sūtra by its author for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is untenable; therefore, he says: "Everywhere."

That which is uttered separately and without being joined together by all the reciters of the Sūtras is justified by a desired cause that pervades all the Sūtras. "The syllable Oṃ is a constituent part of the Sūtra"—
this is what is meant.
For all the Sūtras are intermediate Brahma-vidyās, since each is devoted to the investigation of numerous Vedic passages.

From the force of the scriptural explanatory passage (arthavāda), "The unaccompanied Brahman flows away, and it perishes at the end," it is understood that the utterance of the syllable Oṃ must be performed at the beginning and the end of all Brahma-vidyās.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the modified form (*ūhya*) is distinct from the original mantra;
for if it were, the consequence would be that even the modified portion within a mantra would not be a constituent part of the mantra itself.

Consequently, since reciting the entire *pati-sūtra* at both the beginning and the end would result in redundancy, the syllable *oṃ* is uttered right at the outset as the governing authority (*adhikṛta*).
If it were taught as part of a continuous recitation, this would be understood as merely a portion of the first sūtra;
so that it might not be understood in that way, it is marked separately by the students.
Nor should it be argued that marking it separately is useless because the subject matter (*adhikāra*) can be understood even from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
Because it is only when there is an absence of an internal indicator (*antaraṅga-jñāpaka*) that an external one (*bahiraṅga*) is to be sought;
thus, by stating another reason for the mention [of the syllable] as being non-composed (*asaṃhita*), the alternative establishment of the cause is asserted.

Now, a doubt arises: on the strength of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning the literal sense, should the utterance of the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and end be understood as a modification (*ūha*), or should it be conceived as a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) for something external, like facing the east and so forth?
True.
Even in the case of doubt, inference—by that same indirect route—is indeed a fallacy due to its being "doubtfully otherwise-established" (sandigdhānyathāsiddha).

Furthermore, since the meaning of the syllable *oṃ* can be ascertained through its coordination with the meaning of the sentence of the first sūtra according to the logic to be stated hereafter, the inference has its object sublated (*bādhitaviṣaya*).
Alternatively, he offers a refutation of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) by this [argument]. To explain:

when the syllable *oṃ* is uttered by all Vedic reciters in a distinct form through a transposition of its position, it is—according to the principle already stated—by virtue of being pronounced at the very beginning.

By the statement "it is established solely on the grounds that [the syllable *oṃ*] has been obtained as something present everywhere," the author states that the probans (*hetu*) in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*).
Consequently, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

Thus, when the inference has been refuted, since the status of the syllable *oṃ* as a constituent part of the first aphorism is established through its unobjectionable initial utterance, what was stated is logically justified.

Thus, since it has been established that this treatise is to be explained, and because only that which is the object of the activity of a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*) ought to be commenced, and because the activity of discerning persons occurs only toward that which possesses a purpose, a subject matter, and a connection— [the author] now begins the commentary on the first aphorism, which sets forth the connection with the purpose and so forth in order to induce the activity of a discerning person, by means of the words "that which expresses reality" (*tattvavācin*), and so on. *1,225*
The statement of the purpose and so forth is indeed meaningful.

Now, if the fact that knowledge of Brahman is the cause of liberation were already established by other means of valid cognition prior to the commencement of this scripture, then its statement in the scripture would be useless;
for in a case where something is established by another means of valid cognition, there is no need for instruction [from a treatise].

If, on the other hand, that determination occurs right here [in this very context], then there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*): first, the determination of the purpose and so forth is required for engagement, and only once the purpose and so forth are determined does engagement occur.
Alternatively, if that determination arises from the first sūtra itself, then it must be explained how that occurs in that very place.
How does engagement [with the treatise] occur? And if another purpose were stated for that [purpose], there would be an infinite regress.
For if engagement occurs in that very manner, the same consequence would follow for what comes after; thus, the statement of the purpose and so forth in the Sūtra would be useless.
It is said:
for the mental activity of persons is threefold—
namely, experience, desire, and effort.
In this context, desire and effort directed toward the means [of accomplishment] are called "engagement" (*pravṛtti*),
but not experience, nor desire directed toward the result;
for if they were so, those two would also require dependence upon the ascertainment of a purpose.
For it is not the case that equanimity (*upekṣā*) is not experienced because it is purposeless;
nor is it accepted that pleasure (*sukha*) is not desired simply because it lacks some other purpose.
Furthermore, it is not the case that for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), sacrifices and the like are not experienced as means to heaven (*svarga*) because heaven is disregarded by him.
However, activity directed toward the accomplishment of human goals—characterized by desire or characterized by effort—is not established by its own natural force (*svarasasiddha*).
Indeed, no one desires to eat or exerts effort without first considering the removal of hunger and so forth.
Therefore, whoever is to be incited to action must have that purpose and so forth demonstrated; thus, the mention of the "purpose" (*prayojana*) and other factors in the Sūtra is meaningful. (1.236)
Regarding the inclusion of the first sūtra within the treatise:
