it has been stated that the purpose and so forth [of the treatise] have been explained; however, it remains to be addressed how a listener might develop faith, and how one who lacks faith might proceed.
On this point, some offer the following resolution:
One who has understood that the author of the Sūtra is a trustworthy person will indeed have faith based on his word alone.

Even if the purpose and other such factors are not explicitly stated when determining his trustworthiness, there still arises a general certainty that "this treatise possesses a purpose and so forth, because it was spoken by a trustworthy person.
Nevertheless, this [certainty] is not a factor for engaging in the study.
One does not engage [in an activity] merely because it possesses a purpose and so forth;
rather, one engages because it possesses the specific purpose and so forth that we intend.
And since that specific purpose and so forth is determined from the statement itself, the mention of it is meaningful.

Even when the reliability [of the speaker] is not certain, activity toward [an object] such as plowing is possible simply because of doubt regarding the matter, just as in the case of [seeing] a furrow and so forth.
Now, one might object: doubt is indeed easily obtained even when the purpose and other factors are not stated, provided there is an absence of both proving and subverting evidence;
and the recollection of specific details [is likewise possible].
"It will occur because of a specific desire for that [object].
Do not say so; for whoever proceeds to act based on a particular statement depends upon that very statement for the recollection of the specific [details].
But not independently.
For one afflicted by disease does not, being unrestrained, proceed by his own conjecture as to whether or not "this is a means for the cessation of my disease" in this or that case;
rather, he acts solely on the word of a physician whose status as an authority has been ascertained.
Otherwise, failing to perceive the stated purpose for oneself, one might suspect even that it is useless:

Is this work purposeless like a treatise on examining a crow’s teeth? Or does it have a purpose that is impossible to accomplish, like describing the *sañjīvanī* herb found on the northern peaks of the Snowy Mountains (the Himalayas) which revives the dead? Or does it have a purpose contrary to my own wishes, like a Southerner instructing an inhabitant of Āryāvarta on the manner of marrying his maternal uncle’s daughter?
Alternatively, even regarding a desired purpose, this method may be more arduous than another simpler means available;
it is like advising one who is thirsty to dig a well near the celestial river Ganges.
One should not engage in such actions when there is the possibility of such undesirable consequences.
Nor do these [objections] find any scope even when the purpose and so forth are stated,
for that would entail the destruction of worldly convention;
indeed, no one desists from following the words of a physician or others by entertaining such doubts.
Therefore, it is established that the statement of the purpose and so forth is valid in both ways;
however, this is untenable. For instance:
If this Sūtra were to determine the purpose and so forth by virtue of being the word of a reliable authority (āpta), then, being [merely] scripture (āgama), it would lose its status as a Nyāya-sūtra.

Furthermore, by whichever means of valid cognition—such as the Vedas—the reliability of the author of the Sūtra is to be understood, by that very same means the connection of the treatise with its purpose and so forth would also be understood; thus, the explicit statement of those [elements] would become redundant.
Moreover, the claim that "activity occurs due to doubt regarding the meaning even when reliability is not certain" is far too crude.

For no one would engage in an undertaking that requires immense effort when there is doubt regarding its purpose and so forth; moreover, how could one not suspect the aforementioned succession of evils? Therefore, the resolution is this: this [section] is not merely an instruction on the purpose and other such factors, but rather aims to establish the scriptural purpose and so forth through logical reasoning (*nyāya*). As for the authoritativeness (*āptatva*) of the scripture, it serves merely as a corroborative support for that reasoning; thus, the author of the *Bhāṣya*'s exposition of it is not without purpose.
For this very reason, this sūtra does not fall outside the scope of the treatise (*śāstra*).

Since its necessity for being commenced is established by this same principle—as in the case of the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) and so forth—there is no fault such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*). What, then, is the context (*prasaṅga*) for this sūtra?
What, then, is the context for this sūtra?
It is said:
for the author of the sūtras has the treatise present in his mind by virtue of his intention to compose it.
In this regard, there arises a doubt as to whether this [work] should be commenced or not;
for indeed, both kinds of statements are encountered,
and this is such a statement.
And no distinction is observed by which there might be a determination of one side or the other. [Objection:
But whose doubt is this?
It cannot belong to the author of the Sūtra,
because he has already understood the specific distinction;
otherwise, it would be impossible for him to compose a sūtra intended to provide a definitive determination.
Nor does it arise from another,
because even now the treatise has not been perceived by others;
and since perception has not occurred, it is impossible for doubt to arise through the observation of common properties and so forth.
Not so.

If this treatise were perceived by another person, then, given the occurrence of the aforementioned causes for doubt, that very person—who possesses the recollection of specific details due to a desire for its purpose—would indeed entertain such a doubt. Thus, it is entirely appropriate for the author of the Sūtras himself to address the doubts imagined by others; therefore, the deliberation on the necessity of the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) follows.

Now, this composition on Nyāya— which is an auxiliary to the desire to know (jijñāsā) and is synonymous with investigation (vicāra), inquiry (mīmāṃsā), and reflection (manana)— must indeed be commenced for the sake of establishing that the desire to know ought to be undertaken; for it is impossible to claim that "investigation should not be performed, and the composition on Nyāya which serves as its means should not be commenced," since an investigation devoid of its instruments cannot even arise.
Otherwise, however, it is not so; rather, the inquiry itself must be investigated.
True.

Since both types of activity are observed in the inquiry whose instrument is the reasoning to be expounded by this treatise, and because no specific distinction is seen, doubt arises as to whether [the inquiry] should be undertaken or not.
But surely, since the desire to know [Brahman] is enjoined by scripture in the words "seek to know that," how can there be a lack of specific insight?
Not so;
for, without inquiry, the meaning of the scripture remains undetermined even now, and thus it remains a locus of doubt.
In that case, it follows first of all that an inquiry should not be undertaken.
Why?

Because it is devoid of the four ancillary conditions characterized by the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), the relationship (*sambandha*), and the qualified person (*adhikārin*).
Indeed, the state of being an obligation (kartavyatā) is pervaded by the possession of an object and so forth.

For plowing and the like are observed to be obligatory only when there exists an object such as the ground, a purpose such as the acquisition of grain, and an authorized agent such as a farmer. Since that pervading property is excluded from this [case], it also excludes the pervaded property of obligation; thus, the logical connection (pratibandha) is established.

For indeed, because it lacks a [relevant] object, no desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is produced for a jar situated in the midst of bright light, even though it is in contact with the sense-faculties along with the mind.
Furthermore, because it is devoid of purpose, even a doubtful thing such as a crow’s tooth is not sought after for knowledge.
Finally, due to the absence of a connection, one who desires the knowledge of words—even if that knowledge possesses a purpose and an object—does not apply himself to the study of medicine.
Furthermore, due to the absence of qualification (*adhikāra*), one who desires liberation has no inclination toward the *Vātsyāyana* [treatise].
This inquiry is not concerned with what is not the Self (*anātman*).
If it is asked how there is such a deficiency of subject matter and so forth here, it is as follows:
This inquiry does not, for its part, concern the non-self,
because that which is characterized as grass and so forth is already determined by perception and other means of knowledge;
and it is only a doubtful object that becomes the subject matter of reasoning.
As it has been said:
"Tarka (reasoning) is the deliberation for the sake of knowing the truth of an object whose reality is not yet known, by means of the application of logical reasons.
Furthermore, once an action has been accomplished, an instrument that does not contribute any further distinction [to the result] oversteps the logic of being an instrument (*sādhana*).
Nor does that which is not sought after serve any purpose; likewise, one who lacks such an interest is excluded from eligibility,
because only one who is desirous, capable, and learned is entitled to engage.
Nor is there a possibility of desire for such an object;
for that which is characterized as dharma and so forth is determined to be non-self precisely through other treatises and the like,
and the self likewise [is determined].

There is no [self] at all distinct from the aggregate of the body, sense-faculties, and so forth; and the body and such are ascertained respectively by direct perception and other means alone. If it is argued that the self, though distinct from the body and so forth, is ascertained precisely through the direct cognition "I," which is both indubitable and non-erroneous—then [we reply: [The opponent continues: Indeed, the self, distinct from the body and so forth, is ascertained by the very direct perception of "I," which is free from doubt and error. If this is said, [the response follows:]...
If that is so, then for that very reason, it is not an object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*).

Precisely because, even though knowledge of its true nature has existed from beginningless time, one does not observe the attainment of the desired or the avoidance of the undesired, it is not inquired about by anyone seeking some purpose.
This inquiry does not concern the self, the other-self, or the supreme self.
If it is argued: "But surely this agent, enjoyer, and one associated with defects appears in the notion of 'I';

however, that which is contrary to this must be understood as taught by the Śruti; therefore, there is a desire to know (jijñāsā)," then in that case, like sentences concerning an old ox and the like, or like the inference of coldness in fire, both the Śruti and the desire to know would result in being mere fallacies due to contradiction with direct experience.
For this very reason, the supreme Self is not the object of inquiry,
because it is already understood through such marks as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
If it is argued that that [supreme Self] alone is the object of inquiry, we say no.
Because that [object] is to be known through worldly experience (*laukika-pravedanīya*), it is not something to be expounded by a treatise (*śāstra*).
Indeed, an infant does not require instruction from a treatise in order to infer that sucking at the breast is the means for satisfying hunger.
Even when a treatise explains an object already known through worldly experience, that is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*); it is not its primary function.
If it is argued that there will be an inquiry concerning God (Īśvara), we say no;
for He does not exist at all.
Nor should it be said that, because words such as "God" would thus be meaningless, they would consequently fail to qualify as words.
For it is possible for those [words] to have the individual soul as their referent in some way;
for he [the soul] also exercises desire over his own body, sense organs, and so forth.
Since the meaning is already established, there is the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) in postulating a meaning that is not established.

It has been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not the object of inquiry (*jijñāsā*), because it is already established—either as being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), or as the substratum of self-luminous knowledge, or as being known through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). Furthermore, the inquiry is not concerned with God (*īśvara*);
moreover, is God known through valid cognition (*pramita*) or not?
Inquiry is not possible in either case.
For if it were not [possible], inquiry would be contradicted as being a form of reasoning (*tarka*), because there would be an absence of supporting evidence (*anugrāhya-pramāṇa*);
for it has been stated that [inquiry] "proceeds from the justification of the cause" (*kāraṇopapattitaḥ*).
The meaning is that the "attainment" (*upapatti*) or "assistance" (*anugraha*) of the instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is the means of knowledge, occurs by means of that [cognition].
Furthermore, that which has not ascended into consciousness cannot be an object of inquiry (*jijñāsita*);
however, if it has been cognized (*pramita*), it is already ascertained (*niścita*) precisely because of that.

Nor does such a position entail a contradiction through the consequence that all reasoning would be untenable; for while there may be scope for such [objections] regarding a particular case once a general cognition has occurred,
we do not observe such a state of affairs here.
Furthermore, as for the means of valid cognition regarding Īśvara, it is certainly not perception,
because that [perception] initially makes known his absence;
nor is it inference.
This is because there is no mark (liṅga) connected to that [Īśvara].
Furthermore, scripture (āgama), which is restricted to [the prescription of] what is to be accomplished (kārya), is not capable of making known an Īśvara whose nature is already established.
Nor is there any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that could be assisted by Mīmāṃsā.
Furthermore, if there is to be any scripture at all, it must be declared to be the Veda alone;
for no other source can be suspected [of such authority], and because [all others] are dependent on something else.
Since there is no cause to determine whether the Veda is of human origin or not, its very status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is difficult to establish.

If, however, intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is accepted, then even the words of the Śākyas and others— which contradict the Vedas— would necessarily possess that same status, resulting in the continued invalidity of the Vedas. Furthermore, the validity of verbal testimony itself is difficult to establish, because it is devoid of contact with the actual object and because the manner in which it conveys the meaning of a sentence cannot be defined.
How much less, then, could there be an inquiry into the specific nature of the Veda?
Since it lacks a purpose, no inquiry should be undertaken;
for the purpose of an inquiry into the Lord would have to be either worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) or liberation (*mokṣa*).
Not the first,
because that [purpose], being achievable through minor means such as religious duties (dharma) and so forth, serves as the purpose of other treatises.
Not the second either.
For even that [liberation] is understood through scriptural passages such as "We have drunk Soma," etc., to be achievable by other easy means;
nor is it contradictory for a single action to be the cause of both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*),
since a distinction is established by the presence or absence of factors such as the desire for specific fruits.
And as for this inquiry (*jijñāsā*), in being a means to liberation, does it function directly or through the medium of knowledge?
It cannot be the first,
because that would entail the fallacy of abandoning what is perceptible and postulating what is imperceptible.
Not the second [alternative],
because the scripture stating that "one spreads knowledge through action" leads to the determination that knowledge is achievable by means of another, easier method;
furthermore, if one were to accept that knowledge itself is the direct cause of liberation, that would merely be the postulation of something unobserved.
Nor is it by way of the grace of Īśvara, because the causality of knowledge as a means to grace is nowhere observed; for it is said:
"That action is pleasing to Hari which [leads to knowledge]."
From such passages as these, it is understood that grace (*prasāda*) is accomplished through minimal means such as ritual action (*karman*).
Furthermore, this bondage, which is imagined by the ignorance of the Self (*ātma-avidyā*), deserves to be terminated only by the knowledge of that [Self],
just as silver imagined by the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl is removed by the knowledge of the mother-of-pearl.
Therefore, how could the grace of the Supreme Lord have any utility in liberation, which is characterized by the cessation of bondage?
How much less could his knowledge, and how much less still the desire to know him, be of any use?
Furthermore, if this bondage were indeed ultimate reality, it could not be removed by knowledge.

Furthermore, it is not logical that bondage— which is real, beginningless, and inseparable from the very nature of the Self— should ever cease, just as the nature of the Self itself never ceases. Moreover, if one who is liberated were still in contact with a body, sense organs, objects, and so forth, his state of liberation would be contradicted,
and he would be subject to suffering and other such afflictions.
Because the collection of causes is present, the aforementioned fault applies due to the equality of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

Furthermore, in the absence of a body and so forth, since the pleasure to be accomplished by them would not exist, no one could have a desire for it; consequently, the scripture would result in being without any qualified recipients (*anadhikārika*).
For what person of sound mind would suddenly venture to abandon happiness and its means?
Thus, because it is devoid of any connection to sense objects and the like, there is no need to undertake the inquiry;
nor are its injunctions authoritative.
When it was argued that this treatise (*śāstra*) should not be commenced, the venerable Teacher composed the aphorism: "Om. Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (1.1.1).
Om. Om. Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Om.
Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman.
For the syllable *oṃ* signifies the state of being pervaded; it expresses that which is to be spoken, as well as the pervasion by its qualities.
The Lord alone is the subject matter of the scripture.
As for the claim that the inquiry should not be undertaken because of the absence of a subject matter—that is untenable;
for even though it is impossible for the non-self (anātman) or the individual self (jīvātman) to be the subject matter, it is possible for the Lord (Īśvara) to be so.
In this context, the words *oṃ* and *brahman* were employed by the author of the Sūtras to refute the claim that there is no Lord (Īśvara) distinct from the individual soul (jīva).
By this, the following meaning is indicated:
"One should meditate upon this syllable *oṃ* as the Udgītha."
In such scriptural passages as "Seek to know that; that is Brahman," the words *oṃkāra* and *brahman* are heard with respect to the object to be sought after.
And by means of these two, it is understood to be distinct from the entire phenomenal world consisting of sentient beings and insentient matter.
That appears to be incorrect;
for the first word lacks a known connection (*saṅgati*) with a supermundane object (*alaukikārtha*).

A word does not produce cognition of an entirely unperceived object—such as the eye and other sense organs do—by which we might perceive a previously unknown object through the mere employment of the word.
Even objects such as heaven, the unseen potency (*apūrva*), and the deities are not established merely by the use of words;
rather, they are obtained through the power of the various sentence-meanings present in proximity. Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "It expresses the state of being pervaded" (*otatvavācī*).
The meaning of the syllable *Oṃ* is precisely its fullness of all qualities (*guṇapūrṇatā*).
The word *hi* signifies a reason.
The syllable *oṃ*, first of all, is the designator of the state of being stretched across (*otatva*), gone to (*gatatva*), or entered into (*praviṣṭatva*).
Indeed, this is the form of the root *av*, which has the sense of going and so forth.

From the rule "avateṣyilopaśca," and following the question, "To whom does the word 'Oṃ' refer?", it is stated: "This verbal root *ava* is named *avati*; its function is motion (*gati*) and its function is entering (*praveśana*)."
Since it has been etymologically explained in this very same way elsewhere as well,

so too, whether that [word] refers to the actions or to the agent, in view of the requirement of the action— even in the absence of a secondary word (upapada) and the like— it denotes by its inherent fitness, or by the force of other scriptural passages and so forth, that the syllable *Oṃ* expresses the one who is to be known as being "endowed with qualities," that is, endowed with infinite auspicious qualities such as bliss and the rest.
In both cases, the meaning of the syllable *oṃ* is precisely the state of being filled with infinite, irreproachable, and auspicious qualities;
that same meaning also belongs to the word *brahman*.
Indeed, this form [of the word] is derived from the root *bṛh*, which signifies "to increase" or "to grow."

And likewise, as before, the connection with qualities occurs either by way of fitness (*yogyatā*) or by the force of other scriptural passages such as, "Now, why is it called Brahman? Because great (*bṛhantaḥ*) indeed are the qualities within it.
For words whose meaning is derived from their etymology necessarily depend upon the apprehension of the connection between their constituent parts.
This is what is meant:
for derivative words do not necessarily depend upon the grasping of a conventional relation (*saṅgati*) for the communication of meaning.

Rather, when the meanings of the individual components are understood through the power of etymology (*nirukta*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and the analysis of word-roots (*nigama*), and when there arises the possibility of their combination, they convey a previously unknown meaning that is established [by that very process], rather than otherwise.
This is because they consist of sentences;
as it has been said: "A *śrotriya* is one who studies the *chandas*," and "the employment of words is for the sake of the sentence-meaning.
Furthermore, a sentence does not convey its meaning by depending upon the grasping of conventional relations (*saṅgati*).
Because it would entail the consequence that the meaning has already been realized, and because it is impossible,
there is no identity of meaning between the two words "Oṃ" and "Brahman.
Thus, these two words, "Oṃ" and "Brahman," being etymological (*yaugika*), both establish the object of inquiry as one who is replete with infinite qualities.

Since that [nature] cannot belong to either the living being (*jīva*) or the insentient (*jaḍa*), one who seeks to grasp something distinct from those two finds it possible for such a thing to exist because it has not yet been known; thus, it becomes the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*).
Nor is the fullness of all qualities (*guṇapūrṇatā*) contradictory even in that case, because prior to its realization, a contradictory cognition—which requires a substratum—cannot arise.
And because it is established in this very way through dependence (*pratītya*).

Furthermore, the non-difference of the referent of the word *tat*—which is denoted by the syllable *a*—from the referent of the word *tvam*—which is denoted by the syllable *u*—is expressed by the syllable *m*; and by the word *brahman*, the fullness characterized as being of the nature of all things is denoted.
Such is the explanation;

it is unauthoritative and contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for the claim that the syllable *Oṃ*—on account of its being the source of all or its having a beginning—is by nature eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, and is omniscient and endowed with all powers, and so forth: [this is untenable].

With the intention that the explanation of the word "Brahman" is clearly not in conflict with the proof of a reality distinct from that individual soul (jīva) and so forth, no other interpretation was refuted, and it was rather accepted; [the form] "guṇotateti" is correct. *1,307* $guṇotateti-rūpaḥ sādhuḥ$ (The form "guṇotateti" is grammatically sound).
But how can it be "guṇotatām"? It ought to be "vṛddhirecī" [by Pāṇini 6.1.85].
Not so.
Because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule *omāṅośca*, it is taught that this substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs even in other instances.
Alternatively, this form is derived from the root *ūy* (to weave). But is not that root listed in the sense of "weaving together threads"?
There is no fault because verbal roots have multiple meanings.
How, then, is this [the root *ava*] a quality expressing reality?
Because it is accepted as having the form of the prefix *ava*.

The diversity [of forms] is for the purpose of indicating that it is born from two elements; or rather, there is no fault, as this [word] is preceded by the prefix *ā*. That very meaning of the word *brahman* is expressed by the term *nārāyaṇa*. (Manu 1.1.9cd)

Let it be granted that the meaning of the term *nārāyaṇa* is indeed the fullness of all qualities (*guṇapūrṇatā*), and that through the words *oṃkāra* and *brahman*, there is established the object of inquiry as distinct from both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*).
Nevertheless, one might ask: "What follows for the Lord (*īśvara*)? To this, he says: "Nārāyaṇa."
The phrase "that very [name]" carries over [from the previous context].
The intention is that there is indeed no disagreement regarding the name.
Alternatively, the two terms *oṃ* and *brahman* mentioned by the author of the Sūtras are merely illustrative examples.
In the Śruti passage beginning with "Nārāyaṇa, the great object of knowledge," the word *nārāyaṇa* is also heard as that which is to be desired to be known (*jijñāsya*). Furthermore,
the meaning denoted by the term *nārāyaṇa* is precisely that which is characterized as being full of all auspicious qualities (*guṇapūrṇatva*).
Therefore, it is stated here that even by the word "Nārāyaṇa," that which is distinct from the individual soul (jīva) and so forth is established as the object of inquiry.
This is also an illustration;
words such as "Ātman," "Ananta," and "Īśvara" are likewise to be understood [as referring to the same reality].

For even in their case, [the Self] is heard of as the object of inquiry in such passages as, "One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world," and because [the texts] declare its fullness of attributes.

Nor should it be argued that, because the postulation of a non-worldly (alaukika) meaning would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava), it is better to somehow accept these words as referring to living beings and so forth;
for since it has already been stated that the usage of etymological (yaugika) words would otherwise be inexplicable, there is no need for such a postulation.
Otherwise, even from a sentence, there would be no cognition of a non-worldly meaning.
Because it is possible to explain the conformity to meaning in some way even for worldly objects;
furthermore, in some cases a word follows its primary meaning, while in other cases it follows a non-primary meaning due to the impossibility [of the former].
Nor, however, is it the case that [the word] has only a non-primary meaning;

for even by one who accepts that Vedic words such as "Brahman" and so forth refer to the individual soul (jīva) and the like, some primary denotation endowed with unrestrained fullness must necessarily be accepted.
Therefore, what would be achieved by this [position]?
If it is argued that these [terms] have the individual soul (*jīva*) as their primary meaning, and that the non-perception of that [soul] is caused by the veil of ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no;
for the Teacher himself will provide the rebuttal here.
That very same thing is the meaning of the word *bharga*, and it is the abundance (*bhūman*) of the *vyāhṛtis*.
And from both cultivation and hearing, he [realizes]: "This is indeed the Puruṣa."
Regarding what was stated here— namely, whether or not God is known through the Veda—
the answer is that He is indeed known.
And the fault regarding that position will be refuted;
thus, the connection between the subject matter and the treatise becomes established.
As for what was further asked here—by what means of valid cognition [is this known]—[that shall now be addressed].
Regarding this, we say "by means of the Veda.
As for the question, "How is it that the Veda has the Lord as its object?"—for this reason also, the author of the Sūtras employed the syllable *oṃ* with reference to Brahman.
One might ask how this establishes the point in question; therefore, he states the intention of the author of the Sūtras: "And of the Vyāhṛtis... [and so forth].
The connection is that this is indeed the same meaning.
First of all, the syllable *oṃ* is the designator (*vācaka*) of the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign (*īśvara*).
As it is said: "Oṃ is Brahman."
This is because of such scriptural passages. Therefore, it is understood that he alone is the meaning of the *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*,

since the traditional authority (āgama) stating "the *vyāhṛtis* have the *praṇava* as their meaning" reveals that the three *vyāhṛtis* are explained as being composed of the three syllables of the *oṃkāra*.
Furthermore, it is well known that the commentary and the subject of the commentary must have the same object.
The particle *eva* (only) serves to dispel the misconception that these utterances (*vyāhṛti*) refer to the deities Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya,
since they are already well known as having those very deities as their presiding deities (*adhidevatā*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of the relationship between the explanation and the explained;
for what reason, then, do the Vyāhṛtis have that same meaning? To this, he says: "On account of abundance" (bhūmataḥ).

*Bhūmā* means fullness; from that comes *bhūḥ*. This is a form derived from the root *bhū* in the sense of "abundance" with the suffix *kvip*. It is called *bhuvaḥ* because of its bringing forth (*bhāvanāt*) or producing the world.

This is the form [of the word] derived from *bhavati* itself when the suffix *kap* is applied, with the meaning of "internalized" (*antarṇīta*) included. Because it contains the element *su*, it means "happiness" (*sukha*); thus, *svaḥ*.
For the word *sva* is well-known as a synonym for happiness.
The two *ca*s serve to aggregate other reasons,
as it has been said:
"He is the full one, the best of prosperities, the infinite bliss, who is impelled by his own utterance."

The meaning of the *vyāhṛtis* is established by these very reasons, and not by virtue of their consisting of the three worlds, because that would contradict authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [As it is said:
"Bhūḥ, indeed, is this world."

The meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) in such scriptural passages as these is that they refer exclusively to the Lord who resides within the three worlds. [Verse 1.327] What follows from this? That the meaning of the Gāyatrī is Nārāyaṇa alone.
If it is argued: "Is it not the case that the Vyāhṛtis themselves are the Veda? [the answer is: No.

First of all, it is understood that the Supreme Lord is the subject expounded by the Gāyatrī, because it is established by scripture that the three-footed Gāyatrī is an exposition of the three *vyāhṛtis*. Now, [one might object]: "In the Gāyatrī, [the words] 'That form of the divine Savitṛ, which is most excellent (*vareṇya*), may we meditate upon (*dhīmahi*); may He, whose name is Bharga, impel (*pracodayāt*) our thoughts (*dhiyaḥ*),' thus [it refers to] Savitṛ, whose name is Bharga."
Since that which is to be propounded is seen [to be something else], how can it have the Blessed One as its ultimate referent? To this, he says: "He alone is the meaning of the word *bharga*."
The phrase "due to the connection with supporting and moving" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Furthermore, this is an illustrative indication;
it should also be understood that he is called "Savitṛ" (the Impeller) because he is the cause of the generation of the world.
But it is not the sun; for if that were the case, it would be untenable for the Gāyatrī to have the Vyāhṛtis as its meaning. [As stated:
"Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the center of the solar orb, is to be meditated upon always."
The meaning is precisely this: because it would contradict such scriptural passages [as those cited].
Let it be that Nārāyaṇa is the object of the *gāyatrī*; what follows from this?
Since he is the object of the *gāyatrī*, it is established that he is also the object of the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Since that [Veda], consisting of three divisions, is explained as the *tripāda-gāyatrī*, its division is established by scripture (*āgama*) in such passages as, "The *puruṣasūkta* is its specific part. Now, one might ask: since the *puruṣasūkta* sets forth either the Puruṣa who is a sacrificial animal or Hiraṇyagarbha, how can Nārāyaṇa be the subject expounded therein? The phrase "by means of fullness and so forth" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

It is thus established that [the Self] alone is the meaning of all the Vedas;

"All speech is the direct exposition of the syllable *oṃ*.

The word *eva* (only/just) serves to exclude [the Lord] from being a mere effect or the like.

This effort on the part of the author of the Sūtras is intended to establish, by means of reasoning, that the Blessed One is the subject matter (*artha*) of all the Vedas— a fact already established by such scriptural passages as, "That state which all the Vedas proclaim."
This might be so:
[the opponent argues] that God is the meaning of the entire Veda because He is the meaning of its explanation, namely the syllable *Oṃ*;

or, whatever is the meaning of the explanation of something has that as its meaning—just as is commonly accepted; or else, the entire Veda is centered on God because it is an explanation of the *Oṃ* which is centered on Him. Why, then, is this not a direct inference?

"Just as all leaves are pierced by a single pin, so too is all speech pierced by the syllable Om"—by such scriptural passages, the justification for the meaning of the reason will be established; what is the use of this indirect explanation?

Why resort to the inference from the Veda?
Nor should it be said that a single word is not a means of valid knowledge.
This is not so, because it has already been stated that the authority of words based on their etymological derivation (*yaugika*) is established;
for what is being questioned here is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as supported by *mīmāṃsā*.
Nor is it intended that [the Lord] is merely the syllable *oṃ* and so forth;
rather, what is meant is that He is the entire Veda itself.
If it is asked, "What follows if this is so, namely, that the Lord is the meaning of the whole Veda? [the answer follows].

But how can the Śāstra—which has as its subject matter the logic that serves as a means for following the presentation of the Lord—be said to have the Lord as its ultimate purpose?
It is not so;
for Mīmāṃsā is indeed the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the Vedas in their task of making the Lord known.
Because it is an auxiliary cause, the scripture also has that [Lord] as its object, since it brings about His manifestation.
For surely, when water and other factors act as concomitant causes (*sahakārin*) to produce a sprout from a seed, the sprout is not thereby not their effect.

Not so;
for indeed, the causal factor that performs an action is of two kinds: some possess a specific excellence produced by an operation without any intervention.

Just as an axe, characterized by an excellence of conjunction and disjunction with the upward direction produced by the operations of raising and lowering, becomes the direct object (*karman*) of the agent's activity;
whereas something else, such as a tree possessing the state of being split, becomes so through its connection with the intended result and by means of the intervention of the instrument's operation.

In that case, just as the tree becomes the object (*karman*) of the agent's activity through the mediation of the instrument's activity, so too the activity of the investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) has as its intended goal the very cognition of God by way of the possibility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; thus it possesses the status of being that object.
This may be so.
If there were an investigation into the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) [of verbal cognition],

it would not be so; for even without such an investigation, one observes the comprehension of meaning from the word itself, aided by the perception of the word, the grasping of the convention, and the recollection thereof.

Nor should it be thought that a word produces doubt and error due to defects such as ignorance of its capacity (*śakti*) or intention (*tātparya*), or through misconception; for in that case as well, one might expect the word to yield knowledge of reality even without inquiry, once those defects have been removed and doubt and the like have been dispelled by an investigation into its capacity and intention. This [investigation] would thus become a mere auxiliary (*aṅga*). However, since even there the word is held to produce the knowledge of reality without inquiry—[as in the case of the sentence "this is a rope, not a snake"]—the objection does not hold.
What indeed is this "mere obstacle" that is removed by inquiry?
For the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) is not like this. Therefore, how can there be an inquiry into the Vedic *itikartavyatā*?

In what sense does it have God as its object, and in what sense does the treatise (*śāstra*) have that [God] as its object? Because it is the means for determining [the truth], Mīmāṃsā has God as its object. *1,338* $nirṇayaprayojakatvāt mīmāṃsāyāḥ īśvaraviṣayatvam$ (Because it is the cause of definitive determination, Mīmāṃsā has God as its object.)
To this it is replied: True, this is so;

nevertheless, since a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) occurs only when an obstruction has been removed, the investigation—which serves as the cause for removing that obstruction—is also, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāreṇa*), a cause of the definitive conclusion. Thus, its having the Lord as its object is established.
By this, the following objection is also refuted:
"If God is established by the authority of the Veda, then since He is ascertained from that very source, what is the use of Mīmāṃsā?
For it has already been stated that [Mīmāṃsā] serves to remove the obstacles posed by misconceptions arising from fallacious arguments and fallacious scriptural passages.
For instance, some, not even accepting the authority of the Vedas, maintain that God does not exist at all;
others, however, while accepting that authority, deny His existence by interpreting the words denoting Him as referring instead to living beings and the like.
Others, however, maintain that while Īśvara exists, he is in reality devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Some, moreover, assert that even if he possesses qualities, he is not the cause of the world, but rather remains entirely indifferent.
Some accept that even if he is the cause, he is the material cause (upādāna).

Even if [the Self] is a mere signifier (*nimitta-mātra*), others consider it to possess certain qualities and to be distinct from those qualities; still others have accepted it as both distinct and non-distinct;

and some maintain that it possesses a corporeal form—such being the case amidst these manifold disagreements, since the knowledge of reality does not arise even from the Veda, which is the instrument for such knowledge, it is necessary to remove those misconceptions by means of the Vedic *itikartavyatā* (procedural requirements).

Regarding the statement "the inquiry [into Brahman] is to be undertaken" (*jijñāsā kartavyā*), there is an investigation into the acceptance of the genitive case and the analysis of the genitive compound.

In this context, "inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), meaning "the inquiry of Brahman," and not a dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) such as "inquiry for the sake of Dharma."

Regarding the rule for compounds denoting purpose (*tādarthya-samāsa*), the author of the Vārttika states that the mention of the "original material" (*prakṛti*) must be made, because he restricts the fourth-case compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) exclusively to cases where there is a relationship between an original material and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Thus, the example is *yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post), which becomes *yūpa-dāru*. However, a counter-argument is provided stating that in cases devoid of the relationship between original material and modification—such as *aśvaghāsa* (horse fodder) and others—the forms *aśvaghāsa* and so on are actually sixth-case compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).
Furthermore, there is no relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) here.

Even regarding the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), some maintain that it is formed by the rule "the sixth [case] in the sense of remainder" (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*), while others maintain it is formed by the rule "the sixth [case] in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi*).
In that context, the word "jijñāsya" (to be desired to be known) was stated in order to include the genitive case for the object,
because it is traditionally taught that gerundives (*kṛtya*) take the genitive in the sense of the object;
otherwise, he would have said "jijñāsā asya" (the desire to know of this).

Indeed, the desire to know (jijñāsā) depends upon an object; it cannot be known without an object, though it does not depend on a specific related entity. Since the object is primary, that alone should be stated.
If it is argued that the object is obtained by implication from the mention of the general category of "related entity," we say no;
for it is pointless to accept what is obtained by implication while abandoning what is directly perceived.
If it is argued that, this being the case, the desire to know the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth would also be implied by the initial proposition (*pratijñā*), we say no;
for that [desire] is obtained even without being explicitly stated.
Indeed, there can be no desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) without the desire to know its definition and other such attributes.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a division of the scripture due to having multiple subjects.
This word, employed to dispel the doubt that it might be without a subject, is rightly understood as denoting the ritual action (*karman*) alone.
And in this way, the Sūtra would be in accordance with the meaning of scriptural passages such as "Seek to know That" (*tadvijijñāsasva*). *1,356*

If it is objected that the sixth case (genitive) ending in *karmaṇi* is prohibited from forming a compound because of the rule "the sixth case prescribed by specific rules [such as the genitive of agent] is not compounded," we say no;
for there is the rule: "The sixth case characterized by connection with a *kṛt*-suffix is compounded."
Thus, because of this counter-objection (*pratiprasava*),
the term "to be desired to be known" (*jijñāsya*) is used for the purpose of establishing the primacy of the object (*karman*).
Alternatively, the primacy of the object is indicated by the term "to be desired to be known" in order to dispel the suspicion that Brahman might lack primacy by virtue of being the object.
For in the case of an injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna-vidhi*), Brahman would be subordinate;

but when the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is enjoined with the aim of knowing That [Brahman], how could there be subordination? [This concludes] the investigation into the necessity of supplying the word "to be performed" (*kartavya*).
By the phrase "is prescribed" (vidhīyate), he indicates the ellipsis of the word "it must be done" (kartavya).
[Objection: But that it "comes to be" (bhavati) is established by its very nature.
[Reply: Not so.
For if that were so, it would follow that [the sūtra] is merely a restatement (anuvāda). On this point, some raise an objection:
"Is not the desire to know Brahman (brahmajijñāsā) already established?"

Now, since the inquiry into the meaning of the entire Veda was initiated with the words "Then, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), and because the knowledge of Brahman—being characterized by injunction (*codanā*)—is of the nature of Dharma, there can be no further doubt; thus, [this section] demonstrates the impossibility of the doubt that the subject matter has already been covered and the subsequent resolution thereof. *1,383* $Demonstration of the impossibility of the doubt regarding the subject matter being already understood and its resolution$.
In this regard, some, exhibiting an apprehension of superiority [in their own position], begin the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) as a separate undertaking.

Others, however, say: "Only that portion of the Veda which culminates in action has been introduced and investigated therein; it does not culminate in the reality of things. Therefore, this [work] is commenced in order to investigate that portion of the Veda which culminates in the reality of things."
This suspicion that the meaning has already been explained, as well as its proposed resolution, is untenable;
for since all the Vedas are centered solely on the Lord, the subject matter of all the Vedas is to be investigated precisely here.

Alternatively, with the intention that the *Mīmāṃsā* treatise on the inquiry into *dharma* was undertaken for the sake of investigating *dharma*—which is a secondary meaning of only one portion of the Veda—it may be said: "He alone is the meaning of the word *bharga*."
Thus it has been stated.

In that context, by the phrase "the meaning of all the Vedas," the suspicion that its purpose is already exhausted is dispelled; the first resolution—that it is that very [meaning] and not a subordinate part of a ritual action (*kāryaśeṣatayā*)—and the second, beginning with "all," have both been refuted. The preceding sentence serves to establish that.
"Deserving of inquiry" (*jijñāsya*) is the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*).
And he will explain this in detail with the words "and its state of being an effect," etc. (1.391).
"The man of knowledge is dearest to Me; therefore, only the knower of Him is immortal. (Manu 1.1.11cd)
For, by the force of such statements as "He who chooses Him is attained by Him," one is liberated through His grace alone, from the knowledge born of the desire to know (jijñāsā).

*The Refutation of the Charge that the Inquiry is Purposeless:* In order to dispel the suspicion that the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is purposeless, he explains the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) with the words beginning "the knower."

By the phrase "knowing Him" (taṃ vidvān), the sentence "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here," as well as the subsequent sentence "There is no other path for going," are both included by means of the word "eva" for the purpose of emphasis.
The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the sentences;
by the phrase "he chooses him," the sentence "whomsoever he [the Lord] chooses" is included.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), passages such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" are included;
the two words "hi" (indeed) indicate the reason.
The word "eva" (only/just) is connected with each [term].

For it is understood through the authority of the Śruti passages, "He who chooses him thus" and "Whomever he chooses," that one is liberated from saṃsāra solely by the grace— that is, the supreme favor— of that Brahman Nārāyaṇa, and not by means of ritual action (*karman*) or other such factors.
Although the grace of the Supreme Person is not explicitly heard in the words "him thus," nevertheless,
it is understood by the force of the scriptural statement, "Whomever he chooses.
Although the grace of the Supreme Person is not explicitly heard in the words "him thus," [it is nonetheless implied].
Nevertheless, in accordance with the scriptural statement, "Whomever He chooses," that [grace] must also be understood there;

however, it is not explicitly mentioned because the occasional cause (nimitta) serves as an indicator of the occasional effect (naimittika), for the purpose of determining the means belonging to the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu).
Indeed, "choosing" (varaṇa) is said to be divine grace (prasāda).
Scriptural passages such as "We have drunk Soma," however, must be interpreted otherwise because they possess other possible applications;
furthermore, the supreme grace of the Lord arises solely from the knowledge of Him.
Furthermore, it is understood from the statement "the knower is most dear" that he is not [dear] by means of ritual action (*karman*) and so forth;
for it has already been stated that the term "the knower" culminates in meaning through the medium of an excellence of grace.
Moreover, that statement remains meaningful even if ritual action and the like are considered merely causes of secondary favor.

Furthermore, the knowledge of the Lord is attained through the desire to know Him alone and not by any other means; this is understood from the force of the scriptural injunctions regarding hearing and so forth—such as "He is to be heard"—which, by restating the vision of the Supreme Self (in the passage "The Self, indeed, is to be seen"), prescribe those [means] as its instruments.
As for ritual actions, however, since their status as auxiliary to knowledge is established by way of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), that [scriptural] statement will remain meaningful.
Therefore, the connection is that "the inquiry into Brahman ought to be undertaken.
What is meant by this is as follows: although it is not possible for prosperity in the form of heaven and so forth to be the purpose of the inquiry.
Nevertheless, liberation will still come about,
because it cannot be accomplished by any other means;
for the Blessed One alone is the direct means to liberation.
"Bound by the noose of existence, yet the liberator from the noose of existence"—
from such statements as these;
and the means of accomplishment (sādhana) is twofold.
It is both established and unestablished.
Among these, that which is unestablished must be produced by one who desires a result,
such as sacrifice and the like.

That which is already established must be made to function; for example, an axe or similar tool. Since the Blessed One is an established means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), he must be made to function by one who desires liberation.
And the activity [of grace] is simply the state of being gracious (*prasannatā*), as is seen in the case of kings and others who release people from shackles and the like. [As it is said:
"By whose grace one is liberated from this saṃsāra, which consists of supreme suffering, and not by any other."
This is also because of such scriptural passages as these.
Furthermore, the statement that the operation [of the senses] is primary—as in the definition "perception is the contact of the sense-organ with its object"—is merely figurative.
And the liberator is the grace of the Lord, which is to be accomplished solely through devotion to Him.
"Viṣṇu is pleased by devotion alone, and not by anything else," according to such scriptural statements;
[therefore] the mere grace that is the cause for attaining heaven and other goals is to be accomplished through ritual action (*karman*) and the like.
"However, by [the Lord's] will, the lowest is said to be attained," according to such Smṛti texts.
Whether "grace" (prasāda) is a particular kind of desire or a distinct quality (guṇāntara), there is no contradiction for us in either case.

Devotion to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvarabhakti*) is a continuous flow of uninterrupted love that—preceded by the knowledge of His being possessed of infinite, limitless, and faultless auspicious qualities—is superior in manifold ways to one's own self, one's possessions, and all other objects; and which remains unobstructed even by thousands of impediments. With reference to this, it is said: "Where one sees nothing else" and "That is night for the sage who sees."
Such are the Śruti and Smṛti texts.
Furthermore, this [liberation] does not arise without the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of that [Truth],
for such is observed in the world.
Furthermore, the Blessed One, whose nature is unmanifest, cannot be directly perceived even with a thousand efforts without his grace.

However, it is logical that when he is pleased, he reveals himself through the possession of infinite and inconceivable power. And his grace, which is the means for such perception, consists in [the worship] of a specific form of the Blessed One who is endowed with qualities appropriate to himself and is free from defects, performed with reverence and continuity.

It is not attained except through reflection— also known as *nididhyāsana*— which has been accumulated over a long period and is accompanied by detachment from sense objects and devotion to that [Truth].

Furthermore, *nididhyāsana* is not possible even when *śravaṇa*, characterized by the grasping of the meaning of the scriptural statement, has been performed, if it is devoid of inquiry— also known as *manana*—
because doubt and misconception would otherwise persist in their original state.
For when those two [hearing and reflection] exist, devotion (*ādara*) and continuity (*nairantarya*) and so forth are not possible.

Therefore, because it is a means to liberation by way of the grace of the Supreme Lord through inquiry (*jijñāsā*), and by way of the grace of supreme devotion to the vision of Him, meditation (*nididhyāsana*) must be performed.

As for those who believe that meditation itself, having attained supreme proficiency, takes the form of direct perception (*aparokṣa*), for them the scriptural texts concerning "vision" would result in being merely figurative in meaning.
This might be so:
the word *ataḥ* (therefore) indeed functions to indicate the causal status of that which is under discussion.

In that context, when there is an expectancy for a purpose regarding the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), liberation (*mokṣa*), which was introduced by the word *atha* as a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), becomes connected [as the purpose].
The desire to know is *jijñāsā*.
Nor is the word *jijñāsā* meaningful here in its etymological sense,
because a desire cannot be enjoined, as it is not an object that can be made independent [of the agent].
For this very reason, it is also incorrect to suggest that the term *jijñāsā* indicates the knowledge sought after.

Therefore, the term *jijñāsā* indicates by secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*) an inquiry (*vicāra*) in which the desire for knowledge is internally contained. And the purpose for resorting to this figurative meaning, rather than following its primary usage, is as follows:
This is because it makes known that reflection (*vicāra*) is a means to liberation only through the gateway of knowledge;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of syntactic connection due to the absence of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*).
Furthermore, if the word *jijñāsā* is understood—just like the word *mīmāṃsā*—to denote "reflection" itself, [then the objection does not apply].
Even then, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the means-nature of inquiry for the sake of knowledge will be known.
And thus, since inquiry is the means to knowledge and knowledge is the means to liberation (*mokṣa*), it follows that this [inquiry] must be performed.
Furthermore, because there was a suspicion that liberation and so forth might be obtainable by other means, the [statement] is also restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇatā*).

Furthermore, we do not see anything here that indicates the grace of Īśvara. Nor is it unreasonable for knowledge to be the means to liberation; [this addresses the] doubt regarding the independence from grace between knowledge and liberation.
By this [verse], the grace of God is supplied as the intermediate factor.

For when, due to ignorance of the true nature of the Self, there occurs the superimposition of "Self" upon the body and other non-Self entities, attachment and aversion arise toward what is favorable and unfavorable to that [self].
Impelled by these two, one accumulates activity characterized by merit and demerit.
Consequently, his birth occurs as the conjunction of a new body, sense organs, and so forth, within various wombs such as those of gods, humans, and animals.
From that, there is the experience of suffering; thus, this beginningless flow of cause and effect is called *saṃsāra*.
Through the knowledge of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva*), ignorance and its opposite [misconception] are brought to cessation.
This is because the knowledge of reality has the inherent nature of removing ignorance and false cognition that share the same locus and object;
for it is observed that the knowledge of the true nature of mother-of-pearl removes the ignorance regarding it and the superimposition of silver.
And when false cognition is removed, passion and hatred do not arise.
Because of the absence of causes;
and in the absence of those two, there is neither the arising of active existence (*pravṛtti*) nor the exhaustion through experience of that which was previously accumulated.
And in the absence of active existence, there is no further birth, precisely because of the absence of its cause.
Furthermore, when the causes of the present body and so forth are exhausted, they cease;

and in the absence of rebirth, there is no arising of seedless suffering. Thus, liberation is the absolute cessation of suffering. And since liberation is attainable through the very nature of knowledge, what need is there for the grace of God?

For those who employ a lamp to eliminate the suffering caused by dependence on darkness do not depend upon the favor of some lord; for it is the very nature of a lamp that it dispels the darkness co-spatial with itself. And so says the Nyāya Sūtra: [NS 3.2.40] "The production of light is the cause of the destruction of darkness."
“Upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the removal of each subsequent one, resulting in liberation.
(NS 1.1.2) “Substance, action, time, inherent nature, and the living soul—by whose favor these exist, and by whose indifference they do not exist. (Manu Smṛti 1.14)
"Nothing whatsoever is done without you," and so forth;
for otherwise, even by virtue of having knowledge as one's nature, liberation might occur for someone somewhere without Hari. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.14)
Regarding the statement that liberation (*mokṣa*) is dependent on Hari:

the assertion that liberation is dependent on the Lord (*īśvara*) refers to the Lord’s status as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) in the arising of knowledge and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction. And for that purpose, practices such as his meditation (*upāsti*) are useful.

Thus, since the cessation of ignorance and so forth occurs through the very nature of knowledge—such that in the absence of a cause, the effect does not arise—and because this does not depend upon the grace of Īśvara, this explanation of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is incorrect; therefore, he says: "Substance.
By the word "substance," the principles such as *prakṛti* and the rest are meant.
"Action" refers to merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest consists of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth.
"The living being" (*jīva*) refers to that which possesses self-conceit (*abhimānin*). The word "thus" (*eva*) is to be understood as following the phrase "by whose grace."
By this, it is stated that even the existence of all causes and substrata of produced things is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
According to the Śruti, "Nothing whatsoever is done without you," all purposeful activity is dependent upon Him.
The phrase "is understood from such scriptural passages as this" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
By the word "also" (*api*) in the expression "even by the very nature of knowledge," he indicates that this is a statement of formal acceptance (*aṅgīkāravāda*).
The word "for" (*hi*) expresses a reason.
Since this is so, the previous explanation is established.
[This concludes] the demonstration that bondage is dependent upon Īśvara;
and from this, the following meaning follows.
This might be so,
provided that this bondage of the individual soul were caused solely by ignorance;
but it is not so.
This is because it is understood from the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas that [the world] has the will of the Supreme Lord as its cause.

Furthermore, just as for Advaitins the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is dependent on ignorance (avidyā), and for the Logicians (Tārkikas) and others a substance is dependent on its qualities, it is likewise logical that even that which is beginningless is dependent on the Lord.
For this will be established later by the argument beginning with, "This individual soul has knowledge, bliss, and so forth as its essential nature, just like masculinity and other such attributes."
And the non-apprehension of that state is established by experience;
therefore, it is understood that there exists some obscuring factor,
by which [the self], though consisting of self-luminous consciousness, being veiled, does not know its own true nature.
Nor can desire, action, and so forth themselves be such [a cause],
because even they depend upon further causes. Nor is it logical that each subsequent [effect] arises from each preceding [cause].

Because during deep sleep and dissolution there is an absence of its [the mind's] functioning, it follows that the manifestation of one's own nature occurs by the power of stainless consciousness (*caitanya*).
Therefore, one must accept some primordial substance, distinct from desire, karma, and so forth, which is denoted by such terms as *māyā*, *avidyā*, and *prakṛti*.
[As it is said: "He is asleep due to beginningless *māyā*."
There are also such scriptural and traditional texts as these.
Nor is it logical to ask how even *māyā* can veil that which is self-luminous, for it is precisely as an obscuring agent (*āvaraka*) that *māyā* is known.
The proof for this will be stated hereafter;

moreover, it is not logical for that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) to possess any causal efficacy (*kiñcitkaratva*) by itself, and [such a view] would contradict statements such as "substance and action" (*dravyaṃ karma ca*). *1,424*
**The Justification for the Requirement of the Lord’s Grace:** Therefore,

it is logical that the Supreme Lord alone— by means of His own inconceivable and wondrous power, which is His dependent *prakṛti* consisting of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, and which acts as ignorance (*avidyā*) by being opposed to knowledge (*vidyā*)— veils the self-luminous consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva*), even though that consciousness is its very nature.

And that very [Lord], having joined [the soul] with portions of primordial nature (prakṛti) such as the Great Principle (mahat), ego (ahaṅkāra), and so forth— attained through His own self-mastery (svādhiṣṭhāna)— and having displayed to it agency, enjoyership, autonomy, and ownership of the fruits of actions, which do not actually exist, causes it to experience suffering by way of generating passion and other afflictions.
Thus, since bondage is dependent upon the Lord, He alone must be accepted as the liberator, because no other possesses independence.
It has been stated that when He is indeed pleased, He withdraws His own *māyā*; therefore, this entire collection of means is for the sake of attaining His grace.

Consequently, although the grace of the Blessed Lord is not explicitly obtained from the literal words of the Sūtras, it is a sound interpretation to accept it on the grounds of logical necessity (*anupapatti*).

And the author of the Sūtras will state this: "For from that [knowledge] come the reversal of his bondage. By the reasoning thus stated, it is not the inherent nature of knowledge alone to be the direct means to liberation.
Or, even if that were so, the grace of the Lord (Īśvara) is required.
Because the existence and activity of all causal factors (kārakas) are dependent upon Him, no effect whatsoever can arise without His will.
Furthermore, the purpose of this doctrine of acceptance (aṅgīkāravāda) is the support of the very same point previously stated. To explain:
Even by one who accepts that knowledge is the cause of liberation, it is not possible to discard the will of God,
because [the existence of such a will] must necessarily be admitted on account of [God's] being the impeller of causal agents and so forth.
And if that is so, what is the use of this unestablished knowledge?
Thus, the Lord alone must be accepted as the authoritative source.
"Viṣṇu is the giver of knowledge to the ignorant, and he is the giver of liberation to the wise;
Janārdana alone is the giver of bliss to those who are liberated. (Manusmṛti 1.1.15)

**Restatement of the View of the Vivaraṇa:** As it has been stated, liberation is not something to be produced; rather, once the preceding factors such as false knowledge have ceased, there is merely the non-arising of subsequent flows due to the absence of causes.
In that regard, what need indeed is there for the Supreme Lord?
But [the opponent argues] that those words of His are intended merely as causes for the arising of knowledge and so forth;
this is untenable, because the scriptures state that the purpose of the Lord extends beyond the bestowing of knowledge and the like. To this, he says: "Of the ignorant."
[The Lord] is the giver of liberation from the previously mentioned bondage of *prakṛti*.
Now, if it is asked how there can be a cessation of the beginningless bondage of *prakṛti*,
someone here says:
Neither having a beginning nor being beginningless is the cause for destruction or non-destruction;
rather, it is simply the encounter or non-encounter with a counteragent.

Furthermore, in the world, even that which is beginningless—namely, antecedent negation—is seen to cease; likewise, the cessation of the continuum of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) is asserted by the Sugatas through the excellence of their cultivation of the realization of reality.
For the Naiyāyikas as well, the beginningless stream of false cognition and the blackness of the atoms cease;
for the Sāṅkhyas too, non-discrimination ceases through discrimination;
and for the Mīmāṃsakas, the beginningless prior non-existence of the knowledge of the true nature of dharma at the present time ceases.
If it is argued that there can be no cessation of that which has the nature of an entity from beginningless time, we say no;
for ignorance is indeterminable (anirvacanīya).
"That which is beginningless ceases"—this is the general rule of pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti).
The specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*) is that "the cessation of ignorance occurs through knowledge";
therefore, that alone is more powerful.
*1,430* Refutation of the Vivaraṇa School's View.
[Objection: Is it not the case that destruction is the subsequent state occurring within its own material cause (*upādāna*)?

Therefore, how can there be destruction of that which is beginningless and lacks a material cause? [Response: No, because [destruction] consists merely in the subsequent state occurring within its own substratum (*āśraya*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the blackness of atoms and so forth could never cease.
If it is argued that ignorance does not cease because it differs from non-existence, just as the self [is eternal], we say no;
for why should it not cease, given that it differs from existence, just like antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)?
What, then, is the conclusion?
It has been stated that the connection with the distinction is produced by knowledge and ignorance;
however, that is incorrect.
For instance,
regarding the argument that "it is either with a beginning or without a beginning," and so forth:

in that case, is it being claimed by this [reason] that the absence of a subverting factor (*nivartaka*) is the *upādhi*, or rather that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatā*) due to the presence of a subverting factor?
Not the first,
because it pervades the probans;
not the second.
Because it is unestablished.
For one who asserts that cessation is impossible due to ignorance being beginningless does not accept a remover of that ignorance;
rather, by virtue of its beginninglessness, he infers its very non-existence.

As for the objection raised regarding the deviation [of the reason] in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), that too is incorrect because the reason has been qualified by the property of being an entity (*bhāvatva*).
Furthermore, the argument beginning with "of the Sugatas" and so forth is utterly irrelevant;
for the Nihilists (*vaināśika*) do not admit that mental impressions (*vāsanā*) are beginningless.
Nor is there a continuum distinct from those [moments],
by means of which a deviation [of the reason] could be raised;
nor do the Naiyāyikas accept such a thing.
Nor do they accept a stream that is distinct from those [atoms].
Even the blackness of an atom is indeed with beginning;
for it is not their established doctrine that the first occurrence of the baking of an atom has no beginning. *1,437*
As for that which was stated regarding the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of ignorance:
if that indeterminability consists in being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, what is the use of this when it is irrelevant to the subject at hand?
If it is argued that this is merely a counter-argument, we say no.
If it is argued that because [the reason] is unestablished for the opponent and lacks pervasion (avyāpti),
and since "indefinability" consists in being distinct from both existence and non-existence,
the qualification is therefore unestablished— this is not so.
Because this contradicts your own statement.

For you yourself have defined ignorance as that which is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*) yet is dissolved by knowledge, and then you have presented proofs to establish its existence as a positive entity.
If it is argued that what was intended there was merely its distinction from non-existence (*abhāva*), we say no.
For it is logical that this very [non-existence] serves as a qualification of the cause.
But has it not been stated here:
"Since it is distinct from existence, why should its cessation not be like that of prior non-existence?"
That which was said is not well-said,

because even prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is admitted to be existent. Alternatively, if what is intended by "being dissimilar to existence" is "being dissimilar to a positive entity" (bhāva), [then the objection remains].

There is the consequence of non-establishment due to the contradiction with the acceptance of its distinction from the absence of that [nature], as well as deviation in the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Furthermore, if one seeks to prove the cessation of that [absolute non-existence] as well, there is deviation precisely upon its cessation.
Moreover, since the state of being an entity (*bhāvatva*) does not exist in the self (*ātman*), the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) is difficult to avoid therein.

If it is argued that "nevertheless, the state of being an entity (bhāvatva) is superimposed upon that [non-existence]," then this is equally applicable to ignorance (avidyā) as well; thus, [the reason] remains unestablished (asiddhi).
Furthermore, the utility of stating that there is a relationship of generality and particularity between the two pervasions (vyāpti) must be explained.
If it is argued that the determination of relative strength [between two reasons] depends on this,
does it depend merely on the relationship of general and particular, or upon the presence of such factors as non-deviation?
In the first case, it would follow that the particular pervasion— "the mountain is without fire"— would be stronger than the general pervasion— "that which possesses smoke possesses fire."

Regarding the second [point], why should one explain only the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth by means of the relationship between the general and the particular? Or rather, what is the point of this [distinction] between strength and weakness?
If it is argued that the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is sublated by the specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*), [we reply:]...

Is the restriction [of the rule] that "that which is beginningless does not cease except through knowledge" meant to be (1) a limitation [on its scope], (2) a demonstration of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), or (3) the pointing out of a limiting condition (*upādhi*)?
Not the first;
for it must be restricted as follows: "That which is beginningless does not cease except through knowledge."
Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule that only that which is devoid of beginninglessness can be removed by knowledge; for there is no evidence to limit it to such a case.
As for the relationship of general and particular, it has already been stated.
Thus, the second alternative is not tenable.
If it is argued that because no instance of deviation has been shown,
and since it is established by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*) that ignorance is removable by knowledge, there is a deviation regarding beginninglessness (*anāditva*) in that very case—
then let this alone be stated.
What is the point of the distinction between the general and the particular?

Since it is established that ignorance cannot be terminated because it is beginningless, why could it not be the case that the property of being ignorance (*ajñānatva*) is itself fallacious with respect to that very [beginninglessness]?
If you say, "Let it be so; rather, let it be the counter-argument itself," [we reply:]...
Is it by mere pervasion, or by a pervasion endowed with the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)?
Not the first,
because mere pervasion is not probative.
Otherwise, the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) would be redundant.
In the second case, ignorance, which is the cause of saṃsāra, must be capable of being removed by knowledge,
because it is ignorance.
It would have been said, "like the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
In this case as well, is it by way of a general or particular state?
Furthermore, what is this so-called "cognition of mother-of-pearl"? Is it an absence of cognition, or is it an ignorance that has a positive (bhāva) form?
In the first case, there is a deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For the relationship between an example and the subject of the thesis (*dārṣṭāntika*) does not exist merely through a similarity of words;
otherwise, it would follow that by virtue of their being "cows" (*go*), speech and other such things would also be proven to possess horns.
In the second case, is that [cause] beginningless or not? If it is the first, how could this distinction exist?
If it is the second, then that too is equivalent to the position [being refuted].
Not the third [alternative], because the state of being other than ignorance has an equal pervasion (*samavyāpti*) and because it is a case of "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*).
The author of the commentary himself provides the resolution: *1,445*.
By this, the claim that there is a connection with a distinction produced by knowledge or ignorance is refuted.

Furthermore, as for the argument raised regarding the impossibility of destruction in the absence of a material cause— that destruction is simply a subsequent state occurring within its own substrate—
that too is untenable.

If the subsequent state of the substratum were to be without material cause (*anupādānabhūta*), then the destruction of the dependent would occur; in that case, when a jar is removed from the ground, there would be the destruction of the jar.
As for the counter-argument regarding the blackness of atoms, that too is refuted by the fact that it likewise possesses a material cause.
To this, it is replied:
As for the claim that ignorance is not ceased because it is beginningless, this is either a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) or an independent inference (*svatantrānumāna*).
It is not the first,
because since the beginninglessness of ignorance is established by scripture and reasoning, the reductio would result in a contrary conclusion.
Not the second [alternative],
because it contradicts such scriptural and traditional texts as, "the cessation of all illusion," "they cross over this māyā," and "they cross over ignorance."
Furthermore, even if cessation were possible for that which is beginningless, it would be untenable due to the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).

If it is argued that the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the self’s own cessation serves as such subverting evidence, we say no; for there is no necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*) [between the two].
Because a distinction is established through the presence or absence of a remover;
because it is improper not to accept a proven remover;
and because the inference of the absence of a remover based on beginninglessness is sublated.
By this, the objection that the absence of a remover constitutes a limiting condition (*upādhi*) and that its opposite constitutes a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) has been resolved.

Now, if it is asked: "But surely the destruction of a substance is observed to result from the destruction of its parts and their conjunction; how then can there be destruction here?"—from where does this dual assumption arise?
