If it is argued that destruction is observed even through the removal of each individual [cause],
then let it be so for that which has a beginning;
however, for that which is beginningless, the third mode must also be followed.
Since destruction itself is established as a fact,
if it is asked what kind of destruction there can be for that which is beginningless, the answer is:
it is simply the cessation of its own nature.
The statement that "the subsequent state residing within its own material cause results in the reduction of that cause to mere materiality," and so forth, refers to the object that is the effect.
Now, if ignorance were to cease,
then upon the liberation of one, there would be the liberation of all.
It would not [be so], because it is accepted that ignorance (avidyā) differs for each individual soul (jīva).
In this regard, there is a distinction: "But [ignorance] is one, veiling its own qualities."
This should be investigated according to the scriptures (*āgama*). [Section 1.453]:
"The Establishment of the Cessation of Bondage According to the Siddhānta.
It might be argued as follows:
Even for those who know Brahman, ignorance persists;
and it is by means of that [ignorance] that the authority of the Śruti and Smṛti is maintained.
If it is argued that the direct realization of Brahman—not mere discrimination—is what removes ignorance, we say no.

[Objection: Since even those who possess [such knowledge] are seen to continue in saṃsāra, it would follow that the teachings on Brahman given by humans—such as those of Vātaputrīya—would be [taught] immediately upon the falling away of the body and so forth for those who have directly realized Brahman.
[Reply: Not so.
Do you not remember what was said regarding this matter?
It was stated that the Supreme Lord alone, when pleased, effects the destruction of bondage;
and direct realization is not the means for attaining His grace.
On what basis, then, could he be questioned as to why [faith] does not exist for them?
For it has been stated that the supreme state of devotion is its cause, and its perfection is to be understood through its effects;
this is because the mental states of others are not directly perceptible.
The claim that the grace of the Blessed One is obstructed by *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma) is weak;
for it is impossible for insentient karmas to act as an independent obstruction to the grace of the Blessed One.
If it is argued that even those [karmas] are favored by a specific aspect of His will, [we reply:]...
Because this would entail the consequence of a contradiction between the two wills of the Blessed One.
If it is argued that the grace of the liberator is of such a nature [to obstruct],
then it follows that he himself is incomplete.
Otherwise, how could he speak of the destruction even of *prārabdha* karma?
As for the doctrines concerning the obstruction by *prārabdha* and so forth, they are merely figurative in meaning.
In reality, the Blessed Lord alone is the remover of bondage, even that which is beginningless; thus it has been rightly said: "And He is the bestower of liberation upon the knowers."
But surely bliss is the very nature [of the Self];
and since it is veiled by ignorance, it is established by itself upon the cessation of ignorance.
Experience is exactly the same.
The state of being a subject (*viṣayitva*) is also the very nature of experience (*anubhava-svabhāva*), not an adventitious property (*āgantuka-dharma*).
Therefore, since it bestows liberation, how could it be distinct from the bestowal of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth?
It is said in reply:
The power of the Supreme Lord alone is the primary veil over the true nature of the individual soul (jīva);
ignorance (avidyā), however, is merely the instrumental cause.
Therefore, even when ignorance has ceased, there is no manifestation of complete bliss as long as the Lord himself does not withdraw His own power of bondage from that soul.
For this very reason, the decrease and increase of bliss will be explained [later].
Thus, because it has been stated that bondage is false, liberation does not depend upon it at all.
§ Description of the Falsity of Bondage.
Having thus explained the Sūtra according to his own view, he refutes the commentary of others for the sake of its purification, beginning with the words "the falsity of bondage," and so forth.

For the proponent of Māyā has described in his own commentary and elsewhere that bondage— characterized by agency, enjoyership, contact with defects, action, factors of action, and results— is false because it is superimposed upon the Self.
That is untenable,
because the falsity of bondage was not indicated in the Sūtras.

Furthermore, if one were to describe a meaning not contained in the aphorism (*sūtra*), it would follow that it is not a commentary (*bhāṣya*) because it lacks the defining characteristics of a *bhāṣya*. For those who know the definition of a *bhāṣya* declare: "That in which the meaning of the aphorism is described by means of sentences that imitate the aphorism, and its own words are also explained, is known as a *bhāṣya*."
Here it is said: for the meaning of a sūtra is twofold— the literal (śrauta) and the intended (ārtha).

In this regard, concerning the aphorism *athāto brahmajijñāsā*, since it must avoid being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) and must ensure the engagement of the person in the scripture, the word "should be performed" (*kartavyā*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. Furthermore, once it is established that the term *jijñāsā* (desire to know) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the inquiry (*vicāra*) which is inherently implied and fit for execution, the literal meaning of the aphoristic sentence becomes: "An inquiry into Brahman should be performed by one who is endowed with the fourfold means. This is the explicit (*śrauta*) sense of the aphorism.

By implication, it is established that the knowledge of Brahman is the means to liberation, which serves as a qualification for the seeker; and by proximity, it is established that the inquiry into the Vedānta texts is the means. Thus, both through direct statement and implication, the purport of the aphorism is that one who is endowed with the fourfold means must undertake the inquiry into the Vedānta texts for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means to liberation.
The subject matter to be established has been understood.

Thus, since the falsity of bondage (*bandhamithyātva*) establishes the purpose (*prayojana*) and other elements—which are effectively indicated by implication as being necessary for the engagement of a discerning person with the treatise—it too is indeed the meaning of the aphorism (*sūtrārtha*).
[I.4.70] "The falsity of bondage establishes the purpose and the subject matter."
For the knowledge of Brahman has been aphoristically stated as that which destroys the cause of evil;
and this evil consists primarily in the state of being a knower, as well as agency and enjoyership.
If these were produced by the nature of reality itself, they could not be destroyed by knowledge.
Since knowledge is the very remover of ignorance,
if agency and enjoyership were caused by ignorance, then it would be logical that the knowledge of Brahman is said to be the destroyer of the cause of evil.

Thus, by the author of the Sūtras himself, in composing the sūtra stating that the knowledge of Brahman destroys the cause of evil, it is demonstrated that agency and enjoyership have ignorance as their cause.
Furthermore, Brahman is set forth as the subject of inquiry;
and Brahman is the Self (ātman).
If its perceived form—as "I am the agent" and "I am the enjoyer"—were ultimately real, then, being free from doubt, it could not be the subject of inquiry.
If, therefore, the nature of being an agent and so forth is superimposed by ignorance,
while the ultimate, actionless, partless form of Brahman remains, then it is logical that this [Brahman] is described as an object because of its being concealed;
thus, by the author of the Sūtras himself, in defining the nature of the Self as the subject of inquiry, the falsity of agency and other such non-essential forms is established by the Sūtra itself.
Furthermore, that which is necessary for the falsity of bondage— such as agency and so forth— to be established has also been set forth in the aphorism.
Nor does this entail the fault of having multiple meanings,
because the distinction between what is directly stated (*śrauta*) and what is implied (*arthika*) has already been explained, and because it is an aphorism.
Indeed, this multiplicity of meanings is itself an ornament of the sūtra;
as they say:
"It should consist of few syllables, be free from ambiguity, be substantial, and be comprehensive."
"Those who know the sūtras understand the sūtra to be unimpeded and faultless.
By the term "facing in all directions," he expresses its manifold meanings; as it is said elsewhere as well:
"The wise call them *sūtras* because they are concise, indicative of their meaning, composed of few syllables and words, and contain the essence of everything.
They are "indicative of their meaning" (*sūcitārthāni*) because whatever meaning has been indicated therein constitutes the entirety of their sense.

Therefore, whatever meaning is understood—whether by the power of the words or by the force of the sense—all of that belongs to that [subject] alone; thus, this entire collection of meanings is attained through its majesty.

Consequently, regarding the four requisites required by an injunction—the qualified person (*adhikārin*), the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the connection (*anubandha*)—the commentary beginning with "of the spheres of the notions of 'you' and 'I'" (*yuṣmadasmad-pratyaya-gocarayoḥ*) is indeed consistent with the meaning of the Sūtra, as it establishes the falsity of bondage (*bandha-mithyātva*) which supports the purpose and the subject matter implied by the Sūtra.
It might be argued:
"How could one not be unskilled if, bypassing the literal meaning first encountered, one establishes only the ultimate meaning encountered last?
To this, it is replied:
This might be so,
provided that the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "yuṣmadasmad" were merely an explanatory elaboration of the very meaning implied by the first sūtra;
but it is not so.
What indeed is the purpose of this commentary, even beyond its introductory exposition of the meaning of the entire Tantra?
It is as follows:

the Vedāntas culminate in establishing that the ultimate nature of the Self—which is erroneously regarded as a transmigrating being—is its own essence, which consists of bliss alone, is eternally existent, immutable, and of the single flavor of pure consciousness. This is the definitive purport (*aidaṃparya*) of this treatise.
Furthermore, this [notion] contradicts the appearance that arises as if uncontradicted by what is considered direct perception—namely, "I am the agent," "I am happy," or "I am miserable.

Therefore, until it is established that the nature of the self as something contrary to the essence of Brahman is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), so as to avoid contradicting that [perception], the teaching appears as useless as a statement such as "the old bull" (*jaradgava*). Consequently, for the sake of removing that [misconception] and to prompt the activity of a discerning person, it must first be demonstrated that the self's non-Brahman-nature is a manifestation of ignorance.
"Therefore, this is what is stated by this commentary.
This threefold connection of the initial commentary is also inconsistent;
for it is as follows:

As for what was stated— that the falsity of bondage is implied by the purpose indicated in the aphorism— that is incorrect. For indeed, when something, though established by valid cognition, is logically untenable and requires something else for its own justification, it implies that specific thing and nothing else.
Just as the absence of the living Devadatta from his house implies his presence outside, but does not imply the impermanence of sound;
for what reason?
Because his absence from the house is only logically possible in dependence upon his presence outside.
And thus, if liberation, which has been stated as the purpose [of the inquiry], were to depend upon the falsity of bondage, then it would imply that [bondage is false];
but this is not the case, as he says: "the falsity of bondage."
By the word "eva" (only/just), he indicates that [the state of being pleased] is established in no other way.
How so?
This has been stated: "[He is] pleased because of knowledge."
The Supreme Lord alone brings about the cessation of bondage;
and it will be explained that even for one who possesses truth, cessation occurs through the grace of the Master.
Now, it may be objected that both types of cessation of bondage are observed to occur through direct perception.
Just as there is the release from a real bondage such as shackles through the favor of a king produced by [the king's] perception,
and just as there is the direct release from a false bondage such as being bound by shackles in a dream through awakening alone;
in that regard, a doubt arises as to which position should be adopted concerning the cessation of the bondage of saṃsāra through the knowledge of Brahman, which has been stated in the aphorism.
And thus, there might be an alternative explanation, rather than an explanation that is otherwise impossible.
This is not so;

for since a definitive conclusion is reached through the statement of a specific [reason], the phrase "of those who are ignorant" (ajñānām), which was stated here [in the previous verse] for the purpose of establishing this meaning, must be supplied here as well.
The general statement, "He who knows the Self overcomes sorrow," is set aside by the specific statement.
If it is argued that the Śruti, "Upon seeing Him alone, one is liberated," does not tolerate anything between the act of seeing and liberation, we say no;
for it is logical that the restrictive particle (*eva*) has the purpose of excluding what is impossible (*ayogavyavaccheda*).

Furthermore, this is because it is logical that [liberation] is intended to exclude other [causes], such as the grace of the Lord arising solely from spiritual vision (*darśana*), and not from causes such as ritual action (*karman*).
*1,485* Let it be granted that liberation is possible even without the falsity of bondage;
or rather, let there be the cessation of bondage through knowledge.
Nevertheless, the falsity of bondage does not depend on liberation in this way.
How so?
For the cessation of bondage does not arise from knowledge through the observation of its causal efficacy.
By what means could one rely on the falsity of bondage?
Rather, it is scripture alone that declares the cessation of bondage through knowledge.

Once the relationship between the means and the goal has been established by valid cognition, what inconsistency could possibly exist such that one would have to seek a further justification for its pacification?

Now, it may be objected: although the status of the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya as causes of an *apūrva* is indeed heard in scripture, intermediate *antarāpūrvas* produced by the sacrifices occurring in sequence are postulated for the sake of establishing their capacity to bring about the primary *apūrva* that arises at a later time;
or else, an *apūrva* is postulated so that the sacrifice itself, as heard in scripture, may be established as a means to attaining heaven.
Likewise, [it might be argued that] the postulation of the falsity of bondage is solely for the sake of establishing what is heard in scripture.
This is not so, because of the disparity; for in that case, the postulation of something unprecedented (apūrva) is indeed appropriate.
Because of the rule that whatever comes into being at a later time is the effect of its cause,
and such is not the case here.
If it is argued that even here there is a rule— that knowledge is the very remover of ignorance— that is not so.
Even if that which is real were to cease through knowledge, its non-determination would follow from the absence of any sublation;
furthermore, we shall explain that mere observation and non-observation do not determine pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Thus, the very possibility of the contradictory doubt—that something might be a cause even while lacking existence in the immediately preceding moment—does not even arise.
If it is argued that an objection must be raised to prevent its cessation—
namely, that if even the existent were to cease, the Self would also cease— we say no, because there is no necessary pervasion (vyāpti).
Furthermore, because there is no subverting argument against the opposite position:
why should the self not also cease when beginningless ignorance ceases?
Even though it is false, ignorance, though beginningless, does indeed cease.
If you say that the self is not real,
where have you found this principle that what is real never ceases?
Since you disregard beginninglessness as the cause for non-cessation and instead employ falsity as the cause, why do you not accept that ignorance can cease by any means whatsoever?
What is the use of a restriction regarding knowledge?

If it is argued that knowledge alone is the opponent of ignorance, then—alas!—since the mere presence of the opponent is the cause for cessation, how can there be the cessation of the self (*ātman*)? (1.495)
**The Refutation of the Objections Stated in the Vivaraṇa:** Now, when reality is sublated by knowledge, does that which is sublated reside in the object (*viṣaya*) or in the locus (*āśraya*)?
Now, regarding that which pertains to both [the whole and its parts]:
it is not the first case;

because, in the case of a variegated composite, the cognition of a substance qualified by blue does not exclude its own object, nor taste and so forth inherent in its own object, nor even a contradictory quality such as yellowness.
Not the second,
because the knowledge of a jar and so forth does not eliminate the dharmas residing in the self.
Not the third.
[Objection: Because the relationship between the body and the self is not terminated by the cognition of the body as being the self—[we reply:
Not so, for this has already been answered.

If knowledge were to eliminate that which resides in its substratum, then it would also eliminate dharma and so forth; however, this is impossible because there is no pervasion (vyāpti) here, and because there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary case.
Furthermore, the cognition of a jar and the like is not in contradiction with dharma and so forth.
Furthermore, because the knowledge of the true nature of the self (*ātma-yāthātmya-jñāna*) is the very opposite of bondage, there is a disparity [between it and other cognitions].
It is precisely the knowledge of the true nature of the self that is intended as the object of negation;
however, the cognition of a substance qualified by blue in a variegated whole (*citrāvayavin*) is simply a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
Nor is there any quality of yellowness therein;
for those who know the categories of reality hold that the single form called variegated (*citra*) exists as a pervasive occurrence throughout its substrate.
Liberation does not depend at all upon the falsity of bondage.

Or, let it be that knowledge is the remover of ignorance alone; even so, in this context, liberation does not depend upon the falsity of bondage. Rather, since liberation consists simply in the non-existence of bondage—along with its cause, which is ignorance—that alone should be described. What, then, is the relevance of describing superimposition (*adhyāsa*)?
The falsity of ignorance, however, is like a ball of molasses stuck in one's armpit [difficult to remove],
because it is about to be refuted.
Furthermore, since it is observed that even real poison is removed by the meditation on Garuḍa, liberation does not depend at all upon the falsity of bondage.
If it is argued that "poison is not real," we say no;

for if that were the case, then since even substances qualified by blue color and so forth would be unreal for you, it would follow that their cessation could not logically be brought about. [Objection:
It is real.

That too is false for me. If you argue that it is merely an objection raised by accepting the opponent's position, then that very [objection] has not ceased through knowledge; thus, even that which is false does not cease through knowledge.
If it is argued that what is false is removable by a contradictory cognition, we say no; for the qualification would be redundant,
since non-removal of the self is possible precisely because there is no contradiction.
Even if one accepts falsity (*mithyātva*), a contradiction must still be admitted;
therefore, it is simpler to accept that very [contradiction] as the cause (*prayojaka*), due to parsimony (*lāghava*).
If it is argued that being contrary to knowledge belongs only to that which is false, we say no.
Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If you argue that it is because [the world] is perceived, then by what could even the existence of the Truths (*satya*) be prevented by means of scripture (*āgama*)?
Nor is mere perception the determinant of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
If it is argued that meditation (*dhyāna*) is a mental activity (*mānasī-kriyā*) and not knowledge (*jñāna*), we say no;

for if it were an activity consisting of physical motion (*kriyā-parispanda*), then, being dependent on supersensible [factors], it would itself be supersensible, which contradicts its appearing as immediate (*aparokṣa-avabhāsa*), and there would also be a contradiction regarding its appearance due to its lack of form (*rūpa-rahitatva*).
And if it is held that this is a mental creation, this is acceptable;
for we admit that meditation (*dhyāna*) is the mental observation of an object consisting of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by hearing, seeing, and so forth.
Even though a substance has as its material cause something beyond the senses, its perceptibility is possible, just as in the case of a triad (*tryaṇuka*).
The birth of the material fire from the formless wind is well-known indeed to the Vedāntins;
as for the logicians and others, we shall satisfy them by refuting their theory of atomic aggregation (ārambhavāda).
And thus, the fact that the root *dhyai* has the meaning of "thinking" is established both by Smṛti and by reasoning.
For this very reason, the contradiction with the sūtra stating "like action and mental [states]" is also resolved;
for in all cases, the complete cause of knowledge is independent of the desire and effort of a person produced by an injunction,
since we observe the occurrence of knowledge even in one who does not desire it and does not intend it.
If it is asked, "How then is this knowledge [attained]?"— the answer is no;
for the injunction has fulfilled its purpose merely by making known the relationship between the goal and the means,
and since desire and effort have already achieved their ends in awakening the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), they have no further operation in the perception of mental objects.
Furthermore, its utility lies in removing mental distraction, just as the closing of the eyes removes visual movement.
Moreover, it is well-established that the cessation of evil and so forth occurs through such acts as visiting sacred fords (*setu*).
There is no evidence for postulating an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) in the interim.
Otherwise, there is no evidence for the postulation of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) even in the case at hand;

otherwise, it would follow that one must likewise postulate an unseen force in the present instance as well. If it is argued that liberation would consequently be impermanent if it were accomplished by an unseen force, we reply that this is the same even if it were produced by knowledge.
If it is argued that there is no impermanence because [liberation] is of the nature of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) even though it is produced by knowledge,
this applies equally to its being accomplished by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, since liberation is characterized by the destruction of bondage, it does not depend at all upon the falsity of bondage.
What indeed is this so-called "reality"?
For there is no destruction of that which is false, such as a rabbit's horn.
But surely you yourself have stated that, through the exclusion of false things like a rabbit's horn, destruction culminates in reality?

In that case, I too can certainly say that even when [the argument] is excluded from the real conscious self (cidātman), it results in the false. Although that may appear to be true at first glance, nevertheless, the *arthāpatti* based on the Sūtra is itself blunted by being overwhelmed by doubt.
We shall, however, produce for you a certainty by means of the refutation of the "indefinable" (*anirvācya*).
If it is argued that liberation is simply the cessation of bondage,
this is not so; for the Śruti and Sūtras do not speak thus,
since in passages such as "He crosses over sorrow," they express the opposite.
The author of the Bhāṣya himself has established otherwise the logical implication (*arthāpatti*) of the scriptural statement, "He who is already liberated is being liberated.
Furthermore, the statement in the Sūtra regarding the purpose—that knowledge of Brahman removes the bondage residing in the individual soul (*jīva*)—does not depend upon the falsity of that bondage.
If the statement of the purpose in the Sūtra were that the knowledge of the individual soul removes the bondage residing in the individual soul, then it might somehow require the falsity of bondage.
Nor does the author of the Sūtras state this; for silver superimposed upon mother-of-pearl does not cease merely through the cognition of a jar.

Furthermore, the claim that "the knowledge of Brahman" consists in the experience of the identity of the referent of the term *tvam* (the individual soul) with the referent of the term *tat* (Brahman) is mere idle chatter confined to one's own sectarian circle, as it will be refuted later. *1,536*

Moreover, if bondage were false and if the sublation of bondage occurred through mere knowledge, then once knowledge has arisen, liberation would not require anything else at all; consequently, it would follow that for those who have directly realized Brahman, there would be an immediate cessation of the body and so forth. This constitutes a contradiction with reason (*tarka*) based on the impossibility of such a consequence (*arthāpatti*), which we shall elaborate upon in the third [chapter].
Thus, the claim that the falsity of bondage (*bandhamithyātva*) is described here as being implied by the purpose stated in the Sūtra has been refuted.

Alternatively, he refutes the claim that it is implied by the mention of the "object" (*viṣaya*) with this [verse]. Such a statement in the Sūtra—the mention of Brahman as the object—does not depend upon the falsity of bondage.

For if the *jīvātman* were mentioned in the Sūtra as the subject matter (*viṣaya*), then that might somehow require the falsity of bondage—such as agency and so forth—in order to establish its state of doubt.
However, it is Brahman alone that is here stated to be the subject matter;
for it is not logical that because one thing is in a state of doubt, another thing becomes the object of inquiry.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].

We shall, however, refute the false hope that the Self alone is Brahman. Alternatively, by this [statement], he refutes the claim that the purpose of the passage beginning with "you" and "I" is merely an introductory statement for the meaning of the entire treatise.

For instance, such statements as "But that [Brahman], because of the harmony [of all Vedas]" (Tattusamanvayāt) do not depend upon the falsity of the bondage residing in the individual soul; rather, they declare that Brahman alone— characterized as the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world and entirely distinct from the phenomenal complex (*prapañca*) consisting of both sentient and insentient beings— is what is propounded by the entirety of the Vedas.

For this [treatise] indeed requires only the falsity of the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, which are apprehended through fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*), with respect to Brahman alone.

If this scripture were intended to establish that the culmination of all Vedānta lies in the identity of the individual soul with Brahman, then there would be a need to rely on the falsity of bondage in order to pacify contradictions;
but such is not the case.
We shall explain how this is so.
But surely, since dependence is a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*), how can this be? It is as follows.
In this context, "expectancy" (*apekṣā*) is said to be the capacity of a known fact that is otherwise inexplicable to imply that which makes it explicable.
And so, since the cessation of the bondage of cognition is not inexplicable without the falsity of that bondage, it has been stated that [cessation] does not imply it.
Furthermore, the falsity of bondage cannot be established on the grounds of contradiction with perception. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 1.16cd)

He states another refutation of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding the contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) concerning falsity (*mithyātva*), beginning with the words "falsity also" (*mithyātvam api*).
It is not only that liberation does not depend upon the falsity of bondage; rather, the connection is that even the very falsity of bondage does not exist. But is this not untenable?
For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes an object by its own inherent power alone.
Furthermore, it does not depend upon the prior establishment of the object.

If that were the case, the means of valid cognition would be redundant; moreover, since the preceding means of valid cognition would likewise require such dependence, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, the fact that the object is not established prior [to the presumption] is indeed an ornament of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Once presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has already begun to operate, its own non-establishment (*asiddhi*) need not be taken into account, precisely because it is [itself] already established as a means of valid cognition.
If that is so, why would the fatness of a person known to eat only by day—which is otherwise inexplicable—fail to imply the mastery of an elixir (*rasāyana*) or supernatural power (*yogarddhi*)?
Furthermore, even the non-establishment of those [alternatives] prior to the operation of the presumption is merely an embellishment.
If it is argued that [the object] does not exist at all in the subsequent time, we say no,
because of the disparity.
For an object is not something to be known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) simply because it has not yet been established by means such as the perfection of alchemy (*rasāyana*).

Nevertheless, in the case of a person whose character is well-known, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes what was previously unestablished by way of being sublated [by other cognitions];
it does not, however, establish what is contradicted by a means of valid cognition—this is indeed a well-known principle.
This, then, is the complete causal complex for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
When there is the established status and the incoherence of the implicant (*ākṣepaka*),
and also the establishing nature and the non-contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of the implicate (*ākṣepya*),

then— precisely for that reason— the refutations of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are as follows: its lack of established status, the absence of incoherence [in the implicant], its coherence even otherwise, its coherence in a manner other than [the intended one], and its having a meaning contradicted by valid cognition.
True.

For we also maintain that the falsity of bondage is not a matter to be established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), precisely because it contradicts direct perception (pratyakṣa)—such as the perceptions "I am the agent," "I am the enjoyer," "I am happy," or "I am miserable.
This is what was meant by the statement, "due to contradiction with direct perception."
Alternatively, the construction may be "also because of contradiction with direct perception" (*pratyakṣavirodhato ’pi*).
By this, he combines [the argument] with contradiction by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*),

since the Self— endowed precisely with agency and so forth— is established as known through such signs as movement and the like, as well as through scriptures such as "that which is to be known as 'I' alone."

Alternatively, it was stated that the commentary of the opponents is useless because it describes bondage as being false without being implied by the semblance of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
This [uselessness] is further stated by the phrase "even though it is illogical, because it propounds a meaning contradicted by perception and so forth.
Now, one might object: "Perception has as its object only the essential nature of bondage, but not the absence of falsity within it."

Therefore, how could there be a contradiction with perception regarding either the [inference] based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or the author of the *Bhāṣya*’s demonstration of its falsity?
It is not so;
for perception, when it takes bondage as its object, would take it as either "it exists" or "it does not exist."
Because a cognition that is indifferent to both [existence and non-existence] is not observed;
in the first case, "existence" and "the absence of falsity" are synonymous, so how could there not be a contradiction with perception?
In the second case, there is a contradiction with experience, as well as the consequence that its demonstration would be useless. *1,546*
If falsity were to exist prior to that statement regarding suffering and so forth, [then the statement would not be a means of valid cognition].
An inquiry into the meaning of the scriptural text, "There is no diversity here," might be as follows:
this would be so if this perception were a means of revealing ultimate reality (*tattva*).

But this is not so; for the reality of the Self is indeed proclaimed in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas as being one alone, without a second, indifferent, and of the single essence of infinite bliss-consciousness unconditioned by any adjuncts, according to such passages as "There is no diversity whatsoever here."

Nor can these [scriptural texts]—which, by virtue of their introductory passages and so forth, declare the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) in this manner and are intent upon that [reality]—be made to have a figurative meaning by anyone.

Furthermore, how could perception—which presents an individualized self (*prādeśika ātmā*) overwhelmed by a manifold proliferation of suffering and the like—not be a delusion, since it contradicts that [scriptural teaching]?

This beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*anirvācyāvidyā*), which acts as a variegated wall of impressions from prior cognitions and the latent tendencies of karma and afflictions, obstructs the manifestation of consciousness as it truly exists in its nature as Brahman, and instead projects the state of being a transmigrating soul (*jīvatva*).

The *ahaṅkāra* (I-consciousness) is that which has acquired a specific transformation through being presided over by the Supreme Lord; it is the substratum of the two powers of cognition and action, the single locus of agency and enjoyership, and is directly manifest as a light produced by its conjunction with immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*). This [ahaṅkāra] is designated as the "internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*), "mind" (*manas*), "intellect" (*buddhi*), and "the subject of the notion of 'I'" (*ahaṃpratyayin*) by the proponents of Vedānta, who distinguish it from the conscious Self (*cidātman*) by means of the intellect (*buddhi*), relying upon its specific cognitive power.
And because of the power of vibration, it is called *prāṇa*.
Due to the coloring by that [vibration], agency and so forth falsely appear to belong to the Self,
just as redness appears in a crystal gem due to the proximity of a colored object.

Thus, since the direct perception that "I am the doer, the enjoyer, happy, miserable," and so forth, has been rendered as rotten as a rotten kushmanda gourd due to its contradiction with scripture and other authorities, the demonstration of the falsity of bondage is highly appropriate;
therefore, he says: "If [the falsity]... and so on.
This description of the falsity of bondage— having rendered perception illusory by means of the contradiction with such scriptural passages as "There is neither diversity nor plurality here"—
is a system that merely charms the minds of the ignorant,
provided that those passages were intended to convey the nature of the Self in the manner described.
But it is not so;
for instance,
is the meaning of the sentence understood merely upon its initial presentation?

Alternatively, [the meaning] is consistent with and not contradicted by the aforementioned marks for determining the intended purport (*tātparya*), such as: "The beginning, the conclusion, repetition, novelty, the fruit, the eulogy (*arthavāda*), and the logical justification (*upapatti*) are the marks for determining the purport.
It is not the first [of these].
Because it would result in the futility of the Mīmāṃsā inquiry;

as for the second [alternative], how could this sentence be intended to convey the true nature of the Self as described by the stated definition? For it is contradicted by the powerful reasoning found in the indicators such as the opening statement (*upakrama*) and so forth.

For this very reason, the meaning understood from such statements as "from non-being, being was born" is abandoned because it is contradicted by reasoning, as in: "But how indeed, my dear, could this be so? How could being be born from non-being? And the venerable author of the Sūtras will state in the section concerning the presiding deities (Abhimāny-adhikaraṇa) that even an object perceived from a statement such as "the clay spoke," one must set aside if it is contradicted by reasoning, and accept another meaning. If it is asked, "In what way is there a contradiction with reasoning here? [the answer follows].

Thus, if everything other than the Self— such as suffering and so forth— were to be false by the force of scripture and other authorities, then that very scriptural statement itself would have to be false,
because it is distinct from the Self. Otherwise, its authority regarding itself would be undermined, and it could not establish any meaning whatsoever.
Furthermore, even if this statement were false, it still could not establish the falsity of suffering and so forth;
for we do not observe that a false statement, such as the words "the son of a barren woman," possesses any probative power.

Thus, since this statement—whether false or true—is incapable of establishing the falsity of bondage, it cannot serve as a sublater of direct perception; therefore, the falsity of bondage, suffering, and the like is not established.
The knowers of reality say:
"For we also accept that every bond—characterized by the intellect, the senses, the body, their objects, and their qualities—is indeed superimposed upon the Self.
As it was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:
Since bondage consists in negligence (*pramāda*),
what then is the basis for the effort to dispel the falsity of that bondage?
True.
Nevertheless, there is a difference of opinion on this point.
Such indeed is the view of the knowers of the inner self (*adhyātmavid*):

with respect to action and knowledge, agency and enjoyership—characterized by the state of not being dependent on other causal factors—exist inherently in the self, even though they are dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
This is because it will be stated later that modification—consisting of the penetration by activity (*kriyā*) and so forth—is not a cause for destruction and the like.
The appearance of that [Self] as dependent on another is an error caused by ignorance (*avidyā*).
And ignorance and the rest exist both in their own nature and as related to the Self.

In this way, the intellect, the sense organs, the body, and their objects, though existing as they are in their own nature and under the control of Īśvara, are superimposed as "mine" due to the power of ignorance (avidyā) and other factors.
Even a state of "mineness" that is dependent on another exists.

And not perceiving those [objects] clearly as distinct from the Self, one regards their attributes—such as suffering and so forth—as truly real in terms of "mineness," and consequently regards the transformations characterized by lowliness and loftiness caused by them as truly real.
He proceeds [in this way]. Then, impelled by passion and hatred, whatever he does for the sake of their cessation turns out to be exactly like that; thus he wanders through many wombs.
He never attains the ultimate pacification of those [afflictions] except through the propitiation of the Supreme Person.
The proponents of illusion (māyāvādins), however, consider suffering and so forth to be false even by way of their own nature; as it has been said:
"having conjoined the real and the unreal."

Therefore, it is entirely appropriate to insist upon the refutation of that [bondage]; to make this point clear, even though the illusory nature of bondage was introduced in a general sense, the specific term "of suffering and so forth" has been used.
This is because [the existence of a creator] is contradicted by such scriptural passages as, "There is no other agent than Him," which deny His independence and so on.
Indeed, there is no contradiction between this [scripture] and the scripture declaring the falsity of everything, as there is with [other doctrines] like the existence of a creator.
And the author of the Sūtras will state this in various places (Sūtra 1.1.5–6): "Furthermore,

having placed at the forefront this mutual superimposition of the Self and the non-Self— which is called ignorance— all worldly transactions involving means and objects of knowledge proceed, as do all the scriptures," and so forth.
Another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been presented;
that [objection] is refuted by this very [argument].

For here, there is the triad of worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) characterized as the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; the agent, the object, and the action; and the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment.

By demonstrating that empirical usage is preceded by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of "I" and "mine" upon the body, the senses, and so forth, it has been stated that inference— based on the mark of the effect of empirical usage,
or the impossibility of accounting for such usage otherwise— is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding superimposition.
However, by this [inference], the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the internal organ, the body, the senses, their objects, and their attributes such as pain and the like, is not established.
For even things that exist in their own right are accounted for in worldly discourse solely through the superimposition (āropa) of identity with or relation to [other things].
Nor does mere superimposition imply falsity (mithyātva),
because it would follow that the Self (ātman) would also be false by virtue of being superimposed upon the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth.
Furthermore, the superimposition of the Self upon the internal organ and so forth has been accepted by the opponent;
as it has been stated:
"One superimposes that inner Self, the witness of all, upon the internal organ and so forth through a reversal of [its true] nature."

If it is argued that because there is no superimposition of the nature of the conscious onto the unconscious, but rather superimposition occurs only through their being conjoined, and that all worldly and Vedic transactions are possible by that alone, therefore [the world] is not false— this is equally applicable to the unconscious as well, as has been prattled here by someone. Furthermore, even in the case of mutual superimposition, the sublation of the phenomenal complex of the body, senses, and so forth will be established by means of scripture and reasoning.
"But the conscious self (cidātmā) is uncontradicted, as it has been determined by the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, and the logic not opposed to them.
This is incorrect,
because the Śruti and other texts that sublate the phenomenal world (prapañca) are being refuted.
Furthermore, since these arguments will be refuted later,
and because falsity is established by scripture (*śruti*) and other means of knowledge, such statements as "this very thing called ignorance" (*tam etam avidyākhyam*) would become meaningless.
Indeed, no proponent of a philosophical view asserts [that falsity is established by scripture].
The body and so forth are not superimposed upon the Self in any form whatsoever,
by which a mere superimposition could be established;
furthermore, the Teacher will later refute the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*).
And even without that [self], he will establish conventional usage;
as for the claim that agency and so forth, which reside in the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), appear in the self due to its coloring by that [ego-sense]—
that is incorrect.
Because the notion of "I" has the self as its object. [Objection:
If that were so, there would be an awareness of "I" even during deep sleep, since at that time the self is manifest by virtue of being self-luminous.
Nor does it follow that the effects of ignorance would also be perceived at that time,
because during deep sleep, ignorance has its entire range of transformations uprooted, and thus those effects are absent.
This is not so.
If it is argued that even during sleep the "I" is admitted to be manifest, then the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) should be remembered just as it was yesterday;

for even though there is no rule that what has been experienced must necessarily be remembered, [the ego-sense] would still be remembered because it is nothing other than the self that is being remembered—if this is said, we reply: no.

Because one who has risen from sleep observes the recollection of the experience of the pleasure of sleep, thinking, "I slept happily. If it is argued that [the pleasure] is specifically remembered at that time,
is it being suggested that the memory is vivid?
Or is it colored by a particular object?
In the first case, there would be the production of a light;
but not in the second.

Because the pleasure experienced during deep sleep (*sauṣuptika-sukha*) is not produced by an object, there is no such rule that whatever is remembered must be remembered together with all its related particulars. Therefore, since there is no sublation regarding the primary pleasure and its experience, the hypothesis that the subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) has the non-existence of suffering as its object is rejected. (1.581)

As for the statement regarding the distinction between the Self (ātman) and the ego (ahaṅkāra)—namely, "Now, therefore, the instruction on the ego" and "Now, therefore, the instruction on the Self"—that has been explained otherwise by the author of the Bhāṣya himself.
Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras will state: "For that [Self] alone [is meant by] 'Being' and so forth. Otherwise, how could the all-pervasiveness of the ego be logically established?
Although the ego (ahaṅkāra), established by such Smṛti texts as "the great elements, the ego," and so forth, is indeed distinct from the Self, nevertheless,
it is not the object of the mental impression "I am the agent.
If that were the case, it would follow that the same would apply even in such [Vedic] passages as "I am Brahman."
If it is argued that here too there is a figurative explanation (vyākhyāna), as in the case of "that which is a post is a person," we say no;
for in the passage, "He knew only himself: 'I am Brahman,'" even the faultless Brahman is seen to be designated by the term "I.
Furthermore, [the Lord says], "Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this Māyā."

Furthermore, since even the Lord— who is capable of dispelling the illusion (māyā) that has descended upon Himself— is observed to employ such expressions as "I am the source of all," the distinction between these two is evident even from the words themselves. For the indeclinable word *aham*, ending in the letter *m* and denoting a transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), is never used to refer to the Self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, that which denotes the Self—derived from the word *asmad* ending in the letter *d*—is never employed to refer to a transformation of *māyā*. Thus, if the Śruti were intent on establishing the falsity of everything, it would follow that the Śruti itself is false; consequently, since it would fail to be a means of valid knowledge (*asādhaka*), the falsity of bondage consisting of suffering and so forth could not be established. Therefore, how can it be said [in the previous section] that "perception does not reveal reality" (*na pratyakṣamatattvāvedakam*)? This is the objection.
By the statement "not here, not there," a single cognition arises that everything other than the Self is false; and there is no successive operation (viramyavyāpāra) of that cognition,
because it arises only as directed toward its own object and lacks any operation beyond that.
True.

Although the cognition produced by the sentence at once has as its object the falsity of everything, there is no fault, because the cognitions of the investigator themselves— having divided that object through their own intellect— investigate it sequentially in order to determine the validity of that cognition.
This is the same as in the investigation of the authority of such statements as "I shall remain silent for as long as I live";
furthermore, the opponent has not established that what is false can be a means of proof. (Mānava 1.1.17cd)
Refutation of the Efficacy of the Non-existent:

Now, it might be argued that even if the Vedas and other means of knowledge are false, their efficacy is still possible, because I admit that only that which is false can be efficacious; to this, he says: "Of the false... [mithyāyāḥ].
The construction is: "of those [words] such as the Veda which are false.
Alternatively, *mithyāyāḥ* is an indeclinable that functions like a case-ending.
This is the intended meaning (*abhisandhi*).
By such statements as "not here, not there" (neha nānā), is a person who has already ascertained non-duality being taught,
or one who is the opposite?
Not the first.
Because it would be redundant.

As for the second [position], one who considers that only the true [statement] can be a means of proof (*sādhaka*) [argues]: if this sentence were to establish the falsity of everything, then, being included within "everything," it would itself be false—just as in the case of the statement, "Sound is impermanent."
The word "iti" is impermanent.

Seeing that if this sentence were false it would not establish any object at all— which would entail the undesirable consequence of its own non-existence— how could one admit the contradiction of one's own reasoning merely on the basis of your assertion?
Now, the capacity of a sentence to establish [truth] consists in its generating a valid cognition of the connection between word-meanings.
This is sometimes obstructed by a defect in a word;

sometimes by the failure to grasp the connection [between words]; sometimes by forgetting it; sometimes by the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors; and sometimes by the presentation of a contrary meaning.

Therefore, in this case as well, regarding the statement "not here, not there" (*neha nānā*) and so forth, one must accept that the cause for establishing the absence of proof is simply one of the defects of the words and so on;
why resort to "falsity"?
Are you prepared to assert that even a non-existent sentence possesses such qualities as being composed of flawless constituent words?

By speaking thus, when some matter is contested, you will surely refute the probative force of one who cites the words of a barren woman’s son as an authority against an opponent, by pointing out defects in the words and so forth.
Since its lack of probative force is already established by the very non-existence of its own nature, what is the use of considering defects in the words and such, which occur only subsequently?

If it is argued: "Once it is established that visual perceptibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) lacks the capacity to prove impermanence simply by virtue of its non-existence in sound, what is the point of considering the faults of the word and so forth, which occur only at the final stage? For once it is established that visual perceptibility lacks the capacity to prove impermanence simply by virtue of its non-existence in sound, no further consideration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is undertaken"—then this applies equally to the present case as well.
[Objection: Granted that the reasoning may not be contradictory in relation to the opponent, it will nonetheless be so in relation to the proponent. [Reply:
Not so.

For the proponent (vādin) as well, having established through the scriptural statement (*śrutivākya*) that everything other than the Self is illusory (*mithyātva*), must understand that even that which is illusory possesses the capacity to prove [its own conclusion]. Indeed, prior to the realization of the universal falsity [of all things], he is exactly like his opponent.

Thus, since the scripture establishes the falsity of everything, one must recognize that it is precisely the illusory that functions as the means of proof; consequently, any reasoning (*tarka*) that contradicts this must be refuted.

And since the Veda would establish the falsity of everything only upon the refutation of that [duality], you have not escaped the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). How then could such a person establish the contradiction of reasoning? Furthermore: "Is that [duality] established by you through a false means of knowledge or a true one? If it were established by a true one, duality would be proven; and if it were established by a false one, the means of proof itself would not be established. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 1.18)
Now, it may be thought:
first of all, the fact that perception and the other means of knowledge are instruments of valid cognition is established by experience;
and their falsity is understood through the scriptures and through reasoning.
Do not say, "How is it established that something which is false can be a means of valid cognition (*sādhaka*)?

For it is possible for another means of knowledge, assisted by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a single cognition, to generate a qualified cognition, just as in the case of the perception "fragrant sandalwood.

Alternatively, since the self (*ātman*) who synthesizes both [cognitions] exists, there will be a qualified apprehension, just as there is the grasping of a single object through both seeing and touching.

And thus, since it has been established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) itself that only that which is false (*mithyābhūta*) is the prover, [the opponent] asks by means of an alternative [option] in order to refute the claim that "contradictory reasoning (*viruddha-tarka*) does not [apply] merely on the basis of my own admission": "And that" (*tac ca*);
here "that" (*tat*) refers to the state of being a prover only for that which is false.
The word "and" (*ca*) implies "just as the falsity of that which is distinct from the Self."
The connection is with the phrase "by means of a valid cognition that exists.

The meaning of the question is this: when you present a means of valid cognition consisting of a combination of two means of valid cognition in order to establish that only what is false is a prover, is that [means of valid cognition] itself false or true?
He refutes the position that [the effect] exists by saying: "If [it were] existent... and so forth.

Although the alternative of falsity (*mithyātva*) should have been mentioned first at the time of the inquiry—since it is primary because it is what the opponent intends to establish—nevertheless, between the false and the true, the true is primary in terms of its actual meaning; therefore, the refutation follows that order.
Following the phrase "if [it exists] as something real" (*sacca cet*), there is the alternative of whether it exists in the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or as something other than that.
The promise to refute the first position, beginning with "we shall explain," must be supplied [from the context].
The refutation of the second position—that [the world] exists as something other than the Self—is that it would result in the establishment of duality (*dvaita*).
Thus, the underlying point is that this would contradict the scriptural texts (*śruti*) that establish non-duality (*advaita*).

Nor, however, is the intent merely to avoid contradicting one's own tenets; for that would be inconsistent with the context, as the discussion has commenced by demonstrating that the Śruti cannot establish non-duality due to its contradiction with logical reasoning.
He states the fault in the case of falsity (mithyātva): "And it is not established," etc.
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) or the meaning of the word *tu* (but).
That which is other than the real—that is, that which is false—is not established as a means of proof;
the point is that the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramā-sādhana*) for that which is false is simply not established.
This is what is meant:

for one who, having accepted the pervasion that "whatever is false is not a means of proof," applies this to the falsity of the Veda to show its lack of probative power, will certainly also result in the lack of probative power for the very means of proof adduced to establish the point, since that too is false.
Thus, he would be establishing the probative power of that which is itself false.
And thus, once the validity of this means of knowledge is established, it follows by implication that its validity belongs only to that which is false;

from that, the contradiction of the reductio ad absurdum (tarka) is established; and from that, the validity of this means of knowledge is established—thus, due to the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka*), not even one of these is established. *1,605*
**The Refutation of Objections Regarding the Non-existence of the Prover:** Now, one might ask:

"How can the Śruti, which establishes the falsity of suffering and other phenomena distinct from itself, be in contradiction with reason? To this we reply: Why is there this restriction of the meaning of the Śruti?

If you argue that this is due to the force of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the impossibility of [the world] being a means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*), then, having set aside what has been cognized by that very means, how could one who asserts falsity (*mithyātva*) establish the falsity of suffering and so forth as well? For that too is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
But surely, I have undertaken this effort precisely to render such direct perception fallacious (*ābhāsa*) by means of its contradiction with the Śruti!
If one were to assert a contradiction with scripture on that very basis, how would there not be the fallacy of mutual dependence?
For if scripture lacks authority, there is no sublation [of perception], and thus perception possesses authority;
consequently, scripture lacks authority because it is contradicted by that [perception].
Alas, how could this mutual dependence not also apply to you?
If the authority of scripture is established, then perception lacks authority due to its contradiction with that scripture;
and from that, the authority of scripture is established because there is no sublater [of it]. Thus, the same circularity remains.
If it is argued that this is not so because scripture (*śruti*) is more authoritative, we say no;
for that [scripture] is defective,
and the superiority of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) will be established later.
But why has the demonstration of the superiority of scripture not been done here by simply presenting its contradiction with direct perception?
What is the purpose of demonstrating its contradiction with logical reasoning?
It is said in reply:

For it has been demonstrated by means of an extensive treatise that the other [position] is indeed consistent with the marks of intentionality (*tātparyaliṅga*) regarding the ultimate non-duality (*advaita*).
Therefore, the contradiction with that [non-duality] has been established solely to reveal the opponent's lack of skill in inquiry.
And this [contradiction with non-duality] is an illustration of the contradiction with the opening statements (*upakrama*) and so forth.
And we shall explain that [later].
Now, let it be granted that reasoning is not contradictory;
nevertheless, even though it is false, an object in a dream is a reflection of an object, just as a letter inscribed on a line [is a reflection] of the auspicious or inauspicious.

Furthermore, the redness of a crystal due to the proximity of a colored object, the color and length of a reflection due to the presence of the substrate, and the sun’s disc and its apertures as evidence for the movement of the sun—all these are found to establish distinct objects; thus, because their foundation is shaky, they are fallacious.
This is not so.
For in this case, that which is a proof is not false, and that which is false is not a proof. To explain:
He will indeed explain the reality of a dream, which consists of cognition and its object;
even a line, when conventionally assigned to a letter or a word to a meaning, brings that [object] to mind, so there is nothing false here.
For this very reason, having perceived the line, they pronounce the letter.
The reality of the reflection has been accepted even by the opponent;
we shall likewise establish the reality of the separation.
By this very [argument], the redness of a crystal is also explained.
Length and so forth are indeed inherent in phonemes just as they are in sounds;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that length and other qualities would appear in consonants just as they do in vowels, due to the influence of the accompaniment of sound (*dhvānopadhāna*).
If it is argued that a consonant is not manifested by such a sound, we say no.
If that were the case, one would have to admit a specific quality within the phonemes themselves;
that very quality will be what is denoted by terms such as "length" (*dairghya*) and so forth.
It is the cognition of the sun's aperture and so on that serves as the indicator of impending misfortune.
And this will be explained later;
in the same way, other points should also be inferred.

Therefore, the meaning of the Śruti—that there is no difference in essential nature (svarūpa-bheda) regarding the Blessed One—must be understood as stated by the venerable Commentator, who was a supreme devotee and the foremost among those learned in words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). *1,613*

In our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is the justification of the meaning of the scriptural passage "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*). But surely, even here, there is indeed an inconsistency; for by the word "manifold" (*nānā*), the diverse phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is denoted.
But there is no difference; for if that were the case, it would follow that there is plurality.
It is not so.
This is because, as in the case of the sūtra "muktopasṛpyavyapadeśāt" (BrSū 1.3.2), it is appropriate to understand the statement as having the state (*bhāva*) as its primary referent.
Even if the substrate (*bhavitṛ*) were primary, when the various constituent parts, qualities, actions, and so forth are negated in Brahman, multiplicity itself is what is negated.
This follows the logical principle: "When a prescription or prohibition concerns something with a qualification, they apply to the qualification."
Because negating both would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); because the qualifier is encountered first;
and otherwise, the employment of that [qualifier] would be purposeless.
And because it is seen in such passages as, "A *snātaka* shall not wear worn-out or dirty clothes";
for this very reason, it has been said:
"The denotation [of a word] cannot reach the qualified object, as its power is exhausted by the qualifier.
Any acceptance of a qualified injunction or prohibition in certain cases is done only out of necessity (*agatikayā*).
Furthermore, we shall explain that Brahman possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*).
If it is argued that this being the case, there is a prohibition of what has not been attained, we say no; for it is attained only as an appearance (*ābhāsa*).
And thus [it is said]: “Not even from the standpoint of location.”

We shall demonstrate this in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, the denial of heaven, the unseen potency (*apūrva*), and so forth, applies only to the opponent, as such things are not [admitted by us] and their denial is therefore untenable.
"One only, without a second."
In such passages as these, you yourself, while explaining the negation of internal plurality—whether of the same kind, of a different kind, or inherent—must also provide a resolution to this:

"By that witness who desires the establishment of an existent thing through its capacity as a means of proof, the non-establishment of that which is devoid of distinction has, in fact, been accepted. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.19)
And since that [measure] must be established by another measure without distinction, there would be an infinite regress.

The Refutation of the Proof of the Indistinguishable: Now, just as you do not accept the capacity for proof in that which is false, so too I do not accept the capacity for proof in that which is real.
Because you do not admit the reality of anything apart from consciousness,
and because consciousness, when devoid of the entry of activity, cannot function as a means of proof; in that regard,

since you have stated that the Veda cannot prove the falsity of bondage— lest its own falsity result in its lack of proving power due to your refusal to admit that what is false can be a means of proof.
In this way, it can certainly be argued by me as well, who does not accept that truth is the means of proof:
if perception were true, it could not be the means of proof;
yet you yourself do not admit its falsity.

Furthermore, since even perception lacks the capacity to establish the reality of bondage, the statement "the falsity of bondage also does not [follow] from a contradiction with perception" is untenable.
And in this way, the commencement of the discussion would be rendered impossible at the very outset, due to the mire of misconceptions.
"Therefore, without first investigating whether that [perception] is a valid means of knowledge or not, one should begin the investigation"—
this is not so;
for there is no contradiction even if the perception grasping the truth of suffering and the other truths is itself true.

If it is argued that I have already stated that I do not accept the status of being a means of accomplishment (*sādhakatva*) for an existent thing, he replies to that with the words: "The status of being a means of accomplishment..."
By that proponent of illusion;
the words "of ignorance in the form of a positive entity" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the reason.
Or rather, it indicates what is well-known.

Indeed, by the proponent of Māyā (the Māyāvādin), who desires to establish ignorance as a positive entity, the means of knowledge consisting of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) has been accepted for its proof, [beginning with the statement]: "First of all, perception [establishes it], because one observes the manifestation of immediate awareness in such forms as 'I am ignorant' and 'I do not know myself or another.'"

This is because, by the subsequent statement beginning with "the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya), which consists of the knowledge of the substratum and the counter-positive," it is understood that the witness is the means of perception (pratyakṣa).
And thus, by one who desires the establishment of ignorance through the witness, the capacity to prove [an object] has necessarily been accepted for that which exists,
since the witness-consciousness itself exists.
Therefore, it cannot be said that I do not accept the status of being a prover (*sādhakatva*) for the Existent;
for our intention is that we too have presented the direct perception of the Witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) as the proof for the reality of bondage, such as suffering and so forth.
It is solely by virtue of ignorance that I accept the Witness as the prover.
If you say "not from itself," we say no;
for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Indeed, for you, there exists no reality of ignorance other than its manifestation as a witness (*sākṣin*).

Therefore, since there is ignorance, the witness is established as the means of proof (*sādhaka*), and within that [establishment], ignorance is established; how then is this not a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)?
If it is argued that this is not so because both are beginningless (*anādi*), then the statement "by the power of ignorance" is empty.
For it is not logical that whatever does not depend on anything at all should be dependent upon that [very thing];
however, if there were dependence, one could not escape the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

Thus, in order to demonstrate that there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) accepted by both disputants within his own system, he has presented the opponent’s own admission that a witness of truth establishes ignorance.
Now, in this context, he says that even that is not tenable: "Of the non-distinct," etc.
Indeed, for one who does not accept ignorance as having a positive (bhāva) nature, the evidence of the witness-consciousness (sākṣipratyakṣa) has been adduced regarding that [ignorance].
But that is not appropriate,
because it is accepted that the witness is devoid of all specific attributes (viśeṣa).
Furthermore, the proof of non-distinction must itself be established by you for the sake of the opponent;
it is not already established.
For whatever is a means of proof—whether it be an instrument, a result, or eternal cognition—all of that possesses specific qualities such as genus (jāti) and so forth.
Furthermore, since the opponent has accepted the rule that what is devoid of specific characteristics— such as a rabbit’s horn— is not a means of proof,
for it is not fit to be presented as a proof for any object whose status as a prover is not already admitted; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Now, it may be objected: "Is it not the case that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is employed for the establishment of a real entity?
What then is the purpose of its having specific attributes? This is true;
however, since validity itself is not possible for that which is devoid of attributes, it is precisely for that reason that one pursues specific attributes.
For validity cannot be established in the absence of specific factors such as being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).

If it is argued that ignorance is established merely by its being superimposed upon the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), and that there is no instrumental capacity (*sādhakatva*) belonging to it beyond that; [we reply:]...
In that case, the establishment of ignorance by the witness (*sākṣin*) is not at all tenable;
for it is impossible for you, who profess non-distinction, to demonstrate to an opponent the point that darkness, which is the substrate of light, is established by light itself.
Furthermore, is even superimposed ignorance an object of the witness or not?

In the first case, the status of being an object-possessor (*viṣayitva*) would fall upon the witness (*sākṣin*). In the second case, the very status of being a witness is untenable, according to the rule: "The term *sākṣin* is used in the sense of one who sees directly."
Thus, because such an etymological derivation is impossible, the establishment of that [witnesshood] by means of something that does not have it as its object is unworldly (alaukika). Furthermore,
the claim that even the indeterminate [Self] possesses witnesshood by the power of ignorance is refuted.
However, one who out of impudence says that even a probandum which has not yet established its validity is fit for formal application just like a probans whose validity is already established—

otherwise, when an opponent points out that "being produced" is unestablished for one of the two parties regarding the non-eternality of sound, even the proponent who has the means to prove it would have to remain silent.
And as for my claim that I shall establish the probative force of a witness who is devoid of attributes when there is a dispute,
he should be asked:
"Is this being established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that possesses attributes?"
And as for the claim that it is "without distinction":
not the first [alternative],
because that [distinction] is false for you.
Furthermore, since its status as a means of proof is not accepted according to the reasoning stated by the opponent,
he says "And that," meaning that the second [alternative] alone must be admitted.
What is from this?
This is from that.
Is that means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for establishing non-difference perception direct perception (sākṣāt) or something else?
In the first case, there is mutual dependence;
namely, that the establishment of the witness's status as a prover [depends on the object].
The second case is not tenable.
Because that [distinction] is absent;
he states the refutation regarding the acceptance of another non-distinction: "thus there is an infinite regress."
The word "iti" indicates the demonstration that the proving of even this non-distinction must be accomplished by the very same means of knowledge for non-distinction.
[Objection: But since it was the non-proving of non-distinction that was under discussion, it would be more appropriate to refer to it with the words "sā ca" (and that).
[Reply: True.

Nevertheless, although the capacity of that which was previously shown to be false to establish [an object] has already been refuted by the refutation of the alternatives regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must also be refuted by the refutation of the alternatives such as "possessing attributes" (*saviśeṣatva*) and so forth;
it is for the sake of indicating this that there is a general neuter reference.
By this, the position previously conceptualized—that [the means of knowledge] is existent and identical with the self (*ātman*)—should also be understood as refuted. *1,643*
For those who do not accept the reality of the universe, that [scripture] cannot be their teaching.
Therefore, all worldly transaction is established as being based on truth alone.

He concludes the reductio argument stated in the verse beginning with "If [you claim] falsity... (*mithyātvaṃ yadi...*) by saying, "by those who do not accept [it]," namely, that the status of being a proponent (*vāditva*) is untenable if one does not admit the existence of validity (*prāmāṇya*) and so forth.

Since it is thus the case that what is false lacks the capacity to establish anything, therefore, for those who do not accept the reality of the universe and who maintain that everything other than the Self is false, even sentences such as "not here, not there" (neha nānā) would result in being themselves false; consequently, they would possess neither the status of a proponent nor the capacity to prove their point.

The plural number used in the conclusion is intended to indicate that the singular number in the phrase "of that sentence" (tadvākyasya), which was under discussion, refers to a collection [of sentences].
Alternatively, this is a statement of another over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For it is as follows:

If everything other than consciousness were false, then even the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—which are included within "everything" and constitute the very basis for verbal discourse—would also be false.
Consequently, for the Māyāvādin who does not accept the reality of the universe but accepts its falsity, there could be no status as a speaker, as he would be without any means [of communication].
Why?
Therefore, as stated above, because that which is false cannot function as a constituent part of proof or refutation;

if it is argued that there is an inconsistency (vyabhicāra) because the Cārvākas and Buddhists— who accept the falsity of the entire universe— are nonetheless observed to be proponents of doctrines, we say no,
for they too are subjects of this very same logical consequence.
This refers to those who do not accept this [position], namely the Cārvākas, the Buddhists, and the Māyāvādins.
Otherwise, since the singular form "by you" (tvayā) and "by him" (tena) have been introduced, he would have said "those who do not accept" (anaṅgīkurvantaḥ).
Nevertheless, there is sublation by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇabādha).
This is not so, because the status of being a proponent (vāditva) among the Cārvākas and others is established by perception and other means of valid cognition;
for what is being proposed here is the absence of such proponent-status.
For a refutation consists in the sublation of a proof by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but not in the case of a reductio ad absurdum (*āpādana*),
because the latter has as its object that which is not [the proponent's] own tenet.

Since the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭha*) consists in the abandonment of what is authoritative and the acceptance of what is unauthoritative, and since otherwise there would be the consequence of the total destruction of all limits (due to over-extension), the author—intending to clarify that the stated [consequence] is indeed a *prasaṅga*—states its reduction to the contrary (*viparyaya-paryavasāna*): "There would be no consideration of the strength and weakness of the positions."
"Vyavahṛti" means that by which one transacts;
that is to say, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, which constitute the components of discourse.

Since the means of valid cognition and the rest are the causes for the transaction of discourse, and since the absence of the effect is easily established when there is an absence of the cause, [the definition] is well-established.
