In order to indicate that the "invariable concomitance" (pratibandha) is the root of the three undesirable consequences (atiprasaṅga), the term "pramāṇa and so forth" is employed through its etymological derivation (yaugika-pada), rather than by using the conventional term (rūḍha-pada).

[This is because] in the section concerning the desire to know (jijñāsādhikaraṇa), if one does not accept the existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth, the status of being a proponent (vāditva) would be untenable.

One might ask: "Granted that the conventional usage of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, which are constituent parts of the discourse, may be real; but what follows regarding the bondage consisting of suffering and the rest? To this, he says: "It is conventional" (*vyāvahārikam*).
Because this conventional discourse of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is real, that which is the object of convention, such as suffering and the like, is "conventional" (*vyāvahārika*).
The word "and" (*ca*) connects [the two senses]: not only is there convention, but there is also that which is conventional.
For it is not possible that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) does not exist while the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) exists.
The term "conventional" (*vyāvahārika*) was stated in order to demonstrate that there is no contradiction;
for it has been said here:
"For what reason does the proponent accept the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth?"

Is it because verbal discourse is necessarily pervaded by the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, such that it cannot be carried out in their absence; or because of its being a cause for the verbal discourse to be initiated by the debaters; or because it is established by worldly convention; or else because the non-acceptance of those [means] would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of both the determination of truth and victory?

Even regarding the first [alternative], is it merely conventional usage that is pervaded by the acceptance of the existence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, or is it a convention capable of establishing or subverting?

It cannot be the first, because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*): for even those such as the Cārvākas and Mādhyamikas who do not accept such [means] are observed to have extensive verbal discourse.
For if that very [object] is not established, your effort to refute it is untenable;
if that too is made the subject (*pakṣa*), there is sublation (*bādha*);
and in the second case, the state of sublation remains as it was.
Because my non-acceptance of "beings" (sattva) is established by experience,
your reason is unestablished;
or, if it were established, my desired conclusion would be proven.
Furthermore, in the case of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the presence of the definition of a pseudo-true statement (*sadvacanābhāsa*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

For, even while accepting the existence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) set forth by followers of one school are declared to be incapable of serving as proof and so forth when faced by others who follow a different school and likewise accept the existence of means of valid cognition and the rest.

From this it is known that the sole determinant for a statement being characterized as a semblance of true speech (*sad-vacanābhāsa*)—when it is incapable of establishing a conventional transaction (*vyavahāra*) and so forth—is precisely its possession of those characteristics; it is not the non-acceptance of its existence.
[Objection: But if the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the rest do not exist...
In that case, how could even conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) itself be established as having a subject (*dharmin*),
or how could the systematic arrangement of refutations and so forth occur? For all prescriptions and prohibitions are dependent upon valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Not so.
We do not say that a discussion is commenced by accepting that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the rest do not exist.
Rather, we mean that they are employed by you after being accepted by those who remain indifferent to the inquiry as to whether the means of valid cognition and the rest exist or do not exist.
Thus, let the discussion be carried on by those who engage in debate.
Furthermore, relying upon what kind of rule (*maryādā*) was this objection stated by you when the discussion proceeded?

Was it in a discussion conducted by both the proponent and the opponent having accepted the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; or having accepted their non-existence; or having accepted existence by one and non-existence by the other?
Not the first,
because for one who accepts the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, there is no occasion for such an objection.
Not the second.
Because it would lead to the same consequence for oneself;
nor the third,
because it would result in the introduction of an entirely different discussion.

Therefore, when a discussion has been set in motion after binding an agreement regarding the regulation of conventional usage, remaining indifferent to the acceptance of the existence or non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth;
It must be said that this objection has been stated by you;
thus, there is a contradiction. Nor should it be argued that this objection is not being addressed to the opponent.

What indeed is meant by [the statement] that disciples and others are informed that one who does not accept the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth has no entitlement to engage in debate?
For even with respect to disciples and others, it must be stated that this same fault applies to the Cārvāka and his ilk. And how could that be the case?
Because, whether or not one enters into that discussion, one is incapable of understanding it;
for defeat occurs only within the discussion itself,
not in the second case.

This might be the case if the causality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth with respect to the verbal discourse initiated by a debater were to cease upon the non-acceptance of their existence;
however, this is not possible.
For if that were so, the very nature of the verbal discourse of those who do not accept their existence would not even be established.
Because the reason is untenable.
Now, you might think:
"The existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth is established because they serve as reasons for the discourse of the debater."
And as for the claim that "because of existence there is acceptance, since whatever exists is accepted"—
this is not so.

For when a discussion proceeds according to some established rule of debate, the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth must first be established by you, because they serve as the cause for the verbal discourse of the disputants.
Prior to the debate, however, the two debaters—who desire either the ascertainment of truth or victory over the opponent—must observe whatever is necessary for that desired end to be fulfilled.
Since this is possible for both of them only through a binding agreement on the rules of formal procedure (*vyavahāra-niyama-samaya-bandha*), they enter into such a rule.
And that rule takes the form: "One must proceed by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*)," and so forth.
Nor is it appropriate for the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth to be accepted by those two [the proponent and opponent] in this very same way;
for the commencement of the debate is established by the mere rule of such conventional usage alone.

Even if one accepts the existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth, without such a rule of conventional usage and without the commencement of the debate, the desired determination of truth or victory cannot be achieved for the two debaters.
Nor is it the third [alternative].
For worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) would have to be either the convention of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyavahāra*) or the convention common to ordinary people and the like.
It cannot be the first.
Because it is difficult to define that [object] without the activity of investigation (*vicāra*),
and because the restriction was previously sought precisely for that purpose;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable.

If that were the case, you would be forced to accept [the existence] of the body, the self, and so forth as well. If you argue that these are not accepted because they are subsequently sublated by inquiry, then the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so on must likewise not be accepted if they are sublatable by inquiry; otherwise, they must be admitted. Thus, existence is accepted simply because it is established by worldly convention.
Thus, it is not the case that [the first three alternatives] do not exist;
nor is it the fourth,
because you yourself, having accepted the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, rely upon a fixed rule of discourse during debate.
For we too adopt that very [position] with indifference toward the pursuit of whether means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth exist or do not exist.
If that [position] leads to an over-extension of the consequence (*atiprasañjaka*) for me, then the same consequence applies equally to you as well.

Therefore, since there is no utility for discourse in the acceptance of the existence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, it is untenable to claim that those who do not accept the existence of means of valid cognition and so forth are not speakers (*vādin*). All of this is to be understood as having been ridiculed by him [the author], for instance: * Since the existence of means of valid cognition and so forth is not accepted, the very status of being a "speaker" is impossible for one who does not accept them. * Furthermore, if one does not accept the existence of means of valid cognition, the distinction between a "proponent" (*vādin*) and an "opponent" (*prativādin*) cannot be established. * Moreover, if one does not accept the existence of means of valid cognition, the refutation of the opponent's position would be impossible. * Finally, if one does not accept the existence of means of valid cognition, the establishment of one's own position would also be impossible. Thus, all these arguments are rendered laughable. To explain: [The opponent might argue: "If you say that because we do not accept the existence of means of valid cognition we are not speakers, then by that same logic, you yourself are not a speaker because you do not accept the existence of means of valid cognition. [The author replies: This is not so; for even without accepting the existence of means of valid cognition, the status of being a speaker is possible through the mere acknowledgment of the conventional reality of things. It is like saying, "I am not a speaker because I do not accept the existence of the self," which is a fallacious argument. Therefore, the objection that those who do not accept the existence of means of valid cognition cannot be speakers is invalid. This is what is meant by "all of this is to be understood as having been ridiculed. Thus it is said: "Since the existence of means of valid cognition and so forth is not accepted, the status of being a speaker is impossible for one who does not accept them. Furthermore, without accepting the existence of means of valid cognition, the distinction between proponent and opponent cannot be established. Moreover, without accepting the existence of means of valid cognition, the refutation of the opponent's position would be impossible, and the establishment of one's own position would likewise be impossible. This concludes the section on the refutation of the opponent's objection regarding the impossibility of discourse for those who do not accept the existence of means of valid cognition. Now, the following is the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s omniscience. [The opponent argues: "If the Blessed One were omniscient, he would have to know everything simultaneously. However, since he knows things sequentially, he is not omniscient. Furthermore, if he were to know everything at once, he would be like a lamp illuminating all objects simultaneously, which contradicts the nature of consciousness. Therefore, the Blessed One is not omniscient. [The author replies: This is not so; for the Blessed One’s knowledge is unimpeded and functions without effort, unlike the sequential knowledge of ordinary beings. Just as a powerful king can command his subjects to act simultaneously, the Blessed One’s wisdom perceives all objects without succession. Therefore, the objection that the Buddha is not omniscient because he knows sequentially is invalid. This is what is meant by "the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s omniscience. Thus it is said: "The objection that the Blessed One is not omniscient because he knows sequentially is invalid; for his knowledge is unimpeded and functions without effort, perceiving all objects simultaneously like a powerful king. This concludes the section on the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s omniscience. Now, the following is the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s teaching. [The opponent argues: "If the Blessed One were omniscient, he would teach the Dharma to others. However, since he has entered into the state of cessation (*nirodha*), he does not teach anything. Therefore, he is not omniscient. [The author replies: This is not so; for although the Blessed One has entered into cessation, his previous vows and the power of his compassion ensure that his teaching continues to benefit sentient beings. It is like a drum that continues to sound after the striker has withdrawn. Therefore, the objection that the Buddha is not omniscient because he does not teach while in cessation is invalid. This is what is meant by "the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s teaching. Thus it is said: "The objection that the Blessed One is not omniscient because he does not teach while in cessation is invalid; for his teaching continues to benefit sentient beings through the power of his previous vows and compassion, like a drum that sounds after the striker has withdrawn. This concludes the section on the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s teaching. Now, the following is the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s liberation. [The opponent argues: "If the Blessed One were liberated, he would be free from all defilements. However, since he still possesses a physical body, he is not liberated. [The author replies: This is not so; for the Blessed One’s physical body is merely a manifestation of his skillful means for the sake of sentient beings, and does not constitute a source of bondage. His true nature is that of complete liberation. Therefore, the objection that the Buddha is not liberated because he possesses a physical body is invalid. This is what is meant by "the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s liberation. Thus it is said: "The objection that the Blessed One is not liberated because he possesses a physical body is invalid; for his body is a manifestation of skillful means, and his true nature is that of complete liberation. This concludes the section on the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s liberation. Now, the following is the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s permanence. [The opponent argues: "If the Blessed One were permanent, he would be eternal and unchanging. However, since he undergoes birth and death, he is not permanent. [The author replies: This is not so; for the Blessed One’s permanence refers to the continuity of his dharmakāya, which is unconditioned and beyond birth and death. His appearance in the world is merely a display of his compassion for the sake of sentient beings. Therefore, the objection that the Buddha is not permanent because he undergoes birth and death is invalid. This is what is meant by "the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s permanence. Thus it is said: "The objection that the Blessed One is not permanent because he undergoes birth and death is invalid; for his permanence refers to the continuity of his dharmakāya, which is unconditioned and beyond birth and death. This concludes the section on the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s permanence. [The opponent argues: "If the Blessed One were non-dual, he would be identical with emptiness. However, since he possesses various qualities such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, he is not non-dual. [The author replies: This is not so; for these qualities are merely designations within the realm of conventional truth, whereas his ultimate nature is that of non-dual emptiness. Therefore, the objection that the Buddha is not non-dual because he possesses various qualities is invalid. This is what is meant by "the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s non-duality. Thus it is said: "The objection that the Blessed One is not non-dual because he possesses various qualities is invalid; for these qualities are conventional designations, while his ultimate nature is that of non-dual emptiness. This concludes the section on the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s non-duality. Now, the following is the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s ineffability. [The opponent argues: "If the Blessed One were ineffable, he could not teach the Dharma. However, since he teaches the Dharma, he is not ineffable. [The author replies: This is not so; for the Blessed One’s teaching is itself an expression of his ineffable nature, transcending all conceptual constructs. Therefore, the objection that the Buddha is not ineffable because he teaches the Dharma is invalid. This is what is meant by "the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s ineffability. Thus it is said: "The objection that the Blessed One is not ineffable because he teaches the Dharma is invalid; for his teaching is an expression of his ineffable nature, transcending all conceptual constructs. This concludes the section on the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s ineffability. Now, the following is the refutation of the objection concerning the impossibility of the Buddha’s absence of activity. [The opponent argues: "If the Blessed One were without activity, he would be like a stone. However, since he performs acts of compassion, he is not without activity. [The author replies: This is not so; for the Blessed One’s "activity" is actually the absence of activity, as he is free from all mental effort and conceptualization. His apparent activity is merely a reflection

As for the objection that was stated regarding the position that mere worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is necessarily pervaded by the acceptance of the existence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—
that is incorrect;
for we would indeed establish it in this manner only if such were the case.

The proponent of illusion (māyāvādī) accepts the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, because he engages in worldly discourse; or rather, his discourse is preceded by the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth, because it is a form of discourse, just like the discourse of one who speaks of reality and just like that very discourse itself.

Alternatively, this person is not a conventional agent because he does not accept the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; or his activity is not a [true] convention because it is devoid of being preceded by the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth.
In that case, there would certainly be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Who indeed, being of sound mind, would infer in this manner?
For what reason would it be that if the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth exist, they should not exist?
In that case, they would not be effective means of proof,
because it is impossible for what is non-existent to function as a means of proof;
and if those [means] were not effective, the conventional activity resulting from them could not be accomplished.
And thus, there would be no capacity for speech;
yet this [capacity] exists.
Therefore, the existence of its causes—namely, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—must be admitted, because the Teacher intends this as a *prasanga* (reductio ad absurdum).

Furthermore, it has been accepted that the locus of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is equivalent to the subject matter of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*). Moreover, it has been stated that sublation (*bādha*) is indeed a figure of speech for the reductio.

Even under the view that the capacity for the conventional practice of proving and refuting is pervaded by the acceptance of the existence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, the aforementioned objection is refuted by this very point.

If one were to take either the proponent of illusionism (māyāvādin) or his conventional practice as the subject, and then seek to prove— by means of the reasons "being an agent of qualified conventional practice" or "being a qualified conventional practice"— that he accepts the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, or that [such practice] is preceded by them, then the following would be the case:
"The disputed conventional practice is not capable of establishing the means of proof (*sādhana*) and so forth."

Alternatively, if the proof is stated as "because it is devoid of being preceded by the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth," then the previously mentioned *upādhi* would apply if there were some form of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
However, it has already been stated that this is not the case.
Furthermore, this *upādhi* does not differ from the probans (*sādhana*).

For when the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is not accepted, then their non-existence itself is admitted; thus, there is the fault of the [reason] being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). And that is precisely the specific characteristic of what is called a "semblance of a true statement" (*sad-vacanābhāsa*). Now, as for the objection raised by saying, "We do not say this," and so forth—that was poorly stated.

Since it is impossible to superimpose the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) upon the intellect while abandoning both existence and non-existence, it is illogical for one who is indifferent [to such categories] to accept it.
Furthermore, that which was intended as "indescribable" (*anirvacanīya*) by one speaking in this manner will be refuted later on.
As for what was stated here regarding "what kind of boundary," and so forth:

In this regard, we state that this refutation is directed against one who accepts the non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, as well as against one who, even while perceiving their existence, remains indifferent toward it, thinking "I am [indifferent]. Thus,
the aforementioned fault does not apply.
We do not claim that the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth must necessarily precede the commencement of debate as its cause.

Rather, we show the opponent—who has engaged in debate in some manner—the penalty that debate would otherwise become impossible, and thereby compel them to accept the existence of those causes, namely the *pramāṇas* and so forth.
Nor does this entail the fault of falling into another debate and the like.

If one does not accept the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, the very discussion (*kathā*) cannot be established. By this, the instruction of the student is also resolved;

for it has been stated that, having accepted the opponent’s entry into the discussion, one who engages therein must necessarily accept the existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth as the cause, by virtue of the force of the effect—the discussion already established.
The fault stated regarding the second position is likewise irrelevant;

for we do not include even the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth within the category of causes for the verbal discourse that must be initiated by the debater.
If we did, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the very nature of verbal discourse could not be established for those who do not accept their existence.
Rather, we maintain that it is precisely the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth that constitute the cause of discourse;
and since that [discourse] would not be possible in the absence of their existence, their existence must be admitted.
As for what was said in response to the initial objection concerning the linguistic usage of the disputants:
“By saying this, you must admit the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth at a time subsequent to the commencement of the debate.
And thus, the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth—which is the fruit of the debate—cannot be the cause of the debate;
rather, it is only the rule of conventional practice, such as ‘one must operate by means of the means of valid cognition,’ that is the cause.”
That is indeed already accepted by us;
however, as for one who asserts that even the acceptance of existence (*sattā*) is a prerequisite for engaging in discourse,
he alone should be questioned in this manner:
Furthermore, regarding the statement beginning with "nor [is there] of the means of valid cognition, etc.," which spoke of the complexity of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-gaurava*):
does this complexity of conceptual construction arise from the admission of the existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth, or from including that admission within the category of causes?
It is not the first.
Because its existence is established by the fact that its status as a cause would otherwise be untenable,
and because what has been so established must be accepted by investigators;
whereas in the second case, there is simply agreement.
Regarding the third [point], we first accept the first [part];
what was stated therein has already been largely refuted.
Even if the second [part] were accepted, there would be no fault.
However, such things as the identity of the body with the self are not accepted because they are subsequently sublated by inquiry.
As for what was stated here regarding "the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth," what is meant by that?
Is it that the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is not the cause for the commencement of inquiry?
Or is it that because the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition and so forth is itself sublated by inquiry, it cannot serve as the basis for conventional discourse?
Regarding the first [alternative], there is agreement.
Not the second [alternative],
because in the view that intrinsic validity (*autsargika-prāmāṇya*) is set aside by a sublater (*bādhaka*), that very [sublater] is the determining factor.
Furthermore, the fault stated regarding the fourth position is also refuted by this very [point].
We do not say that the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is the cause for the accomplishment of the fruit of debate;
rather, it is the means of valid cognition themselves.
And since their status as causes is not possible if they are non-existent, their existence must necessarily be accepted.
It might be argued as follows:
even by one who initiates a discussion through a binding agreement on the rules for verbal expression within a fixed context, the existence of linguistic convention must be admitted;
for it is impossible to describe the activity of linguistic convention without admitting its existence.
For action (*kriyā*) is indeed accomplishment; that is to say, it is the attainment of the state of existence for that which was previously non-existent.

Furthermore, the restriction that "the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be brought forth" involves a binding rule because the status of being an instrument of valid cognition is included within that very restriction. Thus, without adopting the nature of causality—which consists in having a fixed prior existence—the [status of being a means of valid cognition] cannot be established.

Furthermore, by the very act of asserting the refutation of objections through the determination of their negation and the binding of rules, and by the determination of the conventional usage of the reality-status of the objects of proof— such as the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other members of the syllogism (*sādhana*)— through their existence,
you have explicitly admitted the existence of each of those very things. Is this not so?
This is what is being said:

having raised the objection that the commencement of a debate is possible even without accepting the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, it was stated that even by these [objections], once a debate has begun, there can be no escape from the previously mentioned refutation, because that which is intended must be established.
That too has been refuted by this very [argument]:

since the acceptance of the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth— which is itself voluntarily adopted as a rule of discourse for the sake of accomplishing the completion of the nature of the debate—
results ultimately in nothing other than that very acceptance, we are speaking to one who, having entered into the debate, is not even aware of his own self-contradiction.
Now, if the effect such as discourse exists, one must somehow admit the existence of its causes, such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued, "Since the effect itself lacks existence, what is the use of the existence of a cause?
[we reply: From what means of valid cognition have you determined the non-existence of discourse and so forth?
If it is argued that this is so because of scripture (*śruti*) and other authorities, we say no;
for those very sources are themselves mired in a dense thicket of numerous fallacies and over-extensions (*atiprasaṅga*).
Thus, once their authority is established, the non-existence of the effects of debate and the like is proven.

Consequently, the fallacious nature of the reasoning (*tarka*) would be established by that [other] "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhi*), and upon that being established, the validity of the *śruti* and other authorities would be established; thus, due to the occurrence of a circular argument (*cakraka*), not even one of them could be established.

Furthermore, the status of the non-existent as a cause will be refuted by the author of the Sūtras himself, so enough of this digression. *The Refutation of the Capacity of Empirical Reality to Establish [Truth]* (2.46)
And its status as a means of proof from the perspective of conventional reality is also as stated before.
This might be so,
provided that we were to accept the non-existence of everything other than the Self on the strength of such passages as "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*);
but it is not so, for what indeed is accepted is merely conventional existence (*vyāvahārikī sattā*).

And thus, since it is possible for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—which fall within all [categories]—to be established as existing conventionally (*vyavahārasat*), the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not follow; therefore, he says: "and as existing conventionally."
The word *ca* indicates a reason;
the word *api* indicates conjunction;
the word *tu* indicates restriction.

Even from the perspective of conventional reality (*vyavahārasat*), the capacity to prove [the thesis] is not established for the opponent, just as it was not established for the previous [proponent] who held it to be non-existent; therefore, there is no escape from the aforementioned logical consequence (*prasaṅga*).
This is the meaning:
if that which is called "conventionally existent" were indeed truly existent, then the demonstration of its falsity would be contradictory.
And the tree of our desire has borne fruit;
the term "worldly affairs" has become meaningless.
Now, if that [worldly state] is non-existent, what further has he done?
Because the undesirable consequence—that in the absence of an existent entity (sattva), there would be no capacity for proof—remains as it was.
Now, one might object: "Existence is indeed twofold: primary (mukhya) and secondary (amukhya).
Among these, that which is not sublated in any manner whatsoever is the primary existence, and it is called ultimate (pāramārthika)."
But for that whose very existence is its cognition, it is a non-primary existent; and from such [an existent], existence is not established. For instance:
Do you think that the existence of a thing is accepted merely from its cognition, or rather from its uncontradicted cognition?
Not the first,
because it would lead to the absurd consequence of accepting the actual existence of water-form in a mirage and similar phenomena.
Even in the second case, it is not so, because among the proponent, the opponent, and the neutral arbiter, there is likewise no cognition of its being sublated at the very time of the discussion;
or rather, because there is an absence of any cognition of its being sublated for anyone, even at another time.
Not the first [alternative].
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For we frequently observe that even what was understood by three persons, or what was understood in a single moment, is sublated by another person or at another moment.

Furthermore, one does not accept that such an object remains existent in that very same way—even though it is unreal—merely out of deference to the cognitions previously produced by two or three persons, even when sublation has already occurred.
Therefore, the second position remains;
and since that [existence] does not exist in the non-primary sense, how could there be the attainment of ultimate reality?
Nor should it be argued that even for the cognition of existence, existence itself is merely another cognition, which would lead to an infinite regress.
Because cognition is ultimately real;
for there is no sublation of it.
If there were such sublation, that very cognition would be uncontradicted and thus ultimately real.
And since there is no difference in the essential nature of cognition itself, consciousness is therefore Brahman alone as ultimate reality.
The non-primary [consciousness], however, is twofold:
that which has *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and that which has *avidyā* as its limiting adjunct.
Among these, the first consists of ether and so forth.
Because it remains uncontradicted until the knowledge of Brahman arises, and because it facilitates worldly transactions such as rejection and acceptance, it is called "empirical" (vyāvahārika).
Indeed, worldly transaction is understood to proceed merely from the realization of its reality for certain perceivers over a certain period of time.

The second is [the error of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like; however, it is not called "merely apparent" (prātibhāsika) because it does not merely disappear at the time of its perception, nor because it is not a cause for rejection and so forth.

Thus, since there are these three kinds of existence, it is logical that the universe, consisting of ether and so forth, is "false" (mithyā) despite being existent, because it lacks ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva).

Furthermore, because it possesses empirical reality (vyāvahārikasattva), the validity of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and other factors included therein is established as a constituent of discourse.
Moreover, the term "empirical" (vyāvahārika) is possible as a qualifier intended to exclude both ultimate and apparent reality. To this, the following must be said:

Is the threefold nature of existence such that what is ultimately real is itself divided into two types—existent and non-existent—based on the distinction of sublation; or is it that there is only one type of existent, which possesses internal subdivisions?
In the first case, the previously mentioned fault cannot be avoided;
for something is not capable of performing an unreal causal function merely by virtue of being known as "existent."
By means of which such [flawed] means of valid cognition and so forth would attain the status of being a constituent of debate;
for if that were the case, even poison, when perceived as nectar, would perform its intended function.
Because it would entail the consequence that there is sublation, delay, or a lack of causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*).
As for the claim that worldly convention is perceived in exactly that way, that will be refuted later.
If it is argued that even causal efficacy is non-existent, that has already been rejected through arguments such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
If it is argued that because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is possible for what exists, it must somehow be admitted even for what is unreal, [we reply:
this is only after the authority of scripture has been ascertained.
How is the opponent to be convinced when, prior to that ascertainment, he maintains that causal efficiency belongs only to that which is ultimately real?

It has been stated that this would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and so forth. Regarding the threefold nature of existence and its indeterminability, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is refuted; for it must be asked: by what means of valid cognition could that threefold nature be established? (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 1.22cd)
Even for that [position], there is no proof whatsoever in the manner described;
by this, the distinction between existence and non-existence is also refuted.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "And the threefold nature of existence..."
The meaning of "by what" is: by that which is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), or conventionally real (*vyāvahārikasat*), or appearance-real (*prātibhāsikasat*).
Regarding the first case as well, the sense is: "Is it by something other than the self, or by the self?"—this is the question we are asking; such is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The meaning is: "And likewise" refers to the question, "By what means would the capacity to prove [an object] be established for that which is false?
Or, it refers to that which was put forward to establish the capacity to prove for that which exists conventionally (*vyāvahārikasat*).
He says, "Of that too," because being the very subject of the inquiry is not a fault.

Just as there is no proof for the capacity of a non-existent thing to establish [anything], so too that threefold existence is not established in any of the various conceptualized positions whatsoever.
Why? Precisely in the manner already stated.
For instance: the self does not possess ultimate existence as something other than [the aggregates], because that would entail the consequence of duality.
Nor can it be established by itself,
because that which is devoid of distinctions cannot function as a prover;
furthermore, even now, the very nature of both the conventional and the apparent has not been established.
That which is not primary is not "existent," even if it possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence;
for [if it were so], the aforementioned fault would follow.
Rather, it is inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*).
Nor is that difficult to explain,
for it is precisely the distinctness from both the existent and the non-existent;
and that, as previously stated, is twofold due to the distinction between the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and the apparent (*prātibhāsika*).

In this regard, since the empirical world (*vyāvahārika-prapañca*), which is distinct from both the real and the unreal, is distinct from the real, its falsity (*mithyātva*) is established by scripture and other means;
and because it is distinct from the unreal, the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth contained within it possess the capacity to prove [objects].
This would be so in some way if the universe were indeed distinct from both the real and the unreal.
He says that this very point is not established: "The difference between existence and non-existence."
The word "of the universe" (*viśvasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
In the phrase "of the existent and non-existent" (*sadasatoḥ*), the genitive case indicates mere relationship;
thus, the meaning is "by means of the existent and the non-existent" (*sadasadbhyām*).
By this—
namely, by the refutation of the conceptualization of valid cognition—
it is as follows:
Is the difference of the universe from both the existent and the non-existent established by a means of valid cognition that is existent, or by one that is non-existent,
or by one that is distinct from both existent and non-existent?
Not the first,
because a proponent [of that view] is untenable;
nor the second or third.
[The opponent replies: "Because the respondent does not agree.

[The proponent asks: "But surely, in this case, one must state the reductio (*prasaṅga*) that there would be no capacity to prove [the point] regarding the distinction between existence and non-existence;
yet, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) in that regard."
Not so;
for it is possible to ascertain the pervasion (vyāpti) with respect to the witness itself.
Alternatively, we shall state a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga): that if existence were absent, its status as a means of proof would not obtain.
If it is argued that "non-existence" (*asattva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) there, we say no;
for that [non-existence] does not exceed the absence of existence (*sattvābhāva*),
and because it is impossible to establish the refutation of that [absence] prior to the proof of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).

By this, the argument that the proof of falsity (*mithyātva*) is established because of being distinct from the real (*sad-vilakṣaṇatva*), and that the status of being a means of proof (*sādhakatva*) is likewise established, is refuted.

For if there were distinction from the real, it would follow that it is non-existent (*asattva*), resulting in the absence of the status of being a means of proof; and if there were distinction from the non-existent (*asad-vilakṣaṇatva*), it would follow that it is existent, resulting in the impossibility of establishing falsity.
Furthermore, since the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) has not yet been proven, it is impossible to refute the two types of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
If the practical usage of "rejection" and so forth were established merely by the distinction from the non-existent, then that [usage] would also follow in the case of shell-silver and the like.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā*, we say no,
because that [distinction] will be refuted later.
This is because mere distinctness is irrelevant to the present context.
Or, let us set aside the formulation of the refutation by means of the rejection of the alternatives such as existence (*sattva*);
the very proof for the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is not tenable.

The scriptural passage beginning with "neha nānāsti" (here there is no diversity) does not state that the universe is indeterminable, characterized by its difference from both the real and the unreal.
For one who asserts that even the real is itself diverse, how could the universe—which is also unreal—be non-different from it? (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 1.24)
Now, one might think:

"The subject of dispute is distinct from both existence and non-existence because it is sublated by knowledge; whatever is so is thus, just as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. This inference is the proof for the world's being distinct from both existence and non-existence.
By the force of this, even the Śruti ultimately culminates in that very point."
That is incorrect.

Intending to show that the inference is fallacious, and because it is encountered first, he first refutes the proposition (pratijñā) with the words: "The difference from the existent... (vailakṣaṇyaṃ sataśca).
The word *ca* (and) serves to restrict;
the two words *api* (also) serve to connect [the terms] mutually.
This is the meaning.
In this context, do the words "existent" (sat) and "non-existent" (asat) denote existence and non-existence,
or do they denote that which is present and that which is absent? Regarding the first alternative, the refutation follows.

In my view, which maintains the distinction between existence and non-existence, the difference of the world—which is existent and of the nature of being—from that which is non-existent and of the nature of non-existence, is itself truly existent.

Likewise, for the proponent of difference, the difference of the world—which is non-existent and of the nature of non-existence—from that which is existent and of the nature of being, is itself truly existent.
Therefore, how could that which has been established by him result in something undesirable for me?

What indeed would be the "irrelevancy" (arthāntaratā) for the opponent, such that even by establishing the distinction between existence and non-existence through such a division, the intended thesis would nonetheless be proven? // 1 //

And if it is intended that there is a distinction from both existence and non-existence for each individual thing, then for me, who maintains the doctrine of the differentiation of entities, the universe— which is an existing entity— is itself indeed existent because of its distinction from other entities, since I accept its distinction from other entities.

For one who asserts a distinction between existence and non-existence, the difference from non-existence— which itself lacks being— is all the more clearly existent; likewise, for one who asserts a distinction within non-existence, the difference of the world’s non-existence from [other] non-existences— which themselves lack being— is itself existent,
because they admit its distinction from other non-existences.

Since the distinctness from existence is itself necessarily existent, how could it be unestablished by that [existence]? (2) *2,77* If it is argued that what is intended by "distinctness from existence and non-existence" is the state of not being the locus of reality (*tattva*),
even so, for the world which is an existing entity, its distinctness from non-existent non-existence— that is, its state of not being the locus of non-existence— is itself existent.
Even the distinction of the non-existent universe— which is an absence— from existence, namely its not being a locus of existence, is itself existent for me,
because I maintain the doctrine of the difference between existence and non-existence.
For if I were to admit that existence possesses non-existence and non-existence possesses existence, how then could there be a doctrine of the difference between existence and non-existence?
And so, how could that which is being established by him not be my own desired conclusion? (3)
Now, if it should be thought that what is intended is the state of not being the locus of both existence and non-existence for each [entity] individually,

then even for the world as an existing entity (*sat*), its distinction from existence and non-existence— that is, its state of not being the locus of the nature of existence and non-existence— is itself inherently existent (*sat*). Likewise, even for the world as a non-existing entity (*asat*), its aforementioned distinction from existence and non-existence is itself inherently existent.
For those who maintain the distinction between existence and non-existence do not admit that a single entity possesses both natures;
for in the case of existence, there is only the nature of existence,
and not the nature of non-existence as well.
And in the case of non-existence, there is only non-existence;
it is not existence either. Therefore, how could that which has been established by him result in anything undesirable for me? (4)

Now, one might think that for each individual entity, what is intended to be proven is its non-being the locus of existence (*bhāvatvānadhikaraṇatva*) and its non-being the locus of non-existence (*abhāvatvānadhikaraṇatva*).

Even so, for me, the world—which is an existing entity—possesses the quality of not being the locus of non-existence simply because it is distinct from non-existent non-existence; thus, it is itself existent.
Likewise, the world—which is non-existent non-existence—possesses the quality of not being the locus of existence simply because it is distinct from existent existence; thus, it is itself existent.
Because he is a proponent of the distinction between existence and non-existence, how could his position not be undesirable? For,
since one part [of his argument] establishes a point already proven, it results in the defeat of the opponent.

If it is argued that there is no fault because both [the universal and the particular] are the means of proof, we say no; for even when the unestablished [particular] is present, the established [universal] does not lose its nature.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the proof of a qualified [entity], we say no.
Nevertheless, this does not avoid futility.

(5) *2.86* If it is argued that no such fault applies because one is proving that what is intended to be an entity lacks the property of being an entity, and what is intended to be a non-entity lacks the property of being a non-entity, we say: no.

Nevertheless, even for the world which exists as a real entity (*bhāva*), its distinctness from existence—that is, its non-inherence in the property of being an entity (*bhāvatva*)—is itself inherently existent.

How is it that for one who asserts a difference in the property of being an entity, there is not just one single *bhāvatva* that is common to all entities? Rather, does the property of being an entity not differ with each individual entity?
And this will be established later;
likewise, even an existent entity (bhāva) will be a substratum for another existence.

In this way, even for the universe which is non-existent and of the nature of absence (abhāva), its distinction from non-existence—namely, its not being a locus of non-existence—is itself existent for me.
How so?
Because even for one who maintains that there is no difference in the nature of non-existence, they must admit that within non-existence itself there is no further distinct nature of non-existence;
and thus, how could that which is not established by him come to be?
Because for the opponent alone, the state of having established the thesis is not avoided. // 6 //
Now, if the intended meaning is that for those things regarded as existence and non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence exists in any way whatsoever;
even so, the very fact that an existing entity is distinct from the non-existent—its not being a locus of non-existence—is itself existent.
Therefore, how could the world, established by that [distinction], fail to be what the proponents of difference (bhedavādin) desire?
This is what is meant:
if antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest are made the subject (*pakṣa*) and it is proven that they are "not the locus of the property of being non-existence" (*abhāvatvānadhikaraṇa*),
then their status as positive entities (*bhāvatva*) would be asserted.
Because it is a rule that an existent (bhāva) cannot be the locus of non-existence;
for two negatives convey the original meaning with an intensification.
Thus, if one were to take space and so forth as the subject and prove that they are not the locus of existence, it would amount to asserting their non-existence.
Because it is a rule that non-existence itself cannot be the locus of existence;
for non-existence is simply the negation of existence.

And since the opponent has accepted the distinction between existence and non-existence regarding the universe, there is nothing undesirable for me, who maintains the distinction between existence and non-existence.
However, it is merely a reversal of existence and non-existence;
and the proof for that is irrelevant to the subject at hand.

(7) *2,91* Since the two things intended as "existence" and "non-existence" are agreed upon by both the proponent and the opponent to not be the loci of non-existence and existence respectively, the property of "not being the locus of existence and non-existence" is further established [as their common characteristic].
If it is argued that, therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply, we say no;
because the distinction of the existent world— including space and so forth— from the non-existent is itself existent, as it consists in being a non-locus of non-existence,
and this is indeed established by valid cognition.

And because the distinction of the non-existent— the world, its prior non-existence, and so forth— from the existent consists precisely in its being non-substantive (the absence of the property of being a positive entity), it is itself existent; indeed,
it is established by valid cognition that this very distinction of the non-existent from the existent is itself existent.
Therefore, how could there be a lack of necessity for the proponent of difference on account of that which he has asserted in a contrary manner?
Indeed, a lack of necessity would exist only if the matter asserted were established;
for this [assertion] cannot be established when it is sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which has as its object existence and non-existence on the conventional level is sublated by inference alone whose object is reality (*tattva*), we say no.
For, according to us, the means of valid cognition whose object is existence and non-existence has reality itself as its object;
otherwise, there would follow the fallacy of a circular argument (*cakraka*) and other such over-extensions (*atiprasaṅga*). // 8 //
To this second point as well, the same answer applies:
even my own distinction of the existent universe from the real is simply my own opinion;
likewise, its distinction from the non-existent or the unreal is also simply my own.
Therefore, how could there be anything undesirable for me by that being established?
Let it be that the self is distinct from the world, like a rabbit's horn;
but how can it be distinct from existence itself?
If it is argued that [the world] is real because it is accepted as such, it is not so.
For me, who asserts the distinction between the existent and the non-existent even while the existent exists, the very fact that the universe is distinct from the non-existent is self-evident;
likewise, for one who asserts the distinction between existents, the very fact that the existent universe is distinct from other existents is self-evident.
Because of its distinction from all other existing things. // 9 //
If it is argued that "being neither existent nor non-existent" means being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent,
even then, for one who asserts a distinction between the existent and the non-existent, the existence's difference from the non-existent is itself existent.
Therefore, how could that which has been established by him be undesirable for me?
If it were argued that the very point already established for the opponent would be proven [by this],

and thus "not being the locus of existence" (*sattvānadhikaraṇatva*) alone is what is being proved, we say no. For for me, the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), the fact of not being the locus of existence— which is simply the distinction of the non-existent from the existent— is itself necessarily existent.
And thus, since the non-existence of the universe would follow from proving by that [reason] its non-being the locus of existence, it would be an undesirable consequence for the opponent alone.
How could there be an undesirable consequence for me, who am refuting the opponent through the employment of an undesirable consequence?

(10) *2,95* Now, if it is argued: "Since the fact of not being the locus of non-existence is established for both the proponent and the opponent, the additional property of not being the locus of existence is also being proved," we say no.
Because it is not established as being undesirable.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a single, pervasive "existence" (*sattva*); rather, existence differs with each individual object.

In that context, when establishing for space (*viyat*) and other such things the property of not being the locus of existence—given that they differ from non-existence—is this intended to mean not being the locus of one existence, or not being the locus of multiple existences, or not being the locus of all existences?
Does this mean not being the locus of unqualified existents,
or rather is it intended to mean not being the locus of existents in any way whatsoever?
It is not the first.

Just as the universe possesses a distinctness even though it is non-existent, so too do I possess a distinctness even though I am existent; moreover, my not being the locus of existence is likewise inherent.
How so?
Because for me, who maintains the doctrine of the difference of existents (*sattva-bheda-vādin*), it is accepted that even what is existent does not have another existent as its locus.
And thus, how could there be an undesirable consequence for me by means of that [reason] which is already established and being used to prove [the thesis]?
In this very same way, the refutation of the fourth [alternative] is also to be explained.
The second and third [alternatives] are not [possible].
The distinction of the universe from the non-existent is, for me, simply its not being the locus of non-existence; the distinction from the existent is its not being the locus of multiple existents;
and its not being the locus of any existence whatsoever is, for me, simply itself.
Its distinction from existence (*sat*) consists in not being the locus of multiple existents.
Furthermore, its not being the locus of all existents is itself existent.
How so?
For one who maintains the doctrine of difference, each individual object is not accepted by all sentient beings; and if it were so accepted, the distinction [between them] would be destroyed.
Consequently, how could that which is undesirable for him come to pass?
Not the fifth,
because the very distinction of the non-existent from the existent is itself that [non-existence],
which necessarily exists.

And since the distinction of the existent from the non-existent is likewise necessarily fixed, how could it not be undesirable for the proponent of difference (bhedavādin) that the universe, by being established through that [distinction], would result in being both existent and non-existent?
For I have indeed accepted the existence and non-existence of one and the same thing:
because it is not the counter-positive of negation with respect to its own limiting adjunct (upādhi), yet it is the counter-positive of negation with respect to another's limiting adjunct.

If it is asked, "Since both [existence and non-existence] are in every way negated, how can there be the consequence of being either existent or non-existent?"—then the distinctness of the existent from the non-existent is itself necessarily established as existent. Therefore, having stated the distinctness of the existent, how could the proponent of difference (bhedavādin) not be contradicted by asserting a distinctness of the non-existent that is itself contradictory?

Likewise, since the distinctness of the non-existent from the existent is also necessarily established, having stated the distinctness of the non-existent, one must see that the subsequent assertion of the universe's distinctness from the existent is likewise contradicted.
Indeed, this contradiction cannot be avoided prior to the establishment of the "inexpressible" (anirvācya).
If you argue that its establishment follows from this very reason [of the contradiction], then why is the proposition "the mother is barren" not also contradictory?
For in that case as well, it would be easy to say that the meaning of the proposition is established by the very reason that is yet to be stated.
If it is argued that, according to the maxim "the meaning of a proposition, once established, is proven by the reason," there is no expectation for a reason in this case, that is true; furthermore,
the very fact that the world is existent constitutes its own distinction from the non-existent, and is itself existent.
It is established by direct perception;
therefore, since that [perception] sublates it, how could the proponent of difference not have an undesirable consequence by asserting that there is an absolute absence of existence?
If it is argued that the means of valid cognition [in question] indicates a non-primary existence, [we reply:]...
I have already stated that, for me, that reality is indeed primary,
because the means of valid cognition and reasoning belonging to others remain immersed in the depths even today.
Some explain this to mean that it would not be something undesirable for you.

In this regard, the resolution should be understood as follows: the negation expressed by the word "not" (*na*) in the rule "not at the beginning of a foot, etc. indicates that [the prohibition] is not absolute.

If it were argued that [the term "existent"] applies to everything, then the established distinction between various existents would be lost; since even Brahman would then be nothing more than mere existence, even that [Brahman] would not exist for us. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.25)

This is another refutation of the third [position]:

if it is asserted as the thesis that the universe is distinct from all that exists—that is, that it does not have existence as its locus—then there is the establishment of a distinction from existence.
For if one does not admit multiple instances of existence, there is no purpose for the use of the word "all."
If it is argued that while there are indeed many [entities], only one is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), we say no;
for you are still striving even now to establish that very [multiplicity],
and in the attempt to prove that [the ultimate reality] does not have that [multiplicity] as its locus, you fall into the fallacy of contradicting your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
In the fourth [verse], he states another objection: "The state of being mere existence," and so forth.

Since existence (*sattva*) whose specific qualities are not intended to be expressed also belongs to Brahman, for that reason, it would follow according to our view that the universe possesses a distinction from that Being-Brahman, namely,
that the universe is not the locus of that [intended] existence.
And thus, because it is already established, that too would not be something to be proven (*sādhya*).

If the probandum (*sādhya*) were "not being the locus of existence whose specific qualities are not intended to be expressed," then even the fact that Brahman is not the locus of existence [in general] would suffice to establish the meaning of the proposition; therefore, this results in the fallacy of proving something extraneous (*arthāntara*). *2,105* *The Refutation of the Definition of Existence according to the Opponent’s View*

Alternatively, what is this so-called "existence" (sattva) that is being established as not being the substratum of the universe? Is it existence as a universal (sāmānyasattva), or is it existence as intrinsic nature (svarūpasattva)?
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "If it is said..."
Distinctness from the universal that follows all things and all objects means, in short, not being its locus.

If this is stated as something to be proven (*sādhya*), then there is the establishment of a distinction from existence (*sat*). If existence itself does not exist, then the proposition (*pratijñā*) that it is not its locus would be meaningless.

This is not like the case of "the locus of a hare's horn," because no such misconception could even arise; furthermore, if one accepts the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), the differentiation of existents (*sadbheda*) is unavoidable,
for there is no universal that has only a single substratum.
If it is argued that there are entities that serve as substrates (sattvādhikaraṇa), then one must state what they are.
If you say they are substance and so forth, then how can it be established that those very things are not themselves substrates?
From the perspective of conventional usage (vyavahāra), everything exists.
If it is argued that this is not so from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), we say no;
for the answer has already been stated.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this response was given from the standpoint of the opponent's own position.

According to his own view, however, one should see that this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*), because he does not accept a universal existence (*sattvasāmānya*) that persists as something distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the other categories. He refutes the second [position] with the words: "the state of being mere existence" (*sanmātratvam*).
Existence independent of [particular] entities means being pure existence (*sanmātratva*), that is to say, existence as its own essential nature (*svarūpasattva*).
That [existence] belongs to Brahman as well; for that reason, there would be no difference between the universe and that Brahman, nor would the universe possess the nature of non-Brahman.
Alternatively, by this [verse], another fault is stated regarding the position that [the world] possesses general existence (*sāmānyasattā*).

For instance, although Brahman is devoid of the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), it nonetheless possesses the nature of pure being (*sanmātratva*) as its own essential existence (*svarūpasattva*). However, Brahman does not become non-existent or indescribable simply because it lacks that [generic] existence.
Therefore, since the absence of [generic] existence is not a cause for non-existence or the like, the universe cannot be a non-locus of that [Brahman’s] existence either.
By this, the position that the nature of Brahman is existence (*sattva*) is also refuted.

The two positions—that existence consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) or in being unsublated by knowledge (*jñānābādhyatva*)—have not been explicitly criticized because their flaws are obvious.

Furthermore, for one who asserts causal efficiency, there is a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since they would be admitting that even that which is false possesses causal efficiency.
Since Brahman possesses existence even while being devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that lack of efficiency is not a reason for its non-existence.
To prove merely that it is not the locus of causal efficiency is irrelevant to the present context and is, moreover, contradictory [to the intended conclusion].
Furthermore, the lack of resistance by cognition is simply its being sublated by that cognition.
And it is quite clear that this does not differ from the meaning of the reason (*hetu*).

Even if another reason were stated, the consequence of [the reason] having as its object either sublation (*bādha*) or what is already established (*siddha*), according to the logic to be explained, would be equally evident.
As for what has been said here:

It is extremely weak [to argue] that "since you also, while establishing the reality of existence and non-existence as two truths, have established whatever it is as existing, I too accept that very thing, and thus there is no failure to define the referent of the word 'existent'. For, by me...
In some cases, "existent" (*sat*) is conventionally designated as a positive entity (*bhāva*); in other cases, it is that which is not the counter-correlative of negation within a recognized locus;
and in yet other cases, it is "corporeal" (*mūrta*) and so forth—all such [definitions] are refuted. (2.112)
Furthermore, even the fact that [an object] is sublated by knowledge is not established for the opponent;
for it is held that the correct knowledge of something already known is precisely what constitutes its being otherwise.
Having thus refuted the proposition, he now also sets aside the reason: "sublatability by cognition. This constitutes the refutation of the sublatibility asserted by the opponent.

The meaning is that not only is the thesis (pratijñā) faulty, but even the reason (hetu), namely "being sublated by cognition" (jñānabādhyatva), is so. The word "but" (tu) distinguishes this from the "sublation by cognition" as intended by the proponent of the established view (siddhāntin).

For the opponent intends as the reason either "being sublatable by knowledge" (meaning being removable by knowledge) or "being the counter-positive of a negation within a locus that has been apprehended.
However, neither of these is established for me, the proponent, regarding the phenomenal world (prapañca).
Therefore, the reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (anyatarāsiddha).
Surely, even you must accept that the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) occurs through the knowledge of God;
otherwise, his status as the agent of dissolution would be untenable,
since only one who possesses knowledge and other such qualities can be an agent.
True;
however, it is not the opponent’s intended meaning that [the world] is removable by knowledge in this manner.
Rather, for that which has ignorance as its material cause, there is a contradiction with knowledge regarding the same object; once the material cause has ceased, it vanishes of its own accord.
As it has been said:
"The cessation or sublation of ignorance occurs through knowledge, together with its own effect—whether that effect is currently present or already dissolved.
And this [sublation] is not what we accept regarding this phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
However, just as a jar is destroyed by the blow of a hammer and so forth, the destruction [of the world] would likewise occur through the operations of God’s knowledge, will, and effort.
If it is argued that this [destruction] itself may be the cause, we say no;

for even such sublation by knowledge is not established for the opponent in respect to a portion of the subject, namely primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the rest, and is therefore fallacious due to being "partially unestablished" (*bhāgāsiddha*).
Furthermore, let it be granted that even reality (*satya*) is destructible by knowledge (*jñāna*).

However, since there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position, the property of being destructible by knowledge is not established due to a lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*); that is to say, it is also unestablished as a pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*).
This [assertion] is merely a "sweet-tongued" concession made from the perspective of the opponent.
If it is argued that since no subverting argument has been presented, the probans' lack of pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi) must necessarily apply to the proponent as well,
and furthermore, if destruction were to occur for what exists, it would follow that consciousness (caitanya) too must perish; then,
since mere destruction is not the necessary determinant of the probandum, the fact of being sublated by knowledge remains unestablished.
It might be argued that [the reason] would also be "unestablished" (asiddha) due to a redundant qualification;
that "perishability" (*nāśyatva*) alone is the reason, and the mention of "in cognition" (*jñāne*) is merely a statement of its essential nature (*svarūpa*);
and that this [reason], being supported by the aforementioned subverting arguments (*bādhaka*), is not "inconclusive" (*aprayojaka*). If this is said, we reply: no.
For even though the nature of the entity (*sattva*) is the same, a distinction has been stated based on the presence or absence of a cause of destruction.

If it is argued that there is indeed sublation (*bādha*)—in the form of a scriptural negation such as "there is no diversity here"—with respect to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) within the accepted limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), we say no;
for this [distinction] occurs only after the meaning of the scripture has been determined.
However, that very [position] is said to be impossible because it contradicts the logic of rebirth (*upapatti*).
Alternatively, it should be understood that being sublated by knowledge (*jñāna-bādhyatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), as it lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*). For instance:
It must be stated whether the "sublatability by knowledge" intended here as a reason is that which you yourself accept, or that which we accept.
If it is the former, it is not established for the opponent according to the reasoning already stated. If it is the latter, there is a lack of pervasion (vyāpti).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Of that which has been cognized."

For, since the sublation (*bādha*) of something known erroneously is precisely its correct cognition (*samyagvijñāna*), we maintain that its being sublated consists in its being the object of that [correct cognition].
And since that [erroneous cognition] resides in the self, which is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the sentence is incomplete [in implying] that it is devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Even if the self is real, it must be admitted by the opponent as well that it is cognized as the body and so forth, and thus becomes the object of the mental state (*vṛtti*) consisting of the correct cognition produced by the Vedāntas.

"Otherwise, the cessation of ignorance would be impossible. This is the definition of sublation (*bādhyatva*). Alternatively, he rejects the [opponent's] example by stating: "sublation by knowledge" (*jñānabādhyatva*).
By the word *api*, the predicate of being "indescribable"—characterized by being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent—is conjoined.
The word *tu* (but) excludes the intended [property of] being sublated by knowledge from that which is not intended [i.e., Brahman].
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "[it has no] establishment" in the case of nacre-silver and the like.
First of all, the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of such things as nacre-silver is unestablished for me, the opponent,
because I accept them as being absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsattva*).
For this very reason, I do not agree with the claim that they are sublated by cognition (*jñānabādhyatva*).
For that very quality of being removable by knowledge is what the opponent intends;
and this is not possible for that which is non-existent,
because such a thing is eternally removed.
Therefore, this is a fallacious example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) that is deficient in both the probandum (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana). [Objection:
But surely, sublatedness (bādhyatva)—defined as being the counter-positive of a negation within a recognized locus—does indeed exist in cases such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
[Reply: Not so.
For otherwise, it would follow that they are real;
and this will be explained later.
If, then, shell-silver and the like are not sublatable, [then...]
(“Certainly! But surely”) there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting all the world and so forth.
“Not so.”
Even in the absence of that which you favor, another form of sublation exists there;
to the question "What is that?", he says: "of what has been cognized."
The term "bādhyatvam" (the state of being sublated) refers generally to that which is to be sublated, namely the object under discussion; it refers back to it as a whole.
Some say that sublation (*bādha*) is the cognition of the non-existence of the superimposed thing, such as "this is not silver.
Others, however, maintain it is the cognition of another, contradictory entity, such as "this is mother-of-pearl."
Each of those two [definitions] individually is non-pervasive,
because both are established as being sublated in the case of verbal cognition (*śābda*) and so forth;
therefore, this [definition] is stated as that which is common to both.

Indeed, the cognition of that which is present before one as being silver and so forth, by means of its being shell and so forth, is the correct cognition (*samyagvijñāna*) of what was previously cognized otherwise.

In the same way, the cognition of non-existent silver—which was apprehended as existent and so forth—by means of its being non-existent and so forth, is likewise the correct cognition of what was previously cognized otherwise.
If it were stated merely that "correct cognition is sublation" (*bādha*), it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) that every correct cognition whatsoever is sublation.
And yet, such is not the common usage;
therefore, to exclude that, it was stated "of that which has been cognized otherwise.

If it were merely stated "the cognition of that which has been cognized otherwise," there would be the over-extension [of the definition] even to the case where, following a continuous stream of error regarding a piece of mother-of-pearl perceived as silver, one subsequently cognizes it as lead, tin, and so forth.
To refute that [objection], the word "correctly" (samyak) was stated. "Otherwise" means with respect to its own essential nature (tatsvarūpa).
By this, the objection that a pot might be known again as a "pot" after having been known otherwise—as a cloth and so forth—relative to other things, is refuted;
for that would result in a fallacious argument (*chala*).
Nevertheless, the objection remains in force regarding the case where a piece of mother-of-pearl, perceived as silver, is subsequently known as white and so on.

If it is argued that, in this way, there would also be the undesirable consequence [of sublation] when there arises a correct cognition—whether belonging to another person or to that same person at a later time—that contradicts what was previously cognized otherwise, we say: not so.
For the root *bādh* is taught in the sense of "churning" (*loḍana*), and that [churning] may pertain either to the cognition or to the object.
First, it cannot belong to cognition itself,
because, being momentary, it is destroyed by its very nature; furthermore,
