it would follow that even correct cognition (*samyagvijñāna*), which is destroyed by a subsequent cognition, would have to be treated as sublated.
Nor [is it a negation] of the object,
because the fragment of mother-of-pearl and so forth remains in its original state, whereas the silver and so forth have been utterly destroyed.
Therefore, it should be said that this is like the churning away of a contrary form brought about by a preceding cognition.
And that being so, what over-extension [of the argument] could there be?
Why then should this need to be stated?
No;
for how would it be known if it were not stated? [It is known] by the force of the statement, "of that which has been understood otherwise."
Otherwise, he would have simply said "correct cognition"; what, then, is the purpose of this [qualification]?
The remainder [of the sense] is that its being an object of that [subsequent cognition] constitutes its sublation (*bādhyatva*). *2,135*
*The Refutation of the Definition of the Ineffable*:
Alternatively, it has been stated that the ineffable is "unreal" (*asat*) in a secondary sense.
In that regard, what is this state of being ineffable?
Is it the absence of etymological derivation,
or is it the absence of the cause for etymological derivation?
It cannot be the former.
Because the etymological definition beginning with "indescribable" (anirvacanīya) is impossible if [the object] exists as a reality;
and regarding the second [alternative], the basis for the etymological definition would have to be either cognition or the object itself.
It cannot be the first.
Since the existence [of such an object] is established for both parties regarding cognition,
the second [alternative] is not tenable.

Anticipating the objection that the Māyāvādin accepts an extraordinary (alaukika) object such as silver according to its appearance, the opponent has stated two definitions of the indefinable (anirvacanīya).
[The opponent claims that] indeterminability consists in being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, and in being sublatable by knowledge.
Of these, he first refutes the former [claim]: "And its distinction from the existent... [and so forth].

The explanations, however, are exactly as before. In that regard, in as many positions as there is a final conclusion regarding the reality of the object, in those cases, since the state of being indefinable (anirvacanīyatva) is not incompatible with existence, one must understand that the fault of "inconsistency of the undertaking" applies to the claim that "the world is not real (*sat*), but rather indefinable."
Furthermore, where there is a conclusion such as contradiction and so forth, one should understand that there is non-pervasion [of the definition].
Alternatively, the opponent maintains that the ether and so forth, as well as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth, are indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*).
In that case, for the universe—including the ether and so forth—which is indeed existent and is cognized as being existent, its very nature of being distinct from the non-existent is itself existent.

Thus, for the entire universe—including superimposed things such as nacre-silver—which is non-existent and cognized precisely as non-existent, its very nature of being distinct from the existent (sad-vilakṣaṇatvam) is itself existent;
whereas in the case of ether and so forth, there is only the state of being distinct from the non-existent (asad-vilakṣaṇatvam).
However, the state of being distinct from the existent is sublated by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa-bādhita).
Likewise, in cases such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there is indeed a difference from the real (*sad-vilakṣaṇatva*);
however, a difference from the non-existent (*asad-vailakṣaṇya*) is contradicted by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, one should observe the following construction: "Since that characteristic is impossible, how could what you have stated not be an undesirable point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? and so forth.

By the phrase "for those who maintain the doctrine of difference" (bhedavādinaḥ), he intends to convey that for the proponents of Māyā (māyāvādinaḥ), the admission of a distinction from existence (sad-vailakṣaṇya) regarding ether and so forth, as well as the acceptance of a distinction from non-existence (asat-vilakṣaṇatva) regarding shell-silver and the like, is merely a stain of dogmatic insistence.
Furthermore, in the phrase "if it is said," one should understand the impossibility and other such defects according to the manner already stated.
By the term "the state of being pure existence" (sanmātratva), over-extension (ativyāpti) is indicated.
For instance,

it is accepted by the proponent of Māyā (the Māyāvādin)— this is the ellipsis— that even Brahman possesses "pure existence" (*sanmātratva*), which means that it is not the locus of actual being (*sattva*).
Because it is accepted that Brahman is devoid of all attributes (*nirdharmaka*),
its not being the locus of non-existence is indeed certain.
Therefore, even that Brahman would have to be existent, yet it would follow that it is inexpressible (*anirvācya*).

Inexpressibility (*anirvacanīyatva*) consists in the inability to withstand analysis in terms of existence and non-existence, but it does not mean being a locus that lacks the properties of existence and non-existence.
If it is objected, "But how could Brahman be inexpressible, since it withstands analysis in terms of existence?", we say no;
for we do not accept the meaning of the suffix *-tva* (in *sat-tva*) as "existence."
Furthermore, since the investigation applied to ether and the like is equally applicable to Brahman as well, how can its indeterminability not be established?
As it has been said:
"Because of the acceptance of its being distinct from everything," and so forth.
And that faulty reasoning will be refuted here and there;
he now refutes the second definition as well: "the state of being sublated by cognition."
If "being sublated by knowledge" means, as stated above, that because things such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell are non-existent, they lack avidyā as their material cause,
then the definition suffers from the flaw of being impossible (asambhavitva).
If, on the other hand, it merely means "being destroyed by knowledge," [then the definition is too broad].

Nevertheless, because [the property] exists only in what is eternal, such as space (viyat) and so forth, and because it does not exist in what is non-existent, such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is not established [therein]; thus, there is a lack of pervasion (avyāpti).

Furthermore, if [the definition] is "being the counter-positive of a negation within a locus of cognition" (pratipannopādhau), that too is not established in the case of space and so forth; thus, there is indeed a lack of pervasion.
The arguments for this have been stated and should be understood from those yet to be stated.

[Objection: Surely you too must admit some form of sublatedness (*bādhyatva*), since it is impossible for a word to be devoid of meaning. Therefore, let that very thing be our definition of the "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*). To this, he replies: "of that which is known by the opponent."
The connection is that this is the opponent's view;

the implication is that since this [definition] also exists in the case of the self, which is inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*), it is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*). In this context, error (*bhrānti*) is simply the cognition of something otherwise than it is.

It should be understood that other doctrines have been refuted by the definitive statement that "sublation is indeed correct cognition (*samyagvijñāna*) which overturns the otherwise-form [of an object] induced by that [initial cognition].
By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he indicates that this is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[This concludes] Prabhākara’s restatement of the position regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Now follows the doctrine of the fivefold misconception (pañcākhyātivāda).

In this regard, some who consider all cognition to be strictly according to its object do not tolerate the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*). For instance: what indeed is this so-called "misapprehension"?
If, first of all, *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) means that an object which has undergone a transformation appears otherwise,
then it would follow that all cognitions of jars and the like are errors (*vibhrama*), because they too would be cases of appearing otherwise.
Furthermore, does the transformation of mother-of-pearl into the form of silver have a cause or is it causeless?
It cannot, first of all, be without a cause,
because it would then be impossible for it to occur only occasionally; therefore,
a cause must be stated for its initial occurrence.
If it is argued that this is a defect of the instrument (*karaṇadoṣa*), we say no;
for it is illogical that a defect belonging to the instrument could be the cause of the transformation of the mother-of-pearl.
Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that at that very moment all objects would undergo transformation into the form of silver.

If it is argued that the cause [of the error] is contact with a defective sense organ, even so, does the transformation into the form of silver occur through the departure of the mother-of-pearl's nature (*śuktitva*),
or without its departure?
In the first case, even another person would not perceive the mother-of-pearl's nature at that time.
In the second case, it would have to be cognized even through error;
furthermore, upon the sublation [of the cognition] when the nature of mother-of-pearl has disappeared, that [silver] would not appear.
Moreover, if it is argued that silver has been transformed into the form of mother-of-pearl, we say no.
This is because there is an absence of a cause for any defect in the instrument [of cognition].
If it is argued that sublation is likewise apprehended by that very same [instrument], we say no;
for if that were so, it would follow that even a jar and the like would be cognizable solely by the potter and others.

If it is argued that [the self] is like pleasure and so forth, we say no; for there is a distinction between the external and the internal, otherwise the aforementioned over-extension (atiprasaṅga) cannot be avoided. (2.154)
Furthermore, if the mother-of-pearl were transformed into the form of silver due to a defect (*doṣa*), then why does it not remain in that very state even when the defect has disappeared?
For it is never observed that the destruction of an effect follows from the destruction of its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
If it is argued that the departure of the solar light—which is the efficient cause for the blooming of a lotus bud—is seen to be the cause for the cessation of that blooming, we say: not so.
For expansion is indeed the separation of petals;
and because of momentariness, that [expansion] ceases as soon as the light of the sun is present.
However, the destruction of conjunction never ceases, while the state of budding, characterized by re-conjunction, is produced solely by the impulse of cold and so forth.
Even if the division were to persist, the claim that its destruction has a cause entirely different [from that of the substance] is trivial;
for if it were argued that it would be like "priority" (*paratva*) and so forth, we say no, because there is disagreement on that point.
If silver were produced [in the cognition] and then destroyed, then there would be a corresponding perception [of its destruction], and not the subverting cognition "this is not silver.
By this, the view that silver arises from a cognition produced by a defective instrument is also refuted.
And what, in that case, would be the purpose of speaking of "defects"?
For instance, the staff, the wheel, and so forth, which are the instrumental causes for the transformation of clay into the form of a jar, are not considered defects.
Furthermore, does that cognition arise from its own objective support (ālambana), or from another cognition?
Not the first.
Because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence:
for silver would arise only when there is the production of the cognition that takes it as its object, and that cognition would be produced only once the silver has arisen.
Indeed, a cognition does not arise without an object.
Regarding the second [cognition] as well, what is its object: is it another cognition of mother-of-pearl, or is it an object consisting of both mother-of-pearl and silver?
Alternatively, it has another object as its support.
Not the first [alternative],
because it would follow that silver would be produced everywhere immediately after the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
Furthermore, there is no rule that the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl" must necessarily precede the cognition of silver in the case of a shell-silver illusion.
If it is argued that the production of the silver-cognition arises from the perception of a common form belonging to the mother-of-pearl as perceived by a defective sense organ, we say no;
for there is no rule that the cognition of silver must invariably follow the mere observation of a common form.
If it is argued that a deficiency of causes is postulated in that case,
this might be so;
provided that the arising of silver were established by valid cognition.
We shall, however, establish cognition through another means.
It is not the second [alternative],
because the very same cause would apply to the previous silver as well, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of an uninterrupted stream of cognitions of silver.
Not the third [alternative], because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Thus, since neither error nor sublation is tenable, the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is not logical. *2,159*
Nor is it logical to maintain that "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*) consists in the appearance of an object as having the nature of another object;
for in that case, does that [nature] exist in the object as the nature of another object, or does it not exist?
In the first case, there would be neither error nor sublation.
Furthermore, everything would be perceived by everyone in its entirety and through its very essence;
for a defect is not a refinement of the sense organ.
If that were the case, nothing at all would be perceived by one whose cause is defective.
Moreover, this being the case, it would follow that the cognition of silver is valid, while the cognition "this is indeed mother-of-pearl" is invalid.
Nor is the second alternative possible,
because the perception of what is non-existent is untenable.
Or, even if it were produced, what is the point of apprehending the silver as a real entity?
By this, the view that "misapprehension" (anyathākhyāti) is the cognition of a thing qualified by an unrelated qualifier is refuted;
for it is impossible to cognize a relationship with a non-existent qualifier.
Or, regarding its arising, what further point is left for the proponents of *asatkhyāti*?
Now, if you say that "cognition having one form is *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension)," that is incorrect.
For even correct cognition would result in being an error because its form would differ from the object due to internal or external characteristics.

Furthermore, the claim that "a cognition which manifests the form of one thing has another as its objective support" constitutes the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), but this is contradictory.
To explain why:

An object of cognition cannot be established merely by its existence or non-existence, because the mere existence of a thing is common to all conditions for all entities; consequently, it would follow that all cognitions have all things as their objects, and thus everyone would possess omniscience. Furthermore, it would result in the conclusion that objects such as the past lack any objective basis.
By this, the status of being an object (*ālambana*) due to its existence in the location in front [of the observer] is also refuted.
Nor is it an object by virtue of being a cause;
for if it were, then since the eye and other [faculties] are also causes of the cognition of form and so forth, it would follow that they too would be its objects.
Furthermore, cognition would not have the past and the future as its objects;
for since the past and the future do not exist, it is impossible for them to function as causes.
By this, the view that they serve as causes by way of being objects is also refuted.
Furthermore, this being the case, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*),
because the very nature of being an object (*viṣayatva*) is what is currently under investigation.
Moreover, in that case, let it simply be called "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*).
What is the use of this futile causality that gives rise to such a calamity? Furthermore, what is this "objecthood" (viṣayatva)?
If it is argued that "that in which an excellence (atiśaya) is produced by something is the object of that [thing]," [then...]
For excellence (atiśaya) must be either cognizedness (jñātatā) or linguistic usage (vyavahāra).
It cannot be the former,
because it is not admitted [by you].
Even if this were accepted, it would follow that the cognition of the past and so forth would be devoid of an object;
for it is not logical for a property to arise when its substratum (dharmin) does not exist.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
For if there were no arising of linguistic usage for one who does not seek that object, it would follow that the object lacks a domain of experience;

furthermore, it would follow that even a staff or similar object being taken up immediately after the cognition of a tiger, a thief, or the like, would also possess the status of being that [cognition's] object.
However, the principle that "whatever cognition has whatever form, that is its objective support" follows the doctrine of the Tathāgata. (2.163)
Nor is it the case that "whatever cognition is produced by contact with a particular instrument has that [instrument] as its object";
for this would lead to the absurd conclusion that the cognition of color and so forth would have space and the like as its objects.
Indeed, it is not logical to claim that the eye, while producing the cognition of color and so forth, is not in contact with space and the like.
Furthermore, recognition (pratyabhijñā), being produced by a cause proximate to that [object], would not have that object as its content;
nor is there any proximity between a sentence and the sentence-meaning,
such that the sentence-meaning could be the object of the cognition generated by that sentence.
Furthermore, it would follow that [the cognition] would have space and so forth as its object;

and since the cognition of the probandum (liṅgin) arises from the cognition of the mark (liṅga) which is in contact with the self, it would follow that the cognition of the probandum has the self as its object.
Therefore, one should maintain that whatever cognition appears as a certain thing, that very thing is its objective support (ālambana).
In this regard, it must be stated whether the mother-of-pearl appears in the cognition of silver or not.
One who says that it does appear is a "beloved of the gods" (devānāṃ priyaḥ) of praiseworthy intelligence;
yet if he were to say that it does not appear—out of respect for consciousness—then how could that cognition have the mother-of-pearl as its objective support?
Furthermore, if silver appears while having mother-of-pearl as its objective basis (*ālambana*), how is the resulting over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to be avoided?
Surely, if the appearance of silver has silver as its object (*viṣaya*), it must be that very silver.
Why should it not be so?
For even when one accepts what is currently perceived as real silver, there is no cause for that acceptance other than the appearance of silver;
indeed, there is no reason to favor the manifestation of one particular silver over another.
If it is argued that there is also the manifestation [of the thought], "There is no silver here," [we reply: so be it.
True.
By the very power of its appearance, the absence of silver is indeed admitted right before one's eyes.
If it is argued that there would be a contradiction between two cognitions, we say no.
Since there will be no contradiction, as will be explained later [in verse 2.166],
we do not perceive any cause for the production of "apprehension of something otherwise" (anyathākhyāti),
nor is the eye and so forth alone the cause.
Because it is determined that [the means] possesses the capacity to produce correct knowledge,
nectar— which is indeed the cause for the destruction of old age and death— can never be the cause of that [knowledge].
For if the cause were identical, it would follow that the difference between the effects is accidental.
Nor can there be a difference in the effect due to a difference in the unseen (adṛṣṭa),
because that [unseen factor] is to be determined only after the difference in the effect has been ascertained,
and because the difference in the effect itself is still a matter of dispute.
The claim that erroneous cognition arises from the sense faculty itself when it is assisted by defects is also incorrect;
for defects merely destroy the natural capacity of causes to produce their standard effects,
but they do not bestow upon them the capacity to produce contrary effects.
Indeed, it is not the case that a *kuṭaja* seed produces a *vaṭa* tree; rather, what indeed does it not produce? It simply does not produce a *kuṭaja* sprout.
Nor should it be said that the capacity of *vetra* seeds burnt by a forest fire to produce a plantain stalk has been observed.
Because a different substance arises through cooking, those [previous states] lack the status of being seeds.
Furthermore, if there were deviation regarding the form demonstrated [by the cognition], then the suspicion of deviation would be unavoidable for the cognition in all cases;
and if that were so, how could we refute the denial of external objects?
For indeed, it is cognition alone that establishes the nature of objects everywhere, and nothing else;
if that cognition were to deviate in some instances,
then it would be subject to doubt regarding deviation in all instances.
And there is nothing other than cognition capable of washing away the mud of that doubt;
and it has been stated that even such [cognition], when its power is contracted by the stain of doubt, is not effective.
Therefore, whence can there be any hope for external objects?
Nor should it be argued that, just as smoke is not suspected of deviating from fire even when earthen objects such as jars do so,
so too one should not suspect deviation everywhere even if a single cognition deviates from its object;
for the two cases are dissimilar.

For even though there is no difference in their being earthy substances, there exists therein a specific intermediate property such as "smokiness" which serves as a means for determining non-deviation;
indeed, there is nothing subverting it there. Therefore, confidence in that case is justified.
In the present case, however, we do not perceive any specific sub-class of cognition capable of dispelling doubt.
Nor should it be argued that a distinction is established based on the presence or absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*),
for even a sublater is itself a locus of doubt by virtue of being a cognition.

Indeed, there is no such thing as a "horn" (i.e., a specific characteristic) belonging to a sublater (*bādhaka*). Furthermore, the absence of a sublater is the same for one who has not yet experienced a sublated error.
If it is argued that the distinction lies in the presence or absence of a corroborating factor (*saṃvādaka*), we say no.
Because this has already been answered:
since even a corroborative cognition is itself a cognition, why would it not also be a locus of doubt?
Furthermore, if one were to seek yet another corroborative cognition for that one as well, how could an infinite regress not occur?
Furthermore, the mutual correspondence regarding a continuous stream of error has been accepted by the opponent;
by this, it should be understood that the distinction characterized by the presence or absence of non-contradiction in the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) produced by cognition is also refuted,
because there is no cause for confidence even when such a distinction is apprehended.
Moreover, it must be explained from where this perceived form of silver originates.

First of all, it cannot be maintained by the proponents of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) that it resides in the object standing before one; for if that were the case, it would contradict the subsequent sublation (*bādha*).
Nor will we say that it exists in another location;
consequently, it follows that this [object] resides within cognition itself.
And thus, the Buddhist proponents of representational consciousness (sākāravijñānavādin) have triumphed. *2,170*
If that is so, what then is the status of such cognitions as "this is silver"?
It is said:
"This is silver" consists of two cognitions, in the form of memory and direct experience.
In that context, "this is here" refers to the apprehension of the mere substance present before one;
this occurs because, due to a defect, the specific universal of "mother-of-pearl-ness" residing in that object is not apprehended.
Thus, "this is here" is the apprehension of the mere substance present before one.
Due to the influence of a defect, there is a non-apprehension of the specific universal of "mother-of-pearlness" belonging to that object;
however, when that [object] alone is apprehended, it produces a memory of silver through the process of awakening a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by virtue of its similarity [to silver].

And although that memory has the nature of apprehending what was already apprehended, due to the influence of a defect, it remains in a form resembling the apprehended [silver], through the loss of the aspect of "having been apprehended" (*gṛhītatva*).

And thus, because the memory of silver and the perception of the object present before one are not mutually distinguished as to their own nature or their objects, these two—the perception and the memory—though distinct, give rise to the practical usage of non-difference and the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the form "this is silver," by virtue of their resemblance to the cognition of nearby silver.
If it is asked, "Why is this so? we reply: no [other reason is needed].
Because it has already been stated that [the cognition] cannot be explained otherwise;
furthermore, there is no dispute that this "this" is an experience (*anubhava*) consisting of a cognition born from the contact of the eye with the object present before one.
And the cognition of silver is certainly not produced by the sense organs.
Because the sense faculty has the capacity to produce cognition only with respect to an object that is in contact [with it];
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of everyone being omniscient.
Furthermore, there is no contact with the distant silver.
This is because its effect, which is direct perception, is never observed;
nor is it tenable to claim that the sense organ produces the cognition of silver merely from contact with a fragment of mother-of-pearl, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Nor can there be a settled distinction based on the presence or absence of defects,
because defects have been refuted by the fact that they produce contrary effects.
If it is argued that the digestive fire (*jāṭharajātavedas*) of one afflicted by the defect of *bhasmaka* is observed to be the cause of the digestion of a greater amount of food, we say no.
Because of the contradiction;
for it is logically established that the defect (doṣa) alone is the cause of the transformation of the food.
Nor should it be asked how a defect performs the function of burning.
Because even in the case of the same effect, a difference in nature is observed:
for it is the *rasas* transformed by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) that cause the nourishment of the body, and not those transformed by *bhasmaka*;
therefore, this [cognition] is not born of the senses.
It cannot be maintained that this [cognition] arises from inference and the like even for those who are devoid of the consideration of logical marks (*liṅga*) and so forth;
therefore, since the present instrument [of perception] is absent, this [cognition] which is being produced must, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), be nothing other than memory (*smaraṇa*).
Furthermore, this is memory because it does not arise in one who has not previously perceived silver, just like a memory that is universally accepted as such.

It is not correct to argue that this non-recollection is due to the absence of the aspect of "that-ness" (tattā), as in the case of a currently perceived object; for there is a deviation from this rule in the recollection of a word-meaning from a word, and in the recollection of Hari, Hara, and so forth. Furthermore, whatever has been experienced is not necessarily recollected in its entirety.
The "this-ness" (tattā) portion is the property being remembered as connected with a past time and place;
and so let there be remembrance, even if,
due to some defect, that "this-ness" portion has been lost.
Nor is there any subverting argument against the contrary position; thus, the reason is not "inconclusive.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that this is not memory because it is produced by the sense organs, on the grounds that it follows the positive and negative concomitance of the operation of the sense organs.

This is because the operation of the sense organ—both its positive and negative concomitance—is exhausted solely in the grasping of the common form present before one, which serves as the cause for awakening the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that is the seed of memory.
If it is objected: "In that case, since a child who has never tasted bitterness cannot logically have a memory of bitterness, how can there be the cognition 'the jaggery is bitter'? We reply:
No, because it was experienced in another life.
Furthermore, recollection occurs for some [cognitions] alone due to the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).

Alternatively, there is no such rule that it is only the apprehension and recollection—when their mutual distinction remains unapprehended—that initiate practical activity and so forth; rather, in some cases, it is the apprehension itself where the mutual difference is not grasped, as in the case of "the conch is yellow."
For here, due to a defect, the yellowness of the bile-substance residing in the rays of light emerging from the eyes is perceived as being devoid of its substrate;
the conch-shell, too, is perceived merely in its own form, devoid of its quality.

Since these two—the quality and the possessor of the quality—are mutually dependent, their non-apprehension of non-connection, along with their similarity [to other yellow objects], results in the practical usage of non-difference and the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just like the cognition of a yellow *cirabilva* fruit and the like.
As for your point regarding the perception of the blackness of collyrium, that is due to its oblique position and because it obstructs the rays of the eye due to its lack of transparency.
But the specific distinction is that bile (*pitta*), being situated within the eye, is transparent like glass and thus not an obstacle [to vision];
likewise is the conventional usage "molasses is bitter.
Furthermore, in some cases of recollection, there is simply no grasping of the distinction [between the object and its qualifier].
Just as it is said, "that jar existed there," by this same method all conventional expressions such as "the wheel of fire" (*alātacakra*) and so forth are to be explained.
Furthermore, even by one who accepts the opposite [view], the non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekāgraha*) must necessarily be admitted.
For when there is the apprehension of discrimination, there is no room for error,
because of their contradiction;
otherwise, the cessation of error would be impossible.

And since everything is thus established from that very [source], what is the use of postulating the opposite? Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).

Even the sublation of the cognition "this is not [that]" is logically possible only by way of negating the conventional usage of non-difference, which is occasioned by the non-apprehension of difference.
And when that [distinction] is established, it is also proven—consistent with worldly consensus—that the two cognitions, whose distinction has not been grasped, are erroneous.
Thus, the formal argument is:
the cognition under discussion is in accordance with reality.
Because it is a cognition, like that which is commonly accepted.

Now, in this context, what is meant by "the disputed cognition"? Is it the non-conceptual sensory awareness of the object present before one? Or is it the recollection of silver arising from the perception of something similar? Or is it both? Or is it the cognition of the identity between the silver and the object present before one? Or is it two distinct cognitions in which the difference has been lost?
If it is argued that in the first three positions there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*),

while in the fourth there is the unestablished nature of the proponent’s locus (*vādyāśrayāsiddhatva*), the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), and contradiction (*vyāghāta*), and in the fifth there is the unestablished nature of the opponent’s locus (*prativādyāśrayāsiddhatā*); [we reply:]...
Not so;
there is indeed the non-conceptual cognition of that which stands before one,
and there is also the recollection of silver produced by the perception of a similar object standing before one.

Likewise, there certainly exists that conceptual cognition arising from it, namely the perception "this is [silver]," which involves the dispute over difference and non-difference regarding the cognition of silver. In this regard, if one intends to propose as the subject of inquiry (pakṣa) merely the apprehension "this is silver"— setting aside the disputed aspects of difference and non-difference— as the cause for the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "this is silver," then what contradiction is there?
Nowhere is there a formulation of a thesis (*pakṣīkāra*) based solely on a discordant form;

for were it so, if one were to formulate as a thesis a sound that is both eternal and non-eternal, or a mountain that both possesses and lacks fire, the seal of inference would be shattered due to the persistence of the aforementioned faults.
Furthermore, only that which is already established [as a subject] is formulated as a thesis.
If even the form of doubt were established, what would remain to be proven? Furthermore, difference and non-difference are the objects of dispute at the time of error.
For if there were a difference between these two cognitions, this cognition [of silver] would have as its object only that which is present before one, and would not know it to be silver.

Even the cognition of silver does not grasp the silver alone; rather, having referred to the object present before one with "this is not [silver]," it prescribes silver-ness for that very object with "this is silver.
However, it merely connects the property of silver-ness to something or other by means of the word "silver."
And since that [error] is not contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could there be any "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*)?

Therefore, those who maintain that theory must assert non-difference (*abheda*), while those who maintain the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātivāda*) must reject it; thus, there is indeed a disagreement.
Consequently, if one sets aside the conflicting aspects and takes as the subject merely the cognition "this is silver," there is no fault whatsoever.

How could the proponent of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory that there is a misapprehension of one thing as another) escape this fault while presenting an argument to prove that the cognition "this is silver" has as its object the thing standing before him? If you say, "I am taking as my subject the cognition which serves as the cause for my activity toward the mother-of-pearl when I seek silver," then let it be said aloud so that the opponent may hear; otherwise, [your position] would be undermined by the cognition of God (*īśvarajñāna*). If you argue that [in our case] there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) because of God’s cognition, then why would you not also face the same sublation (*bādha*)?

If it is argued that non-divine cognition (*anīśvarajñāna*), which is the cause for the activity under discussion, is being made the subject (*pakṣa*), then it would be exactly the same for me as well. If you argue that the qualification is useless because you do not accept a Supreme Lord (*īśvara*), then why would it not be equally useless for you in relation to me?

Furthermore, if you argue that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) regarding the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then the consequence is that you yourself face the fallacy of sublation (*bādhaprasaṅga*) in that very case.

If you say, "I am setting forth this object of dispute: that the cognition of silver is a cognition of silver from which its distinction [from the substrate] has not been grasped through knowledge," this is equally applicable to me as well.
Furthermore, the cognition of silver under dispute has silver as its object because it is a cognition of silver, just like a [cognition] that is universally accepted.
Here too, the object of disagreement should be analyzed in the same manner as before.
This might be so:
what is this so-called "cognition of silver"? Is it the cognition of silver, or is it that which is both silver and its cognition?
Is it (1) a cognition characterized by the verbal expression "silver," or (2) a cognition that serves as the cause for the activity of one desiring silver, or (3) the cognition "this is silver"?
It cannot be the first,
because the meaning of the genitive case is impossible except as the relationship between object and subject, and thus it would be indistinguishable from the probandum itself.
Not the second [alternative],
because it is unestablished for both parties;
for cognition is devoid of form (nirākāra).
Not the third [alternative],
because the meaning of the recollection (*ullekha*) is not established as the object [of the cognition].

Furthermore, if it were produced solely from the memory generated by the knowledge of that [word], there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since it is possible for the word "silver" to be remembered even through the knowledge of the preceding word alone.
Nor is the fourth [alternative] correct;

for there is a deviation [in the reason], since even the cognition "this is a shell" held by those who grasp at distinction (viveka) has the shell as its objective support and thus serves as a cause for that [error].
Nor is the fifth [alternative] correct.
"Because it is not excluded from the previously stated position"—
do not say so.
For the proponent of anyathākhyāti (the theory of misapprehension), is the cognition of mother-of-pearl said to be a case of anyathākhyāti when its object is actually mother-of-pearl?
Or is the cognition of silver directed toward the mother-of-pearl?
In the first case, there is no dispute between us, because it is a case of *yathārthakhyāti* (the manifestation of things as they truly are).
In the second case, that very object which is intended by the opponent through the term "cognition of silver" will serve as our reason (*hetu*).
For instance, the first alternative is not fit to be accepted by the opponent,
because it would entail a contradiction and because it would result in the non-difference between mother-of-pearl and silver.
Not the second,
because it is not accepted;
not the third.

Furthermore, there is the consequence of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) because it is possible that even the cognition of mother-of-pearl could be caused by the recollection of the word "silver" as applied to something else [by convention].
Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable;

for in a case where one has heard the statement, "There is mother-of-pearl here, and beneath it there is silver," the cognition of mother-of-pearl would also become a cause for activity directed toward silver, which would result in its being classified as *anyathākhyāti*.
Nor is it the fifth [alternative],
because it is not included within the positions previously stated.
Therefore, having accepted one of the aforementioned positions regarding what is called "silver-cognition," its defect must be refuted.
Or another alternative may be considered:
"I shall take reality itself as the reason"—this is trivial.

Some, however, accept the meaning of the reason as simply "cognition having silver as its object," and by accepting "not having anything other than silver as its object" as the probandum, they avoid the fault of the probandum being non-different from the reason.
That is incorrect,
because it is subject to deviation in the cognition "silver and pot," and because it is unestablished for at least one of the two parties.
Therefore, the refutation has already been stated.
Furthermore, the property of being a cognition (jñānatva) subsists only in that which is in accordance with reality (yathārtha), because it subsists only in cognitions, just like validity (pramātva).
A mother-of-pearl shell does not appear as silver, because it lacks existence in that form.
Whatever is non-existent in a particular form does not appear in that form,
just as Mount Meru does not appear as a mustard seed.
This identity with silver cannot be apprehended because it is non-existent, like a tortoise's hair.
Therefore, the position of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) alone is superior.
Herein, the refutation of the theory of non-apprehension known as the Prabhākara view is stated.
As for that definition of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) which was refuted up to the words "by the phrase 'the manifestation of another form,'" that is precisely what we accept.
For we admit that *anyathākhyāti* is a cognition that takes one thing as its object under the aspect of something else.

As it has been said: "The apprehension of the non-existent as existent, and the apprehension of the existent as non-existent—this is indeed misapprehension (*anyathāpratīti*) because it is erroneous."
Now, is the nature of one thing [identical] to another existent or non-existent?
We say it is non-existent.
If you object that there can be no cognition of what is non-existent, we say no.
Because that [existence] is yet to be established.
If it is argued, "In that case, from where should the existence of silver also be admitted?", we say:
no one asserts that "silver exists."
We shall indeed explain the nature of *anyathākhyāti* anew later on.
Here, however, someone has prattled as follows:
"It would follow that all conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-pratyaya*), such as 'the cow is spotted' or 'the cloth is white,' would be erroneous."
"Because a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) has identity (tādātmya) as its objective support,
and because that [identity] is absent here"—
this argument is extremely weak.
For instance, upon what does the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) depend for identity?
Is it between a quality, action, genus, or the like, and a substance; or among qualities and so forth themselves; or between the substratum of a quality and the substratum of an action, and so on?
Not the first,
because it is not accepted;
for it is not the intention of worldly people that the meaning of "a white cloth" is "whiteness is the cloth."
Nor is the intended meaning of the expression "the cloth moves" that the movement is the cloth;
nor is the expression "a spotted cow" synonymous with the claim that the state of being spotted and the state of being a cow reside in the individual body alone.
For if that were the case, the expression "Devadatta is stick-bearer" would also entail having as its object the identity between the stick and Devadatta.

If it is argued that, because in verbal usage such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) there is the employment of a cognition whose object is a distinct entity, a similar [distinct] cognition must be postulated here as well— then this applies equally here too,
since the suffix *ac* is prescribed by the rule *arśa-ādibhyo 'c* in the sense of "one who possesses the quality of being pale" (*śuklaguṇa*).
However, in cases such as "he moves" (*calati*), the difference in meaning between the base and the suffix is indeed manifest.
For "cow" (*gauh*) does not denote "cowness" (*gotva*), because if that were the case, the suffix *-tva* would be redundant.
For this very reason, after saying "the white cloth," people explain it as "the whiteness of the cloth.
For this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable.
For it does not occur to the minds of cognizers that the expression "the white cloth moves" has the meaning that whiteness, cloth-ness, and motion are one and the same.

If that were the case, then even the cognition "Devadatta is staff-bearing" or "Devadatta is earring-wearing" would result in having as its object the identity (*tādātmya*) between the staff, the earring, and Devadatta-ness.
However, the third [type of relation] certainly exists.
Those which have one and the same substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) are indeed "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*); the state of being such is "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
And thus, while there is clearly a mutual distinction among qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth with respect to their substratum, there is no distinction among the substrata themselves;
for a thing cannot be its own own substratum.
Nor is it logical for those [qualities] to have a common substratum when there is mutual non-difference; nor does that [quality] possess commonality when there is a difference in its substrata.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for a difference in the substrata of qualities and so forth.
Even though there is a difference between two distinct things, that [distinction] is not the locus of qualities and so forth;
rather, it is another entity that resides in the locus of the qualities and so forth.

And thus, since where there is difference, there is no appearance of non-difference, and where there is an appearance of non-difference, there is no difference, how could there be any over-extension [of the definition]?
Now, is it not the case that the established doctrine of the venerable Sage is that there is no mutual difference between the qualities and so forth and their substratum?
Furthermore, in some instances, both difference and non-difference are maintained.
And as for the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it has been explained as being based solely on difference.
And thus, cognitions such as "the cloth is white" would again result in errors.
Not so;
for we accept that [the object] possesses specific qualities.
We shall explain this clearly in the section on the specific determination [of the object]. Furthermore,

our position— that there is no contradiction with experience regarding the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) as we conceive it— is indeed accepted by you, even though you have rejected the definition of the objective basis (*ālambana*) in the passage beginning with "that which manifests another form" and ending with "by means of a sense-organ in close proximity," in order to establish that contradiction with experience.
Because it is accepted that whatever cognition is produced by a sense-organ in proximity to a certain object, that [object] is the objective domain (*viṣaya*) of that [cognition].

If it is argued that a fault has been stated here as well, we say no; for since the sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*) is also intended to be a cause [of the cognition], the [alleged] objection is irrelevant.
For the contact of the eye and other senses with space and so forth is not the cause of the cognition of color and so forth;
nor is the contact of a sentence with space and so forth the cause for the cognition of the sentence-meaning;
and the contact of the cognition of the mark (liṅga) with the self is not the instrumental cause for the cognition of the object indicated by the mark (liṅgin).
What indeed are those "inevitable proximities" (*avarjanīya-sannidhi*) that you call "contacts"?

If it is argued that the contact between the mark (*liṅga*) and the subject possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*) is the cause of the cognition of the thing marked (*liṅgin*), we say no, because the cognition of the mark itself is accepted as the instrument (*karaṇa*).
By this very [argument], the objection based on the contact between the sentence and the listener's ear is also refuted.
This is because it is accepted that the cognition of the sentence itself is the instrument [of verbal knowledge].

Even so, one might object that in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there would be the consequence of non-objectivity for the element of "thatness" (*tattā*)—since there is no sensory contact between the eye and that element, or between the knowledge of the mark (*liṅga-jñāna*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), or between the knowledge of the sentence and the sentence-meaning. This is not so, because if one were to allow the communication of what is not in sensory contact, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Recognition arises through a sense organ assisted by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of that [object];
the knowledge of the probandum (*liṅgin*) is produced by the knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*) which has as its object a mark pervaded by it;

and the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is generated by the knowledge whose object is a sentence consisting of a collection of words denoting things possessing the property of relation (*saṃsarga*).
If it is argued that there is therefore no over-extension [of the definition], then proximity (*sannikarṣa*) must be admitted.
For proximity is not merely conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth; rather, what is it but mere nearness (*pratyāsatti*)?
Even so, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*) that the self (*ātman*) is the object of the cognition of form.
If it is argued that [the mind] is the instrument because the contact between the self and the mind is also a cause for the cognition of color,
we say no; for what is intended here is the specific (asādhāraṇa) cause.
And because the mind is common [to all cognitions], one might object:

"In that case, visual cognition arising from the eye in proximity to the mind would fall within the domain of the mind. This is not so, because proximity (*sannikarṣa*) is also intended here as a specific, non-common cause.
For the contact of the eye with the object is common to the cognition of substances and other categories;
likewise, other minor objections here must be avoided.

Thus, since the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*) in produced cognition is established otherwise, it is untenable to define it differently as "that cognition which has the appearance of that [object]."
And this being the case, there is no contradiction with experience,
because the appearance of silver is logically accounted for as having that [silver] as its object precisely because it is produced by a sense-organ in contact with the mother-of-pearl.
Nor is there the fault of over-extension.
The distinction [between valid and invalid cognition] is established by the fact that one is produced by defects while the other is not;
otherwise, even if one were to act toward a non-silver object based on the cognition of silver, how could there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?

Furthermore, we shall refute with the demonstration of the unity of cognition that objection which was raised and answered beginning with the words, "As for the appearance as silver... (*yat punā rajatāvabhāsasya*).
Or let it be that the rule is simply this: whatever cognition has whatever appearance, that has that as its object.
Even so, there is no contradiction with experience.
Do you mean to say that there is a contradiction with experience regarding the appearance of silver having the mother-of-pearl as its object, or rather regarding the aspect of "this-ness"?
Regarding the first [point], there is agreement.

For we do not say that "the nature of mother-of-pearl (śuktitva) appears" in this cognition, which would entail a contradiction; rather, we admit that the appearance of the nature of mother-of-pearl is contradictory to the appearance of silver.
In the second case, however, there is no contradiction whatsoever;
or, if there were a contradiction, the cognition "this is silver" would not occur with respect to real silver.
We shall explain the contradiction with experience for one who does not admit that the aspect of "this-ness" (idam-ākāra) is the object of the appearance of silver.
If it is argued that this being the case, it would follow that silver also is an object of cognition, [we reply:
true, this is indeed accepted.
And this does not constitute a partiality for the theory of non-apprehension (akhyāti).
Because the identity of cognition is accepted;
nor does it follow that the cognition "this is silver in the mother-of-pearl" would be an error, because the non-existence of the silver is accepted.

And because the manifestation of identity (*tādātmya*) is admitted, for this very reason it has been said: "the cognition of existence in what is non-existent, and the cognition of non-existence in what is existent.

Furthermore, the Teacher will state [later] how there can be a sublation of the object: that the non-existent silver and its identity with [the shell] possess the status of being objects of cognition.
Nor is there an absence of causes for the production of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti),

because the sense organs and so forth themselves serve as its cause; for it is logically consistent that even those very causes of correct cognition, when defiled by defects (doṣa), function as the causes of error.

Nor should it be said that [the fault] merely consists in the contradiction of the natural capacity [of the action]. For if that were the case, one would have to admit either that the fault does not produce a contrary capacity, or else that the faults themselves possess such a capacity.
In the first case, it must be stated whether animal sacrifice possesses a natural capacity for producing merit (*dharma*), or for producing demerit (*adharma*).
In the first case, how could that which is outside the sacrifice not produce merit (*dharma*)? In the second case, how could that which is included within the sacrifice produce merit?

If you argue that it is due to the influence of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), then you must admit that these auxiliaries, by obstructing the natural capacity [of the act], impart a contrary capacity.
The second [alternative] is not tenable because there is no restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*).
Furthermore, glass and other such substances are also accepted as mere auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) in the production of erroneous cognition;
their status as defects (*doṣatva*), however, is asserted merely on the basis of their obstructing the production of the intended effect.
Because a lustful man conceives the pride that there is a quality in the graceful movements of a beloved woman;
yet, why do parched *kuṭaja* seeds not produce a *vaṭa* sprout in this same way?
This must be said, because of the diversity of the powers of word-meanings;
some [powers] simply obstruct the power of another entity.
Just as in the case of roasting and so forth;
some, by obstructing an innate power, even bestow a contrary power,
such as when the lethal power of poison is obstructed and [the power] to produce health and so forth is produced.

If you argue that entities which impart a capacity are indeed qualities (*guṇa*) and not defects (*doṣa*), then it has already been stated that glass and the like are also merely qualities and not defects.
Now, it is observed that only that which is the producer [of a cognition] is the object of a direct perception (*sākṣātkāri-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, neither silver nor the identity between "this" and [silver] has the capacity to produce [the cognition];
how then can they be objects? Do not say so.
If that were the case, the eternal object of God’s knowledge would not be its objective domain (*viṣaya*),
nor would the "thatness" (*tattā*) component be the objective domain of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

For if one were to accept something as an objective domain merely by virtue of being the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of that [cognition], then even silver and the like would logically qualify as objective domains, since they too are determiners of their respective cognitions.
If it is asked how that which is non-existent can be a determiner,
[we reply: no, for it is logically consistent, just as one speaks of "the commentary of the Gurus" or "the field of the Kurus."
Furthermore, the object of cognition (*prameya*) would lack the capacity to differentiate [perception] from inference and other means directed toward past objects and so forth.
If it is argued that there is a discrepancy because the differentiator exists at times— such as silver— and does not exist at others,
then is this causal efficacy (*kāraṇatva*) something that belongs to what exists at some time or other, or to what exists in the immediately preceding moment?
Not the first,
because it would lead to an over-extension;
as for the second, what is the point of this?

Now, if it is argued that the object— whether past or otherwise— does not itself exclude [the possibility of] inference and so forth by its own power such that there would be a dependence upon its existence,
but rather that a cognition excluded from other objects arises through the power of its own cause;
this is equally true in the present case as well.
Furthermore, even in the case of a real object, it is not the object itself that is the direct cause of perception, but rather the sensory contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*).
And since such contact is not possible with a non-existent object, it depends upon the existence of the object; thus, the object's causality is only indirect.
[Objection: In that case, since contact with a non-existent silver or the like is impossible, how can that cognition be produced by the sense organ? [Reply: No.

This is because it is accepted that the sense organ, being in contact with the mother-of-pearl, produces a cognition that apprehends that very object as having the nature of silver—which is absolutely non-existent.

For this very reason, there is no consequence of the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*). Indeed, *asatkhyāti* would only follow if everything that appears in a contested cognition were non-existent.
And it has already been stated that this is not the case.

Furthermore, as for the claim that if there were deviation regarding the object, there would be a lack of confidence in all cognition, that will be refuted by the Teacher himself when he states that "the validity of cognitions is the rule, while its opposite arises from an exception.

For the witness, which is of the nature of pure consciousness, is invariably true and never assailed by doubt; it itself apprehends the truthfulness of the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*).
The view of Bādarāyaṇa is that truthfulness [of cognition] is established by being assisted by critical examination (*parīkṣā*).
For this very reason, the claim that there is no specific distinction among cognitions as a means for dispelling distrust is refuted.
Otherwise, how could even an opponent have confidence in a subsequent practical activity when there has been a deviation regarding the object in a previous one?
And in the absence of that [distinction], how could there be an understanding of a related meaning through the observation of linguistic usage?
Furthermore, if there is no apprehension of distinction in some cases, how could there be confidence in a qualified cognition elsewhere?
And in the absence of that [confidence], how could there be unhesitating activity?
Furthermore, confidence based on the absence of sublation and so forth has already been refuted according to the opponent's own reasoning.
Moreover, how can the absence of sublation, which occurs only after an activity has taken place, be of any use for an activity that is already free from doubt?

And how can one who accepts the determination of the very nature of a qualified cognition through the absence of sublation and so forth not abandon the doctrine of self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśavijñānavāda*)?
If it is argued that the general rule is set aside by an exception,
this applies equally to the present case as well.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that under the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), cognition would become endowed with an objective form (*sākāra*)— that too is addressed.
That is untenable,
because you admit that it is precisely an absolutely non-existent form that appears;
otherwise, since a form being employed in conventional usage would lack external existence, it would follow that even the conventional usage itself would possess that [non-existent] form.

Furthermore, this process described in such passages as "this is silver" is untenable, because there is no evidence for the existence of two cognitions or for the fact that the cognition of silver is a memory; for the refutations of [the arguments against] qualified cognitions have been answered,
and the [opponent's] inferences have been shown to be fallacious.

As for the presentation of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) regarding the memory-nature of the cognition of silver, that too is untenable because the method of elimination is itself unestablished; this is due to the demonstration that [the cognition] is produced by currently present causes such as a defective sense organ.
Furthermore, the fact that it does not arise in one who has never perceived silver is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it does not apply to things such as the sky.

If it is argued that what is intended is "arising only for one who possesses the cognition of silver," we say no; for even so, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to the latent impression (saṃskāra) of silver and its subsequent practical activity (vyavahāra).

If it is argued that there is no such fault because of the qualification "provided it is a cognition" (jñānatve sati), we say no; for the deviation remains as it was in the case of the determinate experience (savikalpakānubhava) of silver arising only for one who possesses the indeterminate (nirvikalpaka) cognition of silver.

If it is argued that what is intended is the state of being produced only for one who possesses a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) of silver, we say no; for this fails to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) in the case of cognitions of avoidance (*hāna*) and so forth.
Furthermore, this inference is subverted by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being produced by the mind assisted by mere latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Nor can this very reason establish [the probandum] in the subject (*pakṣa*), since the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has already been stated.

Furthermore, as for this property of being a recollection (*smaraṇatva*) which is to be proven: it cannot be a generality (*sāmānya*), since that is not accepted by the Prābhākaras among the qualities (*guṇa*).
If you say it is "not being an experience" (*ananubhavatva*), then what does that mean—is it being other than experience, or being a non-locus of the nature of experience (*anubhavatva*)?
In the first case, since even experience could possess that [property], it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
In the second case, it must be stated what constitutes "experience-ness" (*anubhavatva*);
if you say it is "being other than memory," no.
This is because the definition would over-apply to memory as well, and because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
If it is argued that "the nature of memory is being produced solely from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge," we say no;

for since we accept that memory arises from mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), the subject (*pakṣa*) has an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).
Furthermore, this cognition of silver is determined to have that [silver] as its object because it conforms to the presence and absence of the operation of the sense-faculties;
thus, its object is sublated.
If it is argued that this is not so because the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) are employed for something else, [we reply: no.
Therefore, once its status as memory is established, is it to be assumed that it is subsumed under something else, or is it simply so?
Not the first, because that [other thing] does not exist; for if its existence were established through this very inference, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Not the second [alternative],
because it would follow that even a correct cognition of silver would possess that same character.
If it is argued that "the exhaustion [of the cause] elsewhere is suspected," even so, there is no escape from the fallacy of the "mistimed" (*kālātīta*) reason, as it remains doubtful.
Even if there is a correct experience of silver, how is it determined by you that there is no sublation elsewhere?

If you say it is because of the determination of its being an experience, we say no; for the status of being an experience is itself doubtful due to the suspicion that the operation of the sense organ might have been applied elsewhere.

If you say the determination of its being an experience follows from the correspondence with practical activity regarding the object present before one, we say no; for even the experience of that correspondence remains undetermined.

If it is argued that, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), one should not suspect a futile dissipation [of the cause] elsewhere, this applies equally to the case at hand. By this, the definition of memory as "that which arises from a cause that is not presently present" is also refuted; for in the case of a second or subsequent error, this would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) and the undesirable consequence of the probandum being indistinguishable [from the subject].
If it is argued that memory is the state of representing that aspect [of the object], no; for this is contradicted by direct experience.
By this, the view that memory has as its object an entity conjoined with cognition is also refuted.
By this very [argument], the two counter-inferences (*pratipakṣānumāna*) should also be understood as being subsumed.

This is because it was intended in the first formal argument (*prayoga*) that "this should not be designated as 'memory' because it is devoid of the marks of memory, such as the recollection of the object's specific features.
For this very reason, the process of the cognition of bitter sugar and so forth is also refuted. (2.233)

As for the objection that assuming the opposite [of our position] involves the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*), let it be so, provided that the occurrence of activity and the like can be accounted for by the mere non-apprehension of distinction (*vivekāgraha*).
However, we shall demonstrate that this is not the case.

Furthermore, if this were so, one would not need to admit the existence of the cloth even after having accepted the entire collection of causes up to the final conjunction of the threads, since everything would be accounted for by that alone.

If it is argued that even though the cloth has been cognized, it cannot be negated, and that without it the cognition of oneness and so forth would not be possible—then since this is equally the case in the opposite view (the theory of non-apprehension), why should there be any burden [of proof] for the former?
If it is asked, "What is the proof for the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*)? [the answer follows].
We say that it is indeed an experience (*anubhava*).

For just as, in the case of silver present before one, a single cognition having a qualified object—namely, "this is silver"—manifests either through self-luminosity, or through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), or by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), so too does this [cognition in question]; why then should it not be a single cognition with a qualified object?
For we do not perceive even the slightest distinction between them; or, if there were such a perception, our engagement [with cognition] would not occur.

If it is argued that one [cognition] is "corresponding to reality" (*yathārtha*) because of the existence of such an object, while another is "not corresponding to reality" (*ayathārtha*) due to the absence of that object—despite both being indistinguishable in their objective domain and both appearing as a single entity characterized by that specific object—then this is not so.

For otherwise, even for anyone else, there would be the undesirable consequence that confidence in the unity of a specific object could not be established, and one would be forced to accept the opposite [view].

If it is argued that "there is no cognition at all that grasps the unity of a specific object," we say no; because if one denies a cognition established by experience, one would be forced to deny the very nature of both memory and perception.
Furthermore, the activity of one desiring silver toward mother-of-pearl is inexplicable otherwise than through the postulation of a cognition of it as something else (anyathājñāna).
If it is argued that this activity is possible from two cognitions whose difference has not been grasped— both in terms of their own nature (*svarūpa*) and their objects (*viṣaya*)—
then what is this so-called "difference"?
Is it essential nature (*svarūpa*), or distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), or mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), or else dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)?
Not the first,
because it is impossible for that [object] not to appear when there is the appearance of the object of knowledge within self-luminous cognition.
Not the second.
Because qualities are not admitted to reside in qualities;
because it would follow that one seeking one thing might act toward another, since the non-apprehension of difference is possible everywhere;
and [the third alternative] must be addressed.
Is it that the mutual absence between "this-ness" and "silver-ness" does not appear, or is it the mutual absence between "this" and "silver"?
It cannot be the first,
because it is impossible for that [mutual absence] not to appear in the case of a genus and an individual which cause the recollection of two non-synonymous words.
Furthermore, what is called mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is simply the very nature of one thing as distinct from the other;
since that [nature] is perceived, how could there be a non-perception of it?
For this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable.

Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because the "this-ness" (idantva) residing in the object present before one is perceived as not existing in the silver, and the "silver-ness" (rajatatva) residing in the silver is perceived as not existing in the object present before one; for it is the non-apprehension of the non-relation (*asaṃsarga*) between these two—this-ness and silver-ness—that is intended [by you]. If this is argued, we say no.
For non-association (*asaṃsarga*) is simply the absence of association (*saṃsarga*).
And since that [absence] is, for our opponents, nothing other than the very intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of "this" and "silver-ness," how could it not appear when those two appear?
Even by those who maintain the theory of error (*viparyaya*), the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) must necessarily be admitted.
If it is argued that the same fault applies there as well, we say no;
for we do not admit that difference (*bheda*) consists merely in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the object].

Now, you might think: "The non-apprehension of those two—the property of 'mother-of-pearl-ness' (*śuktitva*) and so forth residing in the object before one which distinguishes it from silver, and the property of 'being in a remote location' (*vyavahitadeśatva*) and so forth residing in the silver which distinguishes it from the object before one—is what causes [the person] to act."
That is incorrect;
for if one does not perceive the "mother-of-pearl-ness" (śuktitva) of the object present before one, a person seeking mother-of-pearl would not act toward it.
And since silver is not present there, if its properties such as proximity were not perceived, a person seeking silver would likewise not act toward it.
But how could there be an activity directed toward what stands before one by someone seeking silver?
Furthermore, one who asserts that the activity of one seeking a different object [occurs] elsewhere due to the non-apprehension of difference must be questioned:
is this very same practical activity [of mistaking one thing for another] due to the non-apprehension of difference, or is it due to the apprehension of non-difference?

Or [it might be argued] that "even everyone [acts thus] due to the non-apprehension of difference. The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it would result in the fallacy of having no determinate cause.
But surely, in all cases, it is only the apprehension of non-difference that prompts action;
likewise, the non-apprehension of difference is also accepted as such because of its similarity to that [apprehension].
For example:

First, even in the case of a cognition intended to be motivating, there is indeed a non-apprehension of difference solely because of the absence of any distinction—both in terms of essential nature and in terms of object—between the two aspects of the apprehension of the means required and the apprehension of the [object] standing before one.
Likewise, here too, a non-discriminating common form is apprehended;
however, the discriminating unique property (asādhāraṇadharma) of both the objects to be known and the cognitions themselves is not apprehended.
And therefore, [it might be argued that] a single impelling condition, having a form similar [to its effect], produces this pair of feelings and the subsequent activity.
This is not so;
for it would fail to escape the fault of having an indeterminate cause.

Furthermore, is it to be postulated that activity occurs solely because of similarity to the instigator, or is there a universal rule that whatever is similar to something performs that same function?
It cannot be the first,
for it would entail the postulation of an unobserved entity (*adṛṣṭa*).
If it is argued that this was accepted out of a desire for worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), we say no; for that [activity] is well-established precisely by accepting its opposite [cessation].
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because one does not observe the cessation of cold from a cluster of *guñjā* berries, which resemble fire.

[Objection: Just as for you, the cognition of silver produced by a fragment of mother-of-pearl resembling silver arises from that which is to be accomplished by silver (i.e., the silver itself), why does activity not likewise arise from two cognitions that resemble a single motivating cognition?
[Reply: It is not so.
This is because it is not accepted that the object is the direct cause of cognition;
rather, similarity functions as a defect, like a cataract or similar impairment.
Furthermore, if these two cognitions were to produce activity based merely on similarity to the motivating factor, why would they not also produce cessation?
For in that case, there exists a non-apprehension of difference (*abhedāgrahaṇa*) consisting in the similarity to the apprehension of a distinct object that would cause cessation.
But [an objection may be raised]: "Just as the non-apprehension of difference produces for you the apprehension of non-difference, why should it not likewise produce activity?
Not so.
Because of irregularity;
for in the production of knowledge, the independence belongs to the causes and not to the person.
And those causes, having fallen into such a collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*), produce a corresponding cognition.
However, [the means of knowledge] do not depend upon the desire of a person, because they merely produce the cognition of what is to be abandoned or what is to be disregarded.
But with regard to action, the person alone is independent, not the cognition;
for even when cognition exists, it is only the person who acts once he has formed a desire.
However, it is not the case that knowledge has arisen merely by the fact that [an object] has been produced; for even in the case of one who is indifferent or mistaken, the same would follow.
Thus, the eyes and other sense organs, when defiled by the fault of non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*), produce error.
But a person ought not to act merely on the basis of a similarity with that which prompts action.
Or, if that were the case, it has already been stated that a discerning person would also desist due to the similarity [of the cognition] to that which causes cessation.
Furthermore, does cognition produce activity toward an object directly, or by means of desire and effort?
Not the first.
For there would be the undesirable consequence of activity occurring even toward things that are to be avoided or disregarded.
In the second case, how could activity arise from two cognitions whose difference has not been apprehended? For effort is the direct cause of activity directed toward the object present before one.
If there were that desire,
there would be an inference of its being a means to a desired end;
yet that is not possible.
Because the property of being silver has not been apprehended as a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

Now, when silver is apprehended, the cognition that it is a means to achieve what is desired arises through the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*)— that is, the apprehension of non-difference (*abhedagraha*)— with respect to that [silver].
If it is argued that [the cognition] produces a desire for what is present before one due to its similarity [to that object], we say no;
