for if that were the case, then because of the similarity consisting in the non-apprehension of difference following from the apprehension of difference, there would result even indifference [toward the object].
Now, let the second position then be accepted.
For instance:
in the case of real silver, there exists both the cognition of the individual instance of silver and the awareness of the universal of silver-ness (*rajatatva*);
yet, there is no cognition of their non-relation (*asaṃsarga*).
It is by this much alone that those seeking it engage in activity toward them;
for they do not perceive an identity between the two,
because there is no identity between the universal (jāti) and the individual (vyakti).
Furthermore, the apprehension of a relation is not the motivator in that case, for the relation between those two is inherence (*samavāya*).
And that is not perceptible,
because of the absence of sense-object contact.

Nor can it be known through inference at that time, because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*). For the logical mark for that [validity] is the perception of a form possessing expectancy together with a form possessing a similar appearance, which is qualified by being the generator of non-contradictory practical activity; and non-contradiction cannot be apprehended prior to the actual engagement [with the object].
Since all of this is indeed operative even in the case of error, how can there be an impossibility of activity in the absence of misapprehension?
Alternatively, the cause of activity regarding a real piece of silver is the apprehension of the difference between the locus of "silver-ness" and [the substrate];
and this [apprehension] exists in the present case as well.
Nor should it be argued that desire is untenable if silver-ness is not perceived in the object standing before one;

for [it might be claimed] that the inference of being a means to a desired end is possible either because the non-relation with silver has not been grasped, or because the difference from silver has not been grasped.
This too is incorrect, because both the non-apprehension of non-relation and the non-apprehension of difference have already been refuted.
Furthermore, this being the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*).

This is because the apprehension of the mere thing (*vastumātra*) and the non-apprehension of relations (*asaṃsargāgraha*) would be identical to indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*). [Objection: The relation between a quality (*rūpa*) and its possessor (*rūpin*) shines forth in determinate perception.
If it is argued that the distinction lies in the fact that non-conceptual [cognition] consists of the mere nature of the object (*vastusvarūpamātra*),

then what is this relationship between form (*rūpa*) and the bearer of form (*rūpin*)? If it is claimed that it is the state of being the object of mutual expectancy between the property (*dharma*) and the possessor of the property (*dharmī*), then is that their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) or something else?
In the first case, even that [object] is indeed manifested in non-conceptual [cognition].
In the second case, is it sensory or supersensory?
If it is the former, how could it not be manifested in a non-conceptual [cognition]?

In the second case, how could it appear in a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*)? If it is argued that, because its perception depends upon the perception of the object itself, it appears in the conceptual cognition even though it did not appear in the non-conceptual one (*nirvikalpaka*), then it follows that there is nothing distinct from the relation itself; thus, the conceptual cognition arises solely from the apprehension of the relation.
Furthermore, indeterminate cognition does not possess the capacity to instigate action.

Moreover, if one were to accept that action occurs everywhere solely due to the non-apprehension of non-relation, then since the action of the middle-aged man would likewise be of that nature, the child would lack the means to infer the knowledge of that relation; consequently, the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding words in their related meanings would be impossible.
There would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of verbal testimony (*śābdapramāṇa*).
Now, one might think:
"The cognizer of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) certainly exists for the person engaged in linguistic practice."
What indeed exists that is not useful for engagement?
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
In this regard, it must be stated whether that subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is necessarily involved in engagement or not.

In the first case, let it be useful for that activity or not; however, it is at least established that without the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), there can be no activity toward the object present before one by someone seeking silver.
In the second case, however, the total abolition of verbal communication remains as it was.
Furthermore, it is untenable to claim that something which is invariably antecedent is nonetheless not a cause.

If you argue that when there is no apprehension of the non-connection between two appearing things, the apprehension of their connection is an unavoidable proximity, we say no; for the opposite could equally be asserted.
And this must necessarily be so.
For it is logical that conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is based on the perception of that which is to be conventionally used (*vyavahartavya*),
and not based on the non-perception of the opposite of that which is to be conventionally used.
Indeed, the conventional usage of a jar is preceded by the cognition of the jar to be conventionally used, because it is a conventional usage, just like the conventional usage of a jar [itself].

The object of dispute is the cognition [of silver], which has as its object that which stands before one, because it generates linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding that object, like a [cognition] that is commonly accepted [as valid].

Alternatively, that which stands before one is the domain of the cognition of silver, because—while not being a means to [actual] silver—it is the object of activity by one desiring that [silver], like real silver.

Furthermore, the cognition of silver under dispute is not different from this [present] cognition, because while there is a difference between what is manifesting and what is not manifesting, it is itself manifesting, like the commonly accepted cognition of silver. Such are the arguments.

Furthermore, the fact that the cognition "this is not silver" possesses the status of a sublater (*bādhaka*) would be untenable in the absence of a contrary [cognition]; therefore, it leads to the inference of such a contrary [cognition].
For if that were the case, it would not have the status of a sublater.
To begin with, its status as a sublater cannot consist in its being a remover of non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*).
Because it would follow that all cognitions would result in the attainment of suchness (*tathātva*);
nor [is it a sublater] by way of interrupting worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*),
because if transaction does not arise for those who do not seek it, it would follow that the cognition "this is not silver" would lack the status of being a sublater (*abādhaka*).

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the cognition of a tiger, a thief, and so forth, would be a sublater [of knowledge], because it also interrupts purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
Nor can it be by way of interrupting the object's fitness for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*);
for even at another time, since there is delusion regarding that same object, it would follow that no activity would ever occur.

Nor can it be [the cause] by way of being an obstacle to worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because once non-discrimination (*aviveka*) has ceased, worldly transaction becomes impossible due to the mere absence of its cause; thus, it is illogical to postulate such an obstacle.
Furthermore, this would result in the cognition of tigers, thieves, and the like being considered sublaters (*bādhaka*).
"Doubt is unreal because it is sublated, like conventional discourse.
For this very reason, the establishment of its status as a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*) is also proven through its well-known nature as an error (*bhrānti*).
This being the case, the inference based on the property of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) should be understood as being subject to the fallacy of "missing the proper time" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
And it is also sublated by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being produced by a non-defective instrument.

By this, the inference [of validity] based on the nature of the cognition of silver is also refuted. Otherwise, one might argue: "The cognition under dispute is consistent with reality, because it is a cognition."
Or one might also argue: "The object is silver, because it is the locus of the practical activity (vyavahāra) regarding silver.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that "the nature of cognition (jñānatva) occurs only in accordance with reality," and so forth—is this "nature of cognition" a universal (sāmānya) or something specific?
The first [alternative] is not tenable,
because the locus is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent.
In the second case, if it is the state of being a cognition occurring in a cognition that accords with reality, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Even if one takes as the subject (pakṣa) the cognition that exists in erroneous cognition (vimata-jñāna), the term "only" (mātra) would be redundant. And if that [term] were omitted from the proposition (pratijñā), the very same fault as in the first inference would arise.

Furthermore, in the phrase "existing only in valid cognition" (yathārtha-mātra-vṛtti), is it intended merely that it does not exist in invalid cognition (ayathārtha-avṛtti), or rather that it does not exist in erroneous cognition (ayathārtha-jñāna-avṛtti)?

In the first case, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*), because it is established that [the property] does not reside in a usage that is not in accordance with reality. In the second case, the qualifier is unestablished for the opponent (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*),
and "residing only in that which is produced by a non-defective causal complex" (*aduṣṭasāmagrījanyamātravṛttitvam*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
And as for the claim that "the mother-of-pearl appears as silver," and so forth—
that too is incorrect;
for in a statement such as "Mount Meru is a mustard seed," even Mount Meru appears as a mustard seed, and thus the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).
Otherwise, one who has heard such a pseudo-statement would not negate it, because [the negation] would not have been occasioned;
for the negation of an established entity is not logical.
Furthermore, if this were the case, there would be no distinction between a statement whose object is sublated, such as "fire is cold," and a meaningless statement, such as "a pot cooks."
As for this [argument] beginning with "the identity with silver," that too is incorrect;
because if that [identity] is not perceived, the locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

Because there is a contradiction in its being perceived, and because the example is equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*), let this suffice; [this concludes] the refutation of Rāmānuja’s theory of misapprehension (*akhyāti*). However, someone else says the following:

This is because of such Vedic scripture as, "He made each one of them threefold," and because of Purāṇic texts such as, "Having come together, they entered into mutual conjunction," and because of Sūtras stating that [each element] consists of the three [qualities].
(line 6) ...

Otherwise, because it has been established through the narrative of Śvetaketu and Uddālaka, even non-duality (*advaita*) would not be the intended meaning of the Śruti. [As it is said:
"Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I am Brahman.'"

Thus, even this restatement of the worship of another deity would not have its own meaning as its primary purport, because it occurs within the context of the section on worship, as in the passage: "Now, he who worships another deity...
and so forth; and in that case, there would be much confusion.
Therefore, this is the intention of the author of the Sūtras: that the causality of the origin and so forth of the world is indeed an intrinsic characteristic (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman.
And thus, by the force of other clear statements of his own, this Sūtra as well has as its sole purpose the definition of the essential nature [of Brahman].
Since, for this very reason, the causality of the origin and so forth of the world is here designated in the Sūtra as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman...
Therefore, the very commencement of this sūtra is not tenable according to the opponent's view;
thus he says: "Hence" (ataḥ).
Therefore, that Teacher of the World also rejected the identity of the individual soul [with Brahman].
For a definition (lakṣaṇa) serves the purpose of distinguishing [the object] from both its own class and other classes;
as it has been said: "The purpose of a definition is the exclusion of those of the same and different classes.

And thus, by this definition, the author of the Sūtras has distinguished Brahman from the living being (jīva), which belongs to the same class, and from the insentient (jaḍa), which belongs to a different class.

How could there be the commencement of a sūtra refuting the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) for those who maintain that such identity exists? It would only be possible if this [definition] were somehow an incidental definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*).
And it has been established that this is the definition of its own nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*).
This undertaking of a definition might be untenable for the Advaitins if this definition were stated for the purpose of excluding the individual soul (*jīva*).

However, when the definition is explained as being intended merely to exclude what is insentient (*jaḍa*), how could the commencement of the sūtra on the definition be untenable for those who maintain the identity of the soul? To this, he says: "Not so" (*na hi*).
For the individual soul cannot be the cause of the birth and so forth of the world.
For whatever lacks that characteristic must be admitted as excluded from it;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of the definition being over-narrow (avyāpti). And this characteristic does not belong to the living being (jīva).
How then is this [self] not excluded by this [definition]?
Furthermore, if the living being (jīva) is not excluded by this definition,
then it too is included within the scope of what is to be defined.

If that were the case, then having raised the objection that the definition would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to the individual soul (*jīva*), the author of the Sūtras’ refutation of that objection—stating that "because there is the designation of another [the Lord], there would follow the fault of not performing what is beneficial" and so forth—would be inconsistent. For no one ever suspects that a definition could over-apply to the very object of definition (*lakṣya*). Or, if such a suspicion were somehow raised, one would have to accept that the *jīva* is also an object of definition; yet, instead of doing so, the refutation of the definition is not applied to it. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the non-performance of what is beneficial. (*hitākriyā*)
And the Lord himself will indeed explain the fault of acting contrary to one's welfare and so forth.
Although the opponent also indeed accepts that the definition [of the soul] serves to exclude [others],

as he says: "Setting aside the Omniscient and Omnipotent [Brahman], it is not even possible to conceive of the birth and so forth of the transmigrating Hiraṇyagarbha from anything else imagined by others— whether from the non-conscious *pradhāna* and the like, or even from a conscious being such as [Hiraṇyagarbha] himself, who possesses limited power of knowledge and action."

Nevertheless, this was stated in order to establish [the point] through logical reasoning. Furthermore, since even the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) asserted by the proponents of illusion (*māyāvādins*) has been refuted by the authors of the Sūtras themselves,
he says "And as for qualitylessness" (*nirguṇatvaṃ ca*) to show that, for this reason as well, the commencement of the Sūtras defining Brahman is not possible for the Māyāvādins.
And the absence of qualities has been refuted by that very Lord himself.
For a defining statement (lakṣaṇavākya), by directly establishing the connection of the definiendum with its unique property, establishes—by implication—the exclusion of it from others.

Therefore, even by this defining statement, the connection of Brahman with the causality of the world's origination and so forth, as well as with omniscience and other qualities inseparable from that [causality], must be established.
And thus, the qualityless nature of Brahman is negated by this aphorism.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that there is no distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman], how can the commencement of the Sūtra— which negates such lack of distinction— be justified? For those who accept the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, as well as the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) of Brahman, this conception of the causality of the world's origin and so forth as being merely extrinsic (*taṭastha*) would result in the impossibility of commencing the Sūtra on defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇasūtra*).

If, by this Sūtra, the causality of the world's birth and so forth were stated as the defining characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman, it would not be so; rather, it is merely an incidental characteristic (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*).

For such causality of the world's birth and so forth does not contradict the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, nor does it contradict Brahman’s qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*). (3.46)
Is it not the case that the proof for [the term] *svalakṣaṇa* has already been stated?
Not so;
for it may mean either "its own characteristics" (*svasya lakṣaṇāni*) or "characteristics of itself" (*svasya lakṣaṇāni*).
Alternatively, it may be because they are not characteristics (lakṣaṇa) due to their being included within its true nature (svarūpa), since that meaning is logically consistent.
If that were so, the designation would have been: "Māyā is that from which this [world] originates, etc., and Brahman is its substratum";
rather than: "Brahman is that from which this [world] originates, etc."
Not so;
for the usage is justifiable through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the expression "that which has the sound [of the river] is the Gaṅgā.

Now, even by one who stands on the bank, the identity of Brahman with the individual soul (*jīva*) and its qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) [are established] through [Brahman's] being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe.
It is contradictory;
for the opponent has cited "the state of being a roosting place for crows" as a definition that stands apart [from the definiendum].
If that were included within the definiendum, then even "the state of being the locus of crows" would have to be the meaning of the word "house."
And consequently, upon the departure of the crow, there would arise the cognition that "one part of the house has been destroyed.
In that case, does the crow's being the locus [of the action] differentiate the house from those things that are not its locus, or not?
If the latter position is taken, it contradicts experience and renders the expression of that [property] useless.
If that is so, how does even the definition of Brahman in the first [sūtra] not exclude the individual soul (jīva),
and how is it not rendered qualified (saguṇa) by association with that?
Not so.

For that individual soul (*jīva*) who, thinking the Self to be inseparable from the aggregate of cause and effect and thus subject to agency, enjoyership, and contact with defects, undergoes affliction— he alone is excluded by this definition. In this regard, there is no contradiction in accepting that the element of consciousness (*caitanyadhātu*) does not differ from Brahman.

Nor is the meaning of the Sūtra that Brahman is the substratum of a real Māyā which is the cause of the real phenomenal world (prapañca), by which Brahman would possess attributes; rather, the meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman is that upon whose support the entire illusory manifestation (vivarta) of the world depends. And this being the meaning of the Sūtra, how could the oneness of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, as well as the attributelessness (nirguṇatva) of Brahman, be contradicted? *3,47*
"The conception that the state of being the cause of the world's birth and so forth is merely incidental (taṭastha) is untenable.
To this it is replied:
Let this matter rest for now.

The theory that the world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) and so forth is rejected because it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and because it will be refuted in the *Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa*.

Furthermore, why should it be accepted here in this Sūtra that Brahman is taught through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as the cause of the origin and so forth of the world from a remote standpoint?
For it is observed that one resorts to secondary indication only when the primary meaning is impossible.
First of all, there is no perception that sublates Brahman’s status as the cause of the world's origin and so forth, because [Brahman] is not an object of perception.
Nor is there inference, because it is sublated by scripture.
Nor is there traditional authority (āgama), because it has scope elsewhere, being intended for such matters as the effortless performance [of rituals].
Surely this is determined through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti):
first of all, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is necessary;
and that [identity] is not possible unless the causality of the origin and so forth of the world constitutes its very definition (svalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, because it cannot be established otherwise, this definition must be understood as pertaining solely to the realm of illusion (*māyā*).
It is postulated that Brahman is defined by the phrase "that from which the origin and so forth of this [world proceed]" only through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
To this, he replies: "Precisely by way of difference" (*bhedenaiva*). (3.48)
But when the primary meaning is possible through differentiation alone, why resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā)?

If, in order to preserve the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, one abandons the literal meaning of the Sūtra and resorts to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then—since the primary meaning of the Sūtra is possible through the very difference between the *jīva* and Brahman that has been accepted—why should figurative indication be resorted to? One might object: "Is it not the case that there is a doubt as to whether figurative indication should be resorted to by adopting non-difference, or whether the primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*) should be adopted by adopting difference?"
We, however, maintain that the second position alone is superior;
for a secondary sense of statements is observed even in some instances when it is resorted to for the sake of preserving what is not [otherwise] authoritative.
This is what was stated: "precisely by way of distinction."
Now, one might object: "How can the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman be considered lacking authority?
Is it not established by such scriptural texts as *tat tvam asi* (That thou art)? If this is argued, we say no; for it is contradicted by logical reasoning (*upapatti*).
For instance: that which is the primary meaning of the word "tat" (that).

By the passage beginning with "Existence alone, my dear," that which is under discussion—the creator of fire, water, food, and so forth; the root, the abode, and the support of all beings; free from even a trace of all defects; an inexhaustible mine of infinite qualities; and who is the primary referent of the term *tvaṃ* (thou), perceived through direct perception and other means—[is established].

Is identity with this [Supreme Being] asserted by this statement by taking up [the individual soul] as it is— accomplished, of little power, dependent on another, defiled by defects, and possessing limited qualities such as knowledge—
or rather, by abandoning the contradictory portions through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?
Not the first [alternative], because due to mutual contradiction and the absence of fitness, there would follow the consequence of it being a fallacy, like the sentence "an old ox" (*jaradgava*).
Regarding the second [alternative], he states the fault: "only by means of difference" (*bhedenaiva*). (3.49)

Just as in the case of "The lion is Devadatta" and similar expressions, one might resort to a merely figurative grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) while not at all accepting the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, on the grounds that the primary meaning of both terms is possible [in that context].
"Why should the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the indicator that both excludes and includes) be adopted? [Objection:

"In this doubt—whether the figurative nature of the words *tat* and *tvam* is to be explained by taking their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as primary, or whether the primary meaning of the words *tat* and *tvam* is to be explained by grasping their coreferentiality as secondary—is there not a reason for deciding between them?"
It is not that [the distinction] does not exist;

for there exists the maxim, "One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family," and because it has been demonstrated in various places that the very difference between the indicative marks of the intended meaning (*tātparyaliṅga*) constitutes their compatibility.

This has been stated as "only by means of difference" (*bhedenaiva*). Furthermore, regarding the claim that the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) establishes the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman through a definition consisting of essential nature alone, by abandoning the contradictory forms— this so-called "abandonment of contradictory forms" is not merely a matter of non-intentionality, as was stated previously.
Now, just as in the case of "this is that Devadatta," there is the impermanence of the contradictory form;
regarding this, he asks: "How?"
How could there be unity for this [Self], which possesses eternal qualities, through the loss of those qualities?
Furthermore, the eternality of the qualities of the Lord will be established in the *Liṅgapāda*.
The phrase "of this Lord" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*),
because even in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), defects such as dependence are eternal.
As it is stated in the Purāṇa: “He has little power and is not omniscient.

(3.56) Now, one might object: the meaning of the soul’s identity with Brahman is achieved by abandoning the contradictory forms, and not merely by disregarding those contradictory forms, nor even by [claiming] impermanence;
rather, it is simply the soul’s identity with Brahman as devoid of attributes (nirguṇa). To this we say: no.
Because it is impossible to define the very state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*). To explain:
Is that which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) different from the Lord who possesses qualities (saguṇa), or is it non-different?
In the second case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that it too possesses qualities, which would contradict its being devoid of qualities.
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "sadaiva" (always).
If this [Self] were always possessed of qualities, then that which is devoid of qualities would always be distinct from it.

(1.1.102ab) If that which is devoid of qualities were absolutely distinct from that which possesses qualities, then—since this [latter] is eternally possessed of qualities—it would follow that the one devoid of qualities is eternally distinct from it;
and thus, there would never be liberation (kaivalya).

But surely, it is by its very nature devoid of qualities; it is only through superimposed false qualities that it is spoken of as "possessing qualities" by the ignorant, just as the sky is perceived as blue due to the superimposition of blueness.
And since the stream of superimposition is beginningless and eternal, its state of possessing qualities is not undesired [as a conventional reality].

And thus, even the teaching of identity by means of abandoning the form of the false contradictory is not untenable, just as in the case of "the sky is formless," or as when another person reveals his own intention by saying, "That which is this silver is mother-of-pearl. To this, [the author] replies: "Not so" (na ca).
Nor can there be the quality of falsity [in that which is indeterminable], because that has been refuted.
"False" (mithyā) means either non-existent or indeterminable.
It cannot be the first [alternative],
because that is not accepted.
Not the second [alternative],

because that which is inexpressible has already been refuted in the very first sūtra. Therefore, "being devoid of qualities" (nirguṇatva), characterized by the absence of qualities, cannot be defined in any way whatsoever.
Now, it may be objected that those who know the categories of existence consider the pentad beginning with quality (guṇa) to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). Let them so consider;
for at present, we are not engaged in refuting the existence of a qualityless entity.
What indeed is it that cannot be described by non-dualists as the qualityless Brahman?
For here, by the word "quality" (guṇa), mere attributes (dharma) are intended.
This is also universally accepted regarding its qualities and so forth;
furthermore, that qualities and the like possess qualities themselves will be explained when refuting the theory that atoms are the originators [of matter].
Now, [it is objected]: "The witness is conscious, solitary, and devoid of qualities."
Thus, Brahman is heard to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
This is not so;
for, being contradicted by the aforementioned logical inconsistencies, that passage must have another meaning.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction, since qualities such as being a witness (*sākṣitva*) would also be [inherently] properties of the self (*dharmatva*).
For a witness is indeed one who sees directly;
as Pāṇini has said:

Regarding the rule "when [the word] *saṃjñā* (name) [is used] for one who sees directly" (*sākṣāddraṣṭari saṃjñāyām*), he says mockingly to one who, despite the fact that being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*)—characterized by the absence of *dharma*—has already been refuted, still accepts it out of mere obstinacy: "Being devoid of qualities," etc. (*nirguṇatvam iti*).
In that case, there would be a state devoid of qualities; otherwise, it would be demonic.

And at that time, even though the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) has been refuted through reasoning, if the state of being devoid of qualities were still pleasing to the opponent, then it would simply be the state of being demonic (*āsura*), characterized by the total absence of all auspicious qualities denoted by the word "quality" (*guṇa*);
for it has already been stated that [such a thing] cannot be defined otherwise.
Therefore, we also accept the identity [of Brahman] with the proponents of Māyā.
By this, it is addressed that the objection raised regarding this definition—that because Brahman is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), it must be "extrinsic" (taṭastha)—is refuted.

For neither the state of being permeated by the performance of various types of effects, nor the nature of possessing the power to produce them, can possibly be included within the pure Brahman that is the object of inquiry.
That too should be understood as refuted,
because the very absence of qualities has already been rejected.

As for what was stated— "This is not a qualification of Brahman, because it is impossible for it to be included within the nature of the unconditioned Brahman since it has the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as its limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*)"—
that will be refuted later. Now,
regarding the faultiness of the claim that "the relationship between a quality and its possessor cannot be defined in terms of either difference or non-difference":

He repeats the opponent’s argument—stated for the sake of establishing that the definition is "external" (taṭastha) because the quality and the possessor of the quality cannot be determined as either different or non-different—in order to refute it:
“Whether there be difference, non-difference, or both, between the object of definition and the definition... (MAnu 1.1.103cd).

It has been stated that what is here primarily declared as the definition— namely, being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world— is intended to imply the possession of all qualities such as omniscience and the rest.

Both of these characteristics must be either different from, non-different from, or both different and non-different from the Brahman that is the object characterized (*lakṣya*). Not the first [option], because,

like Mount Meru and Mount Mandara, the relationship of characterized and characteristic (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) as well as the relationship of quality and qualified (*guṇa-guṇi-bhāva*) would be untenable.
If it is argued that [the relation does not exist] because of the actual existence of a relation, [we reply:
no, because that [relation] also cannot be determined as being either different from or non-different from its two relata.
It is not the second [alternative].
Otherwise, even Brahman, which is non-different from many [individuals], would fall into the state of being manifold;

and thus, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statement that "it is indeed one," as well as the consequence that the defining characteristics (lakṣaṇas) themselves would become multiple.
Furthermore, there would be the fault of redundancy regarding such scriptural passages as, "From which indeed these beings are born";
for the relationship of the defined and the definition, as well as the relationship of quality and the possessor of quality, are not possible if there is non-difference.
For that which is unestablished must be defined by means of that which is established;
and it is not logical for the very same thing to be both established and unestablished at the same time.
Furthermore, one who possesses qualities is the possessor of those qualities.
Nor does one possess that [quality] by means of itself;
nor is it the third [alternative],
because of mutual contradiction.
Therefore, because it cannot be definitively determined, this is not an intrinsic definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa) of Brahman; rather, it is merely an extrinsic definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa).
And by means of that extrinsic definition, there is no contradiction of Brahman’s non-duality.
"Just as that which appeared as silver was actually mother-of-pearl, so too [Brahman] may be characterized by the causality of the phenomenal world (prapañca), even though that causality is illusory.
Having thus restated [the opponent's position], he begins to refute it with the words: "Thus questioned... (*pṛṣṭa*).
Thus it was asked. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.104a)

The word "must be stated" (*vaktavyam*) is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). The phrase "when questioned" (*pṛṣṭe*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇam*); it should also be understood to include "and when refuted" (*dūṣite ca*).
Because the objections are utterly irrelevant, it was simply stated, "when asked," as if asking,
"what is there to be said? In that regard,
although there is no difference between the attributes such as being the cause of the world's birth and so forth, because a distinction does exist, by virtue of that [distinction]...

Thinking that the statement "everything arises" cannot be asserted regarding an undifferentiated reality because the opponent does not admit any specific distinction therein, and because things such as pots—which are admitted to be false—cannot serve as examples, [the author], considering that this must be established only with respect to a real entity, says: "At that time."
...then there is no possibility at all for their identity.
If you thus refute the definition after having asked this question, then there is no way to determine the nature of their identity;
this is the intended meaning.
For the proponent of Māyā (the Māyāvādin) accepts two types of statements as revealing reality (*tattvāvedaka*).
One is the Great Sentence (mahāvākya), which has as its purport the identity of the individual soul and Brahman,
such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and so forth;
the other is the intermediate sentence (avāntaravākya), which has as its purport the essential nature of that [Brahman].

As in "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and so forth; both of these [scriptural passages] must be accepted by the opponent as being based on a single reality that possesses distinctions, for there is no other possible alternative. (3.65)
Among these, first of all, there is no other alternative for the first [position].
If it is asked how so, it is said:

regarding the identity taught by such statements as "That thou art," one must state whether that unity is non-different from the consciousness indicated by the word "That" (tat), or different, or both different and non-different.
Since the position of non-difference is primary because it has been accepted by others, he first refutes that view: "The identity [of the two] is non-difference."
That unity-in-difference is not to be known through scripture, because it is self-luminous.

If identity is accepted as being non-different from the very nature of consciousness, then that identity would not be something to be established by scripture through such texts as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
Why? Because the essential nature, being self-luminous, is eternally established;
and because identity consists of nothing other than that very nature.
For that which is merely manifest is not what is to be established by a treatise,
as that would lead to the consequence of futility.
Furthermore, others accept that self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) consists in being fit for the usage of "immediate" while being non-objective (*avedyatva*).
And thus, it is contradictory [to claim] that it is both self-luminous consciousness by nature and yet something to be established by the scripture.
Now, if it is argued that the scripture does not establish oneness, but rather dispels the delusion of difference;
As it has been said: "But [the cognition] is established as a negator," [we reply]: no, because when identity is being manifested, there is simply no room for the delusion of difference;
for the failure to realize the true nature of things is the cause of such delusion.
If it is argued that oneness does not manifest, we say no;
for this contradicts its being nothing but self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacaitanya*).
If it is argued that even though it is self-luminous, it does not appear due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no; for this would entail the consequence that it would never appear at all.
And thus, since the superimposition of ignorance (*avidyā-āropa*) is impossible when the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not manifest,
for it is not possible for the veil of ignorance to exist partially over an undivided reality.
If it is argued that ignorance is capable of making impossible things appear;
In that case, why is it not accepted as residing in insentient things alone?
For the lack of logical justification is equal [in both cases]. And thus: "It does not reside in insentient objects."
This is incorrect.
The statement "it is not to be known through the treatise" is merely an elliptical expression;
for even if it were something to be propounded by the treatise, its establishment would still occur through that very term itself.

It should also be understood that the statement "Thou art" would likewise be meaningless. If it is argued that the mere word "That" does not remove the delusion of difference, and therefore "Thou art" is meaningful, this is not so.
Because identity is established by that word (*tat-pada*), and because the delusion of difference is dispelled upon the realization of identity;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that it could never be removed.
If identity were not conveyed by the word "that" (tat), it would be impossible for [the object] to be merely the consciousness indicated by that term.
Now, one might ask: how then is the sentence "This is that Devadatta" to be understood?
Even here, if a distinction is not admitted, there is indeed the same impossibility. (3.68)
If there were a distinction [between them], then by force of that very distinction, the falsity [of one] would entail the truth [of the other].
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "Difference."
If it is admitted that identity is distinct from its own nature, there is first of all the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*),
because the proponent of Māyā has accepted that statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) have as their purport an indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*).
Another defect is the undesirable consequence that [identity] would be false (*mithyātva*).
This is because everything other than pure consciousness (caitanya) is admitted to be false;
otherwise, if duality were real, it would contradict non-duality itself.
If you ask, "If unity is false, what is lost? we say no.

Because of the continuation [of the argument] that "it is not to be known through scripture because it is false," otherwise the scripture such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) would become a non-revealer of reality. Furthermore, if the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman were false, then the reality of their difference would also follow.
Why? The meaning is: "by the force of pervasion" (*vyāpti-bala*).
[Objection: But we do not accept a difference between existents anywhere; so how can there be pervasion?
[Response: Not so.
Let the investigation into ultimate reality rest for now.
It is observed that when two trees standing far apart are perceived as one, that unity is false, whereas their difference is true.
Alternatively, for that which exists by its own nature, its non-existence is false; therefore, its opposite is true, as in the case of Brahman.

The occurrence of this reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) is established by relying on a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), namely: "If the state of being unreal and so forth is false, then the state of being real and so forth is true," as they have said:
"But when there is mutual contradiction, no third alternative can exist.
He refutes the third [position] with the words: "Difference and non-difference" (*bhedābhedau*).
If there were both difference and non-difference; MĀnuv 1.105c.

If both difference and non-difference from the essential nature are accepted regarding the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, then it must be stated: are those two non-different from consciousness (caitanya), or different, or both different and non-different?
In the first case, it would follow that consciousness itself is dual, or that the two [difference and non-difference] are one, and so forth.
He states the fault regarding the second [alternative] with the words "tadā" (then).
... for in that case, there would certainly be an infinite regress. // MAnu 1.105cd //
By the word "hi" (for), he expresses clarity for the purpose of demonstrating the lack of a final term (*anavasthā*). For instance:
is that difference distinct from the two things that differ, non-distinct, or both distinct and non-distinct?
In the first case, that distinction would likewise require another, leading to an infinite regress;
in the second case, there are defects such as synonymy with the word itself;
and the third is included within the third [category].
In that case as well, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) according to the method already stated.

Now, one might argue: "There is no infinite regress merely because a difference has another difference, and both difference and non-difference have yet other differences and non-differences; for these do not act as obstacles to production or cognition. If this is said, we reply: No.
Because, in the absence of the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣa*), the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) would be untenable, [the absence] acts as an obstacle to knowledge;
this is what was stated by the words "it would indeed be so."
Although a contradiction can be asserted regarding the acceptance of both difference and non-difference, it has not been stated here because it is obvious.
Likewise, in the position that oneness is different from its own nature, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [Objection:

But surely, even if oneness is non-different from consciousness, it will explain the self’s state of not being manifested by its own natural luminosity, precisely because it is self-establishing (*svanirvāhakatva*).
Alternatively, one might argue: "Let there be both difference and non-difference within the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*);
and even if there is no further difference or non-difference within those two, the practical application of the terms is possible because they are self-sustaining (*svanirvāhakatva*).
This is not so, for the intention [of the author] is that without the admission of *viśeṣa*, it is impossible even to speak of self-sustaining capacity; thus he says: "self-sustaining."
If there should be self-sufficiency, [then one may live by that].

If it were admitted that unity—or even both difference and non-difference—is its own self-establisher (*svanirvāhaka*), then we ask: for "self-establisher" means that which establishes itself; the state of being such is "self-establishment" (*svanirvāhakatā*).
And in the term "of itself" (*svasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
This is because of the grammatical rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65).

Thus, it is stated that within a single sustaining activity (*nirvāha-kriyā*), there exists for one and the same entity both the state of being sustained (*nirvāhyatva*) and the state of being a sustainer (*nirvāhakatva*), which are characterized respectively as the object and the agent.
Furthermore, that state of being sustained and the state of being a sustainer are absolutely non-different from one another, as well as from the substratum (*dharmin*) and the action (*kriyā*).

"Whether [the cause] is identical to or different from [the effect], or likewise whether it is external or externalizing— this distinction would either be a mere synonym or lead to an infinite regress in both cases. (MAnu 1.106b–d)

The term *nirvāhyam* [is used], and the term *nirvāhakam*—by the force of the word "also" (*api*), it would follow that even the collection of words beginning with *nirvāhakam* would constitute synonyms, because they possess the same meaning.
Yet, no one considers those words to be synonyms. Having restated the second [position], he refutes it: "[It would be] possessed of difference" (*bhedavān*).
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "if.

If the meanings such as "being that which is to be carried out" (*nirvāhyatva*) and so forth were not distinct from one another and from the substratum (*dharmin*), then, since those two types of difference would consist merely in the nature of the differencer itself, there would follow the fault of synonymy and so on; therefore, it must be accepted that they are like other differences.
And in that case, by relying on mutual difference or the difference of the substratum, there would be an infinite regress in both instances.

Having thus stated that the meaning of the great sentence is untenable if no distinction is admitted, he extends that same argument to the intermediate sentence as well, with the words "satya" (truth).
The same applies even to [the knowledge of] truth, wisdom, and so forth.
The meaning is that one must state the refutation by formulating such alternatives even with respect to intermediate statements (avāntara-vākya) such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
For instance:
are truth, knowledge, and so forth, absolutely non-different from one another and from Brahman; or are they different; or are they both different and non-different?
Not the first [alternative];

for if that were the case, it would follow that that [Self], being of the nature of the self-luminous Brahman, would be the object of exposition by the scriptures such as "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth;
and furthermore, since the words "Truth," "Knowledge," and so on would become synonyms, their simultaneous employment together would result in logical inconsistency.
Not the second,
because it would contradict your own established tenets (apasiddhānta) and because it would entail that the scripture does not reveal reality, as it would result in its being false.
Furthermore, it would follow that ignorance and so forth would be real; thus,
the third [alternative] is not tenable,
as it entails the consequence of an infinite regress.
And because self-sufficiency (*svanirvāhakatva*) cannot be defined in the manner stated above.
[Objection: But surely there is absolute non-difference between truth, knowledge, and so forth, both among themselves and with Brahman;
yet, even so, the words "truth," "knowledge," and so on, do not become synonyms.
This is because there exists a difference between the primary denotative meanings (*vācyārtha*) [of the two words].

For it is accepted that those words which denote higher or lower universals (*sāmānya*), or which denote Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*), function by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*).

Nor should it be argued that [the second term] is redundant, since if the object indicated by the word "Truth" (*satya*) were itself indicated by the word "Knowledge" (*jñāna*), it would be purposeless.
Furthermore, in the case of a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) involving an additional attribute, the status of being "indivisible in meaning" (*akhaṇḍārthatā*) is not established;
for even though there is no difference in the referent indicated by the secondary sense, the other words serve a purpose by excluding superimposed qualities such as unreality and so forth.
For this very reason, the scripture is not rendered useless.
If it is argued that the scripture has a purpose because it serves to exclude superimposed forms even though Brahman is self-luminous, we say no.

Is it meant that the purpose is the cognition of the exclusion of "unreality" and so forth as a qualification of Brahman, or is it the cognition of the exclusion itself as an independent matter? (3.76)
He states the fault in the first case: "Not by way of exclusion."
... there is no purpose in exclusion;
for if that which is excluded were without distinction [from what remains]... // MĀnuv 1.107bc //
The third case ending is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (itthambhūtalakṣaṇe).
You cannot state that the purpose of the words "real" (*satya*) and so forth is to exclude [qualities] such as unreality by means of their being qualifiers of Brahman.
Why? To this he says: "of that which is excluded" (*vyāvṛttasya*).
The meaning is: "given that Brahman, which is cognized as being excluded [from all else], is without distinction.
And if one accepts distinctions among absences, what wrong have positive entities committed? He refutes the second [position] with the words: "not of that which is excluded."
If the exclusion were not distinct from the Brahman that is excluded, then that independent exclusion would not serve as a purpose,
because it is not what is sought to be known.
One who desires liberation must seek to know either Brahman or its attributes.
In that regard, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not Brahman, because Brahman is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), is one, and is without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*).
Furthermore, if it were not even a property of Brahman, how could it be an object of inquiry for one seeking liberation?
And how could making known that which was not intended to be known constitute a purpose?
Furthermore, do the words "real" (*satya*) and so forth, with respect to Brahman, denote properties such as reality and so on, for the purpose of excluding non-reality and so forth,
or otherwise?
Not the first [alternative], because it is not accepted; thus he says: "not by way of exclusion."

The meaning is that once it is admitted that Brahman, as excluded [from all else], is devoid of distinctions (*aviśeṣatva*), it cannot be said that the purpose of the words is exclusion by way of expressing qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇābhidhānamukhena*).
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "Not of the excluded... (*na vyāvṛttasya*).
That is to say, if Brahman, being excluded [from all else], were devoid of distinction, there would be no presentation of attributes such as reality;
thus, it cannot be maintained that the purpose of the words is the exclusion of non-reality and so forth.
For it is not possible for the word "river" to have the exclusion of "non-river-ness" as its purpose if it does not denote "river-ness" in relation to the bank.
For it is by the presentation of a contradictory form that another contradictory form must be excluded.
As for what was stated— that the treatise is purposeful even regarding self-luminosity through the exclusion of superimposed forms—
that too is refuted by this very [argument].
It has also been stated that when [the Self] is non-distinct and self-luminous, the superimposition of a contradictory form is simply untenable.
Having thus explained the inconsistency of the two statements in the absence of accepting distinctions, he concludes with the word "tad" (therefore).
...that which was indivisible has been divided. MAnu 1.107d.
Therefore, the view that [Brahman] is partless and devoid of distinctions, as propounded by the two statements, should be understood as refuted and discredited; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, he states that the assertion of being "devoid of distinctions" is contradicted by its own action: "nirviśeṣatvam" (the state of being devoid of distinctions).
By this, there would be a state of non-distinction, as in the expression "I am mute."

Just as the statement "I am mute" is contradicted by one's own action— since by this [statement] the absence of speaking is expressed, yet by the very act of speaking there is the state of being a speaker—
so too would the claim that "Brahman is devoid of distinctions" be contradicted by its own activity.
How so?
By this reason—namely, "being without distinction" (nirviśeṣatva)—which has not itself fallen into the category of a [further] distinction;
for it is the absence of distinctions that is intended to be established by the statement, "Brahman is without distinction."
And by the act of demonstration, a distinction characterized by the absence of distinction would result;
yet this very distinction is refuted by the phrase "the indistinct" (*nirviśeṣam*). Therefore, how could there be a contradiction with its own function even in that case?
If it is argued that there is a contradiction with experience (*pratīti*), [we reply:]...
In that case, even this agency of speaking is negated by the statement "I am mute"; so how can there be a contradiction with one's own action in that instance as well?
If it is argued that there is a contradiction with experience, the resolution is the same.
If it is argued that the absence of specific qualities is accepted because there is no means for awakening others,
and not because they are specific qualities of Brahman,
then this statement here too is made precisely because there is no means for awakening others.
In reality, let it be that this [Brahman] is indeed mute;
the intention of the term "nirviśeṣa" (without distinction) is solely the negation of distinctions,
not the prescription of the attribute of being without distinction.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is there a contradiction?
[we reply: Then even in the statement "I am mute," the intention is the negation of speakerhood.
Since this is not the speakerhood of this very statement, how can there be a contradiction in that case either?
If it is argued that there is no contradiction with one's own words in that case, but rather a contradiction with one's own action,
then [we ask] what else is stated in the present case? Let this elaboration suffice.
This has been stated: "as if saying, 'I am mute.
He states the purpose for which this effort is made: "even though [the object] is not distinct," and so forth.
For this distinction necessarily follows, even though [the object] is non-different.

Therefore, by the force of the otherwise inexplicability (*anyathānupapatti*) of both the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) and the intermediate sentences (*avāntaravākya*) in the manner described above, one must accept a specific power called "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), which serves as the cause for resolving this inexplicability, even though Brahman is devoid of difference. This is what is meant: [The text continues: ...this is what is being stated. The meaning is that, although Brahman is indeed free from all distinctions, there exists a particular power within it—termed "distinction"—which accounts for the fact that the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) and the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) can be established between the words "Brahman" and "Thou," and between the words "That" and "Thou," respectively. Otherwise, how could the relationship of signifier and signified exist between the two words "Brahman" and "Thou," given that they refer to the same single essence? And how could the relationship of qualifier and qualified exist between the two words "That" and "Thou," since they denote the same single entity? It is precisely because of this specific power called "distinction" that these relationships are possible. Thus, the relationship of signifier and signified between the two words "Brahman" and "Thou," and the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two words "That" and "Thou," are established through this specific power known as "distinction. Therefore, it is concluded that this specific power called "distinction" must necessarily be accepted.
