The identity taught by the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) and the attributes such as reality (satyatva) taught by the intermediate sentences are indeed non-different from Brahman and from each other;
for there are scriptural texts establishing its single essence, such as "It is to be seen as one alone."
Nor is the aforementioned fault incurred;
for even in an entity devoid of difference, there exists a certain specific capacity by which it is logically consistent that, although it is manifesting, it does not manifest, and so forth.
And you must admit that this specific capacity is understood solely through this very presumption (*arthāpatti*).
[Objection: Even if a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is admitted, the logical inconsistency is not resolved.

For if that particularity is distinct from the entity, then there would be the fault of an infinite regress of distinctions (*bhedānavasthā*) and so forth; and if it is non-distinct, then because the relationship between the particularity and its possessor (*viśeṣatadvadbhāva*) would be untenable, the same problem remains. To this, he says: "And the particularity and its possessor themselves would be self-establishing. (MAnu 1.1.108cd)
Furthermore, one must admit that there is indeed non-difference between the particular (viśeṣa) and the qualified (viśeṣin);
and by the power of the particular, the relationship between the particular and its possessor (viśeṣatadvadbhāva) is also to be established—this is the remainder [of the argument].
Nevertheless, since a mutual regressus ad infinitum might arise through the succession of particulars, he says: "by way of self-establishment" (svanirvāhakatā).
That very particularity (*viśeṣa*) itself brings about the relationship between the particularity and its possessor (*viśeṣatadvadbhāva*) without requiring another particularity.

It must be accepted that, by the power of that [particularity] alone, the status of being both the object to be established (*nirvāhyatva*) and the establisher (*nirvāhakatva*) is accomplished for a single entity.
[Objection: But from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it known that a particularity brings about the effect of differentiation within an undifferentiated reality?
To this he says, beginning with "siddham": "But [in the case] where there is no difference..."
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis;
however, when [the object] is devoid of difference, it is that which restricts another synonymous term, and is thus called "viśeṣa" (particularity). ... MAnu 1.1.109a-c.
The phrase "the regulator of other synonymous terms" is an indicator of its capacity to bring about the realization of all distinctions without exception.
This is what is meant:
through such scriptural passages as "as one alone," the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, and so forth, is understood to consist solely in the nature of pure consciousness.

Even though consciousness is established as self-luminous, its "non-establishment" consists in its being cognizable through synonymous terms; furthermore, the specific difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is understood such that the manifestation of consciousness does not remove ignorance, whereas the knowledge of non-duality (*advaitajñāna*) does remove it. Likewise, the functional differences of duality, such as numerical distinction—namely, that consciousness is one while truthfulness and other attributes are many—are also perceived.

Since neither of these two [effects] can otherwise be accounted for, it is postulated that even though consciousness is devoid of difference (*bheda*), there exists some excellence (*atiśaya*) acting as a substitute for difference that produces its effects;
for there is no other possible recourse.

Thus, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) which apprehends the essential nature [of consciousness], [it is established that] this [excellence] alone accomplishes the function of differentiation.
"Since this [particular] is established, what is the need for seeking further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard?
By this very statement, the definition of the particular (*viśeṣa*) is also stated:
even when difference is abandoned, the particular is that which serves as the cause for the non-metaphorical linguistic usage of difference. (3.87)
"Even by other proponents [of philosophical systems], a particularity (viśeṣa) must be admitted.
Having thus caused the proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin) to admit a particularity, he causes others to admit it as well, stating: "That exists."
... thus there exists [a means] regarding all things without exception. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.109d)
Not only must the proponent of Māyā (the Māyāvādin) accept this distinction with respect to Brahman;
indeed, even those who maintain the reality of the phenomenal world (prapañca-satyatāvādins) must accept that distinction in all substances.
For instance, a cloth and its whiteness are certainly not distinct.
If it is argued that [the two] are not perceived as distinct because they are like two fingers, on account of their being inseparable (ayutasiddha),
then what is this so-called "inseparability"?

If it is argued that they must necessarily exist in the relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), then why should their difference not be recognized by this much alone? Furthermore,
a cloth does not manifest as a locus like a bowl, nor does whiteness manifest as a superstratum like jujube fruits.
What indeed is that which is "that very same thing"?
Nor is this cognition an error,
because there is no subverting evidence.
For a perceptual cognition that apprehends the difference between whiteness and the cloth would indeed be subverting;
since it is impossible for inference and the other means of knowledge to even arise when they are obstructed by a perception of non-difference.
And it has already been stated that there is no perceptual cognition that apprehends difference;
therefore, the non-difference between the cloth and its whiteness is established by perception itself.
Furthermore, effects that appear to be distinct are observed.
The absence of identity in objective referent between the cognition of a cloth and the cognition of whiteness;
the non-synonymy of those two words; the capacity of those words to evoke other non-synonymous words; and the difference in purposeful action, such as the fetching of water.
When it is said, "Bring the cloth," there is no bringing of whatever white object; when it is said, "Bring the white [object]," there is necessarily the bringing of the cloth.
There is no contradiction between these two cases, just as there is none between the expressions "non-cloth" and "cloth" or "non-white" and "cloth."

Furthermore, for one who is blind, there would be no arising of the cognition "this is white," just as there is no cognition "this is a cloth"; and just as there is an absence of the cognition of "cloth" [in the case of the blind], there would likewise be an absence of the cognition of "white.
Moreover, just as whiteness [is perceived] through contact with saffron dye, so too would the cloth [be perceived].
The absence of circularity, or, like a cloth, the absence of the non-reoccurrence of whiteness,
and so forth.
Nor is this cognition an illusion,
because there is no even the appearance of sublation,

and because it is non-contradictory in its practical application (*vyavahāra*) and so forth. Therefore, since these two cognitions— the one of non-difference and the one of difference— are otherwise inexplicable, [the object] must be without distinction.
One must simply assume that there exists some excellence (*atiśaya*) in the cloth, serving as a substitute for difference, by virtue of which all this becomes consistent.
And this excellence, even though it resides in what is non-different, is called a "particular" (*viśeṣa*) because it functions as a differentiator;
in the same way, a particular is to be understood in other substances as well.
If it is argued that there is no need for a specific distinction because the inconsistency [of the position] is resolved by accepting both difference and non-difference, we say:
no. Even for the purpose of establishing the coexistence of difference and non-difference—which are mutually contradictory in one place—a specific distinction must also be admitted.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because [the phenomenon] is well-known,
that is true; however,
when one considers how even such a cognition is established, one must follow the specific excellence of the nature of the thing itself.

This is because it has been stated that the acceptance of *viśeṣa* (particularity) is necessary even for the purpose of avoiding the infinite regress of difference and non-difference (*bhedābhedānavasthā*).
[Objection: Now, if there exists a *viśeṣa* in all things, and that *viśeṣa* is not distinct from the thing itself, [then...]
In that case, it would follow that all things are one; therefore, he says: "The particulars (*viśeṣāḥ*). *Mānava-dharmaśāstra* 1.1.110: "Those particulars are also infinite and mutually distinct;
they exist in all things without exception, being self-sustaining."

Those particularities, which possess their own inherent natures, exist in their entirety as nothing less than infinite within infinite substances; they are not, however, a single entity present everywhere. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
The intention is that the singular number in the phrase "it exists" (*so 'sti*) is employed with reference to the collection [of particularities] as a whole.

But surely, since there is also a single particular (*viśeṣa*) in each individual substance, then such diverse and manifold worldly usages as "the cloth is large," "white," and "moving" would be untenable;
for the production of diverse and manifold effects from a single cause of non-diverse nature is never observed,
as that would entail the consequence of their being accidental (*ākasmikatva*).
And consequently, the acceptance of particularities would be useless; therefore, he says: "The particularities..."

Those particulars (viśeṣas) defined by the aforementioned characteristics are also infinite within each individual thing, even taken without exception; therefore, there is no room for the fault previously mentioned. "Infinite" is an illustrative term (upalakṣaṇa). It should be understood that as many linguistic conventions (vyavahāras) as exist regarding a given object, so many particulars exist therein.
Since there is a multiplicity of particulars for every substance, they must be conceived as being mutually distinct.

Because multiplicity is inseparable from difference; and thus, if there were no difference between distinct substances, it would follow that the substance itself must be multiple. To this, he says: "successively" (paramparā).
The meaning is that multiplicity is possible only through the possession of mutual particularities (*viśeṣa*), because it has been stated that a particular performs the function of differentiation.
Since there would be an infinite regress if one were to admit further particulars for these particulars as well, he says: "by being self-sustaining" (*svanirvāhakatā*).
Previously, there was an investigation into the non-difference of the particular from the substance;
now, however, it concerns their mutual [non-difference], so the difference in meaning is clear.
All of this is established by the very presumption (*arthāpatti*) that proves the essential nature of the particular; therefore, no separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated.
For that which is itself unestablished cannot serve to pacify another lack of establishment;
rather, in whatever way it becomes established, it is postulated precisely by means of *arthāpatti* (presumption) which grasps its own nature.
This is so even though the particular may be perceptible.

Because it will be stated later, "by that which is established through direct perception," nevertheless, one who holds a contrary view cannot be convinced by that alone; thus, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has been introduced. *3,94*
Regarding that for whose sake all disputants have been made to admit a distinction by [the statement] beginning with "of that unity," he now says: "Therefore."
Therefore, Brahman is said to possess infinite qualities, even though it is without differentiation.
Therefore, although Brahman is without division, it is said to possess infinite qualities by virtue of its capacity for differentiation.
This is the answer to what was asked by the opponent—namely, whether there is a distinction between the defined (lakṣya) and the definition (lakṣaṇa)—that Brahman is without division.

As for what was stated here— that there would be the consequence of multiplicity for that which is not distinct from its various characteristics, or the impossibility of the multiplicity of the characteristics themselves,
or the synonymy of words—
Regarding the objection that "the state of being a quality and the possessor of qualities and so forth is untenable," the reply is:
therefore, although it is without differentiation, there is an infinity of specific qualities,
and yet Brahman remains one.

Because it has infinite qualities (*ananta-guṇa*), the relationship between quality and the possessor of quality (*guṇa-guṇin*) exists; thus, the non-redundant statement "Brahman and its qualities" is also appropriate.

Here, although it should have been stated that [Brahman] is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, this expression "possessing infinite qualities" is used in the Sūtra [to indicate that Brahman] possesses infinite qualities.

This is intended to indicate that you yourself, having in mind the definition of Brahman, have set out to establish its proof by propounding the definition of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world.

Thus, it is established that since there is no sublation (bādhaka) regarding the fact that being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world constitutes its own definition (svalakṣaṇa), it is not proper to conceive of it as an accidental or external definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa).
Here, [the opponent] says:

For what purpose is the resolution of all worldly transactions accomplished by accepting the non-difference between the characterized (lakṣya) and the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) on the basis of their specific distinction?
Why is difference itself not accepted?
Furthermore, the relationship of quality and qualified (guṇaguṇibhāva) will arise from the relation of inherence (samavāya).

Furthermore, if the author of the Sūtras intends to reject *samavāya* (inherence), then it is not appropriate to accept it; rather, one must accept that there is some such specific difference in nature (*svabhāvabheda*) between the quality and the qualified object itself.

For it is not logical to postulate the same [inherence] even in the case of Brahman merely because a specific linguistic usage is observed due to the force of a particularity (*viśeṣa*), despite the absence of any actual difference in things like cloth;
this is because there is a lack of any definitive means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it.
For probability is postulated for the purpose of presenting a decisive means of valid cognition (*niścāyakapramāṇa*).
As they have said:
"The meaning of a thesis, once rendered probable, may be established by a reason. (3.95)
"There is no protection for him by means of causes, he who dies at the very moment of birth."
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, it is not that mere possibility alone establishes the meaning; therefore, he says: "In this way, phenomena..."
By the scriptural statement "thus [are] the dharmas," their non-difference is also proclaimed.
By the word "also" (api), even distinction [is implied].
For here, non-difference is understood through the censure of perceiving the attributes of Brahman as separate;
and by the mention of a plurality of attributes in the phrase "the attributes" (dharmān), there is the presence of distinction.
Nor is this merely a restatement of the impermanence of phenomena (*dharma*), for that is not established without scripture (*śruti*).

If one accepts a foundational scripture, that very scripture will be the one expressing the specific distinction; thus it is known that Brahman is indeed without differentiation, yet it becomes the basis for various worldly transactions precisely through the power of its specific attributes. (3.96)

In this regard, having deliberated on whether the status of being the cause of the world attributed by the opponent to Brahman consists solely of its being the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), or solely of its being the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), or both, the third alternative has been adopted. Furthermore, regarding its being the material cause, one [view] holds that it is through transformation (*pariṇāmitva*),
while another holds that it is merely by way of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the illusion of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
All of this will be refuted more thoroughly in the section concerning *prakṛti*.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman, known as Nārāyaṇa and endowed with the two characteristics previously described, is the object to be investigated by one desiring liberation.
Thus ends the section on "Birth" (*janma*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.

[======= JNys_1,1.II: The Section on Being the Source of the Scripture =======] *3,97* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning the fact that the scripture is the source [of the Lord].

Now, the doubt regarding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the status of being the cause of the world, based on the scriptures of the Pāśupatas and others and upon inference, is addressed by the sūtra: *Śāstrayonitvāt* (Because [the Lord] is the source of the scripture).
It has been stated that the causality of the origin and so forth of the world is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman.

Fearing that this [definition] might be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*)—applying to conscious beings such as Hara and Hiraṇyagarbha, as well as to unconscious entities such as Pradhāna—by virtue of the support of the *Pāśupata* and other scriptures and inference, the venerable author of the Sūtras here provides a rebuttal;
therein, he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words: "By the Śaiva and others... (*śaivādyeti*).
But by means of the visible results obtained from the Śaiva and other Āgamas,
other [scriptures] are inferred to possess authority through comparison with their words.
Because it is the word of the Lord... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.113a]
That which was composed by Śiva is "Śaiva";
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), those composed by Hiraṇyagarbha and others are included.
"Attained through them" means attained through the performance of the means prescribed therein.
"Seen" (dṛṣṭa) means "vision" (dṛṣṭi), that is to say, direct perception (pratyakṣa). That which is established by that is "established through what is seen" (dṛṣṭagam).
The remainder [of the meaning] is that the authority of that statement is inferred by means of its result (phala).
The locative case in "pramāṇatve" (in being a means of valid cognition) is a locative of object.
First, a statement that prescribes means for the sake of a visible result is inferred to be a means of valid cognition. By what mark?

Regarding the question of how that which is not connected to its own side (the subject) can serve as an inferential mark (*anumāpaka*), it is said: "attained through the scriptures of the Śaivas and others.
To avoid the charge of non-establishment due to ignorance, it is said: "by means of what is seen."
The word "tu" (but/however) indicates a specific reason for the two types of inference.
In the phrase "īśavākyatvataḥ," the word "ādi" (and so forth) should be supplied.
This is the meaning.
For the scripture propounded by Śiva is of two kinds:
one which prescribes the means directed toward fruits such as *sampat* that are capable of being perceived through direct experience;

the other, however, prescribes [means] whose fruits—such as the class of *saṅkalpa*—are not perceptible, [and which instead establish] Śiva’s perfection in all qualities, such as being the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe, omniscience, omnipotence, and the possession of true resolve.
And he establishes its faultlessness:

first of all, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because when the practice of the means prescribed therein is performed, the result is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself. (3.98)

Thus, the formal argument is as follows: The scripture under dispute is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it generates purposeful activity that bears fruit, like the works of Caraka, Suśruta, and others.
If it were not a valid means of knowledge, it would not produce effective activity, like the speech of a deceiver.

As it has been said: "When there is the comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that means of valid cognition is effective because it possesses the capacity for successful action.

Consequently, having ascertained the supreme reliability (*paramāptatva*) of Śiva, the author of that [first scripture], the validity of the second scripture composed by him is determined by way of that example.
And here is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
The disputed scripture is a valid means of knowledge because it is the word of Śiva, just like that which is undisputed.
In the case of the contrary, the subverting argument is the undesirable consequence that Śiva would not be a reliable authority.
Thus, by means of the Śaiva scripture whose validity has been inferred, [the fact] of Śiva being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world [is established].

The Śaivas maintain that this definition does not apply to Viṣṇu because of his specific designation [in the scriptures]. Following this same method, the validity of various Āgamas and the counter-arguments of those who worship various deities are to be understood.
Furthermore, this is merely an illustration.
Even by means of inference, it is possible to establish that Śiva and others are the cause of the world's birth and so forth, as well as their omniscience and other attributes. For instance:
the earth and so forth have an agent, because they are effects, like a pot.
Action under dispute is produced by a substratum of effort, because it is an action, like that which is commonly accepted;
as for the disputed earth and water,
they are held up by one possessing effort.
Because it possesses weight yet does not fall,
like that which is commonly agreed upon [to be so];
[it follows that] earth and the other elements are destructible by one possessing effort.

By means of such inferences as "because [the world] is subject to destruction, like that which is commonly admitted," once a creator of the general origination, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe has been established, and since such a capacity is impossible for people like us, it follows by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that the Blessed Lord Śiva alone is proven to be the creator of the birth and so forth of the world.
And just as, upon seeing an effect such as a painting, a creator corresponding to its nature is postulated, so too, by the observation of various and manifold effects, [the Lord is inferred].

Even when a creator is postulated, he is established as possessing omniscience and other such qualities consistent with that role. Alternatively, the very fact that the earth and so forth have a creator inherently includes omniscience and the rest; it does not require a separate effort [to prove them].

For creatorship belongs only to one who possesses knowledge of the efficient cause, the material cause, the result, and so forth, and who likewise possesses the volition and exertion corresponding to those.
In this manner, the status of being the cause of the world should also be applied to Hiraṇyagarbha and others by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
Now follows the refutation of the inferences that establish the authority of the scriptures of the Śaivas and others.

Thus, when it has been suggested through both scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*) that others [than Brahman] are the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, the author of the Sūtras has provided a rebuttal.
Neither through scripture nor through inference should others be postulated as the cause of the world.
Why?
Because [the Lord] has the sacred teaching (śāstra) as His source.

The term *śāstrayoni* means that the scripture—consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, as stated in the passage beginning with those words—is its source (*yoni*), cause, manifestor, and authority (*pramāṇa*). The state of being such is *śāstrayonitva*; [the argument proceeds] from that.
This is what is meant:

since the reality that is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world is to be known exclusively through the scriptures such as the Vedas, it is not within the scope of the Śaiva Āgamas or inference; therefore, the status of being the cause of the world should not be postulated for others by means of those [other sources].
However, that very being whom the scripture declares to be the cause of the world must be accepted as such.
This might be so;
yet, if the reason stated in the Sūtra—that [the Lord] is to be known solely through scripture—were established, it would be valid, but it is not so.

Even if [the Lord] is not accessible through direct perception, one might object that His status as the cause of the world can be determined through the scriptures of the Śaivas and others, as well as by means of inference in the manner described;

having raised this doubt, the author—desiring to refute the accessibility of [the Lord] through the scriptures of the Śaivas and others in order to establish the reason stated in the Sūtra—dismisses the inference put forward by the opponent with the words, "If it be said... (iti cet).

If it is argued that there would be an inference of invalidity based on that which possesses deviation (*tadgavyabhicāriṇā*), [we reply: that which is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣāvagata*) and yet exhibits deviation—namely, the deviation from the result—is what constitutes "possessing deviation" (*vyabhicārin*). A statement possessing this is a "statement possessing deviation" (*tadgavyabhicārivākya*). By means of such a statement, serving as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), [the world's being caused by Śiva and others] would be understood. *Mānavadharmaśāstra 1.113bc; Verse 3.104* *Note: The parenthetical phrase "(avagamahetubhūtā)" is reconstructed from the context of the commentary.*
Furthermore, there would be an inference of invalidity based on reasons such as being the statement of a village-chief (gamasyeśa).
This is what is meant:

if, having inferred the validity of the statements of Śiva and others concerning perceived objects through corroboration by perception, one then infers the validity of those concerning unperceived objects—using the fact of being the statement of Śiva and others as the reason and the aforementioned cases as the illustrative example—then [the following applies].

In that case, regarding those very sentences whose objects are perceptible, one might infer their lack of authority—on the grounds that they are seen to have a failure of result through direct perception—by means of the following inference: "The subject under dispute is non-authoritative, because it produces an ineffective activity, like the speech of a deceiver.
Having inferred this lack of authority, one might then apply that same example to those [scriptures] whose objects are imperceptible, using reasons such as "being the speech of Śiva and others."

It is indeed possible to infer the lack of authority [of certain texts] by means of the following inference: "The disputed [texts] are not authoritative because they are the words of Śiva and others, like those [words] commonly accepted [as authoritative].
For not every word of Śiva concerning perceptible objects necessarily produces effective activity;
for it is frequently observed that some produce activity that is fruitless.
If it is argued that even such a statement is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),

and that the failure to produce the result is caused by defects in the agent, the ritual action, or other factors— then even that statement would be invalid. Furthermore, let the correspondence with the result be a mere coincidence (*kākatālīya*), or let it be a "sugar on the tongue" (*guḍajihvikā*) deception employed by those who delude the world, such as Śiva and others.
For when validity is firmly established, one must postulate defects in the agent and so forth as the cause of deviation.
However, for one who posits validity solely on the basis of non-deviation from the result, there is clearly the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
If it is argued that being the word of Śiva is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to correspondence with the result, we say no.
Even in that case, it is inconclusive because there is a failure of the result [to correspond].
Furthermore, does one who considers the Śiva-āgama to be authoritative even regarding its unseen (adṛṣṭa) objects also accept the authority of the Hiraṇyagarbha-āgamas and others, or not?
Not the first [alternative].
Because it is impossible for both [contradictory] views to be authoritative when they are mutually opposed;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because if the mode of inference is identical, a disparity between them cannot be established.

If it is argued that this inference is inconclusive because even if [the words] were the speech of Hiraṇyagarbha, the possibility of invalidity for a single instance remains due to adventitious defects such as deception,
the solution is the same.
By this very logic, the validity of the statements regarding the veneration of caityas and so forth can also be established.
For its proponent has never spoken anything that was not true.

Thus, since the validity of the Śaiva and other scriptures cannot be established, the Creator of the world is not proven by them. [3.107] Now follows the demonstration that there is no room for inference regarding the causality of the world.
If it is argued: "Let the proof of the creator of the world's birth and so forth not come from the Śaiva and other scriptures;
let it rather come from the aforementioned inferences.
Therefore, how can it be said that the cause of the world is to be known through scripture alone?"
Is it being asserted that inference in accordance with scripture is the means of valid cognition regarding the cause of the world, or is it independent? As for the first case, it is indeed accepted.
Therefore, our own position alone is established;
for it will be stated in the *Samanvaya-sūtra* that the scripture has the Blessed One as its sole focus.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "not separately."
Nor is he distinct from the Lord who is to be inferred.
The meaning is that independent inference regarding Īśvara as the cause of the world is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

To explain: first, regarding the inference for the general establishment of a creator of the world, what exactly is being proven—is it that the world is preceded by a creator who possesses direct perception of the causes and so forth?
Or [is it] merely having an agent?
In the first case, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*);
for a potter and the like do not directly perceive the causes of the jar and so forth, such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
If it is argued that for this very reason one's desire is sometimes frustrated,
what does that matter?
For it does not avoid the flaw of the example being devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*).
If, by some means, this were a qualification of the reason, there would be a deficiency in the probans (*sādhana*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
If it is argued that "in that case, let this be a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*)," we say no;
because the qualification is unestablished (*asiddha*).
In the second case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*),
because it is possible for the individual soul (*jīvātman*) alone to be the agent of those unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*).
If it is argued that this is not so because they [the souls] lack knowledge of the causes, we say no.
Otherwise, it would follow that potters and others are not agents.
If it is argued that there must be some supervisor even for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), we say no;
because there is no function to be performed by a supervisor.
First of all, it is not impulsion and so forth,
because it is not a substance;
nor is it the production of an excellence.
Because it is impossible for one quality to possess another quality;
nor can there be a power deposited by something beyond the senses,
since that is not admitted.
Nor is there a convergence of auxiliary causes,
since that is established through unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) alone;
nor is there the capacity to produce an effect.

Because its nature is unperceived (*adṛṣṭa-svabhāvatvāt*). If it is asked, "In that case, why does it not act immediately after its arising? we reply: "No; because of obstruction by another powerful unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth."
Furthermore, how is "being an effect" established in the subject (*pakṣa*)?
If it is argued that it is because of "having come into existence after not having existed," we say no; for that very property is what constitutes being an effect.
Even if there were some degree of difference, [the reason] would be unestablished with respect to a part (*bhāgāsiddha*),
for we certainly do not perceive that mountains, oceans, and so forth come into being after having not existed.
If it is argued that, in the case of substances at least, the concomitance with being an effect is established because they possess parts, we say no.
For "having parts" (sāvayavatva) means either having an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) or having a transformative cause (pariṇāmikāraṇa).
In the first case, there is non-establishment for the opponent (prativādyasiddhi).
In the second case, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, how could one who disputes even the mere fact of being an effect accept that it possesses a cause? (3.108)
If it is argued that the possession of spatial extension by earth and the other elements is indeed experienced through direct perception—
otherwise, how could the presence and absence of a jar on the ground occur simultaneously?—
this is not so; for in that case, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that space and the like are also effects.

Otherwise, how could one say that the existence and non-existence of birds [occur] simultaneously in the sky? For it would be possible to say the same even in that case. The same applies to the case of the primary elements (*prakṛti*).

If it is argued that the parts of earth and the other elements are established by perception—those whose disjunction occurs through digging and so forth, and those whose conjunction occurs through pushing and so forth—is it then being said that "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*) consists in possessing another substance of the same genus that undergoes conjunction and disjunction? Or does it mean "being composed of those [parts]" (*tad-ārabdhatva*)?
In the first case, there is a deviation from the rule due to atoms;

in the second case, the qualification is redundant and, as before, there is the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhi*). By this, the argument that "the action under dispute is produced by a substratum of effort" is also refuted.
Furthermore, as for the inference that earth and water are supported by one who possesses effort,

that too is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), as before. Moreover, why is it not postulated that conjunction (*saṃyoga*), velocity (*vega*), effort (*prayatna*), and even the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) are also obstructors of gravity?
Furthermore, the non-falling [of the mountain] is doubtful and unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*),
because it is possible that a falling [object] is not perceived due to its great size.
By this, the final inference is also refuted.
Furthermore, all inferences would be subject to counter-arguments (*satpratipakṣatā*), such as: "The earth and so forth have no creator, because their creator is not perceived, like space.
And since "non-perception" means "unfitness for our perception," there is no minor flaw whatsoever.
If it is argued that there is a deviation [of the reason] with respect to the happiness of others and so forth, we say no;
for that is apprehended through inference.
If it is then argued that the creator of the earth and so forth is likewise apprehended through inference, we say no.
If the Lord is apprehended through inference and other means, then our own inference is defective;
likewise, if the Lord is apprehended through inference, there arises the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
In this same manner, all independent inferences that seek to establish merely a cause for the world should be refuted. (3.114)
As for the inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*) regarding Śiva and others being the cause of the world, is that [inference] in accordance with scripture or merely independent?
It cannot be the first,
because it will be stated later that the scripture has the Blessed Lord alone as its sole purport.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "Nor as something separate."
The meaning is that separate inference regarding Īśvara, Śiva, and the creator of the world is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "By the state of being male," and so forth.
Precisely by the power of the cause of virility, according to the very path previously described.

By the very path previously described; that is to say, by the very method of refuting the inference regarding the authority of the Śaiva Āgamas, specifically by means of establishing a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*).
The particle "eva" (only/just) indicates that one should not needlessly weary the mind by searching for other refutations when a manifest fault exists.
To the question, "How can being the word of God serve as a reason here? he says: "By the state of being a person," and so forth.
The meaning is that by the phrase "by the very path previously mentioned," only the state of having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatā*) is being extended,
but not that [specific] reason (*hetu*).
The formal argument here is as follows: Śiva is not the cause of the world, because he possesses masculinity, just like Devadatta.
[Objection: But by what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is Śiva established?

Now, from what source is the creatorship of the world established for you as well, who infer it in him by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*)? If you say "from worldly report (*lokapravāda*) and so forth," then let it be the same for me as well.
If it is argued that the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to the Brahman favored by you, we say no;
for this objection is raised against the proponent of pure inference by accepting the position of one who does not admit an Īśvara.

Is it not the case that the inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*) is as follows: "The state of being the cause of the universe resides in Śiva, because, while its subsistence elsewhere is impossible, it is known to reside in something or other?"
If it is asked how this can be its counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*), we say no;
for a counter-argument is possible merely by establishing a contradictory meaning.

Furthermore, from the perspective of formal application (*prayoga*), there is a lack of both valid proof (*pramāṇa*) and purpose in [the opponent's position] being restricted to a single property (*dharmin*). Otherwise, such counter-arguments would not be included elsewhere, which would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they could not function as refutations at all.
Nor should it be said that "let it be so," because the state of being an obstructer (or non-obstructer) is established by experience.
If it is argued that, this being the case, the establishment of a universal (sāmānya) becomes untenable, let it be so; for those inferences have already been refuted. (3.120)
If it is asked, "What follows from this if it is so?", he says: "The fact that the scripture is its source" (*śāstrayonitva*)—thereby establishing the reason stated in the Sūtra.
By this, the fact that the scripture is the source [of Dharma] follows by force from the cause.
By this, meaning by the manner already stated;
"of the cause" [refers to] the world—this is the ellipsis; "by force," meaning by the force of its non-establishment through any other alternative mode. (3.121)
He states that the fact that the cause of the world is not known through inference is also established by the Śruti texts: "Not one who knows not the Veda."
From such statements as "The truth is not known by one who lacks the Veda, nor by mere reasoning," it follows that reasoning can in no way lead to the knowledge of the Lord.
"One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One"; "This understanding is not to be attained through reasoning."
“Neither the senses nor inference [know Him]; the Vedas alone make Him known”;
from such statements, it is understood—the word “iti” being understood as the remainder of the sentence.
The term "tarka" (reasoning) is an elliptical expression for inference (*anumāna*) in general.
"Īśitāram" means the Lord, the cause (or creator) of the world;
[one seeks to know Him] in some way, both generally and specifically.

As for the claim that the omniscience and other attributes of God are established through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) of reasons such as "being an effect," or by some other inference—that too is improper because it is vitiated by counter-arguments. Thus he says: "By means of [the reason] 'being a forest-maker' and so forth, it is easy to establish that the Lord, who is the subject in the form of 'forest-maker' etc., possesses only limited knowledge, simply by virtue of his being a person. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.116) *3,122*
Surely, one might argue that the following syllogism should be employed here: "The Lord is limited in knowledge because he is a person, like Devadatta.
To this we reply: Is the Lord known [as such] or not?

In the first case, since his omniscience is established by that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which [the subject] is established, there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition that apprehends the locus (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇavirodha*).
In the second case, however, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
To this, he says: "Pleasure," [addressing the objection]: "How can it be said that the Lord's state of being a knower of only a little can be established by his being a person?"
To the question "How so?", it is said: "of that which has become the subject (pakṣa) by way of having forest-cutting and so forth as its nature."

The intention is that there is no fault whatsoever in formulating the argument by taking as the subject (pakṣa) that very agent who is established by such [inferences] as "the forest possesses an agent because it is an effect," provided he is qualified by that specific form [of being an agent].
This refers to one endowed with a property (*dharma*) such as "being the maker of the forest" or "having the mountain as his substratum.
For, merely by being the "maker of the forest," one does not thereby become "omniscient."
Because the creator of well-known forests is not omniscient, one might ask:

"If that very same person is the creator of the earth and so forth, why would he not be omniscient? If this is asked, the answer is no; for there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for his existence [in such a capacity].
For the reason of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth cannot establish its unity everywhere in the same way that it establishes an agent.
If it is argued that unity is resorted to on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), [we reply:
no, because for one who postulates an agent in accordance with worldly observation, it is more appropriate to resort to [the principle of] complexity (*gaurava*).
For in the world, the makers of elephants, oxen, donkeys, and so forth, as well as of jars and other such things, are observed to be of entirely different species [from those objects].
Nor should it be argued that if one proves the forest-maker to be omniscient, what need is there for an *īśvara*?
For his status as *īśvara* is [established] by the opponent.
Otherwise, one might ask: "Once the forest-maker is established, what follows regarding the establishment of God?

Not only is it easy to prove [the existence of] someone with limited knowledge, but with the intention of showing that even ignorance of one's own created effects can be proven, he says: "The maker of trees," etc. (*vṛkṣakṛt*).
For one who fells trees does not know every single tree, just as Caitra [does not know] because of his manhood.

The phrase "tree-maker" (*vṛkṣakṛt*) is stated as before to avoid the fallacies of contradiction with the apprehender of the subject (*dharmigrāhakavirodha*) and the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
The term "devoid of a well-known maker" (*prasiddhakartṛrahitā*) should also be applied;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
The term "entire" (*akhila*) refers to that which is accompanied by the specific number of constituent parts, weight, and dimension that initiate [the object].

It is stated as "entire" to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*), since for people like us there exists only the cognition of a tree regarding objects about which there is disagreement.
The particle *hi* indicates the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

There is no rule that whoever is the agent of something must know everything about it; for such knowledge is absent in the case of the potter and others, and because such knowledge is of no utility. (3.126)

Intending to show that, by this very same logic, since a counter-argument is possible in every case, even such qualities as having true volition, being bodiless, possessing eternal knowledge, will, and effort, and being devoid of suffering and so forth, cannot be established by inference, he says: "and so forth."
No inference rivaling such [Vedic] inference is capable of making known the Supreme Lord... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.117c–e).

The word "ādi" (and so forth) expresses a variety of types. [He says that] the collection of inferences regarding the Lord possesses a status equal to that of a mere appearance, because the Lord is endowed with such qualities as having true volitions; thus he states: "And there would be an over-extension."

"...and there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) for such inference. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.117f). The meaning is that if one employs inference—having abandoned the perfection of auxiliary factors such as scripture (*āgama*)—with respect to objects that are entirely beyond the senses (*atyantātīndriya*), an over-extension occurs.
He demonstrates the very same over-extension [of the argument] with the words: "because it is a real entity" (vastutvāt).
Because it is a real entity, a horse has horns; the sky is like a flower; [the earth] is joined with sons;
and the Citriṇī is the sixth taste, for being a taste, it must have something superior to it.
A variegated [cow] is barren.
If it is stated that "the sixth taste possesses another taste," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of the first taste and so forth.
If it is stated that "it possesses a seventh taste," there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).
Therefore, it is said that [the inference] has a superior [counter-example].
The implication is that if the inference for God were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then these [other arguments] would also be valid.
If it is objected that "substantiality" (*vastutva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it exists in things such as jars, we say no.
Because that too is a subject (*pakṣa*).
If it is argued that [the existence of] a horse's horn and so forth is sublated by non-perception (*anupalambhabādha*),
then the same applies to the case of the earth and other things having a creator.
If it is argued that [the object] is not perceived because of its unfitness [to be perceived],
then let the horn of a horse be exactly like that as well.
For is it not the case that what is called a "horn" possesses magnitude and has manifest color?
If it is asked, "How could that particular limb of the body be unperceivable?
then how could the agent— like a potter or similar craftsman— be unperceivable when he possesses magnitude and a body of wondrous form?
If it is argued that [the self] is not perceived because it is bodiless,
then the horn of a horse would likewise [not be perceived] due to the absence of form (*rūpa*). If it is argued that a horn does indeed possess form, [then the same applies to the self].
The agent, too, possesses a body.
If it is argued that the body is not required for agency, we say no;
for what need is there for such a requirement?
For, according to you, there is no pervasion by way of origination from that [body], as there is for the Buddhists.
If it is argued that "the possession of attributes such as dharma is the determinant for being embodied," we say no;
because even that is established by means of [proving] agency.
Now, how is it to be applied here?

[The application is as follows: "If the nature of being an inference were to reside in 'being an effect' and so forth, then it would also reside in 'being a real entity' and so forth, which are not distinct from them. (3.133)

Anticipating the objection that it would be contradictory to undertake this treatise on inquiry and yet demonstrate the inapplicability of inference regarding the cause of the world, he concludes by stating: "By the introductory passage, etc. (upakramādīti).
Therefore, there can be no other inference for it than from signs such as the onset of disease and so forth.
This is an illustration of inference supported by scripture (*āgama*).
For when there is support from scripture, all these [inferences] are indeed merely inferences,
since the constituent factors such as the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) are established by the scripture— which, being authorless, is intrinsically valid.
And because the counter-arguments and so forth are sublated by their opposition to that [scriptural authority], this is the summary.
Thus, since the state of being the cause of the world is to be understood solely through scripture (*śāstra*), it cannot be established by inference (*anumāna*) and the like.
It is established that it is correct to state that the definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*).
Now, regarding the fact that the commentary (*bhāṣya*) of another [author] here is a misinterpretation:
some explain [the phrase] as "the source (*yoni*) of the treatise."
That is untenable because it is irrelevant to the subject at hand;
for being the author of the scriptures is not a reason for being the cause of the world,
as no such pervasion (vyāpti) is observed.
If it is argued that the omniscience of Brahman, which was understood in the preceding sūtra as the cause of the world, is now being clarified as the cause of the Veda, we say no;

for the Veda is also included within the entirety of the world. Furthermore, how could that omniscience—which is not clearly manifested as the creator of the entire manifold universe (prapañca) consisting of infinite categories—be clearly manifested merely as the cause of the Veda, which is but a single part of it?

If it is argued that, in order to establish that Brahman alone is the cause of the world by excluding Pradhāna and others, the omniscience mentioned as the reason is now established by means of its being the source of the Śāstra, we say no;
for this would lead to the fallacy of unestablished premises (asiddhi).
Indeed, one who does not accept that Brahman is the cause of the world will not accept that it is the cause of the Veda.
If it is argued that [the Lord's existence] is established by scripture (*āgama*),
then why is His being the cause of the world not also established by that same means?
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of redundancy with the *Sūtra* on "origination and so forth" (*janmādi-sūtra*) due to the section on "seeing" (*īkṣati-adhikaraṇa*) and others.
If it is argued that "omniscience is not established as the cause of the world because [the Lord] is not the author of the Vedas," we say no;
for if that were so, it would result in the text being a mere assertion (pratijñāmātra),
and such an objection could likewise be raised regarding space and the other elements.
If it is argued that this [objection] will also be refuted in the section concerning space (*viyadadhikaraṇa*) and so forth, we say no;
for in that case, this matter would already have been settled by that very [section].
Furthermore, [this is so] because of the absence of an author of the Veda.
The very doubt that omniscience is impossible is utterly crushed;
for there is no rule that the creator of something must necessarily know it. Furthermore, how does authorship of the Veda prove omniscience?
Whoever is the author of a sentence that conveys a specific meaning necessarily knows even more than that meaning, just as Pāṇini and others do.
If it is argued that since this [author] is the composer of a treatise that conveys all meanings, how could he not be omniscient? We say: no.
What is this so-called "authorship of the Vedas"?
Does it mean composing [words and so forth] by one's own will after perceiving an object through another means of valid cognition?
Is authorship merely the act of utterance?
In the first case, it follows that [the Veda] would be of human origin;
in the second case, omniscience is not established.
If it is argued that the Veda is superimposed upon Brahman— just as [ignorance is superimposed] upon a preceptor and so forth, or as a snake is [superimposed] upon a rope—
then how is the example of Pāṇini and others [to be understood]?
Grammar was not indeed composed by Pāṇini with his own hands.
And if this were the case, how could omniscience be established?
If it is argued that this is because the scripture is a manifestation of the power of his consciousness (*vijñāna-śakti-vivarta*), [we say] no.
Furthermore, it would follow that even space and the other elements possess the power of manifestation,
and it would also follow that the power of concealment and so forth residing in ignorance must be ultimately real within Brahman.
Moreover, what connection is there between the Veda’s power as an instrument of knowledge and Brahman’s power as its agent?
And where has it been found that the power residing in the superimposed object is real in the substratum of the superimposition?
Therefore, that [other interpretation] is indeed a false explanation; the meaning of the Sūtra is exactly as stated above.
Thus ends the section on "Being the Source of Scripture" (*śāstrayonitva*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.

The Formulation of the Prima Facie View:
Om. But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the harmony [of the texts]. Om.
"But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the harmony [of all texts].
Let it be granted that the cause of the world is to be understood solely from the scripture (*śāstra*).

Nevertheless, this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*), since from the scripture itself we perceive that others—such as Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and so forth, as well as Pradhāna and the like—are also presented as the cause of the world.
Nor should it be said that this scripture has Viṣṇu as its ultimate subject, because it has been explained by authoritative scholars as having Śiva and others as its ultimate subject.
Although, according to such scriptural passages as "All names [belong to Him]," it is determined that the names of Śiva and others possess only a secondary power (lakṣaṇā) with respect to Viṣṇu.
Nevertheless, there is no evidence for such an intention (*tātparya*).
For it is a logical principle that "whatever a word aims at, that is the word's meaning.
Furthermore, it is not proper to infer an intention based merely on [the presence of] denotative power (*śakti*).
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument],
and it has already been stated that there exists the explanation of the learned which serves as evidence for the intended meaning (*tātparya*) elsewhere.

Therefore, having raised the objection that this [definition] lacks defining characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), the author of the Sūtras refuted it with the statement: "But that [Brahman is established], because of the harmony [of all scriptural texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*). *Oṃ tattu samanvayāt Oṃ.* (Sūtra 1.1.4) **Exegesis of the Sūtra Statement:** The word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the aforementioned doubt. The word "that" (*tat*) refers to Brahman, which was introduced as the subject of the inquiry in the first aphorism (*janmādyasya yataḥ*). The phrase "because of the harmony" (*samanvayāt*) means because of the concordant connection (*anugama*) of all the Vedānta texts with that very Brahman. To explain: although the various Upaniṣadic passages appear to have different literal meanings when taken individually, they nevertheless possess a single, uniform purport (*ekārtha*) regarding Brahman. This is because they are all connected through the common characteristic of being the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world (*jagad-utpatti-sthiti-pralaya-hetu-lakṣaṇa*). Just as the various sentences regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice—such as "One should offer the Agnihotra," "He offers after sunrise," and "He offers before sunrise"—are unified by their common reference to the performance of that specific rite, so too are all the Vedānta texts unified by their common reference to Brahman. Furthermore, the word "harmony" (*samanvaya*) here signifies the state of being well-connected (*saṃgati*) with the intended meaning, free from contradiction. It does not mean mere proximity or sequence. Thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman is established as the object of knowledge because all the Vedānta texts are in complete agreement regarding Him. In that regard, he states the meaning of the term "positive concomitance" (anvaya) with the words: "those very [same ones]."
These very ones are known by the name of lineage... // MAnu 1.119a //

The terms *upakrama* and so forth are "connected" (*anvīyante*)—meaning they are related and understood as being within the scope of the [text's] capacity and intention; thus, these are called "connections" (*anvaya*) because the sentences are connected by them.
Here, by abandoning the conventional term *upakramādi* (beginning and so forth) and adopting the etymological term *anvaya* (connection), he indicates this.
In understanding the intended meaning of a treatise, neither superficial comprehension nor the words of a commentator serve as a valid indicator;
rather, it is only the introductory statements and so forth that do so,
because they are never deviant.
However, because both common understanding (*pratīti*) and explanatory tradition (*vyākhyāna*) are subject to deviation,

even in cases where they do not deviate, they do so only by virtue of being preceded by an investigation of the opening statements (*upakrama*) and other criteria, and not independently. Therefore, because they are that upon which others depend, it is the opening statements and the rest alone that serve as the marks for determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
He says this very thing: "ta eva" (those very ones).
He connects the statement of the Sūtra with the word "taih" (by them).
When these are correctly investigated,
the primary meaning of all the scriptures is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, and none other.

By this, it is stated that the singular number in the word *anvayāt* (from the positive concomitance) refers to the collective sense; and by that, he indicates their lack of contradiction. The meaning of the prefix *sam-* is "correctly" (*samyak*).

And its connection with the verb "investigated" (*pravicārita*) is shown by means of an implied action (*adhyāhṛta-kriyā*). Now, one might object: since even in the case of the *upakrama* (opening statement) and other indicators, a deviation from the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is sometimes observed—just as in the case of the interpretation of what is already understood—how can they possess the status of a logical mark (*liṅgatva*)? To dispel this doubt, it is stated that [the text] has been "properly investigated. This refers to the deliberation on the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha-vimarśa*) following a determination of relative strength (*balābala*) based on proximity (*sannikarṣa*) and remoteness (*viprakarṣa*), as well as the presence of scope (*sāvakāśatva*) and so forth, among the *upakrama*, etc., and the direct statements (*śruti*), etc.; wherein, in case of conflict, the weaker is sublated by the stronger.
It is a thorough investigation;
therefore, it is not said that the mere presence of symptoms such as an assault constitutes a sign,
by which the pointing out of a fallacy would be consistent.
However, it is stated that the preliminary stages (*upakrama*) and so forth are indeed endowed with the intermediate function characterized by thorough investigation (*pravicāra*);
and it is said that these never deviate from their object.
In the word *pravicārita*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
"When the investigation has been performed" means when it has been investigated in the treatise;
"this is understood" is the completion of the sentence.
The word "saṃ" has another meaning through repetition as "the primary sense" (mukhyārtha).
The word "sarva" is also indeed the meaning of "saṃ.
The phrase "the meaning of the scripture" (śāstrasyārtha) is an explanation of the term "śāstrayoni," which is carried over from the preceding sūtra.
The meaning of that word is "the Blessed One Viṣṇu.
The word "tu" (but/only) is used for emphasis;
its explanation is that there is no other. *3,150*
And thus, the application of the sūtra is as follows:

when the treatise has been thoroughly investigated through the collection of marks such as the opening statement (*upakrama*) and so forth, because the entire treatise is found to be consistently connected (*anvaya*) with the Blessed One alone through the function of its verbal expression— thereby understanding the relationship characterized by power (*śakti*) and intended meaning (*tātparya*)— that which is called Viṣṇu is indeed Brahman.
Because He is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, He is the source of the scriptures (*śāstrayoni*), and not Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, or others.
For being fully endowed with infinite qualities is indeed the primary characteristic [of Brahman].
In that regard, when the scripture is accepted as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is entirely appropriate in its literal sense.

For if it were to function through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth, the qualities would not be obtained in the expressed meaning; furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that those qualities would belong to the expressed meaning itself. Likewise, the infinite qualities cannot be conveyed by only a few sentences.
Furthermore, because it would follow that the subject matter of another sentence would also possess those qualities,
the repetition of the word "saṃ" is justified.
[Objection: Is it not the case that, because of the hearing of the word "that" (*yat*) in the sūtra "From which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed]," Brahman is the subject under discussion?
That very [Brahman] will be carried over here by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) [of ellipsis]. What, then, is the purpose of explicitly mentioning "that" (*tat*) here?
Not so;
for in this context, the word "tu" (but) must be employed for the purpose of excluding other [possibilities],
and its connection cannot be understood unless that [word] is stated.

Because of the rule that "where there is restriction, there is negation of the other," it should not be argued that the cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) will arise through the recurring [word]. For,
by this very [principle], it would follow that the cognition of the relation [of concomitance] would occur through the heard [word] alone.
If it is argued that [the word] is not [used] there because of its lack of utility, we say no; for it is logical that its purpose is to refute the explanation based on common perception.
If it is argued that this is established from the word itself through syntactic connection (*anvaya*), we say no.
Since its purpose can be fulfilled simply by establishing that the "approaches" (*upakrama*) and so forth function as indicators (*liṅga*),
the inclusion of that [word] in the Sūtra is meaningful.

Furthermore, the interpretation that the prefix *sam-* indicates— through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)— that all words refer solely to the nominal stem-meaning of "Brahman" is refuted by the rejection of the theory of indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*).
And this will be refuted later on, so it is not refuted here.

Thus, it is established that the definition is well-founded: by its primary sense, Brahman—known as Nārāyaṇa—is indeed the cause of the origin of the world and so forth, and is that which is to be propounded by the entire body of scriptures consisting of letters, words, and sentences.
Thus ends the section on "Harmonization" (*samanvaya*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_1,1.IV: The Section on "Because of Seeing" (Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa) =======] *3,154* // Now begins the section on "because of seeing."
**Establishing that Brahman is denotable by all scriptures.** *Oṃ. Because of seeing, [Brahman] is not "that which is not based on the Word," *oṃ*.**
"Because of [the act of] seeing; [Brahman] is not that which is not based on scripture.

(BS 1.1.5) Having stated that Brahman is the subject taught by the entire scripture solely through the function of verbal testimony, this section is commenced to raise an objection against that and provide its resolution.
For instance:
"From which words turn back," "without sound, without touch," and so forth, according to such scriptural passages;
and "wherein there is no word accompanied by manifold causal factors."
From such Smṛti passages as these, it is determined that Brahman is inexpressible.
Furthermore, the function of speech is based on substance, quality, action, and genus;
yet Brahman possesses no connection with substance or the other categories.
"Absolute and devoid of qualities," "partless, actionless, and tranquil"—
from such scriptural passages [it follows that He is beyond description].
Therefore, how could His state of being expressible be possible?

Furthermore, the status of being the subject matter of the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*) is possible through the function of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā-vṛtti*) and does not depend upon being the primary denotation (*vācyatā*).
Therefore, because Brahman is not the primary denotation, it is not accessible through the scripture by way of its direct expressive function.
Another says: it is not possible for Brahman to be the subject matter propounded by all scriptures, because there is no means for certain determination.
For the means of determining that [Brahman] are the indicators such as the introductory context (*upakrama*) and so forth;

and while through these one might somehow ascertain that a scripture already understood by people like us has Brahman as its object, it is impossible to ascertain that a scripture not understood by us is intended for that purpose.
"Indeed, the Vedas are infinite";
from this Vedic revelation, it is understood that the scripture is indeed infinite.
And the mastery of an infinite scripture is not possible for us even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Furthermore, the determination that a single portion of the scripture has Brahman as its ultimate purport is fruitless,
because one may suspect that in another portion it teaches the opposite;
and since no alternative is possible regarding an established reality, doubt persists even in this case.

Thus, on the grounds that all scriptures lack authority, it might be argued that Brahman—the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, and complete with all auspicious qualities—is not established.
This being the position reached, the author of the Sūtras first refutes the doubt regarding its ineffability: "Because of seeing (īkṣateḥ), [Brahman] is not 'non-scriptural' (na-aśabdam)."
Because it is seen [in scripture], that which is not based on the Word [is not Brahman]; Om.
He explains that [point] with the words: "Because it is to be seen" (*īkṣaṇīyatvataḥ*). Here, *īkṣateḥ* is a reference to the verbal root.
A mere word whose meaning is not intended to be expressed cannot serve as a reason for Brahman being denotable; therefore, its actual meaning is indicated by this [term].
Nor does even a vision unrelated to Brahman serve as a reason here, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore,

the relationship is not of the nature of agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, because it is not supported by scripture (*śruti*), because there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position, and because it would lead to an undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*).
Therefore, "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) must be stated as having Brahman as its object precisely because of its being the cause;
yet even this is not tenable, as it would result in a lack of grammatical coordination (vyadhikaraṇatva).
Consequently, with the intention that it is the state of being the object of seeing (īkṣaṇīyatva) itself that is intended as the reason, it is said: "on account of being the object of seeing."
Because He is the object of vision, Viṣṇu is indeed the expressible... // MAnu 1.1.120ab //
The word "that" (tat) is carried over from the previous context; by that [word], he says "Viṣṇu.
That which has no expressive word for it is "wordless" (aśabda).
The meaning is "inexpressible.

Regarding the statement "it is not inexpressible" (*nāvācyam*) when one ought to say "it is expressible" (*vācyam*), it is stated—"it is indeed expressible" (*vācya eva*)—with the intention that this serves as a restriction, based on the rule: "Two negatives convey the original meaning with an intensification."
Now, for what purpose is the restriction [expressed by the particle "eva"]?
It is said:
for the aphorism of logic (nyāyasūtra) is indeed for the purpose of determining reality (tattvanirṇaya).
And a definitive conclusion arises only through both the establishment of one's own position and the refutation of the opponent's position,
not by either alone,
as it has been said:
"Ascertainment (nirṇaya) is the determination of the meaning through the examination of the pro and the con.

Therefore, once this ascertainment is made here, both the affirmation of expressibility and the negation of inexpressibility would be proposed, respectively, by the direct statement and by implication.
Furthermore, the reason "being perceivable" (īkṣaṇīyatva) is understood as serving the purpose of establishing both.
And in this way, a definitive conclusion would be reached;
for if it were merely asserted that "it must be stated," the refutation of the opposing position would not have been accomplished,
and there is no other sūtra for that purpose.
Therefore, this explanation is appropriate;
it should be understood in the same way elsewhere as well.
This is what is meant:

Brahman must indeed be expressible, and not inexpressible, because it is the object of the act of seeing, like a pot; and Brahman’s being the object of seeing is established by such texts as, "He sees the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond the mass of living beings," and "One should see the Self in the Self alone."
Thus, it is established by such scriptural passages.
Now, one might ask: what is the contradiction if Brahman lacks the quality of being expressible? [The answer is:
It would not be capable of being perceived.
If it is argued that, in that case, the scripture would be rendered useless and liberation impossible due to the absence of knowledge of Brahman, we say no;
for being denotable (*vācyatva*) is not a pervader (*avyāpaka*), and being perceptible (*īkṣaṇīyatva*) is not a pervaded (*avyāpya*).
Indeed, the cessation of a non-pervader does not entail the cessation of the non-pervaded.
It is not possible [to prove it].
For being "perceptible" (īkṣaṇīyatva) is properly understood as the pervader (vyāpaka), having as its causes direct perception, inference, scripture, and their fallacies;
whereas being "denotable" (vācyatva) is merely the pervaded (vyāpya), being conditioned by the specific function of words.
Not so;
for this perception of Brahman taught for the sake of liberation is not produced by a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*),
because error lacks the capacity to remove ignorance (*avidyā*).
Nor is it produced by perception or inference, since it has been established that [Brahman] is to be understood solely through scripture.
Thus, given the absence of any other means, if Brahman were not even expressible, it would follow that it could not even be seen; such a subverting argument (bādhaka) is indeed possible.

Nor is there an impossibility of pervasion (*vyāpti*), because negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is possible; for there exists a general pervasion such as: "whatever is not the object of a particular instrument is not the object of the corresponding action," just as the sky, which is not the object of an axe or similar tools, is not the object of cutting. (3.165)
Now, it may be argued: "Granted that Brahman cannot be perceived by fallacious means of knowledge, nor by perception and inference, and granted further that it is not denotable;
nevertheless, it will still be perceivable as being indicated by words."
And thus, because there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary case (vipakṣa), the reason (hetu) is inconclusive;
therefore, he says: "Nor... (na ca).
"...and not otherwise; for nowhere has 'being the object of definition' (lakṣyatva) been observed [in the absence of being denotable].
For (hi), because (yasmāt) elsewhere—namely, in the absence of being denotable (vācyatva)—"being the object of definition" is never observed anywhere.
Therefore, since Brahman is inexpressible, it lacks the possibility of being indicated; thus, the implication is that it cannot be perceived even through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
For it is observed that only something already expressible by some word, such as a riverbank, can be indicated by another. *3,167*
"Even that which is inexpressible would be a *lakṣya*, leading to an infinite regress.
Now, one might ask: why could even that which is inexpressible not be a *lakṣya*?
Consequently, since there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), this reductio argument (*prasaṅga-hetu*) is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).
Therefore, he asks: "What is that?"
"What is that?"—thus there would be an infinite regress.
The word "otherwise" (anyathā) carries over from the previous context.

If it were admitted that Brahman, though inexpressible, is still the object of definition (lakṣya), then there would be an infinite regress (anavasthiti) when the inquiry "What is that? is undertaken.
This is what is meant:

for a word that is based on its specific characteristic (*lākṣaṇika*) does not produce a cognition of another meaning merely upon being heard, because its expressive power (*śakti*) has not been grasped therein;
rather, [it produces it] with respect to the denoted object (*vācyārtha*).
Even when one has produced an understanding and perceives its impossibility,
that alone is not sufficient;
for the perception of the impossibility of the literal meaning is merely a cause for its abandonment.
What indeed [is the point] when another object is understood both in its own nature and as being related to the expressed meaning?

For it is observed that in the case of words such as "Ganges," the bank and so forth—which are the indicated (lakṣya)—are already understood both in their own nature and as being related to the Ganges and so forth;
not something whose own nature is ununderstood, such as a tortoise's hair.
Nor is it the case that the bank or similar objects are understood as being related to something else;
likewise, if Brahman is to be indicated by Vedic words, its cognition must be admitted [to arise from them].
And its cognition cannot possibly occur through perception or other means of knowledge, as is the case with the bank and such things.

Then, when a word used in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*) is employed, one who perceives an inconsistency in the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) will have the desire to know (*jijñāsā*): "What is that which is indicated (*lakṣya*) by this? In that case, the word itself must be employed [to indicate it].

If even by that [word] it is not the literal meaning but rather the indicated meaning, then because the desire to know—"What then is that?"—is not yet satisfied, another word would have to be employed as the literal meaning.
If even by that it is again only the indicated meaning, then there would be an infinite regress (*aparyavasāna*) of such desires to know.
If each preceding definition is not established, the subsequent definitions cannot be established, resulting in a collapse of the very foundation.

Furthermore, if [the word] were expressible by some other word, then once that [other word] had been uttered, one whose desire to know [the meaning] has ceased would perceive the derivative (lākṣaṇika) function [of the original word].

If it is argued that even if it were expressible, there would be an infinite regress because the establishment of the preceding [word] is required in order to grasp the relationship [between the word and its meaning], we say no.
This must be stated in the section concerning overestimation (*abhimāna-adhikaraṇa*).

Therefore, since there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) characterized by infinite regress (*anavasthā*) against the contrary position, it follows that if [the word] were inexpressible, the state of being definable (*lakṣyatva*) would not occur; thus, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is logical.
For a word based on its definition (*lākṣaṇika*) does not produce a cognition of another meaning merely upon being heard, because its expressive power (*śakti*) has not been grasped therein.
