For the words "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth denote modifications (*vikāra*),
because the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed in the sense of modification,
and because such modification is possible in the case of the sheaths (*kośa*) beginning with the body.
Alternatively, since all modifications are logically possible within primordial matter (*prakṛti*),
or because the individual selves (*jīva*) who identify with those modifications consist of food and so forth, it is appropriate [to speak of them as such],
just like [describing someone as] "fair" or "dark."
Nor can this sound belong to presiding deities such as Brahmā and others,
as in the expression "Indra is the thunderbolt";
furthermore, the state of being a modification is not possible for the supreme Brahman.
[This is] because [the Self is described as] "changeless," "indestructible," "pure," and so forth.
Although the suffix *mayaṭ* is used both for modification (*vikāra*) and for abundance (*prācurya*),
nevertheless, the word *annamaya* must be accepted as having the sense of modification.

Regarding the body denoted by the word "person" (puruṣa), which is a modification of food produced from plants—as indicated by the statement, "From plants comes food; from food, the person"—it has been said: "This very person is food, consisting of the essence of food."
"Because of the direct designation, 'This very thing is its head,' and because a twofold conceptualization is thus untenable, the sense of 'modification' (vikāra) must be accepted everywhere."
Furthermore, while there are five [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya),
Brahman is only one;
therefore, how could it be denoted by these words?
Moreover, these [elements] are described as being distinct from one another by way of the relationship between body and embodied, and by way of being internal;
however, Brahman cannot be so.
Nor should it be argued that the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is Brahman because it is the innermost of all.
Because it falls within the stream of modifications (*vikāra*),
and because its status as the innermost of all cannot be determined merely by its being the interior of those beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*);
furthermore, the Supreme Brahman under discussion in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" is the "Brahman, the tail, the support" of the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).
Thus, [Brahman] is perceived as consisting of parts;
yet the part itself is not the whole, because that would be a contradiction.
Therefore, all five—beginning with *annamaya*—are not Brahman, but rather something else entirely.
This being the case, the author explains the aphorism that establishes the final conclusion: "He who lies upon the ocean."
The Veda [declares him] to be reclining upon the ocean and the progenitor of all that is born.
"He proclaimed with certainty that 'That alone is the supreme Brahman';
therefore, because the word *brahman* is restricted to that very thing [alone], [it is not used for anything else]. (Manu 1.155)
This [knowledge] arises from the repeated practice of such forms as "Food is Brahman" found in the Taittirīyaka,
and likewise in thousands of other instances within other branches of the Veda that possess this same form.
Hari himself is denoted by such words as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) and others.

In this regard, the portion of the thesis stating that "Brahman is the one consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) has been explained by the following passage from the *Taittirīyaka*: "In thousands of other branches as well, Hari himself is denoted by such words as 'consisting of bliss' (*ānandamaya*)."
In this context, "taittirīyaka" is the citation of the illustrative sentence; "in others" is the designation of those [texts] yet to be determined;
and "of such a form" means those that possess qualities similar to the qualities expressed by the general term denoting the possessor of qualities (guṇin).
In that regard, the reason is "from practice.
Its explanation is: "Those who [meditate on] food as Brahman... "Those who meditate on food as Brahman," [it says].
Those who worship the vital breath as Brahman;
he who knows the bliss of Brahman; and if one knows consciousness as Brahman.
The meaning is that the word "Brahman" is repeated in the verses cited as referring to the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth, such as: "If one knows Brahman as non-existent...
Repetition in its primary sense consists of the multiple mention of the same subject matter.
And since this is not the case here,

in order to address the doubt as to whether it is merely stated more than once— thereby indicating that there is also a single object of reference— the phrase "because it was not stated" (*ityanuktatvāt*) and so forth was employed. This means that [the author] stated it in such a form [as "because it was not stated"].
It is thus stated that this is because the word "Brahman" is heard in the scriptures as referring to the [selfs] consisting of food and so forth.
To the question, "How is this certainty established by the word 'Brahman'? he says: "Of the word 'Brahman'..."
To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "Because of scripture."

The construction is as follows: "Since the Śruti, with its definitive assertion, declared that 'That alone is the supreme Brahman'—referring specifically to Viṣṇu as the one denoted by the word 'Brahman'—therefore [it is so].
To the question, "Even there, on what basis is Viṣṇu the object referred to by the pronoun 'That' (tat)? it is said: "He who reclines upon the ocean."
This has been explained in the first Sūtra:
that the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is an elliptical designation for [the series] beginning with "consisting of food" (*annamaya*).
Now, is it not the case that the proposition in the Sūtra is simply "consisting of bliss"?
To the question, "How then [is this] an explanation by means of passages such as 'consisting of bliss' (ānandamaya)? he says: "It is an indicative mark" (upalakṣaṇatvam).
Words beginning with "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) serve as indicators [of the preceding stages].
"He who consists of bliss" (ānandamaya) and "the former" (pūrva)—those for whom these two exist are "those preceded by him who consists of bliss" (ānandamayapūrviṇaḥ); [this refers to] them.
There might be a discrepancy between this commentary and the text being commented upon if the word "consisting of bliss" here were to denote its own specific category alone;
but it is not so.

However, in this context, the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is intended as an elliptical indicator (upalakṣaṇa) for the terms "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth, which follow the same logical principle.
Likewise, in the subsequent sections, it should be understood that the terms "ether" (ākāśa) and so forth are also elliptical indicators for other terms that share the same logical principle.
And this [definition] is one that does not abandon its primary characteristic (*ajahallakṣaṇā*). Therefore, one should not consider the abandonment of the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).

For this very reason, it should be understood that the objections beginning with "because of the word for modification" (*vikāraśabdāt*), as well as their refutations and independent arguments, are merely illustrative examples. *3,307*
If one were to grasp the sūtras exactly as they are heard [literally], the quality of being "all-encompassing" (*sarvatomukhatva*) would be untenable.
This might be argued:

metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is observed when the primary meaning is sublated, when there is a connection [between the primary and secondary meanings], and when a purpose [for the indication] exists.

In this context, since the use of a direct expressive term (*vācaka-śabda*) is possible, what purpose does the author of the Sūtra have for employing a figurative term (*lākṣaṇika-śabda*)? Nor is this a conventional metaphor (*rūḍha-lakṣaṇā*), which would not require a specific purpose; therefore, he says: "Of the Sūtra... [and so forth].
Because this Sūtra consists of few syllables, it serves to determine all the various recensions;
furthermore, because it provides the means of attainment, there is a separate topical section (adhikaraṇa) concerning it.
If the primary usage were employed,

then one would have to use the expression "consisting of food, consisting of vital breath, consisting of mind, consisting of consciousness, and consisting of bliss"; and in that case, the characteristic of the Sūtra’s brevity of syllables (alpa-akṣara-tva) would be lost.
For brevity of syllables consists in not stating a meaning that is already known either through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or by implication (*artha*).
And we shall explain that this very meaning is understood from the sense of the context.
Therefore, the author of the Sūtras employs a figurative usage (*lākṣaṇika-prayoga*) for the purpose of achieving brevity of syllables in the Sūtra.

Now, if it is asked: "If the Sūtra is accepted exactly as it was heard, what kind of fault is there such that one must explain it through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā)?"—to this he says: "All... [and so forth].
The word "because it has been set forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

For if only what is heard in a single Sūtra were taken into account, then the reconciliation of hundreds of Sūtras with hundreds of statements would indeed be accomplished; however, there would be no definitive determination of all the Śākhās.
These [sūtras] were composed for the purpose of determining the meaning of all Vedic branches (*śākhā*),

because there are no other sūtras [for that purpose]. Therefore, since it is otherwise impossible for them to determine all branches, it is understood that they must be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by abandoning the literal sense alone.
For it is by resorting to indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that the determination of all the Vedic branches (*sarva-śākhā-nirṇaya*) is established.

Now, one might object: "Just as there is an obstacle to accepting the literal sense—namely, the impossibility of the Sūtras being 'facing in all directions' (*viśvatomukhatva*)—so too is the existence of an obstacle equal in the case of resorting to indication;
for since all words could be indicated by the term *ānandamaya* just as *annamaya* and the others are, the commencement of the subsequent section would be untenable. If this is argued:

Is the objection that it would follow that one should not begin new topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning other words that share the same logic? Or is it that it would follow that one should not begin new topical sections concerning other words that fall under a different logic?
Not the first.
Because it is accepted [as such].
Not the second,
because of the lack of parity.
For the [sheaths] beginning with *annamaya* are grasped as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) by virtue of their connection through the principle of uniformity;
but what connection could there be for the others to serve as indicators?
Indeed, indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is never observed to occur without a connection.
The "disturbance" (*upaplava*) consists in being characterized by the nature of sound (*śabdatva*) and by being subject to doubt.
This being so, [the matter] would be fully resolved by the sūtra itself, "But that [is established], because of the harmony [of all texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*).
Alternatively, it may be observed that even when the same logical principle applies, the commencement of a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) is seen.
Since it is argued that [the definition] would not apply under the view that it is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an incidental indicator), he says: "And again... (*punaśca*).

In this regard, even concerning a subject matter where the reasoning (*nyāya*) established in a previous section (*adhikaraṇa*) applies, the commencement of another section is justified because that [previous] reasoning still exists—specifically, due to the presence of a further doubt characterized by the appearance of a new point that would otherwise obscure the logic of the prior section, which serves as the reason for initiating a new section.
What is meant is this:
although the reasoning is the same, the claim that "the meaning of the Sūtra must be exactly as it is heard, since otherwise the commencement of a new section would be inexplicable" is not tenable.
Because it can be established otherwise;

for when an opponent suspects that a certain principle does not apply due to a further doubt, the commencement of a new topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) is for the purpose of demonstrating once again that it is indeed the subject of that principle by refuting that further doubt.
Thus, since there is no room for the charge that the "all-sidedness" (*viśvatomukhatva*) of the system is undermined, it is logical to simply resort to figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*). *3,310*

[Objection: But surely these sūtras do not serve as determiners for all Vedic branches (śākhās), because all branches are concerned with ritual action (kārya) and thus do not have Brahman as their subject matter. Furthermore, the portion of the Vedānta that has Brahman as its subject matter is so small that it can be determined by the sūtras according to their literal meaning, even without resorting to figurative interpretation (lakṣaṇā). So what is the point of resorting to figurative interpretation? To this, he says: "All... [and so forth].
"The Vedas."
For the Veda declares: "That state which all the Vedas proclaim. (Manu 1.159ab)
The remainder [of the meaning] is that he states that all the Vedas have Brahman as their ultimate goal.

As for the reason for specifying only the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) in the Sūtra: if it were intended here as a mere illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), then, because it occurs first, he would have employed the term *annamaya* (consisting of food) instead.
But since the author of the Sūtras employs the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), he indicates an intention to refer to that [bliss] alone; therefore, he says: "consisting of bliss."
But in the case of the form consisting of bliss, it is because of the statement that Brahman is its "tail."
For the name "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) indeed arises from the attainment of the state of Brahman in its entirety.

The fact that the terms "modification" (*vikāra*) and so forth apply equally to the *annamaya* and the others serves as a general argument for their non-Brahman nature. Furthermore, there is an additional and even stronger argument: since it is stated that "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and then "Brahman is the tail, the support" is said regarding the *ānandamaya*, this implies that the entire *ānandamaya*—as the possessor of the parts—is not Brahman. Therefore...
The author of the Sūtras has employed the name "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) in order to indicate that one must remain attentive; thus, an alternative interpretation is stated.

For if the "consisting of bliss" were Brahman, then its constituent part—the entire [self] consisting of bliss—would not attain the status of being truly Brahman, nor would it attain the perfect nature of Brahman.
Consequently, the scriptural teaching that the attainment of the Supreme results from the knowledge of that [Brahman] would be contradicted.
But surely, even in the case of that which consists of food (*annamaya*), there is the impossibility of further [stages]; for it is said: "From herbs comes food;
from food, the person (*puruṣa*)."
"That indeed is this person consisting of the essence of food," and "Of him,
this very [body] is the head"—
do not say so.
This too is included within that [the Self consisting of bliss], because it brings about its modification;

or rather, since the inquiry into the Self consisting of bliss is connected with the subject at hand—given that Brahman, which was declared as the object of inquiry in the sūtra "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," has been stated to be the "tail" (of the Self consisting of bliss), thereby resulting in the conclusion that [Brahman] is not the entire [Self consisting of bliss]—it is appropriate to employ the mention of the name "Self consisting of bliss.

**Another reason for the term *ānandamaya* being indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*) of *annamaya* and the others:** Now, one might object: "Since the absence of indicativeness in the Sūtras would lead to the undesirable consequence that there is no definitive determination regarding all Vedic branches (*śākhās*), let us grant that they are indicative. But from what [reason] does this specific distinction arise—that the word *ānandamaya* is indicative of *annamaya* and the rest? To this, he says: "Of the word *brahman*... [The full Sūtra is: *brahma-śabda-sāmānyād-ānanda-maya-śabdo 'nnamayādīnām upalakṣaṇārthaḥ*. (Because of the commonality of the word *brahman*, the word *ānandamaya* is intended as an indicator for *annamaya* and the others.)
And because of the repetition of the word "Brahman" with respect to the five forms and so forth, [its meaning] is clear. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.160cd)
For the repetition of the word "Brahman" that was stated as the reason for the Ānandamaya being Brahman is equally present in the case of the Annamaya and the others as well.
Thus, if the Annamaya and the rest are not Brahman, how could that [reason]— being inconclusive (anaikāntika)— establish the Brahmanhood of the Ānandamaya as well?

Therefore, by stating that the repeated use of the word "Brahman" common to the [sheaths] beginning with the *annamaya* is the reason [for its being Brahman], the author of the Sūtras indicates that he accepts those [sheaths] as well as being subjects of inquiry (*pakṣa*).
By the word "and" (*ca*), he suggests that the reasons such as "because it teaches the union of this [self] with That in this [state]" are also common [to all the sheaths].
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), Ānanda and others are included;
therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is exactly as stated.
Even though it is designated as a "tail," there is no contradiction with its being complete or being a constituent part of a whole.
Now, one might ask: how can that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya) be Brahman?
For it is stated that "Brahman is the tail," thereby designating Brahman as its tail.
And yet, the word "Brahman" cannot refer to anything else.
If that were the case, it would result in the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) right here.
Nor should it be argued that the word "Brahman" is the probans (*hetu*) only when it is free from exception, and not merely the word "Brahman" in general;
for even in the phrase "the tail is Brahman," there is likewise an absence of exception.
If it is argued that [the Self consisting of bliss] is a limb of Brahman, we say no;
for even now, the fact that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is Brahman has not been established.
Here, the following must be asked:
Does the intention here mean that if the part is full, the fullness of the whole is not logically possible?
Or is it intended to establish that if the whole, which consists of bliss, is full, then its part cannot be full?
Or is it because of the difference between the part and the whole that, while the part may have the nature of bliss, the whole does not possess that same nature?
Regarding this, he states the fault: "Brahmahood... etc.
Brahminhood may exist even in a part, and likewise in the whole by its own nature;
just as the entire state of being a Brahmin belongs to Kṛṣṇa, who has black hair.
For his boundless powers have indeed been demonstrated to the son of Pṛthā.
If Brahman-hood exists even in a part, then it would exist in the whole by itself and without effort;
for since largeness is observed in a whole in dependence upon its parts,
it follows that if a part is complete [in being Brahman], the completeness of the whole is untenable— this is contradictory.
In the second [verse], he demonstrates the absence of pervasion (vyāpti), saying: "Just as..."
And this is well known in the Purāṇa through such passages as, "He plucked out two hairs from himself," and so forth.
It is "entire" (akhilā), meaning without any figurative qualification.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "In the same way, this will also apply to the limb consisting of bliss.
Regarding this, he states the authority: "And it has been shown," etc.
That Pārtha beheld heaven and earth and so forth is understood from his own words;
the word *ca* (and) serves to include the arguments stated in the Purāṇas and other sources.
The word *eva* (indeed), however, is connected to show that this was established by such means of knowledge and is not merely stated as a verbal assertion.

Now, one might object: "In the world, whatever possesses parts is observed to be limited; how then can this be so? To this, he says "Niḥsīmā" (Boundless): because the Supreme Lord, by virtue of His power which brings about the impossible and is unimpeded everywhere, even that which has not been seen elsewhere is possible; what room is there here for the question "How?"? Thus he says: "Niḥsīmā."

Regarding the statement "sīma and sīmā [are both used] in the feminine," this compound has the word *sīmā*—a synonym for *sīman*—as its final member. Even though *sīmā* is the final member of the compound, the form is grammatically correct by virtue of the rule *ḍāb ubhābhyām anyatarasyām*.
This very same response applies to the third case as well.
"Niḥsīmā" (boundless).
The word "hi" indicates a reason; or, it indicates the well-known fact that his head is Nārāyaṇa and so forth. *3,318*
This might be argued:
by the force of the word "Brahman" alone, it is not possible to determine that the Annamaya and the others are Viṣṇu.
[As stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "The Ṛta, the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the Person who is dark and tawny..."
"Ūrdhvaretas, Virūpākṣa, Śaṅkara, Nīlalohita."

Since the term "Supreme Brahman" is heard even in reference to Rudra in this passage from the *Tāpanīya*, he explains the first and second halves [of the verse] as having different subjects: "The Truth... and so forth.
The Supreme Brahman is the eternal truth, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny.
Elsewhere, that which is called Viṣṇu is described as having the semen drawn upward;
however, the inferior one called Virūpākṣa is described by Brahmā as being established in his vow.
The construction is as follows: in the first half [of the verse], the Supreme Brahman called Viṣṇu is stated;
elsewhere, in the second half, that called Virūpākṣa is stated. Thus, it is said that the first and second halves have different subjects.
To the question, "If they have different subjects, how is there syntactical connection (anvaya)? it is replied: "that [is] the one with upward-turned semen" (tat pratyūrdhvaretas).
By this, it is stated that words such as *ṛtam* and so forth are in the accusative case, while words such as *ūrdhvaretasam* and so forth are in the nominative case.
If one asks how there can then be a neuter gender usage, it is said: "the lower Brahman" (*aparaṃ brahma*).
Since the word *brahman* exists even for the individual soul (*jīva*) through a secondary (figurative) application, the neuter gender is used in reference to that.
He explains that [the term] "one whose semen is drawn upward" (*pratyūrdhvaretas*) by saying: "established in that vow."
Since the first and second halves [of the verse] are perceived as having the same subject matter, why is a difference in subject matter postulated? To this, he says: "samāna... (identical).
If the subsequent [term] "blue-and-red" (*nīlalohita*) were to share a common substratum (*samānādhikṛtatva*), then it would be a tautology in the form of "black-and-tawny" (*kṛṣṇapiṅgala*).

That which has a common, single substratum—that is, a locus or object—for both the preceding and the following [terms] is "co-referential" (*samānādhikṛta*); the state of being such is "co-referentiality."

If the first and second halves [of the verse] were to have the same subject matter, then what is stated in the second half— namely, "blue-and-red"— would be a redundant repetition of what was stated in the first half,
because the words "black-and-tawny" (*kṛṣṇapiṅgala*) and "blue-and-red" (*nīlalohita*) have the same meaning.
Therefore, it is more logical to set aside the apparent identity of subject matter and instead accept that they have different subject matters.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent phrase "the overlord of Brahmā, the overlord for Brahmā," one understands that Rudra is the overlord of whom Brahmā is the overlord—that is, he is the "overlord of Brahmā" (brahmādhipati). Since he who has an overlord cannot be the Supreme Brahman, the author, intending to show that the first half [of the verse] does not concern Rudra, says:
"The overlord of Brahmā. This refers to the *Tāpanīya-śruti* cited previously. [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.165ab]
The statement "Ṛta is truth" occurs here in the *Tāpanīya-śruti*; the word "Ṛta" is placed before [the word "Satya"], meaning prior to it or above it.
The construction is that there exists the phrase "Brahmādhipati," which establishes Rudra’s state of being subject to another's authority.
This would indeed be so if the term "Brahmādhipati" were a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
But this is not the case;
for since it is possible that [the compound] is either a genitive *tatpuruṣa* or a *karmadhāraya*, there is no certainty that it is a *bahuvrīhi*. Therefore, he says: "svarita... and so forth.
The term *brahma* ending in the svarita accent will attain the status of a bahuvrīhi compound.
Since the nominal stem *brahmādhipati* ends in the word *brahma* preceded by *sva*, it follows that it must be a *bahuvrīhi* compound;

it cannot be any other type of compound. If it were otherwise, then because the final syllable would be udātta, the preceding member would—by the rule "a word [in a compound] has one vowel that is anudātta" (*anudāttaṃ padam ekavarjam*)—result in having a svarita at its end.
The state of having a preceding member ending in a svarita accent would not occur.
Alternatively, after stating the previously mentioned meaning exactly as it appears in the text, the entire verse should be applied as a response to the aforementioned doubt;
for although the status of being a *bahuvrīhi* compound was already established previously.
Nevertheless, the usage "eṣyati" (it will come) is employed with respect to the ascertainment of that [future state].
If it is asked, "Even though the final vowel of the preceding word is *svarita*, how can there be the status of a *bahuvrīhi* compound?
he replies, "Because it is seen in examples," citing "svāhā."
"O Indra-śatru, increase by svāhā!"—this is the sūtra in the Mahāvyākaraṇa for determining accents when a term has attained the status of a *bahuvrīhi*. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.166)

Since, in the case of "svāhendrashatrur vadhāsi" (O weapon, slay the enemy of Indra), the nominal stem *indraśatru* ends with the word *indra* which has a svarita accent and thus acquires the status of a bahuvrīhi compound, this [other instance] is likewise of that same nature; therefore, the nominal stem *indraśatru* also possesses the character of a bahuvrīhi because of the possibility of it being a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). To this, he says: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, Indra alone became his parasol, according to the subsequent Vedic revelation;
for since the word "Indra" was employed with a circumflex accent at its end,
the mantra would otherwise suffer the defect of lacking its intended accentuation.
Indra became the "śatru" (destroyer) of this Vṛtra;
he did not, however, become Indra’s enemy in accordance with Tvaṣṭṛ’s intention.
From the force of this subsequent sentence, it is understood that the nominal stem *indraśatru* is a bahuvrīhi and not a tatpuruṣa.
And so they have said:
"A mantra that is deficient in accent or phoneme, when incorrectly employed, does not convey its intended meaning;
it becomes a verbal thunderbolt that destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [Vrtra] was destroyed due to a lapse in accent."
Thus:

it is not only that the status of being a *bahuvrīhi* is inferred from the force of the examples when there is a svarita accent on the final syllable of the first member; rather, even in the case of the example itself, it is inferred by the force of hearing the subsequent [member]. He states that there is indeed such an instruction as well: "when the end of the preceding [member] is svarita."

In the *Mahāvyākaraṇa*, regarding the determination of accents, it is stated in the sūtra that when the acute accent (*svarita*) falls on the first member of a compound, a *bahuvrīhi* ending in the masculine gender will result. (Mbh 1.1.167)

The meaning of the sūtra is this: when two masculine words (*puṃsau*) are being compounded and there is a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the vowel at the end of the first member (*pūrvapada*), that compound base (*samāsaprātipadika*) shall attain the status of a *bahuvrīhi*.
Here, some raise an objection regarding an inconsistency; however, that is incorrect.
For it is the established procedure of grammar (*vyākaraṇaprakriyā*) that what is obtained through a general rule (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is subsequently set aside by specific rules (*viśeṣaṇalakṣaṇa*).
As it has been said:
"by means of a definition possessing both general and specific characteristics.
In that case, how is it appropriate to point out a logical deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the general characteristic without first having examined the specific characteristics?
Furthermore, by this sūtra, the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) in the first member of a bahuvrīhi compound is indicated;
since the words *brahma* and *indra* end in a circumflexed vowel (*svarita*),
how could there be any deviation?
As Pāṇini has stated:
"In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first member retains its original accent.
For this very reason, he says, "the determination of the accent."
Otherwise, he would have stated "the determination of compounds" (*samāsanirṇaya*).
Furthermore, this is stated for the purpose of determining a compound through accent when a doubt exists,
as it has been said:

While explaining the purpose [of the treatise] without doubt, the author of the Bhāṣya, having demonstrated the ambiguity regarding whether the word *sthūlapṛṣatī* in the injunction "one should sacrifice a large-spotted ox" (*sthūlapṛṣatīmanaḍvāhīm ālabheta*) is a *tatpuruṣa* or a *bahuvrīhi*, states: "If it has the original accent of its first member, it is a *bahuvrīhi*; if it has the udātta accent on the final syllable of the compound, then it is a *tatpuruṣa*," and so forth.
And thus, to point out a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding that which is beyond doubt is irrelevant.
[Objection: But how can it be said that "the svarita accent belongs to the prior member" (*pūrvāntasvarita*), given that a compound is untenable due to a lack of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*)?
Not so;
for the explanation is that [the rule applies] when there is a circumflex accent on the final syllable of the preceding member within a compound nominal stem (*samāsa-prātipadika*).
Even so, it would follow that [the term] should be *svarita-pūrvānta*.

[Objection: Because in a *bahuvrīhi* compound the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is placed first. [Response: No, because the status of qualifier and qualified is a matter of choice (*kāmacāritva*), or because [the term] belongs to the class beginning with *āhitāgni* (Pāṇini 2.2.37). *3,351*

Furthermore, having established that the two halves of the verse—"Ṛta" and "Satya"—have distinct referents by means of the force of the subsequent statement and to avoid the consequence of tautology, the sentence which was explained in brief is now explained in detail: "Ṛtam... [and so forth].
In the passage beginning with "Ṛtam, satyam, param brahma," the second case ending is used for the objects of reference;
the first case ending, however, applies to Rudra and those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas). *Manusmṛti* 1.1.168.
Regarding the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth), the *luk* elision of the nominative case occurs according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
Alternatively, it may mean "situated in that group of words which stands before 'ityādi' or after 'adharastha'.
If only "dvitīyā" were stated, one would understand only the accusative case as applying to the object (*karman*).
Because the case-ending of the *kāraka* is more powerful,
and that [accusative status] is not possible here,
since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) depends upon an action.
And because there is no action here, it has been stated that [the suffix] follows the word denoting the object (*uddeśya*). In that case, the word *prati* ought to be used.
True;
it will be supplied by ellipsis.
Based on the observation of Vedic usage, one should either follow the word *retaḥ* as ending in *a*, or assume the suffix *ḍa* at the end of the compound.
"One whose semen is drawn upward," and so forth.
The word *ūrdhvaretas* is composed of such constituent parts.
Just as [the phrase] "within the range of Rudra" (*rudragocare*) was previously mentioned, so too should "within the range of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇugocare*) be understood.
Having thus stated the case-endings for the objects and their respective meanings, he provides the formal construction [of the compound] with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, Rudra remains established in his vow toward Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman;
thus indeed should the meaning of the Vedic scripture be understood as "one whose semen is drawn upward" (ūrdhvaretas).

This is stated with the intention that the term "one whose vital energy is drawn upward" (*ūrdhvaretas*) is an illustrative designation (*upalakṣaṇa*), based on the collection of the arguments already set forth; thus it is said: "established in his vow" (*vrate sthitaḥ*).
Furthermore, the meaning of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) is not explained in this way solely by the force of logical reasoning (*upapatti*).
Moreover, he says "Ṛtam" to show that this is also established by the designation found in another Vedic text.
Sadāśiva, the blue-and-red Śaṅkara whose vital energy is drawn upward, meditates upon Viṣṇu as the supreme Brahman, who is the eternal Order and Truth.
For this very reason, the supreme *Nīlagrīva-śruti* of the Atharva Veda declares that Hari alone is the Supreme Brahman in the sacred revelation. 1.171.
"He meditates upon that very [object].
By supplying the word "meditates" (*dhyāyati*) from this context, it is understood that the second case ending is used for the object (*karman*).
When "Atharvaṇī" is mentioned, it might by association be understood as referring specifically to the *Tāpanīya-śruti*;
therefore, it is said: "other than that."
Then what is its name?
It is the *Nīlagrīva-śruti*.
Thus, he states what is obtained by explaining the first and second halves [of the verse] as having different subjects: "the Supreme Brahman."
The phrase "is understood" is to be supplied [to the statement] "Ṛta and Satya" in this Śruti passage.
Therefore, because the first half [of the verse] has Viṣṇu as its subject matter, he states another subverting argument: "That very same... etc.
"He declared that very thing to be *ṛta*; how else could the Śruti be so?
For it directly determines that very [thing] as being *ṛta*, etc.
(Manu 1.1.172). If the first half-verse, "Ṛta is truth, the supreme Brahman," also refers to Rudra, then from that truth, he is indeed *ṛta*.

"The seers declare that this alone is Truth, this alone is the supreme Brahman"— how does this Śruti directly state the truthfulness and other attributes of that Viṣṇu in accordance with the consensus of the seers?
The underlying sense is that, due to mutual contradiction, the lack of authority of one of the two Śrutis would otherwise result.
The scripture "Ṛtam" refers to Rudra’s nature as Ṛta, Satya, Brahman, and so forth;
and the scripture "Tadeva" refers to Viṣṇu.

In that regard, since both [the individual soul and Brahman] are denotable by words such as "Ṛta" due to the force of two scriptural passages, where is there any contradiction? To this, it is said: "of that very [Brahman]."
To the question "How so?", it is said: "they ascertain.
Furthermore, in a case of contradiction, the sublation of the first-heard [text] alone is logical.
This is because that very [first-heard] scripture is more powerful; and this is understood to consist in the sublation of the delusion born from the superficial cognition produced by that scripture.
For a negation of what has not been established is not logical,
nor is there any means of establishing that [identity] other than a semblance of scriptural authority.
Well then, let there be no contradiction by virtue of Rudra being identical with Viṣṇu.
To avoid the charge of tautology, it may be argued that Virūpākṣa mentioned in the second half of the verse must be someone else.
If that is so, then the word "Brahman" refers to Viṣṇu alone; thus, where could there be a deviation from the reason stated in the Sūtra?
For a deviation within the subject of the thesis (pakṣa) is not even to be suspected.

Furthermore, how can the status of Brahman be logically established for Rudra and all others who were non-existent at the time of dissolution and only came into existence from the Lord during creation?
From what source is it understood that they possess birth and other such characteristics? To this, he says: "One" (*eka*).
"One was Nārāyaṇa; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara. (3.357)
Vāsudeva was there at the very beginning; neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara was present.
"Neither Indra nor the Sun, nor Guha, nor Soma, nor Vināyaka"—
from such statements as these, the birth of Viṣṇu pertains to his incarnations.

From such statements as these, it is understood that Rudra and others cease to exist at the time of dissolution, while Viṣṇu undergoes birth. If, on account of possessing birth, Viṣṇu were not Brahman, then the same would apply to him as well; for even he exists in forms such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and thus his birth is real. To this, the author says: "Of Viṣṇu... [referring to the following verse].
"Arising" refers to the discourse on arising;
it pertains to the manifestation [of a Buddha] within the sphere of appearance,
but not to the characteristic of obtaining a physical body and so forth.
To the doubt, "Whence is this [known]? the preceding passage beginning with "one" (*eka*) is connected.
The meaning is that from such passages, one understands Viṣṇu’s persistence even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).
If it is asked, "Even if He persists in His mere essential nature (*svarūpa*), why should there not be an origination characterized by the acquisition of a body and so forth?", we say: no.

Because the existence of intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattva*) is common even to Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and others, there would be the undesirable consequence that expressions such as "not Brahmā" would be logically untenable.
Now, if the word "Brahmā" refers exclusively to Viṣṇu, then how could the term be used for the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth?

And thus, the use of the neuter gender would not be appropriate in view of [the word] *brahman*; furthermore, the phrase "the lord of Brahman" (*brahmaṇo 'dhipatiḥ*) would also be contradictory. Anticipating this objection, he concludes by stating: "The primary [meaning]. (mukhyam iti) //

"Because Hari is the primary Brahman... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.175a]. Now, one might object: "If it is admitted that the word 'Brahman' applies to someone other than Viṣṇu in a secondary sense, then why are the [sheaths] beginning with 'consisting of food' (annamaya) not likewise explained as being secondary Brahmans? For there is nothing here that indicates their status as primary Brahman. To this, he says: "The introduction" (prastāva).
...and even the introductory discourse is supreme. MĀnuv 1.175b.
For here, in the statement "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," there is an introduction (prastāva) and a context (prasaṅga) concerning the Supreme Brahman itself.
Therefore, since it is certain that the subsequent occurrences of the word "Brahman" also refer to the Supreme Brahman, one should not entertain any suspicion of a non-primary meaning here.
The word "api" (also/even) serves to include what is about to be stated.
This [statement] was said while accepting this as an indicator (*jñāpaka*);

however, in reality, because it is the first to be obtained by virtue of the capacity for grasping the word-meaning (*śakti*), and because there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is not proper to assume a non-primary meaning. Thus he says: "The primary... (*mukhya*).
When it is appropriate to grasp the primary sense of "Brahman," the secondary sense is never appropriate.
For when the primary sense is impossible, there occurs the acceptance of a secondary meaning.

If it is asked, "Why should there not be an acceptance of the non-primary even when the primary is possible? [the answer is] no; for there is an invariable concomitance (vyāpti) such that the acceptance of the non-primary occurs only when the primary is impossible. Thus he says: "For when there is impossibility..."

Alternatively, one might ask: "How then can the word *brahman* in passages such as 'He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself' be taken in a non-primary sense? To this he says: "For when [the primary sense] is impossible in some cases... Now, it may be objected that the *annamaya* (consisting of food) and the others are not the Supreme Self, because we hear the suffix *-maya*, which denotes a modification (*vikāra*), and it is logically untenable for the Supreme Self to be a modification of food and so forth.
Nor is there any inconsistency regarding the word "Brahman," since a non-primary sense is possible;
nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction with the introductory context (*prastāva*) and no sublation of the primary meaning, as has already been stated.

Because the suffix *mayaṭ*, which signifies a modification (*vikāra*), acts as a sublater [of the sense of abundance], one might raise the objection that for this very reason the introductory passage (*prastāva*) also constitutes an instruction. To resolve that, the Sūtra states: "Om. If it be said 'no' because of the word denoting a modification, we say no, because of abundance (prācurya). Om.
"Oṃ. If it be argued that [the Self] is not [denoted by the word 'Self'] because of the word 'modification,' we say no, because of abundance. Oṃ.
"If it be said [the Self is not Brahman] because of the word 'modification' (vikāra), we say no, because of abundance (prācurya).

To dispel the impression that the objection and its refutation there concern only the subject of the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), he explains the portion of the established conclusion: "And they have the sense of abundance."
And all instances of the suffix *mayaṭ* used here are explained as having the sense of abundance.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
Regarding the question "In what [scripture]? he says: "In this Śruti. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because they have been established."
This is the meaning:

for the word *mayaṭ* is primary not only in the sense of "transformation" (*vikāra*) but also in the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*), according to the grammatical rule: "*mayaṭ* [is used] in the sense of expressing that which is the subject matter at hand."

Furthermore, the word "Brahman" is not used in its primary sense elsewhere; nor is there a sublation of that which has no other possible application (the *niravakāśa*) by that which has another possible application (the *sāvakāśa*).

Therefore, by the force of the word "Brahman," which has no other application, it is logical that the suffix *-mayaḥ*—which otherwise has other possible meanings—should here signify "abundance. Consequently, one should not assume on the basis of that suffix that the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and the others are not the Supreme Self.
By this, the claim that the word *ānandamaya* does not signify abundance because it falls within a series of modifications (*vikāra*) is refuted by its very internal collapse;

for even in the case of *annamaya* and the others, the suffix *mayaṭ* is accepted as signifying abundance. Furthermore, it would not be proper for the opponent to assert that the suffix has the sense of a modification even in the case of *prāṇamaya*.
Because it is impossible for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) to be modifications of the vital breath;
for if one were to conceive of them as modifications in any way whatsoever, the primary meaning would be abandoned.
This might be argued:
If it is argued that, just as being a transformation of food is impossible for the Lord, so too is an abundance of food,
since that [abundance] would belong to the bodies of the Pāśupatas who subsist on food— [we reply: no,
because here the word "food" does not have its commonly accepted meaning of edible grain.
For the Śruti itself explains the etymology of the word "food" (anna) in the passage: "It is eaten and it eats beings; therefore it is called food.
This form [of the word] arises from the verbal root *ad* when the suffix *kta* is applied in both the passive sense (object) and the active sense (agent).
Furthermore, the state of being an eater of beings is not possible for ordinary food;
therefore, this word "food" (anna) has the abstract state as its primary meaning, denoting both the state of being eaten by beings and the state of being an eater of beings.
Nevertheless, such abundance [of these qualities] is not appropriate for the Supreme Lord.

Since, although being the devourer of beings is possible through its nature as a destroyer, being the source of beings is in no way possible [for it], he says: "the state of being an object of enjoyment."
And here, Hari’s state of being the object of enjoyment consists in his being the primary source of sustenance.

Here, "primacy" (ādyatva) means, by way of figurative application (gauṇyā vṛttyā), the state of being an object of enjoyment (bhogyatva). And this state of being an object of enjoyment is appropriate for Hari, because He is the source of sustenance for all beings.

In the same way, the words *prāṇa*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* must also abandon their well-known meanings—namely, the vital air (*vāyu*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and the intellect (*buddhi*)—and [be understood as referring to Hari]. *Prāṇa*...
Based on the sense that "bodha" (awakening) signifies consciousness (*vijñāna*), its abundance must be established even in the Supreme Self, though it is bodiless;
for otherwise, the meanings of the verses cited therein would not accord with their well-established significance.
Even if the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies abundance (*prācurya*), the designation "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth is not appropriate for the Supreme Self;
for when one says "abounding in that," there arises the implication of even a small amount of its opposite,
as in the expression, "this village abounds in Brāhmaṇas."
"It is not the case that even a trace of ignorance, suffering, or the like exists in the Supreme Self.
"Do not say so," [the opponent replies],
"because the attainment of a contradictory state is not supported by scripture."
For a word meaning "abounding in X" expresses merely the predominance of X in that [substratum];
however, the existence of a contradictory property is to be understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Otherwise, if it were said that "the sacrifice abounds in food" or "the sun abounds in light," it would follow that there is even a trace of famine in the sacrifice or darkness in the sun. (3.367)
"Is it not the case that abundance exists only in relation to its counterpart?
True;

however, this is possible by comparison with the smallness of those same qualities as they exist in other things. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states the intended meaning of the terms *annamaya* and so forth, so that there may be no room for a contradictory cognition, beginning with the words "the great enjoyer."
The meaning of "the great enjoyer" and "the great object of enjoyment" would apply to that which consists of food.
He is possessed of great vital breath, great awakening, and also great consciousness.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is that the Supreme Lord, consisting of food (*annamaya*), is expressed by the term "consisting of food.
It should be understood that the meaning expressed by the term "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) is "the Great Breath," which signifies "great activity.
From the root *man* in the sense of "cognition," with the suffix *asun* in the abstract sense, *manas* is "cognition."
In this case as well, it should be understood that the meaning of the term *manomaya* (consisting of mind) would be [the same as] the term *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness).
From the word "also" (*api*), it should be grasped that the meaning of the term *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) would be "great bliss" (*mahānanda*). [Objection:

But surely, if the Supreme Self were [identical with] those beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*), there would be the consequence of its being manifold; thus, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti which states, "[It is] one only."

Likewise, if [the suffix -maya] meant "abundance," there would be the undesirable consequence of a distinction between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth on one hand and the Supreme Lord on the other—such that one would have to say, "consciousness is abundant in this" and "bliss is abundant in this"—which would contradict such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss.

Furthermore, if the word *manas* were to mean "understanding" (*avabodha*), then since the words *manas* and *vijñāna* would have the same meaning, the separate mention of "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) and "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) would be untenable; therefore, he says: "on account of the distinction" (*viśeṣa*).
Consciousness is also called "mind" (manas) by virtue of its particular and universal aspects.
The speech of Hari, who is of the nature of singular consciousness, occurs through differentiation.
In this regard, three distinct solutions should be understood according to the difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*).

First, although Hari is one and without division, because He possesses the number "many" through the power of His specific attributes (*viśeṣabalena*), it is logical to speak of His multiplicity as the *annamaya* and so forth through such divisions.

Likewise, although Hari consists of knowledge and bliss, even though His nature is that of knowledge, it is indeed logical to speak of Him as possessing those [qualities] through division by means of His specific power alone. Similarly, even though the word "mind" (*manas*) has the sense of "understanding" (*avabodha*), [it refers to] consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The separate mention of "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) and "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) is appropriate according to their distinction;
how so?
By way of the particular and the general, and by way of having the particular and the general as their respective objects.

For the word *vijñāna* denotes specific cognition (*viśeṣajñāna*). However, those particulars which are not cognizable through generalities [are expressed by] the word *vijñāna* in my speech; by the force of its co-occurrence [with other terms], it culminates in general cognition (*sāmānyajñāna*).

Since both the universal and particular aspects exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is indeed logical that the Lord possesses knowledge whose object is the totality of those [aspects].

Nevertheless, the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the others are not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). For it is said: "From this very one, which consists of the essence of food... (*tasmād vā etasmād annarasamayāt*).

Since it is understood from such passages as "There is another inner self consisting of vital breath" that the selves beginning with the one consisting of food are distinct from one another, whereas there is no such difference in the Supreme Self, he says: "Even though there is non-difference."
Even though there is no difference [between them], Hari has declared that "the other" is distinguished by its specific qualities alone.
The meaning is that [the distinction] is by means of *viśeṣa* alone— which, acting as a substitute for difference, accomplishes the function of difference—
but not by means of actual difference (*bheda*),
which would entail a contradiction.
Nor should a break in the caesura (yati-bhaṅga) be suspected here;

for it is said: "In the case of a sandhi, a vowel from the end of the preceding word should sometimes be regarded as the beginning of the following word when considering the caesura; likewise, a *yaṇ*-substitute should be regarded as the beginning of the following word."
Because of this statement, it has already been stated previously that the particular (*viśeṣa*) accomplishes the functions of differentiation, such as linguistic usage and so forth.
In this regard, he states the scriptural authority (*āgama*) concerning the particular: "The words for difference... (*bhedaśabdāḥ*).

But words denoting difference (*bhedaśabda*) would express a specific distinction in Hari because of his distinctness from others; other words such as "Ādi" (and so forth) are called *bhedaśabda* because they are based on difference.
He states an exception to the rule that "they should state the distinction regarding Hari" with the words beginning with "of Hari."
... indeed, the primary distinction between Hari and both sentient and insentient beings.
Even the words of the Brahmatarka are thus... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.181a //
In this way, an exception to the rule "otherwise there would be difference" should also be observed elsewhere;
the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that not only is the previously stated reasoning [valid], but the words of the *Brahmatarka* also convey this.
As for what was stated previously—that there is a designation of even a single thing through division—that [point] did not have its underlying reasoning explained there.
Since this very same argument has been stated merely as a formal proposition, he extends it to that case as well with the words "hence" (ataḥ).
...therefore, that one [Self] is said to be fivefold, beginning with "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth... // Manu 1.1.181b-c //
The word "api" (even) is connected with both "viśeṣabalādeva" (solely by the power of the distinction) and "ekaḥ" (even one);
the phrase "ityādi" (and so forth) is an adverbial modifier of the action.
Furthermore, in the subsequent section (*anuvāka*), Varuṇa teaches that the very reality established in this section is indeed Brahman.
Therefore, he states that the one consisting of food and the others are the supreme Brahman by means of the passage beginning with "Bhṛgu."
...and he will speak this to Bhṛgu.
It has been stated that [the author] will speak of this as being subsequent to the [present] section (*anuvāka*).
Furthermore, its status as Brahman will be established later on.

Thus, since the status of Brahman is established for all five—beginning with *annamaya*—both by the word "Brahman" itself and by the corroboration of the subsequent sections, the suffixes such as *mayaṭ* must be understood as signifying abundance (*prācurya*) rather than material composition (*vikāra*).
"The explanation is appropriate.
[Objection: But here the words "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth are heard; whereas later on...
The words "food" (*anna*) and so forth are themselves devoid of the suffix *mayaṭ*.
Furthermore, when there is a difference in words, there must necessarily be a difference in their causes and a difference in their referents.
It is not logical that the words "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth are synonyms for the words "food" (*anna*) and so forth.
This is because there exists an additional meaning conveyed by the suffix.

Nor should it be argued that this is like the cases of Bhīmasena being called Bhīma, Balabhadra being called Bala, Satyabhāmā being called Satyā, punarnavā being called navā, or kācamācī being called mācī.
Because of the disparity;
for words such as "Bhīma" and so forth denote those [individuals] each separately,
and the word "food" (*anna*) alone is not a denoter of that which consists of food (*annamaya*).
Because it would follow that the suffix *mayaṭ* would have its own inherent meaning [rather than a specific derivative sense],
and it has been stated that *mayaṭ* signifies abundance (*prācurya*).
For when one ought to say "the sacrifice consists of food" (*annamaya yajñaḥ*), the word "food" alone is not employed.
Therefore, since separate entities are taught here and there, how can it be said that Brahman is being taught here as well by virtue of agreement with those [other passages]?
However, because the sheaths (kośas) such as the one consisting of food (annamaya) and so forth are taught here, whereas Brahman is taught there, he says: "By way of being the goal" (prāpyatvena).
The suffix *mayaṭ* has been stated [by Pāṇini] in the sense of "that which is to be obtained"; regarding that as well, something else is now being said.

In the passage beginning with "Having approached this self consisting of food" (*etam annamayam ātmānam upasaṅkramya*), because the suffix *-mayaṭ* is explicitly taught as denoting abundance, nothing else is stated there either; for it is precisely the abundance of food and so forth that is meant by the expression "consisting of food" (*annamaya*). (Manu 1.1.182cd)
For it is stated without distinction; nothing else whatsoever is stated here.

For just as in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, in the sentence "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring," which is intended to enjoin a specific time, the word *jyotis* is a designation for the Jyotiṣṭoma;
yet there is no synonymy between the two words there,
because otherwise it would follow that the word *rājan* (king) is a synonym for the word *rājapuruṣa* (king's man).
For the *jyotiṣṭoma* is indeed a "stoma of lights" (*jyotiṣām stomaḥ*).

For this very reason, there is no denotative function for each [word] individually; rather, by the force of the context (*adhikāra*), one must accept that through the mention of a single part, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the entire word, and thus the identity of the cause and the denoted object is established. In the same way here as well, through the mention of a single part such as food (*anna*) or vital breath (*prāṇa*), and by means of the indication of words like "consisting of food" (*annamaya*), the identity of the words "food" and so forth with the terms "consisting of food" and so forth is to be accepted.
Having accepted the identity [of the meditations], the identity of their designations based upon that [identity] is admitted;
for, by the force of the use of the suffix *mayaṭ* in the place where [the object] is spoken of as being attained,
the sense is that it is not logical for one meditation to result in the attainment of another.
The term *annamaya* is the citation of the nominal stem alone.
The particle *iti* is used in the sense of "beginning with" and is connected to each [term].

Thus, because the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies that which is obtained from this [source], and by virtue of the lack of distinction among the words "food" (*anna*) and so forth—which share a single essential nature as causes—the Supreme Self alone is denoted by those words, such as "abounding in food" (*pracurānna*), on account of being the cause of such abundance.

However, the construction here is not that, having accepted a difference in the subject matter between the two sections (*anuvāka*), something other than Brahman—such as the sheaths consisting of the body and so forth—is taught in this [second] section.

For the first word "hi" is intended to indicate the logical principle that it is not proper to attain one thing through the knowledge of another. The second [word "hi"] indicates the well-known rule that when there is identity of the word, there must be identity of the cause, namely the object denoted. (3.391)

Thus, by means of two sūtras, it has been established that the pentad of terms beginning with *annamaya* denotes Īśvara, and that the suffix *mayaṭ* everywhere signifies abundance (*prācurya*). Now, establishing by another reason that the term *ānandamaya* denotes Viṣṇu and that the *mayaṭ* contained therein signifies abundance, he explains the sūtra "And because of the designation of that cause" (*taddhetuvyapadeśāt*) with the words:
"In the state of being Great Bliss (*mahānandatva*) alone..."
// Oṃ, and because its cause is designated, oṃ.//
And because of the designation of its cause:
"The cause of this very state of great bliss is itself; what else could it be?"—this is clear. (Manusmṛti 1.1.183cd)
... has been stated. // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.184a //

In the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the reason for Viṣṇu alone possessing great bliss is stated in the passage: "For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if there were not this bliss in the ether?
By this it is known that Viṣṇu alone is the referent of the term *ānandamaya*, and that the suffix *mayaṭ* here signifies abundance (*prācurya*).
For if the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) were other than Viṣṇu,
and if the suffix -maya denoted a modification (vikāra),
then the Śruti would have stated some reason for another being a modification of bliss.
The statement regarding the reason for Viṣṇu’s state of great bliss (*mahānanda*) is indeed inconsistent;
by this [statement],
it is implied that the word *tat* in this Sūtra is employed through *tantra* (simultaneous application) as both a genitive and a locative case ending.
Because it has been stated there that Viṣṇu is of the nature of great bliss (*mahānanda*).
Now, one might object: "In this context, it is merely stated that if space were not bliss, neither breathing nor living would be possible for anyone;
however, no reason whatsoever is given for Viṣṇu being of the nature of great bliss. To this, it is said: "Clearly" (*sphuṭam*). [Verse 3.392]
If it is asked how that is so:
it will be stated later that the word "ākāśa" refers to Viṣṇu, on the grounds of its characteristic marks—namely, "Ākāśa [is Brahman] because of its characteristic marks."

And thus, wishing to show that the Śruti—intending to demonstrate that if Viṣṇu were not blissful, the world would necessarily follow as being devoid of activity—intends "being the cause of the world's activity" as the logical reason, he first establishes the pervasion (vyāpti) of that [activity] by blissfulness, stating: "In another Śruti... etc.
... because in another Vedic text it is said: "Having obtained happiness, this person acts;
one who is not happy does not act. (Manu Smṛti 1.184a-c)
The phrase "because" (yasmāt) connects with what follows.
It is connected with the subsequent statement, "it is said in another Śruti," namely the Chandoga Śruti.

The meaning is that in another Śruti it is stated that the activity of the Supreme Lord is inseparable from bliss, as in: "When one indeed attains happiness, then one acts; one does not act having attained unhappiness; only having attained happiness does one act."
And regarding the fact that *pūrṇānanda* (complete bliss) alone is the primary meaning of the word *ānanda*, he cites scripture on this point as well: "The Infinite" (*bhūmā*).
... abundance is happiness; there can be no happiness in what is meager.
Thus it has been said... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.185a //

The meaning is that it has been stated in the *Chāndogya-śruti*—"That which is plenitude (*bhūman*) is bliss; there is no bliss in the limited"—that the primary denotation (*mukhyavṛtti*) of the word "bliss" is indeed full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*).
Although the word *bhūman* denotes a state (*bhāva*), according to the rule "the elision of *bahu* and *bhū* for *bahu*," it signifies the same as *bahu*.

Nevertheless, because the state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*bhavitṛ*) are one, it is said to be "full" (*bhūman*), meaning it is complete and not small; and because of its proximity, it is understood as being "easily.
... For its activity—such as dancing and singing—proceeds from pleasure, while weeping and so forth proceed from pain, and this is due to its being the agent of all. (Manu 1.1.185)
For one who possesses all power, there would be suffering... // MAnu 1.186a //
Here too, the connection is with the words "because" (*yasmāt*) and "if" (*yadi*).
Activity (*pravṛtti*) is fourfold; the remainder [of the definition] is that it arises from an excess of pleasure, an excess of pain, attachment to pleasure, and aversion.
He provides an illustration of activity arising from an abundance of pleasure with the word "nṛtta" (dancing).
The word "of the insane" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He illustrates activity arising from the intensity of suffering with the words: "from suffering."
Some say that pleasure, pain, and the attachment and aversion toward their means are themselves the motivators, as it has been stated: "The defects have the characteristic of motivating.
It is for the purpose of refuting this that the word "only" (eva) is used.
"From pleasure alone, or from pain alone"—
for there is no continuity of thought in one who is insane,
by which he might, out of attachment to pleasure, reflect "this is the means to that" and proceed toward dancing and the like.
Rather, it is simply the intensification of pleasure that serves as the cause for its engagement;
nor is there any consideration that suffering—even for a hell-being who hates it—is the cause for avoiding it, such as through weeping and so forth.
On the contrary, it is established by experience that the mere intensity of suffering itself is the cause in that case.

The engagement in eating and so forth for the sake of attaining pleasure due to attachment to pleasure, and the engagement in removing thorns and so forth for the sake of avoiding it due to aversion to pain, are well-known; therefore, they have not been cited [as examples].
What follows from this? If it is the case that the activity associated with a conscious agent is of four kinds, he says: "Because of being the agent of everything."
The word "and" implies "the non-attainment of happiness.

Therefore, the meaning is that these three types of activity—motivated by the intensification of suffering, for the sake of its cessation, and for the sake of attaining happiness—are not possible in the Supreme Lord.
To the question "Even so, why [is He inactive]? he says: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).
... therefore, he is the impeller solely through his divine play. // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.186bc //

Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is established that the Lord, being the instigator, must act solely out of sport (*līlā*) and from an abundance of bliss (*ānanda*); thus, the inseparable connection between the Supreme Lord's activity and perfect bliss is proven.
Having thus stated the introductory context (*upodghāta*), he states the formal argument (*prayoga*): "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Since the inseparable connection with perfect bliss (*pūrṇānanda*) is thus established through the activity of the Supreme Lord, it follows that this impeller must be endowed with perfect bliss by virtue of his mere sport (*līlā*). Herein lies the formal argument (*prayoga*): [The formal argument: The Supreme Lord is endowed with perfect bliss, because he is an impeller [who acts] solely out of sport. Just as, for example, a person who acts out of mere play is endowed with pleasure. Therefore, the conclusion is established.
The Lord ought to be happy;
for, while being devoid of the three causes of activity, he possesses activity, like a madman.
Furthermore, since the cause must correspond to its effect, through this great activity, great bliss alone is established.
And if he were not to breathe, who else would be a person? (Manu 1.186cd)
Having thus explained the reason established by the intention of the scripture, he elucidates the scriptural refutation for the contrary case with the words "na cet" (if not).

This Supreme Self is called *ākāśa* because it shines (*kāśana*) everywhere; it is full bliss. If this were not so, then, due to the absence of any other cause, nothing at all would proceed. If this did not impel anything, then what person would breathe, or what else would exist?
No one whatsoever would engage in worldly or Vedic activity.

The phrase "due to the absence of independence" is to be supplied. The aphorism, "And it is sung as being precisely that which is described by the words of the mantra," is intended to establish that even the five [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) are the Supreme Brahman, by means of another logical argument. *3,398* Oṃ. ...is observed. // MAnu 1.188a //

Therefore, the [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya) are the Supreme Brahman.
This might be so if even the wording of the mantra were to have the Supreme Brahman as its object;

Since that [term "Brahma-knowing"] can also occur in other senses through a secondary application, and as for how the subsequent text serves to elaborate upon the meaning indicated by the words of the mantra, he provides an introduction in order to explain the meaning of the Sūtra, beginning with the words: "The knower of Brahman."

In the first sentence of the section beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," it is indicated that it is indeed the Supreme Brahman [that is meant], because of the hearing of the word "Supreme" (para) and because of the statement that knowledge of It is the cause of liberation.

And that very [Brahman] is characterized by the words of the mantra as "truth, knowledge, infinite," and is established as being endowed with unique attributes such that it is neither finite nor infinite; therefore, it is the supreme Brahman described by the words of the mantra. For when it is said, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," three doubts arise: what are the characteristics of that Brahman? What is its nature? What is its form? And how is it attained? It is precisely this [Brahman] that is indicated by the mantra. Thus, the doubt regarding the characteristic of Brahman is resolved. As for the doubt concerning its nature, it is stated: "From whom words, along with the mind, turn back. Since it is impossible for the mind and speech to reach the nature of Brahman, it is concluded that Brahman is of an inconceivable nature. Since it is impossible for the light of Brahman to be reached by the light of the sun or other luminaries, it is concluded that Brahman is attained through the light of knowledge alone. Thus, the doubt concerning the characteristic of Brahman has been dispelled. Now, the doubt concerning its nature is being considered. Is Brahman of a sentient nature or of an insentient nature? For indeed, without its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), a thing cannot be known as being distinct from everything else. And how is that [Brahman] known? Is it by accepting that the perceived form is superimposed, such that one thinks "I am that," or otherwise?
Brahman is perceived as complete (*pūrṇa*).
Furthermore, such a direct realization is not possible for us;
what, indeed, could be its attainment that is to be accomplished by knowledge?
For it is eternally attained due to its omnipresence.
To avoid that [objection], the Śruti cites the wording of a mantra:
"With regard to this, this [verse] was spoken.
This means that with respect to those three aforementioned doubts, it is stated as a means of resolving them.
The meaning is that this *ṛc* is being stated.
In that regard, it is the answer to the inquiry concerning the definition [of Brahman] as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
And each of these is a defining characteristic.

Because truthfulness and the other qualities are non-deviant in the manner that will be explained, the distress of opponents— who, having accepted the definition as a whole, seek to investigate the function of each qualifier— is thereby dispelled. The phrase "he who knows" is the answer to the second objection.

Although its magnitude is complete, it manifests itself as having a small magnitude through the power of its own capacity and out of compassion for devotees; it should be known as residing in the cave of the heart as the impeller of all living beings and their instrumental and material causes.
Thus, the phrase "he enjoys" (so 'śnute) is the answer to the third doubt.
His attainment [of Brahman] is not merely a physical conjunction.
Nor is there an attainment of identity and so forth;

rather, in the place of that individual manifestation, there is simply the manifestation of its similarity to [the Brahman] characterized by "desiring the true" (*satyakāmatva*) and other qualities, while remaining absolutely distinct from it.

Let it be so: since the meaning indicated by the first sentence is the Supreme Brahman, the Vedic verse (*mantravarṇa*) intended to dispel the doubt arising therefrom must also have that as its purport.
Nevertheless, as to what is the subject at hand, he explains the meaning of the Sūtra with the word "therein" (tatra).
In that regard, the truthfulness of both the creation and the food and vital breath has been stated;
furthermore, knowledge has been proclaimed through both the mind and higher discernment. (Manu 1.188)
Likewise, its infinity has also been declared by the term "consisting of bliss."
In that regard, the reality of the characteristics [of the elements] is established by the section on creation, namely, "From this very Self, space was produced," and "This person, indeed,
consists of the essence of food."

Thus, it has been stated through the two contexts of food and vital breath— namely, "from this very one consisting of the essence of food" (*annarasamaya*) and "from this very one consisting of vital breath" (*prāṇamaya*)—
that knowledge, which is the defining characteristic of Brahman, is attained by means of the mind.
"From that very one consisting of breath," and so forth, by means of the section concerning the one consisting of mind,
and also by means of consciousness.
“From this very one consisting of mind,” and so forth; this has also been declared in the section concerning that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).
The word *tathā* (likewise) is used for conjunction.
Infinite extent (*anantatva*) is also a defining characteristic of Brahman, according to the passage concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*):
"From this, indeed, which consists of consciousness... (*tasmād vā etasmād vijñānamayāt*).
By the phrase "by this section on the one consisting of bliss" (*ityādinānandamayaprakaraṇena*),
it is indicated that [the Supreme] has also been cited by the subsequent sentences.
Therefore, since all six of the following sections are expositions of the definition of the Supreme Brahman as described in the words of the mantra, [it is the Supreme].
The meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman alone is the Annamaya and the others.
It was stated that its reality is taught through the context of creation;
to the question "How so?", he says: "the state of being existent."
Because it conveys the state of being as it truly is, that is called truth.
Thus has the creation here been described...
The word "sat" (existent) denotes existence;
for there is a scriptural statement that this term "sat" is employed in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness.
"Existence" (*sadbhāva*) means birth;
by the word "existence," procreation is indicated.

Thus, since the word *sat* denotes birth, when it is used as an object (*karman*), the root *yā* (to go) has the sense of causing to go (*ṇyartha*) implied within it. By applying the suffix *ka* according to the rule *ato 'nupasarge kaḥ*, and then [applying] the rule *ayasmayādīni chandasi* to the object [of the compound],...

When the notion of "being" (sat-saṃjñā) exists, it becomes "truth" (satyam). Therefore, because it causes all that is distinct from itself to attain birth—that is, to reach the state of being—it is called "Brahman, the Truth.
Thus, keeping in mind that the meaning of the word "truth" is its being the cause of the birth of the entire universe, [the text speaks] of the Self.
The meaning is that in this section, the creation beginning with "From [the Self] ether," etc., has been declared by scripture.
Let it be granted that being the creator of the world is the meaning of the word *satya*;
nevertheless, it is not logical to claim that the section on creation beginning with "From [the Self] ether" is an explanation of that [word].
Because there is an absence of an explanation of the meaning of the individual parts and so forth, he says: "The world... and so on.
...Brahman is indeed established as that which pervades the true existence of the world. // MAnu 1.190bc //

The creation has been described solely for the purpose of establishing that reality which was referred to by the word "Truth" (satya)—namely, Brahman as the pervader of the existence of the universe—and not for the purpose of explaining its etymological components or similar matters.
What is meant is this:
an explanation does not consist merely in the description of etymological parts and so forth.
However, even that which was stated as a formal position [is relevant here].

And in the present context, when the definition "Brahman is Truth" has been stated, one might raise the objection that this is impossible because the five great elements alone are the cause of the origin and so forth of the world; [in response to this], it is held that Brahman alone is the cause even of the great elements, being contained within them.

Since that which bestows existence and so forth is Brahman alone, and therefore Brahman is the progenitor of the world, its establishment is carried out by the passage beginning with "Space is the self" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.1.2); thus, this constitutes its exposition.
It has been stated that the section concerning the "consisting of food" (annamaya) is the meaning of the word "Reality" (satya); to the question "How so?", he says: "Existence" (sattvam).
... as well as the vital essence and life itself.
Decay is the state of being worn out; that which is bent, they indeed call *sanna*.

Not only birth alone is the meaning of the word *sat*, but life as well—characterized by the maintenance of vital breath—is indeed *sattva* (existence), which is the very ground for the application of the word *sat*.
This is because when it is said, "Devadatta exists," the understanding arises that he is living.
Furthermore, disintegration is characterized by looseness.
Existence (*sattva*) would be the ground for the application of the word "existent" (*sat*).
Why?
Because they say that a disintegrated object is "existent" (*sannam*).
The word *eva* indicates that this usage is indeed primary, based on the grammatical rule stating that the root *ṣad* is used in the senses of "sitting," "perishing," "going," and "fading away.
