Thus, the form *sad* is derived either from the root *ās* with the suffix *śatṛ*, or from the root *sad* with the suffix *kvip*.
Furthermore, this term emphasizes the state of being (*bhāva*).
That which causes the existence, life, or non-destruction of beings to endure is called "truth" (satya).
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "Therefore... (ataḥ).
Therefore, indeed, the very meaning of the word "truth" (satya) is the state of being free from hunger and thirst.
Since it is thus established that being the cause of the destruction of the life-force of all beings is what is expressed by the word "truth" (satya),
therefore the very meaning of the word "truth" constitutes "food-ness," which is the ground for the application of the word "food" (anna).
How so?
For it is because [the Self] is characterized by being the object of dependence (*upajīvyatva*) and characterized by being the destroyer (*vināśakatva*).
And it has been stated that the meaning of the word "Truth" (*satya*) is the section concerning the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "The breath... (*prāṇam*).
The gods breathe after the vital breath, as do humans and animals;
for the vital breath is the life-span of all beings—that which constitutes their movement and their living.

When "sat" is uttered, it signifies the root-meaning of "to go"; therefore, truthfulness is indeed the state of being real (satyatā), while the state of being living (prāṇatva) is... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.1.193a-c]
The gods and others breathe—that is, they move—following the Prāṇa, the Supreme Self, by its impulsion.

That Prāṇa is the Supreme Self, the cause of the life and longevity of all; therefore, it is called "Prāṇa. This is stated in the mantra according to the etymological meaning of the word *prāṇa* as "that by which all beings breathe or live," signifying that it bestows movement and life upon all beings.
Since "sat" is the meaning of the verbal root,
and "going" and "living" are also meanings of the verbal root— by forming [the word] from those two roots with the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvip*, respectively— the form "sat" arises.

Intending that [the root *as*] has existence (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning, the word *satya* (truth) also expresses the quality of bestowing movement or life upon beings, insofar as it causes their existence, movement, or life to proceed.
Therefore, it should be explained that truthfulness (*satyatā*) is the state of being breath (*prāṇatva*), and thus the words *satya* and *prāṇa* have the same meaning.
By this detailed exposition of the meaning of the word *satya* within the context of the *annamaya* and *prāṇamaya* sections, it is implied that it is explained therein.
It has been stated that the meaning of the word "knowledge" (jñāna) refers to the section concerning the mind-made (manomaya).
To the question "How so?", he says: "for the purpose of comprehension."
The element *man* is proclaimed to have the meaning of "understanding. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.1.193c–d)
The term *manu* is proclaimed to mean "awakening" (*avabodhana*), which constitutes a contradiction [with its usual sense].
Consequently, when the suffix *-asun* is applied to that [root] to form the state [of being], both *manaḥ* and *jñānam* come to have the same meaning.

Since it is perfectly clear that the word *jñāna* is the intended meaning within the context of the section concerning that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), it has not been elaborated upon further.

In this context, when the definition "Brahman is knowledge" (*jñāna*) has been stated, there might arise the suspicion that this is not a valid definition because it applies to all conscious beings (*cetana*). To address this, it is explained through these two sections that what is intended here by "knowledge" is not mere cognition (*avabodha-mātra*), but rather that which has as its object the general and specific forms of all things; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition.
Furthermore, it has been stated that the quality of infinity (*anantatva*) is explained by means of the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Not small."

By the very statement that "there is no happiness in the small," the nature of being composed of bliss (*ānandamaya*) has been declared; thus, its infinitude is well-established, for perfect bliss does not reside in what is limited. This commentary on the section concerning the one composed of bliss is characterized by its focus on the etymological definition of the term "infinite" (*ananta*).

What is meant is this: when there is a doubt regarding the impossibility of the characteristic of infinity, the state of consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatā*) is stated to firmly establish and demonstrate that infinity;
[the point being] that the Supreme Lord is infinite because He is full bliss.
But one might object: since the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans is not observed anywhere else, how can this be established?
Not so;
for by the scriptural statement "there is no happiness in the small," it is determined that complete bliss does not exist in that which is small and finite.
The meaning is that there exists a negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*).
[Objection: But surely, like infinity, full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*) is also unestablished.
[Reply: True;
for this very reason, the Śruti establishes it through such passages as "Who indeed could breathe otherwise? (*ko hyevānyāt*).
And this has been stated by the words "consisting of infinite space.
He concludes the meaning of the Sūtra with the word "therefore" (ataḥ).
"For this reason, the expansion mentioned in the words of the Mantras is performed by means of the entire supreme [Vidyā], because... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.1.195a-c).
"For this reason" (*ataḥ*) means in the manner already stated.
The word "hi" (for) indicates well-known fact, while the word "tu" (but) serves as a restriction. [The phrase] "by the subsequent scriptural statement" means by the mantra-text that follows.
Therefore, the connection with the preceding [sentence] is: "Therefore, Viṣṇu alone is denoted by the words 'consisting of food' and so forth. *3,412*

Having thus established his own position through such sūtras as "Likewise, [the Self] consists of bliss because of repetition," etc., he provides the following sūtra for the purpose of refuting the opposing position: "Not the other, because of impossibility. Oṃ, not the other, because of impossibility, Oṃ.
"Not the other, because it is not possible.
Therein, he explains the part of the proposition: "the other."
...the other [matter] is not discussed here.

Neither the individual soul (*jīva*), nor the sheath consisting of the body (*śarīra-kośa*), nor primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is mentioned here in this section concerning the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth.
Why?
Because such [entities] are untenable in this context.
All food indeed comes to those who venerate food as Brahman;
they attain a full span of life.

The meaning is that liberation is understood to result from the knowledge of the [self] consisting of food and so forth, by means of such passages as "those who worship the vital breath (prāṇa) as Brahman";

for if the words "consisting of food" and so on were denotative of the individual soul (jīva) and the like, such [liberation] would be untenable. To the question "Why is it untenable?", he says: "the Person (puruṣam)."
"He who knows the Puruṣa is liberated; indeed, no other path exists"—according to this Vedic revelation, how can one who knows anything else attain liberation?
By this, he indicates the Vedic scripture: "One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journey."
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that 'Him' (tam) is mentioned here, and not Viṣṇu?
Not so;
for, intending to show that the word 'Him' refers back to the Puruṣa under discussion in passages such as "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads," it was stated: "the Puruṣa."
Because of hearing the word "yat" (which), it should be understood as "sa" (he);
[the form] "mucyet" means "mucyeta," according to the rule that "transpositions occur frequently."
There is another path to liberation than the knowledge of the Supreme Person; the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that this is well-known from the Śruti.

Now, let it be granted that liberation arises from the knowledge of the Puruṣa; but if the Puruṣa is something other [than the self], why is there no liberation from the knowledge of another? To this, he says: "The Puruṣa."
The Supreme Person, the Self-born, Brahman, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Great Bliss, Viṣṇu, Bharga, and Om— thus is He proclaimed.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself [is the possessor of these names], and not anyone else; that is, by his own primary function,
these are his names.
Why is this so? Precisely because these [names] belong to Viṣṇu, those who perform sacrifices, give gifts, and so forth while intending for Viṣṇu must utter "Oṃ";
otherwise, that would not be the case.
For it is not possible that those performing an action intended for one [deity] should mutter a mantra whose referent is another.
He states the reasoning for the word *puruṣa* denoting Viṣṇu with the words "by the hymn" (*sūktena*).
"Those who are proficient in the knowledge of the supreme self worship him with this Puruṣasūkta," so says the Paiṅgi-Śruti; therefore, one is not liberated through the knowledge of anything else.
"Those who worship this Nārāyaṇa worship Him with the Puruṣasūkta;
by that it is known that the word 'Puruṣa' denotes Viṣṇu.
Thus the Paiṅgi-śruti declares that the word 'Puruṣa' has the Blessed Lord as its sole referent, because [in the passage] "knowing Him thus," that very one is Viṣṇu. (3.414)
Surely, the same inconsistency applies to the acceptance of Īśvara as it does to the acceptance of anything else.

For instance, in the passage "From herbs comes food, from food the person," the body—which is a modification of food and an effect of herbs—is denoted by the word *puruṣa*. Then, referring back to that with the words "This very person," it is described as "consisting of the essence of food" (*annarasamaya*).
Since it is impossible for that [individual self] to be the Lord,

and since the layers consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya) and so forth fall within its stream, he constructs a foundational framework (pīṭhikā) to dispel this doubt, stating: "designated by the word Brahman."
Having applied the word "Self" (ātman) to that which is denoted by the word "Brahman," he then declared here the fourfold creation of space.

"One who knows Brahman attains the Supreme"; "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite"—thus it should be construed that the word *brahman* is applied to Viṣṇu, who is denoted by that term; and the word *ātman* is also employed [in the passage] "from this very Self" (*tasmād vā etasmād ātmanaḥ*), because of the connection with the phrase "from this very one" (*tasmād etasmāt*).
And by the statement "the ether was produced" (*ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*), he taught the creation of space;

by the phrase "and having employed the word 'Self' (*ātman*) in this section, he taught the creation," he indicates that the nature of being the Self (*ātmatva*) is also intended as a prescribed attribute.
The fourfold nature of creation is due to its connection with the four kinds of space,
not inherently;
for a threefold nature will be stated later.
And thus, the meaning is that he has also taught the fourfold creation of space.
To the question of how there is a fourfold nature of space, he says: "The element... [Verse 3.415]:
"The element, the presiding deity of the element, its body, and the internal controller."
Hari is denoted by the word "space," yet primarily it is Hari alone [who is so designated].
That which shines everywhere as space is, in its primary sense, Hari.
The connection is that [the element] "earth" is what is expressed by the word "space," and so forth.
Among these three, there is an internal regulator.
Furthermore, he says "primarily" to show that all four do not possess the status of being denoted by the word "space" with equal standing.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but).
To the question "How so?", he says: "āsamantāt" (all around).
The word "ā" (in the etymology of *ākāśa*) is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*), for the meaning of the term *ākāśa* is "shining all around" (*samantāt-kāśanam*).
Therefore, since Hari alone shines primarily all around, it should be understood that He alone is primarily *ākāśa*.
Thus, by distinguishing between the primary and secondary [meanings], he declared the creation of the fourfold wind from the fourfold *ākāśa*, according to the manner previously described.
In that context as well, it should be understood (or stated) that by the word "wind" (vāyu), Hari alone is primarily denoted.
To the question "How so?", he says: "By [the word] 'power' (bala)."
Because its essential nature consists of power and knowledge, Vāyu... // MAnu 1.1.202cd //
The word *vaśa* signifies power;
"life" (*āyuḥ*) refers to knowledge,
because the root *ay-* has the sense of "going."

Since roots meaning "to go" have the sense of "to know," and likewise [the scripture] declares the creation of the fourfold fire from the fourfold wind with the words "from air, fire," it is established that in that context as well, Hari alone is primarily denoted by the word "fire. To the question "How so? he says: "Fire... (*3,417*)
... Agni, leading the goat. (Manu 1.202d)
The universe is called *aga* because it does not go (*na gacchati*) by itself and does not proceed (*na pravartate*).
In the word *aga*, the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *nī* with the object *aga* as an attendant word (*upapada*).

Due to the grammatical rule governing that formation, there is the elision of the attendant word and the shortening of the vowel of the root, as this is a case of etymological derivation (*nirvacana*).
Thereafter, with the words "from fire, water," he taught the creation of four kinds of water from four kinds of fire.
In that context, it must be stated that by the term "water" (āpaḥ), Hari alone is primarily intended. To the question "How so? he says: "Water."
...and because they protect [the people] from water... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.203a //
This is the form of the root *pat* preceded by the prefix *ā*;
the shortening of the prefix and the elision of the verbal root occur because it is a formal etymological derivation (*nirvacana*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.
By this it is stated that because [the source] has the form of a woman, it is in the feminine gender, and because it has many forms, it is in the plural number.
The word "eva" (only/verily) is connected with "Hari" alone.
Thus, he declared the creation of the fourfold earth from the fourfold waters.
In that regard, since it has been established that Hari alone is primarily denoted by the word "earth," he demonstrates this with the verse beginning "pṛthivī."
... from which the earth is spread out.
The etymological connection is that she is called "Pṛthivī" because she is spread out (*pṛthita*) here and there;
the root *pṛthu* means "to expand.
Thus, he proclaimed the creation of the fourfold herbs from the fourfold earth, as in the passage: "From the earth, the herbs [arose]."
Since the primary elements (*bhūta*) have already been completed, the mention of the derivative elements (*bhautika*) follows next; this is what remains to be done.
Furthermore, since it is established that by the word "herbs" (*oṣadhi*) Hari alone is primarily intended, [the author] asks "Why? and answers with the words "of those that dwell" (*uṣyānām*).
Because it serves as the substratum for the plants, that very [earth] is named "uṣadhī" (the herb-bearing).
Of those that have been burnt.
*Uṣya* [is derived from] *uṣ*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The meaning of *oṣadhi* is "that in which the burning (*oṣa*) is placed."
The suffix *kip* is applied according to the rule "after a verbal root denoting action, when the locus [of the action] is expressed.
To the question, "How can that which is contained within the medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*) be the substratum (*āśraya*) of the heating (*oṣya*)? he says: "It resides in the medicinal herbs."

Viṣṇu resides in the medicinal herbs; he is resorted to by those who are hungry. [This means] by those whose hunger is not satisfied by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*). He has declared that food comes from medicinal herbs—that is, the creation of the four kinds of food proceeds from the four kinds of medicinal herbs.

In that context as well, the word "food" (anna) is primarily applied to Viṣṇu alone; since it has already been established previously that the etymological explanation—"it is eaten and it eats"—is possible only with reference to Him, it was not stated here.

Thereafter, from the phrase "from that food, the person," he declared the creation of the threefold person—consisting of the body, the ego identifying with it, and the inner controller—from the fourfold food.
Since it is established that even there, by the word "puruṣa," Hari alone is primarily intended, [the author] asks, "How so? and replies with the word "purī" (city).
Because he lies within the city (puri), he is therefore celebrated as Puruṣa.
Now, from that [root]:
*puri* means in the body (*śarīra*). Here, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending of the secondary member (*upapada*).
The vowel *i* of that [root] becomes *u*;
the letter *ś* of the verbal root becomes *ṣ* due to the rules of etymological derivation (*nirvacana*). The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *śī* when it denotes a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Having thus explained the words "self" (ātman) and so forth, he describes their creation with the verse beginning with "kriyā."
The manifestation of Hari as the initiator of activity is his birth;
for there is no other [birth] in ether and the other elements, since the presiding deities possess self-conceit (abhimāna).
The manifestation of the body of the conceited one and of that which has become manifest.
To the question, "Why should it not be actual birth itself?", he says: "Not another," etc.
The word "hi" indicates the well-known scriptural authority of such passages as "He is the eternal among the eternals.
"Abhimāna" is the cognition that "this is mine.
"Janis" refers to the relationship [of ownership].
The term "of that which has come into being" (*bhūtasya*) is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood to include material things such as plants and so forth.
The grammatical connection is that "birth" (*janir*) refers specifically to direct manifestation.

If this is so, and since Hari alone is primarily denoted by the terms *ātman*, *ākāśa*, *vāyu*, *agni*, *ap*, *pṛthivī*, *oṣadhī*, *anna*, and *puruṣa*, while everything else is denoted non-primarily, what is the relevance to the present context? To this, he says:
Thus:
"In this way, [one should know] Hari alone, who has come down even unto the body and so forth. (Manu 1.1.206cd)
In order to understand that very [Self] as having five forms,
the Śruti says, "He indeed is this," after having discarded everything beginning with the elements.
In this context, the word "ātman" (self) is to be supplied before the word "deha" (body).

The Śruti text, "That indeed is this person," having set aside everything previously mentioned—beginning with the elements and ending with the body—refers back by those very words to Hari himself as the subject under discussion.
This is for the purpose of making known that the Creator possesses five forms, beginning with the *annamaya* (consisting of food), within His own body.
This is what is meant:
there is no contradiction with the reference "He, indeed, is this person" if one accepts that the [sheaths] beginning with the *annamaya* are the supreme Brahman;
for it is accepted that this reference refers to that which is denoted by the word "Self."
Nor is it the case that this [Self] is not the Supreme Brahman;
for, based on the context, it is understood that the Self—characterized by truth, knowledge, and infinity—is the very one described as that which must be known by one desiring to attain the Supreme.
Furthermore, it should not be argued that it is improper to set aside the reference to what is immediately proximate in favor of accepting a reference to something remote and previously mentioned.
For it is accepted that even by all terms beginning with "Self" and ending with "Puruṣa," it is precisely that [Brahman] which is the subject under discussion;
nor is the origination of the Lord unproduced,
since it is explained in reference to his manifestation (*prādurbhāva*).
Nor is this explanation lacking in authority,
for it will be established that [the elements] act as causes;
nor does it follow that the creation of the bhūtas and so forth would thereby become unauthoritative.

This is because words such as "ākāśa" and others are admitted to refer to the primary elements (*bhūta*) and so forth, and because their polysemous nature will be demonstrated later. Furthermore, it does not follow that these [words] would also result in denoting mere manifestation.
Since the word *sambhava*, heard in a general sense, can be explained appropriately according to the context,
there is no such consequence that the one consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) would attain the status of being the Self of all as previously introduced.
This is because, even though elements and so forth were introduced, we accept that the reference (*parāmarśa*) pertains to Hari alone, by setting aside those other elements.
Nor is this unreasonable;

for since words such as "space" (ākāśa) and so forth have their primary meaning in Hari alone, He alone is brought to mind with particular intensity. Furthermore, the reference to the Lord (Īśvara) is not purposeless.
This is because [the subsequent section] begins as a new chapter for the purpose of making known that very [Self] possesses five forms, beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya);
and because it has already been stated that its utility lies in explaining its defining characteristics.

Thus, since there is no logical inconsistency in the "consisting of food" being Brahman, one should not assume that those following in its series—the "consisting of vital breath" (prāṇamaya) and so on—are not Brahman. *3,426*
Now, one might ask: what is the use of this elaborate arrangement?
Could this not simply be a reference to the body alone?
Not so.
If that were so, since the person would be complete by the mere statement "this [is] the person," the word "he" (sa) would become redundant.
If it is argued that this is equally true in your own position as well, we say no; with this intention, he says: "He."
Having designated the word "Self" as "he," this [Self] resides within the body of the living being.
The word "this" refers to that which resides within the body of the individual soul (*jīva*).
If it were said merely "residing in the body," it might be understood as referring to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) possessing a body;
therefore, the word "individual soul" (*jīva*) is used.
Furthermore, regarding the reference to the body, one should have simply said, "This person consists of food" (*annamaya*);
the word "essence" (*rasa*), however, is redundant,
as no purpose for its inclusion is perceived.
Furthermore, because "the person [arises] from food" is the subject under discussion;
nor is the word *rasa* redundant even in our view.
For if it were merely said "consisting of food" (*annamaya*), one might understand it as consisting of ordinary, physical food.
Intending to show that [the definition] is meaningful because it serves to exclude those [other categories], he says: "It is 'sāra'..."
This Lord consists of the essence of food alone; He does not consist of the worlds of food.
Thus, he specifies that [essence] which resides in the body by means of the word "rasa" (taste/essence).
For the word *rasa* denotes "essence" (*sāra*),
according to the statement that the words *rasa*, *sāra*, and *vara* are synonymous. Consequently, *annarasa* means the essence of food (*annasāra*).
Among the meanings of the word *anna*, its primary meaning is characterized by being the eater and so forth; thus it is said to be "abundant" in that sense.
Its intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) is that it consists essentially of food (*sārānnamaya*).
The word "iti" (thus) is used to indicate that this is what remains to be understood;
the Śruti qualifies [the subject],
and furthermore:

If this [meditation] were merely a tactile perception of the body, then the teachings that "this is its head," "this is the right wing," "this is the left wing," "this is the trunk," and "this is the tail, the support," would all be entirely useless;
for since the body, head, and so forth are established through direct perception, they would not require such instruction.
But surely, the same lack of logical consistency applies to the case of the Lord (Īśvara) as well.
This is because it lacks parts such as a head and so forth; no, for it will be stated later that "it is like light";
nevertheless, there remains an inconsistency.

If it is argued that because [objects] such as the head of Īśvara are not perceptible, they cannot be designated as "this," we say no; for this is possible through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). With this intention, he says: "This."
The designation "this" refers to the All-pervading Lord as if He were clothed in a garment.
The living soul (jīva) arises from the head and so forth, because it is established in the head and so forth.

The designation "this" (*idam*) can indeed occur through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even with respect to the head and so forth of the Supreme Lord, though they are not directly perceived, because the head and other parts of the omnipresent Lord are established [as being present] in the head and other parts of the individual soul (*jīva*), which are directly perceived; thus he shows the relationship that serves as the seed for figurative indication. Now, one who employs a figurative usage while abandoning the primary usage must state its purpose.

If it is argued that, for instance, in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," the cognition of sanctity and so forth is indeed observed [to arise], we say no; because in the present case, there is a conventional (rūḍha) indication (lakṣaṇā). With this intention, it was stated: "like one covered by a garment."
The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*).

The meaning is as follows: just as even when the knee is not directly perceived, if it is covered by a visible cloth, one points to it as "this" due to the proximity of the visible cloth, so it is in the present case as well.
If it is objected: "Since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) of the primary meaning, why resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?", we say: no.
Because the futility of grasping at a body is evident;
furthermore, it is heard in scripture that liberation comes from the knowledge of the "consisting of breath" (prāṇamaya), which leads to the exhaustion of one's entire lifespan.
Indeed, the absence of death at any time constitutes the full span of life;
and this is not possible without liberation,
nor is it possible while maintaining the appropriation of a body.
He says "him" (tam), because [the statement] "one who knows him thus" (tamevaṃvidvān), and so forth, would otherwise contradict the Śruti.
Upon knowing that, one's liberation shall occur; it cannot happen through the knowledge of anything else in any way.
"Having known that Supreme Self, one sees it directly"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
By this, there is identity of the agent (samānakartṛtā).
Furthermore, words such as "Brahman" should also be stated here as contradictories [of the opponent's position].

Now, when the author of the Sūtras, by stating "on account of the word denoting a modification" (*vikāraśabdāt*), resolved one inconsistency regarding the status of *annamaya* and the others as Brahman, he thereby indicated that all inconsistencies could be resolved through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya provided the resolution of those inconsistencies in that very same place, stating, "In this context, the state of being an object of enjoyment and the state of being food [are not primary meanings]," and so forth.
Furthermore, it would have been more appropriate to place such arguments as "designated by the word *brahman*" in that very same location.
"Because there is no reason for an intervention;
otherwise, it would follow that [the teaching] deviates from the sūtra.
This is not so.
Even for a meaning indicated by that sūtra, there exists a purpose despite the intervention [of other topics].
Here, the fallacious arguments (upapattyābhāsas) that establish the non-Brahman nature of all five—beginning with *annamaya*—are refuted;
however, it is made known by the words "but here" (*atretinā*) that the resolution of the impossibility regarding *annamaya* alone is intended.

Furthermore, regarding the sūtra "And it is not the other, because of the impossibility [of the attributes]," some explain that the self consisting of food (*annamaya*) is not the supreme Self because the reference to the supreme and so forth would be impossible; this too is stated here in order to refute that view. To this, he says:

The individual soul (jīva) alone is the referent of the terms "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth. For it is called "consisting of food" because it is delimited by a body that is a modification of food;
and it is likewise delimited by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss, becoming a modification of those—just as space within a jar is a modification of the jar.
By this, its nature as consisting of breath and so forth is established.

And thus, the reference "this very person" (sa vā eṣa puruṣaḥ) becomes more appropriately connected when understood as referring to that [self] as having those [breaths] as its limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Furthermore, the word "essence" (rasa) will serve to exclude the grossest portion residing in food.

Furthermore, the designation "this" (idam) attains its primary meaning in all cases beginning with the *prāṇamaya*, because it is logical to mention even that which is already established as being predominant in a context where limbs such as the head and so forth are to be described.
Thus, [the soul's] possession of a body, its state as a whole possessing parts, its connection with pleasure and the like, and its having Brahman as its tail—all this becomes consistent.
Nor should it be asked: "Why then are the sheaths consisting of the body and so forth not accepted?"

Furthermore, this would be in accordance with another Vedic text which says, "May my self consisting of food, the self consisting of vital breath, the self consisting of mind, the self consisting of consciousness, and the self consisting of bliss be purified. Since the term "Brahman" and so forth are not applicable to the sheaths (*kośa*s), [the terms] "otherness," "interiority," and "being the body" are possible even for the individual soul (*jīva*) when considered in relation to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). (3.4.34)
But surely there is an inconsistency even in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*).
For the word "Brahman" cannot be established without the Supreme Self as its substratum, [as it is defined] by the etymology:
"it is eaten and it eats."

The state of being the first of all and the devourer of all; the fact that He is the object of worship for all the gods and others, as in "the gods [worship] Prāṇa"; the fact that He is beyond the reach of speech and mind, as in "from whom words turn back"; and [the state of being] consciousness, as in "the gods [worship] Vijñāna."

Thus, being worshipped by all the gods, being the eldest, being the creator of all preceded by the volition "He desired," and being the inner self of all— these and other such qualities cannot possibly belong to the individual soul (jīva), which is endowed with only limited knowledge, power, and so forth; furthermore,
the designation of Him as the cause [of the world] would be inconsistent.
Furthermore, the explanation based on the wording of the mantras would be contradicted;
nor is liberation possible through the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva).
This is not so.
This is due to a failure to understand the meaning of the Upaniṣads;
for here, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is intended.
Among those [scriptural] statements, those that appear to contradict [this identity] refer to the nature of the transmigrating soul as conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
However, terms such as "Brahman" refer to the essential nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is established by its own inherent character.
Furthermore, the intention here to express identity is understood precisely because the syntactical unity of the passage would otherwise be inexplicable.
Nor is there any lack of grounds for this determination; thus, it is the Supreme Self alone that is denoted by the terms beginning with "consisting of food" (annamaya).
The very nature of the great space (mahākāśa) is what is conventionally designated as the limited space; as it is said:
"As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart.
However, the property of being limited to a span (vitasti-mātratva) does not belong to the great space.
Nor is it untenable that "Brahman is the tail, the support";
for the meaning is logically consistent: Brahman is the tail—the abode, the foundation, and the innate essential nature—of this individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, "it is not the other."
In order to dispel the doubt that this is untenable, there is the sūtra: "And because of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśāt*).
*3,436* // Oṃ, and because of the designation of difference, Oṃ.
And because of the designation of difference:
"Because of the teaching of difference, stating 'this [is] in the sun and in the person,' there is no non-difference of this [Self] with the individual soul (jīva)... (Māṇḍūkya Āraṇyaka 1.1.211a–c).
And with the intention that the word "ca" (and) there has the sense of a conjunction of propositions, he explains the Sūtra: "The sun... and so forth.
This might be so in some way,
if the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman) were intended to be expressed in this Upaniṣad;
but it is not so.

"‘That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun, that is one’"—since in this passage the distinction between the individual souls (all those designated by the terms ‘person’ and ‘sun,’ both inferior and superior) as the objects of governance and the locus, and the Supreme Self as the governor and the presiding agent, is indeed taught;
and likewise: "For having obtained the Essence, he becomes blissful."

Thus, [the relationship] is shown as that between the attainer and the attainable by the words "For when he..."; as that between the worshipper and the object of worship by the words "he approaches...";
and as that between the one who reaches and the goal reached by the words "Out of fear of him... [and so forth].
Thus, the teachings concerning difference should be understood as being based on the relationship between the governed and the governor.
As for what was stated— that the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the syntactical unity of the texts (*vākyaśābalya*) is the proof here— [that remains to be examined].
That is incorrect; for it is precisely by taking the sentences as referring solely to Brahman that they are rendered consistent.
Therefore, the individual soul (jīva) is not denoted by the terms "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth. *3,438*
Now, how can it be said that there is no non-difference between this Supreme Self and the individual soul (jīva)? For their non-difference is established through inference;
and thus, by the method already stated, why should the soul not possess the nature of being composed of food (annamaya) and so forth?
Nor is there a contradiction with the teaching of the aforementioned distinctions;

for, due to the contradiction with inference, it is established that that very [teaching] has another purpose. To resolve this doubt, the Sūtra states: "And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference. He explains that as follows: "Not by inference."
... inference does not act according to one's own will.
Since bodies are considered diverse as the abodes for my enjoyment,
the notion that "these are bodies" and so forth is indeed required for the knowledge of reality.
Because it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.213a]
Oṃ. Furthermore, because it is desired, there is no dependence on inference. Oṃ.
And because of [the nature of] desire, there is no dependence on inference.
The term "disputed" (*vimatāni*) is stated in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) regarding those bodies that are currently accepted as such.
If [it is argued]: "Because these are bodies..."
The meaning is "because it is a body";
"like my own body, etc. is the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such [inferences] as: "The sense organs that are perceived in opposition [to one another] are indeed my instruments, because they are sense organs, like those [organs] perceived in agreement.

Now, it may be objected: these inferences establish the non-difference of the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) in each respective body, but not the non-difference of the individual souls (*jīva*) from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

In this regard, one might suspect the following inference: "The individual selves (*ātman*) do not differ from the supreme self (*paramātman*) in reality, because they possess the nature of being a self (*ātmatva*), just like the supreme self.
However, this is not the case.
Not so;
for it is not possible for there to be direct non-difference among individual souls (*jīvas*) whose very nature is conditioned,
because that would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition.
Consequently, the inference results in non-difference in its unconditioned form;
and thus, how could there not be a connection with the subject at hand? This is because the knowledge of reality has the knowledge of reality as its purpose.
It is not required;
the meaning is that it does not serve as a cause for the knowledge of reality.
Why?
Because it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition.
The word "hi" indicates an illustrative example. Thus, the formal argument is as follows:
The inference held by others— that "the bodies are conscious" and so forth—
is not a cause of knowledge that accords with reality,
because it contradicts valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the inference that seeks to prove that fire is not hot.
To the objection that a valid inference might exist even if it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, it is said: "acting according to one's own will."
He explains that as follows: "The sense-faculty," etc.
For inference that proceeds according to desire is indeed undermined by the fear of contradicting the scriptures and perception.
"Akṣa" means direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Inference (*anumāna*) should also be included here; thus, it refers to that which is supported by both perception and scripture (*āgama*).
The meaning is that [the mind] is abandoned out of fear of contradiction with that [truth].
"Acting according to desire" means possessing an activity that follows human whim.
To the question, "But what subverting argument (bādhaka) has been stated here regarding the counter-example (vipakṣa)? he says: "Where? (*kutra*). 3.439.
... where would it not find its proper occasion? (Manu 1.213d)
The word "kim" (what) is used in the sense of an objection;
the meaning is that it would find scope everywhere.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because it is dull (*jaḍa*)."

"By what reason can such [propositions] as 'the Self alone is insentient because it is a real entity' or 'consciousness is insentient because it is an object of cognition,' or 'space is solid,' be refuted? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.214)
"The self is insentient and not a substratum of knowledge because it is an entity, like a jar; space is dense and composed of compact parts because it is an object of cognition,
like a stone"— such [arguments] contradict the direct perception of the witness.
An insentient object such as a jar and consciousness are contradictory to the inference: "It [consciousness] is insentient because it is an object of cognition, like the self."
Because the effect of consciousness is not perceived in any way whatsoever;
by the first word [of the verse], there is the inclusion of that which contradicts scripture, such as: "Wine may be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa because it is a liquid substance, like milk."
The word "by what" (*kena*) is used in the sense of an objection.
The ellipsis is: "If [the inference] were to be an inference even though it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge.

The meaning expressed is: "If an inference of unity, despite contradicting perception and so forth, were to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then why would the example cited not also be [valid], since there is no distinction [between them]?"
Now, how should it be formulated here? He says that it should be according to the standard arrangement, using the particle *eva*.
If it is objected that in that case there would be a contradiction with the words of the proposition (*pratijñā*), [the response is as follows].
Let it be so;
for this [objection] is no more weighty than the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge,
and it is equal in the case of the opponent's inference as well.
The rebuttal to that is also equal in this case.
[Objection: But in the proof "space is solid," there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to time and so forth. [Reply: No, because they are equivalent to the subject (pakṣatulyatva).
"What is to be said on this matter will be stated further below. [Objection:

But has the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) not already been established at the very beginning with the words "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*)?
Likewise, it has also been established by the Sūtra concerning birth and so forth (*janmādi-sūtra*).

Since it has already been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is one [with Brahman], if one were to prove that again here as well, it would result in redundancy; therefore, he says: "Not the individual soul" (na jīva).

There is no tautology here due to any doubt regarding the sūtras on the diversity of living beings, because they serve to illuminate other statements; thus, the section beginning with "separately" (pṛthak) is complete.

In this treatise, whenever the intention to express unity is invoked in various sections, the establishment of difference is carried out within the sūtras by highlighting the statements regarding the differences residing therein. Therefore, because there is a difference in the underlying purport (tātparya), one should not suspect redundancy. To illustrate:
When a doubt regarding non-difference arises within the *jijñāsā* (enquiry) statements, the very word *brahman* occurring therein serves to establish difference;

likewise, when it is suspected that the *brahman* to be enquired into is the individual soul (*jīva*), the establishment of difference is achieved through the definition stated in the preceding statement—such points are to be inferred by oneself.
In this very same manner, [the Sūtra states]: "And because there is a designation of difference, [He] is other."

In such passages as well, the fault of tautology must be avoided. Now, one might object: "If this is so, then non-difference would never have been refuted in its own right. To this, he says: "separately" (pṛthak).
Fullness is the primary [point],
because the proof of difference has been examined independently;
for even though non-difference has been refuted by virtue of its being the subject of a specific context, the refutation of its essential nature is established by implication.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, as this is merely a statement of the actual state of affairs.

Alternatively, since the avoidance of redundancy occurs in this manner, the sūtras beginning with “And where there is a comparison” (*ata upamā*) appear, from the perspective of the literal meaning as it is understood at first glance, to be intent upon [establishing] difference.
This was stated for the purpose of refuting that [view];
for in the very phrase "because of the separate teaching," the full completion of the demonstration of their difference finds its conclusion.
Although this will be understood from the commentary that is about to be composed,
there is no fault in stating it here for the sake of clarity. Furthermore,

the position that the sheaths of the body and so forth are what are denoted by the terms "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so on has already been refuted by the general objection that "the other [interpretation] is untenable."
In order to refute [the opponent's position] by means of a specific fault, the Sūtra states: "And it teaches its connection with this in this.
Oṃ, it teaches its connection with this in this; Oṃ.
In this [context],
he teaches its connection with those [sheaths] beginning with "consisting of food" (annamaya), since he praises them as its fruits.
Therefore, to claim that these sheaths exist in both places is an extreme rashness.

Because the Śruti praises— that is, declares— in both places, in both Anuvākas, that this very one who is described as "one who knows thus" (the knower of Brahman) attains union with, or reaches, the states consisting of food and so forth as his fruit; as in the passage beginning,
"He enters this self consisting of food," and so on.

And as for the passage beginning, "Having approached this self consisting of food," and so forth, the interpretation that these [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food are "sheaths" (kośas) is an extreme rashness, rooted in a failure to consider what precedes and follows. For it is not possible that the attainment of sheaths such as the body can be the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman.
This is because it would contradict such passages as "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow," and because the body and so forth are themselves of the nature of sorrow.
This might be so if the attainment of the stages beginning with the "consisting of food" (annamaya) were being described here.
But this is not the case, because the word "approaching" (*upasaṅkrama*) has the sense of "transgressing"; therefore, he says: "And approaching...
[Verse 3.446] ...and indeed, approaching is indicated in relation to what is designated as the second.
The prefix *upa* should prevent him from speaking of transgression.

Regarding that which was taught in the second [section]: it refers to one who speaks of "transcending" (atikrama) that which is called "approaching" (upasaṅkramaṇa)—namely, the approaching of the [self] consisting of food and so forth, which is stated as the object by means of the accusative case. That is to say, it refers to one who explains the word expressing "approaching" as having the meaning of "transcending."
The prefix *upa* would preclude [the sense of attainment];
thus there would be a contradiction with the prefix *upa*,
because the root *kram* preceded by *upa* has the meaning of "attainment" (*prāpti*).
He states another fault: "of that which has not been heard," etc.
How, moreover, could one provide a place for an unheard-of or excessive word?
The word "again" (punar) serves to aggregate another fault;
[it refers to] those devoid of shame who conceive of abandoning what has been heard and what has not been heard.
He states the intended meaning of the two sentences [beginning with] "śruta" as follows: "śrute" etc.
For by explaining it in this way, one would have to abandon the heard word *upa* and supply the unheard word *ati* in its place;
thus, there would be both the abandonment of what is heard and the postulation of what is unheard,
and both of these are grounds for embarrassment.
We do not, by abandoning what is heard [in the text], perform an insertion of what is not heard, whereby this fault would arise.
If it is argued that—since indeclinables have multiple meanings—the prefix *upa-* is explained as having the meaning of *ati-*, we say no;
for without a restrictive factor, it is illogical to abandon a well-established meaning and adopt an unestablished one.

For it is not the case that simply because indeclinables have multiple meanings, the word *antaḥ* (inside) must be understood as having the meaning "outside" (*bahiḥ*). Rather, this is established only by following usage and other factors. Having thus established this, he states a fault even while conceding [the opponent's point]: "only at death" (*mṛtāveva*).
For it is only upon death that the abandonment of that which consists of food is truly accomplished.

For, since the abandonment of the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya*)—and by the word "and" (*ca*), also of the sheath consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*)—is accomplished precisely at death, because death consists in the relinquishment of the body; therefore, since the passage beyond the sheaths beginning with *annamaya* has already been stated by the very mention of "departing from this world" (*pretya*), it would follow that there is a redundancy in stating again, "he approaches this self consisting of food. Thus, the mention of passing beyond them would be a mere repetition.
Furthermore, it would be consistent with the opening statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," if the text were intended to convey attainment.
Therefore, the *annamaya* and other sheaths (*kośas*) are not [the objects of attainment]; rather, it is Viṣṇu alone.
Even if the sheaths mentioned in other passages were intended as objects of purification—as indicated by the evidence of prayers for purity—there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Moreover, those [beings] beginning with "consisting of food" (annamaya) are distinct from these [five sheaths] beginning with "consisting of the essence of food" (annarasamaya), because of the introductory statement and the complementary passage "He indeed is the essence" (raso vai saḥ). Thus, by the logic of different terminology (śabdāntara-nyāya), they will be shown to be other [entities]; therefore, everything is faultless. Having thus explained the sūtras as being intent on establishing that all five, beginning with the one consisting of food, are the Supreme Brahman, this subsequent textual section is intended to refute the interpretations of others.

It begins: therein, the proponents of illusion (māyāvādins), considering that all five sheaths beginning with "consisting of food" (annamaya) are [merely illusory], explain these sūtras as demonstrating that Brahman— referred to in the phrase "the tail, the support of Brahman"— is to be known as the primary reality in its own right.
For instance: first of all, the four beginning with "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) are indeed sheaths that are modifications of food and so forth.

Thus, while there is a continuous stream of the suffix *mayaṭ* used in the sense of modification, how can it be maintained—suddenly, according to the maxim of the "half-chariot" (*ardhacarati*)—that in the case of "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) alone, the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies abundance and has Brahman as its object?
If it is argued that this is because the context concerns Brahman as described in the Vedic mantras,
then it would follow that the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and the others are also Brahman.

If you say that the "consisting of food" and the rest are not Brahman because another entity is heard of within them, whereas the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is Brahman because no such other is mentioned, we say no.

Even there, because it was stated that Brahman—the subject under discussion in the passage "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—is the "tail, the support" of the *ānandamaya* (the one consisting of bliss), the five sheaths beginning with the *annamaya* (the one consisting of food) are postulated solely for the purpose of making that Brahman known.
[Objection: But how can Brahman, which was mentioned as the tail of the *ānandamaya*—just like the *annamaya* and the others—be the primary subject itself? [Reply: It is not so.

This is because Brahman is the subject under discussion by virtue of its own primary importance. Nor should it be argued that even when Brahman is known as a limb of the *ānandamaya*, its status as the subject under discussion is not lost, since the *ānandamaya* is Brahman;
for if that were the case, the inconsistency would arise that the very same thing is both the whole and the limb.
And if one of the two must be accepted, it is more appropriate that the tail alone is Brahman,
because the word "Brahman" is heard there; but not so for the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because the word "Brahman" is not heard in reference to it.
This is because the verse beginning with "asanneva" refers to the Brahman described as the "tail of Brahman";
for here the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is not being referred back,
but rather the Brahman mentioned as the tail is being presented as the primary subject itself.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to doubt the existence or non-existence of that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya), since it is established by experience.
How then, one might ask, can there be a statement regarding its being a "tail"?
The phrase "tail-like tail" is used for the sake of providing a basis;
furthermore, because the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) possesses limbs such as joy and so forth, and because it is embodied, it follows that Brahman would also possess attributes,
whereas Brahman is in fact devoid of attributes.
This is because of the scriptural teaching that [Brahman] is beyond the reach of speech and mind.
Furthermore, even if the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies abundance (*prācurya*), when it is said that [Brahman] "abounds in bliss" (*ānandamaya*), a small amount of suffering is also implied;
for in common worldly usage, abundance is necessarily dependent upon the existence of its opposite in small measure.
Furthermore, suffering is not possible in Brahman.

Moreover, since the beloved and so forth exist as distinct entities in each body, if the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) were also distinct, it would follow that Brahman too is distinct in each body;
and that is not tenable.
This is because of the scriptural statement regarding its infinity.
Nor would the Vāruṇī knowledge of Bhārgava be contradicted in this way,
for since the suffix *mayaṭ* is not heard there, the two have different scopes.

Furthermore, because it is stated that "this self consisting of bliss" (*etam ānandamayam ātmānam*) is to be transcended—just as the selves consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the others are—it follows that the self consisting of bliss is not Brahman. Since the suffix *mayaṭ* is heard at the end [of the series], it must be understood to apply to the preceding terms as well; thus, even the one preceding [the self consisting of bliss] should not be considered Brahman.
However, for one seeking knowledge of Brahman, the teaching of that [self consisting of bliss] will be appropriate as a means [to reach Brahman].
[Objection: If that is so, then how are the Sūtras [to be understood], given that they are observed to be intent on establishing that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is Brahman? [Reply:
It is not so.

In the event of a conflict between the Vedas and the Sūtras, according to the maxim "when there is a quality [in doubt], an improper assumption [should be made]," the Sūtras can be interpreted in some way or another.
Therefore, all five sheaths beginning with the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) are not Brahman.

Although this has already been refuted by the explanation of the Sūtra, he refutes it clearly once more for the benefit of the students, starting with the words "those who [regard] food... (*ye 'nnam*).
Those who [practice] the meditation "Food is Brahman" and so forth through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Furthermore, the Vedic word, which speaks of the attainment of those fivefold forms, exists in two locations for those who deny them. (Manu 1.219)
How could she endure any other form of existence apart from darkness?
The phrase "ityādi" (and so forth) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).

The term "pañcasvarūpāṇām" (of the five natures) is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) and not a numeral-determinative compound (*dvigu*), because there is an absence of the conditions for a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning and so on.
It speaks of attaining that;
the remainder [of the sense] is "as the fruit of knowledge.
"Two places" refers to two sections (anuvākas).

For those who deny this, it is said: if the pentad beginning with *annamaya* were not Brahman, then [the following would be inconsistent]: in the verses cited with respect to *annamaya* and the others, there is the statement "those who meditate on food as Brahman" in the first section (*anuvāka*), and in the subsequent section, "he understood that food is Brahman."
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the statement that it is Brahman;
for there is no other authority for the tail being Brahman than this very word "Brahman. [Objection:
But this is taught as a means to the knowledge of Brahman.
If it is argued that [the Self] is not taught as being Brahman, we say no; for it is stated through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya),
and this coreferentiality is not figurative.
If that were the case, the attainment of that [Brahman] by the knower would be contradicted;
nor has it been stated that there is any transgression of the text in that regard.
Furthermore, it should not be argued that the word "Brahman" does not apply to the *ānandamaya*, because the verse concerns the "tail."
If that were so, it would follow that the verses beginning with "consisting of food" (annamaya) would likewise have to be understood in that same way.
Furthermore, this [interpretation] is adopted either on account of a subverting argument (bādhaka),
or simply as it stands.
Not the first, because the subverting arguments have already been refuted.

As for the second [alternative], however, one who denies Brahman—which is the very object of the Veda—would incur rebirth in hell through the wrath of those who take pride in the Veda, just like the Buddhist who denies the Veda. *3,465*
It was stated that [the syllable] resides in two places,
and it will be said later that this [syllable] belongs to Bhṛgu.
In that context, he elaborates upon the nature of Brahman as described in the subsequent explanatory passage with the words "Adhīhi" (Teach!).
"Teach me, O Blessed One, Brahman," he said; thus addressed, [the teacher] taught him starting from food and vital breath.
He said: "O Brahmin, how is that not so..."
"Study and teach," because the sense of the causative suffix (ṇi) is inherent;
"O Blessed One, O Blessed One."
The suffix *ru* is used for the vocative case in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), according to the rule "matuvaso ruḥ saṃbuddhau chandasi.
Varuṇa was questioned by Bhṛgu, as it is said: "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa (*vāruṇi*), approached his father Varuṇa."
"Teach me, O Venerable One, about Brahman.
To him he said this:
"Food, breath, sight, hearing, mind, and speech."
The meaning is that, because it has been stated as the answer to the question regarding Brahman, food and so forth must indeed be Brahman itself.
Now, if it is objected that there is a difference in subject matter because the suffix *mayaṭ* is not heard there [in the case of food], we say no; for this objection has already been answered.
Furthermore, just as in the verses cited regarding the "consisting of truth" (satyamaya) and so forth, there would be a difference in scope due to the non-occurrence of the suffix *mayaṭ*;
if it is argued that this may be so, we say no, because if that were the case, the citation of those examples would result in an inconsistency.
If it is argued that there is consistency because the intention is to praise those [beings] such as those consisting of food (*annamaya*) from which the modifications [of the self] arise, we say no;
for that is incompatible with the verse concerning the one "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*).
If it is then argued that, precisely because of that incompatibility, it must be assumed that the words "food" and so forth refer to the beings "consisting of food" and so on themselves:
Therefore, in this case as well, one must accept that it is the self consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the others that are being spoken of by virtue of the context;
for this narrative was told as a corroboration of the matter already stated.
Consequently, it is the self consisting of food and the others that are spoken of here.
And because these [teachings] are stated as answers to Brahmā’s questions, they must be Brahman itself, as otherwise it would be logically untenable;
for although it is explicitly stated that "this is the knowledge of Bhṛgu and Varuṇa, which is established in the supreme ether," it is indeed the knowledge of Brahman.
Nevertheless, a logical argument is presented for the sake of investigation;
or rather, because this [case] shares the same status regarding its proof and refutation (*samānayogakṣema*). *3,468*
This might be the case:
merely because they were spoken as answers to the question regarding Brahman, it does not follow that food and the rest mentioned by Varuṇa are Brahman itself;
for their instruction is also logically consistent as being means for the knowledge of Brahman.
For instance,
in the inquiry regarding the second moon, even a branch that does not have the form of a moon is called "the moon" because it is a means for the cognition of the moon;
or as, in the inquiry regarding Arundhatī, the large star situated near her is taught as being Arundhatī herself.
[The opponent argues: "Because it serves as the door to the knowledge of Arundhatī;

and the status of being a 'door' is indeed appropriate for the body and so forth—denoted by words such as 'food'—with respect to the knowledge of Brahman, since it functions by way of warding off outward-directed activity.
[The author replies: Not so.
Is it that a deviation [of the reason] is being urged by this?
Or is another way of establishing [the conclusion] being suggested? Or is that [deviation] being ascertained?
He states that the three positions are incoherent: "The gate," he says...
"That is the gate," according to the proponent;
how could they know the approach? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.221bc).
"That food and so forth" means the manner of the teacher's instruction occurring after one has approached [the teacher] for the sake of attaining knowledge of Brahman;
"how" is used as an interrogative particle to introduce an inquiry.
The meaning is that they do not exist.
The point is that this doubt arises from a failure to understand the manner of the teacher’s instruction.
To the question "How is it that they do not exist?", he says: "To one who has approached [the teacher]."
... for [the teacher] has thrice accepted her who has approached him for instruction. (Manu 1.221d)
Only the ultimate reality (brahman) should be taught,
and not just anything whatsoever;
even when there is a lack of understanding, that very same reality must be explained again and again through different words.
And the door must be described as being the door itself, not as having that [door] as its essence;
for smoke is not demonstrated as having fire as its essence.
The example of Candra and others is likewise unestablished.
"Āgamas" refers to the Vedas;
"those who know the tradition" refers to the authors of the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas.
Moreover, these two [terms] have the sense of mutual conjunction (*samuccaya*).
If that is so, let it be that Varuṇa, out of ignorance regarding the method of instruction, taught something else.
Not so.

With the intention that such an absence of knowledge is possible for a world-guardian (lokapāla), he concludes the refutation of the doubt regarding the instruction on the door with the word "tat" (therefore).
Therefore, whatever [untruth] the Lord of the Quarters might say to one who has approached him for instruction—[the opponent asks]:
"Could it not be that Varuṇa spoke non-Brahman as Brahman to the one who questioned him merely for the sake of deluding him? To this, he replies: "He should not speak [untruth]. (1.223ab) *3,470*
How could he speak of Brahman? For the Lord of Waters is not a deceiver.
The word *kim* is used in the sense of a censure; the meaning is "one should speak only as a Brahmin. The reason for this is given by the phrase "for he is not a magician" (*māyāvī na hi*).
The meaning is "because of being authoritative.
For it is well known that Varuṇa, the guardian of the quarter, possesses knowledge of the true nature of the intended object;
and his non-deceptiveness follows from his status as a father.
Because Bhṛgu was fit for the knowledge of Brahman;
because the fault of approaching [the teacher] inappropriately had been removed by the phrase "having approached";
and because it is impossible for one who is called a "lord of waters" due to presiding over the element of water to possess impaired faculties.
And since the intention to speak is established through instruction alone,
for this very reason the Śruti says that Vāruṇi approached his father Varuṇa.

Thus, it is stated that the fact that food and the others were spoken of by this authoritative person (Varuṇa) as answers to questions concerning Brahman constitutes the reason for their being Brahman.
Now, one might object: let food, vital breath, and mind among those things mentioned by Varuṇa be of the nature of Brahman;
for there is no inconsistency in the words "food" and so forth having the sense of "the eater" and so on.
But how could the eye, the ear, speech, and sound be Brahman?
For regarding the words "eye" and so forth: it is called the "eye" (*cakṣus*) because one sees (*caṣṭe*) by means of it;
it is called the "ear" (*śrotra*) because one hears (*śṛṇoti*) by means of it.
If it is argued that "speech" (*vāk*) is so called because one speaks by means of it—since the word implies an instrument—and since it is impossible for Brahman to be an instrument, we say no;
for that etymology is possible even when applied to the agent. Thus he says: "He speaks" (*caṣṭe*).
It is called "the eye" (cakṣus) because it sees; it is called "the ear" (śrotra) because of hearing;
and speech (vāk) is indeed Brahman, the cause of creation, maintenance, and so forth, because of its speaking. (Manu 1.224)

By the word *eva*, [the author] refutes the interpretation that it is an instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, the definition of Brahman— that it is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all beings, as stated in the passage, "From which indeed these beings are born"— would have been taught [if it were so intended] regarding food and the like.
And therefore, he says "this is Brahman" with the word "sṛṣṭi" (creation).
The connection is that because it has been stated to be the cause of creation and so forth, for this reason also it is Brahman.
[Objection: Even so, the two sections (anuvākas) cannot refer to a single entity, because of the difference in number and the difference in designation.

Previously, indeed, five [sheaths] beginning with *annamaya* were mentioned, but not those consisting of the eye, ear, and speech; and later, six beginning with food (*anna*) were mentioned, but not consciousness (*vijñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*). To this, he says: "And that... (*tac ca*).
And that [eightfold form] is illustrated in the Vāghūla recension as being accompanied by consciousness and bliss, distinguished by the characteristics of creation and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Since, in the Bādhūla recension, that group of six beginning with food, together with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and bliss (*ānanda*), is declared to be Brahman in its eightfold form,

the intention is that— in accordance with that— there will be a unity of number and designation by supplying the three beginning with sight (*cakṣus*) from the first section and consciousness and bliss from the subsequent one.
Alternatively, the word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate another reason;
for here too [it is said]: "He understood that consciousness is Brahman," and "He understood that bliss is Brahman."
Indeed, by considering the subsequent sentence as well, the ellipsis of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*) is understood here;

for it would not be logical that Varuṇa taught one thing while Bhṛgu understood another. But why is it that even what is stated in the Vādhūla recension [is not considered]? To this he says: "separately."
This has been stated here in order to indicate that only those who know the many branches [of the Veda] possess the proper qualification for this.
Now, one might ask: "Why is it not stated here, as it is in the Vādhūla branch, that both [the insertion and the extraction] are the same? To this he says: "āvāpa...
"Because they say that the branch [of the Veda], through the process of insertion (āvāpa) and extraction (udvāpa), is the supreme state. (Manu 1.226ab)

The nature of the various recensions (śākhās) is such that they establish the true nature of the Supreme Lord by means of adding what has not been stated elsewhere in one place, by means of removing what has been stated elsewhere in another place, by means of both these methods together, or by means of the complete collection [of all texts].
Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Now, even so, it may be argued that it is not logically tenable for food and other things taught by Varuṇa to be Brahman.
"Having understood that, he again approached his father Varuṇa"—
from this statement regarding Bhṛgu's return even after having received instruction,
it follows that if what was previously mentioned were indeed Brahman, then the act of approaching him again with the words, "Teach me, O Venerable One, Brahman," would be purposeless.
By this, however, it is known that the Brahman previously taught was not [the ultimate].
For instance, if someone gives silver to one who has requested gold, and having accepted it, the recipient reflects upon it and then requests again, "Give me gold."
Therefore, one standing nearby knows that what was previously given was something else entirely and not gold;
likewise here, he dispels the doubt with the words "since" (*yataḥ*).
(Manu 1.1.226cd) "Since the elements are born," and so forth, by these very characteristics [he knows].
Later, having perceived each individual form through austerity alone, the Guru attained direct realization of everything that had been declared.

For those who, having received the command of their guru with a desire [to learn], have ascended by means of austerity alone, yet say "this is not the Veda," there is both the loss of what was heard and the acquisition of what was not heard. (Manu 1.228)
Since they have attained the status of being direct definitions, there is shame in speaking of them [as such] in those [other] statements.
The meaning is this: one should not, on the grounds that the subsequent approach would otherwise be inexplicable, assume that what was previously taught is not Brahman;
for the subsequent approach can be explained in another way.
To explain:
For Varuṇa, having instructed Bhṛgu in Brahman through both its general indication and its defining characteristics, said:
"You have not achieved your purpose by mere hearing alone;
for mere hearing is not a means for the direct realization of Brahman."

Since direct realization alone is the means to liberation, you must therefore perform the austerity consisting of reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). Having thus instructed him, [the teacher] explained that because it is impossible to realize everything simultaneously, one must first attain the state called "food" (*anna*) through reflection and meditative absorption.

Having directly perceived the form of the Blessed One, he approached his teacher once again to offer him that most unprecedented wealth obtained through the teacher's grace, desiring to perform reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) for the sake of directly realizing the other form known as *prāṇa*, and seeking the teacher’s permission;
such was also the case regarding the other form.

In that context, although one ought to say "Grant me permission," the fact that he says, "Teach me Brahman, O Blessed One," is for the purpose of dispelling [the student's] egoism (*ahaṅkāra*). Now, let it be granted that there is an *arthāpatti* (presumption) here; yet, since that [presumption] is exhausted by other possible explanations, a doubt remains: does the student approach again because the previous [teacher] was not a knower of Brahman, or is it, as stated above, for the sake of seeking permission?
And because there is doubt, it is not possible to determine that the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and the others are Brahman.
Not so;

for, since they possess characteristics such as "from which these beings are born," and because there is the indicative mark of being perceived through austerity itself, the determination of the latter alternative is logically established.
For this characteristic is not possible in the body and so forth;
nor is austerity required for the direct realization of that knowledge which is established by its own nature.
Furthermore, because the former [Brahman] was not Brahman, he approached it again, and having performed austerity, he understood: "Food is Brahman."
One should indeed say, "Not from food alone," and so forth.

Thus, for those who, even when the scriptures declare the nature of Brahman, imagine that it is not Brahman despite being heard as such, there would be both the abandonment of what is heard and the acceptance of what is unheard; therefore, enough with refuting such utterly baseless positions—it only brings shame upon ourselves.
The meaning of the words is indeed clear;
however, the Blessed One did not explain the inconsistency with the syllables of the Sūtra,
because that [inconsistency] had already been accepted by the opponent himself.

For one who considers his own explanation to be inherently incoherent, to provide a demonstration of that very point to him would be like killing what is already dead; it would only bring shame upon the refuter himself.
Therefore, he says:
"In this manner, when his statements—which serve as the subject matter—are subjected to refutation, it is we alone who feel shame.

Having explained the sūtra "And because of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśāt*), the opponent stated that the mention of "because of the designation of difference" was made by relying on a false distinction between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*). With the intention of showing that this is untenable, [the author] says: "In proximity" (*samīpe*). (3.481)
Because it is repeatedly stated that liberation is proximate to the enjoyment of [the fruits of] merit. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.229cd)
If the difference between the individual soul and the Lord were false, then that very falsity would itself be false.
In passages such as "having approached this Self consisting of bliss" (*etam ānandamayam ātmānam upasaṅkramya*), [the meaning is] in the presence of the Supreme Lord;
in passages such as "he enjoys" (*so 'śnute*), [the meaning is] together with Him.
For proximity and coexistence are not possible without distinction;
nor is it logical that even in liberation what remains should be false,
for that would entail the falsity of the very nature of the Self.

Alternatively, having stated "because of the designation of difference," one might wonder, "Could this not be a false difference? To dispel such a doubt, he explains the sūtra "And He teaches its connection with Him" in another way:
"By this [explanation], because the meaning of the suffix *mayaṭ* is conceived in two ways, the opinion of others, even if it exists, does not shine forth among the wise. (Manu 1.1.230c–f)

Having thus refuted the interpretation of the proponents of the five sheaths (pañcakośavādins), who are Māyāvādins, [the author] now refutes by extension the view of those such as Bhāskara and others—who follow the Sūtras exactly as they are heard—by stating "by this" (*eteneti*). These latter explain that the four sheaths beginning with the one made of food (*annamaya*) and the one made of bliss (*ānandamaya*) are respectively the four [sheaths], while the one made of bliss alone is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). It is their opinion that he refutes by way of analogy.

By this very demonstration that all five— beginning with the *annamaya*— are indeed Brahman, [the author] states an additional fault regarding those who maintain there are only four sheaths (*catuṣkośavādinaḥ*), as opposed to others who maintain there are five sheaths (*pañcakośatvavādinaḥ*), in the assemblies of the virtuous, the learned gatherings: "And because of the conceptualization of two distinct meanings for the suffix *mayaṭ*."

As for the argument stated here—that the suffix *maya* signifies "modification" (*vikāra*) in the cases of *annamaya* and so forth, but signifies "abundance" (*prācurya*) in the case of *ānandamaya*—that has already been refuted previously.
[Objection: But surely the sequence of "modification" was broken at the very point of *prāṇamaya*.
[Response: In that case, then...
There would be an additional fault in assuming that the suffix has its own inherent meaning (*svārthikatva*).

[Objection: Having begun with the explanation of the Sūtra, is it not irrelevant to refute the erroneous explanations of others? [Reply: No; because it is for the purpose of strengthening one's own explanation. With this intention, he concludes the subject matter of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, the divine Nārāyaṇa is primarily designated by words that express all qualities without exception,
as well as by general terms for the possessor of qualities.

The Blessed One alone is primarily designated by the terms "vital breath" and so forth when referring to the internal, and likewise by the terms "food" and so forth when referring to the elemental. (Manu 1.232)

Although the present section was undertaken for the purpose of establishing the coordination of words denoting qualities and those denoting the possessor of qualities, he summarizes another point established by the logic of a "conclusion established by the context" (adhikaraṇasiddhānta):
"And by those pertaining to the inner self."
