For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the introduction of the section.

It would be untenable to conclude that the Blessed Lord alone is primarily denoted by all the words— whether they denote the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), generalities, or qualities— which refer to the internal self (*adhyātma*) such as breath and speech, or to the external elements (*adhibhūta*) such as food and herbs.
Because this meaning has not been stated previously.
[Objection: But was it not said that this word "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is intended as an illustration?
[Reply: True.
For an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) pertains to a meaning that is relevant to the subject at hand and is logically consistent;
otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, it is neither relevant to the present context nor logically tenable to establish that all these words denote the Blessed One alone through their primary mode of signification (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*).
For instance,

in the sūtra "From which [proceeds] the origin and so forth of this [world]," eight characteristics of Brahman, such as being the cause of the world's origin and so forth, are stated. In that very context, at the third sūtra, scripture is declared to be the means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of those very same passages with respect to Brahman was proposed.

Therefore, the demonstration of the concordance of precisely those passages—in which the causality of the world's birth and so forth is perceived—with the Supreme Lord is relevant to the present context;
it does not apply to all [passages].

Because there is no demonstration of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world in all [other] cases. Furthermore, even if it is established that a word denoting that which is perceived as the locus of the causality of the world's origin and so forth refers to the Blessed One through some mode of signification (vṛtti), the over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition is certainly not avoided.
For it is not the case that the bank, which is the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the word "Gaṅgā," does not possess the quality of being the site of a cowherd settlement;
therefore, what is the use of supporting a primary denotative function (*mukhyavṛtti*)? Furthermore, it is untenable to support a primary denotative function for all words in the Blessed One alone.
For conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*yoga*) are the primary modes of function; even between these two, conventional usage is stronger than etymological derivation.
However, there is no conventional usage of words for the Blessed One.
But that [yoga] exists only elsewhere; however, yoga is possible there as well,
yet it is equal to that which exists elsewhere.
And thus, words function primarily only with respect to distinct objects, because both conventional usage (rūḍhi) and etymological derivation (yoga) exist [in that regard],
but not with respect to God.

Since the mere application [of the term] is possible in some way or another, one might suspect that this is a misinterpretation because there would be no consistency or logical justification for the author of the Sūtras to establish that all words refer primarily (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*) to the Blessed One alone. Anticipating this, he first demonstrates the consistency by stating: "janmādi" (beginning with birth).
By the aphorism "janmādy asya" (the origin, etc., of this), the definition of Brahman was proclaimed for the sake of establishing its entirety of attributes... [Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 1.1.233a-c]

Now, in the first aphorism, "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," the word *brahman* is employed to indicate that the object of inquiry is complete with all perfections, thereby distinguishing it from the individual soul (*jīva*) and other entities.

In the second aphorism, "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]," the causality of the world's birth and so forth is stated as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman for the sake of establishing that very perfection.

Therefore, by these two aphorisms, both the completeness of all qualities such as bliss (as the thing to be established) and the causality of the world's birth and so forth (as the means of establishment) are introduced as the subject matter.
This has already been explained by us previously.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "It is rooted in the treatise."
... because it is rooted in the scriptures. (Manu 1.1.233d)

Both of those— the primary and the secondary definitions— were stated in the third sūtra as being "based on scripture" (*śāstramūla*) or having "scripture as their sole authority" (*śāstraikapramāṇa*), in order to exclude [the definition] from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) when such was suspected through inference and other means. Consequently, in the fourth sūtra, when there is a suspicion that scripture might have another purpose,
the remainder [of the argument] is that it is appropriate to assert the connection of *all* words with the Lord, and not merely of a few words.

Even though the treatise is designated as an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is complete in all its qualities, from what [source] is the application of the word "all" to be asserted? To this, he says: "The application" (*anvaya*).
The lineage of all words is that which makes known the entire essence of qualities.
Since it is the concordance (*anvaya*) of all words—not just a few—that makes known the entirety of the qualities (*guṇa*), the connection [of the sentence] is as follows:
for the sake of establishing the totality of qualities from the entire scripture, that very [concordance] must be asserted.

Otherwise, if the concordance of a particular word were not asserted, the quality intended by its meaning would not be established in the Blessed One, and there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

And since the *samanvaya-sūtra* has already asserted the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all words [with Brahman], how could the author of the Sūtras' subsequent elaboration (*prapañcana*) of that [concordance] be irrelevant?
By this, it should also be understood that the primary mode of signification (*mukhyavṛtti*) is consistent [with the Sūtras],
because that too must be asserted in the *samanvaya-sūtra*.

Because, if it were used in a non-primary sense (*amukhyavṛtti*), there would be the consequence that the qualities denoted by those words could not be attained; and because, if it were applied to the primary object of denotation (*abhidheya*), there would be the consequence of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Having thus resolved this inconsistency, [the author] addresses what was stated by the opponent: "It is not logical that the Supreme Lord alone should be the primary referent of all words."

Since etymological derivation (*yoga*) is possible for [the word *īśvara*] elsewhere as well—just as it is for the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)—and since there is no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for the Lord [alone], whereas that [conventional usage] is predominant elsewhere; therefore, he first refutes the equality of etymological derivation in both cases with the words "The word... (*śabda*).
Because the grounds for the application of words are primarily and consistently present in it.

Since supreme sovereignty and other qualities, which are the grounds for the application of words such as "Indra," have a primary connection with that Supreme Lord, words like "Indra" denote Him alone.
For it is His supreme sovereignty that is indeed limitless and independent.
If one asks, "If it were the same elsewhere, what would be the distinction? it is said in that regard: "In the case of other objects."
Because they are causes for the smallness of other meanings, and because they serve as the basis for those [meanings], words possess the capacity to denote them... // MĀnuv 1.1.235a-c //
Because in other objects such as Purandara and others, the cause for the application of the word— namely, sovereignty and so forth—
is limited; for it is restricted by place, time, and essential nature,
and because even that which is limited serves as a cause for the Blessed One.
This is what is meant:
for *yoga* is indeed a function (*vṛtti*) that follows the meaning of its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*).
And in whatever measure the meaning of the parts increases, to that same extent an increase in the function of *yoga* must also occur.
Because it is illogical for there to be a lack of diversity in the effects when there is diversity in the causes;
furthermore, the meaning of the constituent parts [of the word "artha"] is unlimited and independent in the case of the Supreme Lord,
whereas in other objects it is limited and dependent on another.
Therefore, how can there be equality of yoga in both cases?
Rather, since "great yoga" (mahāyoga) applies to Īśvara while elsewhere there is merely "yoga," He alone is the primary referent of the word.
To refute the claim that words have no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) with respect to Īśvara, he says: "bahulā... [and so forth].
...due to excessive and frequent practice. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.235d)
"...the point to be proven would simply be that it is conventional (*rūḍha*).
Because of the frequent application [of the term], the collection of words is established as being conventional for Hari;
this is the formal argument (*prayoga*).
Words whose meanings are subject to doubt are conventionally established in reference to Hari,
because they possess extensive and frequent usage,
just like words such as "Nārāyaṇa" and others.

Since the state of being used [in common parlance] exists both for etymological (*yaugika*) words and for non-primary (*amukhya*) ones, the term "frequently" (*bahula*) was stated. Since frequent usage also exists for non-primary words whose primary meanings are unknown, the term "excessive usage" (*atiprayoga*) was stated;
for excessive usage is indeed usage by those who are venerable (*pūjya*).
And "worthiness of worship" (pūjyatā) is the absence of being preceded by a lack of discrimination.

Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of primary usage (rūḍhi), etymological usage (yoga), metaphorical usage based on convention (rūḍhopacāra), or metaphorical indication based on convention (rūḍhalakṣaṇā);
for in those cases as well, because primary usage is present, they belong to the class of similar instances (sapakṣa).
For those [words] function through collective application (*samāhāra-vṛtti*).

Now, it might be argued that this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because there is no actual usage of words such as "Indra" and so forth for the Supreme Lord; to this, he says: "conventional usage" (*rūḍhi*).
For conventional usage is considered to be of two kinds,
according to whether it is acquired by those who are ignorant or by those who are learned.
In this context, "conventional usage" (*rūḍhi*) refers to the observation of frequent and extensive application as an indicator of such convention.
"Attainment" (*āpti*) means connection.
The point here is that although there is an absence of such frequent and extensive application among the unlearned, because it exists among the learned, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*).
Let it be that words have conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) even with respect to Īśvara;
nevertheless, because that [usage] exists in the world as well, there is indeed equality [between the two].

And since it would therefore not be tenable that Hari alone is the primary denoted meaning, he says: "mukhyā... (*Mānava-dharmaśāstra* 1.1.236d): "...for that [usage] is indeed primary for the learned."
Since that conventional usage is primary—being inferred from the extensive application by the learned—therefore there is no equality; this is the remainder [of the argument].
To the question "In what way is it primary?", he says: "vidvad... (by the learned).
The Vedic usage of learned scholars is derived solely from etymological derivation (yoga).
For it is said that "learned usage" (vidvadrūḍhi) is inferred from frequent Vedic employment;
and it is quite clear that this [learned usage] is primary (mukhya) compared to that which is inferred from purely worldly employment.
Now, one might ask: how can it be called "Vedic"?
One might argue that the suffix *ṅīp* should apply here according to the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* and so forth;
but this is not so,
because [the specific form] is intended to manifest his supreme Vedic character.
Alternatively, since Vedic usages exist within this [work] as indicators, when the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule "arśādibhyo 'c," the form *vaidikī* is obtained.
Or else, it is established through its usage as meaning "from the mouth of Vedic persons."
He states another reason: "That" (seti).

The fifth case ending is used when there is a cause for concealment (*lyablopanimittā*), because that usage based on the conventional knowledge of the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*) is perceived precisely without abandoning etymological derivation (*yoga*).
However, unlike the conventional usage of the unlearned (*avidvadrūḍhi*), which is equivalent to a mere arbitrary convention (*saṅketa*), that [usage of the learned] is primary (*mukhya*). *3,500*
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Therefore, Viṣṇu is the primary referent... MAnu 1.237c.

Since, in this way, the term *mahāyoga* applies primarily and by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) to Viṣṇu alone, whereas elsewhere it consists merely of etymological connection (*yoga*) and non-primary usage, it is therefore established that Viṣṇu is the primary referent of all words. He concludes: "Thus, having done so."
... having placed [it] in his heart, the Lord [spoke]. (Manu 1.237d)
...he establishes the systematic connection. // MAnu 1.1.238a //

Keeping this connection and this logical reasoning in mind, the author of the Sūtras establishes—through the principle "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition"—the primary application of all words denoting general qualities to Hari.
Therefore, this interpretation is indeed correct.
Thus ends the section on the "One Consisting of Bliss" (Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa) in the venerable Nyāyasudhā.
[======= Section on Being a Semivowel (Antasthatva) =======] Now begins the section concerning the state of being a semivowel.

// Oṃ, because of the teaching of His attributes within [the heart], Oṃ. // *3,502* Because of the teaching of His attributes within (antas taddharmopadeśāt), [it is established that the Self is atomic].
BBs_1,1.20 / This might be so.

If the author of the Sūtras, by stating "because of repetition" (*abhyāsāt*) in the case of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), had intended this much as his final meaning, then the subsequent sections beginning with "on account of the teaching of its attributes within" (*antastaddharmopadeśāt*) would not have arisen at all, since their purpose would already have been accomplished by that alone. For it is precisely by resorting to conventional (*rūḍhi*) and etymological (*yoga*) meanings directed toward other referents that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) proceeds in those cases.
As stated in the Bhāṣya:

"In that regard, since the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) directed toward another object is a 'conventional usage of the ignorant' (*avidvad-rūḍhi*), it is weaker than the 'conventional usage of the wise' (*vidvad-rūḍhi*) directed toward the Blessed Lord;

and since etymological derivation (*yoga*)—which depends on a basis for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) limited by the Blessed Lord—is weaker than 'great yoga' (*mahā-yoga*) which depends on an unlimited and independent basis for application, its weakness has already been established. Therefore, what room is there for a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*)?"
True;

nevertheless, since there exists a further doubt, the commencement of another section (adhikaraṇa) is justified. With this intention, [the author] first presents the further doubt and then shows the purport of the section beginning with "On account of the teaching of its attributes within" (antastaddharmopadeśāt), starting with the words "Of the gods" (devānām).
Oṃ. [The Self within the sun is Brahman] because of the teaching of its attributes. Oṃ.
... having apprehended the power of the gods in that regard ... // MAnu 1.238b-c //
The Taittirīyas recite:
"Having entered within, this agent who moves within the moon by means of the mind—
though he exists together [with them], the gods do not perceive him."
In this regard, there is a doubt:
is this one who has entered within the supreme Self, or is it someone else? For the moment, the prima facie position is that it is someone else.
Why? Because Indra is the king who rules over the world;
Tvaṣṭṛ, who transforms forms; the wise one; Brahmā; Indra; and Agni, the foundation of the world.

By the scriptural passage beginning with "The Self during the day is Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati," and by the indicative mark of Aditi in the verse "Seven yoke the one-wheeled chariot," as well as by the designation of Him as the cause in the scriptural passage "Food is Brahman" and so forth, the determination was made in the preceding section (adhikaraṇa).

Nor can the scriptural mention of Indra and others be led elsewhere, because these terms are both conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in Purandara and others, and etymologically derived (*yaugika*). Now, it was argued that conventional usage belongs to those who are ignorant, while the etymological sense— being dependent on the Supreme Lord— is secondary due to its limited basis.
True;
that would apply to objects such as food, medicinal herbs, and the like,
but not to [deities] such as Purandara.

In this regard, since the grounds for the application of terms such as "Indra" and so forth—namely, supreme sovereignty and the like—are present there in their unlimited and independent form, the primary etymological derivation (*mukhyayoga*) is established.
For indeed, among those who are powerless, such as vassal kings and the like, sovereignty and so on are both limited and dependent upon others;
but how could it be otherwise for the gods, whose powers are unimpeded?
And thus says the Śruti:
"Indra is indeed the most powerful among the gods," and other passages of this kind.
Furthermore, [the author] himself [explains] the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of those very words in that context. (Manu 1.1.238cd)

Even the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of words such as *indra* for [deities like] Purandara and others is indeed primary (*mukhya*), as it pertains to learned persons (*vidvat-sambandhinī*), given that their extensive application is observed in mantras such as "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra" (*indrasya nu vīryāṇi pravocam*).
For if those [words] were not intended to refer to them, their employment in rituals such as their sacrifice would be untenable.
Nor should it be argued that independent and unlimited sovereignty and so forth are contradictory for multiple beings;
for Indra and the others are of the nature of the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, He alone, through the power of His body, assumes various designations when differentiated by the distinctions of their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
If it is asked, "Whence is this known?
we reply first of all that it is because the syntactical unity of the statements contained within this section would otherwise be inexplicable.
For instance:
That which was described as having the characteristics of the *ānandamaya*—namely, "invisible" and "without self"—is here stated as "the gods do not know it.
Furthermore, the scriptural references and indicative marks (*śruti-liṅga*) such as Indra and others are used in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
And a single sentence cannot have multiple objects [of reference].
It occurs because of contradiction,
as it has been said:
"A sentence is one because of its unity of purpose, provided that there would be mutual expectancy if it were divided."
And there is no reason here for the abandonment of one [aspect] upon the acceptance of another;
likewise, there is a Purāṇic statement:
"I, Bhava, and you—all this has Nārāyaṇa as its essence," and so forth.
For this very reason, the designation of difference must be explained as referring to something other than that [Brahman]. And this being so, there is no lack of a determining factor;
for while attributes not superimposed upon [Brahman] can exist in the superimposed [individual soul], the reverse is impossible.
Therefore, it is Indra and the other deities themselves who are presented as having entered within.
Thus, there is the capacity of the words "Indra" and so forth to apply to those gods—Indra and the rest—independently and without limit as the grounds for their application.
Consequently, the implication is that the words "Indra" and so forth possess the function of *mahāyoga* (great metaphorical application) there.

Likewise, having raised the suspicion that there is an even greater conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of those words— such as "Indra" and "Purandara"— with respect to those gods like Purandara, [the author states] that they apply even directly (*svayam api sākṣād api*), meaning even in relation to the learned (*vidvat*). (3.513)
Having established that Viṣṇu has ascended [to the highest state] by means of those attributes which consist in abiding at the edge of the ocean... // MAnu 1.1.239a-c //
The author of the Sūtras himself [establishes] in the sūtra "Because of the teaching of His attributes within" that it is Viṣṇu alone who has entered within; [as stated in the mantra]:
"Within the ocean, the seers [know Him], whose egg-shell they call the vital heat."

The statement "Brahmā obtained [it] through austerity" is because it teaches attributes such as being situated within the ocean, being the potency of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and being attainable through the austerity of Brahmā;
and because these [attributes] are established by Śruti and Smṛti as being the qualities of Viṣṇu.
Nor is there any contradiction with the Śruti and indicative marks (liṅga) concerning Indra and others.
This is because their sublation is established by the force of the "unrestricted" (niravakāśa) indicative mark;

nor is it the case that those [indicative marks] themselves lack an unrestricted scope, for it is proven through such passages as "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni," and so forth, that there exists in the Blessed One a well-known conventional usage among the learned.
Furthermore, since Mahāyoga is well-established [in scripture],
it is well-known from the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and other sources that the supreme sovereignty and so forth residing in Indra and others are limited and dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
Even in the case of Śakti, there is merely a superiority relative to those such as ourselves, but not absolute unrestrained power.
Otherwise, there would be the contradiction of multiple lords.
Even the conventional usage among the learned is based solely on the proximity of the Lord.

Thus, by means of the attributes of Viṣṇu—such as residing within the ocean and so forth—the fact that "entering within" resides in Viṣṇu is established, as well as the fact that words such as "Indra" and others are conventionally rooted in Viṣṇu.
This is an elliptical indication;
therein, having established its etymological derivation (*yaugikatva*), [the sūtra states]:
"And because there is a designation of difference, [the Self] is other [than the body]. (BBs 1.1.21) *3,515*
...and he again restrained them from their assault.

Now, one might object that, according to the reasoning already stated, since the gods are identical with the Supreme Lord, it is entirely possible for them to abide within the ocean and so forth; thus, having raised the doubt once again that the gods themselves are non-different from the Lord, [the author] addresses this with the sūtra: "And because there is a designation of difference, He is other."
And this [Self] is distinct from Indra and the other gods, because it enters within them;
for there is a designation of distinctions based on specific objects, such as "the Self of Indra," and there is no evidence for their non-difference.
Nor is there a confusion of scriptural passages.
The meaning is that [the author] refuted [the objection] on the grounds that it has been stated that everything is subordinate to Īśvara,
and because the Purāṇa concerns the excellence of Īśvara’s presence;
here, however, he merely restates the objection with the words "But again" (atra punar).
By specifying "by those very [means]," the objection that this sūtra on difference is redundant because it would otherwise be a mere repetition is refuted.
Although this word consists of an indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is no fault, as it is determined here by virtue of being connected with multiple names such as Indra and others.
Some [commentators] take these two sūtras [together] with the passage: "Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun..."

They explain [the passage] as being intended to establish the lordship of the person within the eye and the sun mentioned in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*— namely, "this person who is seen within the eye"—
but it was stated that this very [explanation] must be refuted.
For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-commencement of the sūtra *antaropapatteḥ* (Because of the occurrence within).
If it is argued that this [sūtra] was commenced with reference to the sentence, "That person who is seen within the eye—that is the Self," we say no;
for if there were a division of sentences and a consequent division of topics (*adhikaraṇa*), it would follow that the scripture would never reach its conclusion.
Moreover, attributes of Brahman such as immortality and so forth are present there as well.
[Objection: But surely the undertaking of that [section] will be due to a suspicion of additional [attributes]. For instance:

The expression "this is seen" is employed with respect to an object that is directly perceived; however, Brahman is beyond the senses and thus cannot be the object of such a designation. Yet, this [expression] is applicable in the case of a reflection.

[The opponent argues: "Since the shadow-person (*chāyāpuruṣa*) is understood from the first direct designation [of the Self], the immortality and other qualities perceived in the intellect colored by that [shadow] must somehow be explained as mere praise.
This was stated by one who is bewildered by the fear of redundancy;
for here too, there is a direct designation, namely: "This person who is seen within the eye."

In this regard, since that [interpretation] will apply here just as it was accommodated for the Supreme Self, what further doubt can there be? If it is argued, "Then let the very passage cited by the opponent serve as the subject-vacana (viṣayavākya) here,
and in that case, the phrase 'entering within' and so forth will apply," we say no.
Because, through the designation of distinctions such as place and so forth, that very [Self] appears there as the illustrative example;
therefore, the explanation of those impoverished in their knowledge of sentences is to be disregarded.
Thus ends the section on "Being Within" (*antaḥsthatva*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNYS 1.1.VI: The Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇam) =======] *3,521* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇam).

Having thus explained the concordance of words concerning the divine realm (adhidaiva), the author of the Sūtras now desires to establish the concordance of words concerning the elemental realm (adhibhūta). Since space (ākāśa) is preeminent among the elements, he declares its concordance with Hari: "Space [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark" (ākāśastalliṅgāt).
"Space [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark. The Chandogas recite: "What is the goal of this world? "Space," he said.

"Verily, all these beings arise from space alone; they dissolve back into space, for space is indeed greater than these, and space is their ultimate resort. This is that Udgītha which is higher than the high; this is infinite.
Regarding this, there arises a doubt.
Is this "ether" (ākāśa) the Supreme Self or the elemental ether?
For the moment, it is concluded that it is the elemental ether.
Why?

Because the word "ākāśa" is well-known in the sense of the primary element (bhūta) through both its etymological derivation (*yoga*) and its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Indeed, "expansion" (*ākāśana*), meaning the state of providing space (*avakāśatva*), is obtained from the etymological analysis of the word "ākāśa," and that is well-established in the case of the primary element.
Furthermore, in both common usage and the Veda, the word "ether" (ākāśa) most frequently refers to the elemental ether.
But one might object: could it not be the Supreme Self, on the strength of the indicative marks (liṅga) such as "All these indeed..."?
We reply: no, because direct statement (śruti) is more powerful than an indicative mark.
Nor does strength reside in the multiplicity of the indicative marks;
for even so, there would be no determination due to their equality,
and yet there is not even such equality.
As they have said:
"Power is twofold: by way of multiplicity and by way of intrinsic nature.
Of these two, that which is intrinsically powerful is that which is dependent [on others], and so forth."
Between the artificial and the non-artificial, the non-artificial is indeed superior.
Therefore, in accordance with the Śruti—which possesses the power of an intrinsic nature understood first—the indicative marks (liṅgas) should be applied in some manner. [Objection:
But has this not already been resolved by the sūtra, "On account of the teaching of its internal attributes" (Antastaddharmopadeśāt)?

Just as the word "Indra" and others, the word "ākāśa" (ether/space), though applied to the physical element in a non-primary sense, is rightly understood to denote the Lord through the force of great yoga (*mahāyoga*) and the conventional usage of the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*), thereby producing the cognition of Him; this is all the more so by the power of the unconditioned indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Since there is no further doubt whatsoever, this Sūtra need not have been commenced.
In this regard, he demonstrates an even greater doubt with the words: "For [it would be] desired... and so forth.
For whatever movement belongs to sentient beings arises through their grace;
how then could cavities and the like, which are by nature insentient, arise from that?
... for the purpose of removing such doubt. (Manu 1.1.241a)

It is logical that words such as "Indra" are used in a non-primary sense when applied to [beings] like Purandara, because an unlimited ground for application— such as sovereignty— is impossible [for them],
and even a small amount [of such power] is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
And it is logical that the primary sense [of the term] applies to the Supreme Lord, who possesses independent and limitless sovereignty and other such qualities.
Furthermore, the property of providing space (*avakāśatva*), which is the ground for the application of the word "space" (*ākāśa*), cannot be limitless in the elemental [ether],
because it is not absent at any place or at any time.
Nor is it dependent upon Īśvara.
For sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is a desire belonging to a conscious being, consisting in the forms of raining, commanding, protecting, and so forth.

Since that [desire] depends upon adventitious causes such as knowledge and volition, and because it is itself adventitious, it is logical that it is dependent upon the grace of the Supreme Lord, both by way of its cause and in its own essential nature.

Furthermore, the grounds for the application of terms such as "space" (ākāśa), namely "hollow-ness" (vivaratva) and so forth, do not depend upon the Supreme Lord either through the medium of adventitious causes such as cognition,
because they reside in non-conscious entities;
nor do they depend [on Him] by way of their own essential nature.
Because it is its very nature and not adventitious,
the application of the word "space" (ākāśa) to Īśvara is not possible;
for he lacks even the slightest quality of providing room (avakāśa).
Therefore, the remainder [of the commentary] is that this was formulated as a sutra in order to remove the excessive doubt that the word "space" (ākāśa) refers to the primary element (bhūta) itself.
The term "vivara" and so forth is an indication where the abstract state (bhāva) is the predominant factor.
By the inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth), it indicates that the mention of "opening" (vivara) is an elliptical illustration (upalakṣaṇa) intended to include "space" (ākāśa).
"From the Supreme Lord" means "dependent upon Him. The word "how? (*katham*) is used as an objection. (3.527)
But surely, it has already been stated here that "the ether is the Supreme Self because of its characteristic marks";
nothing further has been said to cover the previously mentioned prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). Therefore, he states another meaning of the Sūtra: "The ether... [and so on].
And even the name "space" [is derived from Hari]; furthermore, it must belong to Hari because of the superior and unprecedented indicative mark [of the suffix -ya]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.1.241b–d)
Indeed, another has raised the doubt that the name "Ākāśa" [belongs to Hari] by force;
however, that is not correct.
For the name "Ākāśa" belongs to Hari because of many indicative marks, such as being "higher than the high" (*parovarīyas*) and so forth, which leave no room for another interpretation.
The word "denotative" (*vācaka*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Here, although it is indicated in the compound as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), its connection with the subsequent term "even beyond" (*parato 'pi*) is not untenable, because it is mentally distinguished by its quality of being more excellent (*varīyastva*).

While one might have said "from that which has the cause of the origin of all beings as its antecedent" (*sarvabhūtotpattikāraṇatvapūrvāt*), it is stated as "from that which has the excellence of the higher and lower as its antecedent" (*parovarīyastvapūrvāt*).
For even though [the qualities] such as being the cause of all beings are perceived first, they can somehow be explained as applying to the elemental [air] (*bhūta*) as well;
however, qualities such as "being higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) cannot be applied there in any way whatsoever. To explain:
*3,529* Thus it is said: [text follows]
Having stated "space" as the answer to the question regarding the destination of this world—namely, the question concerning the earth's destination—it is asked: how can this be so?
For the earth is indeed an effect of water, and [the destination] must be within that very [water].
Having raised the objection that [the dissolution] occurs in those very [elements] because it is logical for them to be the destination of the earth,
he says "all" to show that this is not so, because they are the root causes.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the scriptural text "from the Self, space was produced," the Self must be mentioned [as the subject of the word "all"]; for in an investigation concerning the elements, it is space alone that ought to be mentioned. Furthermore, it is not contradictory to say "all" even though space is itself an element.
This is because, as in the statement "He created all this," it is logical to include that which is distinct from those [elements];
nor is there any inconsistency with the restrictive particle (*eva*),
since there is no other [cause] that originates the elements through a traditional succession.
How is it the cause of the origin and so forth of the elements?
He says: "Because it is the eldest among the elements"—for space is indeed more ancient than these four elements.
It is not only because it is the cause of origination and dissolution that [ether] is the "goal" (gati);
rather, he says "ether is the ultimate resort" (ākāśaḥ parāyaṇam) because it is also the substratum for the scriptural teaching that the effect resides within its causes.
Furthermore, the phrase "of this world" (*na cāsya lokasya*) is a designation for the collection of living beings (*prāṇinikāya*);
otherwise, even the word "all beings" (*sarvabhūta*) would refer to that [collection].
Moreover, in the statement "he should not lead the world beyond its foundation," it is the earth (*pṛthivī*) that is the subject under discussion.

Furthermore, it is not possible to explain "being higher than the high" (parovarīyastva) and so forth in such a manner [as figurative]. For "being higher than the high" is indeed the state of being the absolute supreme in an unqualified sense;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its meaning being redundant with the word "greater" (jyāyān).
Furthermore, because it has been stated that "this syllable 'Om' is the Udgītha," its status as the Udgītha cannot be interpreted otherwise in any way.
If it is argued that this is a mere figurative attribution (āropa), we say no; for such an interpretation would reduce the Upaniṣads to the level of childish play.
Furthermore, infinity with respect to space is simply not possible for that which has limits in terms of place, time, or attributes;
moreover, a relative [infinity] contradicts the subject at hand.
As for the earth, its nature is to move toward the center: "O gentle one, your *sāman* is indeed finite."
Having thus rejected [the opponent's view], what more could one possibly do by asserting that space itself is finite?
Therefore, its infinity is indeed non-figurative (*nirupacarita*).
[Objection: But was it not already stated that the scriptural testimony regarding space (*ākāśa-śruti*) is likewise without scope (*niravakāśa*)?
True;
that was poorly stated.
For it is not possible for space, which is delimited by place and time, to possess an unlimited capacity for providing room.
Nor is it independent, because it is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
Why is that? To this he says: "The sky."
"By whose ordinance this [space] gives the path to those who breathe," and by such statements... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.1.241a-c].
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is a summary of [qualities] such as "endowed with all elemental qualities.
By this, that which was stated—that the application of yoga is impossible for the Supreme Lord—is also resolved.
The remainder [of the meaning] is that in space, the quality of being a giver of room is understood to belong to the Lord as well, separately, just as it does to space.
We shall, however, state the proof [for this].
Therefore, it is established that the Blessed Lord Hari is the primary and ultimate referent for all words denoting elemental space (adhibhūta) as characterized by ether (ākāśa).
Thus ends the section on Ether (Ākāśādhikaraṇa) in the venerable Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_1,1.VII: The Section on Vital Breath =======] *3,535* Now follows the section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa).

Now, desiring to establish the concordance of the term "breath" (prāṇa) with the internal [Self], [the author] composed a sūtra for that purpose because of its primary importance: "Therefore, breath [is Brahman]. (Sūtra 3.3.10)
Oṃ, for this very reason, [it is] the vital breath; Oṃ.
For this very reason, [he became] Prāṇa.
It is heard in the Taittirīyaka:
"Therefore, you indeed became Prāṇa."
The great enjoyment of Prajāpati is his arm, which is about to be made; [the question arises] whether it breathes the gods or not.
In this regard, there is a doubt.

Is this *prāṇa* the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or the principal vital breath (*mukhya*)? Although the term *prāṇa* may apply to the functions of air and so forth, it cannot be the subject of doubt here because the meaning of the sentence is in every way untenable; for a conscious being is never addressed by an insentient thing with the words, "You have become thus."
What, then, is the position reached? That it is primary.
Why?

Because the word *prāṇa* is used predominantly in both common parlance and the Veda to denote the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), and because the etymological derivation "that by which beings breathe" (*prāṇanti anena*) is possible for it;

[an objection is raised: "But this too has already been refuted by the previous reasoning, so it does not necessitate the commencement of a new Sūtra. Therefore, he shows the further doubt with the words: "With respect to the internal self" (*adhyātmam*).
... through internal positive and negative concomitance, because the [breath] and so forth are observed to have it as their cause. // MAnu 1.241bc //

With reference to the self (*ātman*), that which exists as the locus of its experience is the "internal" (*adhyātma*) body; within that, "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) refers to the act of breathing, i.e., life.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), the other [vital breaths] are also understood to be included.
The phrase "of the principal one" (*mukhyasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
In this context, the remainder of the sentence must be supplied as follows: "The vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone ought to be the primary [subject] here.
Consequently, the meaning is this:
in that case, the sublation of the mention of Indra and so forth, or the mention of ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth, is appropriate.
Because the primary basis for the application [of the term] is impossible elsewhere,
yet possible in the case of the Supreme Self;
and this is not so in the present context.
For they [the vital breaths] possess the quality of being the cause of the impulse for living, which is the ground for the application of the term "prāṇa";
and that [quality] is possible in the primary sense.

When the primary [body] exists, life and so forth occur; when it does not exist, they do not. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the primary body is observed to be the cause of life and the like.
But surely, it is observed that life and so forth follow the positive and negative concomitance of modifications of air;
yet you seek to prove that the primary air (mukhya) is their cause—how are these two points consistent?
Not so.
"Because the primary [breath] has a body that is a modification of air.
Alternatively, it should be explained as "because the causality of the vital breaths and so forth is not observed," with the word "of the Supreme Self" being understood as the ellipsis.

The meaning is this: causal agency is indeed to be inferred through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), yet we do not perceive any such concomitance that would establish the Supreme Self as the cause of life and so forth—which are the grounds for applying the term "breath" (*prāṇa*).
Alternatively, what is stated here in the sentence "you have made the gods breathe" is the animation of the sense organs (*indriya*).
Furthermore, that all living beings characterized by Prajāpati possess the capacity for experience—
both of these [characteristics] are observed primarily in the individual self (adhyātma) through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and not in the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Therefore, because it accords with reasoning, this statement refers exclusively to the individual self as its subject matter.

Furthermore, there is no mark of God (*īśvaraliṅga*) here that is unconditionally established (*ananyathāsiddha*) as in the previous case, by which we might accept a sublation of the Śruti; such is the remainder of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). [Objection:
If this is so, then this Sūtra does not serve as a "covering" (i.e., a refutation); therefore, he states its intended meaning: "For it is an extended application (*atideśa*)."
For such is the nature of extended application.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the reason.

Thus, when the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached through such an additional doubt, the author of the Sūtras has extended (*atideśa*) the aforementioned method of refutation to this case; therefore, it should be understood that this Sūtra indeed serves to dispel the stated doubt.
Alternatively, what is the point of this elaboration on the suspicion of an additional [objection]?
Why should the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) not simply follow the Bhāṣya as it stands? To this it is said:
for such is the nature of an extended application (atideśa) that when there is an increase in the suspicion, the refutation remains the same.

If there were no distinction in the case of the doubt, then, since it would have been resolved by the previous [argument] alone, the extension of the former principle (*nyāyātideśana*) would be purposeless;

for if every doubt were resolved by a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), it would lead to the undesirable consequence of the treatise never reaching its conclusion. Furthermore, if the resolution were not specified as distinct, how could there be an extension based on "precisely this" (*ata eva*)? This was stated for the sake of instructing those of duller intellect.
In the Bhāṣya as well, he says "because it is well-known" (*prasiddheḥ*) in order to accept all of this.
He states "the indicative mark" (*liṅgam*) to explain the principle of extension (*atideśa*).
The indicative mark (liṅga) shall indeed be more powerful... // MAnu 1.1.243(c) //
The word "Hari," which is to be mentioned later, is connected here as well by way of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokana) maxim;
thus, it is connected with the word "eva.
Alternatively, this is an explanation of the word "balavat" as a restatement of the word "eva" found in the sūtra.
As in the case of the statement, "He is known from the word alone";
for the words "since" (yataḥ) and "therefore" (tasmāt) must be supplied.
Consequently, this is the meaning:
Hari alone must be the vital breath (prāṇa) here. Why? Because a Vaiṣṇava mark is heard in this context:
"Śrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives."

Thus, because the state of being the Lord of Śrī-Lakṣmī—heard in the immediately preceding sentence—is so powerful that it cannot even be conceived of as belonging to anyone else, [the breath must be the Supreme Self].

Now, it was argued that the scriptural mention of "breath" (prāṇa) is also without scope, since the grounds for the application of the word "breath"—namely, being the cause of the act of breathing and so forth—are observed through positive and negative concomitance in the primary sense (the vital air), whereas they are absent in the case of the Supreme Lord; to this, too, the same answer applies.
The "mark" (*liṅga*) consisting in being the cause of breathing and so forth means, in short, the property that serves as the ground for the application of the word "prāṇa.
It would apply primarily (*mukhya*) to Hara alone, and not to Mukhya [the vital breath].

for the status of being the speaker has already been established by the very statement that Indra is teaching about the Self.
Nor is it for the purpose of identifying the speaker as Indra, because that [statement] does not convey him as such.
For us, however, it is meaningful to illuminate the underlying reasoning: that Viśvāmitra, the composer of this distinguished hymn, could not have taught it otherwise than as Indra himself. *3,582*
He concludes the meaning of the preceding statement with the words: "Therefore."
Therefore, by means of words found elsewhere that conform to the principles already stated, the one god Nārāyaṇa alone is described from every perspective; there is no doubt about this.
The phrase "by those consisting of names that have departed elsewhere" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"By the aforementioned reasonings" is an explanation of the word "therefore" (tasmāt).
Those [reasonings] in which the stated logic resides are described as such.
On all sides, it is contained within all the Vedas;
its single meaning is the primary one.
There is no doubt in this matter.
The view of some is that this "endowment" (samanvaya) is stated in a figurative sense (lakṣaṇayā), whereas the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that it is in the primary sense (mukhyavṛttyā).
Therefore, one should not entertain doubt here due to this disagreement, because the means of determination has already been stated; such is the meaning.

Alternatively, he explains by this that even though the reasoning has been stated, one should not entertain a doubt—arising from beginningless latent impressions (anādivāsanā)—concerning whether something else is the primary object of expression.

When the Blessed One, acting as a teacher who functions like the Omniscient One for the sake of imparting the truth, has thus explained the Sūtras, the disciples might form the notion that these [Sūtras] have only this much meaning.
To refute that, he says: "Vāsudeva and so forth."
He exists everywhere as the fourfold form through Vāsudeva and the others,
or else he is declared to have five forms with respect to each respective substratum.
Or rather, for every sūtra, for every word, or even for every syllable.
The meaning is "as Vāsudeva and so forth.
The word "ca" (and) serves to collect the other alternative views that will be stated hereafter.
Since it is mentioned at the end of the first quarter (pāda), it appears that this belongs to this very quarter.
To refute that, it is said: "In every respect."
In all the quarters as well, the compound particle *athavā* indicates an alternative position (*pakṣāntara*).
He possesses five forms by virtue of being Nārāyaṇa and so forth.
The word *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
Furthermore, the three particles "atha," "api," and "vā" are connected respectively with the three phrases beginning with "pratisūtram" (in each sūtra), and so forth.
To the question, "How is it known that this form is being expounded here? he says: "By those... (*tair iti*).
[The verse continues: "...by those various specific methods of reasoning, scripture, and logic. (Manu 1.1.250cd)
The word *nyāya* signifies "manner" (*prakāra*),
or it refers to the meaning of "reasoning" (*nyāya*) that is distinct from direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The remainder [of the sense] is that differentiation (*viveka*) is to be understood through those well-known marks established for each respective form, which serve to distinguish them from [other forms such as those defined by] direct scriptural statement, designation (*samākhyā*), and so forth.

Now, one might ask: how can there be a conceptual alternative regarding the reality of whether [the Lord] has four forms, five forms, or even per adhikaraṇa, per sūtra, or per syllable? To this, he says: "Because of fitness."
... as is the capacity, according to [the verse]: MĀnUv 1.1.250d.
All these positions are intended by the author of the Sūtra;
they are understood without overstepping the capacities of persons.
It should be understood that, in consideration of those [capacities], the presentation of alternatives is appropriate.
To the question, "In this way, why do the sūtras have a supramundane meaning?", he says: "In the Bṛhattantra."
... by means of the authority of the extensive tantras.
The ellipsis is that the meaning of the sūtras should be understood in this way;
and the phrase "having many meanings," which is about to be stated, is also connected here.
If that is so, why is it not explained in that way? To this he says: "Even though it has many meanings."
... although it contains many meanings, it is spoken for the sake of being easily grasped by the intellects of men, because it summarizes [the essential points]. (Manu 1.251b–d)
The word "sūtrajātam" (the collection of sūtras) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
It is "spoken" (ucyate), meaning it is explained (vyākhyāyate).
If the word *buddhi* has the sense of "knowledge" (*jñāna*), then *graha* means "the object of apprehension" (*grāhya*); this is a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary focus.
The object (*artha*) is precisely the state of being graspable; for that purpose [the mind is directed]. When the mind is the object, "grasping" (*graha*) means the act of grasping.
With the intention that this treatise is not merely devoted to explaining a fragment of the meaning of the Sūtra and thus should not be disregarded, he says: "the treatise. (*3,586*)
This treatise, too, contains manifold meanings... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.1.252a //

Even though he did not provide a complete explanation of the meaning, one should not suspect that the *Bhāṣya* is of little significance simply because it was called "this" (*ayam*) [referring to the *Sūtra*] and because it is a re-arrangement of it; thus he says: "And the *Bhāṣya*... (*bhāṣyaṃ ca*).
...and the commentary is of extreme length.
Because it contains a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has an expansion (*vistara*) by means of an exceedingly great object," one might object:
"The fact that these two possess many objects is contradicted by non-perception.
To this he says, "They are indeed omniscient," with the intention that such non-perception is caused by a deficiency in the conditions for explanation.
Only those who possess great knowledge understand the specific distinction between these two.
Having thus stated this incidental [discussion] and established the connection with names well-known elsewhere, he concludes the proof of the definition with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, Viṣṇu possesses great qualities because his names are not redundant.
The meaning is: because [the Lord] is the denotation of all names found in the entirety of the Vedas.
How, by that alone, is there the possession of great qualities?
Because the names are etymological (yaugika) and because they are non-redundant (apunarukta).

Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in this commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna*— the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda— composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha as an elucidation of the meanings of difficult words and sentences.
Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2 *3,590* // Now begins the second quarter of the first chapter.

[======= JNys_1,2.I: The Section on Omnipresence =======] In order to establish the distinction between the preceding and following sections of the second chapter, as well as their internal unity as a single discourse, he shows the subject matter to be expounded with the words: "of those whose nature is the *liṅga*."
The function of words whose nature consists of gender-attributes is considered to reside in the supreme Nārāyaṇa... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.2.1a-c]

The *liṅga* is *dharma*; it is like the self (*ātman*). Those for which this [dharma] is the cause of their manifestation are "those whose nature is the *liṅga*" (*liṅgātmaka*). Alternatively, the word *ātman* has the sense of "essential form" (*svarūpa*), because of the metaphorical treatment of the cause and the effect as non-different.
The phrase "of those found in all the Vedas" implies "those well-known elsewhere.

[Objection: But were not the [words] in the preceding section also merely indicative (*liṅga*) in nature, even though they were integrated [into the context], because they are etymological (*yaugika*)?
Otherwise, since the qualities would not be fully attained, the effort to establish their possession [by Brahman] would be futile;
nor can it be argued that this is meaningful because the qualities mentioned in the specific context are obtained,
for in that case, accepting the function of the words [in their primary sense] would be rendered useless.
And it has been said that words function through [multiple] modes of application (yogavṛtti).
How then is this distinction possible?
True.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, for this statement is made in accordance with superficial cognition (*āpātapratīti*), just as in the case of [terms] well-known elsewhere.
Since function (*vṛtti*) also includes indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth, it was stated that "the primary meaning" (*mukhyārtha*) follows;
thus, "primary function" (*mukhyavṛtti*) is obtained.
It is contemplated and established in this "foot"—this is the ellipsis. *3,594* // Oṃ, because of the teaching that is universally established, Oṃ.

Some explain that this section (adhikaraṇa) is intended to establish that the Supreme Self is to be meditated upon as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth, based on the scriptural statement that He is "mind-made, whose body is breath, and whose form is light.
Being of the opinion that this is incorrect, [the author] says: "Omnipresence."
Because the teaching is established everywhere;
first, however, omnipresence is investigated.
The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis.

The meaning is that in this section [of the chapter], the quality of being situated in heaven—which was mentioned in the passage beginning with "this Self in this [body] and that Self in heaven"—is established first as belonging to the Supreme Lord; it is not, however, His being an object of meditation by virtue of qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*).
The meaning is that since attributes of the Supreme Lord, such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth, are clearly manifested, doubt and the like are untenable.
Now, one might object: "But qualities such as being composed of mind (*manomayatva*) are also perceived as attributes of the embodied soul.
This is not so; for those [attributes] have scope [as applying to the Supreme Lord] according to the principle established in the *Ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*.
For even that which is perceived last can establish the alteration of that which was perceived first—provided it is without [other] scope—whereas the latter has scope.
[Objection: But how is it, then, that for us as well, [attributes such as] "consisting of the eye" and so forth lead to the position of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
It is said:
When there is a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on another reason, those [other reasons] are presented merely as supplementary support (*abhyuccaya*).

For example, in the case of the opponent in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, even though the "order of sequence" (*prāyapāṭha*) has been refuted, it is presented in the *Prāṇa-adhikaraṇa* merely as supplementary support.
He demonstrates the utility of establishing omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) for the present topic with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
"Viṣṇu, stationed here and there, awakens their respective powers. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.2.2ab) "Awakening" (*prabodhana*) means causing [the power] to be directed toward its specific function.

One might ask: "Is he not capable of awakening the power even while remaining at a distance, such that he would need to be stationed here and there? To this it is said: "even from afar" (*dūrato ’pi*).
That Lord is far superior even to those, being capable of all things through mere sport.
...in order to make this known. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.2.3a)

Although that Lord Viṣṇu is capable of awakening those respective powers even from afar, nevertheless, it is investigated here that he is omnipresent in order to demonstrate that he remains in various places merely as a sport (līlā) and acts as the awakener of those respective powers; such is the connection.
This is what is meant:

it was previously stated that the primary powers, such as the vital breath (prāṇa) and others, which effect the falling down and rising up of the body through their own exit and entry, are dependent upon the Lord contained within them;
however, that [statement] is untenable.
Because the Blessed One lacks omnipresence,
that [omnipresence] is indeed to be understood solely through the scripture (*śāstra*).

Suspecting that the scripture— beginning with "He is in this" and so forth— is intended for something else, it is stated here that the omnipresence of Hari is logically established in order to substantiate the meaning already explained.
Alternatively, one might raise the objection that all-pervasiveness (*sarvagatatva*) need not be attributed to Hari,

because, like bliss (*ānanda*) and other such qualities, or like his creatorship (*sraṣṭṛtva*) and so forth, it lacks the status of being a "quality" (*guṇatva*). Anticipating this, [the author] clarifies that what is intended here by "all-pervasiveness" is not merely the state of being conjoined with everything, but rather [his being all-pervasive] by virtue of being the impeller of their respective potencies (*śakti*).
Therefore, it is stated by this [sūtra] that its demonstration is appropriate.

Alternatively, one might raise the objection: "It is not omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) that is to be established here, because that will be demonstrated in the section concerning invisibility (*adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa*). Anticipating this, the present [sūtra] states the difference in intent: that while omnipresence alone is [the subject] there, here it is the power to awaken those respective potencies (*tattacchaktiprabodhakatva*).

Alternatively, having raised the objection that this section need not be commenced because the Lord’s abiding within the earth and other elements will be discussed in the *Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa*, he explains [the difference] by stating that here His being internal to those things is described as the impeller of their powers (*śakti*), whereas there it is described as the provider of their existence (*sattā*) and so forth. Or else, having raised the objection that this is already covered by the *Antaḥsthatva-adhikaraṇa*, he states that while there the Lord’s abiding within a limited number of objects such as the moon is mentioned, here His inclusion within all objects is declared.
Thus he states the distinction of what is to be established by this [verse].
Alternatively,
"omnipresence" (sarvagatatva) means being in conjunction with all corporeal substances.
Alternatively, the possession of the dimension of the supremely great is well-established;

if that were the probandum here, then the objection based on "having a small abode" would be untenable, as its meaning would already have been covered by the section concerning invisibility and so forth.
Anticipating this objection, he explains "omnipresence" (*sarvagatatva*) in another way:
"It is the awakener of those respective powers.
[Objection: This is not possible, because of the prohibition of such a compound by the rule *kartari ca*. [Response: No.
This is because of the counter-exception (pratiprasava) [stated] "and by the sacrificer and so forth.
Alternatively,
it is "prabodha" in the sense that "from which there is excellent awakening" (prakarṣeṇa bodhaḥ), formed with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).
The awakening of the powers is "śaktiprabodhaḥ";
and from that [comes the form] "ajñātaḥ," where the suffix *kap* is applied. *3,604*
On this point, the Sūtra states: "And because of the designation of [the Self] as both the object and the agent of action."
The meaning of this is as follows:

because it is said that "it praises itself to another" (*ātmānaṃ parasmai śaṃsati*), and because in the act of praising the self is designated as the object (*karman*) while the body is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*), this all-pervading entity is not the embodied one (*śārīra*).
For it is impossible for the object and the agent to be one and the same in a single action.
For Devadatta is neither the agent nor the object in the act of cutting. In this regard, is the state of being both object and agent pervaded by difference, or not?
It is not the first [alternative].
Because there is no means of restriction, the pervasion is not certain.
This might be argued:
it is well known that an agent is the substratum of action.
That which possesses a result produced by an action inhering in another is called the *karman* (object).
For example, a village possesses conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is the result of the action of going (*gati*) inhering in Devadatta.
If being the *karman* were based solely on possessing the result of the action, then Devadatta—who also possesses that conjunction—would also undesirably follow as being the *karman*.
And if that were the case, the accusative case would apply in the sentence "Devadatta goes to the village" (*devadattaṃ grāmaṃ gacchati*).
Therefore, because it contradicts the grammatical definition, the distinction between the object and the agent is necessary.
This is not so.
Because Devadatta, from whom [the village] departs, would also incur the status of being an object (*karman*) due to possessing a portion of the fruit of the action of going inherent in Devadatta;
and consequently, there would be such usage as "Devadatta goes from Kauśāmbī to Pāṭalīputra.
Furthermore, since future objects and the like do not possess the fruit of actions such as desire directed toward them, they would not have the status of being objects.
For in the absence of that [object], the production of a result therein is not possible.
If you say, "Let it not be so," we reply:
no, because that would contradict the fact that desire and the like are transitive verbs (sakarmaka).
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the accusative case could not be applied to words denoting such [objects].
Moreover, even in the case of a jar or similar object existing in the present, no result produced by cognition or the like is perceived. To explain:
It cannot be "cognizedness" (jñātatā),
because that will be refuted later and because desire and other mental states do not produce it.
Nor is it the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth,
because those arise only within the self;
nor is it conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
Because that [agency], in the form of conventional activity (*vyavahāra*) and so forth, resides in the agent;
and because [agency] in the form of material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth does not extend to things to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*).
Therefore, agency is independence with respect to action (*kriyā-svātantrya*).
And it must be stated that being the object of that [action] is what constitutes "karmatva" (the state of being an object);
nor do we perceive any contradiction whatsoever between those two.
Otherwise, even the concept of a "karmakartṛ" (an object-agent) would become impossible.
Furthermore, there is indeed the co-occurrence of other grammatical factors (*kāraka*s),
as seen in such usages as *kāṃsyapātryā bhuṅkte* ("he eats from a bronze vessel") and *kāṃsyapātryāṃ bhuṅkte*.
Likewise, what contradiction is there in the co-occurrence of the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kartṛ*)?
But surely, a distinction between the object and the agent is indeed perceived,
and no deviation is observed;
therefore, there is a certainty of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Not so;
for it will be stated later that mere observation and non-observation do not establish pervasion,
nor even the non-observation of deviation.
"I know myself" [is known] from that perception;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the direct realization of the self is impossible.
Nor is the self merely inferable by means of constant inference, because direct perception (sākṣātkāra) cannot be denied.
Someone says: "This self is to be determined through mental perception."
Nevertheless, this [self] is indeed the agent and not the object;
for its immediacy is established by its mere appearance in the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya), which has the self as its agent.
This is because an object-status distinct from that [agency] cannot be defined.
It is merely an empty statement.
Furthermore, is the cognition "I" transitive or not?
The position that it is not contradicts experience.
Since the root *jñā* (to know) is always transitive and its object is not perceived [in this context],
it must be stated what its object is in the first case;
it cannot, at any rate, be something other than the self (*ātman*).
Because the notion of "I" is not observed in relation to things such as a jar.
If it is argued that pleasure and so forth belong to the self, [we reply: no, because [the notion of "I"] pertains to that alone.
Because it would follow that the self is not established as an object, and because it would follow that there would be such linguistic usage as "I am happiness.
If it is argued that the agent is the substratum of cognition and the object is distinguished by happiness and so forth, [we reply: no.
Thus, the identity of the agent and the object of action is established at least partially.

Furthermore, for one who is practicing yoga and perceives the self as free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), the notion of "I" cannot have anything other than that self as its object; therefore, it must be admitted that this notion is either objectless or has the self itself as its object, since there is no other alternative possible. (3.614)

Another [view], however, holds that the cognition produced by the eye or other senses in contact with a jar or similar object establishes the object as its *karman* (the objective) through the nature of the manifestation of the triad;

it establishes its own form through self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*); and it establishes the self as the substratum (*āśraya*). Thus, the self does not possess the status of being an object (*karman*).
Nor is there a failure to establish its direct realization; thus he says:
"He should be asked:
what is this so-called self-luminosity of cognition?"
If you argue that it is "self-luminosity through its own action," then you are like one fleeing from the fear of a scorpion who falls into the mouth of a venomous snake; for,

in order to avoid the contradiction inherent in the relation of object and agent— which depends solely on its own definition— you instead accept the relation of action and object, which is contradicted by everyone in the world.

For action is held to be produced by the object and the agent; and it is not appropriate for that which is produced and that which produces to be one, because action consists in the internalized sequence of prior and posterior states.
And it is not logical that the very same thing should be both prior and posterior with respect to itself.
If it is argued that self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) consists in being established without dependence on another illumination, we say no.
Otherwise, it would follow that even objects such as jars possess self-luminosity;
for jars and the like do not require another light for their own establishment,
but rather [require] light itself.
If it is argued that [the definition] is "establishment independent of a light external to itself," we say no;
for since there is no dependence on itself, the qualification "external to itself" is redundant.
If it is argued that [the self] is established independently of manifestation, no; for that would involve a contradiction.
[Otherwise,] even things such as a rabbit’s horn would [be so established].
Furthermore, it would lead to the undesirable consequence [of over-extension] regarding attainment (*siddhi*).
If it is argued that "it is the state of being a manifestation that serves as the cause for one's own linguistic usage," we say no;
for we observe that it serves as the cause for linguistic usage only with respect to its own object, and not with respect to what is not its own object.
Because it is untenable for [the quality] itself to be the cause of its own linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
However, examples such as the *bahuvrīhi* compound where the quality is included in the cognition (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) need not be cited here,
since it is accepted that the quality itself is also the object of the compound.
Furthermore, the self does not appear in visual cognition,
because it is an immaterial substance, like space;
otherwise, it would follow that it possesses form.

If it is argued that there is the employment of form as an object (*karman*) in the act of manifestation (*prakāśa*), we say no; for this qualification is redundant against one who maintains that whatever is manifesting manifests precisely as an object.
By this, any suspicion of another [logical] reason (*prayojaka*) in the case of inference is also refuted.
Furthermore, if the self were to manifest even though it is not an object of that [cognition],
then alas, why would taste also not manifest in a cognition of color?
If you say it is because [taste] is not its substrate, [we reply:]...
In that case, does everything related to cognition appear within cognition,
or is it only its substrate?
In the first case, there would be the over-extension [of the definition] to the eyes and other sense organs.
In the second case as well, a restrictive factor must be stated;
for it is not the case that "this is a jar" appears as the self.
Rather, the cognition "I know the jar" is quite another, having as its object the self qualified by the knowledge of the jar.
The establishment of the self will also occur by way of being an object;
by this, the establishment of the self through self-luminosity is also refuted,
because it is impossible to define that [self-luminosity] as anything other than its own nature, which— like the light of the sun— is not distinct from itself.

Thus, it is established that the relationship between agent and object is not pervaded by difference (*bhedavyāpta*). Furthermore, because of the designation of [the same entity] as both object and agent (BBs 1.2.4), [one might ask]: "In that case, how can it be taken up as a cause? To this, he says: "The object... (*karmeti*).
... there is generally a distinction between the action and its agent. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.2.3ab)
As long as there is a distinction between the object and the agent within a single action, pervasion (vyāpti) certainly exists; however, this is the general rule (autsargikī).
The meaning is that it is not, like smoke [pervaded] by fire, something that cannot be restricted.
If it is asked, "What is gained from that?", he states in sequence that two faults have been avoided: "Even non-difference," and so forth.
Non-difference may also exist within the particular; that [particular] is powerful and remains unrefuted.

Since there is a difference between the object and the agent by default (*utsarga*), it therefore qualifies its own object by excluding it from the scope of the default rule; thus, "qualification" (*viśeṣa*) is an exception (*apavāda*). When that [exception] exists, there may also be non-difference (*abheda*). And so: "I know myself," and so forth.
Thus it is established:
since a general rule (*utsarga*) is powerful in establishing its own object when there is no exception (*apavāda*),
and there is no exception in the present case.
Therefore, its inclusion here as a reason is also appropriate.
For just as the general prohibition against harming any living beings— expressed as "one should not harm any beings"— is set aside by the injunction to harm the animal in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice,
yet even when it has been set aside, there remains authoritative proof for the non-performance of the harming of Brahmins and others.
But if that is so, then it can certainly be said of knowability (*prameyatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) as well:
there is a general pervasion (*vyāpti*) of knowability by impermanence,
while permanence exists in cases such as space (*ākāśa*) due to an exception (*apavāda*).
Because there is no such objection, [the reason] establishes impermanence in sound and so forth;
consequently, the fallacy of being inconclusive (anaikāntika) would be eliminated.
Not so.
For when an object has been cognized by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose scope is general, there occurs a sublation (*apavāda*) by one whose scope is specific;
consequently, a cognition that had previously applied to everything abandons that [general] object and finds its rest elsewhere.

However, there is no acquisition through any means of valid cognition of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), such as there is for the prohibition of harming all living beings.
What indeed is this "knowability" (*prameyatva*)?

Since it is perceived as existing in conjunction with both permanence and impermanence, there is no room for the application of the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) in that case either.

If that is so, then since the relationship between agent and object is also observed to be established in terms of both difference and non-difference, how can there be any room here for the principle of the general rule and its exception?
Do not say so; for the relationship between agent and object consists precisely in the nature of subjectivity (pratyaktva) and objectivity (parāktva).
For the time being, this must be reconciled either through distinction (*bheda*) or through qualification (*viśeṣa*) due to the apparent contradiction.
In this regard, it has been stated that distinction is primary, whereas qualification is a substitute.
Furthermore, there is no appearance of parity between the primary and its substitute;
therefore, it is rightly said that while difference is established in a general sense, the specific [exception] arises through an apavāda (exception).
We shall explain later how the principle of utsarga-apavāda (general rule and exception) is possible even in the absence of a persisting universal.

Just as a relation that possesses an *upādhi* lacks the status of being a constituent part of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), so too a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) that possesses an *upādhi* lacks the status of being a constituent part of the refutation (*dūṣaṇāṅga*). What is extraordinary about this? And this will be explained later.
It has been stated that "omnipresence" (*sarvagatatva*) is what is being established in this section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Is that [the term "all"] intended as a mere enumeration or as an indicator of other things?
In the first case, there would be a loss of the "omnipresence" (viśvatomukhatva) of the aphorisms,
