yet the aforementioned fault does not apply;
for in that case, there exists a distinction between what is called "power" and what is called "manifestation."
And it has already been stated previously that this [particular] is what effects the differentiation of the action.

Furthermore, if that particular were distinct from each other and from the qualified entity, then why would there not also be a distinction between the power (*śakti*) and its manifestation (*vyakti*)?
Furthermore, if it were non-different [from the universal], there would be a confusion of linguistic usage and so forth; therefore, he says: "possessing particulars."
... is distinguished. // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.2.6d //
Even though he is non-different... // MĀnuv 1.2.7a //
The term "distinction" (viśeṣa) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
We maintain that this distinction is indeed non-different;
thus, the previously stated logical inconsistency does not apply.
For even though it is non-different [from the agent], it is admitted to possess specific qualities;
the meaning is that it is its own destroyer.
But if this is so, then the eternality of action must likewise be admitted in other cases as well.
If it is argued that by accepting both the potential (*śakti*) and the manifestation (*vyakti*), all faults are avoided—
then let this be accepted, provided there is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its eternity;
for only when such an uncontradicted means of knowledge exists [can this be maintained].
And this conceptualization occurs because it cannot otherwise be explained in the case of conventional usages that are contrary to that [permanence].

Furthermore, there is no unassailable means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the permanence of actions such as those of a jar; however, there is such a means of valid cognition for the permanence of the action of the Supreme Lord and others—thus he says: "and action, etc. (*kriyādiśca*).
For scripture declares that action and so forth are its very nature.
By this, the third [position] is also refuted;
for by this [argument], he indicates the scriptural passage: "His power is declared to be indeed manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are innate."
"Intrinsic" means existing as long as the substance exists;
regarding this, he cites a clear scriptural authority: "Knowledge," etc.
"Knowledge is eternal, action is eternal, and strength is the power of the Supreme Self"—
thus says the Paiṅgi Śruti.
Alternatively, the former scriptural passage was cited in the context that "power itself is action," while the latter concerns the eternality of action;
or else, the former concerns its essential nature (*svarūpa*),
because that is the subject of dispute.

The second [alternative], however, concerns the eternality of its cause. Let it be that the activity of God is eternal; but is the activity of others necessarily non-eternal? To demonstrate the distinction by means of another proof, he says: "By power," etc.

...but it should be understood that the eternity of action and so forth exists only insofar as their causal capacity (*śakti*) exists; elsewhere, however, there is non-eternity. *Mānava-dharmaśāstra* 1.2.8b–d.
Thus is the statement on the true nature of beings... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.2.9a //
"In existence" means in permanence;
by the word "etcetera," knowledge and so forth are included.
Alternatively, "permanence" refers to stability.
Consequently, it is stated that for as long as the power of knowledge, action, and so forth exists, the knowledge and other faculties must also exist for that same duration.
Some maintain that there is no such thing as "power" distinct from the conjunction of the essential nature and auxiliary causes;
however, this view contradicts the scriptural passages and other authorities cited above.
Nor is it merely its own essential nature,
because it is perceived as being in a relationship [with something else];
nor is it merely an auxiliary cause.
This is because [the scriptures] teach that [fire] possesses intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*) and so forth.
Furthermore, there is indeed such conventional usage:
even though fire possesses the capacity for effects such as the production of a *sphoṭa*, it does not produce them due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), such as contact with a body.
In this context, first of all, the mere nature of fire is not denoted by the word "capacity" (*śakti*),
because that would entail the redundancy of the possessive suffix *-matup*.
Nor does it denote the presence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-samavadhāna*), since the absence of such [auxiliaries] has already been stated.
If it is argued that the universal of combustibility (*dahanatva-sāmānya*) itself is the causal capacity (*śakti*),

then how is it that there is nothing distinct from the conjunction of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)? If it is further argued that the universal is also included within the class of auxiliary causes, [the response follows].
Is that [power] perceptible or imperceptible?
In the first case, upon seeing a fire, there would be no desire to know its capacity to produce a blistering burn.
Nor is it the second case.

Because this would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Or, if you were to accept it in that way, then that very power (*śakti*) is simply what we [Advaitins] maintain.
Furthermore, the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of clay, thread, and so forth is established by perception and other means of valid cognition.

Its status as the cause of jars and other such things, however, is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). And the means for grasping this positive and negative concomitance is the universal (sāmānya);
and it has been accepted even by the opponent that this universal is established through perception and other means of valid cognition.
Moreover, causality is neither the essential nature [of the cause] nor the conjunction with auxiliary factors;
for the essential nature is understood independently of positive and negative concomitance.

Since one must seek the conjunction of auxiliary causes for the cause itself, one must therefore admit that the causality of clay and other materials toward a jar and so forth is something entirely beyond the senses.
That very thing is what is accepted by the proponents of power (*śaktivādin*) as "power" (*śakti*); let this elaboration suffice.
Now, one might ask: what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for action?
We reply that it is perception itself when the action resides in a perceptible substance, because we observe the manifestation of "moving" as something directly present (*aparokṣa*).
Because the cognition of motion follows the presence and absence of the operation of the sense faculties;
otherwise, it would follow that even color and other such objects would not be perceived.
Now, if it is thought:
Action is not perceptible,
because no specific quality distinct from disjunction and conjunction is perceived in a substance as it moves;
as for this cognition that "it goes," [it is based on inference].
It is argued that [the cognition] has as its object an action inferred from conjunction and disjunction,
and that the operation of the sense organ consists in the apprehension of the conjunction and disjunction which serve as the inferential marks.
This is incorrect.

Whether the inferential nature of the cognition of action and the fact that the operation of the sense organ is exhausted elsewhere are postulated once its non-perceptual status has been established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or otherwise— [we reply:
it is not the first case,
because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*).
As for what was stated, namely "because of non-apprehension," that is unestablished, because it is unestablished for the proponent.

For one who accepts that [the object] has a non-mediately manifest appearance cannot be made to understand [the contrary] merely by the statement "because of non-perception," since that would lead to the same consequence for things such as jars.
[This applies to] the object of dispute.
If it is argued that [the action] is not perceptible because it is an action, like the action of an atom, we say no;
for we accept that even the action of an atom is perceptible to yogis.
Therefore, if the qualifier "for those such as us" is added for that purpose, it is redundant for the opponent.
Furthermore, why could it not be argued that the subject of dispute, form (rūpa), is imperceptible because it possesses the nature of form (rūpatva), just like the form of an atom (paramāṇurūpa)?
If it is argued that this is not so because it contradicts empirical experience (*pratītivirodha*),
the same applies to the case at hand as well.
If it is argued that the perception of non-sensuousness is invalid because it is contradicted by inference (*anumānaviruddha*), [the same response follows].
If it is argued that the cognition of the perceptibility of form should likewise be so [i.e., non-existent], because inference does not arise regarding an object that contradicts direct cognition,
this objection is equally applicable here as well.
Now, if you say that the non-perceptibility of the form of an atom is caused by the lack of magnitude in its substratum,
that is not so.
Because it will be stated later that even an atom possesses magnitude;
furthermore, why not assume that the same [reason] is the cause for the imperceptibility of atomic action as well?
If, then, action were perceptible, [it would be perceived].
If it is argued that the cognition "it moves" would arise even when only a single individual action has occurred, we say no;
for this would apply equally to conjunctions and disjunctions as well.
And thus, there would be no inference of action either.
Now, if you think that the perceptibility of conjunction and disjunction is established in the same way as [the perception of] an army or a forest,
then why should it not be the same for action as well?
Not the second [alternative].
The threads are not perceptible, but are instead to be inferred from the effect, which is the cloth;
for it would follow as a conceptual error that the operation of the sense organ is employed only at the time of grasping the cloth.
Furthermore, it is the opponent's view that conjunction and disjunction have two substrata.
For us as well, the pair of conjunction and disjunction has two substrata;
and action, being inferred from those two, would have to be inferred in both places.
Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "the post moves" occurring even with respect to the post, just as it does with respect to the hawk.
Now, it might be argued: "It is not action in the post that is inferred, but rather [action] in the hawk itself;

for when the hawk, while falling, produces a disjunction from its previous location, or while rising, generates a conjunction with a subsequent location, it is impossible for the action of the post to be the cause."
But [it might be argued that] when the act of flying (śyena) is inferred, its conjunction with and disjunction from other locations become possible;
however, that is untenable.

For if the production of conjunction with and disjunction from another location by means of the motion of a post were impossible for the hawk, then another motion conducive to that effect would have to be postulated in the hawk.
But how could there be any cessation of the inference of motion in the post?
For it is a general rule that the cause must reside in the same locus as the effect that is perceived.
If it is argued that since everything is established by means of the action of the hawk alone as conceived [in the mind], the action of the post (sthāṇu) is of no use, we say:
no, because such an alternative is untenable.

For instance, is the inferential mark (liṅga) an indicator of the object only when it possesses both pervasion (vyāpti) and the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā), such that this much constitutes the complete causal complex for inference?
Or is it merely the possession of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)?
Not the first, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the abolition of inference regarding things that are neither cause nor effect.

Furthermore, it is contrary to common experience (*alaukika*) to claim that what is not invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with something else does not indicate that thing when it is perceived somewhere, on the grounds that it is useless [to do so].
But in the second case, why is there no inference of action in the post?
If it is argued that even when [action] is inferred, it is set aside for fear of the complexity of conceptualization (*kalpanā-gaurava*), [we reply:
no, because such fear does not exist regarding an object established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But surely, in the case of the inference for God as well, there would be the postulation of multiple gods if this were so?
It would not;
because of the difference.
For the state of being an effect (kāryatva) regarding the earth and so forth, while making known merely the existence of an agent, remains indifferent as to whether that agent is one or many;
therefore, when the suspicion of its being many is refuted by the principle of the complexity of postulation (kalpanā-gaurava), it culminates in [the conclusion of] oneness.
But in this case, since action is inferred in the post itself through an effect characterized by conjunction and disjunction, how can that [action] be removed by the complexity of postulation?
Now, it might be argued:
"Since there is another way to account for it, there is no inference of action in the post;
nor should it be said that this is a fault of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) rather than of inference (*anumāna*)."
"Otherwise, if there were a suspicion that [the effect] could arise in another way, then even in the case of inference, doubt regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) would result"—
this is untenable; for in this case, when a post (*sthāṇu*) is perceived, one might indeed suspect that the conjunctions and disjunctions [produced by it] would be entirely causeless.
Or [one might argue] that they should become [the hawk and the quail] by means of that very same action performed in the form of a hawk.
Not the first [alternative], because a doubt regarding what is already contradicted cannot arise;
nor the second.
Since the causality of something belonging to one [entity] by means of abandoning what belongs to its respective parts has never been observed elsewhere, no groundless doubt can arise.
If it is argued that action (*karman*) itself is observed to be such [a cause], we say no;
for that is what is currently being postulated.
But in the theory that action is directly perceived, this fault does not arise, because it is possible to follow the nature of that [action] as it is apprehended.
Furthermore, if action were inferred from conjunction and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "it moves" persisting as long as the entity exists.
If it is argued that [the action] does not exist because the action is destroyed by conjunction, we say no;
for even the destruction of the action is difficult to comprehend according to the doctrine that [such destruction] is imperceptible.
Indeed, the arising of an effect is not invariably concomitant with the destruction of its cause.
By which conjunction and production could the destruction of action be inferred?
For even upon the production of a cloth, the conjunction of the threads and so forth is not destroyed.
Nor has the production of a conjunction ever been experienced as being invariably concomitant with the destruction of action.
If it is argued that as long as the action persists, there is a constant proximity for the arising of conjunctions and so forth,
then does it follow that as long as the cause exists, another effect must be produced?
Let it not be that as long as the conjunction of the threads exists, there is a continuous production of a succession of cloth-pieces.
As long as the existence of karma persists, the production of conjunction is not certain.
Furthermore, since both conjunction and disjunction are imperceptible in the invisible ether (*ākāśa*), there would be no such cognition as "the bird falls through the sky.
If it is argued that this cognition is based on the conjunctions and disjunctions of many birds within the ether, which is a composite entity consisting of extended light-particles, [we reply:]...
Nevertheless, since the impossibility of perceiving the movement of the light from a lamp has not been avoided,
furthermore, the appearance of the movement of the eyes and so forth in the dark would be difficult to account for.

Furthermore, if the motion of Devadatta were inferable in the same way as that of the solar orb, then the cognition of "moving" would arise in both cases; otherwise, it would not arise in either case,
because there is no distinguishing cause.
Furthermore, since the production of conjunction and disjunction is possible through action alone, what is the use of postulating an intermediate action? Thus, the existence of action is untenable.
It is not possible for the production of conjunction and so forth to arise from action;
for it has been established elsewhere that such a specific conjunction and the like initiates an effect either in its own substratum or in that which is inherent in it.

For the conjunction of the body and the self is indeed the cause of the action of the body; how then can conjunction and disjunction with a location in space arise from that [action]? The same should be understood in other cases as well.
Not so;
for if that were the case, it would follow that even the specific conjunctions and other factors that cause action would lack the status of being causes of action,
since a mutual conjunction of threads does not possess the quality of being a cause of motion.
If it is argued that while the absence of that [effect] may apply to conjunction in general, it might still occur for a specific kind of conjunction,
then why would the capacity to initiate [an effect] in another location not likewise apply?

Furthermore, if this were the case, how could action (karman) produce conjunction and so forth elsewhere by abandoning its inherent connection with the substratum and the substrate-inherent [quality]?
If it is argued that this [nature] is established in that very way because it is inferred from such an effect,
then let this nature be postulated by relying on a mere internal distinction of the cause of the action itself;
for indeed, the postulation of a property-bearer (dharmin) is more cumbersome than the postulation of a property (dharma).
Therefore, it is established that action based on perception is indeed perceptible.
Thus ends the section on "Being the Eater" (*attṛtva*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= JNys_1,2.III: Guhādhikaraṇam =======] *3,672* // Now begins the section on the Cave (guhādhikaraṇa) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
Oṃ. For by seeing that [reality], the two selves indeed enter into the cave; Oṃ.
"Because they have entered the cave, for they are both the Selfs; on account of that perception.

Regarding the statement "the two who drink the reward," there arises a doubt: does it refer to the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), or rather to the Supreme Lord alone? On this point, the initial position is that it refers to the individual soul and the Lord.
Why?
This is because of the dual number;
nor can the objection be resolved by the principle of the section concerning the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya),
for there is no subverting evidence [to that effect].

Furthermore, because the experience of the fruits of karma would be impossible [if they were distinct], and because in the view that there is a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), the designation could occur through metaphorical transfer according to the "umbrella-bearer" analogy— this being the position reached— the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that this passage teaches only the one Supreme Self (paramātman),
on account of the characteristic marks of being hidden in the cave and the qualification by the word "Brahman."
In that regard, the experience of the fruit of karma has been established by the Blessed One in the Bhāṣya;
however, a clear resolution for the dual number has not been stated.
Therefore, he says "and duality" in order to provide that resolution.
...and duality is not possible for a single entity. MAnu 1.2.9b.
This is what is meant:
one who asserts that the dual number is untenable when referring to the Supreme Lord alone should be asked,
"In what way is it untenable?"
If it is argued that the dual number denotes duality and that internal differentiation is not appropriate for the Supreme Self, we say no;
for there is no grammatical rule (anuśāsana) stating that the dual number denotes duality.
If it is argued that the number two, which is denoted by the dual number, is contradicted in the Supreme Self both by its non-difference [from all things] and by its oneness, we say no;
for the number two is observed in a jar that possesses oneness through non-difference [of its parts] when it is accompanied by another substance.
Now, if it is thought that duality is not possible for that which is devoid of any other substance because of contradiction,
then this [objection] stands:
not only is the enjoyment of the fruit of karma impossible for one who is free from the phenomena of saṃsāra, [but so too is duality].
However, duality is possible for that which is undivided and which consists solely of the substratum of unity.
In response to the inquiry "How so?", he explains the aphorism "And because of the qualification" (*viśeṣaṇāt*) by another method, stating: "That which is the bridge... (*yaḥ setuḥ*).
And because of the qualification:
"That which is the bridge," for it is qualified by the expression of oneness.
Regarding duality, there is first of all no contradiction characterized by existence and non-existence with respect to non-difference and unity,
because that [contradiction] does not exist.
Nor is there the state of being the victim and the slayer.
Because it would entail the consequence of their coexistence;
however, the absence of identity (tādātmyābhāva) is not relevant to the present context.
Therefore, only non-coexistence (sahānavasthāna) must be asserted.
And the seed for that [inference] is the necessary perception of two things through mutual exclusion;
however, this does not exist [in the present case],
as in the phrase "the two drinking the Truth."
Thus, because the two substrates of duality under discussion are qualified by the singular term “the bridge” (*yaḥ setuḥ*),
there is the comprehension of their being a substrate of non-dual unity; that is to say, they are understood as one.
Nor is there the apprehension of only one [of the two] here,
because there is no differentiator;
by this, the following point is also refuted.

"Regarding the point where the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was established as 'the intellect and the individual soul' by another [author], and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established as 'the individual soul and the Lord'—

for indeed, since the author of the Sūtras, having declared in the aphorism *'But that [is Brahman], because of the harmony [of the texts]'* that the harmony [of the Upaniṣadic passages] refers exclusively to the Supreme Self, it is that very same [Supreme Self] who must be elaborated upon through the explanatory statements."
One who seeks to establish the concordance (*samanvaya*) of this statement regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) would abandon the initial context (*prakrama*).
If it is argued that this fault does not apply because there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), we say no; for such a subverting factor has not been demonstrated.
If you argue that it is a dual number, then there would likewise be no acceptance of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), because their identity is accepted.
If it is argued that the distinction between the two is merely conceptual,
then let duality be established as a twofold nature belonging to the Lord alone by virtue of His marvelous and inconceivable sovereignty;
in this way, the Sūtra would be consistent with its introductory context.
"And the scripture reveals reality.
Now, one might ask: should it not have been stated as "by means of the singular number" (*ekavacanena*)? Why is it stated as "by means of the expression of oneness" (*ekatvavacanena*)?
The meaning of the suffix is [expressed] by numbers such as singularity and so forth,
as it has been said:
"The dual and singular endings are used for two and one."
The meaning is "of duality and unity.
Otherwise, it would have been "in two and in one.
Therefore, it is correct that "the expression of unity" (*ekatvavacana*) means simply the expression of unity.
Elsewhere as well, it should be understood that the designation is primarily intended to express the state (bhāva).
Thus ends the section on the Cave (guhādhikaraṇa) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_1,2.IV: The Section on the Intermediate [Topic] =======] *3,677* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning the intermediate [topic].
Oṃ. [The intermediate state exists] because of the arising [of a new birth] in between. Oṃ.
"Because [the intermediate state] arises in between.
Regarding this, it was stated that the application of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in the form of the absence of action is being considered;
however, that is incorrect.
Since the sūtra asserts only the entity (bhāva) and does not mention action (kriyā), he explains the word *antara* as having both meanings: "antar" [means both].
Abiding within and providing delight, he is declared to be the "Inner One" (Antara);
and because he takes pleasure (ramaṇa) and is perceived by means of the word "Self" (ātman), he is so called.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied by the rule "after the root *ram*, preceded by the word *antaḥ*,

[the suffix] *ḍa* follows when *ñam* is intended"; furthermore, the elision of the prefix (*upapada*) occurs according to the rule "the *uṇādi* suffixes are diverse," and this was indeed the intention of the author of the Sūtras.
Otherwise, as in the case of "Because of the teaching of His attributes within," he would have said "because of the logical possibility of being within";
and in that case, the Sūtra would have been more concise.
By using the word "within" (*antara*), he asserts this very point. But is it not the case that,
"this person who is seen within the space (*antarikṣa*)..."?
"This is the Self," he said;
this is the illustrative statement here,
and in this context, it is understood as being situated within the eye.
It does not possess the status of being the agent of delight;
rather, that which is stated in the Śruti alone must be affirmed by the Sūtras.
To the question, "How then can the author of the Sūtras affirm the agency of delight when it is not mentioned in the Śruti? he says: "And delight... (ramaṇaṃ ca).
The first "and" (ca) indicates that it is not only the state of being situated in the eye, but also the act of delighting and the agency of delighting.
The second "and" indicates that it is not only in the Sūtra, but also in the Śruti.

By the word "ātman"—that is, by this term "this self"—the meaning is according to its etymological derivation (*nirvacana*): that which measures (*māti*) or experiences (*anubhavati*) what is to be taken (*ādeya*), namely what is to be accepted (*upādeya*), such as happiness and the means to happiness.
[The suffix] *kvip* is applied to the roots *dā* preceded by the prefix *ā-* and to the root *man*. (Pāṇini 3.2.680)
And because of the mention of one distinguished by bliss:
the other sūtra, "And because of the mention of one distinguished by bliss," establishes that the other eye is the Supreme Lord.
In this case, the word "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) is redundant because the meaning is already complete by the mere mention of "pleasure.

If it is argued that the word "qualified" is intended to express the relation to pleasure, we say no; for it could equally well have been stated as "by the mention of being possessed of pleasure" (*sukhitva*).
If this were the case, the Sūtra would be unnecessarily brief;
moreover, it would be improper to mention the connection with pleasure [alone] in the passage:
"Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman."
Because the Śruti mentions only "bliss" (sukha), he explains it otherwise as follows: "qualified," etc.
And because it possesses distinguished happiness... // MAnu 1.2.11a //
In this context, the term "distinguished by bliss" does not denote the possession of that [bliss] such that it would be something not to be adopted;
rather, it refers to the excellence of bliss, characterized by its fullness.

For if one were to say simply "because it is designated as pleasure," there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since pleasure exists elsewhere as well; therefore, the inclusion of the qualification is purposeful. Now, how is the analysis (*vigraha*) of this compound to be understood?
[The term] "excellent" means distinguished by happiness.
How then is it said to be "excellent happiness"?
There is no fault here, for this is merely an explanation of the meaning.

For "sukhena śreṣṭhaḥ" would mean that he is best by virtue of that happiness; thus, excellence is a property of happiness. Alternatively, it follows the rule: “kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye” (the words beginning with kaḍāra may optionally precede in a karmadhāraya compound).
Thinking that the qualifier should be placed at the end [of the compound], he stated "qualified happiness" (*viśiṣṭasukha*).
How, then, can the suffix *matup* be employed, since it is not mentioned in the scripture?

This is intended to make it known that [the Self] possesses that [pleasure] by means of its own nature as pleasure through its specific power (*viśeṣa-śakti*). If it is objected: "In this interpretation, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*), because the 'distinctness' (*viśiṣṭatva*) which qualifies pleasure is not mentioned in the scripture," we reply: No.
Because between the primary and the secondary, the primary alone is to be accepted;
and since the excellence of happiness has been stated in the Śruti, he says: "and the state of being Brahman" (brahmatvam). ... "And the state of being Brahman is excellence. (Manu 1.2.11b)
The meaning of the word *brahman* is the state of being Brahman (*brahmatva*), which consists of a specific excellence of bliss and distinction;
that is to say, it is what is expressed by the word *brahman* in the phrase, "What is *ka*? It is *brahman*."
For the word "Brahman" denotes fullness (*pūrṇatā*).
When there is a requirement for a substantive to which it refers, since there is no reason to abandon what is proximate, it connects with "bliss" (*sukha*) alone.
"Because of non-abiding and because of impossibility, it is not the other. (BBs 1.2.17)

Having established that the one within the eye is the Lord (Īśvara), the Sūtra—*anavasthiterasambhavācca netaraḥ* (3.2.39)—is intended to refute the position of the opponent who claimed that it is Agni himself who is spoken of here as the controller of both the eye and the sun. Its meaning is as follows: The meaning of this [Sūtra] is: because of the lack of stability and because of impossibility, it is not the other. 1. **Lack of Stability (Anavasthiti):** If it were Agni, he would have to reside within the eye at all times. However, Agni is observed to be unstable, moving from place to place; he does not remain fixed within the eye. Furthermore, the scriptural description of the "person within the city" (*puruṣa eṣo 'ntarāditye*) and the "person within the eye" (*puruṣo 'ntarakṣiṇi*) implies a single, stable subject, which is inconsistent with the nature of Agni. 2. **Impossibility (Asambhava):** Moreover, it is impossible for Agni to be the controller of the sun. Agni is subordinate to the sun; the sun is the source of light and heat for Agni. It is illogical for a subordinate entity to exercise control over its superior. Furthermore, the qualities attributed to the inner being—such as being the ruler of all, the lord of all, and the source of all worlds—are impossible for the elemental fire. Therefore, the "other" referred to by the opponent is not the intended referent; rather, it is the Supreme Lord. This concludes the refutation of the prima facie argument.

If the fire were the controller of another living being, there would be an infinite regress, as that [second] being would require yet another controller; furthermore, since both possess the same status of being living beings, the relationship of the controlled and the controller is impossible. Therefore, it is not the case that fire is what is referred to here by its abiding in the eyes and so forth. This [objection] is untenable.
Because it contradicts itself.
For we also accept that the souls of Brahmā and others are the controllers of the souls of humans and so forth;
in that case, if the impossibility of another [controller] residing [within them] applies to you, why should it not apply to us as well?
And just as it is not so for us, so it is not so for another; therefore, he prepares the introductory framework (pīṭha) to correctly explain the Sūtra with the words "anyonya" (mutually).
And there would be no mutual determination if there were no divine ordinance.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
The term "of sentient beings," which is to be mentioned later, is also connected here.
"The mutual determination of sentient beings" refers to the state of Brahmā and the others acting as regulators for one another.
However, the state of being subject to restraint for humans and others would only be possible if there were an impelling force in the Lord’s act of restraining;
for otherwise, there would be no possibility of avoiding an infinite regress.
For the chain of impellers ultimately rests upon the Supreme Lord, who is independent of anything else.

By His decree, the relationship of the constrained and the constrainer will exist among others. In the absence of the Lord as the ultimate restrainer, a mutual constraint between things would not be possible.
Because there would be no means to avoid the impossibility of non-cessation [of bondage].
Now, one might object: "The distinction that Brahmā and others are the controllers (*niyāmaka*) while humans and others are the controlled (*niyamya*) is simply their inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
To this we reply: as he will state later, "Nor is it based on office," and because [this distinction] persists even in liberation (*mokṣa*).

Because of the statement, "due to what is said regarding those situated in the presiding maṇḍala," and because one might ask, "In our own system, what indeed is the dependence upon the Supreme Lord? he says: "of sentient beings."
The specific nature of volitions, which is also derived from the Lord, [is what constitutes merit].
The distinction characterized by the relationship between the governed and the governor that exists among conscious beings such as Brahmā and others, as well as humans and others,
is simply their inherent nature (svabhāva).
"Nothing exists, whether moving or unmoving, that could be without me," according to this statement;
otherwise, the Lord's sovereignty over all things would not be possible.
Furthermore, others might maintain independence;
for others have accepted that even though space is beginningless, its status as a substance depends upon its possession of qualities (guṇavattva),
and by the Advaitins, the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman is held to depend upon ignorance (avidyā).
For that which is always governed by a lord is called its "nature" (*svabhāva*),
whereas that which is [governed] only occasionally is called "non-nature" (*asvabhāva*). (*3,685*)
If this is so, what follows? He says—namely, that the meaning of the Sūtra is established without self-contradiction—by means of the words "mutually" (*anyonya*).
Therefore, if there were mutual restriction, there would be either an infinite regress or an impossibility.

The meaning is as follows: since a mutual restriction is logical only when God is accepted, and not otherwise, it is therefore correct that the author of the Sūtras stated the fallacies of infinite regress (*anavasthiti*) and impossibility (*asambhava*) when an opponent attempts to establish a mutual restriction without accepting God.
Now, one might ask: what is the difference between infinite regress and impossibility?
Because in both cases there is an equal impossibility of activity. It is said in reply:
for in the case of infinite regress, activity is blocked because its root is not established beforehand.
But when [the existence of the property] is impossible, the distinction lies in its being understood through similarity and non-exclusion;
for example, it is said in response to one who claims that "smell is perceived in water because of its connection with earth": [this is not so].
"Why could it not be that its perception [of water] occurs on earth due to a connection with water?
For there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary].
By this, it is stated that this articulation of a fault is directed against one who does not maintain the existence of a Lord (anīśvaravādin).
To the question, "What is the fault in one who asserts that, having accepted Īśvara, Agni is spoken of here as being situated within the eye and the sun? he says:
"If Īśvara is indeed the controller, and he alone is the one first encountered, why is he set aside? Why is there this useless postulation of another [deity]? (Manu 1.2.13)

If Īśvara were accepted as the controller of all, then why would they abandon Him—who is the first-arrived one, perceived through such means of knowledge as immortality and so forth by virtue of His abiding directly within the sun? Furthermore, for what reason is the postulation made that He exists among Īśvara and the sun and others merely as a redundant supervisor of fire?
[This is because] those arguments leading to the prima facie position have already been refuted in the Bhāṣya.
It has been stated that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for either abandoning the Lord (*īśvara*) or postulating fire in the middle.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "It is faulty" (*doṣavatī*).
Therefore, that [marriage] should never be performed in any way if it is defective.
The fault consists in the abandonment of what is heard and the assumption of what is not heard.
By the first word "eva" (only), he states that these two faults are unavoidable.
Therefore, because there is an absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in both cases.
That conception of remaining [in the center] by abandoning the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) should be understood as expressing an alternative meaning of the sūtra;
for there is no basis for conceiving of a stay in the middle of the fire.
And because it is impossible to abandon the Lord (Īśvara) who has already been understood [in other contexts], it cannot be anyone else.
This is what is meant:
regarding the fire that is being presented here as residing in the eye and the sun, is this stated without accepting an independent Lord?
Alternatively, having raised the alternative "or by admitting [the existence of God]," the author of the Sūtras stated the refutation for both positions;

or else, having determined that the opponent is a non-theist (nirīśvara), the author of the Sūtras stated the [fallacies of] infinite regress and impossibility— such is the meaning of the preceding text.
To the question "How is that certain?", he says: "If [it were] God... and so forth.
If the Lord who controls all were accepted by the opponent,
then why would he, being the first to arrive, be set aside? And for what reason is this useless hypothesis of his existence maintained?
However, because it would lack a basis (*nirnimitta*), that [position] should not be undertaken at all;
for the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) is by no means devoid of foresight,
otherwise he would be as fit to be disregarded as a madman.
The proponent is certainly not entirely lacking in discernment;
for if that were the case, he would be as worthy of neglect as a madman, yet he has formulated all these conceptual constructions.
Therefore, we understand that the intention of the author of the Sūtras is this: "This [proponent] is one who denies the Lord."

[======= Section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) =======] *3,689* // Oṃ. The Inner Ruler [is the Supreme Self] with respect to the divine and other realms, because his specific attributes are designated [in the scripture]. Oṃ. //
The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) is [the Self] because his attributes are designated in relation to the deities, the worlds, and so forth.
[Objection: But this has already been established by the immediately preceding [section];
for being the Inner Ruler consists in being a controller while abiding within.
This very point was stated as "upapatterantara" (due to another reason).

Nor is it intended that there is no regulating factor (*niyāmakatva*) in that case; for if that were so, the objection—"because of non-abiding and impossibility"—would result in being irrelevant. Therefore, in order to demonstrate the distinction between the objects of knowledge (*prameya-bheda*), he states the doubt to be removed by this section: "ramaṇam" (pleasure).
Delight does not belong to one who exerts excessive effort; it arises precisely from the absence of distraction.
In the previous section, it was stated that Hari, abiding in the eyes and other organs, is their impeller while they experience pleasure;
that is incorrect, because it is self-contradictory.
Indeed, one must apply extreme effort for the sake of restraining the sun and other [planets],
because it is observed that effort conforms to its function;
and for one who exerts excessive effort, mental distraction is inevitable.
Furthermore, delight is not possible for one whose mind is distracted;
therefore, to be both a regulator and one possessed of delight is a contradiction.
And what is contradictory cannot be established even by a hundred reasons.
As it has been said: "And from such manifold activity, there would be even greater affliction.
The word *eva* is used for the purpose of ascertaining the previously stated pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
With this as the solution, the author states the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) with a hidden intention, beginning with: "If it be argued... (*iti cet*).
If this is so, why can there not be a universal restriction for everyone?
In this context, the remainder of the sentence is "this is the answer.
For that Supreme Lord who possesses the universal governance and the state of being the inner ruler of all—why can his sporting not be possible? This is the subject under discussion.
The intention is that, in order to dispel this doubt, the state of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all is stated here as the reason.
[Objection: But is this not like giving a *khārī* measure of oil to one who has gone to beg for a mere *piṇyāka* cake?
For, it was argued that since the one who governs the sun and other deities is subject to mental distraction, his taking pleasure [in the body] is not logical.
The state of being the controller of all has been stated;
for, due to excessive distraction of the mind resulting from that, pleasure cannot arise.
Therefore, he reveals the underlying intention with the words: "by one's own self."
For an object that is not restricted by its own nature would indeed be opposed to itself;
but how could that which possesses its own inherent existence, power, and so forth, be opposed to itself?
It is observed that whatever object is not determined by Devadatta himself— meaning its existence, cognition, and activity do not depend on Devadatta—
that very object becomes contrary to Devadatta’s own self and causes distraction of his mind;
however, this world has its existence and so forth dependent upon the Lord of the World.
How, then, could that cause distraction of his mind?
Or rather, if this universe were not regulated by the Lord who is one's own self,
it would not possess existence and other attributes dependent upon Him.

For at that very time, it would be contrary to the nature of the Supreme Lord; and one should apply the thought that this is not so. The state of being the Inner Controller (*antaryāmitva*) is not merely the status of a regulator, as in the case of a king or similar authority.
Rather, it is said that [the Lord] is the bestower of existence and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmyadhikaraṇa) in the venerable Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_1.2.VI: Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇam =======] *3,692* // Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning invisibility (adṛśyatvādhikaraṇam).
// Oṃ. [The Brahman] possesses qualities such as invisibility, because of the statement of its attributes. Oṃ.//
"Because of the mention of its attributes, [Brahman is] that which has the qualities of being invisible and so forth" (BBs 1.2.21).
Here, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of those attributes—such as invisibility and the rest—stated in the passage beginning with "that which is invisible," is established as belonging to Brahman.

Since their nature as the very essence of Brahman has been accepted according to the method explained above, the author raises an objection against any further doubt regarding this by using the word "guṇa" (attribute).
If entities such as qualities and actions were non-different [from Brahman],
how could non-difference be compatible with Brahman, whose nature is the absence of [such] attributes?
If qualities such as bliss, actions such as withdrawal,
states such as omnipresence, forms such as those consisting of food (annamaya), and limbs such as the tail are accepted as non-different [from Brahman], then they might indeed be so;
for there is no impossibility in their being real entities, as will be explained later.
Furthermore, since other untenable positions have already been refuted,
it is not logical that qualities such as invisibility and so forth are non-different from Brahman;
for those qualities are non-existent, whereas Brahman is existent.
[The opponent objects: "Because the identity of existence and non-existence is contradictory. [The author] replies: "Not non-existence."
And the distinction that "non-existence is not existence" would generally prevail.

For here, that which is other than the visible is the invisible; its state is invisibility (*adṛśyatva*). Thus, by words such as "invisibility" and so forth, the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the visible and so on is denoted—just as that which is other than a horse is a non-horse (*anaśva*), and its state is non-horseness (*anaśvatva*).
Furthermore, it is not its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and so forth,
because a compound is impossible due to a lack of semantic compatibility.
If it is argued that the meaning [of the term] should be "the state of being opposed to the visible and so forth," we say no;
for the types of opposition characterized by non-coexistence, mutual destruction, the relation of killer and killed, and existence and non-existence are impossible [in this case].
And since the contradiction of identity does not exceed mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*),
then, because non-existence is mutual non-existence and existence is [its opposite], there would be no distinction or difference between these two even in the world.
This being the case, what inconsistency could there be with respect to Brahman itself?
The word "mostly" (*prāyaśaḥ*) was stated with the intention of what will be explained by the phrase "for its absence" (*tadabhāvo hi*).

Alternatively, since all four types of absence (*abhāva*) might be understood by the term "absence," the word "mostly" was stated (expressed) in order to include specifically mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*).
For mutual absence [is distinct] from prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the others.

It is more extensive because it is restricted to each individual object, and because there is no prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) or other such absences that possess an eternal and beginningless relation.
[Objection: But surely, relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) is distinct from prior absence, destructive absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*).
Is it different from the substratum (dharmin) or non-different? Not the first, because it would follow that even Brahman would possess differentiation.
And likewise, because this would contradict such scriptural passages as "Thus are all phenomena," and so forth;
nor should it be said that this [teaching] is not heard regarding Brahman.
Because it is well known through such expressions as "without lineage" (*agotra*) and "without color" (*avarṇa*),
that which lacks lineage and so forth is indeed described in that way.
In the second [case], what is the purpose of determining it by means of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)?
One should simply say "non-existence," for in that way, there would be an explanation of all the scriptures.
To this, we reply:
The prior non-existence and other forms of non-existence are indeed distinct from the substratum (dharmin),
because they do not perish even when the substratum perishes.
For instance, even when the ground where there is an absence of a jar is destroyed by digging and so forth, the absence of the jar continues to persist.
Furthermore, the status of being a locus (*dharmitva*) for the ground and so forth is merely conventional (*prātītika*), not established by reality.

For this very reason, after stating that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a distinct category (*tattvāntara*) just like existence (*bhāva*), [the author] declares that mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is the very nature of the locus (*dharmisvarūpa*) because its essence consists of both existence and non-existence.
[Objection: But in that case, would it not follow that Brahman is likewise [merely conventional]?
True;
for the absence of connection with genus and so forth is admitted to be distinct from Brahman.
For just as a staff is a qualification of Devadatta,
so too the absence of lineage and other such attributes is a qualification of Brahman;
and there is no contradiction with the Śruti.
This is because, in that case, the state of possessing the absence of being [the object] is intended to be expressed as its *dharmatā* (essential nature).
Furthermore, such a conceptualization does not apply to Ānanda and others, as it is said:
"Ānanda is Brahman."
Because of such statements as these,
and because there is no subverting evidence,
therefore mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) itself is the very nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*) in other cases; thus, it must likewise be accepted in the case of Brahman as well.

However, since the state of being devoid of genus (*gotra*) and so forth is itself of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), there is no inconsistency whatsoever in its being the very essence of Brahman; thus, this point is not further investigated here.
But he who does not accept anywhere that mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpatā*) should be questioned as follows:
What is the cause of this non-acceptance?
Is it due to contradiction, or rather due to the absence of valid cognition?
Now, if it is argued that [the property] is excluded because of the existence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*),
then it must be explained how there is a contradiction between mutual non-exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*) and the locus (*dharmin*).
If it is claimed that this is due to their being of the nature of affirmation and negation, respectively:
How is that so? If it is argued that it is because of the presence or absence of the negative particle (*nañ*), he says in response: "The non-existence of that" (*atadbhāva*).
"Non-existence of that [identity] and otherness—there is no difference whatsoever between them."
For the cloth's state of being a non-pot and its difference from a pot are one and the same;
this is because no distinction is perceived between the two expressions "it is a non-pot" and "it is other than a pot.
Furthermore, since the employment and non-employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) do occur, there is a deviation [in the logical reason]; such is the meaning.
In another place, he demonstrates the fallacy of deviation: "the absence of defects."
Even among worldly people, it is well known that the absence of defects constitutes a quality.
Health is a quality, and non-cruelty is a quality; thus, the absence of disease and so forth— which is the negation that is the object of the application of the negative particle (*nañ*)—
possesses the nature of a positive injunction and the nature of a quality, insofar as it is not the object of the application of the negative particle.
This is well known in both worldly and Vedic transactions;
furthermore, this is an illustration,
for lack of magnanimity is a fault.
Thus, it is well known that the absence of a quality constitutes a fault;
for this reason as well, "inconstancy" (vyabhicāra) is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the demonstration that mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is the very nature of the locus (dharmisvarūpa) is not a mere product of imagination.
However, in order to show that this is also the intention of the author of the Sūtras,
he says— “adṛśyatvādikān” (those beginning with invisibility)— indicating that this very deviation was pointed out by the author of the Sūtras as well.
Therefore, the Lord himself has declared such qualities as invisibility and the rest.

Since the employment or non-employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) does not constitute a contradiction with non-difference, the author of the Sūtras—in order to indicate that very point—states that [the Self] "has qualities such as invisibility" (*adṛśyatvādiguṇaka*); he thus asserts the identity between the qualities such as invisibility, which are expressed by the negative particle, and those qualities that are not of that nature. Otherwise, he would have said "visibility and so forth" (*dṛśyatvādi*).

By this [argument], contradiction (*virodha*)—whether characterized by having a counter-correlate (*sapratyiyogitva*) or lacking a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogikatva*)—should also be understood as refuted.
[Objection: If existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) were thus identical, then the contradiction defined by existence and non-existence would not exist anywhere;
and if that [contradiction] were absent, even the very report of contradiction would vanish.
If it is argued that there is a direct contradiction between existence and non-existence, and through them, between their respective loci,
we ask: do you assert a contradiction between existence and non-existence in their unqualified forms and thereby deduce the absence of the other, or between them as delimited?
Regarding the first [alternative], however, he says that it is the production of radiance: "bhāva... and so forth.
Furthermore, the contradiction between existence and non-existence does not prevail everywhere.
By the word "everywhere" (sarvatra), he indicates its non-distinctness;
the sense is that the absence of a cloth is observed where there is a jar.
Regarding the second [alternative], however, the sense is that the probans (āpādaka) is unestablished (asiddhi); with this intention, he states its nature: "For the absence of that... and so forth.
For the absence of that is the opposite of its presence; it is nothing other than that.
He indicates the well-known nature of experience in both cases by means of the word "hi" (for/indeed).
[Objection: But does not all this fall within the third [category]?
[Reply: True.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, for it is considered separately defiled due to its intensity.
Let us then consider the second position: that there is a lack of evidence for the fact that mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is the very nature of the locus (dharmisvarūpa).
This is not so; for it must be accepted by everyone that difference (bheda) is the essential nature of a thing.
Otherwise, there would follow the fault of infinite regress and so forth;
furthermore, since it is impossible for non-existence (*abhāva*) to have a nature distinct from its own essence, it would entail the absence of difference (*bhedābhāva*).
Moreover, since mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is nothing other than difference itself, how could it not be the very nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpatva*)? *3,706*
Now, it might be thought:
"We accept that difference is threefold:
distinctness (*pṛthaktvam*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)."
And [the category] "own-nature" (svarūpa).
Among these, all three types are possible in the case of substance (dravya),
whereas in the pentad beginning with quality (guṇa), only two types are possible.
Since distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) cannot exist there because it is a quality (*guṇa*),
whereas in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), there is simply a difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*);
for if one were to accept mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) in that case, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, although mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is a type of difference, and although difference itself is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of things],...

Reciprocal non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) does not have the nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*), because reciprocal non-existence is a distinctness that is separate from the difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*); therefore, he says: "as separateness" (*pṛthaktva*).
If they imagine three distinct differences based on the absence of separateness and its nature,
then the faults such as the excessive burden of conceptualization (kalpanā-gaurava) and others will arise there as contradictions.

Non-existence is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). That which has that as its nature—wherein the subject (*dharmin*) is of that form—is "of that form" (*tadrūpa*). By the inclusion of the word "first" (*ādya*), both the abandonment of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved are included.
In that context, however, the meaning is: "if one were to conceive it in such a way."

To address the objection that accepting distinctions among separateness (*pṛthaktva*), mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and essential difference (*svarūpabheda*) would entail the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*) and so forth, he says: "As for separateness... (*pṛthaktva...*).
The distinctions of separateness, otherness, and difference are always expressed through synonyms by worldly people, and likewise in every respect by those who follow the Vedas.
Otherness (*anyatva*) is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Difference (*bheda*) is difference of intrinsic nature (*svarūpabheda*), as in: "A cloth is distinct from a jar; it is not a jar, but rather a cloth.
Otherness, mutual non-existence, and difference of intrinsic nature are all employed by both worldly and Vedic people as synonyms, either sequentially or individually, within distinct sentences.
It is never by means of entering into a single statement.
This is what is meant:

just as the conventional designations "jar," "pitcher," and "pot" are synonyms, and since they arise from one and the same cause, to postulate multiple causes such as "jar-ness" and so forth would involve the fault of conceptual proliferation (*kalpanā-gaurava*).

Just as those who perform conventional designations such as "pot" and so forth perceive their cause as being a single unity precisely because they employ these designations alternately, so too, if one were to accept that [the cause] consists of three, there would be the abandonment of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved.
Thus, [regarding] individuality...

Since even the primary linguistic usages are synonymous, and since their function is accomplished by a single distinction of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), it would involve conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*) to postulate three distinct causes.
For it is observed that those who invariably do not employ them together regard difference and so forth as being one and the same.
If one were to conceive of a triad by means of excluding that [duality], there would be the abandonment of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved.
If it is argued that there is no simultaneous usage because of their inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*),
then let there not be the usage "the pot does not exist" immediately after saying "separate from the pot."
Having stated "it is not a jar," why should one not say "it is separate from the jar"?

For it has been demonstrated by the opponent himself that while separateness (*pṛthaktva*) necessarily entails mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and so forth, mutual non-existence does not necessarily entail separateness.
Furthermore, there is no such rule that what is invariably concomitant must not be mentioned together.

If it is argued that the properties of earth, water, fire, air, and mind— such as possessing action, corporeality, priority, posteriority, and velocity— are established by the very observation of their usage in that [author’s] own text,
and that ordinary people (*laukika*), being intent only on practical purpose,
do not employ them all together because the purpose is accomplished through the usage of even one of them, we say no.
For even the followers of the Veda conduct themselves in this very same way;
thus it has been said:
"even by the followers of the Veda."
Furthermore, the postulation of a difference in the application of synonyms could only occur if there were some instance where they were not applied as synonyms;
otherwise, such a consequence would absurdly follow even in the case of conventional usage regarding jars and the like,
yet this is not the case.
How else could such a groundless conceptualization be tenable?
This has also been stated by the words "in every way" (*sarvaśaḥ*) and "constantly" (*satatam*).
Now, it might be thought:
first of all, there is a clear distinction between separateness (*pṛthaktva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*);
for while separateness is defined by reference to a limit (*avadhi*).
Mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), however, is defined by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Furthermore, the rule "anyārāditarart-" prescribes the ablative case (*pañcamī*) when used in conjunction with words expressing distinctness (*pṛthaktva*).
This is because of the statement that "the word *anya* signifies a different object (*arthagrahaṇa*).

Otherwise, in expressions such as "the cloth is different from the jar" (*bhinno ghaṭāt paṭaḥ*) or "the cloth is another object than the jar" (*arthāntaraṃ ghaṭāt paṭaḥ*), the ablative case would not occur,
as there is no other grammatical rule [to account for it].
And thus, if mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) were simply separateness (*pṛthaktva*), then in the case of "the cloth is not a pot," the ablative case would also have to occur;
but such is not the case.
Therefore, we know that separateness is something other [than mutual non-existence].
And "mutual non-existence" (anyonyābhāva) is distinct from these two;
furthermore, the distinction of essential nature (svarūpabheda) is distinguished from both of these,

But how can that establish its being the supreme Self?

Because it is possible [to apply the term] elsewhere as well, he explains [the reason] by saying: "because He is the Lord of all. (4.15) "Because of the teaching that the Plenum (bhūman) is superior to the state of perfect serenity (saṃprasāda), [it follows that] the Plenum is Viṣṇu, who possesses an abundance of bliss. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23.1; Mahābhārata Anuśāsana Parvan 1.3.2cd) ...Because He is the Lord of all, the Plenum is Viṣṇu, who is supreme in bliss. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.3.2cd)
The prefix *adhi* indeed denotes the Lord (*īśvara*). Thus, since no specific [deity] is mentioned, it follows that He is the Lord of all. Nor is this unproven.
Because it has been stated that name, speech, and so forth possess a progressively superior sovereignty over one another.
[Objection: "In that case, does it not follow that the phrase 'from serene joy' (samprasādāt) is redundant, since it is not required? [Response: No;
with the intention of stating a further reason, he explains: "It is characterized by an abundance of pleasure" (sukhādhika).
That by which one becomes serene is *prasāda*, which is bliss (*sukha*).
Perfect serenity is *samprasāda*.
By accepting the relationship between quality and the possessor of qualities, the intended meaning—that [the self] is superior to pleasure—is stated.
"Since" (yasmāt), therefore (tasmāt); the word "therefore" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. *4,18*
[======= Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa) =======] Oṃ. It is the Imperishable, because it supports everything up to the ether. Oṃ.
"The Imperishable, because it supports everything up to the ether.
(Brahma Sūtra 1.3.10) It has been stated that the "Imperishable" mentioned in the passage, "This indeed is that Imperishable, O Gārgī," is none other than Brahman.
In this regard, the Sūtra says:
Oṃ, and because of the exclusion of other states, Oṃ.

This has been explained in the Commentary as stating another reason for establishing that this syllable is Brahman; furthermore, it is now explained by the words "therefore, as if contradictory," etc., as serving to resolve an objection. To explain:
This is not the imperishable Brahman:

"It is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long; it is without redness, without shadow, without darkness, without air, and without space; it is unattached, without taste, without speech, without mind, without eyes, without breath, without happiness (or lineage), without measure, without interior and without exterior; it eats nothing whatsoever."
Because the syllable *it* is heard as being "not gross" and so forth;
and this [quality] is not possible for Brahman.
For by words such as "not gross," there would either be the designation of minuteness (*aṇutva*) and the like, which are the opposites of grossness and so forth.
Or [the term "not gross"] may terminate merely in the exclusion of grossness and so forth.
In the first case, there is a mutual contradiction;
for by the phrase "not gross," an atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*) would have to be expressed.
And by the term "not minute" (anaṇu), largeness (mahattva) is indicated;
yet it is not logical for both to exist in one [entity],
since they are observed to function through mutual exclusion.
In the same way, a contradiction should be seen here in the statement "neither short nor long.

Nor can the contradiction be avoided by resorting to the view that a single entity endowed with a specific dimension is called "minute," "large," "long," or "short" depending on its relation to something superior;
for, like a jar or other such objects, it would be inexpressible [as possessing those qualities].

Furthermore, because there is no other substance with superior or inferior dimensions, in the second case it follows that Brahman is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). And thus [the Sūtra says]: "Because of the teaching well-established everywhere."

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with what was stated [in the sūtra]: "The Self [is meant], because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving, and because of the presentation of form."
In this regard, having first accepted the initial position, he states the rebuttal indicated by the word "ca" (and): "ataḥ" (therefore).
And because of the exclusion of other states:

"Therefore, having explained even that which appears as contradictory, one should apply the statement—though endowed with seemingly contradictory characteristics—to Hari in its true sense. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.3.3)
Brahman alone... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.3.4a //

Since Brahman is indeed endowed with characteristics that appear contradictory, therefore— even though a statement may appear to convey two mutually opposed meanings, or even if it is not clearly perceived— it must be explained according to its true nature and applied to Hari; this is the intended construction (*yojanā*), meaning it is capable of being so applied.

Alternatively, since the identity of the Imperishable with Viṣṇu has been established through its support of the sky and other attributes, one should explain even those passages that appear contradictory by interpreting them according to their true meaning and applying them to Hari.
In response to the inquiry, "How is this explained according to the true meaning?", the word "by means of contradictions" (*viruddhaiḥ*) is connected [to the previous argument].
Or else, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be connected with what precedes.
Since Viṣṇu is superior to happiness, therefore He is the Plenum (*bhūman*).
[In the phrase] "as if contradictory" (*viruddhavat*), the word "contradictory" (*viruddhaiḥ*) is connected as the reason for the proposition. This is what is meant:
*4,19* This is what is being stated:

It cannot be argued that if the Imperishable (akṣara) were Brahman, there would be no scope for such scriptural passages as "not gross" (asthūla) and so forth; for we accept the interpretation that words such as "not gross" denote qualities like minuteness (aṇutva) which are the opposite of those [grossness and so on]. Nor can it be said that, this being the case, there is a mutual contradiction between the texts.
This is because the subsistence of contradictory attributes in Brahman is established by the Śruti and other authorities. [Objection:
It has been stated that Brahman is endowed with contradictory characteristics;
however, this is a contradiction, like saying "my mother is barren."
For if largeness, smallness, and so forth are contradictory,
how then could that which is endowed with them be one?
This is because contradiction consists in the impossibility of coexistence.
If that one [entity] were joined with them, how then could they be contradictory?
Anticipating the objection that this is because coexistence is the very nature of non-contradiction, he states and explains: "Those... (tāni).
Those characteristics exist in Him, yet they do not exist elsewhere;
however, attributes such as "not gross" and so forth exist in Govinda without contradiction.
By this statement, "Brahman is endowed with contradictory characteristics," we intend the following:

those marks such as "not gross" and so forth, as well as "atomicity" and "greatness" and so forth—which do not exist together elsewhere than in Brahman—exist indeed together in Govinda without contradiction; that is to say, they coexist.

However, it is not asserted that they abide in one place while accepting their mutual contradiction, which would result in a logical inconsistency. This is the meaning of the particle *ca*, used here for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
By the word "Govinda," he indicates that even the direct perception of Yaśodā and others is an authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding this matter. This is the underlying intention:
why should atomicity, magnitude, and so forth not be accepted in Brahman simply because of a lack of evidence?
Or is it because of contradiction? Not the first, [as in the statement]:
"Subtler than the subtle."

This is because, in that case, the authority [of the argument] rests upon such scripture as this, upon the inference from the observation of both effects, and upon the aforementioned direct perception.
Regarding the second [alternative], is there a contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is there a mutual contradiction?
It is not the first.

Because no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is seen that contradicts [the absence of parts], whereas [the existence of] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth is contradicted by the aforementioned means of cognition and is therefore "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
Furthermore, does the conjunction of atoms with space occur in a single part of space?
Or is it space itself?
In the first case, what is meant by "a part"— is it a constituent member (*avayava*), or a distinct location (*pradeśabheda*)?
Not the first,
because it is not accepted [by us].
As for the second, is this [space] the very nature of space itself, or is it something else?
The first [alternative] is included within the last;
the second is also contradicted by one's own admission; but if one accepts that [the self] is adventitious (aupādhika), there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya) and so forth.
Not the second [alternative],
because it would follow that the conjunction with a drum would also possess that same nature; and if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving sound everywhere.

Therefore, space must be admitted as atomic for the sake of conjunction with atoms; thus, there is a deviation [from the rule]. Nor is the second alternative tenable, because of mutual contradiction everywhere else.
For that [contradiction] must be conceived either because it is observed everywhere as non-coexistence, or only in some cases; or else,
is it everywhere except for those points of dispute?
Not the first,
because coexistence with Brahman is seen through scripture and other means;
nor the second.
This is because, although space and mind exist in mutual exclusion, there is no contradiction between their respective properties of being an element (*bhūtatva*) and being formless (*amūrtatva*);
otherwise, both would not exist in earth and the other elements. Nor is it the third [alternative].

For it would follow that there is an impossibility of the coexistence of eternity and being knowledge, as well as bodilessness and being an agent— qualities which everywhere else exist in a state of mutual exclusion— within the intellect of God and within God himself. Furthermore, for one who accepts that conjunction and the like reside in specific locations (pradeśavṛtti), it is not appropriate to accept that such location-residence constitutes residence in parts (avayavavṛtti).
Because that [property] is absent in space and so forth;
and because if one were to admit that a property belonging to one thing could reside in another, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Rather, what must be stated is simply the state of having a common locus with its own absolute non-existence.
And thus, since existence and non-existence are everywhere else found to be unable to coexist, how could there not be a contradiction?
If you say "because they are observed [to coexist]," that applies equally to the case at hand as well.
Therefore, nothing remains but the mere question: "How indeed can those things which are everywhere else found to be unable to coexist actually coexist?"
In this regard, the resolution is that the very nature of the entity (*vastu-svabhāva*) is simply such. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
because that [undesired consequence] is excluded by the presence or absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that this being so, no systematic arrangement of statements should be adopted anywhere, we say no;
for when determining the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one must accept that "it is thus.
For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsā is not rendered useless. *4,34*
Thus far, the scriptural passage's subject matter being Brahman has been established by adopting the position that words such as "not gross" (asthūla) denote minuteness (aṇutva) and so forth.

Now, he explains the Sūtra with the intent that there is no fault even if [the passage] is intended to signify the cessation of grossness and other qualities—namely, with the words "anyā... (others...).
The Śruti declares the removal of other entities' natures, such as grossness and so forth, in the case of Nārāyaṇa; it does not, however, state that he lacks his own nature.

Other entities than Brahman are objects such as jars and the like; those which are of the nature of that [Brahman]—namely, grossness and so forth—which are insentient, dependent, effects, subject to destruction, and which cannot coexist with atomicity and other such qualities—in the absence of such grossness and so forth in Nārāyaṇa, it is said: "neither gross nor atomic."
Such is what the scripture declares;

however, its meaning is not that [the world] lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva), for if it were so, there would be a contradiction with what has been stated. Why, then, is the meaning of the scripture thus restricted?
One might ask: "Why could it not be that the very meaning is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*)? To this, he says: "*Sarvadharmā*...
"Regarding this [matter], the Vedic revelation (*śruti*)—beginning with 'All dharmas, all names, all actions, and qualities have been heard of;
faults have also been heard of, but they are not [to be practiced]' and so forth—is the authoritative means of knowledge. (Manu 1.3.6)
The meaning here is that not only in this case, but also regarding the previously mentioned atomicity, magnitude, and so forth, the Supreme Lord possesses an intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvatva*).
In this context, in the passage beginning with "the doctrine of the shadow" (*ācchāyamatama*), it should be understood that there is indeed an unrestricted function (*asaṅkucitavṛttitva*).
Having formulated this explanation by means of its own words (*svaśabdena*) because it was obscured by many terms, the author of the Sūtras—
By means of the word "ca" (and), he has combined with it the previous explanation which concerned only a few words.
From this point onward, the subsequent sūtras have clear meanings within the Bhāṣya itself; therefore, there is nothing further to be said regarding them.
It was also promised: "I shall provide an exposition of the Vidyā known as Paramā.

For the sake of establishing both of these, he briefly demonstrates the principles of the subject matter, the prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa), and the established conclusions (siddhānta) regarding the sections and topics of this chapter, beginning with the word "liṅga."
The indicative mark, the commonality, the words, the location, the indicative mark, and the favor;
again, the words, the indicative mark, and the words—these are to be examined here as they occur twice.
Excessiveness, the non-mention of gendered words, contradiction, non-perception, absence of positive concomitance, and confusion regarding contrary scriptural statements. (Manu Smṛti 1.3.8)

The delusion that there is an absence of scope for the [Vedic] indicative mark (liṅga), the same regarding the pair [of marks], the plurality of such [marks], the contradiction of what has been stated, and the resulting understanding of the meaning— these are the arguments against the prima facie positions (pūrvapakṣas) in the verse beginning with "all this. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.3.9)
