But those very [reasonings] that are powerful, being devoid of any other alternative, are to be known as the established conclusions (*siddhānta*); and they are seen everywhere.
And since this has been explained by the Teacher himself in the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*, it should be understood from that very source.

Having stated the principles of the established doctrine (*siddhāntanyāya*) indicated by the sūtras, he also speaks of those explicitly mentioned [in the sūtras] with the words "mukta" (liberated), etc.

The state of being approached by the liberated, superiority over the vital breaths, as well as distinction from all else, the nature of his own being, and likewise action preceded by reflection; 1.3.11.

The state of being a sovereign, the imitation of the sun and other luminaries, the name Vāmana, the trembling of all things, and the fact that those words cannot be established by anything else [belong to him]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.3.12)
The state of being nameless and formless, the status of being the foundational authority for all distinctions,
and [the powers] such as universal sovereignty and the rest— these were demonstrated by the Lord of the Vedas.
For this very reason, after stating previously that they "are seen," it is stated here that they "are demonstrated.
The phrase "in every way likewise" connects both with what precedes and with what follows:
namely, "likewise [there is] superiority over the vital breath (prāṇa)," and "likewise [there is] superiority in every respect."

The intrinsic nature [of Brahman] is distinct from everything, as is the case with the support of the sky and so forth; the word "tathā" (thus) in the phrase "action preceded by reflection is thus" is connected with what follows,
thereby including such qualities as being free from evil.

The meaning is as follows: the imitation of the sun and so forth, as well as the quality of illuminating everything, and the fact that those [specific] words cannot be established by anything else—this constitutes the impossibility of the word *jyotis* (light) applying to anything other [than Brahman]. That which has a supporting means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is described as such; the state of being that is "the state of having a supporting means of knowledge" (*upajīvyapramāṇatā*).

"Tāḥ" refers to the arguments for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Now, it may be objected that fourteen topics (*adhikaraṇa*) are understood from the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) in this section (*pāda*), yet only twelve subjects (*viṣaya*), along with their prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and established (*siddhānta*) arguments, have been stated here; and a topic cannot possibly exist without its subject matter and other such elements.
If it is asked how this is so, it is as follows:

"Bādarāyaṇa [holds that there is eligibility] even above that, because of the possibility; for [the Śūdra's status] is indicated by the hearing of his grief regarding that [exclusion], and by his running toward it."
These two sections are not for the purpose of establishing *samanvaya* (the concordance of the Vedas with Brahman).

Rather, the first is for the purpose of establishing the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of gods and others for Vedic knowledge, while the second is for the purpose of establishing the absence of such eligibility for those outside the three *varṇas*. It is to make this known that there is no mention of the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth of these two sections.
Otherwise, even in that case, students would fall into the error of fruitless exertion by searching for a relationship of concomitance (*samanvaya*). [Objection:
But surely these two points need not be investigated here, because they are irrelevant.
For instance, conjunction is of two kinds:
that characterized by inclusion and that characterized by immediate succession.
In that regard, first of all, the former [of these two topics] is not possible within these two sections (*adhikaraṇa*),
because you yourselves have stated that it is not included in the first chapter characterized by "Concordance" (*samanvaya*);
and since those which are not included in a chapter cannot possibly be included in a section (*pāda*).
The *uttara* (subsequent) [connection] is also sixfold, distinguished as:
incidental (*prasaṅga*), introductory (*upodghāta*), arrived at its proper occasion (*avasara-prāpta*), causal (*kāraṇa*), effectual (*kārya*), and having a single purpose (*ekakāryatva*).
Among these, first of all, it does not exist in the first [sense].
Because there is no recollector [of it],
the second [alternative] is not [tenable];
for the matter at hand would be established even without that.
Not the third,
because it is already included within the remainder of the possession [of the faculties].
Not the fourth.
The fifth case is not applicable because no cause for a subsequent series is perceived;
nor is it the effect of a preceding series, as such a causal relationship is not observed.
Nor can it be the genitive case, because [the object] is not produced by the preceding, this [present], or the subsequent [rule].
Therefore, since this [objection] finds no place here, he says: "And there is a governing authority (adhikāra)."
Furthermore, the qualification for these duties and their forfeiture have been considered as a matter of course.

Even though there is no logical connection (*saṅgati*) characterized by inclusion (*antarbhāva*), the eligibility of the gods for the knowledge of the Veda and its absence in the case of Śūdras and others have been considered here as a matter of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*).
The sense is that this incidental discussion is reinforced by the statement in the preceding sūtra regarding the fact that [Vedic study] has human beings as its eligible subjects.
Furthermore, there is no risk of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in investigating what follows from what is already under consideration.
This is because [the status of a statement] is determined by the presence or absence of a purpose;
and in the present case, there exists a purpose such as the justification for what was stated in the phrase, "The Viśvedevas worship. (4.50)
But how can it be said that they are "cintitau" (masculine dual)? According to the rule "in case of conflict, the subsequent [operation] prevails," the feminine gender should have been used.
Not so.
One should supply the words “these two objects” (*itāmau viṣayau*) as an ellipsis. [JNYS 1.3.VIII:

The Section on the Divinities] Here, there are two sūtras intended to raise an objection regarding the eligibility of the gods for Vedic knowledge: “Jaimini [holds that there is] no eligibility because of the impossibility [of the gods] in the Madhu-vidyā and others,” and “[there is no eligibility] because of their presence in the light.”
The meaning of this is as follows:
gods are not entitled to Vedic worship and the like,
because there is an absence of Vedic injunctions directed toward them.
If it is argued that the injunction itself, such as "one should meditate upon the Self," takes those [attributes] as its object, we say no;
for a conceptual dilemma (vikalpa) is untenable.
For instance:
do they have the qualification for all forms of meditation taught in the Vedas, or only for some?
Not the first,
because they lack the capacity to be enjoined in all cases;
for it is one who desires the fruit to be accomplished by them that is enjoined therein.
And that is called a fruit which has not been attained and for which the means have not been performed; moreover,
the desire of the gods for the fruits of all forms of worship and so forth is not possible.
This is because meditations on honey and so forth have the attainment of the state of a deity as their fruit,
and that [state] has already been attained by them;
furthermore, even the knowledge to be accomplished through meditation exists eternally established, since it consists in omniscience.
For this very reason, the second [position] is not tenable.

Furthermore, since Jaimini also thinks thus (*jaiminirapyevaṃ manyate*), and because an injunction is impossible—given that the intermediate result and the ultimate purpose (the *pada* and so forth) have already been attained—and on account of Jaimini’s own statement, it follows that the gods lack qualification (*anadhikāra*). Having reached this conclusion, [the following is said] for the purpose of refuting it:
The Sūtra:
"Oṃ; Bādarāyaṇa [maintains that] there is indeed [the Lord], for so it is; Oṃ."
The injunction for the sake of that fruit is established once meditation has been refuted.
Since Jaimini has established that there is an injunction regarding a matter not otherwise proven for the sake of another purpose,
and since this is the opinion of Vidyādhirāja, there is therefore no contradiction between those two.
In this regard, there is no refutation for the statement of Jaimini cited by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).
Should it therefore be understood as invalid simply because it contradicts the view of the Blessed One?
Not so.
He says, "for the sake of its fruit," because there is no contradiction since their objects are distinct.
The word "that" (tat) refers to what is well-known from such scriptural passages as, "Having become one of the Vasus themselves," and so forth; that is,
when the true nature of Brahman has been established and known.
This is a locative of reference (*viṣayasaptamī*).
The connection is that "there is an injunction for worship.
"For another purpose" means for the sake of a different result.

Likewise, the phrase "the injunction for meditation on an unestablished object" also carries over here. By supplying the word "iti," it should be construed with "is the opinion. [This refers to] those two views. (4.61)

Now, one might ask: what is that other fruit, and how can it be an object not established for all-knowing beings, such that even for the gods the prescription for worship would be possible? To this, he says: "Liberation."
In liberation there is no distinction of fruit, nor does everything manifest;
therefore, even for the gods, constant worship is indeed appropriate.
And that which manifests does not exist at all times;
therefore, it is for the sake of both [the manifesting consciousness and the object].
The word *hi* has the sense of "because.
Now, it might be objected that it is contradictory to say that everything is not manifested to all-knowing beings;
but this is not so.
He says "eternal" because omniscience is not established for anyone other than the Supreme Lord.
The perfect knowledge of Viṣṇu is eternal, free from increase or decrease,
clearly manifest and exceedingly lucid, and it pervades all things without exception.
The knowledge of others is always limited to specific objects and acquired gradually;
however, [the Buddha's knowledge] is complete, having as its object all things without exception.
The word "tu" (but/however) is used for emphasis.
The word "of Viṣṇu alone" is to be connected [to the preceding].
"Having a subject that is clear and most clear" means being supremely clear.
Now, is it not the case that clarity consists in a cognition having a specific object,
and that this is already covered by the word "complete" (pūrṇam)?
Not so.
This is because clarity, like immediacy and so forth, is accepted as a quality of cognition that does not depend on an object;
and because that [clarity] is established by experience for Brahmā, i.e., Hiraṇyagarbha.
"Pervading all things without exception" means having as its object all things other than the Supreme Brahman.
Here too, the word "thus" (evam) is to be connected;
however, the meaning is not that it possesses the aforementioned qualification because it has all objects as its domain.
Here, the separate mention of the realization of Brahman is for the sake of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so");

whereas the mention of the realization of Viṣṇu is intended to indicate that since omniscience is characterized by the knowledge of Viṣṇu, it is impossible for others to possess it. "Pertaining to limited objects" means having as its domain only a few things other than the Supreme Lord.
By this, the aphorism *bhāvam* is explained.
And in this regard, the statement cited in the commentary beginning with “as long as there is service” (*yāvatsevā*) serves as the authoritative proof.
Is it not improper to claim that there is no contradiction between the views of Jaimini and the Blessed One?
For Jaimini must either maintain that the meditations (*vidyās*) possess fruits and so forth distinct from those mentioned in the scriptures, or he must maintain that they do not.
In the first case, how could he declare them to be without qualification (*anadhikāra*) for the rites?
If it is asked, "But how is there no contradiction in the second [case]?", we say: no;
for the Blessed Sūtrakāra (Jaimini), being a knower of all particulars, spoke with clarity.

Jaimini, however, was a knower of generalities; not knowing other results and so forth, he did not refute [the possibility of eligibility], but rather accepted what was heard literally and stated that there was no eligibility. Thus, because the lack of contradiction is established, he says: "and so forth."
These and other such distinctions, however, always reside in the heart of the Lord of Knowledge.
But Jaimini and others, because they possess knowledge of the general principles, spoke thus;
therefore, this doctrine of the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa) is not at all contradicted by the wise.
The word *iti* has the sense of referring back to what was stated as "liberation" (*mokṣa*).
The word *tu* is to be construed as "but [the power] of the Lord of Knowledge.
They abide in the heart.
Therefore, he spoke clearly; this is the ellipsis.
From that [arises] the lack of qualification for the deities and so forth.
Thus it is said.
The meaning is "confused.
To provide a justification for this as well, the preceding sentence beginning with "nityam" (eternal) should be considered.
"Vidyeśa" is the concluding term.
In order to indicate that this same principle should be applied elsewhere as well, it was stated [in the commentary] that "Jaimini and others" and "by the virtuous" are meant here.

Thus ends the third section (pāda) concerning the first subject matter, in this commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna*— the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda— composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha, which explains the meaning of difficult words and sentences.
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
Chapter 1, Quarter 4:
[The Section Concerning that which is Based on Inference] (Ānumānikādhikaraṇam) *4,67*
Now begins the section on "That Which Is Based on Inference" (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.

That the meaning of the [first] section (*pāda*) is the demonstration of the application of words well-known elsewhere [to Brahman] is established either from the *Bhāṣya* itself or by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Furthermore, the distinction between those [terms] well-known elsewhere and those well-known only elsewhere has been demonstrated in the *Bhāṣya* itself; therefore, it is not stated here. "Should it not be [the case that Brahman is] inferential according to some? No, because of the apprehension of what was presented through the metaphor of the body; and Scripture shows this. (Sūtra 1.1.5) ॐ ॥

If it be argued that for some [the soul] is also inferable, we say no; because [the text] shows that it is grasped as presented through the metaphor of the body, and [scripture] further demonstrates this.
Here, having cited the passage: "Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Person," [the Sūtra continues].
It has been established that the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) refers to the Supreme Brahman itself.
Regarding this, what was stated by the opponent—"If the unmanifest is the Supreme Brahman, then it would follow that it is inferior to the Puruṣa;
and that is not tenable"—is addressed as follows:
"Because it would contradict all the Vedas and other authorities"; in order to refute that, the Sūtra states:
"Because it is dependent on that, it is purposeful."
"Because it depends on that, it is purposeful.
He explains its meaning as follows: "one who suffers."
But words such as "suffering," "bound," and "inferior" apply to Brahman because it is the cause of dependence upon those states. ... MAnu 1.4.1a-c.
The mention of "the unmanifest" (avyakta) is an illustration;

for instance, in passages where suffering and other qualities incompatible with being the Lord of All are perceived— such as in "Jīvas alone are subject to suffering" and "Others enter into various wombs," and so forth.

Since the connection of all those [terms] is established here, there is no mention of "the sufferer" (*duḥkhin*) and so forth. Even though words such as "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refer to Brahman, there is no contradiction with any scripture, because although Brahman itself lacks inferiority and the like, the primary causes (*pradhāna*) and others—which possess those qualities—are subordinate to Brahman; for this reason, [Brahman is called] "the sufferer."
It is accepted that even words such as "bound" (baddha) and "inferior" (avara) apply to Brahman.
This is what is meant:
for it is precisely by the force of words such as "suffering" (*duḥkha*) that the state of being a sufferer (*duḥkhita*) and so forth is established;
consequently, a contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be pointed out.
Furthermore, words such as "one who suffers" (*duḥkhin*) do not necessarily denote the inherence (*samavāya*) of suffering and so forth;
rather, they denote merely the relation [of possession] expressed by the formula "this belongs to him.
And a relation, like inherence, can also be one of ownership (*svāmya*).
"In that regard, [the objection] is: 'He is without suffering and without fault,' and 'All names enter into Him.

Since these two scriptural passages, which allow no other possibility, would otherwise be untenable, what inconsistency is there in accepting that the application of words such as 'one who suffers' occurs by virtue of His being the controller of suffering and so forth?
(4.71) Let it be so in the case of those [words] ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*).
How is it [applied] in the case of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, such as *baddha* and others that are conventional (*rūḍha*), like *avara* and so forth? It is as follows:
for the word *baddha*, its status as the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of binding (*bandha*) is the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Thus, that word applies to that which possesses [the property];
and by the phrase "that which possesses," only a general relation is expressed,
because there is no evidence for a specific relation.
The same should be understood regarding words expressing other *kārakas* as well.
Words such as *avara* (inferior) and so forth, which function based on causes such as inferiority (*avaratva*), are to be applied in exactly this manner.
Furthermore, [it is taught that] "the meaning of a verbal root arises from the nominal stem" (*prātipadikād dhātvarthaḥ*).
Thus, when the suffix *ac* is prescribed after roots ending in *ṇic*, the application of words such as *avarādi* is quite easy;
this would be the explanation for cases where inferiority (*avaratva*) and so forth are understood through the word itself.
But how is it in cases such as "The Puruṣa is higher than the Unmanifest," where the status of being lower and so forth is obtained through the sense [of the words]?
For an explanation based on logical reasoning (*upapatti*) cannot take the place of the literal word.
It is said in reply:

By means of the ablative case in the word *avyaktāt*, only this much is obtained: that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) serves as the limit (*avadhi*) in relation to the transcendence (*paratva*) residing in the Person (*puruṣa*).
Nor is there any rule that by the expression “that belongs to him” (*tad asyāsti*), only inherence (*samavāya*) can be understood.
This is because it is logically consistent even in terms of its being the owner (*svāmitva*).
Consequently, that which possesses the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*) with respect to "remoteness" (*paratva*) must, by implication, possess the state of being "near" (*avaratva*).
However, that which is the owner of what resides in the "remote" must, by implication, possess ownership with respect to "nearness" and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. *4,76*
This might be the case:
although the general relation expressed as "this belongs to that" is said to be the basis for the application of terms such as "one who suffers" (*duḥkhin*),
nevertheless, it is only inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth, and not ownership (*svāmitva*).
Since primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*) follow actual usage,
and such usage is observed to be based solely on relations such as inherence (*samavāya*) and the like,
rather than on the relation of ownership (*svāmitva*).

For this very reason, in the rule “*tadasyāstyasminniti matup*” (Pāṇini 5.2.94), the particle *iti* is employed to indicate the intended meaning. Therefore, it is not the case that words such as "suffering" (*duḥkhin*) apply to Brahman solely on the basis of its being dependent upon that [suffering]; rather, there is also usage based on the cause of dependence upon it. Thus he says: “the Queen” (*rājñī*).
...just as there is defeat for a queen. (Manu 1.4d)

The meaning is as follows: since defeat occurring in one who is accompanied by a servant is dependent upon the king, the word "defeated" (*parājita*), which is caused by that defeat, applies to the king himself—as in "Bhadrasena is defeated. Furthermore, if the possessive suffix (*matup*) did not function through its connection with the owner (*svāmin*), even expressions such as "Devadatta possesses cows" (*gomān devadattaḥ*) would not be possible. He explains this very point with the words: "sovereignty" (*svātantryam*).
For independence and its dependence [on another] are indeed the causes for the application of words.

Since independence [of the self] with respect to things belonging to others—just as suffering and other such grounds for linguistic application (*pravṛttinimitta*) appear to belong to those things themselves—is also a cause for the application of words such as "suffering" (*duḥkhin*), because both instruction (*anuśāsana*) and usage (*prayoga*) are identical in both cases;

therefore, the connection is that words such as "suffering" also apply to Brahman by virtue of the logical implication of what has been stated, based on the reason of its being dependent upon those [states]. *4,79*
Let it be that even independence (*svātantrya*) is a ground for the application of words; however, it is only secondary (*amukhya*),
because its usage in that sense is not frequent.
Because of the abundance of usage, being directed toward that [the individual soul] alone is primary.

Thus, since words such as "suffering" (duḥkhin) and so forth are primary when applied to the individual soul (jīva) and secondary when applied to Brahman, the statement "But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the harmony [of the texts]" (tattu samanvayāt) would be untenable; to this he says: "Sovereignty" (svātantryam).
In that regard, autonomy would be primary... // MAnu 1.4.2c //

In that regard, between autonomy (*svātantrya*) and being inherent in that (*tadgatatva*), autonomy alone should be the primary ground for the application of the word; the meaning is that it is not "being inherent in that.
It has been asserted in sequence that autonomy is both the cause for the application of the word and the primary [ground].
Desiring to establish that very sequence, he states the subverting argument against the non-acceptance of freedom as the cause, beginning with: "From where? (kutaḥ).
...how else could victory come to the queen? (Manu 1.4.2d)
Otherwise, if independence were not the cause for the application of words, how could there be the word "conqueror" (*jayin*) applied to a king on the basis of his victory?
How so?
"O Queen, I shall sit upon my own power; whence is victory?
From nowhere at all"—this is the meaning.

Since victory does not reside in the king, if independence were not the basis for the application of the word [‘victor’], then, due to the absence of such a basis, the application of the word ‘victor’ to the king would not occur.
But this is not the case;
therefore, independence (*svātantrya*) must also be accepted as a cause.
If it is argued that the term may be used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*), we say no.

The suffix -in is used here because of the similarity of the causal factor (nimitta), for otherwise the opposite case might also arise. Although defeat (*parājaya*) is the subject under discussion, the mention of victory (*jaya*) is for the sake of establishing a universal concomitance (*vyāpti*). *4,82*
He establishes that independence is the primary cause with the words: "For not... (na hi).
For the title "victorious" is not applied to a servant as long as he remains under another, even though he possesses only the mere appearance of independence. (Manu Smṛti 1.4.3)
The word *hi* means "because.
The words *tāvat* and *yāvat* function as adverbs modifying the action.
Even though victory belongs to another—that is, even though it resides in the servant—[it is attributed] to the king merely by the appearance of independence with respect to that victory.

The connection is as follows: as long as the word "vijayin" (the victor) is employed, it is not used in reference even to a servant who is the locus of victory, because [the servant] is merely related [to it]; therefore, sovereignty (*svātantrya*) must be primary in that case.

While one should have said "because of sovereignty," the expression "merely by the appearance of sovereignty" is intended to highlight the principle of *kaimutya* (how much more so), implying: "If this is so even when there is only an appearance of sovereignty, how much more so in the case of the Supreme Self, whose sovereignty is non-figurative (*anupacarita*)?"
If it is argued that the abundance of usage [of a word] for a king is caused by the ignorance of servants, we say no;
for such usage is observed even when the servant possesses knowledge.
Indeed, the abundance of usage is not the cause of primary denotation.
If it is argued that [the word] is seen even in usages such as "ajñāta" (unknown), "mukhya" (primary), and "lākṣaṇika" (indicative/metaphorical),
that is true; however,
due to the abundance of usage, its primary status resides precisely in those [other senses].
When an opponent objects that independence (*svātantrya*) is secondary because it lacks predominance, this [author] states that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
However, predominance is not being established by means of the frequency of usage,
such that the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would be relevant.

Although one might argue that the abundance of usage here is otherwise established— by virtue of being caused by primary ignorance (*mukhyājñāna*) and so forth— or that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), nevertheless, following the direction of the Sūtra "Because of denoting the world" (*jagadvācitvāt*), this is understood by the students themselves; thus, [the opponent] has stated that the reason is simply unestablished (*asiddhi*).
If it is asked, "How then is primary status established?"— surely,
if its own form (*svarūpa*) were the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), then when a servant is bound or dead,
there would be the usage: "The king is bound," or "The king is dead."
But this is not the case;
therefore, we know that ownership is not the basis for the application [of the term].
Nor should it be said that when a word is in usage, one merely follows after its basis [for application].
But it is not the case that the application [of the rule] is based on the existence of a cause;
for this principle has as its scope non-primary applications,
and in those cases, the cause is not the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
However, that is only one part of the case;
for in the primary application, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is indeed the cause.
For it is not the case that, simply because the word "lion" is not applied to a tiger, the word "Aupagava" would likewise fail to be applied to the offspring of Upagu.
Here it must be asked: what is this so-called "usage" (prayoga)?
Is it, as some suggest, that the power of words (śabdaśakti) has its root in usage, and that grammar [is based on that]?
What, then, is the meaning of "utterance"?
It cannot be the first [alternative], because that consequence is accepted; nor can it be the latter, because the conclusion by contrapositive would be unestablished.
Regarding the second [type of reason], he states that it is established otherwise: "The servant, the kinsman, and so forth... (4.87).
"The servant, the kinsman, and so forth, would be a cause for doubt regarding a king's fitness to be bound and so on; therefore, they are not at all employed [as reasons]. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.4)
Intending to express that a servant or a kinsman is dependent upon the king, one does not employ such expressions as "the king is bound" or "the king has died.
What is the reason?
It is simply because such usage would be a cause for confusion.
But this is not so, because independence is not a cause.
Why? Because independence is a cause of doubt; for even a king is subject to imprisonment and other such conditions.
This is what is meant:
independence is indeed the cause for the application of a word, but the absence of usage is caused by an obstructing factor.
For upon hearing the expression "the king is bound" or "the king is dead," a person of refined intellect would have doubt:
is this said because a servant dependent on the king is bound and so forth, or is it because the king himself is bound and so forth?
Since expectancy, proximity, and compatibility are present in both cases, the cognition of two distinct meanings is unavoidable.
Nor does the fact that the form of the usage has ceased—on the grounds that "let there be no doubt"—imply that independence (*svātantrya*) is not a cause [of the cognition].
For it is not the case that fire, when obstructed by gems, mantras, and so forth, is not the cause simply because it did not burn.
It is not merely the state of being a cause of doubt that constitutes an obstacle to the application [of a rule],
since doubt can be removed through a detailed explanation,
as it has been said:
“From the explanation, the specific meaning is understood; for it is not the case that [a word] is not a defining characteristic due to doubt.

Otherwise, even the usage *rājā jayī* (the king is victorious) would not be possible, since in that case too a doubt would arise according to the aforementioned method. Therefore, he says: “because of the inauspiciousness.”
Because words are inauspicious when used by a king in an inauspicious context,
and because such a word would be unpleasant, its employment should be avoided.
The word *tu* is used for emphasis.
The term *śabdasya* (of the word) is in the singular to denote the genus.
This is because there exists a fitness (*yogyatā*) for the connection [of the word] with inauspicious things such as the imprisonment of a king.

Because the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors are clear, there is the possibility that words such as "the king is bound" might generate an occasional perception of inauspiciousness, such as the binding of a king.
Furthermore, since the expression of inauspiciousness regarding a king would cause displeasure to the king and his ministers, the use of such a word would be precluded.
This is the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*).
It is not merely because doubt has arisen that there is an absence of application;
rather, it is solely due to the apprehension of misfortune caused by the displeasure resulting from doubt.
It is certainly not because independence is lacking in causal efficacy.
If it is argued that, in that case, one should not even say "the king is defeated," [we reply:
because it is well known that the king wins or loses victory precisely through his servants, no doubt arises [regarding the agency].
Indeed, there is simply an absence of such usages as "the king is bound" and so forth.
But that [ownership] does not occur because it lacks a cause;
rather, how can it be ascertained that it occurs due to the obstruction of the aforementioned doubt?
Nor should it be said: "Let this ascertainment not exist."

Even the suspicion that the absence of application might be established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*) can undermine both reasoning (*tarka*) and inference; for even for the proponent (*vādin*), certainty is indispensable, otherwise there would follow the failure to ascertain the coordination (*samanvaya*) based on independence. Therefore, he says: "But the qualities... (*guṇāstu*).
But such are the qualities that are employed therein, even in their entirety.
Such words are caused by their master;
wherever they occur,
if they denote auspicious qualities, they do not bring about even a slight inauspicious impression.
In that case, however, all of them are employed,
as in the examples "the king has conquered" and so forth.

The meaning is that it is determined through the discrimination between what has been attained and what has not been attained that the very suspicion of non-purposefulness is the cause for the absence of application, and not that independence itself is a non-cause;
this is why it was stated, "all [of them] indeed."
Nor is there this rule that linguistic usage must occur only when a formal cause (nimitta) is present;
for indeed, grammarians have stated grammatical rules (lakṣaṇa) for an infinite number of words.
And since their usage is not observed, it was not mentioned because it is obvious.
Thus, having established that independence is both the cause for the application of words and their primary [meaning], he says: "In the case of those worthy of honor... (4.94).
"In the case of those worthy of honor alone, independence is specifically the primary cause. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.6cd)
Since words such as *svāmin* (master), *jayin* (victorious one), and so forth are employed for those who are venerable,
it is known that independence (*svātantrya*) is the cause for the application of these words;
and because they are used especially and predominantly for those who are venerable, and not for servants.
By this it is determined that autonomy (svātantrya) regarding the application of words is also the primary cause, because it resides therein.
To the question, "What follows if this is so?", he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, because defects are extremely remote and even doubt is impossible—
given that defects reside in Viṣṇu when considered from the perspective of the intellect of the wise— [the Veda is authoritative].
And even words denoting faults are intended to signify Viṣṇu’s absolute sovereignty.

Since sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is the primary cause, the connection [of the text] is as follows: with the intention of referring to sovereignty, even words denoting defects—such as "suffering," "bound," and "inferior"—are employed in reference to Viṣṇu, as in such passages as, "Only the individual souls (*jīva*) are suffering.
Just as there is no usage such as "the king is bound" despite the existence of the actual cause [of bondage], so too there is no usage such as "Viṣṇu is suffering."

"How could it not be so even here? For even in this case, there is the possibility that the occasional fear of Viṣṇu and his devotees acts as an obstacle. To address this, he says: "Because of the defect," and so forth.
Because of such scriptural passages as "He is without desire, He is blameless," there is a certainty that defects are utterly remote from Viṣṇu;
for, from the perspective of the intellect of a wise person, it is impossible for there to be any doubt regarding the presence of defects in Viṣṇu or regarding him as their object.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that [the inference holds] both because the causal conditions are present and because there is an absence of any obstructing factor.
This is what is meant:
even though the causal basis exists, the cessation of Vedic practice would indeed arise from fear of Viṣṇu and the Vaiṣṇavas;
and the cause of that is their displeasure.
In this regard, there is a doubt as to whether Viṣṇu’s faultiness is being stated by this [passage].

The cause of that [doubt] is the sentence's capacity to generate the cognition of both meanings. And the cause of that [capacity] is the presence of semantic fitness (*yogyatā*) and so forth in both senses.
And this [capacity] does not exist in the present case;
for since the Vaiṣṇavas possess a certainty regarding the faultlessness of Viṣṇu as the Supreme Lord, the determination of such capacity is untenable.
Otherwise, that same [capacity] would undesirably follow even in the case of sentences such as "the old ox" (*jaradgava*).
Even though displeasure may arise in one who does not understand the intention of the statement, nevertheless, what follows from the cessation of employing words with a virtuous intent?
This too has been stated: "with regard to the intellect of the wise.
The Vedic usage *viṣṇavi* is employed in order to demonstrate one's own supreme status as a follower of the Vedas. *4,100*
In this regard, he also cites scriptural authority, saying "Vāsudeva":
the Vāsudeva-śruti declares that there is no inauspiciousness whatsoever in Viṣṇu.

Since auspiciousness and inauspiciousness exist elsewhere, one should not speak of inauspiciousness regarding Viṣṇu; for, from the perspective of His absolute sovereignty, there is no fault in speaking of what is inauspicious.
He says: "This is worthy," the remainder being understood.

Since there is no inauspiciousness—such as suffering and the like—in Viṣṇu, there is no fault or harm resulting from speaking of inauspiciousness in relation to Viṣṇu; for, due to the absence of suitability, there is no cognition of any other meaning, especially when considering his absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*).
Therefore, the implication is that words such as "duḥkhin" (suffering) and others are also employed for Viṣṇu in the Veda.

However, in other cases—such as when referring to a king and so forth—since both auspiciousness and inauspiciousness are possible, there arises the appearance of another meaning due to the possibility of such fitness; thus, because of the suspicion of potential misfortune, one should not say things like "the inauspicious king has been bound. This is the meaning.
He illustrates, by means of this example, how a single word may in some cases be a cause of misfortune by conveying a fault, while in other cases it lacks that quality:
"Excessive eating is a fault among men, but never so in the case of Hari. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.10ab)
Just as when it is said, "Devadatta is a glutton," one understands both that he possesses much food and that he is blameworthy;
for according to the Smṛti, "Excessive eating is not conducive to heaven," both qualities are possible in Devadatta and thus appropriate [to be understood].
For this very reason, one who is afraid of Devadatta does not employ such a construction [with respect to him].
However, in the case of the Supreme Lord, because worldly attributes are absolutely impossible, it is not so;
rather, only qualities such as being the destroyer of all are perceived.
Regarding that, the application [of the analogy] is as follows;
he states the illustrative example with the word "thus":
"In this way, words such as 'suffering' and so forth are uttered with reference to independence. (Manu 1.4.10cd)
No faults whatsoever exist in Hari...
The defects are the causes of defects.
For the first example as well, the corresponding point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*) must be supplied.

How then is the perception of suffering and so forth in the Supreme Lord stated to be a cause of harm in such passages as "He becomes non-existent"? To this, he says: "by means of the cognition of that [suffering, etc.]."
...are said by those whose intellects are fixed on that [world] to be cause-makers of defects;
therefore, those words denoting defects are, in that very context, expressive of virtues. (Manu 1.4.11)
The meaning is that this is said with the intention of considering suffering and the other [qualities] as residing in that [Self].
Therefore, the Śruti summarizes its own stated point:
"Hence it is established that the Supreme Self is denoted by such terms as 'the Unmanifest' (avyakta) and so forth."
Thus concludes the section on the Inferential (Ānumānika) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
*4,103* [======= Jyotirupakramādhikaraṇam =======] Now begins the section on the Commencement with Light (Jyotirupakrama) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
Oṃ. But [the soul] has light as its point of departure, for so it is studied by some. Oṃ.

"But that which begins with light, for thus it is studied by some. (BBs 1.4.9) Regarding the statements occurring in the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" and "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring," there arises a doubt: does this [word *jyotis*] refer consistently to Brahman, or not?
"No," says the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).
For instance: is the meaning of the sentence here Brahman, or is it the meaning of the word?
Not the first,
because the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and so forth is understood as the meaning of the sentence.
Not the second.
For regarding these words, do they denote Brahman by convention (*rūḍhi*) or by etymological derivation (*yoga*)?
Even in the first case, is the conventional usage of those words for Brahman based on their well-known nature as spring and so forth, or is it entirely distinct?
It cannot be the first.
For, due to their being insentient, non-eternal, and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even Brahman would be subject to those same defects.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because it is improper to accept that [the word "Brahman"] has multiple meanings.
For there is no authoritative evidence for the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of words such as "spring" (*vasanta*) and so forth with respect to the Lord (*īśvara*).
Nor is there any purpose in resorting to such conventional usage for the sake of establishing a coherent connection (*samanvaya*),
since the perfection of all attributes (*guṇapūrṇatva*) remains unproven.
Nor can it be established through etymology (*yoga*),
because since the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the term is predominant, its primary meaning cannot be established;
furthermore, we do not perceive any such etymological derivation (*yoga*) either.

Furthermore, in the case of *yoga* (etymological derivation), one must accept the division into base (*prakṛti*) and so forth, as well as the division into prior and subsequent members (*pūrvottarapada*).
In that regard, does the base and so forth denote Īśvara or not?
In the first case, the *yoga* is untenable because of a lack of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*).
In the second [view], the coordination of all words with Brahman is untenable,
because [terms such as] *prakṛti* and so forth have other referents.
Furthermore, if all words were to have Brahman as their sole referent, the uselessness of case-endings would follow, as would the abolition of the performance of ritual actions.
Because the factors of action (kārakas) possess their form only through being connected with an action, and because there is no word denoting an action [in the case of the Upanishads],
and because another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is seen to be the instigator of performance;
therefore, the Sūtra on Concordance (Samanvaya-sūtra) is untenable.

To this it is replied: as for what was asked— whether the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the sentence with Brahman consists in that of the sentence as a whole or of its constituent words— we say, first of all, that it is of the words.
Nor is there an impossibility of its functioning, because yoga exists; intending this, he explains it by saying "born."
Because the light born from that [syllable Om] is Hari, it is the syllable *ṣaḥ*, which has the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
*Jirjātam*:
from the root *jan*, the suffix *ḍi* is added according to the *auṇādika* rules; *otīram*:
from the root *av*, the suffix *ktin* is added.

That light in which the born world is woven and pervaded exists by way of the form of *prāṇa*, because of its nature as the letter *ṣa*; for the Śruti declares: "The letter *ṣa* is *prāṇa*, the Self."
That which is both light (*jyotis*) and six (*ṣaṣ*) is "jyotiṣaḥ"; its vocative case is "jyotiṣa. [The rule] "from *āyajña* and from *ayajña*" ... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.12c //
In the sense of the abstract state (bhāva) of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice),
the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule "the prescription of *ka* in the sense of *ghañ*."
The absence of *samprasāraṇa* is Vedic; [thus] from *yaj* comes *yajña*. Alternatively, the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of the agent according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*pacādyac*).

And thus, "āyajetaḥ" means that which has been obtained from here by means of sacrifice—whether by a sacrifice, by ritual action, or by a sacrificing person. It is "āyu" because it is life, or because it extends everywhere. It is "yajetaḥ" because it is obtained through sacrifice. Therefore, [the compound] is "āyajetaḥ."
The meaning is that he is the enjoyer of all sacrifices and is to be attained by the performers of sacrifice through the gateway of knowledge.
His vocative address is "O Āyajeta.
... And they dwell because of the spring (*vasanta*). (Manu 1.4.12d)
The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *vas* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134;
thus, that which dwells is "vasa.
After the root *tan*, the suffix *ḍi* is applied according to the Uṇādi rules.
It is called *ti* because it extends (*tanoti*).
According to the rule "the addition of a phoneme and the transposition of a phoneme," there is the addition of the letter *n* to the preceding word.
The term *vasantī* is derived from *vasan* (dwelling) and *ti* (the suffix *ti*), meaning "he dwells";
that is to say, he exists pervasively.
The vocative form of this is *vasante*.
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
But because the covering has been removed, go... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.13ab).

The suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule "the suffix *ḍa* is seen after *amehacchada* even in other cases. Since *ga* means "gone" and *cha* means "covering," such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, that from which these have gone is *gaccha*; this is the vocative form *gaccha*.
This is the explanation of the mantra beginning with "O Indra, come" (*indrāgaccha*). ... Hari, being told "Eat," [acted as] the destroyer of living beings. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.13bc)
The word *su* is a substitute for the word *bhūta*, and *kṣvaḥ* is a substitute for the word *kṣaya*; there is also the augment *m* added to the preceding member.
This [formation] belongs to the class beginning with *pṛṣodara*.
Alternatively, the suffix *ḍva* is applied to the root *kṣi* in the sense of "decay."
This [world] also is awakened by Him; for this world is offered as an oblation (*huta*) into Him, and thus it is called *Huṃ*. 1.4.13cd.
The suffix *mak* is applied to the root *hu* (to sacrifice) in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
By the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
Since the universe is offered into this Viṣṇu Himself at the time of dissolution and so forth, the meaning is that He is both "Huṃ" and "Asau" (He).
Because no specific karma is mentioned, it is called "the world" (*jagat*).
Because of its clarity, it is declared to be *phaṭ*. 1.4.14a.
From the root *sphuṭa-vikasane* (meaning "to burst open"), the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
There is the elision of the letter *s*,
and the vowel *u* is replaced by *a*.
Because it is manifest—that is, because it is evident to one's own self and because its function is uncontracted—or [because it is] "the moment of the hero" (*kavara-kṣaṇa*);
from this [comes] *kavaca*... // MAnu 1.4.14bc //
The meaning is that "kavaca" is a form derived from this very root, namely *kava*. There is only this much suffix: *ac* added to the root *kavati*.
It is called *kavaca* because it protects (*rakṣati*). ... Because [the king] always conducts himself through the sixfold policy (*ṣaḍguṇa*), [he is called] *vaṣat*. ... // MAnu 7.14c-e //
The root *vṛt* means "to turn" (*vartane*); with the suffix *ḍa*, it becomes *vaḥ*, meaning "that which turns.
It is called *ṣaṭ* because its nature consists of the six qualities (*ṣaḍguṇātmakatvāt*).

"Vaṣaṭ" consists of "vaḥ" (you) and "ṣaṭ" (six); its intended meaning is that [the six qualities] exist, and so forth. The six qualities are sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion.
... by virtue of being directed toward that [deity], for them [the syllable] *vauṣaṭ* ... // MAnu 1.4.14ef //
*Viḥ* refers to Viṣṇu; for there is a scriptural statement: "The words *aka*, *ya*, *prati*, *saṃbhūma*, *sakha*, and *āhā* are designations of Viṣṇu."
The six qualities existing in that [state] are *vauṣaṭ*.
There is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending (*saptamī*).
This is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
Because those six qualities are inherent in it, it is called "vauṣaṭ. Thus it is said. *Mānavadharmaśāstra 1.4.14f*
And thus, O Blessed One, there is no inconsistency in [the mantra] being a name (nāman), because the qualities residing therein are also of that same nature.
This very point has been stated: "thus indeed" (ity eva).
If that is so, how is it said "it is told"?

There is no fault, because this is used in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and not in the sense of the object (*karman*). Since he accepts what is his own, Janārdana is called "Svāhā. (Manu 1.4.15ab)
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the roots *hṛ* and *jah*,
both of which, when preceded by the prefix *ā*,
signify acceptance (*svīkāra*).

"O Svāhā!"—one who accepts as one's own the sacrificial oblation and so forth belonging to others, which are perceived as one's own through delusion because of their inherent nature (*svabhāva*), is called Svāhā;
and since he is also a horse (*aśva*), the term "Svāhā" is used as a vocative. *4,126*
Because virtues bow down before him, he is called "Anna" (Food).

The suffix *asun* is applied in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the act of bowing; its neuter gender follows the [convention of the] word itself. The connection with "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) is established by way of suitability.
By the act of bowing, he indicates an absolute connection.

Alternatively, it may be explained thus: with regard to this Supreme Lord, the qualities—namely Brahmā and the others—are subordinate, and they bow, that is, they become humble. Having accepted this syntactical connection through the function of yoga (yogavṛtti), he states the purpose achieved: "Thus, without remainder... (*ityaśeṣa*).
Thus, Janārdana alone is primarily denoted by all words— whether they express actions, names, or sounds— through their words, syllables, vowels, and so forth.
Therefore, [the merit] possesses infinite qualities... // MAnu 1.4.17a //
Thus, according to the direction stated,
there is an inconsistency regarding the meaning of the case endings;
for verbal words are those consisting of finite verb forms (*ākhyāta*).

The words ending in nominal suffixes (*subanta*) are [the] "names" (*nāman*). By the principle of "one" (*ekaḥ*), it eliminates the distinction that would otherwise be obtained; for if there were a distinction in the referents (*abhidheya*), the state of having infinite qualities (*anantaguṇatā*) could not be established.
Primarily by way of figurative application (*yogavṛtti*).
The phrase "by means of words whose names are actions" is restated as "consisting of words, phonemes, and vowels.
It is not only by means of those consisting of words and phonemes, but also by means of those consisting of accents such as the acute (*udātta*) and so forth.
But surely, if phonemes (varṇa) themselves possess the capacity to denote meaning and terminate in an inflectional ending, they are simply words;
so for what purpose is there a separate mention of them?
We reply: it is intended to distinguish between those consisting of a single phoneme and those consisting of multiple phonemes.
The ellipsis is that "the state of possessing infinite qualities is established.
The word *hi* indicates [the reason] "because they are not synonyms.

By this, it is stated that the opponent's argument—that accepting the syntactical connection of words based on mere conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is purposeless because the possession of infinite qualities is not established—is refuted.
But is it not the case that the infinite qualities of the Supreme Lord are not established by the Veda merely through the fact that an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is possible?
For an etymological derivation, being constructed by the intellect of the commentator, can occur in another sense or otherwise.

Otherwise, the sentence "the white one runs" (*śveto dhāvati*), employed with the intention that "the leper (*śvitrī*) is performing purification," would result in the unintended object of knowledge that "a dog is running away from here. Therefore...
It has been said: "By means of revelation" (*śruti*).
For this [dharma] is indeed established through the purport of the revelation (*śruti-tātparya*). (Manu 1.4.17b)

This would indeed be the case if the scriptural passages beginning with "He becomes spring" (vasanta) did not have as their purport the qualities of the Supreme Lord through the etymological interpretation according to the method stated;
however, we shall demonstrate that such a purport does exist—this is the sense of the word "hi" (indeed).
He states another purpose for accepting the figurative application (*yogavṛtti*) [of the names] in the verse beginning with "vijñāna."
Since all words have consciousness as their ultimate referent, there is no fault [in this view].

The meaning is this: since all Vedic words are accepted as having the Supreme Lord as their referent for the sake of knowledge through etymological derivation (*yogavṛtti*), and because they are endowed with infinite qualities, the objection raised regarding impermanence and other defects—which was based on accepting conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) such as [the word] "spring" (*vasanta*) and so forth—does not apply.
By this, [the word] "light" (*jyotis*)...
Thus, the purport of the Sūtra has been stated in brief.
In this way, by demonstrating that each word of the Karma-kāṇḍa is consistently applicable to Brahman, the untenability of the Samanvaya-sūtra has been refuted.
Now, he refutes it even by accepting the position that the connection is with the sentence as a whole: "Even when accepted... (aṅgīkṛte 'pi).
Even if it were accepted, there would be no fault in the consistency of the statement.

The meaning is that even if the concordance (*samanvaya*) of sentences is accepted, there is no fault whatsoever—namely, the inapplicability of the *Samanvaya-sūtra*—even because of the acceptance of the concordance of sentences such as "dwelling in Brahman" (*brahmaṇi vasantaḥ*).
By this, the intended purport of the sūtra "Because of the connection of the sentences" (*vākyānvayāt*) has been stated.
Now, an objection is raised here: "It was said that the concordance of sentences with respect to Brahman is not possible."
Regarding the statement "because it is understood that [the Veda] is devoted to the performance of the constituent parts," he says in response: "by virtue of being for that purpose."
Because ritual action and the like are possible as means for that purpose, [the teaching is] for those of limited intellect.
The word "tat" refers back to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
In the phrase "those of small intellect," the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive,
as in the expression "the lover of Ahalyā."
The ellipsis is "there is no inconsistency in the syntactical connection of the sentence.
For indeed, sentences concerning the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the *āhavanīya* fire, and so forth, do not terminate in that alone without purpose;
rather, they are directed toward the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices.
Likewise, the entire ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) does not culminate in insignificant or unstable fruits;
rather, it exists solely for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman,
because the rituals and other practices taught therein serve the purpose of attaining that knowledge of Brahman.
The intention is that this is based on such scriptural passages as, "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting.
Now, one might ask: is the word-by-word coordination (*pratipada-samanvaya*) of the *karmakāṇḍa* with Brahman that has been stated appropriate, or not?
If the position is "no," it need not be explained.
If the first [position] is taken, one might ask: "What is the point of accepting this syntactical connection of the sentence? To this, it is said: "those of small intellect."
This will be elaborated upon later;
by this, the intended meaning of the sūtras beginning with "for another purpose" has been stated. *4,133*
[Objection: Surely, even for those of limited intellect, the sequence of the individual words (*pratipadānvaya*) alone will be the cause of the knowledge of Brahman;
so what is the use of the sequence of the sentence (*vākyānvaya*)? To this, he says: "Who? (*ka iti*).
"Who [knows] the application of the meters?"—thus from the Śruti... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.4.19a]

The meaning is that, because the application of Vedic words— as indicated by the Vedic scripture stating, "The wise one has taught the application of the meters"— is impossible for those of small intellect to understand,
the explanation of the syntactical connection of the sentences is stated [here]. This is the remainder [of the sense].
[Objection: "In that case, then, the derivation of the connection of each word (*pratipada-samanvaya*) by means of *yogavṛtti* (etymological derivation) should not be performed.

For it is heard [in scripture] that there is no one qualified [to do so], stating: 'What wise man would proclaim the etymology of the Vedic meters (*chandas*) as being *yogavṛtti* with respect to Brahman? No one at all. Indeed, one who sings among the deaf does not truly sing; therefore, he says: 'The meaning of *yoga*... [and so on].
...the knower of the reality of the goal of yoga; Brahman alone exists, and there is indeed no other... // Manu 1.4.19bc //
The meaning of yoga is *yogārtha*;
its reality (*tattva*) is its accordance with fact (*yāthārthya*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin these two meanings.
"This is the meaning of this scripture"—this is the ellipsis.
He establishes this by asking: "Who? (ka iti).
... for the word "ka" has both meanings. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.19d)
According to the Vedic scripture, "Ka is indeed Prajāpati," the word *ka* has the meaning of Brahman; moreover,
it is well known that the interrogative particle *kim* functions in the sense of negation (*ākṣepa*).
And thus, since the word *ka* has both meanings, if it refers to Brahman, there is no lack of qualification because its capacity for knowledge through etymological derivation (*yogavṛtti*) is stated;

if it refers to the sense of questioning (*ākṣepārthatva*), there is no lack of qualification for others besides him, and therefore the acceptance of the syntactical connection of the sentence is appropriate.
But how is this so?
There is no fault [in this], whether due to repetition or because it is the nature of the system (*tantra*).
And the proof for this is the impossibility of [the meaning] being otherwise.

(4.135) If Brahmā alone knew the connection of the meanings of words through their etymological derivation (*yogavṛtti*), then "that which has appeared to a single person does not differ from what is composed [by humans]."

By this logic, it follows that the relationship between word and meaning is something produced (*kṛtaka*), and so forth. Furthermore, the eternal connection of words with their meanings—as stated by Jaimini in the sūtra, “But the connection of the word with its meaning is innate” (*autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena saṃbandhaḥ*)—would be abandoned. Therefore, he says: “Of that too... (*tasyāpi*). 4.136.
Since it is certain that even for that eternally established [word], its nature is indeed knowledge,
the eternal connection of words with their meanings is by no means negated.

Even though there is only a single cognizer, nevertheless, for him, there occurs only the valid cognition (*pramiti*) of the relationship between word and meaning—which is already established, already existing, and already known—rather than mere conjecture (*utprekṣā-mātra*). Since this matter is determined through scripture (*śruti*) and other means, the construction [of the argument] is as follows:
we do not at all abandon the eternal connection of words with their meanings as stated by Jaimini.
This is what is meant:
this fault would arise if Brahmā’s knowledge of the relationship between words and their meanings were of the nature of mere conjecture;
but it is not so.

However, the relationship that was realized in a previous birth and was already self-established is understood in this birth through the grace of the Lord, according to the analogy of one waking from sleep.
And thus says the Śruti: "He who [created] Brahmā," and other passages of a similar nature.
This is so because there is corroboration by the cognition of another person regarding a portion [of the text];
and likewise, the Smṛti says:
"Those [Vedas] were heard in another birth," and so forth.
For this very reason, the Śruti says, "He is the knower" (*āveda*).
By this, the view that a scripture possesses multiple distinct authorities is also refuted.
Thus ends the section on the commencement with light (*jyotir-upakrama-adhikaraṇa*) in the venerable Nyāyasudhā. (4.1.38)
[======= JNys_1,4.VI: Section on the Archetype (Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa) =======] [======= JNys_1,4.VII:
Section by Which All Are Explained (Etēnasarvavyākhyātādhikaraṇa) =======] Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the Section on the Archetype.

Now, he states the concise purport of the two sections—“And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples,” and “By this, all [other views] are explained, they are explained”—with the words: “And the words for women... and so forth.
"And [Brahman is] the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.

(BBs 1.4.23) "By this, all [objections] have been explained; they have been explained. (BBs 1.4.28) "And all words denoting women, though having a negative sense, are also designators of Brahman. (MAnuV 1.4.20ef)
Feminine gender words such as *prakṛti* and so forth are feminine terms.
Prohibition (*niṣedha*) means negation (*abhāva*), that which is prohibited. Thus it is said: "it is prohibited."
Negation is non-existent; it follows that words have both [existence and non-existence] as their objects. (4.139)

In this regard, not all sūtras have been commented upon; otherwise, the initial proposition (pratijñā) would be contradicted. Therefore, considering that [the commentary] has already been explained by stating the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth, he states the subject matter, prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), established conclusions (*siddhānta*), and logical reasons for every section, beginning with the words "contradictory" (*virodhī*).
These various locations are intended for the separate application of all those who prohibit women, on account of the abundance of conflicting opinions in every respect. (Manu 1.4.21)
Alternatively, here by the first verse the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) are stated;
"contradictory" (*virodhin*) means those things which are opposed to supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*).
The term "all" (*sarva*) refers to those other than what has been stated or will be stated.
The term "abundance" (*bāhulya*) denotes things characterized by abundance.
The term "cause" (*kāraṇa*) denotes intermediate causes.
"Strī" means those that have the feminine gender (*strīliṅga*). "Niṣedhinaḥ" refers to those for whom a negation (*niṣedha*) is to be expressed;
or alternatively:
The suffix *in* should be understood as following a *dvandva* compound;
in that case, meanings such as "contradictory" (*virodhin*) and so forth are to be taken,
with the word "of words" (*śabdānām*) supplied as the ellipsis.

If it were said that "all these places and topics contained within this section are the purposes for the coordination (*samanvaya*) of these words," one might understand that the coordination of every single word is established [by each individual topic]; therefore, the word "separately" (*pṛthak*) was used. Furthermore, there would be contradiction with all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the derivation [of meaning] would also be impossible.
Mutual contradiction, contradiction between the effect and its possessor, the feminine gender, and negation—these are the reasons for the prima facie arguments. (Manu 1.4.22)
The restriction of being untouched by defects, the multiplicity of word-meanings,
as well as the multiformity of the Lord, characterized by manifestation and non-manifestation.
The production [of the world] from one's own body, as well as the non-manifestation of the wicked—
these and other such arguments establish the final doctrine directly here.

By the word "all" (*sarva*) itself, the subject matter of the *Samākarṣa* section is also included, because that [section] serves the purpose of resolving the objections raised against the subject matter of the *Jyotiḥ* section. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning of these and other points is to be understood from the *Nyāyavivaraṇa* and other works. Having thus briefly explained the sūtras beginning with "evam ānumānikam" (*Thus [the Self] is known through inference*), he explains the *Samākarṣādhikaraṇa* and the *Jyotiradhikaraṇa* somewhat further by means of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*) method, starting with the words "anvayaḥ" (*continuity*).
For instance:
regarding the *Samākarṣādhikaraṇa*, is the syntactical connection (*vākyānvaya*) being established there the intention of the author of the Sūtras or not? If it is the former, then it must be stated.
Is the connection with the previously mentioned pratipadā logical or not?
If it is not, then it should not be stated [as such].
But if it is logical, then while that primary [pratipadā] exists, this [other one] is redundant.

Furthermore, if the "connection of the sentences" (*vākyānvaya*) were his own view, then the mention of Jaimini and others in such sūtras as "But for the sake of another purpose, Jaimini [thinks so]" (*anyārthaṃ tu jaiminiḥ*) would be redundant. Moreover, the threefold connection of the sentences has been stated thus: "Āśmarathya [holds it to be] a sign for the establishment of the proposition"; "Auḍulomi [holds it to be so] because of the state of one who is about to depart"; and "Kāśakṛtsna [holds it to be so] because of the persistence [of the Self]."
If there were no mutual contradiction between them, there would be no difference of opinion; but if there is a contradiction, how can it be considered the intention of the author of the Sūtras?
Furthermore, if the syntactical connection of the sentences is not intended by the author of the Sūtras, then it ought to have been refuted by a refuting Sūtra.
But this is not the case;
therefore, to explain how this is so, he says: "The positive concomitance" (anvaya).
"The etymological derivation of all words cannot be easily understood"—
by stating this, he expresses the view of Jaimini and others which leads to aversion toward the world.
The Blessed Lord, the sovereign of knowledge, himself brought about the cessation of suffering.
For if the connection [of all words] with the path [of practice] were stated, those of duller faculties would become averse to the path of liberation.

Indeed, it is impossible for those of duller faculties to know that all words are directly connected with Brahman through their primary (mukhya) mode of signification; as the scripture states: "Who knows the meters? (KaU 2.8).
And without that knowledge, there is no liberation;
nor is it reasonable to engage in what is impossible, since we do not observe engagement in such things as churning the sky or its hairs.
And so they have said:
"A wise person should not undertake calamities that end badly, actions where the loss equals the gain, or things that are impossible."
Therefore, let this liberation be set aside;
let us instead proceed for the sake of dharma and other goals whose means can be practiced.

Thus, the Blessed One, the author of the Sūtras, himself refuted the worldlings' aversion to the path of liberation by showing the connection of the statements, declaring that this is indeed the view of Jaimini and others.

Thus, since the syntactical connection of the sentence is indeed intended by [the author] himself, the absence of a sūtra for its refutation is not a defect; and since a word-by-word connection is also logical, its exposition is entirely appropriate. Nevertheless, because a word-by-word connection lacks the necessary capacity for those of dull faculties who are averse to the path to liberation, the statement of the syntactical connection of the sentence is made in order to provide consolation by demonstrating an alternative means.
It is said that [the point] has been established.
If so, it was argued that the mention of Jaimini and others is redundant; to this, he replies: "Of his own disciples."
In order to establish his own disciples, he has set forth his own doctrine partially.
Having understood this, he spoke here concerning the relative gradations among men.
The phrase "of Jaimini and others" is to be understood as a supplement [to the preceding].
Here, by the mention of Jaimini and others, it is not said that this doctrine belongs to them alone;
rather, it is meant that my own doctrine was understood by Jaimini and others only in part.
And this [praise] is for the sake of their renown;

for disciples who are commended by their teacher attain fame in the world. Now, one might ask: how could these three mutually contradictory modes of syntactical connection be intended by the author of the Sūtras? To this, he says: "The gradation" (tāratamyam).

By stating that there is a gradation of states among men who possess limited qualifications, it is implied that the difference between various views arises from the systematic arrangement of these differing states, and not from contradiction.
By this, the statement beginning with "Even though [it] is accepted" (*aṅgīkṛte 'pi*) should be understood as having been explained.
In the *Jyotir-adhikaraṇa*, [the meaning of] all words [is established] in the Supreme Lord through the mode of figurative application (*yoga-vṛtti*).
The grammatical derivation of the word has been stated;
however, that is not tenable,
because etymological derivation is impossible unless the constituent elements, such as the root and so forth, lack any other referent.

For if one does not accept that words such as *jāta* (born) refer to something else [than the Lord], the etymological derivation "that in which the born are woven" (*jātamotaṃ yasmin*) is not possible. However, if the base form (*prakṛti*) and so forth were to refer to something else, then the position that all words denote the Lord would already have been established.

Furthermore, it has been stated that if words such as "spring" (*vasanta*) were taken to refer to the Lord, it would result in the abandonment of the performance of rituals and the collapse of worldly conventions; therefore, he says: "In those... (*teṣu*).

"And because of the instruction based on conceptual construction, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth; for conventional usage is accepted with respect to those various objects. (BBs 1.4.10) (MAnu 1.4.27cd)

"Because of the multiplicity of purposes, because there is no contradiction in each respective case, and by virtue of the capacity for instruction and so forth, power is understood to reside in Viṣṇu. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.28) The "multiplicity of purposes"—namely, the derivation [of words], logical consistency, the possibility of performing ritual acts, and the non-interruption of worldly transactions—serves as the cause. Thus, regarding those various objects well-known as being denoted by their respective words...

The term "conventional usage" (*rūḍhi*) is an illustration; since "function" (*vṛtti*) is accepted, therefore, without abandoning their respective meanings, the power (*śakti*) of all words is understood to reside in Viṣṇu by the force of [the evidence of] instruction, indicative marks, context, and so forth.
Although this much alone ought to be stated here:
This is not a fault;
for it is accepted that all words—even those denoting the Blessed One—also possess well-known conventional meanings.
Indeed, since words such as *jyotis* (light) are admitted to have dual referents, namely the light [of the sun] and the non-dual Brahman, there is no loss of ritual practice or worldly communication.

The etymological justification is that when the word *jātamota* functions with reference to the Supreme Lord through a distributive application (*avayavavṛtti*) to its constituent parts, it is accepted that either of the words *jāta* or *mota* [retains its primary sense]; thus, the derivation is established.
Furthermore, by taking even those constituent parts as referring to something else, the possibility of deriving the word *jāta* for the Supreme Lord remains.
Nevertheless, this might be so.
It should be understood that this was stated in order to dispel the doubt as to why it is precisely so if words were to have multiple meanings.
For instance, the capacity of words to denote other referents must indeed be accepted for the sake of establishing the aforementioned purpose.

Furthermore, the fact that all words denote the Supreme Lord must necessarily be accepted for each respective term, based on the authority of such scriptural teachings as "All names enter into Him" and "All these are indeed Ṛks," as well as through the power of word-roots, indicative marks, and so forth.

By this, the intended meaning of the sūtra, “And because there is instruction based on conceptualization, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth” (*BSū* 1.4.15), has been stated.

If all words possessed both meanings [the primary and the secondary], then [such passages as] “Indra is superior to the universe” and “In the beginning, this was non-existent” would [also be subject to that interpretation].
How is this so in such passages?

Because the two [meanings], such as being the supreme among all and so forth, are contradictory, it is impossible for both meanings to apply here. Even if the words were to express both meanings, there would still be a contradiction therein.
If it is argued that one must accept that the intended meaning (tātparya) lies in only one of those two, [we reply:
even in that case, it is not known which is to be accepted and which is to be rejected; therefore, he says: "Nevertheless" (tathāpi).
Nevertheless, when there is a conflict with this [general rule], its denotative power is set aside.

Although it has been stated in general that words have both types of meanings, nevertheless, when there is no contradiction with the Supreme Lord as the primary referent, any other primary reference is set aside.
The word "tu" (but/however) is intended to highlight this distinction.
First of all, it has been stated by the opponent himself that being intent upon both is contradictory;
furthermore, if one of the two must be abandoned, it is not proper to abandon the Supreme Lord,
because that would contradict other statements whose intended meaning is certain.
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is appropriate that only the other [meaning] be abandoned.
If this is so, then there is a contradiction with [the sūtra] beginning with "because of the teaching of conceptualization" (*kalpanopadeśāt*) and so forth;
for in that context, it was stated that all words have both meanings as their referent. If you say this, we reply: no.
He says "non-contradiction" because that [Dharma] culminates in a state free from reproach:
"But when there is no contradiction, many purposes are considered to be based upon this. (Manu 1.4.29cd)
The word "many" (*bahu*) has multiple meanings. "Accepted" (*matāḥ*) means intended in various respective sūtras.
[Objection: But even if there is no contradiction, is it not improper to accept both meanings?

Since that [objection] would contradict the restrictive determination [of the sūtra], "But that [is so] because of the harmony [of all texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*), it was stated: "as being the root of this."

This refers to those for whom the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) is the root—that is, the primary [cause]; their state is "thatness" (tattā). The instrumental case here is used in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūtalakṣaṇe). The restriction (avadhāraṇa) is employed to exclude any other primary [cause].
But it is not merely another object;
the sense is that this would contradict the stated purpose. By this, [the objection] "and this is not illogical" [is refuted].
The objection that there would be polysemy has also been resolved, because the primary meaning is one and the same.
[Objection: But surely in the case of Purandara and others as well, words such as "Indra" are applied through both conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*yoga*).
Conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*yoga*) are said to be the two primary modes of function (*mukhyavṛtti*).

Therefore, just as in the case of words such as "akṣa," it is logical that for words such as "Indra" both [conventional and etymological meanings] are the primary denotations; it is not the case that [the primary meaning] is the Lord alone. To this, he says: "For from this... (*ito hi*).
For it is from this [source] that others have derived their authority; indeed, its status as a basis for reliance rests upon this very fact.

It is true that even Purandara and others are the objects of the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of words such as "Indra" and so forth; nevertheless, that [conventional usage] derives precisely from this Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

And because, insofar as they are the objects of etymological derivation (*yoga*), the Supreme Lord alone is the basis of support (*upajīvyatva*), therefore He alone is the primary meaning, not Purandara and the others.
