For the Supreme Lord alone, who possesses unbounded sovereignty and other attributes by His very nature, is the object of both etymological derivation and conventional usage for words such as "Indra."
And it is well known that, in the case of Purandara and others, [the application of the name] is due precisely to their proximity to Him and because He is the cause of their activity.
Whatever is denoted by a word through the proximity [of another factor] is secondary (*amukhya*), while anything else is primary (*mukhya*).
For example, in the case of the word *dagdhṛ* ("burner"), iron and fire [are both denoted].
And it is not the case that the referents of words such as *akṣa* [are mutually...]
"There is a disparity because there is dependence on something else.
[Objection: If this is so, then it follows that even the Lord (Īśvara) would possess only a secondary status, since the application of the word [to Him] occurs only in dependence on another object.

Indeed, it is not possible for words such as "jyotis" (light) and so forth to apply to the Blessed One without depending on the fact that words like "jāta" (born) and others have other meanings; therefore, he says:
"Its establishment and its dependence upon that... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.30c).
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
This fault does not exist;
because, in the case of the Supreme Person, it is only the cognition of the application of those various words that depends on other referents, but not the actual application itself.
For the color of a jar is not dependent upon the lamp merely because it is perceived in dependence on the lamp;
just as in other cases the application of a word depends solely on the Supreme Lord, we do not observe any such dependence on anything else in the application [of words] to the Supreme Self. (4.155)
And for this reason as well, he says that this fault does not apply: "And [it] is dependent."
And it is dependent upon the will of Hari.

That dependence on other meanings in the application of words to the Supreme Lord is based solely on the will of the Blessed One, and not because there is no other recourse; therefore, this does not result in a loss of primary meaning for those words.
For the creation of one who employs roots and so forth by His own will is not dependent on another.
Nor does a person with efficient organs, walking for the sake of sport while leaning on a staff by his own will, become one whose movement is dependent on that staff.

If, in this way, the application of words elsewhere occurs through proximity to Hari and so forth, then is it not the case that for all words in the world—just as the word "burner" applies to iron—their function is merely secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?
If that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no distinction between the Ganges and its bank.

Anticipating the objection that this strikes at the root of the meaning stated in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa*—that it is like an axe placed at the base—he concludes the point previously stated with the words "Therefore," etc.
Therefore, while Viṣṇu possesses the supreme primary sense, other deities possess the primary sense [only in a secondary way].

It is not the case that for words such as Indra and others, when applied to Purandara and others, there is merely figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), as is the case with the word "burner" applied to iron; for this is established by conventional usage (rūḍhi) and direct denotation (abhidhāna).
Furthermore, because the signs of yoga, such as supreme sovereignty and so forth, exist [in other cases]; however,
this is due to the fact that in the case of the Supreme Lord, both conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*yoga*) are independent and unrestricted,
whereas elsewhere they are dependent upon Him and limited.
This distinction between the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary (*amukhya*) has been stated specifically with respect to the primary sense (*mukhyārthatā*).
Thus it was said: "the state of being supremely primary" (*paramamukhyatva*) and "primary-ness" (*mukhyatā*).
Furthermore, there are three modes of operation for a word: the indicative (*upalakṣaṇā*), the secondary (*gauṇī*), and [the primary]. (Manu 1.4.31cd)

After the word "gauṇī" (secondary), the word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied. Demonstrating this very point, he states the definitions of the functions beginning with the "paramamukhya" (primary-primary) by means of the verse beginning with "pravṛtti," and so forth.
In that regard, the primary mode of application is twofold:
*mahāyoga* and *mahāyogarūḍhi*. However, *mahārūḍhi* is not possible here.
Because it has been stated that "it is obtained through yoga alone," he describes the nature of Mahāyoga therein with the words, "of the cause of activity."
The abundance of causes for worldly activity and the state of being the supreme goal should be understood.
The meaning obtainable through etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is the cause of its application; its abundance constitutes its limitlessness.
Although independence (*svātantrya*) should also be mentioned here, it is omitted because it is the subject under discussion.

Nevertheless, since the exclusion of the other is established by even one [of these factors] alone, and since the purpose of the defining words (*lakṣaṇapada*) is precisely that much, it was not explicitly stated.
The construction is: "It should be understood as the 'supremely primary'.
Now, one might object: multiplicity is a property of the cause for the application [of a term].
Furthermore, while the state of having frequent occurrence belongs to the denotatum,
the quality of being the primary [meaning] for another belongs to the word;
how, then, can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)?
This is not a fault, because it is used figuratively (*upacaritatvāt*).
It refers to that [activity] of a word which depends upon a cause of engagement that is either unlimited or independent.
The intended meaning is that this function, characterized by great yoga (*mahāyoga*), is to be understood as the supreme primary sense (*paramamukhyatā*).
Describing the nature of the conventional usage based on great yoga (*mahāyogarūḍhi*), he says: "In that regard... (*tatra*).
In that regard, if there is such devotion to it, what need is there to mention the abundance of practice? (Manu 1.4.32cd)

If there were an abundance of usage for a word precisely in that sense where the cause for its application is unlimited, then what need is there to say that such a function possesses "paratā," that is, supreme primacy? In this context, it should simply be stated that when a word has an abundance of usage in a particular sense which possesses an unlimited ground for application, that word's function therein— characterized as *mahāyoga*, *rūḍhi*, or *lakṣaṇā*— is its supreme primary function (*paramamukhyavṛtti*).
The statement by way of *kaimutya* (a fortiori) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt;
for it is as follows:
is the definition here merely the abundance of applications, or is it qualified by an unlimited motive for its application?
Not the first,
because it would be a mere conventional usage and thus incapable of being the primary sense.
Not the second.
Since the status of being "paramamukhya" (supremely primary) is established by the very cause of its unlimited application, any further qualification would be redundant.
Nor does a distinct category arise through their combination;
for if that were the case, a combination of the unestablished (*asiddha*) and the contradicted (*bādhita*) would constitute another fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
In this case, only the second [alternative] is accepted;
nor is the aforementioned fault incurred,
because the status of being "supremely primary" is established by the mere qualification.
Because that [quality] is established all the more by the existence of the substantive;
for we do not employ the qualified term merely to establish its primary or supreme status,
but rather to establish another mode of expression consisting of a collective aggregate.
And there is no over-extension [of the definition],
because of the disparity;
for what is intended is indeed an abundance of usage that depends on an unlimited range of grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
It is not merely a collection;
and for this reason, the phrase "when there is an abundance of causes for engagement" should be applied there.
Furthermore, such a great yoga does not enter into this [category].
Because what is intended there is the absence of excessive application [of the term].
Regarding this, one might ask: "Which usage applies to Viṣṇu, by which it is said that he possesses supreme primacy? To this, he says: "Both."
Both [the manifest and the unmanifest] are seen in Viṣṇu, as are all words in every respect.
Both, that is, the two modes of occurrence,
are perceived by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
this is the meaning of the phrase "in every respect" (*sarvaśas*) regarding words.
The terms such as "Nārāyaṇa" possess both great etymological derivation (mahāyoga) and conventional usage (rūḍhi); for others, there is only great etymological derivation.
Alternatively, he demonstrates by this [verse] what was stated previously: that [the term] has its supreme primary application (paramamukhyavṛtti) in Viṣṇu.
Both [the abundance of causes for engagement] and the abundance [of means] are [required].
Alternatively,
the restatement of what has been cognized is the duty of an investigator, not the fabrication of an object according to one's own whim.
And these two modes of activity are not established anywhere by means of valid cognition;
therefore, they are not to be defined. This is what has been stated here. As for the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), however, they will be explained later.
Now, might these not be "yoga" (etymological derivation) and "yogarūḍhi" (hybrid formation)?
Is this doubted because of a lack of distinguishing factors, or rather because of a lack of a cause for intending that [specific] meaning?
It is not the first case.
Because that has already been stated;
nor is it the second [alternative], because [the text] establishes Viṣṇu’s primacy by first declaring that even derivative and other types of meanings are non-primary. (4.165)
Primary function (mukhyavṛtti) is also threefold:
etymological derivation (yoga), conventional usage (rūḍhi), and etymological-conventional (yogarūḍhi).
Among these, the function that depends upon the ground for application (pravṛttinimitta) is etymological derivation.
For example: "potter," "descendant of Upagu," and "king's man."
But surely even these [words] are not derivative (*yaugika*); rather, they are simply conventional (*rūḍha*).
The employment of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*) is merely for the sake of etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*).
As it has been said:
"These [words] are rooted like trees," and so forth—this is not so.

Since there is no reason to deny the distinction between word and meaning, which is perceived through the methods of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*), the students themselves should infer this; with this in mind, he states the essential nature of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) as follows: "In usage... and so on.

The predominance of mere usage (*prayogamātrabāhulya*) is called "conventional" (*rūḍhi*). When a word has a predominance of mere usage with respect to a particular meaning, its function there is called "convention. The inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding dependence on the meaning of the parts, similarity, and so forth. By this, it is distinguished from primary etymological usage (*yoga*), from "convention-derivation" (*yogarūḍhi*), and from metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
"Abundance" (bāhulya) is a statement regarding their essential nature. Śākaṭāyana maintains that all [words] are etymological (yaugika) and that there are none that are conventional (rūḍha).
That is incorrect,
because words such as *ghaṭa* (pot) and *paṭa* (cloth) are frequently observed [to be used in that way].
If it is argued that these too are merely derivative (*yaugika*) based on suffixes such as the *uṇādi* group, we say no.
Because no conformity with the meaning [of the parts] is observed,
and because, ultimately, one must rely on the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) for that specific sense;
where there is extensive usage dependent upon the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), that is "etymological-conventional" (*yogarūḍhi*).
Just as words such as *paṅkaja* (mud-born) are well-known to refer to the *tāmarasa* (lotus) and so forth, it was not explicitly stated [in the verse].
Some maintain that a combination of etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is improper because of contradiction and futility;
for instance:
Etymology (*yoga*) is a function based on the constituent parts [of a word], whereas convention (*rūḍhi*) is an indivisible function;
indeed, it is not logical for these two to coexist in a single instance.
Furthermore, there is no purpose whatsoever in accepting both etymology and convention simultaneously.
The claim that words such as *paṅkaja* (mud-born) are accounted for by their well-established conventional usage alone is incorrect;
for we do not say that a "conventional-derivative" (*yogarūḍhi*) is a mere combination of the derivative (*yoga*) and the conventional (*rūḍhi*),
which would entail a contradiction.

Just as conventional (rūḍha) indication differs from mere indication, and conventional-figurative (rūḍhagauṇī) differs from mere figurative indication due to the frequency of usage, so too this third mode of operation is distinct from mere conventionality because it depends on the ground for application (pravṛttinimitta), and from mere etymological derivation (yoga) because of the abundance of usage. Furthermore,
should words such as *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") be accepted as being merely conventional, or are they etymological?
Not the first [alternative],

because it contradicts the understanding of the meaning of the individual components and because it contradicts grammatical rules such as "the suffix ḍa is applied after the root *jan* when the locative case ending is present."
For by this very same reasoning, it would follow that [the term] is merely etymological (yaugika) and lacks actual existence. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because it would then follow that the term could be applied even to frogs and the like.

If it is argued that, as in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*), there exist well-known (*prasiddhi*) and not-so-well-known (*aprasiddhi*) usages despite an equality of expressive power (*śakti*), caused by the frequency or infrequency of conventional usage, we say no, because of the disparity.
For words such as "cow," [their primary] function is universally accepted...

Indeed, only when it is determined through the treatise (*śāstra*) that a word has multiple meanings must one search for other causes, such as common usage (*prasiddhi*), [to explain its application]. However, the capacity (*śakti*) of these words has not been established in this way across multiple referents. Furthermore, by stating rules such as "the root *śam* [takes the suffix *kan*] in the sense of a name" and "the roots *ram* and *jap* take [the suffix *kan*] in the sense of an elephant and a spy respectively," the author of the treatise has already accepted this mode of operation (*vṛtti*), even while mentioning limiting conditions (*upādhi*) distinct from the meaning of the word's parts; so, enough of this.

Having thus defined the primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*), which is immediate and known through words such as "denotative" (*abhidhāyaka*), he now defines the non-primary functions—the secondary (*gauṇī*) and the indicative (*lakṣaṇā*)—which are mediated, beginning with the verse starting "prayoga... (the application...).
It should be understood that the cause for the secondary application [of a word] is either similarity connected with usage or a relationship. ... MAnu 1.4.34a-c.
The connection is with that which is joined to the formal application (*prayoga*).
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an optional rule (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).
The word "also" (*api*) serves to include the definition of secondary function (*amukhyavṛtti-lakṣaṇa*) along with the definition of primary function (*mukhyavṛtti-lakṣaṇa*).
The term *amukhyatā* (non-primacy) is an adjective qualifying the function (*vṛtti*), even though that function is subordinate within the compound, having been mentally separated [from the word].
The meaning is that it should be understood as the cause for the non-primary functions—namely, the secondary (*gauṇī*) and the indicative (*lakṣaṇā*).

When a word is employed in a certain sense, its application elsewhere by taking as its motive a similarity to that [primary] sense, distinct from its own etymological ground (*pravṛttinimitta*), is the secondary function (*gauṇī*).
It is said that figurative function (*lakṣaṇā*) is the operation [of a word] based upon a connection with that [primary meaning].
Someone says:
"There is no such thing as a secondary function (*gauṇī*)."
Since similarity also, as a type of relation, is included within *lakṣaṇā*,
[the author] has defined *gauṇī* first even though it was mentioned later, in order to refute that [view];
for in this way, its independence would be made known.
If someone were to say:

"There is no such thing as indication (lakṣaṇā), because it is included within metaphorical usage (gauṇya), since the relationship [between words] consists of similarity in the form of occupying the same location and so forth," then what should be said in reply?
If it is argued that worldly cognition is not thus,
then do worldly people perceive similarity as a relation?
In that regard, the secondary (gauṇī) [metaphorical] usage is of two kinds.
This is due to the distinction between conventional and non-conventional usage.
Among these, the first is as follows:
for example, the application of the word "cow" (*gava*) to a clay cow and the like.
The second [type] is, for example, "the Vāhīka is an ox.

Here, some maintain that the qualities such as dullness and sluggishness, which accompany the primary meaning (*svārtha*) and are indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*), serve as the basis (*nimitta*) for the word "ox" functioning with reference to the Vāhīka.
That is incorrect.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that there is no distinction between secondary indication (*gauṇī*) and metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, when the word "cow" is applied to a *vāhīka*, it is devoid of any logical justification for the qualities being indicated to serve as the cause [of the application].

Moreover, the claim that another quality is indicated from the similarity of the indicated qualities, and from that, the possessor of the qualities (*guṇin*) is indicated, is not supported by experience.
Others maintain that the qualities residing in the object for others are indicated through non-difference from the qualities accompanying the primary sense;
this too is incorrect,
because the distinctness of those qualities will be established later.
And because there is an absence of a [primary] cause (*nimitta*) in the case of the Vāhīka,
it has been rightly stated that "secondary usage" (*gauṇī vṛttiḥ*) is a function for the sake of another, having as its cause the fact of being a substratum of similar qualities.
Furthermore, indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is also twofold.
This is due to the distinction between the conventional (rūḍha) and the non-conventional (arūḍha).
Among these, the first is as follows:
"The king goes."
The second type is, for example,
"the cowherd settlement on the Ganges.
Some say that indication (lakṣaṇā) is defined as the cognition of something invariably concomitant with the primary meaning.
In such cases as "their cots are crying," there would be no metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā);
and there would be [indication] for an object inferred through a mark (liṅga) perceived from the word itself.
Now, if it is argued that "inseparable connection" (avinābhāva) here means merely a relationship in general;
Nevertheless, there is an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in the case of indication by indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*);
for in that case, the function does not relate to what is denoted (*abhidheya*),
but rather relates to what has been indicated (*lakṣita*).
If it is argued that just as things were previously opposed, they have now become unified with one another,
and that this meaning is connected to the subject matter through such a succession,
then what is the point of this cumbersome conceptualization?
Let it be as stated: "the connection is associated with application.
If it is argued that there is another function called "manifestation" (*vyañjanā*), we say no;
for it is not accepted that this [function] constitutes the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*) by way of inference.
As it has been said:
"For that [implication] is an inference based on the mark of the words";
however, the ācārya himself will state that the function of intention (*tātparya-vṛtti*) does not exceed [the scope of] that [inference]. *4,205*
Is it not the case that the secondary (gauṇī) function operates by depending on the inapplicability of the primary meaning, its similarity [to another], and a purpose;
whereas the indicative (lakṣaṇā) function depends on the inapplicability of the primary meaning, a connection [between the primary and the indicated], and a purpose?
As it has been said:

“When the primary meaning is sublated, and there is a connection [between that primary meaning and another], then another meaning is indicated— either through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) or for a specific purpose (*prayojana*)— that is *lakṣaṇā*, a metaphorical operation.”
Thus [it is asked]: "How is it that only similarity and relation have been mentioned? To this, he says: "The previous... and so forth.

...in the case of the primary connection (*pūrvayoga*), there is the apprehension of another [meaning]. (Manu 1.4.34d) A lack of logical consistency (*anupapatti*) is not the cause for resorting to a secondary function (*amukhyavṛtti*),
because the observation of such inconsistency occurs only after the application [of the word] has already taken place.
However, the perception that the primary meaning is untenable is the cause for grasping a non-primary meaning;
for this very reason, it is not required by the word itself, nor by the speaker.
But it is by the cognizer alone [that this is determined].
For a word, by virtue of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), first brings the primary meaning itself to the mind;
and since the cognizer does not venture to abandon that meaning all at once, he requires the impossibility [of that primary meaning] for that very purpose.
Therefore, this [discussion] should not be raised in an inquiry into the causes of usage (*vṛtti*).
Furthermore, the purpose (*prayojana*) is not the cause of usage;
rather, it is only when the primary [meaning] is available for our own use in employing words that [a secondary meaning is resorted to].
Why do the speaker and the listener consider [the word] "non-primary" (amukhya) to be employed?
Therefore, it need not be stated here.
In this context, the mention of "inapplicability" (ayoga) is also an indication for "purpose" (prayojana).

Just as non-connection (*ayoga*) is universal, so too is the purpose (*prayojana*) not [universally required] in the case of established secondary (*gauṇī*) and indicative (*lakṣaṇā*) functions, because they do not depend on it since they are equal to primary denotation (*abhidhā*). It is not expressed by its own name (*svaśabda*) in order to indicate this distinction, for such a term would lack foundation. While one might say "the adoption of the non-primary when there is no connection with the primary," the statement "the adoption of the subsequent when there is no connection with the preceding" is intended to include cases such as indication of the indicated (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).

Indication by indication (lakṣitalakṣaṇā) is not resorted to merely because the primary sense is impossible; rather, it is resorted to when even that which has been indicated [by the primary sense] is impossible.
Therefore, this claim that "the primary sense is sublated" is incorrect. *4,211*
Furthermore, just as there is a gradation even among primary functions when they are accepted, so too is there one among secondary functions.
If one asks why, we reply: it is because of the proximity or remoteness of the comprehension of the meaning.

Now, one might object: "By forming a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) based on the relations of similarity and connection, and then applying its elision (*lup*), everything will be established; why then resort to accepting a non-primary mode of operation (*amukhyavṛtti*)? To this, the following is stated: if, according to the method described, the word *go* (cow) denotes both the actual cow and the Vāhīka man, and the word *gaṅgā* (Ganges) denotes both the river Ganges and the bank, then it is indeed primary denotation (*abhidhā*) itself [that functions].

In that case, upon the utterance of the words "cow" (*go*) and "Ganges" (*gaṅgā*), there would first be a cognition of the cow and the Ganges, and only when their connection is subsequently considered would there be a cognition of another meaning; however,
such a sequence of cognition does not occur when words like *harītakī* are uttered.
However, when both the tree and the fruit are perceived independently, the restriction to one or the other is made by virtue of the context and so forth;
and this subsequent apprehension exists in the case of the prior non-connection.
Therefore, we know that there is no such thing as "denotation by way of implication" (abhidhā) in either case.

[Objection: But surely, since the non-occurrence [of a fact] is the cause for the cognition of another fact, let this be simply "presumption" (arthāpatti); what is the use of resorting to the power of words?
For instance:
is this object understood from a word composed by a reliable person,
or otherwise?
Not otherwise,
because that [logical necessity] is absent in cases such as the speech of a madman;
however, in the first case, it is simply a matter of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
Because another meaning is postulated due to the contradiction between the speaker’s reliability and the impossibility of the perceived meaning,

this would indeed be the case if the speaker’s reliability were certain. However, if that word lacks the capacity for that [other] meaning, how could his reliability be ascertained when he is speaking something incoherent?
Therefore, the power of the word (*śabda-śakti*) must necessarily be resorted to for that purpose; thus everything is clarified.
By this, the following point is also refuted.
As for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view—
that the Supreme Lord cannot have the primary sense [of the term] because yoga is weaker than conventional usage (rūḍhi)—
this is untenable, since it is logical that great yoga (mahāyoga) possesses greater strength than mere conventional usage among the ignorant.
Since the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the learned has also been stated, it follows all the more that the etymological derivation (*yoga*) accompanied by that convention is even more appropriate.

Regarding what was stated—"Both [meanings] are seen in Viṣṇu"—and what was indicated—that the specific etymological derivation is stronger than the conventional usage—he establishes that point with the words: "This very... (*etameva*).
For it is said here that they call Him who is truly so by names such as "Śatarcīn" and others; the inclusion of the word "santam" (being) serves as an emphatic restriction.

He clearly demonstrates, through direct intent and with etymological explanations, the predominance of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) over etymological derivation (*yoga*), as well as the "learned convention" (*vidvadrūḍhi*) found therein, on many occasions. (Manu 1.4.36)
"Because he praised him for a hundred years, they call him the Śatarcins; though he is this very [Agni], they call him the Śatarcins.
And because he placed all this—whatever there is—in the middle, therefore they are the Madhyamas; though they are this very [Agni], they call them the Madhyamas."
Such is the Śruti. Together with its etymological explanation (nirukti), it is accompanied by the application of the term in its yogic sense;
therein, "gām" refers to the Supreme Lord as its object.
He demonstrates the conventional usage among the learned (*vidvadrūḍhi*) for all words indicated by terms such as *śatarcī* and so forth,
because it is stated that "they declare [it thus].

Furthermore, the fact that he shows this many times, even very frequently, makes it known that it is due to the direct intention (*añjas-tātparya*) itself, and not merely as a secondary or incidental mention (*prāsaṅgikatvena*).

Furthermore, by the use of the word "existent" (*santam*) here and by the restrictive particle "this very one" (*etameva*), the Śruti demonstrates the superiority of the yoga pertaining to the Blessed Lord over worldly convention.

Wise men, through the aforementioned yoga, declare this very Supreme Self—who exists as the referent of names such as "the hundred-versed one" (*śatarcī*)—to be denoted by the words "the hundred-versed one" and so forth. However, they do so only in a secondary sense regarding those like Madhucchandas whose meanings are fixed by convention; for this meaning is understood through the force of the two words [in the compound].
By the word "existent" (*santam*), it is stated that the primary meaning is not like how one calls what is not the Ganges "Ganges," but rather [it is] Hari;
for the purpose of establishing that, the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) "they call him" (*ācakṣate*) is connected.
By the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), however, [the primary meaning] of another [term] by that word—[is excluded].
Thatness (tattva) is being negated;
however, a total negation of everything is not tenable,
because it would contradict the purpose previously stated.
From this, it is understood that there is a negation of being denotable [by words] due to [Brahman's] equality with the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).

When it is stated that the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) exceeds the conventional meaning (*rūḍhārtha*), it is established that the specific etymology pertaining to that [etymological] sense possesses greater force than worldly convention (*laukikarūḍhi*).
In some places, the reading is "avadhāraṇā" (restriction).
The construction here is that [the author] demonstrates two things: the word "existent" (*santam*) and the term "restriction" (*avadhāraṇā*).
Since this is so, what has been stated is logical.
He establishes that Viṣṇu is denotable by all words even through other scriptural passages, beginning with "aḥ iti."
The syllable *a* is declared to be Brahman; by its explanation, it is likewise considered [the essence] of all words. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.37a–c)
In the Śruti passage, "‘Aḥ’ is Brahman," the fact that the letter *a* denotes Brahman is stated;
otherwise, the use of the particle *iti* would be purposeless.

In the Śruti text, "The letter *a* is indeed all speech," it is stated that all words are explained by the letter *a*; however, since direct identity is contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge, it is necessary to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which explains and that which is to be explained to have different objects.

Therefore, by reflecting upon these two statements, it is understood that Brahman is expressible by all speech. Furthermore, in this Śruti passage (Ai. 2.3.8): “Having separated from speech that which is ‘Om’ and that which is ‘not,’ and having removed from it what is harsh and what is excessive, the seers discovered [Brahman] and were satisfied in the Name, for it is established in the Truth”—in this, among speech and the collection of words, that which is the word ‘Om,’ meaning that which signifies assent, [is the means of its expression].

That word "no" which has the sense of negation, and that which is cruel in meaning— that is, harsh— within this speech, as well as that which is excessive— that is, harsh— in sound; [all these are to be avoided].
This is an elliptical expression;
having separated and investigated the entire collection of Vedic words, the wise— those possessed of discernment— [realize that everything] is dependent upon Name.
They discovered— that is, they came to know— the grounds for the application of those words, which are dependent on names because they are made manifest by names, and thus subordinate to names.
And when that feeling had been attended to and matured, immediately thereafter they became satisfied, having accomplished what was to be done and were liberated; thus,
the state of having accomplished what was to be done is described for those who know it by name alone.

"Knowing him thus"—from this, it is heard that liberation comes from the knowledge of the Supreme Lord alone. Since both [the injunctions regarding names and the promise of liberation] would otherwise be inexplicable, it is understood that all Vedic names have the Supreme Lord as their referent; thus he says: "Name... (4.219)...
"The knower of names has accomplished his purpose. (Manu 1.4.37d)
Furthermore, the Veda declared that all the syllables and the preceding and succeeding words of all the Vedic Saṃhitās have the form and meaning of the name "Viṣṇu" and that they establish Him.
By this, it is understood that all syllables and all Saṃhitās indeed establish Viṣṇu alone; thus he says: "By the name of Viṣṇu."
Then he declared that the nature of the meaning of the name Viṣṇu resides in the *saṃhitā* and other [Vedic recensions].
To the question "Where did he say it?", he recites that statement according to its meaning: "And the letter ṇa," and so forth.
And pronouncing the letter *ṇa* and the letter *ṣa*, which consist of strength and exertion; (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.38cd)
Likewise, the study of the Saṃhitā is preceded by that knowledge. (Manu 1.4.39ab)
"The letter *ṇa* is strength (*bala*), the letter *ṣa* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the self (*ātman*).
Thus, by stating that the letters *ṇa* and *ṣa* contained within the name of Viṣṇu signify the power and activity of the Supreme Lord, the Veda immediately thereafter says:
"He who knows these two letters, *ṇa* and *ṣa*, as joined together in the *ṛc*s"—meaning that among all *saṃhitās*, the letters *ṇa* and *ṣa* are joined together in the *ṛc*s.

The meaning is that he who knows that the very same reality which is established by the letters *ṇa*, *śa*, and their combination is established everywhere by all preceding and following letters and their combinations— he, knowing this, has declared that the study of all *saṃhitās* must be preceded by the knowledge of the identity of meaning with the name of Viṣṇu.

Now, it might be argued that here the capacity to convey the meaning of the letters *ṇa* and *ṣa* is being predicated of all the letters and so forth, but not the status of being the name of Viṣṇu; for surely the letters *ṇa* and *ṣa* alone do not constitute the name of Viṣṇu. To this he replies: "Because of their being prefixes (*upasarga*)."
Let it be [a prefix] by virtue of being a preposition (upasarga), and likewise let *ud* [be so] by virtue of its meaning "habitual tendency" (tācchīlya).
The letter *ṇa* and the letter *ṣa* are considered [together] as name and form (*nāmarūpa*).
Although there are other letters belonging to the name Viṣṇu,

nevertheless, because the prefix *vi-* functions as an upasarga that qualifies the meaning of the subsequent word, and because the suffix *-un* has the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), it is subordinate (*upasarjana*).
Since the Veda is considered primary for one who reflects upon it, there is no fault in regarding both the letter *ṇ* and the letter *ṣ* as being intended in their very nature as names;
for it is said that "prefixes [occur] in connection with a verb," yet here there is no connection with a verb.
How, then, can it have the status of a prefix? Do not say so; [it is used] in the sense of "ending an action" (*ṣontakarmaṇi*).
Because it is accepted that [the root] consists of two forms, namely *ṇu* and *stu*, the derivation of the suffix expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika-pratyaya*) is thus justified.
He states the purpose of the scriptural citations (śruti) that have been quoted: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Therefore, there is a complete correspondence in Viṣṇu of the nature of vowels, syllables, and words.
This applies even to the Veda; how much more so, then, to that which exists in the form of sentences?

The meaning is that the word-by-word coordination and the sentence-level coordination of all words [referring] to Viṣṇu, which were previously stated, are established by these very scriptural passages (*śruti*).
The scriptural passages dependent on logical reasoning (*upapatti*) have been cited earlier;
now he cites those that clearly demonstrate the coordination of both words and sentences—beginning with the verse "ghoṣāḥ."
All sounds and all the Vedas, as well as that state which all the Vedas [seek].
"The first creator, the bestower of names upon all the gods, is Indra, Mitra, and likewise Indra"—such is the Vedic revelation (śruti). *Manu Smṛti* 1.4.42.
In a matter not covered by the aforementioned means of valid knowledge...
“Indeed, all these *ṛc*s, all the Vedas, and all sounds are but a single utterance (*vyāhṛti*), namely the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) themselves.
“The goal which all the Vedas proclaim,” “Indra, Mitra...”
“They call him Varuṇa, they call him Agni; he is the divine, fair-winged Garuḍa.
Being one, the sages call him by many names: they call him Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan.
“Whom they call Indra, whom they call Varuṇa, whom they call Mitra, whom they call the Truth.”
"He is the first creator, Viśvakarman; he is the first Mitra and Varuṇa of the living beings;
he who alone is the bearer of the names of the gods."
These are the sentences taken up by these representative citations (*pratīka*);
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of passages such as "all names" and so forth is intended.

In this context, the first, second, and final scriptural passages serve as the authority for the two types of reconciliation (*samanvaya*); the others, however, pertain to the reconciliation of sentences (*vākyānvaya*).
When names such as Indra and others refer to the Supreme Lord, [the text reads]: "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra."
For the fact that such statements have that [Brahman] as their ultimate purport is established.
This very point has been stated by the Blessed One himself through the opening [of the work], expressing the entire logical connection (*anvaya*). (Manu 1.4.43b–d)
To the objection, "Since no sūtra is seen that establishes this meaning, why has this matter been stated as being outside the sūtras (utsūtrita)? he says: "That very [sūtra]," and so forth.
This very point has been stated by the Blessed One himself as the author of the Sūtra; it is not being stated here in a manner that contradicts the Sūtra.
And so says the Sūtra:
"But because they begin with light, for thus it is studied by some."
By stating that "jyotiḥ" (light) is to be taken as the pratīka of the sūtra, he indicates that the reading "jyotir-upakramāt" found among others is indeed a corrupt reading.
Alternatively, one might ask: "How can the word 'all' (sarva) convey the meaning here when only light (*jyotis*) is mentioned?
We reply: "Because the word 'light' is used as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
To the question, "How is it understood that the intention is to use it as an illustration?", it is said: "By the one who says [it is] from the introductory context (*upakrama*). (4.223)
For here, having stated the proposition "It is light," the reason is given in the words, "Because it is so studied by some";
and this is its meaning:
“Since it begins with ‘This one has illumined this world,’ having established that opening statement, the text continues with ‘Those indeed... and so forth, [concluding] ‘One alone.
Thus, if the intention here were merely to establish the application of the word ‘light’ (jyotis), then something should have been said to support only that;
what use would there be in introducing the support for its being denotable by all words?”

It is not the case that there exists no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is a particular (*viśeṣa*), by virtue of which a proof could be established through the medium of a universal (*sāmānya*).

Therefore, it is understood that the author of the Sūtra, employing a means of valid cognition whose object is everything, intended the word "light" (*jyotis*) to be used in its secondary sense (*lākṣaṇika*).

Furthermore, it was stated that the proposition "Because of the coordination of all [words]" (*kiñca tattu samanvayāt*) asserts the coordination of all words in Brahman, not merely the coordination of a few words;
and it was also said that the remainder of the chapter proceeds for the purpose of explaining that.
In this regard, the coordination of the words relevant to the context has been established through the sections beginning with the "Consisting of Bliss" (*ānandamaya*).
In this quarter (pāda), there is a systematic application (samanvaya) of words such as "contradiction" (virodhi) and so forth.

Furthermore, since words denoting the sequence of ritual actions and the like remain, and since this present section (adhikaraṇa) is still to be established, one understands—by the method of elimination—that this [quarter] is for the purpose of establishing the samanvaya of those [words]. Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "bruvatā" (by one who speaks).

Let it be granted that there is here the proposition of the concomitance of all words; nevertheless, the method (*nyāya*) for demonstrating that [concomitance] therein is [expressed] by the passage beginning with "born" (*jāta*) and "perished" (*ota*), and so forth.
Since it was stated that this was not set forth in the Sūtra, it was therefore said: "Because of the introduction."

By employing the introductory statement, "He [Brahman] worshipped this world," and stating that "thus indeed one [text] reads," the author of the Sūtras has said exactly what we have stated; for [the identity of the subject] is seen throughout this entire [section] from the beginning.
And how this is so has been stated in the passage beginning with "this very [thing]," etc. (*4,224*).
Having thus explained the sūtras beginning with "that which is inferential" (*ānumānika*) through both summary and detail, he refutes the interpretation of others. To explain:
Some describe this immeasurable basis [of the objection] differently:

"The claim that the *pradhāna* is not based on the Veda (*aśabda*) because of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*), as stated in the sūtra, is unproven; for in certain recensions (*śākhā*), words intended to designate the *pradhāna* are actually heard."
Therefore, as long as this [objection] is not refuted, the doctrine that Brahman is the cause cannot attain stability;
hence, this chapter (pāda) is commenced in order to demonstrate that the Pradhāna is not based on the sacred word (aśābdatva).
He refutes that very point [as follows]: "It is not the case that [the object] is merely denotable by words."
It is not the very fact of being expressible by words that is denied here of the Pradhāna.

The point is this: it would be untenable to claim that the fact that *pradhāna* is not denotable by words is refuted right here in the first chapter; for if that were so, since it would not be included within the definition of "harmonious convergence" (*samanvaya*), it would follow that the chapter itself is irrelevant.
[Objection: But was it not already stated here that the non-verbal nature of *pradhāna* is established in order to ensure the stability of the "harmonious convergence"?

And if that were so, how could there be an inconsistency? Do not say so; for if that were the case, it would follow that [inconsistency] would be included within the definition of non-contradiction (*avirodha*).
Otherwise, the meaning of the second chapter (*adhyāya*) would also be solely for the sake of stabilizing the concordance (*samanvaya*), and thus it too would have to be discussed here;
however, it is not tenable [to claim] that only the designation by words (*śabdavācyatā*) of the *pradhāna* is being negated here.
Because there is no distinction [between the two].

Furthermore, in this section (*pāda*), it is either the state of being denotable by words that express the cause of the world and so forth that is denied of the *pradhāna*, or the very state of being denotable by words itself.
Not the first; for in the sentences cited here, such as “The Unmanifest is beyond the Great” and “In whom the five groups of five people [dwell],” [the term *avyakta* appears].
Because in such passages as these, the Pradhāna is not heard of as the cause of the world,
someone says:
"In the phrase 'the Unmanifest is beyond the Great,' the word 'beyond' (para) expresses temporal remoteness."
Therefore, the suspicion that [the past] is a cause is raised;
that is incorrect.
Is being a cause merely a temporal distance, or is it something to be inferred by means of that [distance]?
Now, [the third alternative] is possible;
it is not the first or the second, because even for two things that lack the relationship of cause and effect, a relation of priority and posteriority is observed.
Not the third [alternative],
because mere possibility cannot be the motivating factor for such an extensive collection of sūtras.
If it is argued that causality is understood in passages such as "the one unborn," etc.:
In that case, what will be done with the Supreme Brahman?
For you have explained that [the passage] concerns the elements of fire, water, and food;
and thus it does not transcend the common worldly proverb: "When a mouse is carried off by a tiger, what loss is there? [Or when a mouse is carried off] by a wolf..."
"What is the benefit in [the word] being led [to that meaning]?
To this, the following response is offered:
"In this case, it is not the very denotability by the word of the primary object that is being negated."
"Because it is not applicable to the subject at hand.

For if the Pradhāna were established as being verbal in nature, its mere essential nature would be proven; yet, the proof of its mere essential nature does not cause any deficiency in the definition [of the Pradhāna].
This is because the opponent, unlike us, has not asserted that all words are in harmony with [the Pradhāna].
Nor has Brahman been introduced there by negating Pradhāna,
such that it would be of use even according to our own position;
this is what was stated.
It is not tenable that here the expressibility of the Pradhāna by words is being negated without reference to its entry into Brahman;
furthermore, the expressibility of the Pradhāna by words should have been negated immediately after the section concerning "seeing" (īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa).
It is not tenable [to claim] that it is prohibited here after having transcended the three quarters, because no reason for such an intervention can be established.
Furthermore, the meaning to be established by a chapter (*pāda*) is such that it is that which is established by all the sūtras contained within that chapter;
and in this [fourth] chapter, [this is not the case] for all [the sūtras].
There is no rule in the Sūtras that the primary [reality] must exclusively be negated as being denotable by words—
which would make this the meaning of this section—
since such a restriction is absent in passages such as "as the cause" (kāraṇatvena).

If it is argued that even in that case, by way of a succession, that very same [primary meaning] is what is to be established, then—since such a succession can be easily asserted even for a word-meaning that has already passed—the negation of the primary status of the word's denotation applies here alone; thus, there is no [contradiction]. For that is indeed a word-meaning which is not established elsewhere. (4.233)
Having thus refuted the meaning of the word in general, he now refutes the explanation of the first topical section (adhikaraṇa) with the words: "It is not merely being denotable by a word."
Regarding the sūtra beginning with "ānumānikam" (the inferential), which has been explained by the opponent as follows:
"The inferential—that is, the *pradhāna* determined through inference—is also perceived in the form of a word among certain followers of Vedic branches;
for it is recited in the *Kāṭhaka*:"
"Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest; greater than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. In this regard, those who have such names...

Furthermore, those very entities— the Great One (mahat), the Unmanifest (avyakta), and the Person (puruṣa)— which are established by tradition as having such a sequence, are recognized here [in this text].
In this context, the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) refers to the Pradhāna by virtue of both its conventional usage (rūḍhi) and its etymological derivation (yoga).
If it is argued that, because it thus possesses a verbal designation, its being "beyond words" (aśabdavatva) is untenable, we reply:
this is not so.
For this statement from the *Kāṭhaka* does not have the *pradhāna* as its primary referent.
Here we ask:

is it merely the fact that the *pradhāna* is denoted by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) occurring in the *Kāṭhaka* that is being negated here, or is it being asserted that it is not denoted by any word whatsoever anywhere?
The answer to the first [objection] is as follows:
It is not tenable that in this passage from the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, it is merely the designation of the *pradhāna* by the term "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) that is being negated.
Because the state of being "non-verbal" is not established by that alone.
Regarding the second [alternative] as well, is it denied by way of the primary (paramamukhya) function, or is only the status of being denotable by a word negated?
In the first case, that much is indeed admitted.
In every respect, it is only the state of being denotable by words that is here negated regarding the Pradhāna; thus, the second [interpretation] is not tenable.
Why? To this he says: "sarva... (all...).
From a compendium of all the Vedas, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas.
The phrase "because of the inclusion of the primary [cause]" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In the Veda, the followers of the Atharva-veda recite: "She who is the producer of transformations, the unknowable, the eightfold-formed, unborn, and eternal;
she is meditated upon by Him, and being presided over by Him, she is stretched out and impelled again," and so forth.
However, when the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are cited, they should be examined [for their own authority].
But has it not already been stated here that the "Pradhāna" consisting of the three guṇas, which is well-known from Smṛti, is not what is being spoken of here?
Therefore, whatever is cited [from those sources] is indeed contradictory [to our position].
Therefore, he cites a passage from the Itihāsa which establishes the Pradhāna as being endowed with characteristics such as consisting of the three guṇas: "Sattva... and so forth.
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas— these qualities born of Prakṛti bind the imperishable embodied self within the body, O mighty-armed one."
...in the form of such statements as these... // MAnu 1.4.46a //
By the phrase "and so forth," there is the inclusion of [the elements] such as "earth, water, fire, and air.
The connection is that this refers to the inclusion of the *pradhāna*, which is endowed with the nature of possessing the three *guṇas* and other qualities as established by such statements. (4.234)

Furthermore, if that which is denoted by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) in the statement "The Person is higher than the unmanifest" is not the Pradhāna, then something else must be explained as its referent.
But has this not already been stated by the author of the Sūtras himself: "Because [the elements] are apprehended as being arranged in the form of a body"?
"Know the self as the rider and the body as the chariot"— the body which was previously presented in the form of a chariot is here grasped by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta),
both because of the context and because of the method of elimination.
The author of the Sūtra did not say this at all;
for if that were the case, he would have said, "because of the apprehension of the body as arranged in the form [of a statue].
Or, let it be granted that for some reason the qualifying term is placed last.
But this must be addressed:
how is it that the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) denotes the body? For this is not a conventional usage.
Nor is conjunction possible,
because the body is manifest.
But has this not already been refuted by the author of the Sūtras?
"But that [body] is subtle because it is worthy of that [state].
Even though this body is manifest, its root— its material cause, consisting of the subtle elements characterized as fire, water, and earth— is nonetheless unmanifest.
Because that subtle [principle] is beginningless, it possesses unmanifestness;
furthermore, the terms "effect" and "cause" become conflated, as in the verse:
"Mix the intoxicating drink with milk."
Regarding the phrase "thus, as it is," this must be explained: what is being stated by this?

Is it the body itself that is spoken of here, such that the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) is used figuratively for it, because the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) consisting of fire, water, and earth— which serve as the primary material cause of the body— are unmanifest due to being beginningless?
Or rather, is it that the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) themselves are denoted by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*),
while the word "body" is used for them figuratively,
because the body is their effect?
He states the fault in both positions with the words "where."
Or if even that which consists of fire, water, and earth is accepted as the material cause;
When it is asked, "Which is the primary cause: beginningless nature (pradhāna) or primordial sin? [the answer follows].
In that statement,
if the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) is not intended to have another meaning,
namely, that characterized as the Supreme Brahman;
Rather, it is held that the primordial material cause of the body, consisting of fire, water, and earth, is indeed the beginningless subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*).

In the first case, it exists in its own essential form; in the second, it is denoted by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). If it is then asked, "In that case, is this not the Pradhāna?", what fault is there in that?
By this, it is denied that [the term] "goes.
This is the intended meaning:
in no way, indeed, can you claim that the word *avyakta* refers to Brahman.
However, [the term "unmanifest"] may denote either the body composed of subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) and its effects, or the subtle elements themselves;
whereas others hold it denotes *pradhāna*.
If the causality of the unmanifest is intended, then both of these positions constitute an opposition to the doctrine of Brahman (*brahmavāda*).

If one accepts [the existence of] a body, the refutation of *pradhāna* is futile. However, if there is no intention to assert its status as a cause, then since neither of the two positions is contradictory, what is the point of this insistence on adopting one and rejecting the other? For it would be fruitless and incoherent. Alternatively, [it may refer to] the beginningless, insentient material cause (*upādāna*), namely the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) such as sound...
If the denotatum is accepted, the claim that "the primary [meaning] is not [the name]" is empty speech, because the primary meaning is defined by that [denotatum];
the intention is that dispute regarding the name itself is impossible. (4,241)
But surely this very doubt has been refuted by the author of the Sūtras himself with the words: "Because it is dependent on that, it is purposeful.
This may indeed be so.
If we were to accept that fire is an independent cause consisting of water and earth,
this would not be the case.
Because its dependence upon Brahma is accepted;
and this must necessarily be admitted.
For that [scripture] is meaningful;
for without it, Brahman’s status as the cause of the world cannot be established. To this, it is replied:
What is meant by this?
It is that there is agreement that the Pradhāna exists,
but there is disagreement regarding its properties, such as independence and so forth.
If this is so, then while the Sāṅkhya may urge that the Pradhāna possesses independence and so forth,
you must instead demonstrate its dependence and other such qualities.
What is the use of this effort to refute the claim that words such as "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) refer to the Pradhāna?
For here, the independence of the *pradhāna* and so forth does not appear;
on the contrary, from the statement "the *puruṣa* is superior to the unmanifest (*avyakta*)," the subordination of the unmanifest to the *puruṣa* is understood.
This has also been stated: "If it is merely said that 'the *pradhāna* is spoken of here,' what fault is there?"
"But when it is stated that [the cause] is independent,
it is not said here in this manner"; thus,
the section beginning with "like the cup, because there is no distinction" (*camasavad aviśeṣāt*) also serves to demonstrate that the Pradhāna is not based on the words of the Veda (*aśābdatva*).
They explain it thus:
"The one unborn [nature], red, white, and black, giving birth to many offspring of similar form..."

"In this mantra— 'The one unborn [soul], indeed, lying along with her while she creates many offspring of similar form, rejoices; another unborn [soul] abandons her once her enjoyment has been experienced'— since the Pradhāna is established, how can it be said that [the Sāṅkhya doctrine] is not based on the Word (aśabda)?"
To this it is replied:
Just as in the mantra “the ladle is face-downward,” [one does not understand] independently that “this is the name of that ladle”;
Thus, it cannot be definitively determined,
because there is no distinguishing characteristic;
for attributes such as having an upward-facing base can be applied to anything in some way or another.
Likewise, even in the passage "the one unborn," it cannot be determined that the Pradhāna is being propounded,
because there is no distinguishing characteristic [to that effect].
This, however, is untenable:
"The Cow is without beginning or end; she is the progenitor, the source of past and future;
white, black, and red; she is the fulfiller of all desires for the Lord."
This is because the determination [of the meaning] is established through the designation of the scriptural passage beginning with those words.
Furthermore, the word *ajā* cannot here be accepted as referring to a she-goat based on its conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*),
because this is a context concerning knowledge (*vidyā*).
Nor is it the supreme Brahman,
because redness and other qualities are impossible [in it],
and because its being an object of enjoyment is untenable.
For this very reason, it is not the individual soul (jīva) either, because it is mentioned separately as the enjoyer;
nor is it any other insentient entity.
Because non-arising is impossible;
therefore, she is unborn by nature, due to the absence of birth.
It is red, white, and black because it consists of the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas;
moreover, the fact that rajas and the others are red and so forth is well-established in the scriptures (āgamas).
And the living being (jīva), being attached to these, transmigrates.
It is also well-established that one who is unattached is liberated;
for if this were not so, the mantra would fall into the state of having no object of application.
Now, [it may be argued] that the mantra does not indeed fall into the state of having no object of application.
For the author of the Sūtras himself says, "Beginning with light" (*jyotir-upakramā*).
In this mantra, the Ajā (the Unborn) is established as beginning with light, having the nature of fire, water, and food.
Why? Because...

"That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food"—thus some indeed study [the Upanishads] as teaching that heat, water, and food possess forms such as red and so forth.
By virtue of that designation, even here,
the *ajā* is to be understood as consisting of fire,

water, and earth; for it is logical that she, being the material cause of the fourfold collection of beings, possesses the quality of giving birth to many offspring and, by virtue of her insentience, the quality of being an object of enjoyment.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Unborn," etc.
When the Śruti declares, "The one unborn female," what fault is there then? ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.47c-e //

If it is accepted that what is propounded here in this mantra is a transforming, insentient [pradhāna] characterized by fire, water, and food, then when the position is taken that the scripture "the one unborn" refers to this very prakṛti, what fault is there?
None at all. *4,246*

If it is argued: "But how can it be that [the Brahman] does not exist? For the non-scriptural nature (*aśabdatva*) has been established by the statement 'Because of seeing [it], it is not non-scriptural' (*īkṣaternāśabdam*)," [we reply:
No, because we have explained that [passage] otherwise; with this intention, it was said: "In every respect" (*sarvathā*).
...if there exists in every way something insentient that undergoes transformation.
The meaning is that it is unavoidable.
This is the underlying intention here:
indeed, it is as the cause of the world that the Unborn (ajā) is perceived in this context.

She is to be established as Brahman by one who speaks of Brahman through her nature as Brahman; but if she were established as consisting of fire, water, and food, why would even the form of Pradhāna not be accepted?

If it is argued that this is not the case because the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is equal, since fire, water, and earth are also dependent upon the Supreme Lord, and therefore there would be over-extension in those cases as well; [we reply: no.
If that is so, then what is the point of refuting the mantra’s reference to primordial nature (*prakṛti*)?

Rather, even while accepting its reference to primordial nature, one must establish that [the world] is dependent solely upon God by the force of such statements as, “He who alone presides over the source. (4.247)
Furthermore, the word "unborn" (aja) is neither conventional nor etymological when applied to fire, water, and so forth;
for,
according to scriptural passages such as "It created that fire," their non-origination is impossible.
Nor is the feminine gender appropriate,
nor is the singular number;
if it is argued that this is because of the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), we say no.
Now, if it should be thought that there exists some single, insentient, and beginningless substance which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of fire, water, and earth,
and that the application of words such as "unborn" (*aja*) is justified through metaphorical usage because [the world] is its effect—
then let that very [substance] be what is propounded here.
If it is argued that this is so because words attain their primary mode of operation (*mukhyavṛtti*),
then what wrong has been done by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) who asserts that "Prakṛti" is what is being expounded here?
For Prakṛti is defined by those very characteristics.
Furthermore, since dispute is impossible regarding what is merely a name, this has been stated as "the one unborn.
But has not the answer already been given here: "because it is taught as a conceptual construction"?
"Just as in the Madhu-vidyā and other instances, the sun and so forth are conceived of as honey and so forth,
so too here, because there is an instruction on conceiving fire, water, and food as the Unborn and so forth, there is no contradiction"— this is incorrect.
Because there is no purpose for such conceptualization;
for this is not a poetic work intended merely to delight the minds of common folk.
For this very reason, even the illustrative example has been refuted.
Someone else explains "kaścijjyotirupakrama" differently:
"jyotis" means Brahman.
Since this *ajā* (the Unborn) has that [Brahman] as its beginning and that as its cause, it is not independent;
therefore, his first sūtra would be redundant,
as its purpose would already have been fulfilled by this one alone.
Furthermore, by the very statement "because it is dependent on that" (*tadadhīnatvāt*),
the fact that the Pradhāna begins with light (*jyotirupakramatva*) has already been established;
this same point must also be demonstrated in the examination of the Sāṅkhya system.

If it is argued that it is incorrect to say there is no fault even if this scripture has the Pradhāna as its primary purport— on the grounds that the restrictive determination in the sūtra, "But that [Brahman], because of the harmony [of all texts]," would be untenable— we say: no.
Even if fire were dependent on water and food, that would not resolve the problem.
[Verse 4.354: "Let it be so for the opponent; but how is there no fault for you? To this he says: "For us... [etc.]
For us, however, the Blessed One alone is the supreme and primary object;
everything else is accepted as being established merely by way of being secondary.
For all words as well, figurative usage and the like are excluded because of their inapplicability.

In our view, however, the meaning of the restrictive statement "because of the coordination" (*samanvayāt*) is this: the Blessed Lord alone is the single, supreme primary referent (*paramamukhyārtha*) of all words, and no other.
Therefore, whatever is conventionally established as the referent of a particular word, all of that is accepted as being nothing but His primary referent.
When the primary sense is not applicable, even a secondary (gauṇa) sense may be accepted.

This being so, what inconsistency is there in accepting that words such as *ajā* refer to the Supreme Brahman through their most primary function (*paramamukhya-vṛtti*), while also denoting Pradhāna through their primary sense alone?

[Objection: If that is the case, then why is the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) in the Sūtra explained as being for the purpose of excluding other meanings that might be considered the most primary?
Why should it not be explained as being for the sake of excluding other mere objects of expression?

Nor is there an impossibility of the stated purpose, since that purpose is established either through a secondary (amukhyā) mode of operation or by mere conventional designation (saṅketa). If this is argued, we say no.
He says—“the two meanings”—because the author of the Sūtras himself has accepted the aforementioned multiplicity of meanings for Vedic words in another work.
He recites that very [verse]: "Of effects," and so forth.
They know the cause of all effects to be the first, the highest object of speech to be the word, and the supreme perfection of yogas to be your supreme state.
Thus... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.51a]
Among Vedic utterances, this is the supreme object of expression; compared to it, all others are secondary objects of expression. Why is this so?

The supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) of yogas and yogic practices; it is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) because things are accomplished therein. Indra and the others, however, are merely inferior accomplishments.
Why is this so?
Because for effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, [the Self] is the primary cause,
whereas Nature (prakṛti) and the others are secondary causes.
"pada" means its own essential nature (svarūpa). They know that which is superior to that.
Although conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is powerful merely by virtue of conveying a meaning without delay, [it is not so here].
Nevertheless, considering that yoga alone is more powerful because it is the cause of specific knowledge (*viśeṣajñāna*), it is precisely that which has been adopted.
Although two meanings are not explicitly stated there, the existence of another meaning to be expressed is understood from the qualification "the highest" (*uttama*).
For this very reason, it was previously stated, "having intended" (*abhipretya*).
He states another proof for the fact that Vedic words have both meanings, beginning with the word "buddhau."

... because both [words] are established through etymology (yoga) and conventional usage (rūḍhi), and because there is no reason to abandon either, they are held to have both meanings. (Manu 1.4.51a–d)
"Yoga" refers to the Supreme Lord, who is the object of the function of yoga;
"rūḍhaḥ" means well-known by convention, such as [the word] *prakṛti* and so forth.
This is the meaning.

To begin with, for one who has mastered the connection between words and their meanings and has understood the principles of verbal cognition, upon hearing words such as "ajā" (the unborn), the Pradhāna— as well as Brahman— ascends to the intellect;
and the validity of cognitions is indeed intrinsic.
It was established in the first sūtra that invalidity depends upon sublation;
however, there is no sublation here in the acceptance of these two meanings,
by which even what has ascended into the intellect would have to be abandoned.
Therefore, by the force of this unassailable cognition, it must be accepted that all words possess both meanings.
He explains this very point with the verse beginning "viparīta... (contrary...).
In the absence of a contrary cognition, the prior ascertainment is indeed the cause; but where that [prior ascertainment] would be erroneous, it is futile, as in the case of a delusion.
The phrase "the cause of acceptance" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. That is a contrary cognition;
even though it was stated as the cause of acceptance, it is the aforementioned ascent.
Being futile,
it does not serve as a cause for acceptance;
"just as an error."
The meaning is: "just as well-known errors such as [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
Alternatively, the thesis and the reason are stated as follows: "Words such as 'goat' (aja) have two meanings, because they are so established in cognition that is free from sublation."
By this [verse], he expresses the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
In that regard, it should be understood that in the first half of the verse, the statement "just as the cognition of a pillar, etc. is also an expression of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Now, one might object: "But here, the causality of the non-born (*ajā*) is being asserted."

If it is argued that the *pradhāna* must be abandoned—even if it has entered the mind—because it is contradicted by the fact that [the cause] is described as having the characteristics of Brahman, we say no.

For while being the mere efficient cause (*nimittamātratva*) is a characteristic of Brahman, being the material cause (*jagadupādānatva*) exists in the *pradhāna* as well; thus, its being for that purpose (i.e., being the cause) is established. Bearing this intention in mind, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, that Śruti declares Pradhāna to be the material cause of the world.
Regarding the phrase "because of being included within the number," they explain this [in the Śāṃkara-bhāṣya] as being intended to demonstrate that the Pradhāna is not based on the Word (aśābdatva).
For instance: "In the phrase *yasmin pañca pañcajanāḥ*, another number five is heard as the object of the number five,
because two words 'five' are observed."
These five sets of five do not amount to twenty-five;

for, by including those twenty-five principles well-known in Smṛti through the number twenty-five well-established in Śruti, it would follow that Pradhāna and the others possess scriptural authority. To this, it is replied:

One should not entertain the hope that even by including them within the category of "the calculable" (saṅkhya), primary matter (pradhāna) and the like can be considered to possess scriptural authority.
Why?
Because of their diversity.
For these twenty-five principles are diverse; they possess no common property in groups of five by which the number "five" could be applied to each set within the twenty-five.
Indeed, without a single unifying basis, numbers such as two and so forth do not apply to things that are distinct.
And because of the surplus:
for there would be a surplus of the number twenty-five over both the self and space.
For if the self were included within the twenty-five, there would be a contradiction with the statement regarding its being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the phrase "in which" (*yasmin*).
There is a contradiction in mentioning even space separately.
Do you mean to suggest that the system of twenty-five principles is entirely without authority,
or that this statement is not intended to be definitive on that point?
He states that both positions are untenable with the words "yattad" (that which...):

"That which is the unmanifest, consisting of the three qualities, eternal, composed of being and non-being, the Pradhāna, they call Prakṛti—the undifferentiated [yet] possessing differentiation. (Manu Smṛti 1.4.53)
It consists of both the existent and the non-existent, and consists of both cause and effect.
They call the *pradhāna* "non-specific" because it is not an effect, and they call the *prakṛti* "specific" because it possesses specific qualities and is an effect.
The explanation of the term "possessing specific qualities" is given by the words "by the five."
The wise know this group of twenty-four principles to be derived from primordial matter (pradhāna), consisting of five, five, four, and ten respectively.
Thus spoke the Lord himself, the sovereign of all knowledge, in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

"Brahman is filled by the five great elements (mahābhūtas), the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the four—intellect (mahat), ego (ahaṅkāra), mind (manas), and intellective faculty (buddhi)—and the ten sense organs.

Since the author of the Sūtras himself established twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) in another work by stating, "The wise know this group of twenty-four to be the effects of Pradhāna," the first alternative [that there are only twenty-four] is not tenable.
If it is argued that this [statement] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), [we reply:]...
Is it of that which is cognized or of that which is imagined?
In the first case, the establishment of the principles occurs through those very means of valid cognition.
Not the second, because it would be purposeless.
If it is argued that [the citation] is for the purpose of refutation, we say no;
because that is impossible.
For it is not possible that a restatement in one text could constitute a refutation in another text.
The second [alternative] is not tenable,
because there is no contradiction.
As for what was stated— that it is because of diversity— that is incorrect.
Furthermore, for the author of the Sūtras as well, it would follow that statements such as "by five" would be untenable due to the absence of any comprehensive categories (*saṅgrāhaka*).

If you argue that in that case there are such comprehensive categories—namely, being an element (*bhūtatva*) and so forth—then those very same [categories], namely being an element, being a subtle element (*tanmātratva*), being a faculty of cognition (*jñānendriyatva*), being a faculty of action (*karmendriyatva*), and being other than those, exist in the Śruti as well; thus, the situation is the same.
Nor is there this rule that the application of a number cannot occur in the interval without a collective term:
for instance, "Śatakratu did not send rain for five and seven years," and "This vow is to be performed for nine and five years."
Because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in such cases;
and as for the argument that "it is because of over-extension" (*atireka*),
that too is incorrect.
Because the followers of Patañjali accept Īśvara;
and because the interpretation "and space" as meaning "space and so forth" is logically consistent.

Furthermore, this statement is either accepted by the Sāṅkhya in its own treatise for the purpose of establishing the twenty-five principles (tattvas), or it is suspected [by the opponent] due to its plausibility.
Neither of the two [interpretations] is possible;

for the phrase "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*) does not convey the number twenty-five. Indeed, if "five-people" (*pañcajana*) were a compound, the second word "five" (*pañca*) would not be connected with the first word "five" (*pañca*).
Because a qualifier cannot be connected with a subordinate element,
nor can it be connected with the word *jana*; for since no expectation arises as to how many "five persons" there are, a qualifier would be inappropriate.
Even though it is not a compound, it cannot first be connected with the word *pañca* (five),
because the relationship of qualifier and qualified is impossible between two things that have the same referent;
nor can it be connected with the word *jana* (person).
Because there is no further expectancy;
for even if there were some degree of expectancy, the number ten would be obtained.
[Objection: Is it not the case that "pañcajanāḥ" is a collective dvigu compound?
When "five" is used as a qualifier for that [group], twenty-five results;
just as when it is said, "five groups of five cakes," twenty-five cakes are obtained.
Not so;
for if that were the case, the masculine gender would be untenable—enough of this.
The misinterpretation of the sūtras beginning with "by being the cause" (*kāraṇatvena*) contains manifest flaws, and thus it has not been refuted [here]. *4,283*
They explain that this section, beginning with "And the primordial nature" (*prakṛtiśca*), is for the purpose of establishing Brahman as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world;
for it is thus:
It has been stated that Brahman is the cause of the world, according to the sūtra: "From which the birth, etc., of this [world proceed.
In this regard, a doubt arises: is it as the material cause (upādāna) or as the efficient cause (nimitta)?
[The text continues: "He thought; He created Prāṇa."

Since it is heard that [Brahman] acts preceded by such reflection, it might be concluded that Brahman is merely the efficient cause; to this, it is replied: "And [Brahman is] the material cause as well, because there is no contradiction with the stated reasons and the cited examples. Brahman is not merely the efficient cause, but is also the material cause (*prakṛti*), that is, the substrate (*upādāna*).
Why? Because there is no contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For in this way, neither the proposition nor the example are contradicted:
"By which the unheard becomes heard."
