Thus, the knowledge of everything is asserted through the knowledge of Brahman;
and this is only logically possible if [Brahman] is the material cause,
because the effect is not distinct from its material cause.
For there is no separation of the effect from its efficient cause, as is seen in the case of a carpenter being distinct from the palace [he builds].
And there are scriptural examples: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay... and so forth.
These and others are recorded as being the objects of appropriation (*upādāna*).
Furthermore, the ablative case in the phrase "from which indeed these beings [arise]" indicates its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*).

Because of the specific traditional rule (smṛti), "the source (prakṛti) of the agent of birth," and because of the teaching regarding intention— namely, the instruction on becoming manifold preceded by the declaration, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"— both its status as the efficient cause (nimittatva) and its status as the material cause (upādānatva) are understood.
"And because both are directly stated.
For this reason as well, Brahman is the material cause:
"All these beings, indeed, arise from space alone; they merge back into space."
Thus, because both origination and dissolution are recorded as having Brahman itself as their direct cause;
for it is well known that whatever originates from something and into which it dissolves, that thing is its material cause (*upādāna*),
just as the earth is the material cause of rice and other grains.

Furthermore, the dissolution of an effect is never observed to occur anywhere other than into its material cause (*upādāna*). This is because of the scriptural statements regarding the Self’s being both the object and the agent of action, such as "through self-making" and "by transformation," and specifically from the declaration: "He made Himself by Himself. (Vyapadeśāt)
Brahman is the material cause (upādāna).
But how can that which is already established be something being made? Through transformation (pariṇāma).
It is indeed logical that the Self, though already established as prior, transformed itself through a specific mode characterized by modification (*vikāra*).
Alternatively, the phrase "because of modification" (*pariṇāmāt*) may be treated as a separate aphorism;
for by such passages as "Being and Non-being became [Brahman]," the modification of Brahman itself into the form of a transformation is recorded through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Therefore, Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*); for it is also celebrated as the "womb" (*yoni*), as in the passage: "That which is the womb of beings."
Thus, Brahman is sung as the "source" (yoni);
and the word "source" is understood in common worldly usage to denote the material cause.
Therefore, Brahman is the material cause. *4,284*
He refutes this with the words "And not... (na ca).
Nor is it said that Brahman is denoted by the word "prakṛti" as the material cause. If one asks why it is not so stated,
the answer is that the meaning of a sūtra must be explained in a way that is not contradicted by other means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, Brahman’s status as the material cause (upādānatva) is contradicted by the Śruti and other authorities;
for that which undergoes transformation (pariṇāmikāraṇa) is called the material cause,
just as clay and gold are the material causes of jars, necklaces, and the like.

He asks: "Since the transformation of Brahman—characterized by the assumption of another nature and synonymous with 'modification' (vikāra)—is prohibited in the Śrutis and other scriptures, how can it be stated as the meaning of the Sūtra? To this he says: "Avikāraḥ" (without modification). The Self, Hari, is eternally without modification, ever-pure, and eternal.
He possesses the power of consciousness that is eternally of one form, and his nature is bliss.
Changeless, imperishable, pure, free from affliction, undecaying, immortal, non-worldly yet the creator of the world, unborn— he who is supreme is thus described.
That which is changeless, incomparable, eternally of one taste, and imperishable—
what the people learned in the Vedas know as Brahman and the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Thus, according to what is declared in the Śruti and the Purāṇas, Janārdana is not subject to modification.
The term "unchanging" (*avikāra*) is connected with both [of the preceding] terms, "eternal" (*sadā*) and "pure" (*śuddha*). Change occurs in two ways:
of the substratum (*dharmin*) and of its attribute (*dharma*).
In that regard, the first [position]—that it exists eternally and so forth—is negated;
the second—that it is always of a single form—is negated.
He is described as such because his power of consciousness is of a single form and free from modification.
The object of comparison is similarity; that which is not similarity is non-similarity (*anaupamya*).
It is of a single flavor, devoid of internal differentiation.
Or, it consists of the nature of primordial bliss (*pradhānānanda*);
the ellipsis is "it is understood that [Brahman] is not subject to modification.

Furthermore, since the idea of Brahman undergoing modification is contrary to reason, he first states the various modes of modification in order to explain this, beginning with the verse: "Dependent on another... (*parādhīna*).
The attainment of excellence dependent on others is an irreversible transformation.

"...there would be a modification, as in the case of milk and so forth" (Manu 1.4.60ab). To begin with, modification is of two kinds: the acquisition of a specific quality and the transformation of the substrate.

In this context, "attainment of distinction" (*viśeṣāpti*) refers to the transformation of mere attributes while the substratum (*dharmin*) remains in its original state; whereas "occurrence of the transformation of the qualifier" (*viśeṣiparivartavṛtti*) is the transformation of the very nature of the substratum itself.
Both of these types of transformation are dependent upon something else.
And each of these is twofold:
irreversible alteration and reversible [alteration].
It should be understood that the individual types are not explicitly mentioned here because they are self-evident.
Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in the statement.
The phrase "like milk and so forth" provides an illustration for the four [stages].
The meaning is that it is like the transformation of milk and other substances into the state of curds and so on. *4,292*
In that regard, the attainment of an irreversible distinction is, for example, the transformation of a dark fruit into yellow.
For in that case, the substratum remains in its original state, since the conventional designation "fruit" does not cease even when it has become yellow.

The emergence of yellowness through the mere disappearance of blackness is not without cause, as in the case of [objects] due to sunlight and so forth; nor does it ever revert again, just as in the attainment of a specific state that is irreversible.
The transformation of gold, which possesses the form of an earring and so forth, into a bracelet and so forth—
in this case as well, the substratum remains in its original state,
because the conventional usage of the term "gold" is observed even when it has attained the state of being a bracelet and the like.
However, through the loss of its state as an earring, it has come under the control of the goldsmith and others in the form of a bracelet;
and this [bracelet] is reversible, because it can once again be made into an earring. (4.293)
An irreversible transformation of the specific quality is as follows: for example, the state of milk becoming curd.
For in this case, there is no persistence of the substratum in its former condition.
Because once the state of being curd has occurred, the conventional usage of the term "milk" is no longer perceived;
rather, it is the very milk, which constitutes the substratum, that becomes curd through the application of coagulation and other factors.
Furthermore, milk does not come into existence again by the cessation of its state as curd.
The transformation of the substratum (dharmiparivarta) is reversible,
as in the case of silverness [appearing] in a piece of gold;
even here, there is no cognition of the substratum remaining in its original state.
Because no usage of "silver" (śulba) is observed in the sense of "white" (tāra),
how indeed could silver itself have become white by depending on medicinal herbs?
Through the cessation of its dullness by the power of potent medicinal herbs, copper is produced;
nor is a fifth mode observed, whether it be possible or heard of in scripture. (4.294)
If such a transformation exists, what follows from this? To this he says: "Not at all."
...he would never truly belong to Hari at any time.
The term "kvacit" (in some cases) is used in the locative sense of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*).
This is the intended meaning:
it has been demonstrated that every transformation whatsoever is dependent upon another.
Moreover, this [transformation] has never been observed to occur in that manner;
for if it were so, it would occur at all times.
Furthermore, there exists no cause whatsoever for a modification of Brahman.
Because, prior to creation, in the passage "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," other entities are excluded;
nor is time or anything else admitted by the opponent [the Sāṃkhya] to exist during the dissolution.
Furthermore, even if this were admitted, it would result in Brahman being dependent on another.
Let it be that in insentient things transformation is dependent on another;
however, conscious Brahman undergoes transformation into the form of the world solely by its own will.
If it is argued that this is so because of such scriptural passages as, "He made Himself His own self," we say no;
for in the case of an intelligent being, a desire to become a manifold world consisting of various objects and forms is simply untenable.

For even a madman does not desire for himself that which is of the nature of misfortune, much less one who possesses discernment; nor is it the case that Brahman does not know the nature of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) to be misfortune.

If it is argued that this conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) does not constitute an undesirable state for Brahman because it would otherwise entail the consequence of Brahman being non-omniscient, we say no;
for it is a contradiction to claim that that which has transformed into the form of suffering and so forth does not possess the nature of suffering and so forth.
For this phenomenal world is not, as it is for the proponents of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādins*), merely imagined by you,
because you accept its reality;
however, its possession of suffering and so forth is not desired.
If it is argued that the intention is not that it has that nature [of being desired], we say no;
for if that were the case, even the state of being pleasant would not be something desired, and consequently, one would not exert effort toward liberation. (4.296)
Furthermore, if Brahman is devoid of misfortune, it must be stated whose misfortune this is;
if you say it belongs to the *jīva*, [we reply: no.
Is it different from Brahman or non-different? Not the first, because that would contradict your own established tenet (apasiddhānta).
In the second case, how could there be no harm for Brahman?
If it is argued that [Brahman] is both different and non-different, [we say] no,
because by virtue of its non-difference, the consequence of harm would follow.
Furthermore, this position will be refuted [in the Sūtra] by the words, “And for this very reason, it is like a reflection” (Upadeśa Sūtra 3.2.18).
Moreover, even in the case of a conscious being, modification is seen to depend upon visible and invisible causes; how then could it occur in Brahman by His mere will alone?
If it is argued that this is possible because He possesses all powers (*sarvaśaktitva*), [we reply: no.
For one who is not desirous [of worldly ends], the possession of all powers is impossible.
Brahman is not to be determined by logic, such that considerations regarding the suitability or unsuitability of analogies would be applicable here;
rather, it is established solely through scripture.
If it is argued that scripture declares the origin of the phenomenal world independently of anything else, we say no;
for if that were so, it would follow that the science of inquiry (mīmāṃsā) would have no occasion to arise.
Moreover, this doctrine that [Brahman] is beyond the scope of reasoning is appropriate only where there is no contradiction among the Śrutis;
and it has already been stated that such is not the case here.
Therefore, it is not tenable to assert that Brahman is subject to modification in a general sense.
Nor [is it so] in a specific sense;
for instance, it is not tenable that this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is a transformation of forms belonging to Brahman itself while its own essential nature remains unaltered.
Because it would contradict scriptural passages such as "not gross" (*asthūla*).
If it is argued that this is possible from the perspective of its own nature (*svarūpa*), [we reply] no,
because grossness and so forth are produced in the very nature itself.
For the state of being a bracelet does not arise for gold without the departure of its state of being a ring.
If it is argued that this is so with respect to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), we say no;

because [the object] possesses the presence and absence of grossness and other qualities due to the difference in time, one might [erroneously] think, "This is the intrinsic nature," and "This is not."

For it is impossible to maintain the distinction that "the manifestation of the world is not its own nature," since you do not believe that Brahman undergoes the state of becoming the phenomenal world through any other cause, by which [manifestation] it would not be its own nature.
Furthermore, if the nature of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañcākāratā*) were irreversible, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning dissolution (*pralaya*),

and it would follow that liberation— characterized by the attainment of the state of Brahman devoid of phenomenal manifestation— could not exist. As for partial transformation (*ekadeśapariṇāma*), however, it will be refuted later.

Nor can it be argued that the world-phenomenon (prapañca) attains its form through the loss of Brahman’s own nature, for this would entail the non-existence of Brahman at the time of its persistence, resulting in the conclusion that the knowledge of Brahman is without a basis (*nirālambana*).
Furthermore, if that [loss] were irreversible, Brahman would never exist; such is the general direction of the argument.

Regarding this, some—like one blind man following another blind man—cite such sūtras as "Prakṛti" and others, asserting them to establish that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe.

Having explained [the previous view], fearing the multitude of refutations already stated, he declares the intended meaning of the Sūtra: "Brahman has as its body the Pradhāna, which is of the nature of consciousness and supremely subtle"— a fact established by such Śruti passages as, "He who dwells in the unmanifest, whose body is the unmanifest," and so forth.

And thus, since the *pradhāna*—presided over by Brahman and having Brahman as its essence—is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, it is Brahman alone that is accepted as the material cause of the world.
Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
To this, he replies: “The very fact of being the material cause... [and so forth].
If its status as the material cause is intended to be nothing other than its status as the point of departure (apādāna), [then there is no distinction].
That has been accepted by you, O father... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.61a //

By speaking in this way, one would be asserting that Brahman possesses the status of an *apādāna*—characterized as the limit of departure (*apāyāvadhitva*)—in the production of the world, just as a father does at the birth of a son.

This is because Brahman, who is in every respect changeless, is declared to be the *apādāna* by virtue of being the presiding controller of the *pradhāna*, which is subject to modification and constitutes His body.
And such is the nature of [Brahman’s] material causality (*upādānatva*).

"We ourselves have indeed accepted this, so we have no hostility toward it here. [Objection: "If the status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādānatva*) has been accepted, how then can it be refuted? To this, he says: "But not... (*na tu*).
...but not through his being the soul of the universe. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.61b)
The view accepted by Bhāskara and others— that Brahman, which is pure consciousness alone, comes into existence as the self of the universe— is not accepted by us; therefore,
its refutation is indeed appropriate.
The intended meaning here is as follows: although the status of Brahman as the material cause of the world, as established by others, is not in fact contradictory to our own position,
nevertheless, that is not the meaning of these Sūtras.
For instance: what is the purpose of this exposition?
It is not, first of all, the refutation of the distinction between efficient and material causes, as Bhāskara [does].
This is because *pradhāna* is accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*).
If it is argued that being the presiding controller of a changing entity is itself the primary sense of "material cause," we say no,
because this contradicts common worldly understanding.
For investigators must formulate definitions in accordance with worldly convention,
and not constrain worldly convention according to their own personal intentions.
And in the world, [the material cause] is that which possesses transformation (*vikriyāvat*).
Thus it is said.
Now, the followers of Patañjali maintain that *pradhāna* alone is the independent material cause of the universe, while Īśvara is merely its favorer;
in order to refute that, [it is stated that] *pradhāna* is essentially identical with Brahman, being the body of Brahman.
If you say that it is being established here that even its status as material cause belongs to Brahman alone,
then that argument is misplaced,
for it ought to have been addressed in the section on the system (samayapāda).
And it will be argued that [the cause exists] "because of its non-existence elsewhere.
Therefore, this is not the intended meaning of the Sūtra.

Regarding the example stated as "because of being the father," the proponent of the theory of Brahman’s transformation (brahmapariṇāmavādin), disregarding the point at issue, says: "The father is indeed the material cause (upādāna) of the son; therefore, this example is not appropriate."
To this, he says: "And not," etc.
Nor is there any transformation of the spider, its progenitor, or its mother.
The first word "ca" is used for emphasis;
the second is a restatement of what has been said by others. By employing the word "janitr" (begetter), he demonstrates that his own work is equal to a mantra.

The Blessed Teacher indicates [this] by the traditional rule that "the mantra is the progenitor. Since the father and mother would naturally be understood here due to the context, the specific mention of the spider and its mother serves to refute even this [notion].
As for that which was stated by the proponents of the transformation of Brahman:
"In Brahman being the cause of the world, just as a spider emits [and withdraws]..."

"In the statement, 'I am the father of this world, I am its mother,' because of the employment of analogies such as the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*), it is precisely the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) that is intended;
for spiders and the like are the material causes with respect to their threads and so forth."
And as for what was stated there [in the commentary]: "For it is sung as the source (*yoni*)," and:
"Even though the word *yoni* [is used] in the passage, 'O Indra, a seat has been prepared upon the source (*yoni*)'..."
In such passages, the meaning of "place" (*sthāna*) and so forth is understood;
nevertheless, by the force of the example to be stated later—"just as a spider [produces its web]"—it is determined that [the term] denotes the material cause (*upādāna*).
Thus, the statement from the *Brahmatarka* which is about to be cited is also explained.
If it is asked, "From where [does it come]?"—
in this regard, since fathers and so forth, as well as sons and so forth, consist of a combination of the sentient and the insentient, four positions are possible:
either the appropriation is directed toward the sentient father and so forth, or...
Either toward an insentient son and so forth,
or toward a sentient son and so forth by an insentient father and so forth,
or toward an insentient son and so forth [by a sentient one].
Regarding that, he states the reason why the first three positions are untenable: "because of being sentient" (cetana-tvāt).
Because it possesses consciousness, that food indeed exists in the form of an effect.
Because both of the first two are sentient; because either one of the latter two is;
but he accepts the fourth, for it is said, "that food indeed."
The food consumed by those [spiders] such as the *ūrṇanābhi* and others refers, in short, to the constituents (*dhātu*) of their bodies which have been transformed from that [food];
the meaning is that it becomes transformed into the form of effects such as threads and so forth.
This is what is being said:
This is indeed the extracted meaning of the analogies concerning the father and others:
that the food consumed by the father and others becomes the material cause for the insentient portion residing in the son and others, which constitutes their body.
Because no other alternative is possible,
and this is not undesirable to us:

at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the effects beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*)— having been swallowed by the Supreme Lord— return to the state of *pradhāna*, which serves as His bodily form.

Furthermore, this is because it is accepted that the Pradhāna serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for its effects, such as the Mahat and the rest. By this, the objection that the spider and other such beings are not transformative (*vikārin*)—
lest it follow that the production of threads and so forth occurs without a material cause— is also refuted.

Thus, it has been stated that because Brahman is understood through scripture, Purāṇas, and reasoning to be changeless (nirvikāra), it cannot be the material cause (upādānakāraṇa) of the world, but rather its instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa) alone.
Now, he says "by way of being the source" (apādānatayā), meaning that for this reason as well— since only instrumentality has been taught by scripture, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and reasoning.
The status of being the creator of the universe is preceded by intelligence, insofar as he is the source (apādāna).
This has been stated respectfully in the Bhāllavi-Śākhā and in the Brahmatarka:

"The status of being the creator of the universe" (viśvakartṛtva)—when this alone is mentioned, it would be understood as a detached agency (taṭasthakartṛtva), like that of a potter or similar craftsmen.
To exclude that [interpretation], it is stated [in the text] that he is the material cause (upādānatayā).
When it is stated that [something] possesses the status of an *apādāna*, it does not follow that the other [status] is undesired;
for since the *upādāna* is also a specific kind of *apādāna*, there is no contradiction between its being an *apādāna* and its being a non-*apādāna*.
And when there is an intention to specify the *apādāna* (the point of departure), as in the case of a tree in relation to the falling of leaves, only its status as a limit (*avadhi*) is perceived;
therefore, it has been stated that [the Lord] is the universal agent (*viśvakartṛ*).
Nevertheless, the qualification "preceded by intelligence" (*buddhipūrvaka*) is redundant.
"It is because the agent is necessarily possessed of intelligence.
Not so;
for what is intended is knowledge of every particular detail.
This is what is meant:

God, possessing the intellect and other faculties directed toward all effects, actions, instruments, results, and objects, favors them through an external form and impels the internal powers of transformation and so forth belonging to primordial matter (pradhāna) and the rest; thus, when the effects such as the Great Principle (mahat)—which are transformations of primordial matter and constitute His own body—cease to exist, He becomes the limit [of manifestation].
We shall demonstrate the state of being full of reverence;
he recites those very two statements in sequence, beginning with "by the mere will."
The creation of the Lord, who is forever changeless, proceeds from His mere will.
This is the nature of the Infinite One by which the world arose from dust;
Janārdana formerly consumed the universe at his will, beginning with his own body.
He created [them] like a mother and father, or like a spider [creating its web].
The meaning is simply that it is not [perceived] by way of transformation;
the reason for this is stated as "of the unchanging.
To the question "For what purpose is it designated? it is said: "as its own nature (svabhāva)."
To the question "How [is this so] due to the absence of grasping?", it is said: "Because of passion."
By him was impelled the *pradhāna*—characterized by the word "rajas" and consisting of the three *guṇas*—which became the world;
through this explanation, his reverence [for Him] is perceived.
From his own body, which is the foundation consisting of *sat*, *cit*, *ānanda*, and so forth.
Alternatively, from its own body as the primary material cause,
it is similar to what was previously consumed and withdrawn in a former kalpa.
Or, it means that which has previously been experienced and exists as a subtle state of appropriation (*upādāna*).
By the word "eva" (only/indeed), he indicates that it is not like clay or other such materials.
The word "vā" (or) serves to aggregate the examples.
He explains the phrases "from one's own body" and "previously consumed" with the word "pradhāna."
The Lord is the primordial matter that undergoes transformation, yet he himself is eternally changeless.
The term "unchanging" (*nirvikāra*) serves as a justification for what was expressed by the word "indeed" (*eva*).
Here too, as before, the emphasis is understood.
By the phrase "prior to being conscious," three formal arguments (*prayoga*) are indicated.
Father and son do not stand in the relation of material cause and its effect (*upādāna-upādeya-bhūta*), because they are both conscious, like Devadatta and Yajñadatta.
The son and so forth, being unconscious,
are not produced with the conscious father and so forth as their material cause.
Because it is insentient, like a jar; and a sentient being, such as a son, does not have an insentient entity, such as a father, as its material cause,
because he is sentient, like Brahmā.

And because the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is ascertained in all cases, he first establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding the second [alternative]: "otherwise, there would be no modification of consciousness."
For where there is anything insentient, there could never be a modification of consciousness;
for if, indeed, in any place or at any time, a modification of consciousness were observed in what is insentient, then this pervasion (vyāpti) would be violated.
But such is not the case—this is the meaning.
If it is argued that the world, beginning with the Mahat, is perceived as the effect of Brahman, we say no; for this remains unproven even now,
as it has been refuted by the aforementioned and the yet-to-be-stated means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In the third [verse], he establishes pervasion: "Not that which is insentient."
Nor can that which is a modification of the insentient ever become sentient.
The explanation is as before.
Thus, even in the first case, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) should be established by showing that the conscious [principle] is not perceived as a modification of the conscious.
Alternatively, the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest are not modifications of the conscious.

Keeping in mind that Brahman’s being the material cause of the world is contradicted by another logical argument—namely, "because it is insentient, like a jar"—the author establishes the pervasion (vyāpti) of this [argument] with the words: "Not [if it were] sentient... and so forth.
If it is argued that jars and other such things are also transformations of Brahman, we say no; for they are known through valid means of cognition to be transformations of clay and the like.
If it is argued that [they are transformations of Brahman] through a lineage of causes, [we reply: so be it.
If that is the case, then it would have to be said that they themselves are not modifications of volition,
but rather its causes; and if so, why should they not serve as an illustrative example?
If it is argued that there is then a deviation (vyabhicāra) in respect of its causes, we say no; for those very causes constitute the subject (pakṣa).
If it is argued that there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) in respect of pleasure, pain, and so forth, we say no.
Because it is admitted that these [effects] are modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
By this, the following argument is also refuted:
"The world has a single, non-different efficient and material cause, because it is an effect produced through prior deliberation, like pleasure and so forth."
Furthermore, there is the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to jars and other such objects;
if these too were made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkaraṇa*), there would be sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*).
[Objection: But if the insentient world were a modification (*vikāra*) of the sentient, what fault would there be?
If that were so, then even a conscious entity would be a modification of the unconscious;
since this is not the case, he says: "not unconscious."

This is the underlying intention: if the Great One (mahat) and the rest were a modification (vikāra) of Brahman, then it would follow that they must possess a conformity to its essential nature (svarūpa);
for in the effect, one observes a conformity to the essential nature of the cause.
Objects such as jars are seen to be transformations of clay and to follow the nature of clay;
however, this is not the case here.
Therefore, [the world] is not composed of the Great Elements (mahābhūta), and so forth.
It is a modification of Brahman.

Furthermore, if the relationship between a modifier and its modification were admitted without following the nature of the cause, then why should a conscious being not also be admitted as a modification of the unconscious?
Yet this is not accepted by the opponent.

For if that were the case, then regarding the sūtra "The self [exists], because of its presence when the body is present," one would have to provide a rebuttal against the Cārvāka— who asserts that this conscious body is merely a transformation of the four elements—

by asking how consciousness, which does not exist in the elements, could arise in their product; the answer would then be that it occurs just as the power of intoxication arises in the substance of wine.
Furthermore, if the Cārvāka were to object that even in the case of wine, the demonstration of a subtle form of intoxicating power would be contradicted;
or else: "The Brahman and the world do not stand in the relation of material cause and effect, because they are dissimilar, like Devadatta and a jar.
If it is argued, "But we observe that even dissimilar things such as clay and a jar do indeed stand in the relation of material cause and effect," we say no.

Because it is intended to demonstrate the distinction between the nature of volition and the nature of non-volition, [the author] states "and" (ca) in order to express the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) for the sake of ascertaining the pervasion (*vyāpti*), prior to stating another inference:
"And the nature of one thing is not seen to belong to another, even when that other is modified. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.67ab).
Furthermore, the word "api ca" (moreover) serves as a conjunction of logical arguments.
Regarding the state of transformation (*vikṛtitva*), in the condition of being transformed, one thing appearing in the form of another—that is, being a modification of another—is not observed.
The meaning is that a modification and its substrate are never perceived as distinct from one another in any instance.
Regarding this, he states an illustrative example: "No."
The difference between milk and curd is not perceived by anyone anywhere.

The meaning is that the distinctness of curd from that milk of which it is a modification is not seen by anyone anywhere; thus, the exclusion of the relationship between a modification and its substrate is established through the non-perception of such distinctness. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "From the Omniscient One."
For the world is indeed experienced as being other than the omniscient Brahman.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because";
therefore, the ellipsis is that there is no relationship of modification and modified between those two.
This is the formal argument (*prayoga*) here:
The world is not a transformation of Brahman,
because it is perceived as being distinct from it;
for whatever is perceived as distinct from something else is not a transformation of that thing, just as a jar is not a transformation of a cloth.
And whatever is a modification of something else is not perceived as distinct from it, just as curd [is not distinct] from milk;
or rather, the world and Brahman are neither the modification nor the modifier of one another.
The formal argument is: "Because they are perceived as being distinct from one another, like a jar and a cloth.
Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because it is heard in scripture that "He who knows all" (Savajña) is Brahman;
because the absence of knowledge in the world is inferred from the total non-perception of the effects of knowledge;
and because there is a rule that two substrata possessing contradictory attributes must necessarily be distinct from one another—it is said with this intention: "from the Omniscient One" (sarvajñāt).

If it is objected: "But since a distinction between the modification and the modifier is admitted, how can this be a valid reason?"—it is not so, because the very perception of their distinction constitutes the reason.
Does it then follow that the jar and the cloth are non-different merely by virtue of your own admission?
Because [the object] is perceived.
Not the first [alternative], because by my own admission, only pure difference is what is apprehended.
Nor the second.
Because it is unestablished.
Or, the non-perception of difference is intended as the reason.
[Objection: But is this reason not unestablished?

If it is argued that non-difference is apprehended through the inference, "The world is non-different from Brahman because it exists, like Brahman," we say no; for this has the same logical status as a fallacious argument, such as "A piece of gold is non-different from gold because it exists, like gold. Thus he says: "Non-difference [is not established]."
There would be no distinction between a donkey and a horse based on mere existence alone.
"If the world and Brahman were to be established"—this is the ellipsis for "then. [The result would be] a mere trifle, like iron or a skull-fragment.
But surely this is exactly what is desired!
If it is argued that this is not so because I have accepted the non-difference between the dross and the gold, we say no;
for by the word "non-difference" (abheda), the absence of difference (bhedābhāva) is intended.
If it is then argued that there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in this regard:
The world is absolutely different from Brahman because it lacks conformity with its nature;
this [reasoning] applies to your inference as well.
The resolution regarding the contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the same in both cases.
If it is argued that the qualification "nowhere" [in the claim] "I have no absolute difference anywhere" is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), we say no;
for that would entail the consequence of the non-existence of liberation (*mokṣa*).
For instance, you maintain that liberation is attained through knowledge and through the cessation of karma;
yet in this regard, even that which is called "knowledge" may actually be ignorance.
If karma, even when active, were to become ceased, how could it be a means to liberation?
If its status as such were due to its being knowledge (*jñāna*), then ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth would likewise possess that status.

If it is argued that knowledge and so forth are absolutely non-different from the nature of knowledge and so forth, yet are different-and-non-different (bhedābheda) from the nature of ignorance and so forth— and therefore there is no confusion of effects—
even so, because one's own effect must be produced through its non-difference from ignorance and the rest.
In this way, liberation as well would be non-liberation, being non-different from saṃsāra;
for if it were liberation by virtue of the existence of the nature of liberation, then saṃsāra too would be so.
Alternatively, if this non-difference, being unperceived, is not useful for causal functions (*arthakriyā*),
then it would have to be accepted merely out of a perverse obsession (*vyasanitayā*).
It has been stated that this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of that [Brahman], because it is devoid of conformity with the true nature of Brahman.
In this regard, is it intended that emptiness is the absence of conformity with all intrinsic natures, or is it the absence of conformity with some [intrinsic nature]?
It is not the first.
Even in the absence of a universal concomitance [of the cause], we observe that jars and the like are transformations of clay and so forth.

It is not the second [alternative], because the relationship between a transformation and its substrate is established through the concomitance of existence (*sattva*). Therefore, he says: "non-difference" (*abheda*).

Non-difference is the relationship between a modification and that which undergoes modification. [Objection: But surely the existence inherent in gold is not present in a small piece; so how can this consequence apply?
Is it then that the very essence of Brahman is the ether and so forth?
If you say "yes," it is not so,
because there is a lack of valid evidence.

For, according to such scriptural passages as "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth; they are the truth of truth," it is established that the truthfulness of the vital breaths has the sense of being dependent upon Brahman.

If it is argued that the general existence (sāmānyasattā) of Brahman alone is what persists through space and the rest, then why is the existence of gold not likewise persisting in a small piece of it (*kharva*)? (4.323)

Now, if you think that the cause itself becomes the effect— this being the doctrine of the proponents of transformation (pariṇāmavādins)— then it must necessarily be admitted that the effect follows the nature of the cause, which is its own inherent essence. Otherwise, the statement that "the cause itself becomes the effect" would be a hollow assertion.
For if there were no conformity to an invariable nature, it would follow that the cause itself lacks conformity.
Furthermore, gold does not have the nature of mere existence (sanmātra),
such that its transformation could be something insentient.
"But [this is so] provided there is the persistence of non-deviating properties such as 'gold-ness' (suvarṇatva).
If that is the case, then how could the world be a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman?
For Brahman does not have "pure Being" (*sanmātra*) as its sole nature.

However, because scriptures such as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28) reveal that consciousness and the rest also possess a nature that is non-deviant from it [Brahman], the case is not equal;

for the persistence of consciousness, bliss, and so forth is not found in the phenomenal world (prapañca). If it is argued that curd—a modification of milk—is seen to be devoid of the persistence of sweetness, which is the non-deviant nature of milk, we say no.
Because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the collapse of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*).
Furthermore, once it is ascertained that curd is the effect of milk, sweetness cannot be postulated as the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of milk;

or, if sweetness were indeed ascertained to be the inherent nature of milk, then there would be no fault in postulating that when the milk perishes, its cause [sweetness] serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the curd.

Furthermore, since the immutability of Brahman has been established through both scripture and inference, there is no contradiction in stating these two reductio ad absurdum arguments (*prasaṅga*) and their contrapositives (*viparyaya*) against one who maintains that Brahman— whose essential nature and character are never lost— is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world. By this, the objection that the same defect applies equally to the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) as the material cause of the world is also refuted.
Now, it may be thought:
Brahman is admitted to have two forms, namely, that consisting of infinite bliss and consciousness, and that consisting of pure existence.
Of these, by the first form, it is the efficient cause.
By the second [alternative], appropriation is [established];
therefore, no fault has been stated.
For it is thus:

As for what was stated regarding its being changeless (*nirvikāratva*), that is not a refutation of [the doctrine of] *śakti* and so forth, because it pertains to the object of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

There is no contradiction with reason even if one accepts that Brahman, which possesses the power of existence (*sat-śaktika*), transforms through its instrumental cause—the power of consciousness—while being designated by terms such as *prakṛti* and *pradhāna*; for there is no fault even if consciousness and other qualities do not persist [in the effect], since the world has as its material cause (*upādāna*) that which consists of existence (*sad-ātmaka*).
Because constant accompaniment exists,
the perception of otherness is not contradicted by the Omniscient One; it is precisely for that reason [of non-apprehension] that there is no grasping.
Anticipating the objection that the appropriation which exists as a real entity is perceived as distinct from that [self], he says: "by means of experience."
If transformation occurs through a part, there must indeed be a distinction between the two parts.
If it is accepted that Brahman undergoes transformation through its conscious aspect while maintaining its changelessness,
then it must be stated whether there is non-difference between those two experiences, or both difference and non-difference.
There is no non-difference [between the two], because both would then necessarily undergo transformation and so forth, rendering the conceptualization of two distinct parts useless.
Nor can there be both difference and non-difference, because non-difference would entail the consequence of their total confusion.
If it is argued that difference obstructs the effect of non-difference, then what is the use of a non-difference that serves no purpose?
Therefore, one must simply accept that there is absolute difference between the two parts. (4.329)
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That which is the portion..."
That portion which is not subject to modification—that alone is our Lord.
There are two entities that are absolutely non-different from one another:

therein, one is changeless and is solely the efficient cause (nimitta) of the world; the other, however, is transformative and is solely the material cause (upādāna) of the world. In accepting this, we—who maintain that the Lord is the sole efficient cause—have no dispute whatsoever.
Because we have accepted that which is changeless and the efficient cause of the world as *Īśvara*, and that which is subject to transformation and the material cause of the world as *Pradhāna*;
and because there is no dispute [on this point], [it is said] "and it is *prakṛti*," and so forth.
"The very non-commencement of the sūtras"—
this was stated according to the opponent's own admission;
however, it should be understood that, according to his own view, it refers to "that which is a real entity."
For a part cannot exist without a possessor of parts;
nor does any possessor of parts exist for that which is subject to modification and its modification.
[Objection: But surely there exists the object of dispute?

If it is argued: "The proponent who maintains the distinction between the cause (nimitta) and its material source (upādāna) accepts that Brahman-hood belongs to the cause alone; however, I maintain that it belongs to the aggregate of existence (sat), infinity (ananta), bliss (ānanda), and consciousness (cit). Therefore, this section (adhikaraṇa) is commenced for that purpose," then what is this so-called "Brahman-hood"?

Does it consist in possessing the name "Brahman," or in possessing the meaning of characteristics such as being the cause of the world? He refutes the first [position] with the words: "Of distinct things... (bhinnānām iti).
If it be argued that the name "Brahman" refers to the collection of these [elements] when they are combined.
He states his acceptance with the words "that would be so.
Consequently, this is the meaning:
if there is no dispute regarding the object, then the formal legal proceeding (*adhikaraṇa*) should not be commenced at all.

Because no dispute is raised by the opponent regarding the mere word; even if one were to raise it, it would not be a treatise on grammar (*aśabdaśāstra*). This must also be distinguished in the second case.
Are "Being," "Consciousness," "Bliss," and so forth, each individually Brahman, distinct from one another?
Or are they not Brahman, but rather only their aggregate that is Brahman? Not the first [alternative].
Because it contradicts such scriptural passages as "One only, without a second," [the opponent's view is untenable].

Even regarding the second [alternative], what is this so-called "collection" (*samudāya*)? Is it a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) having those [parts] as its material cause, or is it a number (*saṅkhyā*), or a conjunction (*saṃyoga*)?
He states the fault in all these cases with the word "Brahman."
For in that case, Brahman would not be the material cause of the universe anywhere at all.
The word "tadā" means:
when one accepts the positions that have been formulated and held in mind;
that is, in some particular position.
By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he expresses the well-known fact of the impossibility [of this].

For in this case, it would follow that either Brahman as the material cause or its possessor of qualities is the material cause of the world; thus, the entire universe could not have Brahman as its material cause.
This is because the powers residing in the material cause or its possessor of qualities cannot possibly exist in the effect-substance or its qualities.
Because it is impossible for [Brahman] to be that material cause (upādāna) and so forth;
or alternatively, it should be explained that because Brahman is an effect and possesses qualities, its status as the material cause of the universe is not possible.
In this context, "Brahman as the material cause" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).
It should also be observed that it is not logical for [the self] to have Brahman as its cause.
This might be argued:
this entire collection of inferences is subject to the fallacy of the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
Because of contradictions such as: "From which indeed these beings are born," "From the Self, space was produced," and "That from which there is the origin, etc.,
of this [world]," [the rule] "The source (prakṛti) is the cause of the agent of birth" [would apply].
Thus, the ablative case is prescribed when the *prakṛti* (material cause) is characterized as the *upādāna* (source);
and so it has been illustrated:
"An arrow is produced from horn."
"A scorpion is born from cow dung"; and in this case, the relationship between material cause and its effect is well-established. This, however, is inconsistent.

The fifth [case-ending] intends to establish that [the cause] is the material cause (*upādāna*). However, this sūtra does not prescribe the use of the fifth case-ending with respect to the material cause.
Now, it might be argued:
First of all, the fifth case-ending is prescribed for the ablative (*apādāna*),
according to the rule "the fifth case is used for the ablative. And acquisition (*upādāna*) is a specific type of ablative.

Because of the traditional rule (smaraṇa) that "the source of the agent of birth is the *prakṛti*," the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*), which is prescribed for the ablative (*apādāna*), will apply even when there is a material cause (*upādāna*). And this being so, it does not follow that the status of being a material cause is necessarily unestablished by the fifth case ending.
Because the specific recollection [of the source] is what is to be grasped, he says: "From a horn... (Manu 1.4.71):
"An arrow from a horn, dūrvā grass from sheep's wool, likewise a scorpion from cow dung—[in such cases as these], the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) is accepted."
The word "tathā" (likewise) is connected with the second example.
Thus, in the first set of examples, the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative point of departure) for the horn and so forth with respect to the arrow and so forth is intended;
the phrase "as the meaning of the fifth case" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
This is an illustration; it should also be understood that this applies to the Sūtra as well.
This is what is meant:
This might indeed be so in some way, if the meaning of the Sūtra and its illustrative examples were something imagined by others.
But it is not so.
What, then, is expressed by this rule, "the source (prakṛti) of the agent of the verb jan- [to be born]"?

It means that whatever substance is the source—the material cause, conjoined with the object, and serving as the limit of departure—of the agent of the verb jan-, that is, of the thing being born, is designated as the *apādāna* (ablative) kāraka.
Even in the examples, the fact that horns and the like serve as the limit of cessation (*apāyāvadhi*) in relation to arrows and the like is precisely what is conveyed by the fifth case ending;
this very point he elaborates upon with the verse beginning "upādāna" (Vākya-padīya 3.7.10).
Even though here a state of being a portion of the material cause is observed, nevertheless,
the very state of being the source [of creation] should serve as the illustrative example for Brahman.

Although in this case, such as with respect to the horn and so forth, one perceives the state of being a part of that which serves as the material cause (upādāna) for the arrow and so forth, nevertheless, the status of being an *apādāna*—characterized by being the limit (*avadhi*) of departure (*apāya*)—is what exists; that alone would serve as the illustration for Brahman.
The meaning is that it would be an example for the sense of the ablative case (*pañcamyarthatā*), but not for the status of being a material cause (*upādānatā*).
This is the intended meaning:

for the horn and so forth, by one part, serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the arrow and so forth, while by another part, it becomes the causal agent (*kāraka*) as the limit (*avadhi*) for the bow; because if that [part] were absent, it would be impossible for the other part to function as the material cause.

For although mung beans, māṣa beans, and the like produce a sprout only through that portion situated within the husk, nevertheless, those portions which have been sown after being deprived of the husk lack the capacity to generate a sprout.
In that case, it is precisely the state of being a limit (*avadhi*) that constitutes the ablative (*apādāna*), and it is this that is expressed by the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*).

By that analogy, for Brahman as well, by virtue of the fifth case-ending, there exists only the status of being a limit conjoined with the predominance of being the material cause (*upādāna*); however, it does not follow that [Brahman] possesses the status of being a material cause itself.
But how, then, is the usage "from primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the great one (mahat), from the great one comes the ego (ahaṅkāra)," and so forth?

To this we reply: even there, the fifth case is used for that which serves as the limit—the untransformed portion—conjoined with a transformed portion. But what is the case where everything is transformed?
In that case, the ablative case should certainly not be employed;
for people do not say, "curd is born from milk," but rather, "milk itself has become curd."
Wherever an application [of a term] is observed, it is either figurative or based on the postulation of another meaning for the sūtra.
Now, one might think:
"The horn itself is the material cause of the arrow."
There is no distinction such that some parts are the material cause (*upādāna*) while others are its limits;
for if that were the case, the usage "an arrow is produced from a horn" would be untenable.
Moreover, whether this ablative case (*pañcamī*) refers to the material cause or to a limit, it should have been stated as "from the parts of the horn" (*śṛṅgāvayavāt*).
Nor should it be argued that, in that case, let there simply be the status of a limit (*avadhitva*);
for that would entail the consequence of production without a material cause (*nirupādānotpatti*).
Therefore, since the horn itself is the material cause, the ablative is heard there, and thus the ablative occurs in the sense of a material cause (*upādāne pañcamī*).
To this, he says: "No, indeed."
For it is not the very act of grasping that is [the cause] here...
In this context, it should not be said that the horn and so forth are the material cause (*upādāna*),
because it is established by valid cognition that the untransformed portion is entirely distinct from the arrow, the sprout, and so on.
The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that otherwise, the determination that "this is its material cause" and "this is not" would be untenable.
To the question, "How then is the usage 'from a horn' (*śṛṅgāt*) employed?", he says: "Because of the weight of external parts" (*bāhyāvayavagauravāt*). (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.73b)
The external [parts] are those other than the transformed ones, which exist in the form of arrows; because of their heaviness and multiplicity, they constitute the limiting parts (*avadhi*).
This is what is meant:

when some parts have been transformed, since many remain, the application of the word "horn" occurs either through the production of another horn or through the mere arising of the cognition of a horn. (4.343)
Now, one might ask: "From where does this conception of a different meaning [for the Sūtra and so forth] arise?
We reply: "Because of the contradiction between the word and its meaning.
For *upādāna* means that by which an effect is taken up—that is, accepted as its own nature (*svarūpa*).

"Apādāna" is that by which something is taken away (*apādīyate*) or abandoned (*parityajyate*) in the course of an action; thus, there is an obvious contradiction [in applying this term to the material cause].
Furthermore, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, rejecting this rule on the grounds that it could have been stated otherwise, has indicated that this very meaning is the intended sense of the sūtra.
If, then, the sūtra "the source (*prakṛti*) of the agent of birth" were to prescribe the technical designation "ablative" (*apādāna*) for the material cause, [it would be redundant].

How, then, does he state that this [definition] has already been covered by the rule *dhruvam apāye ’pādānam*? For the status of being fixed (*dhruvatva*) does not belong to the *apādāna* itself in the context of separation (*apāya*).

Therefore, when the designation *apādāna* is prescribed by this [rule] for the portion of the limit (*avadhibhāga*) which is indeed conjoined with the *apādāna*, the criticism of the author of the Bhāṣya becomes applicable.
Likewise, even by those who are correctly interpreting the Sūtra, it has been stated that this is merely an elaboration (*prapañca*) of that very [point].
Otherwise, previously the term "ablative" (*apādāna*) was taught,
whereas here it is the "object of grasping" (*upādāna*).
For he would not have stated that "the limit (*avadhi*) is the basis (*upādāna*)" if they were one and the same thing;
therefore, it is understood that this meaning is also accepted by them.
Alternatively, let the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) be used even for the basis (*upādāna*).
Nevertheless,
the determination of [the cause] as the material cause (*upādānatva*) based on the ablative case ending in *yataḥ* is not tenable,
because that suffix has multiple meanings.
If it is argued that this has already been stated by the phrase "due to the recollection of the specific [meaning]," then what is this "recollection of the specific"?
If it is argued that it is by means of the inclusion of the verbal root √jan, [we reply:]...
In that case, passages such as "From the Self, space was produced" would not be cited as examples.
Furthermore, why is it determined that the word *yataḥ* is in the ablative case?
Because the suffix *-tasi* is applicable to all case endings.
If it is argued that [the word *ākāśa*] has the same meaning as "the self" (*ātman*) because of the term "truth" (*satya*), we say no;
for that [usage of the ablative case] is intended to express a specific distinction according to the rule in the fifth chapter: "The source of the earth" (*bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ*).
Because it has the sense of being the limit for the manifestation of benefit;
and thus it has been illustrated:
"The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," meaning it is first perceived there. Let this suffice for the detailed explanation. (4.359)
Alternatively, as for what was stated— that the universe is not a transformation of Brahman because it is perceived as distinct from it—
that is incorrect, because the argument is subject to deviation in the case of arrows and similar objects.

For arrows and the like have horns and the like as their material cause, and being distinct from that material cause, they are perceived as distinct from it; therefore, with a hidden intention, he says: "from the horn."

In such cases as these, even with respect to arrows and the like, horns and the like are intended to possess only the status of *apādāna*, characterized by being the limit of departure (*apāyāvadhi*),
and not the status of *upādāna*.
Therefore, because there is an absence of being a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the perception [of the reason] as distinct does not deviate from the probandum (*sādhya*) in that case.

Now, one might ask: "How can it be said that horns and the like are not the material cause (*upādāna*) of arrows and the like? If that were so, since no other material cause is perceived, it would follow that arrows and the like arise without a material cause. To this, he reveals the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) with the words: "The material cause... (*upādāna*). *4,360*

Even though horns and the like possess the status of an *apādāna* (ablative source) in the sense described, it does not follow that arrows and the like must be said to lack a material cause (*nirupādānatva*).
This is because we accept that certain constituent parts of the horn and so forth do indeed serve as the material cause for the arrow and other such objects.
Nor, therefore, does the problem of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) remain in its original state.

Although in this case, for instance in the horn, it is observed that the arrow and so forth constitute a single constituent part (*ekadeśa*) [of the material cause], nevertheless, in this context, only that specific constituent part which has been described as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the form [of the effect] in the horn and so forth could serve as the analogy for Brahman;
for it is precisely from that [constituent part] that the distinction (*bheda*) of the arrows and so forth is perceived.
But it is not the portion that constitutes appropriation;
therefore, because of the absence of that [appropriation],
this is what is meant:

For among the parts of things such as horns, some are the material cause (*upādāna*) of arrows and the like, while others are the efficient cause (*nimitta*). Among these, even if the term "cause" (*hetu*) applies to those that are efficient causes, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*),
because they are included within the class of similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

But as for those things which have become the substratum (*upādāna*), even when entering into their opposite, the causal operation (*hetuvṛtti*) does not occur therein; so how could there be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*)? However, one who, out of impudence, thinks that there is no status as a substratum here—
However, it is merely the state of being a material cause;
thus, there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva). He should be questioned as follows:
What is intended here: is it that the horn as a composite whole is the material cause while remaining undestroyed;
or rather, that all its constituent parts remain [as the cause] while the horn is undestroyed; or else, that all its constituent parts [are the cause] once the horn has been destroyed?
He says "not today" with the words "for not."
Regarding the phrase "here on the horn":
the meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving the horn as well, just as one perceives gold.
He states that the second [alternative] is not [the case] with the words "nahi" (for not).
It is not tenable that all those parts, such as the horns and so forth, remain merely as material causes for the arrow while they themselves have not perished;
for if that were the case, it would follow that the horn and the arrow occupy the same location. He indicates this with the word "hi" (for). He says "not the third" with the words "na hi" (for not).

In this regard, since in all cases of the parts of a horn, the status of being material causes such as the arrow and so forth is untenable after the destruction of the horn, there is no lack of exclusivity (anaikāntya); this is the meaning of the word "hi" (for). To the question "Why is it untenable?", he says: "External," etc.
Because parts that have not undergone transformation are perceived as external to the effect;
and because if that which has not undergone transformation were also a material cause (*upādāna*), it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Objection:

If the horn has perished, how is it that even after the arrow has been produced, there still exist the cognition and the linguistic usage of "horn"? To this, it was said: "because of its heaviness" (*gauravāt*).
The resolution is as before:
let there be no deviation in this case regarding the perception of difference.
Nevertheless, that which was stated—that a modification of the non-conscious is not conscious—is here contradicted.
Since it is observed that conscious beings such as scorpions are produced from non-conscious things such as cow dung, he says: "And not... (na ca).
Nor does consciousness arise there from that which is unconscious.
In that regard, concerning the birth of scorpions and the like from cow dung and so forth:
it is well known that the conscious being is beginningless, due to the desire for food and other factors practiced in previous lives;
otherwise, in the absence of prior karma, even birth would be impossible.
Even if it were somehow possible in the interim, it is entirely impossible at the initial creation;
so how can this groundless objection be raised?
True;

nevertheless, because [this view] has been introduced by another [author] into his own work, and because if the arising of the conscious from the unconscious were non-existent, it would contradict common usage such as "a scorpion is born from cow dung," he says: "by way of being the material cause" (*upādānatayā*).
...by way of being the basis of appropriation. // MAnuv_1,4.74a //
The connection is with what precedes.
We do not deny mere causality, which would contradict conventional usage; rather, we deny it in its capacity as a material cause (*upādāna*).
Because that very [subject] is the topic under discussion:
if cow dung and so forth are not the material cause (*upādāna*) for the scorpion and so forth, then what kind of cause is it?
He asks, "What then? because [he wonders] by what means the occurrence of conventional usage arises.
He states the answer: "The ablative (apādāna)."
What then? For the material cause (upādāna) is indeed insentient;
it is observed [only] in relation to this sentient being who has entered the body that is its effect.
Of this [entity] denoted by words such as "scorpion" and so forth;
for it is observed, which means that its emergence from that [source] is perceived.
Now, it might be argued that the status of being an *apādāna* (ablative source) is accepted only in part.
True;
it was stated with reference to that body—that [the soul] resides within the body of effects.

The meaning is: "belonging to the body which has cow-dung and so forth as its material cause. Here, the word "and" (samuccaya) signifies a conjunction; by the term "scorpion and so forth," two things are expressed: the body and the conscious being.

In that regard, non-sentient things such as cow dung serve as both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*apādāna*) in the production of a non-sentient body, acting as the material cause in one respect and the efficient cause in another.
However, for a sentient being, whose birth is characterized by manifestation, [cow dung] serves merely as a condition (*nimitta*),
because it is the cause of the deity.
And because it arises in that very place,
for this reason the designation "of this" is made as if it were a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, in the case of departure, it is simply the ablative (*apādāna*) as the point of reference.
Therefore, there is no violation of the stated rule.

Having thus set forth the proofs for the absence of Brahman’s status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, and intending to refute the proofs adduced by the opponent, he first refutes the scriptural passage cited as the meaning of the Sūtra—“because of the transformation of that which is not sequential” (*kramasyāprayojakatvapariṇāmāt*)—with the words: “And ‘being’ (*sat ca*)... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.1).
"Truth became that which is true"—thus his universality is not being asserted.

"In truth there arose that which is true and that which is untrue, the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and unconsciousness, the real and the unreal; truth alone became [the world].

In this scriptural passage, it is not stated that this Brahman possesses the nature of the universe consisting of the two classes—the manifest and the unmanifest—denoted by terms such as "truth" (*satya*) and so forth.
Why is this not the case? To this he says: "Having created that... (*tatsṛṣṭvā*).
"Having created that [world] by his mere word, because the universe was already established [in his mind] beforehand. (Manu 1.4.75cd)
"He created all this,
whatever exists here. Having created it, he entered into that very thing."

For, by the statement, "Having entered that, it became the real (sat) and the unreal (tyat)," it is understood that this universe, consisting of the formed and the formless, arose even before Brahman had become the real, the unreal, and so forth.
This is what is meant:
this existence as the Truthful One (Satyadādin) and so forth does not arise from the creation of the universe,
because it occurs at a time subsequent to the creation of the universe.
Whatever action occurs subsequent to another, it is not that [other];
just as when it is said, "he walks after having eaten," the walking is not the eating which occurred previously. Otherwise, the sentence would result in an incoherent meaning.
For clay, gold, and so forth do not become jars, earrings, and the like after having created them and then entered into them.

Alternatively, the universe is not intended here as the referent of words such as "existent" (*sat*) and so on; therefore, one should employ arguments such as: [the universe is not that] because its origination occurs at a time prior to the existence [of the word], just like food, and so forth.
To the question, "What then is the meaning of the Śruti? he says: "Because of existence" (*sattvāt*).
Because it exists, because it is inferred, because it is Vedic, because it cannot be correctly described,
because it is the substratum, because it is its own substratum, because it is knowledge, and because it is difficult to know.
Because it is free from the seventy-three forms of suffering, because it cannot be attained by the wicked,
and because it is eternally pervaded by the qualities of the virtuous and is the form of the Controller,
Brahman itself is indeed described as such through its form as it exists in the world.
If Brahman alone, through its association with qualities such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth, is called "existent" (*sat*) and so on even in the absence of the world-state (*jagadbhāva*),
then there would be no logical connection for the phrase "having entered into that.
For there is no utility in the world-entering [of Brahman] either in its association with qualities like existence or in its being denotable by words such as "existent."
Nor does it follow that [the Self] exists at a time prior to that;

moreover, if this were the case, there would be a contradiction with established usage, because words such as "satya" (truth) and so forth are well known to denote the formed and the formless in passages such as, "Two indeed are the forms of Brahman. Therefore, it is said: "by means of the form belonging to the world."
Although Brahman is always endowed with attributes such as existence and is always denotable by words such as "existent" independently of anything else,
nevertheless, there is a fixed rule that it is denotable by specific words only through the specific forms inherent in those respective entities.

Thus, since Brahman is denotable by words such as "existent" (sat) by virtue of its form as it exists within the manifest and unmanifest world, it is connected [in the text] with the phrase "having entered into that."

It is precisely because of the proximity of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) that even the manifest and unmanifest (*mūrtāmūrta*) are appropriately denoted by words such as "Being" (*sat*) and so forth.
It is "Being" (*sat*) because of its existence (*sattva*) and its excellence; it is "All-pervading" (*at*) because of its all-pervasiveness (*tati*).
The suffix *ḍyat* is applied to the root *tanu-vistāre*. It is called *nirukta* because it belongs to the Vedic tradition;
for that which is stated with certainty (*niścayena ukta*) is indeed *nirukta*.
Indeed, Brahman cannot be definitively expressed by anyone other than the Veda;
because it is impossible to describe it correctly, it is "unexpressed" (anirukta).
Although it is not definitively stated, it is thus called "unexpressed."
Nevertheless, because of the contradiction with the term "unexpounded" (*anirukta*), it is stated that [the Veda] cannot be properly or completely expressed.

Now, one might ask: why is it not explained as being "unexpounded by means of a pramāṇa other than the Veda"? It is not so, for that would entail the abandonment of the subject matter at hand (*prakṛta*).
For it is the context [of the discussion] that "it is not defined by the Veda.
Furthermore, since speech is a property of sound, it is incorrect to say that it is not defined by perception and inference.
Moreover, since the Smṛtis are of the nature of the Veda, the contradiction remains as it was.
Furthermore, the preeminence of its greatness is obtained here;
it is called the "abode" because it is the support of the world,
for all things are determined and proceed within it.

The substitution of *l* for *r* occurs here by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules). Alternatively, this form is derived from the root *lī* (in the sense of "adhering") preceded by the prefix *ni*, with the suffix *lyuṭ* applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
It is "without abode" because it has itself as its own support;
that is, it is that for which no abode exists apart from itself.
It is "consciousness" because it is of the nature of knowledge and of the nature of specific cognition (*vijñāna*).
It is called "non-cognition" (*avijñāna*) because it is difficult to find and difficult to know;
that is, there exists no cognition of a living being (*jīva-jñāna*) capable of penetrating all its specific details regarding its object.
Furthermore, it is "truth" (*satya*) because it is a reality (*sat*), due to its correct pervasiveness (*samyag-vyāpti*) and its status as the cause for both the past and the present.
From the root *tan* with the suffix *ḍ*, the form is simply *tat*. With that, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *sat*.
From the root *yat* meaning "effort," with the suffix *ḍ* and the internal causative sense (*antarṇīta-ṇyartha*), the form is *yam*.
Then there is a *karmadhāraya* compound.

Because the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *bha* is applied by the rule "In the Veda, [the word] *ayas* and so forth [are treated as *bha*]," the substitution of the *jaś*-sounds (i.e., the change of *s* to *r*) does not occur.
It is called "untruth" (anṛta) precisely because it cannot be attained by the wicked,
and not because of its falsity;
for although it is "not-ṛta" (anṛta) in the sense that the ṛta has not been reached, [it is nevertheless true].
Nevertheless, this was stated by the wicked in order to avoid contradicting such scriptural passages as, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme.
The word *hi* (for/indeed) indicates the well-known fact that Brahman is not false.
It is "truth" (satya) because its nature is that of a controller pervaded by the qualities of the eternally virtuous.
Here, "by virtue of being eternal" (*nityatvataḥ*) constitutes one explanation; for it will be stated later that the words "eternal" (*nitya*) and "truth" (*satya*) possess the same meaning.

The word *sat* refers to the qualities of the virtuous (*sādhuguṇāḥ*), according to the statement: "In the sense of existence (*sadbhāve*) and in the sense of goodness (*sādhubhāve*). Their pervasiveness or abundance is expressed by the letter *ta*.
As before, the suffix *ḍvi* is applied to the root *tan* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
Because he is the nature of the driver (*yantṛ*), he is *Yama*. [The suffix] *ḍa* is applied to the root *yama*, meaning "to cease" (*uparama*).
This means that he is the one who impels his devotees toward an abundance of virtuous qualities.
Because of the statement "it existed," there might be the suspicion that Brahman's existence and so forth are with a beginning; therefore, it is said "eternally" (*sadā*) to dispel that doubt.
And its connection is with each [individual] instance.
If one asks, "In that case, how is the usage 'it became' [justified]," he says: "manifestation" (*vyakti*).
For the manifestation of the aforementioned qualities among men occurs in relation to the Puruṣa; thus, the application of such expressions as "it was" and "it will be" is appropriate here.
The manifestation— that is, the cognition— of the qualities described by words such as "existence" (sat) and so forth,
occurs only when creation exists, in relation to the person who is the instructor of men; for this is the reason.
And here, even though Brahman is an eternal attribute, the usage "Brahman became the existent, etc. (sad-ādi) is appropriate;
from this, the meaning of the Śruti is established as follows:
having created the universe consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest, that very Brahman, by being its impeller, [pervades] that same universe through various forms.
Having entered [the world], because prior to creation there was an absence of teachers and disciples possessed of bodies and senses, it existed as something whose qualities were unperceived;
but now, since teachers and disciples possess bodies and senses, it has become something whose qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest, are perceived.
By this, it is stated that the supreme Lord’s creation is for the sake of those who are fit to know His own qualities.
As it has been said:
"This very state of abiding (vihāra) here serves for the production of my own embodied nature, like prosperity itself for the sake of prosperity.
(*4,387*) He concludes the refutation of the transformation into Brahman with the words: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, the Lord of Ramā is the one and only creator of all things without exception, and is devoid of transformation.
The connection is that [Brahman] is indeed changeless and yet the agent of everything without exception.
"One" is the conclusion regarding that which was refuted— the view that Brahman is divided into two parts—
or it is a restatement of the reasoning already given concerning the impossibility of transformation.
Therefore, the connection is that "the status of Brahman as the material cause is not the subject matter of the *prakṛtyadhikaraṇa*"; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
To the question, "What then is its subject matter?", he says: "By means of words" (*śabdaiḥ*).
She is designated by words such as "prakṛti" and others which are feminine in gender.
The word "iti" implies that "this is the meaning" is the ellipsis.
By this, it is also indicated that there is no lack of coherence, because the refutation of erroneous explanations serves the purpose of strengthening one's own explanation.
Now, since there is still subject matter remaining to be stated, how can a conclusion be drawn?
For instance,
it was stated that "because there is no contradiction between the proposition and the example" must first be refuted;
this is true.
It will be refuted by the refutation of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).
If it is argued that, in the passage concerning the teaching of covetousness, the statement “May I become many; may I be born forth” must be critiqued, we say no.
He says— “May I become many”— because this [passage] has also been explained by the very same method of explaining the statement, “Being and non-being” (sat ca tyat ca).
"May I become many"—it is indeed by this very path that he [the Self] is joined.
