"Of that very same unchanging [reality]" is the gloss of "by the aforementioned path," namely,
"by means of each respective form."
...in the form appropriate to each respective [occasion]. // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.80c //
The meaning is that the purport of the Vedic scripture, "He desired, 'May I become many,'" is [the manifestation] through infinite forms that impel those respective infinite categories of objects.
If this were the case, then the subsequent statement, "He created all this," would be inconsistent.
For it is not logical to state an action other than that which was intended by the purpose; nor is the Lord independent or one whose desires do not come true. Therefore, he says: "for that purpose."
"...for he created the world for that purpose. (Manu 1.4.80d).

Immediately after the desire for the state of having many forms as the regulator of various objects, because the state of being a regulator depends upon those who are regulated, "for that purpose" means for the sake of having many forms as a regulator.
First, it created the world as that which is to be governed; then, having assumed many forms as the governor,
it entered into that very world.
The meaning is that since the construction of the sentence is logically consistent, how could there be any inconsistency here?
By this very [explanation], the scriptural passage, “He made himself his own self,” is to be understood as having been explained.
For it is not heard here that the Self creates itself as the manifold world (prapañca);
moreover, the teaching of both [Self and world] is refuted by the very mention of the spider analogy. Indeed, [the analogy does not apply], for that which is being produced from the spider...
And for that which dissolves into that very [thread],
the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) is the material cause (*upādāna*);
however, it has been stated that this is simply the food consumed by it.
The notion that this is the source (*yoni*) has already been refuted; therefore, the conclusion is indeed appropriate.
Immediately after the false explanation, he repeats it in order to refute it: "And that which...
(4.391). "And that which is this very unmodified Brahman [appearing] as the universe is false."
That which is perceived by a dull vision is called "creation" (sarga).
That Brahman is perceived as the universal self— that is what is called "creation"— this much is the same even in the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda).
Therefore, it was stated that [Brahman] remains indeed unmodified.
From what does its unchangeability follow? To this it is said: "one" (*eka*).
This means it is without a second (*advitīya*) and without parts (*niravayava*).
To explain: does the transformation of Brahman into the form of the universe occur by itself,
or rather through another cause?
Not the first, because it is not observed anywhere.
As for the example cited— “like milk and so forth”— that is incorrect, because time and other factors are present [in those cases as well].
If it is argued that [it occurs] by its own will, we say no;
because there would be no purpose.
If it is argued that this is its very nature, we say no.
Because it would entail the loss of [his] discernment;
nor the second,
because he is without a second.
Furthermore, nothing partless has ever been observed to undergo transformation.
If it is argued that space is perceived as possessing conjunction and so forth, we say no; for the subject under discussion is the transformation of a substance that lacks a cause.
However, since atoms and the like are not established by their own nature, and because it is impossible for that which is unmodified to appear as something else, it is said: "it is false" (*mṛṣā*).
By the word "false" (mṛṣā), the indeterminability of the universe's identity with Brahman and the perception thereof is expressed;
that is, just as a rope remains unmodified yet falsely appears in the form of a snake and so forth, so it is here.
If it is then asked, "In that case, another material cause for the universe must be stated," it is therefore said: "only by those of dull vision."
"Dim vision" means that vision by which one becomes dim-sighted; the meaning is "by that illusion.
Alternatively, it is stated as "only by dim vision" in order to avoid the possibility [of it being anything else].
It is "dim vision" because it is both dim and vision; the meaning is "by that delusion."
Since even error would result in the reality of the universe because it conforms to the object, it is said: "false" (mṛṣā).
This very fact—that Brahman is the substratum for the superimposition of false manifoldness—is what is expressed by the statement "Brahman is the material cause" (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
This is what is meant: by the sūtras beginning with "And the material cause" (*prakṛtiśca*), the status of Brahman as the material cause of the world is stated according to the manner described.
And its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is not by way of undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitayā*);
rather, it is solely by virtue of being the substratum for the false delusion of the manifold world, which is itself a transformation of ignorance.
Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
He begins his refutation with the words: "It is said."
That which is asserted by the proponent of the theory of illusory transformation (vivartavādin) regarding Brahman—
its refutation is now stated;
thus it should be construed by repeating [the phrase].

And that [is not so]; either the negative particle *nañ* must be understood as recurring [from the previous statement], or one asks "Why not? by means of an alternative (*vikalpena*), saying "It is so" (*seti*).
Was that limited vision of his directed toward that very Brahman, or did it go elsewhere?

Since the view that the universe is a transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman must be refuted, the question regarding the basis for a limited perspective is inappropriate; therefore, it was said: "She" (*sā*).

The meaning is that it is so described because of its manifestation as a transformation characterized by many forms that are unreal and contrary to reality, while remaining a single entity undeviating from the ultimate truth (tattva), and because it has that [truth] as its material cause (upādāna).
The sense is that once the [notion of] "weak vision" has been refuted by the demonstration that its substratum cannot be established and so forth, all of this is thereby refuted.
"Of that alone" means that upon which the entire universe depends as its illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).
"Belonging to something other than that" means belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*).
The word "what" (*kiṃ*) is connected to both [sides].

For some proponents of illusion (*māyāvādinaḥ*) believe that Brahman itself, through its own ignorance (*svāvidyā*), undergoes a transformation (*vivartate*) into the form of the world, like a dream and so forth.
They hold that Brahman, standing in the position of the original object (*bimba*), is the cause endowed with the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*).
Others hold that individual living beings (*jīva*) are each bound by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Still others maintain that Brahman, reflected through *māyā* and *avidyā*, is the cause of the world; and that while Brahman is the substratum for what is contrary [to its true nature], the living beings are bound by ignorance.
Some maintain that it is the individual souls alone who, through their own ignorance, delude Brahman into appearing in the form of the manifold world (prapañca) for each of them;
and because of this similarity, there arises the appearance of oneness in the world, just as when many people perceive a second moon.
Furthermore, they hold that from the perspective of its own essential nature, Brahman is the cause of the world.
In this context, without intending to specify internal subdivisions, the alternatives were presented as being twofold.

By stating "other than that" (*tato 'nyagā*) instead of saying "residing in the individual soul" (*jīvagā*), the author has also indicated the following alternative: "Is that [individual soul] other than Brahman, or not other than it, or perhaps neither?"
Regarding that, he refutes the second position—that [the effect] enters into the first [cause]—with the words: "If [it were] from Brahman... and so forth.
If Brahman were [the cause], where would his omniscience be? ...

If there were error (*bhrama*) regarding the universe on the part of Brahman, then, since error is preceded by a lack of specific knowledge (*viśeṣājñāna*), that too would have to be admitted of Brahman.
And in that case, he would not possess omniscience;
and if omniscience does not reside in Brahman, then where could it reside?
It cannot reside in the living self (*jīva*),
because that would contradict direct experience;
nor can it reside in the insentient (*jaḍa*), because consciousness alone is impossible therein.
And thus, there would be the futility of such scriptural passages as, "He who is omniscient.
If it is argued that even the omniscience of Brahman is merely due to delusion, we say no.
This is because even a cognition of such-and-such a kind is opposed to specific knowledge;
otherwise, even for one who possesses the knowledge of mother-of-pearl, that ignorance would not be contradicted, leading to the undesirable consequence that error could never be eliminated.
Furthermore, this is merely an illustration.
Since there is no difference in Brahman, an error caused by its non-manifestation is not possible;
however, its own nature is established through self-luminosity,
for if it were unestablished—
It should also be understood that an error is even more impossible because no substratum is perceived.
He refutes the first [alternative] of the second [position] with the words: "If it were directed toward another."
If otherness were [established] by itself from another thing...

If it is accepted that the universal delusion has as its locus a living being (*jīva*) distinct from Brahman, then—since it is impossible for the locus of a delusion to be itself imagined by that delusion—it would follow that the difference between the *jīva* and Brahman is intrinsic;
consequently, this would result in a contradiction of your own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
[Objection: Let the difference between the *jīva* and Brahman be real.
It might be argued that the proliferation of non-self (anātma-prapañca) is imagined through delusion within Brahman; therefore, he says: "No."
The vision of one who is not joined with the body does not exist; therefore, that [vision] arises from itself.

Although the proponents of Māyā do not think in this way, nevertheless, it is praiseworthy to demonstrate the logical inconsistency within that very [system] for one who has set out to refute the meaning of the Sūtras; thus begins [the discussion].
It is not only that individual souls (jīvas) distinct from Brahman are unreal (akalpita).

However, since the perception of the objects of that state is not possible for one devoid of bodily connection due to the absence of the senses, for this reason it must be admitted that the senses—which are the cause of superimposition—and their substratum, the body, exist even without conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). For the opponent does not consider this phenomenal world to be established by the witness-consciousness alone, as is the case with pleasure and so forth, or with silver and so forth; rather, he maintains that the body and senses possess an origin. And its cause must be admitted to be self-existent (*svataḥ*). (4.410)

Let it be granted that for individual souls (jīvas) other than Brahman—along with their causes, as well as their bodies and sense organs—the state of being constructed by delusion (bhrānti) holds true;
for delusion must exist prior [to them] as the seer, the instrument of seeing, the substratum thereof, and the cause thereof.
However, one might argue that the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is distinct from those [souls], is what is constructed by delusion; to this, he says: "of the embodied ones" (dehinām).
If embodied beings and their bodies were not produced from causes, it would be due to delusion.
What is it that is imagined there through delusion? ... MAnu 1.4.84a
By the word "cause" (kāraṇa), there is the inclusion of the sense organs which are the causes of cognition, as well as the body and sense organs which are the causes [of those].
The word "established" (siddhāḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. What [is the meaning of] "what" (kim)? It is used in the sense of an objection (ākṣepa).
In that case, [the question arises] whether [Brahman exists] in this phenomenal world (prapañca) or in Brahman itself;
for there is no phenomenal world apart from the infinite living beings, their causes, bodies, and sense organs.
The underlying point is that even objects of experience exist solely for the sake of sustaining the bodies and sense organs.

And thus, not only would there be a contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), but—as the remainder of the argument implies—it would also follow that the sūtras beginning with "And the primal nature" (*prakṛtiś ca*) would be rendered devoid of subject matter.
Now, it may be objected: "But was it not stated that 'if otherness were inherent [in the thing], then otherness would belong to something else'?"

Since even the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is established through illusion, and since one considers that the delusion regarding external and internal objects arises from Brahman as if it were distinct due to illusion, he says: "The distinction also... [bhedo 'pīti].
... even if the distinction [between them] arises from delusion.
The connection is as follows: not only is conceptual proliferation (prapañca) [unreal],
but if even the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is accepted as being born of error and established by error,
then there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśrayatā).
Here, by the term "mutual dependence" (*anyonyāśrayatā*), a circularity (*cakraka*) is expressed, because that too involves mutual dependence among many factors.
To the question "In what way is there mutual dependence?", it is said: "Because of error" (*bhrānteḥ*).
Since error has its root in ignorance, it depends upon the perception of difference.
Because error has as its cause the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that is positive in nature, which is the ground for the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman;
and because that ignorance is dependent upon the distinction [it seeks to conceal];
one might ask: "Since ignorance is beginningless, how could it be dependent upon a distinction? To this, it is said: "Not [due to] ignorance."
There is nothing that imagines through ignorance, because there would otherwise be the fallacy of mutual dependence.

Since there exists nothing other than the individual soul (jīva), distinct from Brahman, that could be the projector of ignorance; this is what is meant: [of the individual soul and Brahman]... *4,412*... [of the individual soul and Brahman].
The delusion by which difference is established depends upon ignorance,
because it is accepted that both the nature and the object of delusion are effects of ignorance.
Although the error whose object is difference is the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*),
nevertheless, for that [consciousness] which is unattached, a state of being conjoined with a superimposed object does not arise without ignorance (*ajñāna*).
And that ignorance is dependent upon duality,
because it is accepted that even though it is beginningless, it is conceptually constructed by delusion; otherwise, it would follow that it is real.
Furthermore, it is accepted that error resides in the individual soul,
and without the conceptualization of difference, the individual soul itself would not exist.
Nor is it logical that the superimposition of ignorance occurs upon Brahman alone;
for since it is possible for everything to have that [Brahman] as its substratum, the "half-old-woman" logic (ardhajaratīya) is untenable.
Therefore, because delusive cognition, the individual soul, and their distinctions depend on one another, there is a circularity (cakraka).

Alternatively, since difference is imagined through delusion (*bhrānti*) and delusion itself depends upon difference, this [verse] has stated the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). It should be understood that ignorance (*ajñāna*) was inserted in the middle precisely for the sake of explanation.
By this, the position of the doctrine of the individual soul’s ignorance (*jīvājñānavāda*)— [is refuted].
This too is refuted,
because the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) and so forth is equally present.
If it is argued that there is no fault because it is like the case of the seed and the sprout, we say no.

Because of the disparity; for in that case, there is no fault due to the difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), whereas no such difference exists between the individual instances of the ignorance (*avidyā*) of living beings (*jīva*). *4,415*
What was stated—that [the self] does not belong to one joined with a body, and so forth—is untenable; for even the body and such are constructed by delusion.
Nor is there an absence of a cause in that regard, since a previous body and so forth exist.
And there is no infinite regress in this way because it is beginningless;
do not say so.
Because the perception of bodies and so forth is impossible at the initial creation;
for it has already been stated that this matter is not established by the witness-consciousness alone.
Furthermore, even if this avoidance of infinite regress were possible, [it would still be untenable].
If it were established by valid cognition that even the preceding and preceding-most bodies and so forth are established through delusion,
then otherwise— in this very way— there would result the unavoidable consequence of an infinite regress in all cases.
And there is no proof for this.
[Objection: But how can there be no proof, given that such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity here" exist? To this, he says:
"But if it were an error," [it means:]
"But if [the world] were illusory, this statement would not hold, because it falls within that [category of error].
Alternatively, one might raise the following objection: "This entire argument is merely a fallacy (ābhāsa), as it lacks a conclusion that reaches the opposite [of its premise];

for scriptures such as 'Not here, not there' declare that the entire phenomenal expansion (prapañca), including the ether and so forth, is imagined through delusion. It is in response to this that the following has been stated.
For the meaning of the Veda should be accepted as that which is not contradicted by reason;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting even such passages as "the blind man found a jewel," and there would follow the consequence of not undertaking the treatises on inquiry.
Furthermore, the statement "not here, not there" (*neha nānā*) and so forth would contradict reason;
for instance,
if everything beginning with the ether were established through delusion, then this Śruti, being included therein, would likewise be so established.

If everything such as space and so forth were superimposed through delusion (*bhrama*), then all of it would be established by delusion; and since this scripture (*śruti*) is included within that [reality], it too would be so.
Furthermore, because that which is superimposed by delusion is non-existent (*asad*), the scripture—being itself non-existent—could not be the cause for the cognition of its meaning.
The word *bhrama* is well-known among others [i.e., opponents] to refer to both cognition and the object; thus, the term "state of being delusion" (*bhramatva*) was employed.

Although this matter was already described in the first sūtra, there is nevertheless a distinction: whereas the elaboration (*prapañca*) therein concerned the internal, here it concerns external objects.
Furthermore, this is a repetition of what was already stated for the purpose of further explanation. *4,419*

[Objection: Surely this entire phenomenal world, although established by delusion, is indeed empirical (*vyāvahārika*). Therefore, the scripture (*śruti*) included within it will also be a cause for [attaining] the goal because of its empirical nature. To this, he says: "Empirical nature... [and so forth].
For its status as conventional reality depends indeed upon its being non-sublated.
This is the meaning of the verse.
This might indeed be so if the conventional reality of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) could possibly be accepted by you.
But this is not the case;
for the conventional nature of this phenomenal world (prapañca) would only exist if it were non-sublated.
This is what is meant:
If phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) were admitted as being conventional,
then it would follow that it must also be admitted as non-sublatable;
yet you do not admit it as such.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to accept even the conventional [truth].
For if one were to establish the acceptance of its reality, that would be establishing what is already desired,
since the opponent also accepts its reality in some sense.
Therefore, it was stated that [the reason] resides only in non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*).

Now, one might object: "Since even sublatable things such as silver in a shell are objects of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) consisting of recognition and verbal designation, this logical argument (*tarka*) lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*. To this, he says: "The sublatable... and so forth.
"That which is sublated does not perform a causal function" (MAnu 1.4.86c).
True, that which is sublated—such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—is not a causal agent;
however, [the cognition of] supernormal knowledge and the like is an object of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
Nevertheless, it does not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*).
For it is not observed to produce the causal efficiency appropriate to silver, such as the fashioning of a bracelet and so forth.
In this context, what is under discussion is that conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*) is characterized precisely by the capacity for causal efficiency.
It does not have the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth as its object,
because it has been established that the sacred scripture (*śruti*) generates cognition of the meaning [of reality].
Therefore, there is no deficiency in the constituent parts of reasoning (*tarka*).
But is it not the case that sublation is a property of the substrate, such as mother-of-pearl,
since it has been stated [in the sūtra] that "[it is the sublation] of what has been cognized otherwise"?
If even mother-of-pearl and the like perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), how can it be said that what is sublated does not perform causal efficiency?
It is not so; for here we rely upon the definition of sublation as "being subject to negation" (*niṣedhyatva-lakṣaṇa-bādhyatva*), which is accepted by the opponent. *4,421*

[Objection: "But even so, since one observes that unreal things such as the enjoyment of a beloved woman in a dream possess causal efficacy (arthakriyā), such as the emission of the final element, the logical argument (tarka) lacks pervasion (vyāpti-vikala). To this, he says: "And not... [na ca...].
And even a dream is not false for us.
"‘Dream’ refers to an object perceived during the dream state;
this is our view, that of the followers of Bādarāyaṇa.
If it is argued, ‘In that case, let there be a breach of the pervasion (vyāpti) in my view, since I have accepted [dream objects] as false,’ we say no."
Because it cannot be accepted as such by the follower of Bādarāyaṇa.
Now, one might ask: "How is it that for Bādarāyaṇa, a dream is not false? To this he says: "It is a latent impression (vāsanā)."
Because that [dream-object] is also admitted to be produced by latent impressions (vāsanā).

Since the author of the Sūtras, by stating that even such a dream is "mere illusion" (māyāmātra), accepts it as being produced by latent impressions (vāsanā), it is understood that he does not consider that dream to be false;
for no one would attempt to determine the cause of something that does not exist.
Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras' established doctrine must follow the Śruti;

and since the Śruti, by speaking of an agent for the objects of a dream, intends precisely their reality, the falsity [of those objects] was not intended by the author of the Sūtras—this he states with the words "For he... (*sa hi*). This is also supported by the statement, "...because of the sentence 'for he is the agent'. (*Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.87c*)

Now, one might ask: "How can a dream not be false? For the author of the Sūtras himself will state its falsity by saying 'it is mere illusion' (māyāmātra). To this, he says: "Because of latent impressions" (vāsanā).
The term "mere illusion" (māyāmātra) does not intend to convey that the dream is false; rather, it signifies that it is produced by latent impressions (vāsanā), and therefore it is not false.
How this is so will be demonstrated later;
or it may be construed thus: because we accept that the forthcoming sūtra establishes [the fact] that [the world] is produced from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Not only by virtue of the arguments to be stated hereafter is falsity not the meaning of the sūtra.
But he says "for that" (*sa hi*) because it is on account of scripture;
or rather, the object of a dream is not eternal from the beginning, because it would subsequently contradict [the laws of] karma (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth.
Nor is it perishable along with its substratum, because neither a material cause nor an efficient cause can be identified;
and no other possibility is feasible.
To the question, "In that case, how is it not false? he says: "It is a latent impression (vāsanā)."
The ellipsis is "there is no absence of appropriation" (*nopādānābhāva*). Alternatively, it connects with the preceding phrase as "not false" (*na mṛṣā*).
Having thus examined appropriation (*upādāna*), he establishes the cause [of its falsity] with the words "for" (*hi*).
If Īśvara is known as the cause—this is the ellipsis;
or rather, it connects with the preceding phrase "not false.
[Objection: But then, how is it that [the world] is said to be "like a dream or an illusion"?
Because of such statements as these, which describe a dream as being an error, he says: "The state of waking."
... for the notion that it is waking is indeed an illusion.
The word "iti" has the sense of "beginning with" or the sense of "illustration.
That which is the state of being awake for the observer who [thinks] "I am awake,"...
Furthermore, this appearance— whether it be the identity of these objects with the things perceived during waking vision,
or their being produced from external materials such as clay— is an illusion.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is "because it is sublated.
The intention is that, in comparison to that [sublation], there are the statements of the Śruti and so forth.
Now, one might object: in the case of the delusion of a snake in a rope...
Even for a non-existent snake, the performance of causal functions appropriate to a snake—such as fear and trembling—is observed;
likewise, the capacity to produce satisfaction is found in a flower garland superimposed upon a snake.
Therefore, since there is a breach of the pervasion (vyāpti) in this reasoning, he says: "In the case of the snake... [etc.]
For even in cases such as the delusion of a snake, there certainly exists a cognition of that very kind.
Just as there is no sublation [of the cognition] by the statement "there was no snake here," so too there is no sublation by the statement "the cognition of a snake did not arise."

The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that [the cognition] persists as "it was indeed so," and because the status of being an error is accounted for merely by the discrepancy between the object and its representation.
To the question, "What follows if the cognition nonetheless exists? he says: "That very [cognition]."
That alone is capable of purposeful action... // MAnu 1.4.88c //
By the word "eva" (only), [the existence of] snakes and so forth is excluded;
for even when a snake or the like is present, if cognition is absent, fear, trembling, and so forth do not arise.
And since that [fear] arises from that [cognition], trembling and so forth are indeed the effects of the cognition, not the effects of the snake;
whereas crawling toward it, biting, and so forth are the effects of the snake.
Death, too, is caused by the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu-vyākulatā*).

And since that [disturbance] occurs not only through poisonous substances but also through fear and so forth, it follows that the snake or other such agents do not possess causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) even for the victim.

Now, is it mere cognition that produces fear and so forth, or is it cognition as delimited by an object? Not the first, because even the cognition of a jar would then result in producing fear, simply by virtue of being a cognition.
In the second case, the object cannot be the rope and so forth, because it would follow that even the cognition "this is a rope" and the like would be a cause of fear and so on.
If, on the other hand, the snake and so forth were the qualifier, then it too would necessarily be a cause of fear and so on. (4.428)
Regarding this, someone says:
"This is not a fault,
because the object such as a snake, which functions to differentiate the cognition, does not enter into the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) produced by that cognition."
In expressions such as "he does not dwell in the land of the Kurus" or "he studies the commentary of the Guru," even the qualifiers possess the status of a *kāraka*;
however, their function is fulfilled merely by excluding [the agent] from the over-extended domains of "land" and "commentary."
That is incorrect;
for even in that case, one must necessarily admit that the snake and so forth possess the quality of being a differentiator (*vyāvartakatva*).
For indeed, the state of being a differentiator consists in being the producer of a cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-buddhi*).
Even there, if the objection is avoided by accepting [the existence of] cognition, the reductio ad absurdum remains as it was because of the inclusion of the differentiating property;
regarding this, he says: "of such a kind."
The meaning is: "of the same kind as the cognition that apprehends a real snake.
To begin with, the cognition of a real snake is experienced as being distinct from the cognition of a jar and so forth.
Moreover, exclusion is everywhere observed to be produced by the connection with an excluding property (dharma),
and the object itself is not the excluding factor.
Because that [property] does not belong to it;
for only what is connected can be an excluder,
otherwise there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that the connection with the object itself must be the differentiator, we say no; for such a connection, being of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, does not exist [in the case of mental perception].
Therefore, one must admit some property residing solely within the cognition itself.

Furthermore, just as a distinction between two cognitions produced by different causal complexes—consisting in their being indirect (*parokṣa*) or direct (*aparokṣa*)—is admitted even without an external adjunct in the form of an object, why then should an intrinsic distinction not be accepted even in the case of a direct cognition?

Moreover, the specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) resulting from the cognition of a snake would not be possible without an excellence residing within the cognition itself; for it is not the case that...

Merely by virtue of being related to Devadatta, a *kalam* seed produces an effect distinct from the effects of other *kalam* seeds; yet, as for this distinction— whether it arises from a correct causal complex in the case of the cognition of a real snake,
or from an incorrect one in the case of the cognition of a false snake— there is no difference whatsoever.

Therefore, since the cognition of a snake and the like produces fear and so forth by means of its own internal specific quality rather than through the inclusion of an external object, the snake itself has no causal efficacy.

Thus, where purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is certain, there is no falsity; but where there is falsity, there is no purposeful action. Consequently, there is no breach anywhere of the pervasion rooted in reasoning.
Thus he concludes with the word "that" (tat).
"...that [consciousness] is real and performs a causal function. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.88d) [Objection:

But surely, if the capacity to perform a causal function (*arthakriyākāritva*) is excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), namely that which is false, it must likewise be excluded from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), such as Brahman; thus, it would be an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason.
Furthermore, one cannot argue that a causal function has been stated for true cognition.
Since that [Brahman] as well is subject to misconception because it is included within conceptual proliferation (prapañca), he says: "But Brahman... and so forth.
Brahman, however, is that which performs purposeful action, whether through another or by itself;
for it has been accepted as such by that very [author] himself... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.89a-c].

Indeed, by that very proponent of illusion (māyāvādin), Brahman has been admitted to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) even more eminently than the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because it was stated in the *Janmādi-sūtra* to be the cause of the universe.
Therefore, since it falls within the class of similar instances (*sapakṣa*), one should not consider the reason to be "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇya*).
[Objection: But surely, the causal efficiency of Brahman as admitted by me is not intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).
But [it exists] only in dependence on another, because it is accepted that illusion arises from that [dependence].
Therefore, one might ask: how can that which is the basis for the consequence (āpādaka) enter into the similar class (sapakṣa)? To this, he says: "from another" (parataḥ).
The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) has indeed been admitted as belonging to Brahman;
whether that [efficiency] arises from itself or from another is irrelevant to the present context.
For we have not asserted that causal efficiency must be produced by something else.
Or it may be introduced by another;

otherwise, since it would be possible to state that smoke and the like—which were employed in a general way—are "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) because they do not enter into the similar class (*sapakṣa*) in their specific form, there would be a refutation of that [general application]. *4,435*

It might be argued that this [objection] does not mean that Brahman’s capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is dependent on another in the sense of being subject to another like a wooden automaton, nor that it requires a purpose or other factors like a potter.
However, just as impurity in the sky is indeed inactive, so too does causal efficiency (arthakriyā) appear in Brahman due to its connection with *māyā*, though it remains inactive.
Furthermore, such a thing cannot constitute a member of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) for the probans; therefore, he says: "because [the property] is extrinsic" (*paratastva*).
...and there is no means of valid cognition for extrinsic validity. Mānava 1.4.89d.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "of Brahman's capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyākāritva*). Valid cognition (*pramā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when its nature has been determined by something else (*parataḥ*). *4,436*
This is the intended meaning here:
Is the purposeful activity of Brahmā, such as the creation of the world, perceived or not?
If it is not, how can it be stated as a defining characteristic?
And for what is the nature of being illusory admitted?
Even if it is well-known, it is certainly not established by means of perception or inference,
because it is not within their scope.
Therefore, it must be stated that [it exists] by the Veda itself;
and if so, how can it be illusory?
Does it follow, then, that everything perceived in the Veda is real?
Certainly;
however, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it remains exactly so.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of Brahman being dependent on something else that could serve as a subverting factor.
If it is asked, "How can there be truthfulness merely through the absence of sublation?
we reply: because validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
For if validity were extrinsic (*parataḥ*), it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and thus no valid cognition could ever be ascertained.

If it is argued that scriptural passages such as "it is fruitless" and "it is inactive" constitute sublation [of the opponent's view], then, once causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) has been accepted by the opponent on the strength of such scripture, the passage expressing that— namely, "He created all this"— [is likewise established].
In such cases, scriptural testimony (*śruti*) would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), because there is no lack of validity other than the falsity of the matter it sets forth.
Furthermore, since there is no distinction [between them], [the scripture states]: "partless and actionless."
Thus, since this scripture contradicts this [position], why should it not be considered non-authoritative regarding the existence of an external world?
We shall discuss another point later.
Now, let it be that only that which is uncontradicted performs causal efficiency; I accept that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is likewise uncontradicted.

Even though there is an absence of absolute non-sublatability, it is nonetheless unsublatable prior to the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self; therefore, the scripture included therein will also be an authority because of its secondary reality. To this, he says: "secondary."

Since we both always agree that the non-primary truth-cognition is a means of valid knowledge, let that [primary] cognition remain as a means of valid knowledge; for there can be no disagreement between us on this point. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.90)
By the word "always" (*sadā*),
he indicates that this object of cognition (*prameya*) has already been established;
consequently, the fault of redundancy (*punarukti*) is avoided.
"Let it remain; it need not be spoken"—this means that such valid cognition (*pramā*) is a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) sublated by the knowledge of Brahman.
Or, because that scriptural statement is not a valid cognition, "let it remain."
For the falsity of phenomenal proliferation (prapañca-mithyātva) is its object;
nor is that [falsity] the very nature of Brahman,
because it is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (sopādhika).
Consequently, its sublation is necessary;
and it is well known that that which has a sublatable object is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

Even though it has a sublatable object, one might argue that it possesses validity because its object was not sublated prior to the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, it is said: "not primary" (*amukhyā*).
"Truth" means that which has an uncontradicted object;
for we shall explain later that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not become such by having its object contradicted after a lapse of time.
Let it be so; however, since [the Veda] is untrue both in its own nature and in its objective content, the Śruti is contested as being a means of proof.
Nevertheless, one might ask: why should that [distinction] not be put forward as a proof for the falsity of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)? To this, he says: "For not... (na hi).
For it is not possible for one who has gone astray to achieve success anywhere.

If that were the case, there would also be the presentation of the fallacies of the unestablished nature of the subject (*svarūpāsiddha*) and the mistimed (*kālātīta*), because even in those cases, mere superimposition (*āropa*) is easily available; this is the intended meaning.
It might be argued as follows:
Let this inquiry into the existence or non-existence of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) rest;
for it is by means of the pramāṇa alone that the object of cognition (prameya) is established.

Otherwise, even for you, there would follow the consequence of the cessation of all discourse due to the absence of pramāṇas when refuting the falsity of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) and establishing its truth.
The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that you are proposing must be either true or false.
It is not appropriate for you to state it as true to me, because I do not accept that what is true possesses the capacity to establish [an object];
for where there is truth, there is no entry of causal activity (*kriyā*), and where there is entry of causal activity, that is not true.
Nor should it be said that you have accepted the witness as a prover of reality;
for even if its presentation might somehow be possible in the case of pleasure and so forth, it is impossible in the case of the external manifold,
since this [witness] has the external means of valid cognition as its object.
Otherwise, it would follow that there are no blind or deaf persons and so forth;
and since that [perception] alone is the subject under discussion here, nor is it non-existent because it has not been denied by you, he says: "the state of being a means of proof" (*sādhakatvam*).
For the validity of the witness who is present before us both is fully acknowledged;
therefore, let that not become a matter of dispute between us.
The connection is with the word "of truth" (satyasya).
The term "correctly" (samyak) refers to the primary sense alone, and not by way of being a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established incidentally).

The word *hi* indicates the well-known fact that every object, whether in a state of being known or unknown, is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*). The indeclinable *tat* means "by that," namely, by the witness.
The doctrine of universal transformation would not exist; that is to say, we shall refute it.
And this is merely an illustration.
It should also be understood that we establish the reality of the entire universe by means of that very same [consciousness].
And so it will be said:
"No arrangement of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth, has been accepted by me."
But all this is stated according to the opponent's own method;
therefore, how can you say to me, who do not accept anything [of my own], that "you have accepted the probative force of witnesses"? To this, he says: "If... (yadīti).
If nothing has been accepted, then even the state of non-acceptance is not itself accepted;
thus one would be mute, and therefore our position is not contested.
"One who has no acceptance" (*anaṅgīkṛta*) is one for whom no acceptance (*aṅgīkāra*) exists;
its state is "the state of being unaccepted" (*anaṅgīkṛtatā*).
The meaning is "the condition of not having been accepted."
The two occurrences of the word "iti" indicate the reason. If the opponent should say, "I have not accepted anything at all," then he should be addressed as follows:
Do you accept that the self is not accepted by you in every respect, or not?

In the first case, since nothing at all has been accepted, your own position is abandoned; thus, even the non-acceptance of the self would not have been accepted, so the second alternative alone must be accepted.
And if that were so, you would be mute.
For it is improper for one who is indifferent to both acceptance and non-acceptance—like a corpse—to engage in speech;
thus, for one who maintains silence, we are not his opponent. What more need be said here?
This is true.
In reality, we have desisted from all [activity] and, resting our burden upon the solitary reality of Brahman—the self-luminous conscious Self—remain happily, having accomplished our purpose.

As for those who wish to determine the truth by introducing an investigation based on a system of means and refutations devised by themselves, we say to them: "This system of investigation of yours is not sound.
To this they reply: "Do not speak thus!"
Even so, one must necessarily admit the invalidity of the opponent's established system of inquiry;
otherwise, the exposition of that [system] would be futile.
Now, you might think that while admitting only that much, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth is not admitted.
That is not so;

for it is impossible to demonstrate that an alternative system is incorrect without relying on means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the like. If you argue: "We say that your own proposed system is incorrect because it is internally contradictory, but we do not admit any means of valid cognition in this matter," we reply: no.
For one must also accept this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): that "whatever contradicts the system one has accepted for oneself is incorrect.
If it is argued that this too is merely based on what has been accepted by the opponent, we say no.
Is the opponent informed of the incorrectness of his own system after having himself realized it, or without having realized it at all?
In the second case, there would be deception.
If it is argued that this is exactly the same in a debate for victory (*vijigīṣukathā*), we say no;
for even a student is to be made to understand [the truth].
In the first case, it must be understood by oneself through this or some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
How, then, can there be a non-acceptance of *pramāṇa* and so forth?
For it is precisely the instrument of valid cognition (*pramiti-karaṇa*) and the like that constitutes the acceptance of *pramāṇa* and the rest.

Therefore, it must be stated that those who remain indifferent to the acceptance of existence and non-existence (or truth and untruth) acknowledge the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth;
and this [position] has already been refuted previously. *4,448*

Having thus refuted the view that the universe is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, he states the proof for its reality (*sattā*) in the verse beginning with "The universe" (*viśvam*).
"All that he has perceived is true," "He knows the truth of this according to its actual state"—all such scriptural passages declare the reality of the universe. (Manu Smṛti 1.4.93)

By the phrase "in accordance with reality" (*yathārthataḥ*), he cites the Vedic scripture: "The Seer, the Wise One. If it is argued that the scriptures are concerned only with conventional truth (*vyāvahārikasatyatā*), [we reply: no.
[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence that even the statement "That is the truth" would have to be so [unreal].
If you argue that this is because it contradicts another scriptural passage, then here too there is a contradiction with the scriptural passage, "This was indeed non-existent."
If it is argued that there is no intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) because it does not serve a human purpose (*apuruṣārthatva*), we say no;
for the knowledge of the supreme majesty of the Lord, such as His being the creator of a real universe, is itself the cause (or motive) for attaining the human goal.

Furthermore, the reality of the phenomenal world is contrary to the secondary human goal—the attainment of non-duality—which is to be accomplished through the knowledge of the Self devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañcātma-jñāna*).

If that is so, then the reality of Brahman as well is equally [inapplicable], for it is opposed to liberation, which is characterized by the attainment of emptiness obtained through the cultivation of emptiness.
If you argue that the latter is not consistent with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
we shall reply that this [the former] is the same.

Inference (*anumāna*) regarding the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatā*) should also be understood as its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), since this has already been established by the demonstration of the reasoning (*tarka*) mentioned previously.

Thus, once the reality of the universe is established through both scripture (*āgama*) and inference, he also states [the point] regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*): "Reality," etc. (*satyatvam iti*).
And the reality of the sky and so forth is established by the perception of the witness.
The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a collection of proofs (*pramāṇasamuccaya*).
It means not only internal [objects] such as pleasure and so forth, but also external [objects] such as space and so forth;
or alternatively, it means that even among those, time, space, direction, and so forth have their reality established directly by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣisiddhasatyatva*).
The phrase "of space and so forth" (gaganādeḥ) is stated in order to indicate that pillars, jars, and the like are [to be understood] in the manner that will be described later;
otherwise, since the universe is the subject under discussion, that alone would be carried over here—what would be the purpose of this?

If it were merely said "the Witness" (sākṣī), there might arise the doubt that the reality of the universe is not established as known, because a witness is not a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), or else, if he were a means of valid knowledge, the triad of means of valid knowledge would be violated.
To exclude that [possibility], the word "perceptual" (pratyakṣa) was stated; this will be explained further on.
For if only "perceptual" were said, it would not have been stated as a means of valid cognition for the truth of supersensuous objects.

Moreover, since the reality of even those things perceived by the senses is not established by external perception alone without the witness (*sākṣin*), he says "the witness. He states that this point is already established by the fact that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) admitted by both disputants exists in our own position; nevertheless, it is restated once more in order to further substantiate it. *4,455*
Some maintain that space and other such entities are perceptible by the eye because they appear immediately after the operation of the visual faculty, as in the case of a bird flying here;
however, that is untenable.
Because it is a substance devoid of form (*rūpa*), the causal complex for visual perception (*cākṣuṣatā-sāmagrī*) is incomplete;
otherwise, it would follow that the self (*ātman*) and wind (*pavana*) would also be visually perceived.
If it is asked, "How then does this appearance arise? [the answer follows].
We say that [the relation] is established by perception as being connected with space and so forth;

for a qualified cognition such as "sandalwood is fragrant" is indeed observed even when [one part of the object] is presented by another means of knowledge, as is the case for others in the instance "there is an absence of a jar here on the ground. *4,459*
Another says:
"This condition depends upon a circle of light";
that is incorrect.
If it is argued that [the whole exists] because the cognition "here is light" is observed here as well, we say no; for ordinary people do not possess a cognition of a whole based on its parts.
For they do not employ the conventional designation "body" with respect to the hands and so forth;
rather, they do so precisely because [the body] consists of them.
Furthermore, even if this were the case, the cognitions "this is earth" and "this is a triad of earth-atoms" would be difficult to account for.
If you argue that [the cognition] depends on parts brought forth by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then why not likewise justify the cognition "a bird is here" and so forth by depending on space (*ākāśa*) and the like, which are of such a nature?
In this way, common worldly experience would also be followed.
Even so, if it is argued that space may still be known through inference, we say no;
because there is an absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*). *4,462*
Now, it might be thought: "Sound, first of all, is established by perception;
and it is a quality because, while possessing a universal, it is perceptible by a single external sense organ of persons such as ourselves, just like color."
Because it is a quality, it must reside in a substance, just like that [color];
thus, by way of generality, the existence of substance is established (or: once substance is established).

“Sound is not a specific quality of a substance possessing touch, because, while being perceptible, it does not originate from the qualities of its causes, and because it does not persist as long as the substance exists,
like pleasure and so forth.”
If sound were a specific quality like touch, it would follow that it could not be perceived;
for sound is perceived either when it has reached the ear or when it has not reached it.
If [the sense organ] were to grasp what has not been reached, there would be an over-extension;
however, reaching is not possible for either sound or hearing.
For that reaching cannot occur through the movement of the auditory organ.
Because for that [sound], which is devoid of form, motion is impossible;
nor does it come by way of the sound itself, for it is not capable of coming after abandoning its substratum, such as a conch-shell.
Because it is a quality (*guṇa*);
nor is there proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of the auditory faculty through the arrival of the conch and so forth.
Because that [conjunction] is not perceived;
nor [is it produced] through a succession of the production of other sounds,
because a quality is an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) only with respect to its own substratum or a quality residing in its own substratum.
Furthermore, between the conch and the ear, there exists neither the conch nor any substance produced from it.

Therefore, setting aside the conch and other such causes, [the sound] abiding in another substratum reaches the region of space within the ear-cavity by way of the analogy of waves and ripples; it is perceived in this manner and not otherwise—this is established.
Nor is it a quality of the self (*ātman*),

because it is perceptible by the external sense organs, because it can be apprehended by another self, because it does not inhere in the self, and because it is perceived as distinct from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), just like color and other such qualities.
Furthermore, it is not a quality of space, time, or the mind.
Because it is perceptible and because it is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa),
when other possibilities are excluded by negation, a substance distinct from those [other substances] is established by the method of elimination (pariśeṣa).
That is space (ākāśa).
Thus, this is the meaning of the proof:
sound resides in a substance distinct from the non-eternal substances,
because it possesses the nature of a quality (guṇatva) while being subject to sublation in its occurrence therein, just like color (rūpatva).
This is improper, because it would entail the absurd consequence that those congenitally deaf would have no perception of space and so forth;
consequently, there would be no cognition that "there is no light here."
If it is argued that space is inferred from those [objects] by means of the absence of corporeal form (*mūrta*), we say no;
for this is established otherwise through the absence of other corporeal objects.
If it is argued that the absence of a corporeal object must have a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), [we respond as follows].
True;

nevertheless, if that [subject] is not cognized, there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). And if it is cognized, since it is cognized precisely as possessing its own substratum, there is no room for inference. *4,471*
Furthermore, is sound the subject of the thesis as consisting of phonemes, or as being of the nature of resonance?
Not the first,
because its status as a quality is not established.
Nor can its existence be established by the aforementioned inference;

for just as the self is so [perceived] despite the fact that jars and the like are not apprehended by a single sense-faculty, there is no contradiction in a substance being apprehended by a single external sense-faculty.
If sound were a substance, it would not be apprehended by an external sense-faculty.
If it is argued that there is a necessary connection because a partless substance cannot be apprehended by the external sense faculties, we say no;

for even though a partless entity might be apprehended by the senses, since there is no subverting evidence against its being apprehended by the external sense faculties, the necessary connection remains unestablished.
In the second case, however, even if the substance that serves as the substratum is established, space is not thereby established;
for it is possible that [the quality in question] is a quality of earth and so forth.

This is because, in the theory of baking in a pot (*piṭharapāka*), the two properties of being non-preceded by qualities of its own causes and existing as long as the substance exists—while being perceptible—are shown to be deviant with respect to the color and other qualities belonging to that pot.
And for what purpose should it be stated that "while being perceptible"?
If you say it is for the sake of excluding the color and so forth of the atoms of earth, [we reply: no.
Why should that be excluded?
If you say it is because it is cognized [as such],
then since sound is also cognized as having its locus in conch shells and the like, it would likewise have to be excluded at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The qualification must indeed be accepted;
nor do we perceive any subverting argument against its being a specific quality of something possessing touch.
As for non-perception, it does not apply here.
For it is possible for the auditory organ to reach [its object] through movement, just as the visual organ does;
however, the impossibility of such movement for that which is formless occurs only after the establishment of space (*ākāśa*).
If it is argued that, were the auditory organ to perceive by going to the object like the visual organ, there would be no doubt regarding the direction of the sound; [we reply: [this is not so].
If there were no reaching of the object and no grasping of its excellence, even the determination of direction would not occur;
moreover, certainty is far superior to doubt.
Alternatively, the occurrence of sensory contact may be established through the arrival of parts of the conch shell and so forth.
Nor is the aforementioned fault applicable,
because [the case of] the nose and its contact with odor shares the same logical status.
Furthermore, the two reasons for [smell] being a quality of air are unestablished.
And this reasoning is untenable;
it is not thus logical,
because the ear, by virtue of its grasping a specifically determined object, is an external sense faculty (*bahirindriya*).
If it is argued that this is not so because there is a rule that an external sense organ must possess a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) belonging to the same class as its object—
and that if sound were composed of air (*vāyavīya*), it would follow that the ear-organ would likewise be composed of air— the answer is no;
for [the definition of a sense organ is] "that which perceives its own specifically determined object."

If the meaning [of the definition] is that sound is the apprehender of that which is not apprehended by other sense-faculties, it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the mind (*manas*).

If the intention is that it is the apprehender of that which is *only* not apprehended by other sense-faculties, it is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because it is the apprehender of existence (*sattā*) and so forth. Furthermore, even if it is an external sense-faculty, there is no rule that it must possess a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the same genus as its object.
Because there is a deviation [of the rule] in the case of the eye, which grasps oily substances;
furthermore, we see no contradiction even if the ear is composed of air,
since it is possible for each sense organ to have its own specific object due to the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
If it is argued that the nose and the other [senses] would likewise possess a single primordial nature,
let it be so; however,
since there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), there will be another way of accounting for them based on that very fact.
If it is argued that "sound is not a quality of air, because, while being a specific quality, it is not perceived by the sense of touch, like odor," this is not so;
for there is no subverting argument against the contrary position.
Otherwise, even color and other qualities produced by heating would not belong to earth.
It might also be argued that [sound] is like smell because it is not cognizable by the sense of smell;
furthermore, why should it not be a quality of the self (*ātman*)?
For just as pleasure and other qualities are perceptible despite the fact that dharma and so forth are imperceptible, it is possible for this [sound] to be perceptible by an external sense organ.
Otherwise, even the quality of bitterness would not exist as a property residing in eight substances by virtue of being perceptible;

if that [bitterness] were established, there would be a contradiction (bādha), and if it were not established, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā). If this is argued, we say no, because the same [fallacy] applies to the inference by elimination (pariśeṣānumāna) as well.
And what is the meaning of "being perceivable by another self"?
If you say it means "commonality among multiple perceivers," that is not so, because the reason is doubtful and unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*).

If you argue that this fault does not apply because there is a fundamental recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) through the inference of a [single] continuum (*santāna*), then by that same inference, pleasure and other such states would also be common to multiple perceivers.
There would be no inconclusiveness [of the reason],

because the recognition of the original [entity] is possible through that which is inherent in the self alone, according to the analogy of waves and ripples, and because there is no subverting argument against the contrary position.
Another says:
The claim that it is not perceived as residing in the perceiver because it is perceivable by another self is unproven.
If it is argued that its existence is established because it does not inhere in the self, we say no.
That too is unestablished.
If it is argued that its existence is established because it is perceived as distinct from the ego (ahaṅkāra), we say no;
for since one observes, "There is pleasure in my foot," "There is pain in my head," and "My mind is distressed," there is a deviation [of the reason] with respect to pleasure and so forth.
If it is argued that apprehension is valid cognition (*pramiti*), we say no; for [the reason] is unestablished due to doubt.
Or rather, why should it not be a quality such as time (*kāla*)?
If it is argued that [ether] is not so because it is perceptible, we say no;
for then touch would also follow as being non-composite (non-atomic) due to its perceptibility,
and there would be no subverting evidence against time and other categories possessing specific qualities.
If it is argued that its establishment is not through the eye precisely because it is devoid of that [eye], we say no;
for otherwise, its establishment will be explained [later]. *4,487*
Furthermore, in all these cases where concomitance is observed, mere restriction (*saṅkoca*) is simpler than the postulation of another substance.

As for the inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*), it possesses a qualifier that is unestablished, namely, a substance distinct from the eight [known] substances. And if that were established, the inference would be redundant.

If the proof were simply "it subsists in something distinct from the eight substances," then because it would also be excluded from the generality (*sāmānya*) that resides in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, it would be an inconclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) reason.
If you argue that the formal argument (*prayoga*) is: "The substratum of sound is distinct from others, because it is the substratum of sound; [the negative instance] like earth," [we reply:

no, because when each of the multiple distinctions having earth and so forth as their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) is being proved, water and the other elements constitute the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and since the reason does not reside there, it remains inconclusive.

If it is argued that there is no fault because, when the means of proof is fully assembled, the qualification is already well-established, and since non-existence (*abhāva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), and since the non-existence of a non-existence is an existence (*bhāva*), it is possible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) without depending on a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), we say:
no. For even so, the cognition by way of negation (*pratiṣedhamukhena*) cannot be avoided.
"The substratum of sound does not differ from other things because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), like a jar"— this [inference] is also countered by a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).

Furthermore, in the case of attempting to prove a single difference that has everything as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*), there is the additional fault of sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*),
since we observe that differences themselves also possess differences corresponding to their respective counter-correlates.
Or, let it be that the existence of space as a substrate for the quality of sound is established through inference;
nevertheless, the establishment of unmanifest space (avyākṛtākāśa) occurs through the witness-consciousness alone,
because there is no inferential mark (liṅga) to prove it.
The non-duality of space will be discussed in the section concerning the ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*).

Since even those who are congenitally deaf possess a cognition of space, scripture (*āgama*) is not the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding it; thus, the sky is established by direct perception (*sākṣi-siddha*) alone.
The directions (*diś*) are merely parts of that [space] and are not a separate substance; therefore, they too are established solely through direct perception.
We shall discuss other matters on their proper occasion.
(Now,) let it be granted that space and so forth are established by a witness (*sākṣin*).
Nevertheless, its existence—characterized by being devoid of sublation throughout the three periods of time—is not thereby established.
Since even well-known things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell are seen to be sublated, he says: "of that which is established by the witness."
That which is established by witnesses can never be sublated,
because those witnesses are free from defect;
for the validity of cognitions is inherent.
Invalidity, however, arises from the sublation by defects;
and the knowledge of the witness is not produced by defects,
because it is beginningless.
In the same way, if there were unreality even in liberation, that same consequence would follow;
for due to the contact with the defect of ignorance, the Witness (sākṣin) has the appearance of an object to be sublated.
If you say "it is you," no;
for it has already been stated that the connection with ignorance is untenable according to your own view, and we also admit that ignorance is merely another effect [of Māyā]. *4,496*
In that case, does it not follow this:
the nature of space and so forth is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*),
whereas its state of being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time is established by that which apprehends the validity of the witness-consciousness?

Since validity (*prāmāṇya*) also does not exceed the state of having an uncontradicted object, the claim that "the sky and so forth possess reality" is incorrect; therefore, he says: "all... [and so on].
The fact that it is not sublated at any time is perceived by the witness itself.

The ellipsis is "the non-sublatability of ether and so forth. The sense is that it will be stated later that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) alone is the grasper of the validity of the witness-consciousness itself.
Alternatively, the very nature of ether and so forth is established by the witness-consciousness.

It has been stated that its state of being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time is established by means of the apprehension of its validity. Now, since it will be explained that the witness (*sākṣin*) has as its object a reality that is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time, [the author] says "at all times" (*sarvakāleṣu*), meaning that its apprehension of space and so forth exists precisely as qualified by the absence of contradiction at all times.
[An objection is raised: But how is time itself established?
Because the witness perceives non-sublatability at all times, he says: "For time... and so forth.
For time is directly perceived as a witness, as it is experienced even during deep sleep.

For in deep sleep, because the sense organs have ceased their activity, there is no operation of external perception, inference, or scripture. Nevertheless, the manifestation of time persists even then, since one who has awakened from deep sleep observes the retrospective reflection: "I slept happily for this long a time. Indeed, a retrospective reflection on that which was not experienced is not possible.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument].
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is understood that it is indeed cognizable by a witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*).
Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*):
Time is cognizable by a means of knowledge distinct from external perception and the like,
because it is perceived even when those [other means] are absent;
for whatever is perceived as "in this" is cognizable by a means of knowledge other than that [substratum].
Just as a smell perceived while the eye is absent is cognizable by the olfactory faculty distinct from it;
this might be so,
provided that this reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) were occurring during deep sleep.
This is not so;
rather, having experienced the past time of deep sleep at that very moment, the absence of suffering belonging to that state is inferred. Therefore, he says: "past."
The past and future times as well are not within the range of the senses.

Regarding one who has arisen [from sleep], is the recollection of pleasure refuted by accepting that time is experienced by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), or by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
In the first case, our desired conclusion is established,
because the opponent also accepts that time is cognizable by the witness-consciousness.
In the second [view], however, this [objection] applies:
[the two cases] would fall within the scope of non-witnesses, being objects of means of knowledge other than the witness.
Alternatively, let it be granted that the present time is cognizable by the witness on the strength of the experience occurring during deep sleep.

But since the past and future times are not objects of cognition for the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), how can the state of being unsublated throughout the three periods of time be established for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by that witness? To this, he says: "The past... etc.
By the word "api" (also), the phrase "in the case of perception by a witness" is drawn in [from the previous context].
To the question "Why?", he says: "Not."
The two objects of perception are the domain of direct perception (*sākṣin*) and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And they are indeed perceived.
Therefore, the meaning is that they are the domain of direct perception. *4,501*
If it is asked, "How is this so? [the answer is: It is not so;

for it has already been stated that time is not cognizable through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it appears even to those who are congenitally deaf. Nor is it cognizable through scripture (*āgama*).
Inference also proceeds by taking time itself as the subject (pakṣa) or something else;
it is not the first case, as he says: "to take [it] as the subject."
Because it is impossible to form a formal proposition (pakṣa), inference does not apply there.
If time is not established, [the reason] fails due to the unestablished nature of its locus (āśrayāsiddhi);

if it is established, it is impossible to make it the subject of the thesis because that would result in proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). This same response applies to the second case as well.
The phrase "because it is impossible to make [it] a subject" (*pakṣīkartum-aśakyatvāt*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood as meaning "because the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti-smaraṇa*) and the cognition of the property of being a subject (*pakṣadharmatā-jñāna*) are impossible," with the words "without the cognition of time" (*kāla-pratītim antareṇa*) being the necessary supplement. *4,503*
He elaborates on that very point with the words: "This, indeed..."
All this— that which is visible or within the range of memory—
indeed exists as inlaid with time, which is established by the witness.
Therefore, nothing whatsoever can be remembered or even seen without that [mind]... // MDh 1.4.98a-c //

Because everything—whether it be that which is the object of memory (*smṛti*) as "that," or that which is perceived as "this"—exists precisely as inlaid with and connected to time established by the Witness (*sākṣin*);

therefore, the meaning is that without that time—that is, without the manifestation of time—it is impossible either to remember anything such as a pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, or to perceive a subject (*dharmin*) and so forth.
This is what is being said:

For a person who has previously experienced the pervasion, when a subject (dharmin) is being perceived or remembered, there arises—either from the perception or the recollection of the pervaded property (vyāpyadharma)—the recollection of the previously experienced pervasion; the subsequent mental synthesis (anusandhāna) of that which is pervaded within the subject is inference (anumāna).
And this is the cause of inferential cognition (anumiti), characterized by the valid knowledge of the connection with the pervader (vyāpaka).
Furthermore, all cognitions, which consist of the nature of memory and experience, do not merely apprehend an object; rather, they apprehend it as characterized by time.
For it is precisely as "that" (*tat*) that memory arises.
Furthermore, "this is form" does not mean that its reality consists solely in its connection with a prior time.
Likewise, an experience produced by the eye and other senses arises as "this is [it]"; even that produced by inference and so forth arises as "it was," "it is," or "it will be."
Furthermore, this "presentness" and so forth is nothing other than the state of being related to the present time and so on;
and since this is established by the experience of everyone, it cannot be denied.
Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence that time would be visible to the eye and so forth.
This is because a cognition qualified by a particularity established through perception is logically possible;
likewise, even cognitions whose objects are universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) and so forth are not able to take as their domain an object of their own that is unqualified by time,
since they too arise only in such forms as "this is that."
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That... (tad iti).
For since that [Self] is eternally established, there would be no occasion for inference.

Since time is eternally established, its existence is already proven by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) at the very moment of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth; therefore, there would be no occasion for an inference of time. For an inference finds its scope only when a matter is not yet ascertained. However, regarding an object that is already ascertained, for others [who maintain the reality of external objects], it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), while for us [the Yogācārins], it would be a case of the locus being unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Thus, having refuted all inferences concerning time in a general manner, he refutes them specifically with the words "tadetad" (this very thing).
For instance, the commentary of others states: "Time is characterized by the notions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, and slowness and quickness.
Thus, some explain it in this way.
There is, first of all, the cognition "this one is older" regarding an elder, and "this one is younger" regarding a youth;
this is a cognition of the transposition of "older" and "younger," because it is distinct from the cognitions of "older" and "younger" produced by spatial direction (*dik*).
Likewise, there are cognitions such as "arrived simultaneously," "arrived not simultaneously," "arrived after a long time," and "arrived quickly.
These six cognitions are the marks of time.
How so?
Because these [cognitions] arising with respect to objects such as an elder are not possible without time;
for their objective support (ālambana) is not merely substance and so forth,
since it is distinct from the cognition of those [categories].
This is incorrect;
for instance,
[the notions] "that," "the supreme," and "this is the subordinate" [would be untenable].
This is an illustration of "simultaneous" and so forth;
that is to say, it refers to that which is perceived, whether as an object of sight or as an object of memory.
All of that exists precisely as inlaid by time, which is established through direct perception;
therefore, because that [time] is eternally established, there would be no occasion for inference.
"Therefore" is itself an elaboration of the phrase "not without it."
The connection is "it is not possible.
This is what is meant:
[the objects] such as the distant and the near.
First of all, it has been stated by the opponent himself that the conditions (*pratyaya*) have as their object a mass (*piṇḍa*) qualified by time.
And since the time, which is the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), flashes forth precisely upon the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*), how can that [time] be inferred by means of it?
For a staff is not inferred by the cognition of a man with a staff (*daṇḍin*). *4,508*
Now, if it is argued that because this [cognition] is a qualified cognition, it must be preceded by a cognition of the qualifier,
and since no qualifier exists apart from time, time is thus inferred— then this is not an inference of time.
