However, this is an inference based on cognition;
and that is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because one accepts a cognition qualified by a time established by direct perception (*sākṣin*). *4,509*
Now, it might be argued that once the connection with time has been inferred through the presence of wrinkles, gray hair, coarseness, and so forth,

this Bhāṣya constitutes an inference of the instrumental cause (nimitta) based on the fact that the cognitions of "prior" and "posterior" are effects— this being directed toward one who is in disagreement.
But this is not so.
For its connection with time— or rather, its connection with some substance— is inferred from the state of its body.
Regarding the first case, it must be stated whether the prior time is established by this inference or not.
In the first case, that [time] would be established as eternally existing, because it is established by the eternal witness prior to the inference of that time.
In the second case, since the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), there would be no occasion for inference.
Furthermore, [regarding] wrinkles, gray hair, and [roughness]...

If time were inferred as a cause based on the state of the body's directions (i.e., its physical condition), then because that [state] would be established as permanent, its connection with time would likewise be established as eternally present even during states such as the absence of wrinkles and grey hair; thus, since this would be established even for a permanent atom, there would be no occasion for inference, as the subject of the inference would be sublated.
Now, it might be argued that a long duration of time is inferred.
That is not so;
for is this "brevity" (bahutva) of time simultaneous with [the existence] of atoms?
Or [is it] like actions, by virtue of their being prior and posterior? Not the first, because that relation too is eternally established; not the other.
Because that time is eternally established;
for it is accepted as being eternal.
Not the second [alternative].

Because that [existence] is eternally established, it would result in proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhanatva*). If it is argued that the negation of the other [alternatives] will be effected by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), we say no; for the determination through elimination is untenable.
Others, however, explain it thus:
"remoteness" (*paratva*) consists in having a birth separated by a greater number of revolutions of the sun;
and "nearness" (*aparatva*) consists in having a birth separated by a smaller number of movements of the sun.
Simultaneity is the state of being distinguished by the performance of a single action at once;
non-simultaneity is the state of being distinguished by many such actions;
and duration is the state of being distinguished by many successive actions.
Rapidity (*kṣipratva*) consists in being qualified by a few actions.
Time is inferred through the cognitions of that [rapidity].
For the movements of the sun depend upon their own proximity when producing specific cognitions regarding the multitude of objects.
Because, while not being proximate by its own nature, it generates a specific conventional usage,
like the fragrance of sandalwood; and because, while lacking a direct connection, it is related to that which is connected through a mediated relationship.
It is like the blueness associated with a cloth.

Therefore, that substance which is the cause for the indirect relation—consisting of inherence in that which is conjoined with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyogisamavāya*)—between a mass and the movement of heat, is time.
This too is incorrect.
This is because the cognition of a qualified object is established through the very proximity of essential nature (*svabhāvapratyāsatti*), just as in the case of "the ground is empty of a jar.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that cognitions such as priority, posteriority, and simultaneity could not occur regarding non-existence;
yet, a cognition such as "two non-existent things have arisen simultaneously" is indeed observed.
If it is argued that this is not so because there is no sublation (bādhaka) regarding this relationship, we say no;
for the very fact of [the quality] inhering in something else is the sublation.
If it is argued that this is established by postulating another substance as the conveyor (upanāyaka), [we reply: ...

If it is argued that, since there is no obstacle to explaining the absence of a jar on the ground by postulating a third relation between them, one need not postulate an unperceived relation when a qualified cognition can be explained by means of a natural (inherent) relation alone— then it follows equally that, when a qualified cognition such as "prior" or "posterior" arises, why should one postulate an unperceived substance? The two cases are identical.

This has been stated: since those specific causal conditions would be eternally established, and since they would be established by their very nature (*svabhāva*) alone even without postulating a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), there would be no occasion for inferring a distinct substance. Thus, by this, the qualification "while not being proximate by its own nature" is shown to be unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, it is shown that the mere capacity to produce a specific conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Is this not an unequal comparison?
There is proximity between the ground and the absence [of a jar];
therefore, even in the absence of a [inherent] relation, there will be a qualified linguistic usage.
This is because the perception [of the sun] is impossible to deny,
and because it would be useless to postulate another relationship; furthermore, there is no proximity between the movements of the sun and the physical body.
"Therefore, it must exist as some other substance in between.
Not so;
for we observe a specific cognition, namely the cognition of a jar, even in the absence of its presence [as a substance].
Furthermore, in the opponent's view, we do not perceive any proximity of the absence to the ground.
Or, let there be another substance that brings the solar rays into contact with the mass;
why then could that not be earth or some other element?
If it is argued that [the upward motion] does not occur because there is no contact with the sun (*taraṇi*) or the mass (*piṇḍa*), we say no;

for even though each one individually is non-pervasive, it is logical that many of them together, through a multiplicity of conjunctions with what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*), can bring about the action.
Nor should it be said that those [conjunctions] do not exist at the time of reaching the sun and the mass, because they are not perceived.
Because subtle things must be inferred,
and there is no reason for a definitive determination [between alternatives]; for even in the case of doubt, it is impossible to establish a conclusion through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
Because the postulation of a property is simpler than the postulation of a substratum;
or else, why should it not be space?
It should not be so.
If it is argued that [the soul] possesses specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) like earth and other substances, we say no;
for even a blue substance possessing specific qualities is observed to transfer its blueness to a cloth.
Furthermore, the capacity to transmit the motion of the sun is either the very nature of the substance, or an imperceptible power (atīndriya-śakti), or a cooperative power (sahakāri-śakti).
Not the first,
because it would entail the consequence [of this being true] for mere substance.
Not the second.
Because it is not accepted [as a reason].
Even regarding the third [alternative], one must distinguish whether it is pervasion by that [quality] or the absence of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
We, however, say that it is indeed pervasiveness [that constitutes its nature],
for otherwise, the same consequence would follow for the mind as well.
If it is argued that if pervasiveness were the causal factor [for being an object of cognition], then it would follow that the Self (ātman) is also such, we say no;
for its lack of pervasiveness will be stated later,
and even if it were pervasive, there is no undesirable consequence.
Indeed, the capacity of an intermediate substance to bring about an action is nothing other than its conjunction with both [the agent and the object];
this is the same for many substances as it is for a single one.
This applies if it is space (*ākāśa*).
If it is argued that one could transfer a property residing in another thing to a different thing through its own relation,
and that in such a case everything would be transferred everywhere because there is no distinction, we say no; for it must be postulated that the transfer occurs only in a restricted manner.
For the postulation of a substratum (dharmin) is more cumbersome than the postulation of a mere property (dharma);

otherwise, the same consequence would apply even to time. If it is argued that [the objection is invalid] because of the difficulty of its being ill-founded due to the lack of opportunity for its establishment or non-establishment, we say no.
Due to the lack of understanding regarding the nature of entities,
immediately after observing a specific cognition, many alternative positions arise:
is this [cognition] based on an essential relation, or is it dependent upon an additional relation?
In the second case as well, one must consider whether the cause here is a direct connection or one mediated by another substance;
and in the latter case, whether that substance is one among those already established or something else entirely.

Examining the subverting arguments in every instance, whatever subverting argument one perceains regarding the established substances, how could one not apply it when postulating even an unestablished one?

And because the intended meaning here is that one who, while investigating and considering a refutation according to its own nature, abandons the vice of the "burden of conceptual construction" (kalpanā-gaurava), would certainly find pleasure in the much lighter position;

for this very reason, there is no fault in the *prasaṅga* [reductio ad absurdum] being based on what is established for the opponent (*para-prasiddha*). This is precisely the intended meaning. *4,534*
Furthermore, is this reductio (*prasaṅga*) valid in reality or merely a semblance? Not the first,
because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is destroyed after the cognition of time.
In the second case, how could one cause [the opponent] to abandon the idea that space possesses the capacity to bring about action?
Otherwise, even the refutation of *jāti* (universals) would not be possible.

Or, let it be granted that space—which possesses specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*)—lacks the capacity to bring about action; however, this might apply to *diś* (direction), because it is devoid of specific qualities and is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*).
If it is argued that [the universal] does not [exist] because it is established as being the bringer about of conjunction, we say no;
for even if it brings about both [conjunction and disjunction], there is no subverting evidence.

Furthermore, one should simply assume, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), that it generates determinate and indeterminate cognitions according to the difference in its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
"Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating a distinction even with respect to time.
This has been stated [as follows]:

Since that specific cognition is established by means of earth and so forth—which are eternal, constant, and well-known—there is no occasion for inference regarding a substance that is not already established. *4,538*
Others, however, maintain that by the two terms "remote" (*para*) and "near" (*apara*), the qualities of remoteness and nearness residing in the bodies of a youth and an elder are apprehended;
these two, either as being the substratum for the non-inherent cause (conjunction) or as producing the relative cognition which is the efficient cause, lead to the inference of time.
That too has been refuted by the reasoning already stated.

Furthermore, if the objects of the cognitions of "prior," "posterior," and so forth are either the movements of the sun or the states of priority and posteriority themselves, then let there be an inference of time.
And this is not the case,
because it is perceived that only the distinctions of time function as qualifiers; for instance:

When ordinary people and investigators employ expressions such as "this is past" and so forth, and are asked what their meaning is, they are seen to explain it by saying, "This has existed for a long time," and so on.
In that regard, the nature of time is established through direct perception (*sākṣisiddha*).

That their plurality and so forth are known sometimes through direct perception and sometimes through inference and other means has also been stated in the two verses beginning with "tadetad. In this same manner,
the fact that the directions (diś) serve as logical marks for cognitions such as "prior" and "posterior" must also be refuted.
Not finding this ancient path acceptable, others have proposed new inferences regarding space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*):

"The subject under dispute, which is an effect, is produced from two substances devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), because it is an effect, like the conjunction of the two internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
This too is incorrect.
Because there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if one were to employ (or imply) a plural number in the probandum (*sādhya*),
nor is there an absence of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).
This is because there exists a multiplicity residing within the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the conjunction of two internal organs;

and as for the argument that "the mind is conjoined with the mind because it is corporeal, like the body," this is subject to doubtful deviation (*sandigdhavyabhicāra*) in the case of lightning and the like, which are not momentary. *4,547*
Another says:
"The dimension of the supremely great (paramamahat-parimāṇa) resides in four substances, because it is a dimension, like the dimension of the minute (aṇutva).
In this regard, if [the reason] refers to that which resides in space or the self...
If the subject of the proposition is taken as "dimension," then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because selves are many.
Even if the argument is formulated by taking "oneness" as the basis through the property of being a self (*ātmatva*), there is still a contradiction;
for it is impossible for two dimensions to reside in four substances.
Size indeed resides in each individual substance;
for this very reason, there is no inclusion of that which belongs to time and so forth [in the subject]. Furthermore, there is the additional fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

Furthermore, the following argument is untenable: "The universal of the dimension of the supremely great (*paramamahatparimāṇasāmānya*) resides in multiple individual substances that are devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), because it is a genus (*jāti*) that constitutes the terminus of the gradation of dimensions, like the genus residing in the dimension of the minute (*aṇuparimāṇa*).
For the universal of the dimension of the supremely great must be either the genus of dimension (*parimāṇatva*) itself or a subordinate genus within it.
In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving the already established (*arthāntaratā*), since this [property] can be established even by means of the mind;
furthermore, there are the fallacies of sublation (*bādha*) and the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because the existence of a universal residing in multiple instances will be refuted later.
Nor is the second case [valid].
Because that [position] will be refuted,
and because it constitutes a different point from the proof of the phonemes.
Furthermore, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to include many more categories within the place of "many" (*anekapadasthāna*).

If you argue that let there be a plurality of time (*kāla*) and space (*diś*), and that the ninefold nature of substances (*dravya*) is established by the unity of their subsumers (*upasaṅgrāhaka*)— just as with the self (*ātman*)— then [the category of substance] would end up being either space or time.
It would not be the case that this [reason] establishes both [the probandum and its opposite].
If you say, "Let it not be so," we reply:
no, because of the pointlessness of the multiple terms.
Because if one [of the two] were established, it would follow that the other would be a different matter (*arthāntara*);
furthermore, the impossibility of both the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) will be explained later, so enough with this prolixity.

Concluding the point already stated—that the non-sublation throughout the three periods of time of the entire phenomenal world, beginning with space, is established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*), he explains it [further] with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, it is held by the Witness that what is perceived as faultless is true.

There is no defect in that by which [the world] is cognized—that is, by that which has made it its object through cognition, or by perception and so forth, which are themselves free from defect; thus, the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), such as the sky and so on—meaning its non-sublation throughout the three periods of time—is established as the view of the Witness (*sākṣin*). The phrase "by means of the apprehension of validity" and so forth is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
This is the intended meaning:
space, time, direction, the self, the mind, and pleasure and so forth are established directly by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin);
but other categories of objects are [established] according to their respective [means of knowledge].
They are accessible through the senses, logical marks, and verbal testimony.
Furthermore, cognition, characterized by both existence and non-existence, apprehends its own object solely as existent,
not as non-existent.
Nor can it be argued that [the cognition] does not arise in the form of indifference,
nor that the cognitions "the jar exists" and "the jar does not exist" would be untenable due to tautology and contradiction;
for the cognition "the jar exists" has as its object existence related to a specific place and time.
In some cases, it is for the purpose of excluding a contrary expectation; in others, it is due to the relationship between the commentary and the text being commented upon;
and as for the phrase "it does not exist," its purport is the negation of existence in relation to specific places and times.
For there is no restrictive rule that what exists must exist at all places and times.
Furthermore, the validity characterized by correspondence to reality, which resides in cognition, is apprehended by that very factor which apprehends the cognition;
and it is undisputed between proponent and opponent that the cognizer of cognition is the witness (sākṣin).

And thus, when the witness (*sākṣin*) apprehends the validity of a cognition, it necessarily apprehends the very reality of its object—the entire phenomenal world—characterized by non-sublation throughout the three periods of time. For if there were sublation, defined as the non-perception of the existence of an object (whether eternal or non-eternal, all-pervading or non-all-pervading) within its own locus, time, and mode, then what would be the meaning of saying that "the validity of the cognition was cognized by the witness"? It would be meaningless.
If, then, the witness (*sākṣin*), which grasps the very nature of cognition, were to determine the reality of the phenomenal world while grasping its validity,

then it would likewise establish even things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell as real, since that same witness also grasps the nature of cognitions such as "this is silver" and thereby grasps their validity as well.
Nor is it the case that the validity of cognitions such as "this is silver" simply does not exist.

It is not logical to ask, "Let it be apprehended by the witness," for one could equally say, "Why should cognitions whose objects are the phenomenal world (prapañca) be apprehended by the witness at all, given their lack of validity? Therefore,

by one who desires to establish the reality of the phenomenal world through the witness, it must be admitted that it is the very nature of the witness— the apprehender of cognition— to apprehend its validity.
And since such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has been stated, it was said: "without fault" (*adoṣa*).
This is the meaning:
the witness, while apprehending the cognition, does not apprehend that "this is indeed a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*).
Rather,
it is by the established rule that if a cognition possesses a fault, it is invalid, whereas one without fault is valid.

However, when one intends to determine validity through the desire for the truth, then—having ascertained the absence of defects by means of an investigation characterized by the presence or absence of agreement or disagreement with similar or dissimilar cognitions—one determines validity; whereas upon perceiving a defect, one determines invalidity.

Furthermore, regarding the cognition of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), even when searching diligently for a defect and failing to find one, one determines its very validity; thus, its reality is established by direct witness (*sākṣisiddha*).
And this is not the case with [erroneous cognitions] such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell,
because validity is not determined when the defect is not perceived, whereas upon perceiving that defect, invalidity is ascertained.
If it is objected: "But is not the validity even of cognitions such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell determined?
Otherwise, how could there be action free from doubt?
[The reply is: True.
This [cognition] is not a determination through the form of direct perception;
rather, we shall explain that it is mental.
And since the mind is susceptible to contact with defects, validity is not established by that alone. (4.564)
Now, if the witness-cognition, assisted by a verification, were to apprehend the validity of a cognition, then there would be an infinite regress;
for even a verification is capable of determining the validity of another only when it has itself been ascertained as valid,
and not otherwise.
Thus, even in that case, another investigation must be introduced.
Furthermore, a witness whose status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has not been ascertained, being himself unstable, lacks the capacity to ascertain the validity of another;

therefore, for the sake of ascertaining his own validity, there would be a dependence on further investigations and a dependence on other cognizers, resulting in nothing but an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus it is said.
He said: "And because of examination, etc."
And the truthfulness of the examination itself must be considered by him alone.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the witness is included; the word "ca" has the sense of "but"; and "truthfulness" means being in accordance with reality.
By that witness alone, and not by one accompanied by (or joined with) examination;
the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that this matter is established through experience.
Therefore, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), or [it serves as] a reason (*hetu*). *4,566*
This is what is meant:
indeed, investigation (*parīkṣā*) is the application of reasoning for the purpose of ascertaining the absence of defects;
and an object that is doubtful is the subject matter of reasoning.
And doubt arises only when there is the presence of factors that lead to two opposing alternatives.
Thus, wherever there is such doubt due to the possibility of a defect, only in those cases is there a need for investigation, and not elsewhere;
nor is there a doubt regarding defects in every case.
Because there is no attainment of an object already established by perception,
there is, for the time being, no infinite regress of investigation.
To explain:
For one who has heard the statement, "There is water here in front," a doubt arises as to whether this is rooted in error and the like, or not;
for human words are seen to be of both kinds.
Thus, while doubting the matter, one approaches it and infers from specific features of its appearance and so forth that "this is water."
In this regard, too, there arises a doubt:
is this [cognition] a valid inference or a fallacy?
For one observes both correctness and incorrectness among those who grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other such factors.
One who has just approached water, even after inferring specific tastes immediately following its consumption, remains doubtful as before;
however, one who has drunk the water experiences the pleasure of the absence of suffering caused by thirst and the like, and thus does not doubt it.
This is because pleasure and its absence are established by direct witness (sākṣin), and no contrary state is ever perceived.
Nor does doubt arise there even on the basis of the generality of being perceived, because there exists a determinative cognition focused on the specific [nature of the object];
otherwise, since doubt would not be eliminated, it would follow that no practical activity could occur.
And since there is no doubt in the absence [of such a factor], there can be no investigation preceded by it; how, then, could there be an infinite regress?

For this very reason, the infinite regress of investigation regarding the determination of the validity of perception is also avoided. Furthermore, an infinite regress of cognizers simply does not exist.
The witness (sākṣin), by virtue of being self-luminous, grasps its own validity;
this much is the distinction here.

In cognitions produced by the senses, inferential marks, or words, the witness—keeping in mind the two-fold course [of truth and error] throughout the beginningless cycle of transmigration—is not able to determine immediately that "this is a valid means of knowledge."
However, it is only by means of the ascertainment of the absence of defects that [the validity] is established;
and one is not able to ascertain the absence of defects by oneself alone.
However, it is only when accompanied by investigation (*parīkṣā*) that [the cognition] proceeds;

and in the case of investigation arising from the senses, inferential marks, or verbal testimony, it follows further investigations according to the previous logic until it directly descends upon its own object, such as pleasure and so forth.
And since no change into something else has ever been perceived regarding its own self, doubt is absent; thus, one desists from pursuing further investigation.
Indeed, cognition, by its own nature, is not able to apprehend both itself and its validity;
however, its capacity to grasp validity is obstructed by the suspicion of defect in that means of knowledge.
Therefore, it is only through a formal determination (*vyavasthā*) that it touches upon that [validity].
However, we do not accept that [validity] is determined [by another means].
Rather, once the obstacle has been removed through investigation, one determines its validity by its own inherent power.
Nor should it be argued that even if this demonstration [of the treatise] lacks validity, it too must be apprehended as self-evident because it is equal [to the cognition it seeks to establish].
Because of this disparity:
for when determining validity, it can only be established that examination functions merely to remove obstacles;
since once the obstacle has been removed, the witness's apprehension of validity occurs independently of that examination.
For if there were a requirement for cooperation, there would have to be a dependence on that [cooperation] in every case;
and thus, as has been stated, there would be an infinite regress.
Otherwise, the status of being a cause would be contradicted.
Furthermore, invalidity has never been determined by a witness who is independent of examination,
such that we could perceive its function as the remover of obstacles;
rather, because it occurs universally, it is simply the cause [of doubt].
If it is argued that its universal presence is otherwise established because the obstructing factor is universally present, we say no;
for when the obstructing factor has ceased and there is the apprehension of invalidity,
it is logically consistent that examination (*parīkṣā*) serves as the cause.
If it is argued that this being so, there is respect [for the tradition], we say no;
for there is no evidence to establish that it is impossible to determine the specific [cause].
Nevertheless, [the cognition] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of investigation.
If it is argued that its being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) is suspected, [we reply: no;
for since a universal presence of an obstructer is never observed anywhere, the suspicion of its being otherwise established is dispelled.
Otherwise, there would be such a state [of being otherwise established] for auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) everywhere.

If it is held that the extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) of validity arises because validity enters [into the cognition] in some manner as something distinct from the cognizer of the knowledge, then there is no contradiction whatsoever even if one accepts that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) alone possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) while everything else is extrinsic. This is the summary; the detailed exposition, however, [should be understood] by oneself.
The Teacher will say:

"Now, it might be thought that even when a witness apprehends the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge, it consists only in the absence of defects related to a certain time and a certain person."

However, it is not the case that there will never, anywhere, or by anyone, be any deviation from its own purpose; for if this were so, how could the truth of the universe—characterized by the absence of absolute sublation—be established by that [means of knowledge]? To this, he says: "Otherwise... (anyathā).
Otherwise, why is it not suspected that the entire universe might suddenly cease to exist, despite the existence of means of valid cognition such as scripture and reasoning?
If witnesses do not grasp validity characterized by the absence of sublation in every respect, why is it not suspected that even the complete Brahman would cease to exist like the phenomenal world?
To the objection that this is because there is no cause for such cessation, it is said: "accidentally" (*akasmāt*).

But surely [it may be argued] that by such scriptural passages as “Truth, Knowledge” and “That is Truth,” and by such inferences as “Brahman does not possess cessation, because it is distinct from ignorance and its effects,” [Brahman is established as eternal].

Since an illusion without a substratum and without a witness is never observed, nor is a sublation without limits, and since the reality of Brahman is understood through the otherwise inexplicability of the superimposition of the phenomenal world (prapañca), it is said— referring to the phrase "not this"— that [Brahman is known] from the Śruti.
The meaning is that the cessation of these means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, should likewise be suspected.
This is what is being said:
"The Witness does not apprehend the absolute validity of the means of valid cognition, such as perception and so forth, which have the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as their object."
But one who says, "It is only for that moment," must be asked:
Do witnesses have the capacity to grasp absolute validity, or not?
In the first case, how could one not accept the absolute validity of perception and other means of knowledge whose objects are the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)?
In the second case, one would likewise not accept the absolute validity of the Vedas and other scriptures that establish the reality of Brahman;
and thus, the absolute non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*) of Brahman would not be established.
Furthermore, because there is an absence of both proving and refuting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*), its sublation (*bādha*) might also be suspected.
And in that case, even that cognition would not be knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), and thus no effort toward it would be undertaken.
If one were to say that [the capacity] exists in some cases and not in others, then a restrictive principle (*niyāmaka*) must be stated. *4,574*
Now, if Brahman were subject to sublation, why would it not have ceased [to exist] after this much time?
Therefore, since it was free from sublation prior to this, one might think that sublation cannot be suspected even later.
This is not so, because the answer has already been stated.
For even this [perception]— which has the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as apprehended by a witness (*sākṣin*)— its absolute validity is not established;
otherwise, the same would be unavoidable for perception and other means of knowledge that apprehend the phenomenal world (*prapañca*),
since there would be no factor to establish a distinction between them.
He states another refutation: "Prior to this," etc.
If there were no course of transmigratory existence because of its prior non-existence in this way, [then liberation would be impossible].
"Because it is so," meaning because there is no cessation [of the world].
The connection is: "If it is not suspected that there is a cessation of Brahman. The word "then" (tarhi) is to be supplied.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "the goal would be cessation.
This is the intended meaning:
since there was no cessation prior to this, is it an inference based on the possibility of the absence of cessation in Brahman?
Not the first,
because even a possibility, being of the nature of doubt, lacks the capacity to remove suspicion.
Not the second.
If that were the case, it would follow that there is no cessation of transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti) or of ignorance (avidyā);
for the root-ignorance prior to this [moment] has not ceased.
Otherwise, there would be a logical inconsistency (vyabhicāra) with respect to that very [ignorance].
Furthermore, things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell cease even though they had not previously ceased, because it is impossible for that which has already ceased to cease;
therefore, there is also a contradiction. *4,578*
The phrase "otherwise," and so forth, is explained differently: otherwise,
if the witnesses do not apprehend the absolute validity of perception and other means of knowledge which grasp the phenomenal world (*prapañca*),
why is it not suspected that the entire universe— including space and the rest— would perish or cease to exist in the very next moment?
And in that case, all worldly activity would cease to exist due to the absence of the Supreme Lord's desire to withdraw [the universe] and so forth; therefore, it is said: "spontaneously" (akasmāt).
(See page 1117 for the full context.
But surely it is by the will of the Lord alone that the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas establish the dissolution of the phenomenal world;
furthermore, there is the inference: "The destruction of the universe is not without a cause, because it is a destruction, like the destruction of a cloth."
To the question, "How then can such a doubt arise?", it is said: "By scripture" (śruti).
The cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed the absolute absence of their validity; the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is as before.
Now, [one might object]: "But prior to this, there was no proliferation (*prapañca*)."
A fainting fit occurred suddenly;
how then could it be suspected even later? To this he says:
"Prior to this."

In this regard, is the pervasion (vyāpti) that "whatever did not exist previously will not exist later," or rather, "whatever was previously destroyed without a cause will likewise not be destroyed later," or else, "whatever is without a cause will not come to be"?
The previous statement was made for the purpose of establishing that;
however, the first [position] is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence that there is no cessation of transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti) or of ignorance (avidyā).
Not the second,
because it would entail the cessation of saṃsāra.
For it is thus:
Knowledge is the cause for the cessation of saṃsāra;
yet, because it is of the nature of ignorance, it is itself merely saṃsāra. Furthermore, there is no other means to bring about its cessation.
And likewise, if one accepts that nothing whatsoever ceases without a cause, there would be no possibility for the cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*).
If it is argued that knowledge (*vidyā*) itself is the cause of its own cessation because it is the sole adversary of ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no;
for if that were so, then the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) too would [cease] by itself in the subsequent moment.
There might be the apprehension that [the cognition] will cease;
for this very reason, even the third [alternative] is not possible.
He explains the very point already stated: "In a sentence... (*vākya*).
If it were established by the corroboration of the statement, its authority would likewise depend upon witnesses.

Alternatively, it was stated that there is no "course of transmigratory existence" (saṃsṛti-gati), because the course of saṃsāra is established by scripture and other means of knowledge, and because the reason [for its non-existence] is qualified by the fact that such a course is not so established; therefore, he says: "By the sentence... (vākya).
If, after the suspicion of even Brahmā’s cessation has been raised, one were to say that there would be a certainty of the absence of cessation based on scriptural inference;
or if one were to think that upon the occurrence of a sudden subsequent moment, the suspicion of dissolution would arise only through the will of the Supreme Lord as inferred from scripture;
or if one were to assert that the cessation of saṃsāra would occur through scriptural inference;
In that case, it must be stated by whom the validity of that [word or other means] is ascertained.

If one accepts that it is by the witness (sākṣin) and not by another, then since cognition is known by the witness, it would follow that the apprehension of its validity is extrinsic (parataḥ); therefore, one must say that it is by the witness alone.
If it is asked, "What follows from that? [the answer is as follows:]
Does the witness perceive the validity of the statements and so forth that establish the reality of Brahman and other such matters as being merely temporary, or as being absolute?
In the first case, since Brahman’s non-sublatability and so forth would not be established by him, the aforementioned doubt would not be dispelled.
Regarding the second case, however, he says: "That validity... (tatprāmāṇyam).
Its authority is established just as a witness establishes it;
for it remains steadfast at all times, having set aside all deviation.
Why then would he not establish the reality of the universe, which is thus proven by its being perceived through the senses? ... Mānava 1.4.103a-c.
The word "yathā" (as) is connected both here and below.

Just as a witness establishes and perceives [an object] existing in the present time, so too does he perceive it with stability across all times; such is the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of that [scripture], such as the passages establishing the reality of Brahman and so forth.
The word "hi" indicates what is well-known to others. It explains stability itself by means of the phrase "having set aside and rejected deviation and sublation."
The meaning is that the witness does not merely apprehend the validity of statements such as "Brahman is truth" at that particular time, but rather its ultimate [validity] alone.
Alternatively, the word "yathā" (as/how) is connected only with what follows;
the meaning is that it establishes and apprehends only the ultimate [truth].

The phrase "the explanation of this very [point] is as follows" (*asyaiva vivaraṇam evam eveti*) requires the word *iti* to be supplied. This means that at all times, this very [object] remains exactly so; it never undergoes sublation characterized by the withdrawal of its objective status. Thus, having excluded deviation, one perceives it with stability precisely for that reason.
Alternatively, the word *eva* (indeed) signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The witness establishes the absolute validity of statements concerning Brahmā and others, and grasps it as such.
For this very reason, he establishes even their objects—Brahmā and the rest—as being free from any deviation whatsoever due to their stability at all times.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that the non-sublation of the object is included within the absolute nature of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
The word "evam" (thus) expresses the conclusion of the proponent.

If this witness, grasping the absolute validity of such means of knowledge as "if that is true," were to establish the non-sublation of its object— Brahman and so forth— at all three times, then likewise, grasping the absolute validity of sensory and other cognitions regarding the universe, he would certainly establish the non-sublation of the universe included therein as well.
The meaning of the whole [statement] is that this is because there is no distinction.
Now, one might object: "Let the witness accept the absolute validity of perception and the other means of knowledge;
but from what source does his own status as such [a witness] derive?"
And since, for that reason, the establishment of the truthfulness [of the Veda] would not follow, he says: "Being free from defects" (nirdoṣā).
...due to the power of faultless knowledge.
The witness (sākṣin) also establishes that [nature] by virtue of its capacity for faultless cognition;
otherwise, even the reality of Brahman and so forth would not be established.
Alternatively, the witness apprehends the absolute validity of such statements as "That is Truth."
To the objection—“Why might not even that which arises from the senses, such as visual perception, have validity only for the immediate moment?”—he says: “nirdoṣa” (faultless).
How then could even that which arises from the senses not grasp absolute validity?
For that too possesses the existence of a capacity consisting in the nature of faultless cognition.
Alternatively, is it that a witness is never able to grasp absolute validity anywhere?
Or is it that he is capable in some cases but incapable in others?
The answer to the first alternative is "otherwise," and so forth.
The response to the second [objection] is: "In the case of a sentence" (*vākya*).
This would be so if cognition arising from the senses and so forth were faultless;
however, it is not so.
Because its object is the manifold world created by ignorance, like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth.
If it is asked, "Upon what does ignorance depend?",
we reply that it depends upon the individual soul (*jīva*).
But has not the objection already been stated here as well, namely, "it is other than itself"?
This is not so;
for even that difference is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Nor is there any fault such as circular reasoning (cakraka),
because it is established by the Śruti and other authorities that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is produced by the ignorance of the individual soul (jīva).
Furthermore, since there is no room for reasoning (*tarka*) regarding an object already established by valid cognition (*pramita*),
there is no fault of the non-existence of what is to be postulated; for it is accepted that the entire universe is produced by a single ignorance (*ajñāna*).

This is because the existence of the world of living beings and insentient objects as something distinct from that [Brahman] is established as being merely imagined. For the doctrine of a single jīva (ekajīvavāda) is the core conviction of the proponents of Māyā;
however, the doctrine of many jīvas (bahujīvavāda) has been introduced for the sake of engaging those of duller intellect. Therefore, he says: "one," etc.
If it is asserted that the universe was created by a single knower, that is false;
"the universe was created by many knowers" would be the reply to that.
It is said by the proponents of the theory of Brahman’s illusory transformation (brahmavivartavāda): "It is false, because it lacks a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
This is what is meant.
This might perhaps be so,
if the entire universe were imagined through the ignorance of a single individual soul;
but this is not the case.
Because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For the Veda and other authorities will be correctly explained immediately below.

Furthermore, if the Lord, along with many others such as Brahmā and those impelled by him, were the efficient cause through their knowledge, desire, and effort, that would contradict the existence of the Veda and other authorities. *4,591*

Furthermore, one who asserts that everything consisting of sentient and insentient beings is imagined through the ignorance of a single soul (*ekajīva*) must be questioned: "Is this one soul you yourself, or is it another?

If it is another, then since bondage and liberation would not apply to you—who are imagined by that other's ignorance—your adoption of renunciation (*pārivrājya*) and so forth would be rendered useless. Even in the first case, do you perceive the souls of the opponents and others, or not?
Regarding the first [alternative] as well, [one must ask]: do they exist or do they not exist?
He refutes the first [position] with the words "of another" (*parasya*).
He who, though knowing the reality of another, is a thief of his own self and says, "The other does not exist"... // MAnu 1.4.105a-c //
The construction is as follows: he who, even while knowing the reality of another—such as an opponent—says "the other does not exist," is a thief of his own self (*svātmataskara*).

The meaning is that for one who perceives both himself and the other as real, the statement "I alone am real; all individual souls and insentient things are imagined through my ignorance" contradicts his own experience.
There is no powerful means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that everything imagined through your ignorance is non-existent,
such that even perception itself would be sublated.
For it is not the case that things like a city of Gandharvas, though perceived as existing, are accepted as being absolutely non-existent.
However, this is because it is sublated by powerful evidence;
otherwise, why could you not be someone imagined through the opponent's ignorance?
And in that case, due to the lack of certainty, there would be no engagement for the sake of liberation. *4,592*
He refutes the second and third [alternatives] with the words: "What? (kimiti).
... why would he speak like a madman? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.105d)
If the opponent, such as the respondent, does not perceive living beings, or perceives them but sees that they do not exist, then why would he speak like a madman?
One should not enter into discourse,
nor should one compose or explain a treatise;
otherwise, like a madman, one would be disregarded as neither a worldly person nor an investigator.
Why would one not speak?

For if one were to speak, one might fall into the path of the insane; therefore, he says: "In the absence of another... (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 1.4.106a): "For speech is useless in the absence of another..."
Since speech exists for the purpose of awakening another,
and since it would be useless in the absence of another, one should not employ speech that is useless;
for how could one who employs such speech not be insane?
"In the absence of another [position], the statement is meaningless;
for I too say nothing at all. To this, he says: "If... (yadīti).
If it is not stated [by the thief], then one should declare the whip, the *vetra*-reed, or other such things as his answer. (Manu 8.106b–d)

If it is said, "I have never said anything at any time," then for one who denies a fact known to all the world, there is only the punishment due to a thief— one whose own actions contradict his words— not a further reply. If you say, "In reality, nothing is being said," then are those who speak even in conventional discourse considered discerning people when they do so while certain that no object of cognition exists?
By this it may be said:
previously, in order to establish the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the contradiction with external reasoning regarding the scriptural passages cited by the opponent was demonstrated.

Now follows the subsequent section of the text, which first demonstrates the internal inconsistency [of the opponent's view] and then provides a non-contradictory interpretation of those [scriptural passages].
Alternatively, while the general inconsistency common to all the scriptures was previously elaborated upon,
the specific inconsistency unique to this [particular opponent's position] is now being established.

Having first recited the two verses beginning with "If, in that case, the manifold world (prapañca) were to exist," he states the logical inconsistency in the opponent's intended meaning: "The manifold world... and so forth.
If conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) existed, it would undoubtedly cease;
this duality is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), for in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) there is non-duality (*advaita*).
If conceptual construction were to cease because it had been imagined by someone, then this teaching would be for that purpose; for duality does not exist in that which is not known.

In this [verse], both the two words "if" (*yadi*) and "it would cease" (*nivarteta*), as well as the phrase "they say the reality of the universe" (*viśvasya satyatām āhuḥ*)—[these constitute the objection]. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 1.4.109a–c)
Now, one might object that since these scriptural passages were cited by the opponent as being included within the Sūtras, their inconsistency and so forth should have been addressed first.
True;
nevertheless, [this is done] because, if everything were imagined through the ignorance of a single jīva, [the following would apply].
It was stated immediately prior that there is no means of valid cognition [for this]; and in this context, it is understood at first glance:
"When the individual soul, asleep through beginningless māyā, awakens."
Because it has been stated thus,
this [attainment] occurs first due to its compatibility with both; therefore,
in these two verses, the two occurrences of the word "yadi" (if) and the two uses of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) should be removed.
And this is an elliptical indication;
"it should be known" is also to be understood,
as is "by someone."
"Truthfulness" (*satyatām*) is an elliptical expression;
it should be understood as including "beginninglessness" (*anāditām*) as well.
"They say" (*āhuḥ*) means "they make [it] understood."
And thus, the remainder of the argument is that there would be an inconsistency in explaining [the passage] as being intended to establish the falsity of the universe (*viśvamithyātva*).
For if the intention here were to assert the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then it would have been stated: "This phenomenal world which is seen as if it exists will cease to be."
It should be stated that "the conceptual construction imagined through ignorance will cease.
However, if the initial words [of the two sentences] are devoid of meaning or possess contradictory meanings,
then it is understood that these two sentences, through their employment, are intended solely for the purpose of demonstrating the two undesirable consequences (*prasaṅga*).

"Just as [one might say], 'If the mountain were devoid of fire, then it would also be devoid of smoke,'" since the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) culminates in its contrapositive, the capacity of the statement to establish precisely the non-existence [of smoke] and so forth is obtained; thus, by refuting the opponent's position, the intended meaning of the scripture has been indicated. Clarifying that, he first states the meaning of the word "should know" (*vidyeta*): "vidyeta" [etc.].
...and also the origin of knowledge. Mānava 1.4.109d.

This form of the word expresses only its origination, but not its existence; thus, the meaning of the verbal root is stated. By the word "ca" (and), destruction is indicated through the phrase "it would cease."
He confirms this with "not at all" (natu bādham).
To the question, "On what basis is the root *vid* understood to have the meaning of 'origination'? he says: "videti."
For [the word] "vid" in this context is derived from this verbal root (dhātu) ... MAnu 1.4.110ab.
Regarding the phrase "vid-otpattau": it is from this root [vid]. The meaning is "from the root" [as] explained by the root itself.
The connection with the preceding [text] is that one should understand that the root *vid* has the sense of "origination."
The term "dhātoḥ" (of the root) is either in the genitive case;
the ellipsis to be supplied is "because of its explanation.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that although this explanation of the root may be unknown to those of dull intellect, it is indeed well-known to those of great learning.
Nevertheless, why is it that there is only origination?
Why is there no existence (sattā) here? To this he says: "only origination."
For indeed, the fivefold diversity of the phenomenal world is generally characterized by origination and is pervaded by cessation. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 1.4.110b–d)

For here, by the force of the word "if" (*yadi*) and so forth in the phrase "If proliferation (*prapañca*) were to exist, then it would cease," it is understood that this is a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum).
And a *prasaṅga* is rooted in pervasion (*vyāpti*).
This is because its definition is: "A *tarka* (hypothetical reasoning) is the deduction of an undesirable pervader (*vyāpaka*) upon the acceptance of the pervaded (*vyāpya*)."
And thus, there is a necessary pervasion (vyāpti) between the state of "existing" as the premise (the *āpādaka*) and the state of "ceasing to exist" as the consequence (the *āpādya*);
for arising itself is what is pervaded by ceasing,
not mere existence.

Because our [position] is subject to deviation and the opponent's [position] is contradictory, existence (*sattā*) cannot be the meaning of the word "is" (*asti*), as it lacks the fitness for the observed positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Rather, it is only origination (*utpatti*) that is the meaning, because of its fitness for that [concomitance].

The word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) is stated in order to exclude total destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). This "mostly" means "for the most part" (*bāhulya*), namely, the coexistence of both arising and cessation.
Thus, it is effectively stated that the intended qualification of the *āpādaka* (the logical ground) is "while being an existent" (*bhāvatve sati*).
By this, it should be understood that the misconception of those with little knowledge regarding the explanation of the elements (*dhātu*) is refuted.
[Objection: Now, "arising" (*utpatti*) is defined as the acquisition of existence dependent upon causes.
Since there is no existence in a non-entity (*abhāva*), and because a non-entity lacks the possibility of occurrence, the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) is redundant.
Not so.

What is this so-called "existence" (sattā)? Is it a form that persists [in all things], or is it the very nature [of each thing] itself? Not the first, because it will be stated later that such [an enduring existence] does not even exist in things like jars.
Not the second [alternative],
because it will be stated later that "in the case of non-existence, there is the non-existence of its existence, and there is destruction," and so forth.
But even in this interpretation, there is no fitness for logical concomitance (*anvaya*).
Just as for a logical inference, a conclusion by way of contraposition is inevitable;
likewise, if the phenomenal world were produced, it would necessarily perish.
Yet, it does not perish.
Therefore, one should not say that [the world] is not produced;
for this is not tenable,
since the arising and destruction of the manifold world, beginning with the earth, are perceived through valid means of knowledge.

For this very reason, it is also untenable for the undesirability of the consequence (*āpādya*)—which constitutes a member of the *tarka*—to be established; therefore, he explains the word "prapañca" otherwise: "prapañca" [means...]
... conceptual proliferation consists of the fivefold division. MAnu 1.4.110d.
This word *prapañca* does not denote the expansion of the universe,
by which the aforementioned fault would arise;
rather, *pañca* refers to a group of five.
In the word *pañcaśatau* (in the group of five hundred), because the word *vā* is used, it is accepted that the word *pañca* itself is also a *nipātana* (an irregular formation).
*Prapañca* means "excellent five" (*prakṛṣṭaḥ pañcaḥ*). And its excellence arises from being knowledge that is a factor for liberation (*mokṣāṅga-jñāna*).
And that [fivefold nature] is established only for the pentad of distinctions, based on such statements as:
"Having understood the difference between those two, one is liberated; otherwise, one is bound. Therefore, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consists of the fivefold distinction.

And since that [distinction] is of the nature of the eternal essence of the individual soul, the Lord, and primordial matter (prakṛti), it is indeed beginningless and eternal; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
However, the author of the *Ṭīkā* maintains that "distinction" (bheda) is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
And that [non-existence] can only be removed by the attainment of mutual identity;
for it has been observed in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) that the very arising of the counter-positive constitutes the destruction of the non-existence.
Furthermore, since there is never any identity (tādātmya) between entities, the difference even among impermanent things is itself eternal.
Others also say: "And the three are established as eternal."
If it is asked, "On what basis is it said that the word *prapañca* denotes the fivefold difference?
we reply: "Precisely because the [other] interpretation proposed by others is untenable.
And he says, "Because of the scriptural passage having the same meaning," namely: "The individual self (*jīva*)," etc.

The distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, likewise the distinction between the insentient and the Lord, the mutual distinction among individual souls, the distinction between the insentient and the individual soul,
and the mutual distinction among insentient things— this is the fivefold phenomenal world of distinctions.
Thus, this Truth is indeed beginningless... // MAnu 1.112a //
And here, the words *ca* and *tathā* serve to conjoin [the terms] with one another;
the two words *eva* have the purpose of excluding difference (*abheda*) and non-conjunction (*sāhitya*).
This fivefold division of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) has been explained.
The meaning is: "If conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) were to exist," and so forth.
By the phrase "this [world] is indeed real and beginningless" (*so 'yaṃ satyo hyanādiśca*), it is understood that here too two propositions must be formulated externally.
Among these, the subverting argument against not accepting its beginninglessness is: "if it were with a beginning" (*sādiśced*).
"...if it were with beginning, it would meet with destruction. (Manu 1.4.112b).
By this, the first half of the first verse is explained.
Intending that the subverting argument against the absence of truth should be inferred by oneself, he concludes with the word "duality" (*dvaitam*).
"Duality does not exist"—this is the view of the ignorant.
Thus, according to the sacred revelation... [Manu 1.113a]
Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "unperceived" (ajñāta) becomes as stated.
Since it has not been explained by another scriptural passage, he explains the term "mere illusion" (māyāmātra) with the word "is considered" (mata).
... was measured and protected by means of the science of Hari known as Māyā.

From the roots *māṅ* (to measure) and *traiṅ* (to protect), by the rule "there is the prescription of the suffix *ka* in the sense of *ghañ*," the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), resulting in the form *mātram*.
It is observed that a single suffix can be applied even to two verbal roots, as in *adbhutam* from the roots *ad* and *bhū* (in the example *adbhūbhyāṃ ḍutac*).
[As it is said: "The singular conceptualization (*prajñapti*) of Viṣṇu is expressed solely through words."
Therefore, it is appropriate [to say] "by the knowledge of Hari called Māyā.
He explains that "non-duality is the ultimate reality" by the phrase "the supreme object."
Hari alone is the supreme goal; everything other than him is mediocre or inferior.
The proof for that is: "it is other than that."
Therefore, since anything other than Hari is either mediocre or inferior, Hari alone is the supreme goal.
As for the statement, "Conceptual differentiation (vikalpa) shall cease," this is self-evident if the phenomenal world were real; thus, it has not been further explained here.
The application here is as follows:
"When the individual soul (jīva), asleep through beginningless illusion (māyā), is awakened, it then realizes the non-dual (advaita) which is unborn, sleepless, and dreamless. Thus [it is said].

In the preceding verse, having described the "sleep" of the multitude of individual souls— characterized by their knowledge being veiled by insentient matter (prakṛti) and so forth through beginningless māyā, which is either the supreme Lord’s wisdom or His will— and having likewise described their "awakening," characterized by indirect knowledge regarding the reality of the supreme Lord and other principles through that very same [māyā],
direct perception (aparokṣajñāna) has also been stated.
By this, the distinctions between the individual soul and the Lord, between the insentient and the Lord, and between the individual soul and the insentient have been established;
for when a person is bound or liberated by the will of the Lord through fetters and so forth, the threefold distinction is observed.
[As stated previously: "The source of all entities. *4,620*
Thus, the mutual distinction among the individual souls (*jīvas*) denoted by the term "beings" has been stated.
From that very fact, the mutual distinction among the insentient veils (*āvaraṇas*) is also obtained by implication.
And regarding the distinction of those five [categories], it is said: "by beginningless *māyā*" and "unborn and sleepless."
Through the force of such qualifiers as these, its beginninglessness (*anāditva*) is also established.
These two verses are intended to demonstrate both the reality and the beginninglessness of this fivefold division.
First, he establishes its beginninglessness by demonstrating a refutation (*bādhaka*) regarding the contrary position (*vipakṣa*): "The manifold world (*prapañca*)... [and so forth].

Furthermore, it should be understood that the undesirability of the cessation [of duality] consists in such consequences as that if the distinction between the insentient and the living being were to cease, then because the living beings would fall into insentience, the scriptures on liberation (mokṣaśāstra) would become useless.
He states the means of certain determination regarding the pervasion [of this point], as in the phrase "there is no doubt.
Having thus established the beginninglessness of the fivefold duality, he states the proof for its reality: "It is mere illusion" (māyāmātra).
Since this duality denoted by the term "phenomenal proliferation" (prapañca) is, according to the manner explained above, merely illusion (māyāmātra), it is therefore real;
for that which does not exist cannot be an object of the Lord’s wisdom,
as that would entail the consequence of it being an error.
Nor is that which does not exist protected by anyone.
In this context, the state of being two is "duality" (dvitā);
the group belonging to that is "dualism" (dvaita).

It should be understood that [the word "non-duality"] is neuter because it denotes a general category (*sāmānya*), whereas its connection with *prapañca* (phenomenal proliferation) is obtained from the context. To the question, "In that case, how is it stated that 'there is non-duality of all existents' and so forth?", he says: "Non-duality... (*advaitam iti*).
This attribute of the Supreme Lord’s non-duality (advaitatva) that has been stated is not intended to mean the absence of a second entity; rather,
it is [meant] from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ).
The fifth case ending [is used] when the cause is concealment (*lyablopanimittā pañcamī*).
This is said with reference to the meaning already stated;
or else, the suffix *tasi* has the sense of the seventh case.

Regarding the phrase "having the supreme goal as its object," he states the following sublation [of the opponent's view] in the case of not accepting the reality of differentiation: "conceptual construction" (vikalpa).
If this conceptualized distinction under discussion were imagined by some factor such as ignorance, it would then cease— just like the appearance of multiple moons—
and would be sublated;
yet it is not sublated.
Therefore, it is not imagined, but is indeed real. He concludes: "Because of the teaching."
Thus, because it follows from such instruction and accords with scripture and other means of valid knowledge, this alone is the doctrine of the wise:
that which concerns the reality of difference and so forth.
The notion that "duality does not exist," however, occurs only when the ultimate reality is not known.
Therefore, [the author] states "this is a false doctrine.

Now, in order to explain the scriptural passage beginning with "Have you asked for that instruction?"— which has been accepted as the meaning of the Sūtra by both the proponent of transformation (pariṇāmavādin) and the proponent of illusory manifestation (vivartavādin) so as not to contradict their respective propositions— he provides the following commentary.
In this regard, the explanation of those who maintain the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavādinaḥ*) is as follows: "Or did you ask for that instruction,

by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known?"— here, because the world is a transformation of Brahman, the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of that [Brahman] is asserted with the intention of its non-difference from it.

In this regard, Śvetaketu—being ignorant that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of everything and perceiving a difference even between the material cause and its effect—asked, "How indeed, O Venerable One, can that be the instruction? because he had never observed the knowledge of one thing resulting from the knowledge of another. To this inquiry, [the Teacher], intending to teach that the world is non-different from Brahman by virtue of being its material cause, first established the non-difference of the effect from the cause as proven by common worldly experience.

And he demonstrates that knowledge of one leads to the knowledge of the other: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay';
just as, my dear, by means of a single nugget of gold, everything made of gold would be known..."

"The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'iron' alone is the truth. Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of iron would be known—"the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'iron' alone is the truth"—so it is.

The meaning of the three examples is that, just as jars and other products resulting from the transformation of a single lump of clay are known through the knowledge of that [clay] because they are non-different from it, so too is the case here.
Anticipating the objection, "If there is non-difference, how can there be the status of being an effect?", he says, "A mere verbal handle" (*vācārambhaṇam*), for the sake of conventional usage.
In the word *vācā*, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the genitive.
The mention of "speech" (vāk) is an indicator for the functioning of all the sense organs.

A "modification" (vikāra) refers to the object denoted, such as a jar, while a "name" (nāmadheya) is the designation for that object. Thus, it has been stated that there is a real mutual distinction between the jar and its designators, due to differences in their essential nature, function, and conventional designation.

If it is argued that there is mutual difference because of these reasons, then by those very same reasons there must also be difference from the cause; in order to refute this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he says: "Only as clay is it real."
The word "iti" expresses a manner.
In whatever manner and by whose existence clay exists, in that very same manner the earthen object exists as real;
it is not independent [of its cause], like a horse or a buffalo.

The proponent of the theory of illusory manifestation (vivartavādī), however, explains: having asserted that "by the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all," when there is a desire for an illustration, it is said: "Just as, O Somya..."
This is what is meant:
by knowing a single lump of clay in its ultimate nature as clay, all things made of clay, such as jars and the like, become known, because there is no difference in their essential nature as clay;
for modification is merely a verbal handle, a mere name.
It is merely by way of speech that one begins by saying "it exists," [referring to] modifications such as a jar, a bowl, or a water-pot;
however, in terms of the actual nature of things, there is no such thing as a modification.
"For this is merely a name, which is unreal;
'it is clay alone' is the truth"—thus has this illustration of Brahman been handed down in scripture.

In that regard, the proposition that through the knowledge of one thing everything is known, as well as the illustrations of the lump of clay and so forth, are intended to show that modifications are but illusory appearances (*vivarta*). Thus [it is said].
That [modification] is not understood from the sentence directly;
rather, it must be stated that it is understood through the force of the supporting statement, "a mere beginning in speech.
Therefore, explaining that very [statement] first, he states the meaning of the word *vācārambhaṇa*: "begun by speech" (*vācārabdham*).
But that which is initiated by speech and based on convention is called a "name" (nāman). Manu Smṛti 1.4.114ab.
But surely the word *ārambhaṇa* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*;

and *lyuṭ* is prescribed in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), or as an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), not in the sense of an object (*karman*). Nor can it be argued that *lyuṭ* occurs in the sense of an object according to the rule “*kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*” (Pāṇini 3.3.113).
Because it is impossible to explain the inclusion of the term *bahula* (in the sense of "mostly") as referring to the object (*karman*) without a powerful restrictive rule;
and because it would contradict one's own statement that "the word 'beginning' is not applicable to that which has no beginning."
If it is asked, "How then is this explained as 'commencement'?", do not say so;
for we accept that the word *ārambhaṇa* (commencement) denotes existence itself (*bhāva*).

The compound *vācārambhaṇa* means "that which has its commencement or production (*ārambhaṇa*) by means of speech" (*vācā*), that is, by the vocal organ (*vāgindriya*). The elision of the third-case ending (*aluk*) occurs because of the rule stating:
"The feminine suffix *ṭāp* is also applied after stems ending in a consonant, as in the examples *vācā*, *niśā*, and *diśā*."
Alternatively, this is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that whose support is speech" (vāg-ālambana);
the explanation of its meaning is that it is "called speech" (vāg-ākhya).
The word "tu" (but/however) is used for emphasis and is connected with what follows.

Since the status of being a modification (*vikāra*) is already obtained from the phrase "merely a verbal handle" (*vācārambhaṇa*), the word "modification" would be redundant; therefore, he states the intended meaning [of the Sūtra] with the words "sāṅketya" and so forth.
By the term *vācārambhaṇa*, only a conventional name (*saṅketika-nāman*) should be expressed;
however, the explanation of the etymological meaning (*avayavārtha*) is solely for the sake of clarity.

For example, since the word "eye" (*cakṣus*) is derived from the etymology "that by which one sees" (*caṣṭe 'nena iti cakṣuḥ*), the expression "one sees with the eye" does not involve a redundancy of meaning regarding its function as the instrument of seeing.

In that state, because the literal meaning of the individual parts is not intended to be expressed, the term *vācārambhaṇa* is likewise a conventional synonym. ... [The modified form is] manifold. (Manu 1.4.114b)
He states the meaning of the word "vikāra" (modification): "that which is modified."

It is stated that the term *vikāra* (modification) is derived from the root with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), as in "that which is modified by this. Furthermore, he states another point that establishes its state of being modified: "by fire," and so forth.
He states the meaning of the passage "various things are called 'earth'—that alone is the truth" with the word "tu" (but).
But the Vedic name "earth" and so forth is eternal.
The meaning of the word "truth" is eternal.
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis.
By the word "ādi" (etcetera), items such as iron and gems are included.
The connection is that whatever is a refined name, such as "clay" and so forth, that alone is eternal.
"Vaidikam" (the Vedic) refers to the justification for that [statement].
And thus, the construction is as follows:
"vācārambhaṇam" means conventional; "nāmadheyam" means a name; and "vikāraḥ" means that which possesses origination.
Therefore, it is impermanent.
Why?
Because of its manifold nature.
Because it possesses various forms according to human desire,
names such as "clay" and so forth are eternal and beginningless due to their Vedic nature.
Nor is there the fault of a discrepancy in gender in the phrase "the modification is a verbal handle," because the words "name" (*nāmadheya*) and "modification" (*vikāra*) have fixed genders,
and the word "verbal handle" (*vācārambhaṇa*) functions as an adjective qualifying "name."
And because qualifiers are dependent upon the qualified,
for this very reason, although one could simply say "conventional" (*sāṅketika*), he said "conventional name" (*sāṅketya-nāman*).
For when something is commenced by speech, that is its name— a modification characterized by birth.
Speech is the manifestation of names in various forms, because there is no difference between the form and that which possesses the form;
or, according to the interpretation stated in another text, it means "because it is subject to modification, it is like arising and perishing"— if that is the case, then:
There is no suspicion whatsoever of a change in gender.
But one might ask: why is it stated here that conventional names possess the quality of arising and perishing, whereas the names of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) are beginningless and eternal?
This is for the sake of the primary subject—the knowledge of all through the knowledge of Brahman—and as a secondary illustration for us, just like [the example] here.
Because it lacks utility;
therefore, since it is inconsistent, this is not the meaning of the scripture.
Not so.
Although this [example] does not serve as an illustration for the opponent in the same way,
nevertheless, it will be employed as another illustration for the knowledge of all through the knowledge of Brahman, according to the principle:
"as by that, so would that be known."

Intending to follow the context of what has been previously discussed, he says: "Because of its preeminence. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.115) "Because of its preeminence, even a person who is ignorant of the Prakṛti is called 'learned' by the virtuous if he knows it thoroughly; likewise, one who knows the eternal Self is [so called]."
This is what is meant:
because it is produced and impermanent, the conventional name is secondary due to its dependence on something else;
because it is beginningless and eternal, the conditioned is primary due to its independence from anything else.

In this context, just as conventional knowledge arises through the mere knowledge of the refined (saṃskṛta) [language] by virtue of its predominance— meaning that whatever fruit results from that knowledge, such as being within the sphere of the conduct of the learned, comes to pass— in the same way, whatever fruit results from the knowledge of the entire world— including the non-predominant elements such as impermanence (*anityatva*) and so forth, as well as those mixed with deities, rituals, and the like— all of that [fruit] belongs to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is predominant by virtue of its permanence (*nityatva*) and other qualities.
It is obtained through knowledge;
it is included within its fruit.
Here, by the phrase "even an ordinary ignorant person," it is indicated that this [attainment] is in consideration of the fruit.
If it is argued that, in that case, the "knowledge of all through a single knowledge" would be secondary (*amukhya*),
that is true;
for even by another [teacher], it cannot be explained as being primary (*mukhya*).
If that were the case, it would follow that a person who has already seen clay would have no desire to know about specific forms such as jars or bowls;
for common folk do not say, "The learned man is like a fool.
Therefore, the word "by the wise" (sadbhiḥ) was used.
In this way, the remainder of the statement "one who knows the eternal Self" is to be understood according to what has been said above.

Now, one might ask: how can the word *satya* mean "eternal," given that there is neither conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) nor etymological derivation (*yoga*) for it? To this, he first demonstrates the etymological derivation: "that which is ever-present" (*sadātana*).
"Truth is that which is eternal"—thus it is always said by the wise. The word "truth" (*satyam*) is to be understood as recurring [in the definition].
By the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the term "truth," it is indeed expressed as being eternal.
