"But it is not metaphorically designated" indicates that the basis for this etymological explanation is provided by learned grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*).
From the word *sadā*, in the sense of "that which exists therein," the suffix *-tyap* is applied according to the rule "after an indeclinable, *-tyap*."
Thus, when the suffix *tyap* is applied, the substitution of *sa-* for *sadā* optionally occurs by means of a word-split (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule “*sarvasya so 'nyatarasyāṃ diḥ*”.
From the word *sadā*, the secondary suffix *ḍya* may optionally be produced in the sense of "belonging to that" (*bhava-artha*).
And the letter *ta* replaces the letter *da*.
Now, he also demonstrates its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) with the words "and its application" (*prayogaśca*).
"And there is usage [of the word] later on...
(MĀnUV 1.4.116c). The connection is that in this subsequent section (prapāṭhaka), there is indeed usage of the word "truth" (*satya*) precisely in the sense of its eternity.

In order to demonstrate that very application, he recites the passage—“When old age overtakes it, or when it perishes, what then remains of it?”—in its sense as: “He should say: ‘This is not worn away by its old age; it is not slain by its death; this is the true city of Brahman’” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1), beginning with the word *jarā*.
...if old age should overtake him. (Manu 1.116d)
This body perishes; what remains of it thereafter?
It is not slain by murder, nor does it decay through old age.
"This is the true City of Brahman," for it is indeed eternal.
When this body reaches old age or when this body perishes,
then— having been asked whether the Supreme Self contained within this body remains like the space inside a burning house, or whether it perishes like a cloth or similar object—
the answer is that this Supreme Self does not grow old with the aging of this body.
By the killing of this, one is not killed;
rather, this Brahman is called a "city" (pura) because of its fullness, being true and eternal—this is the resolution stated.
The word "iti" connects with what precedes it.
To the question, "In this case as well, why does the word 'truth' (satya) mean 'eternal' (nitya)? he says: "For only in the sense of eternality... and so forth.
In this context, the word *satya* is appropriate if it means "eternal," because destruction is the subject under discussion; however, there is an inconsistency if it means "real."
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that untruthfulness is not the subject under discussion.
To clarify this very point, although it would have been sufficient to read only "this is the true city of Brahman," the preceding sentence has also been included;
its connection is indeed with what precedes.
If it is argued that the absence of old age and death in Brahman is stated as the reason for its reality, we say no;
for you do not admit of any reality apart from Brahman.
Because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of reality;

for it is unestablished that bodies possessed of old age and so forth are unreal, and because there is likewise an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—since unreal things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell lack old age and the like.
[Objection: Even so, why is the passage concerning "the origin of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) recited three times?
We say that this is intended to provide another example.
In that case, there would be six examples;
and it is exactly so.
If that were the case, the three examples of Sanskrit words would have to be stated all at once.
It is not so;
for those [examples] must be stated precisely when the discussion of their respective referents occurs.

If it is argued that even so, the employment of three words is unjustified—since if each word were taken as an illustration individually, it would lead to an infinite regress, and if they are taken as a collective indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), the purpose is achieved by even one—[we reply] no;
for this same objection applies equally to the employment of the triad of illustrations beginning with the lump of clay.
When the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is profound, the employment of a triad is not a fault.
"But [you may argue] that it is indeed a quality because it serves as a cause for the clarity of the intellect;
[we reply] that this is the same in the case at hand as well.

Having thus explained the statement beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*) according to his own view, [the author proceeds to] the theory of illusory transformation (*vivartavāda*).
He states the fault in [this] explanation: "The beginning is merely a matter of speech."
When it is said that [the world] is "a mere modification of speech," to assume it is false is an invention not heard in the scriptures.
It has been stated that "utterance" (ukti) means "word" (śabda).
When it is explained that "having its origin in speech" (vācārambhaṇam) refers to the falsity of words, the word "being" (sati) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
For instance:
Is the explanation that "that which has its origin in speech" (vācārambhaṇam) means "false" (mithyā) made by relying on conventional usage (rūḍhi),
or rather on etymological derivation (yoga)?
In the first case, since there is no authoritative evidence (pramāṇa) for such a conventional usage, it would involve the postulation of what was not heard in the scripture (aśrutakalpanā).
Furthermore, [the opponent argues that] the second [interpretation], namely that "commencement" (*ārambhaṇam*) means "that which is commenced" (*ārabhyate*), is also untenable.

For even so, since a genitive case would be required by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix, accepting a third case (instrumental) involves the assumption of what is not heard in the text (*aśrutakalpanā*).
Moreover, because the suffix *lyuṭ* is not prescribed for the object (*karman*), there is indeed an assumption of what is not heard.

Even in this view, since falsity (mithyātva) is not obtained, there is the assumption of what was not heard [in the scripture]. If it were so on the mere basis of being "begun by speech" (vācārambhaṇa), then that would follow for Brahman as well.
If it is argued that falsity is obtained by explaining it thus: "The modification is merely begun by speech, but does not exist in reality," we say no.

Since the scripture itself states "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*), to explain it as "false" by merely adding the word "mere" (*kevala*) is nothing but the assumption of what was not heard in the text.
He states another refutation: "it is a tautology."
Repetition is the name [of the fault]. ... // MAnu 1.4.119a //
The word *iti* is to be supplied here;
or rather, by the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*), it is connected with both [the preceding and the following].
The subsequent [text] explains that "name" refers merely to a name, for this is indeed false.
Since its meaning is already conveyed by the phrase "a mere beginning in speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*), the term "name" (*nāmadheyam*) would be redundant.

Alternatively, if the explanation were that both the modification (*vikāra*) and the name are "a mere beginning in speech," even so, since it is possible for both the denoted object and the denoting word to be grasped by the word "modification" alone, the inclusion of "name" would still be nothing but a redundancy.
Based on the scriptural passage beginning with "it was differentiated by name and form," he states another fault: "of this [word] 'iti'."
... thus, the word "iti" would be rendered meaningless. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.119b)
For the opponent intends to assert the reality of the clay;
in that case, one should simply say "the clay alone is real," and the word "iti" is indeed entirely redundant.
For it [the misconception] sometimes effects a reversal regarding the object itself, sometimes regarding the reason, and sometimes regarding the sense of "in this way."
In some cases it has the sense of "beginning," in some cases the sense of "manner," and in some cases the sense of "completion."
And it does not possess meaning through any one of these aforementioned senses;
for us, however, there is "comprehension of the object from the word."

Thus, when the sense of "clay" is already present, the justification for [the use of the instrumental case] is for the purpose of grasping the actual form of the word by setting that [meaning] aside. Furthermore, since even for the proponent of transformation (*pariṇāmavādin*), the use of the third case in connection with a *kṛt* suffix is accepted, and since the suffix *lyuṭ* is explained as denoting the object (*karman*), there is no syntactic connection between these words—namely, "the modification is a mere beginning of speech, a name. Consequently, the introduction of other words [to supply the missing links] is desired, which constitutes the postulation of what was not heard in the text (*aśrutakalpanā*).

Since the name itself could be included by means of grasping its modification (*vikāra*), the repetition would be redundant, and the word *iti* would be purposeless; this has not been stated because it is obvious. [Objection:
But was it not said that the word *iti* expresses a manner (*prakāra*)?
How, then, can it be said to be purposeless? It is replied:
this is stated for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that there is a difference between cause and effect.
In this regard, by one who explains that "the clay is real because of its existence, and for that very reason the earthen object is real," it must be stated: what kind of existence is intended?
If it is existence as intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattā*), then there is no distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*).
For how could one who considers there to be a difference between cause and effect accept that the effect possesses its own nature precisely through the very nature of the cause?
Or [if you argue] it is the general existence (*sāmānyasattā*).
That [reason] is inconclusive;
for it is not the case that because a horse exists as a reality, that non-existent horse does not differ from a buffalo.
Now, if it is intended to say that "that which has its existence dependent on the existence of clay is 'made of clay' (mṛṇmaya)," [then...]
Nevertheless, since [the pot] also has its existence dependent upon the existence of the potter and others, there is indeed an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*).
Furthermore, this is contradictory (*viruddha*);
for whatever is dependent upon something else is not that very thing.
Therefore, since it is not useful for establishing what is intended to be proven, the word "iti" is indeed meaningless even according to his own view.
Now, intending to explain the illustrative sentences beginning with "Just as, my dear," according to his own position, he first states the fault in the interpretation of others: "One... [etc.].
And [the terms] "a single lump" and "a jewel" would likewise be redundant. (Manu 1.4.119cd)
When there is the intention to express the state of being a modification... [MĀnava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.120a]
In this collection of terms, the first word is "ca" (and).
The word "iti" is connected to each [term].
"Vaiyarthya" means being devoid of meaning and having a contradictory meaning.
By the word *eva*, he states that futility (*vaiyarthyam*) is unavoidable;
the meaning of the word *ca* is "and" (*ca*), intended in the sense of a figurative transformation (*vivarta*).

When it is intended that through the knowledge of one thing there is the knowledge of all—on the grounds that the world is a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman and is superimposed upon it—it would be as if, by knowing clay, everything made of clay were known.

When iron is known, everything made of iron would be known; when black iron is known, everything made of black iron would be known. Since this much [knowledge] would suffice for completeness, the three single words—namely the words "lump," "jewel," and "nail-cutter"—as well as all words, would become devoid of meaning.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction in meaning because all things made of clay and so forth do not share the same modification from a single lump of clay;
for even in the case of a single thing made of clay, superimposition does not occur upon a single lump of clay,
so how could it occur for all of them?
If it is argued that [the object] is established by reasoning (*yukti*), then its status as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is untenable because it is a subject of dispute (*vivādapada*).
For an example is defined as "that object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding (*buddhisāmya*) among both worldly people and investigators."
For thus say the experts in logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*).

However, since jars and the like are established by uncontradicted perception and other means of valid cognition, it will be explained in the refutation of the theory that [objects] are mere aggregates of atoms (*paramāṇupuñjavāda*) that reasoning itself is merely fallacious.
Even if [the world] were superimposed, the terms "one" and so forth would still be entirely redundant, because "everything" does not reside in a single thing.

[Objection: But surely, by the words "by one" (ekenākena), the oneness of the supreme cause is intended; by "as a mass" (piṇḍena), its orientation toward effects; and by "all" (sarvam), the multiplicity of effects.
Therefore, how can there be redundancy?
[Response: Not so.
Because in the statement of the Dārṣṭāntika, if that [distinction] were intended, the redundancy here would remain unremedied.
Furthermore, in the first two examples, there exists merely a relationship of cause and effect; however, the terms "one" (*eka*) and so forth are indeed redundant.
But this is not tenable in any way, as in the example: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter...
For since a nail-cutter is a final constituent (antyāvayavin), it is impossible for it to be a cause with respect to another piece of iron.
But why does he say that everything arises in dependence upon a single [cause]? He says: "And not... (na ca).
... nor the clipping of a single fingernail;
and [his] everything shall be made of black iron. // MAnu 1.120bc //
The word "and" (ca) connects with the second "and" (*sarvam ca*).
If there is no intention to express transformation (*vikāra*) or manifestation (*vivarta*) in these three examples, then what is intended? To this he says: "Therefore... (*ata iti*).
... and therefore, it is indeed based on similarity. (Manu 1.4.120d)
But here, by the path already described, the intention is to express both eternality and predominance.
The meaning is that other [theories] have been refuted; the word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the others with one another;
and the word "tu" (but) qualifies the quality of permanence.
Eternality (*nityatva*) serves only as a means of establishing primacy (*prādhānya*), and not as an independent basis for the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one.
One must distinguish that the three examples, such as the lump of clay, concern the domain of similarity (*sādṛśya*),
whereas the passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*) concerns the domain of primacy.
If it is objected, "Since the illustration of 'having its origin in speech' (vācārambhaṇa) has already been explained, what is the purpose of stating it again?", we say no.

This is because the intention is that even that which has been stated for the sake of facilitating comprehension can be expressed together with what was not previously stated in a single sentence; with this in mind, it is said: "stated" (uktā).
The teacher has explained elsewhere that through the knowledge of one [thing], there is the knowledge of all due to similarity; this should be considered here as well.
Likewise, the internal distinctions among the examples of the lump of clay and so forth should also be understood.
Now, even in this view, [the text says]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."
The fault [in the opponent's view] is the lack of coherence in the subsequent passage beginning with "ityādi.

For us, however, there is a utility [for that passage] insofar as it serves to elaborate upon the relationship between cause and effect and so forth; therefore, he says: "prādhānyeti" (by way of predominance).
The detailed account of creation and so forth is for the purpose of understanding their relative importance.
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), its abiding during dissolution, the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa), the entry into the form of the individual soul (jīva), and so forth are included.
When it is stated that the fruit of knowing everything arises from the knowledge of Brahman because of its preeminence, the doubt may arise as to why it possesses such preeminence.

The extensive treatise has been composed precisely for the purpose of establishing that [creation and so forth] as a means of attaining that [liberation]; therefore, how could there be any inconsistency? The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis, meaning:
"but not for the purpose of establishing [the Lord's] being the material cause and so forth."
For the appropriator does not perform an action preceded by reflection,
nor is there an intermediate presiding agent;
or rather, the connection is "and this [appropriator]."
Therefore, it is stated that even such passages as "The nature of fire has departed from fire" are intended solely for the purpose of establishing the primacy of the Supreme Brahman;
and so it has been said in the Bhāṣya. *4,659*
He concludes the refutation of the theory of illusory manifestation (vivarta) with the words: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Therefore, by no means whatsoever should there be a doctrine of non-retrogression.
"By whatever path."
Whether from the perspective of Brahma-avidyā,
or from the standpoint of individual (jīva) avidyā, or according to the doctrine of a single jīva;
Either by way of the doctrine of many souls,
or by the establishment of one's own position,
or by the refutation of the opposing position.
The ellipsis to be supplied is "it has been investigated," whether by means of reflection on reasoning or by means of reflection on scripture.
The word "upapanna" (established/proven) is to be supplied [as the object of negation].
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "tad" (that).
Therefore, those who seek what is auspicious must certainly abandon this, as it is fraught with incalculable faults.
That is the doctrine of illusory manifestation (vivarta).
Or rather, it is from this [reasoning]:
"Because that very [doctrine] is beset with innumerable faults. This is its further explanation.
This alone is correct;

however, the meaning of the Sūtra should not be understood according to the manner stated by him. By this, it should be understood that the objection regarding the incoherence of refuting the opponent's view is also dispelled.

If there are faults that have been stated in excess, then they should be pointed out by those engaged in formulating refutations; why then cease? To this he says: "by way of their being innumerable. (*4,660*)
Because the faults are innumerable and for fear of excessive prolixity, I shall now desist... // MAnu 1.4.123a-c //

Since the faults are exceedingly numerous, after mentioning some of them, one should conclude by means of an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for others; and since an illustration is achieved even by this much, one desists.
All [the categories] must also be mentioned; why then are they mentioned merely as illustrations? To this it is said: "In the text... (grantheti).
For if the text were excessive, there would be no inclination on the part of the listeners [to study it];
thus, the meaning is that [the author] acted out of fear that what had been composed might as well remain uncomposed.
This applies if [the object] is neither the material cause nor the locus of the delusion.
Regarding the question of what kind of causality of Brahman for the world was intended by the Sūtra "From which [arise] birth, etc.," he says: "From that."
... Then Viṣṇu, free from fatigue and preceded by his will, creates the universe like a father... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 1.4.123cd //
The meaning is that the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth has already been refuted.
By the phrase "preceded by the will of the Father," he intends [the Lord's] causality as an agent (*kartṛ*).
Since the status of being the agent of diverse and manifold effects would entail defects such as exhaustion and the like, he says "without effort" (*aśrama*).
This has been stated in the Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa:
"Or rather, by the word 'āśrama' (the state), he intends this:
'But [it is] superior, because of the designation of difference.'"
By such statements as these, fatigue and other such qualities will be refuted in relation to Brahman;
furthermore, there is no possibility of fatigue or the like arising from [Brahman's status as] an apādāna (ablative source) or similar grammatical roles.
For this reason also, the author of the Sūtras intends precisely "agency" (kartṛtva).

Thus, at the conclusion of this chapter, he summarizes the result of the systematic reconciliation of all the Vedas with Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman—the result being the establishment of the definition stated in the Sūtra beginning with "birth and so forth" (janmādi)—in the verse beginning with "Pūrṇa."
... whose nature consists of the full remainder of all qualities.
Each [of these] is full and limitless.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Śrīmad-Brahmasūtrānuvyākhyāna* composed by the venerable teacher Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.
